ideas.name: Rolling Half-Kelly Ledger Sizing
ideas.entry_rule: Entry SIGNAL is a fixed harness held constant across the sweep (reference harness: enter long at next bar open when close crosses above the highest high of the prior 20 bars). The idea is the QUANTITY rule. Maintain a rolling ledger of the last N=100 closed trades of this strategy on this symbol. Let W = (count of trades with P&L>0)/N, A = mean P&L of the winners, B = mean absolute P&L of the losers, R = A/B. Compute f_star = W - (1-W)/R. Set risk_fraction = min(max(c*f_star, 0), 0.02) with c = 0.5 (half-Kelly). initial_stop = entry_price - 2*ATR(14). shares = floor(risk_fraction * account_equity / (entry_price - initial_stop)). If f_star <= 0 the signal is SKIPPED entirely and no position is taken until a later recomputation gives f_star > 0. Before 30 closed trades exist, use a flat 0.5% risk_fraction. Recompute after every closed trade.
ideas.exit_rule: Held constant so the sizing effect is isolated: stop at entry_price - 2*ATR(14), otherwise exit at next bar open when close crosses below the lowest low of the prior 10 bars. No target, no time stop.
inputs: rolling trade ledger (win rate, avg win, avg loss)
params: minimum ledger size before Kelly engages
ideas.why: Kelly sizing maximises the expected log of wealth, i.e. the long-run geometric growth rate. Thorp shows half-Kelly retains 0.75 of the full-Kelly growth rate while the probability of doubling before halving rises to 8/9, so it buys most of the growth for a fraction of the ruin risk. Estimating f from the strategy's own recent trade ledger makes the size adapt to genuine edge decay: when the edge disappears, f_star goes negative and the rule stops trading before the equity curve does the telling.
ideas.source: Edward O. Thorp, 'The Kelly Criterion in Blackjack, Sports Betting, and the Stock Market' (2006/2007), open PDF at https://gwern.net/doc/statistics/decision/2006-thorp.pdf and https://web.williams.edu/Mathematics/sjmiller/public_html/341/handouts/Thorpe_KellyCriterion2007.pdf - half-Kelly growth/drawdown result is in the fractional-Kelly section.
ideas.novelty: Not an indicator at all - the trade is identical, only the share count changes, and the rule can veto trades. A moving-average cross has no concept of its own recent hit rate; this does, and the position size is a closed-form function of it.

ideas.name: ATR Unit Sizing with Correlation-Capped Portfolio Heat
ideas.timeframe: daily (caps recomputed daily; entries can fire intraday)
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. QUANTITY: N = ATR(20) in dollars per share. One 'unit' = floor(0.01 * account_equity / N). Before submitting, evaluate four caps against currently open positions using rolling 60-trading-day Pearson correlation of daily log closes: (1) max 4 units in any single symbol; (2) max 6 units summed across any set of symbols whose pairwise correlation to the candidate is >= 0.70; (3) max 10 units summed across any set with 0.35 <= correlation < 0.70; (4) max 12 units net long and 12 units net short across the whole book. If adding this unit would breach any cap, the signal is rejected outright (not shrunk).
ideas.exit_rule: Each unit carries a stop 2N below its own fill (2N above for shorts) where N is the ATR(20) at that unit's entry. Whole position also exits at next bar open when close crosses below the lowest low of the prior 10 bars.
inputs: daily close series for all open + candidate symbols
ideas.why: Equal-N sizing makes one unit of any symbol carry the same dollar volatility, so a book of ten names is not secretly a book of one. The correlation caps address the failure mode that kills volatility-sized books: ten uncorrelated-on-paper positions all being the same beta trade on a bad day. Rejecting rather than shrinking keeps each surviving trade at full size, which preserves the per-trade edge instead of diluting everything.
ideas.source: Original Turtle Trading Rules (Curtis Faith / Richard Dennis programme), public PDF at https://oxfordstrat.com/coasdfASD32/uploads/2016/01/turtle-rules.pdf - unit formula '1% of account / (N x dollars per point)' and the 4/6/10/12 single-market, closely-correlated, loosely-correlated and single-direction caps.
ideas.novelty: The caps are a portfolio-level state machine that can veto an otherwise-valid signal. Nothing in the existing 32 looks at what else is already open, and none of them size by volatility parity.

ideas.name: Inverse-Realized-Variance Volatility Target Overlay
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. QUANTITY: sigma_hat = stdev of the last 20 daily log returns * sqrt(252) (annualised realised vol). target_shares = floor( (target_vol * account_equity) / (sigma_hat * close) ) with target_vol = 0.15, capped so that total gross notional across the book never exceeds 2.0 * equity. Enter at next bar open with target_shares.
ideas.exit_rule: Base exit unchanged (stop at 2*ATR(14), opposite-signal flat). PLUS a continuous rebalance leg: at every daily close recompute target_shares; if |current_shares - target_shares| / target_shares > 0.20, trade the difference at the next open. So the position is trimmed automatically as realised vol expands and added back as it contracts, without any price-based signal.
inputs: 20-day realised volatility of daily log returns
ideas.why: Volatility is strongly autocorrelated at daily and monthly horizons while expected return is not, so scaling exposure by the inverse of recent realised variance raises the Sharpe ratio mechanically: you hold less when the denominator is about to be large. Moreira and Muir document large alphas from scaling by inverse prior-month realised variance across equity factors; Barroso and Santa-Clara show an autoregression of monthly realised variance has out-of-sample R-squared of 57.8%, which is what makes the scaling implementable in real time.
ideas.source: Alan Moreira & Tyler Muir, 'Volatility-Managed Portfolios', NBER Working Paper 22208, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w22208/w22208.pdf ; Pedro Barroso & Pedro Santa-Clara, 'Momentum has its moments', Journal of Financial Economics 116(1) 2015, 111-120 (6-month realised variance scaling, OOS R^2 57.82%).
ideas.novelty: Size is a continuous daily function of realised variance and the position is trimmed mid-trade with no price trigger - the engine's fixed-size, fixed-exit structure has no equivalent. Distinct from ATR risk-per-trade sizing because it targets portfolio return volatility, not per-trade stop distance.

ideas.name: Conditional Volatility Targeting (de-risk only into weakness)
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. QUANTITY multiplier is a 2x2 state: let RV20 = 20-day realised vol of daily log returns, RV252_median = median of RV20 over the last 252 days, and TREND = (close > its 200-day simple moving average). Multiplier = 1.0 when RV20 <= RV252_median (regardless of TREND); = 1.0 when RV20 > RV252_median AND TREND is true; = 0.4 when RV20 > RV252_median AND TREND is false. shares = floor(multiplier * base_shares) where base_shares = floor(0.01*equity / (2*ATR(14))).
ideas.exit_rule: Base exit unchanged. The multiplier is re-evaluated each daily close and existing positions are scaled to match at the next open (sell down to 40% on a state change into the de-risk quadrant, buy back up when it clears).
ideas.why: Unconditional inverse-vol scaling cuts exposure during high-volatility rallies, which are often the most profitable stretches, and that drag is a documented cost of plain vol targeting. Conditioning the de-risking on volatility being high AND the trend being down keeps full exposure through high-vol upside and only cuts into genuine stress, which is where the tail risk actually lives.
ideas.source: Alpha Architect, 'Conditional Volatility Targeting', https://alphaarchitect.com/conditional-volatility-targeting/ - the finding that volatility targeting should be conditioned on the return state rather than applied unconditionally. Specific thresholds and multiplier pinned by me to make it testable.
ideas.novelty: A different rule STRUCTURE from idea 3, not a parameter change: exposure is a discrete function of a two-variable regime state rather than a continuous 1/sigma. The two will disagree most in high-vol uptrends, which is the whole point of testing both.

ideas.name: Equal-Risk-Contribution Book Allocation
ideas.entry_rule: When one or more base signals are live, do not size them independently. Each daily close: build the set S of symbols with an open position or a fresh signal. Compute Sigma, the covariance matrix of daily log returns over the last 60 trading days for S. Solve for weights w >= 0, sum(w) = 1, satisfying w_i * (Sigma w)_i = w_j * (Sigma w)_j for all i, j (cyclical coordinate descent, 50 iterations, initialise at inverse-volatility weights). Target notional for symbol i = w_i * equity * gross_leverage (gross_leverage = 1.0). Enter or top up at the next open whenever actual notional deviates from target by more than 25%. Cheap fallback variant worth sweeping separately: skip the solve and use w_i proportional to 1/sigma_i, which is the exact ERC solution when all pairwise correlations are equal.
ideas.exit_rule: A position exits entirely on its own base exit signal (stop at 2*ATR(14) or opposite signal). On any exit, the remaining book is re-solved that night and every surviving position is resized to the new ERC weights at the next open - so exits change the size of every other open trade, which the current engine cannot express.
inputs: daily log return series for all book symbols
params: shrinkage on the covariance estimate (Ledoit-Wolf intensity 0/0.2/0.5)
ideas.why: Sizing each trade independently means the book's risk is dominated by whichever cluster happens to have the most open positions. ERC forces every position to contribute the same share of portfolio variance, which is the risk-budgeting analogue of diversification and, unlike minimum variance, does not require any expected-return input. Maillard, Roncalli and Teiletche prove the solution exists and is unique for any positive-definite covariance matrix, so the solve is well-posed.
ideas.source: Sebastien Maillard, Thierry Roncalli & Jerome Teiletche, 'The Properties of Equally Weighted Risk Contribution Portfolios', Journal of Portfolio Management 36(4), 2010 - the w_i(Sigma w)_i = w_j(Sigma w)_j condition, the uniqueness result, and the equal-correlation reduction to inverse-volatility weights.
ideas.novelty: Position size becomes a function of the whole open book rather than the individual trade, and exits trigger resizing of unrelated positions. No entry indicator in the existing 32 has any cross-sectional component.

ideas.name: Notional-Equity Drawdown Ratchet
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. Maintain a separate variable notional_equity, initialised to starting capital. Track peak_equity = running maximum of actual account equity. current_dd = (peak_equity - actual_equity)/peak_equity. Let k = floor(current_dd / 0.10). Set notional_equity = actual_equity * (0.80 ^ k). Size every trade off notional_equity, not actual equity: shares = floor(0.01 * notional_equity / (2*ATR(20))). notional_equity is only restored to actual_equity when actual_equity makes a new all-time high (k resets to 0).
ideas.exit_rule: Base exit unchanged (2*ATR(20) stop, opposite-signal flat). The ratchet never closes a position early - it only starves new ones. Variant worth testing: also scale OUT of existing positions to the new notional size on the bar the ratchet steps down.
params: recovery rule (new all-time high vs recovering half the drawdown vs linear unwind)
ideas.why: Fixed-fractional sizing already shrinks with equity, but only linearly, which is far too slow to stop a strategy that has genuinely broken. A convex ratchet cuts size 20% per 10% of drawdown, so 30% down leaves you at 51% of normal size on 70% of the capital - about a third of the original risk. The asymmetric recovery rule (only reset on new highs) means you re-lever only after the strategy has proved it still works, which is the whole point.
ideas.source: Original Turtle Trading Rules, 'Adjusting Trading Size' section - 'when the account dropped 10%, all unit sizes were cut by 20%, with further reductions at every additional 10% drawdown'. Public PDF: https://oxfordstrat.com/coasdfASD32/uploads/2016/01/turtle-rules.pdf
ideas.novelty: State depends on the equity curve, not price. Note this is NOT the same as equity-curve trading (idea below) - it never switches the strategy off, it only makes it smaller, which avoids the binary on/off overfitting problem.

ideas.name: MAE-Percentile Adaptive Stop
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness, unchanged. The stop level is the idea, so nothing about the entry changes except that a warm-up of 50 closed trades is required before the adaptive stop engages (use 2*ATR(14) until then).
ideas.exit_rule: Run a shadow ledger of the base strategy with NO stop over the last 200 closed trades. For each trade record MAE in ATR units: MAE_atr = (entry_price - lowest low between entry bar and exit bar) / ATR(14) measured at that trade's entry (mirror for shorts). Take the subset of trades that were profitable at their eventual exit and compute k = the 90th percentile of MAE_atr over that WINNERS-ONLY subset. The live stop is entry_price - k * ATR(14)_at_entry, fixed for the life of the trade. Recompute k every 25 closed trades. Position also exits on the base opposite signal.
inputs: per-trade MAE from the shadow no-stop ledger
ideas.why: Sweeney's insight is that the stop should be placed where the price behaviour of trades that eventually work changes character. If 90% of eventual winners never went more than 1.7 ATR against you, a stop at 1.7 ATR costs you almost no winners and cuts every loser short. Choosing an ATR multiple by optimisation fits the multiple to the sample; deriving it from the winners' MAE distribution fits it to a mechanism, and it re-derives itself as the strategy's character drifts.
ideas.source: John Sweeney, 'Maximum Adverse Excursion: Analyzing Price Fluctuations for Trading Management' (Wiley, 1996); and Sweeney, 'Using Maximum Adverse Excursions for Stops', Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities V.5:4, pp. 148-150, https://store.traders.com/-v05-c04-usingma-pdf.html - the scatterplot of final P&L against MAE and the winners-only stop-placement rule.
ideas.novelty: The stop distance is an estimated statistic of the strategy's own historical trade paths rather than a chosen constant, and it is re-estimated live. This is a fundamentally different object from any fixed ATR or percentage stop.

ideas.name: MFE Give-Back Trail
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness, unchanged.
ideas.exit_rule: Two-phase. Phase 1 (before the trade works): fixed stop at entry_price - 2*ATR(14); track MFE_atr = (highest high since entry - entry_price)/ATR(14)_at_entry on every bar. Phase 2 begins the first bar MFE_atr >= 1.0. In phase 2, cancel the fixed stop and exit at the close of any bar where unrealised_profit < g * peak_unrealised_profit, with g = 0.60 (i.e. you have handed back 40% of the best open profit this trade ever showed). Additionally hard-exit at a limit set to the 80th percentile of MFE_atr over the last 200 closed winning trades, recomputed every 25 trades.
inputs: running peak unrealised profit per trade
params: evaluate give-back on close only vs intrabar
ideas.why: A distance-based trail (chandelier, ATR stop) gives back a constant number of dollars regardless of how big the trade has become, so a 10R winner and a 1R winner surrender the same amount. A proportional give-back rule surrenders a constant FRACTION, so the stop tightens in absolute terms exactly as the trade gets valuable, which is what you want if you believe large excursions mean-revert. The MFE-percentile hard target caps the trade where the empirical distribution says continuation stops paying.
ideas.source: Maximum Favorable Excursion as defined by John Sweeney (op. cit., Wiley 1996) - MFE as the largest unrealised profit during a trade, used here to set both the give-back reference and the hard target. The percentage give-back structure itself is synthesis; the MFE distribution supplies the target.
ideas.novelty: Exit is a function of the trade's own peak open profit, i.e. path-dependent in a way no price-level stop is. Two trades at the same current price exit differently depending on where they have been.

ideas.name: Volatility-Scaled Asymmetric Triple Barrier
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness, unchanged. At the entry bar snapshot sigma = ATR(14)/close.
ideas.exit_rule: Three barriers all set at entry and never moved. Upper (profit) barrier = entry_price * (1 + pt * sigma * sqrt(h)). Lower (stop) barrier = entry_price * (1 - sl * sigma * sqrt(h)). Vertical (time) barrier = exit at the close of the h-th bar after entry. Defaults pt = 2.0, sl = 1.0, h = 20 bars. Exit on whichever barrier is touched first, tested intrabar against the bar's high and low; if a single bar touches both horizontal barriers, assume the LOWER one filled first (conservative, avoids the classic backtest lie). The three exits are mutually exclusive and one always fires, so holding period is bounded by construction.
params: sqrt(h) time scaling on vs off
ideas.why: Fixing all three barriers at entry as multiples of the entry-bar volatility makes every trade risk the same amount of volatility-adjusted move and gives every trade the same amount of time to work, so the trade population is homogeneous and the resulting statistics are comparable across regimes. The sqrt(h) scaling is the diffusive scaling of price under a random walk, so the barriers grow at the rate the price is expected to wander - a barrier not scaled by sqrt(h) is effectively a much tighter stop at long horizons.
ideas.source: Marcos Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning' (Wiley, 2018), Chapter 3 - the triple-barrier method: two horizontal barriers for profit-taking and stop-loss plus one vertical barrier for the expiration timespan, with barrier widths set as multiples of estimated volatility.
ideas.novelty: The time barrier is a first-class exit with equal standing to the price barriers, not a fallback, and the asymmetry (pt != sl) is a deliberate structural parameter. The engine's current fixed exit has no bounded horizon at all.

ideas.name: R-Multiple Stop Tightening Schedule
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness, unchanged. Record R = 1.5 * ATR(14) at entry as the trade's risk unit.
ideas.exit_rule: Trailing stop = highest_high_since_entry - m * ATR(22), where the multiplier m is a step function of the trade's PEAK R-multiple achieved so far, peakR = (highest_high_since_entry - entry_price)/R: m = 3.0 while peakR < 1; m = 2.0 while 1 <= peakR < 2; m = 1.5 while 2 <= peakR < 3; m = 1.0 once peakR >= 3. The stop only ever ratchets upward (take the running maximum of all computed stop levels) - it never loosens even if m widens back. Exit at the next bar open after a close below the stop. Mirror for shorts using lowest low.
inputs: running max of the stop level
ideas.why: A fixed-multiple chandelier makes a single implicit bet: that the same amount of room is right at 0.5R and at 5R. Early in a trade you want room because noise dominates and the position is small in P&L terms; late in a trade the accumulated open profit is the largest thing at risk and the marginal continuation is less certain. A monotone tightening schedule expresses that directly, and the ratchet-only rule guarantees the stop is monotone in time so no trade ever gets a wider stop after being profitable.
ideas.source: Base structure is Chuck LeBeau's Chandelier Exit (long stop = n-day highest high - ATR(n) x multiplier), documented at https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/chandelier-exit. The state-dependent multiplier schedule keyed to peak R-multiple is synthesis - LeBeau's original uses a constant multiplier.
ideas.novelty: Differs from a plain chandelier the way an adaptive filter differs from a fixed one: the multiplier is a function of realised trade progress, so two positions on the same chart at the same time can have different stop distances depending on when they were opened and how far they got.

ideas.name: Breakeven-Plus Stop with Bounded Re-Arm
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. Additional state: each distinct base signal carries a re_arm_credit initialised to 1.
ideas.exit_rule: R = 1.5 * ATR(14) at entry. Initial stop at entry_price - R. The first bar whose close is >= entry_price + R, move the stop to entry_price + 0.1*R (covers commission and expected slippage) and leave it there - no further trailing. Exit on that stop, on a fixed target at entry_price + 3R, or on the base opposite signal, whichever comes first. RE-ARM: if the trade is stopped out at breakeven-plus (not at -R, not at target) AND the base entry condition is still true on that bar's close AND re_arm_credit > 0, re-enter at the next bar's open with a fresh -R stop and decrement re_arm_credit to 0. No further re-entries until the base signal goes false and fires again.
params: re-arm requires the signal to still be true vs a fresh cross
ideas.why: A large multi-market exit study found breakeven exits ranked near the very top of fifteen exit types, close behind stop-and-reverse. The known cost of a breakeven stop is whipsaw: trades that would have worked get scratched at zero. The bounded re-arm is the cheapest possible repair - it recovers the trade at most once, so the worst case is one extra -R, while the best case is recapturing a full winner that the breakeven stop threw away.
ideas.source: KJ Trading Systems, 'What 567,000 Backtests Taught Me About Algo Trading Exits', https://kjtradingsystems.com/algo-trading-exits.html - fifteen exit types over 40 futures markets, 5 bar sizes and 5 entry methods; breakeven exits reported as 'almost as good as Stop & Reverse'. The re-arm leg is my synthesis to address the whipsaw cost that plain breakeven exits carry.
ideas.novelty: The re-arm makes the exit and the entry co-dependent - a stop-out can immediately generate an entry - which the current one-entry-one-exit engine cannot represent at all.

ideas.name: Stop-and-Reverse Always-In Structure
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. Long when the base long condition fires, short when the base short (mirror) condition fires. Position is opened at the next bar's open for a fixed volatility-parity size: shares = floor(0.01 * equity / ATR(20)).
ideas.exit_rule: There is no stop, no profit target and no time exit. The ONLY thing that closes a position is the opposite base signal, at which moment the position is flipped to the same size on the other side in a single order. The book is always in the market, long or short, from the first signal onward.
params: sizing rule for the flip (constant vs vol-parity)
whether a flip is allowed on the same bar as the previous entry
optional catastrophic stop at 10*ATR as an insurance leg
ideas.why: Every stop, target and time exit is a bet that the exit information beats the entry information. A 567,000-backtest sweep across fifteen exit types, 40 markets, 5 bar sizes and 5 entry methods found stop-and-reverse produced the highest return on account across nearly every slice, and that adding more exit machinery consistently made things worse. This is the null hypothesis the whole domain should be measured against: if none of the clever exits beat the one that has no exit, the exits are noise.
ideas.source: KJ Trading Systems, 'What 567,000 Backtests Taught Me About Algo Trading Exits', https://kjtradingsystems.com/algo-trading-exits.html - 'Stop & Reverse Exits are the best', outperforming across all 40 markets, all bar sizes and all entry types; combined/complex exits degraded performance.
ideas.novelty: It is the deliberate removal of the exit structure, which for an engine that currently hard-codes one is a genuine structural change and the correct control for every other idea in this list. Requires the engine to support short-side symmetry and same-bar flips.

ideas.name: Hazard-Rate Time Stop from Bars-to-MFE
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. Warm-up of 50 closed trades required; use a flat 20-bar time stop until then.
ideas.exit_rule: From the last 200 closed WINNING trades, record for each the bar index (counting from the entry bar) at which its MFE occurred. Let T = the 75th percentile of that distribution, rounded up. Every open position is closed at market on the close of bar T after entry, regardless of P&L. A wide disaster stop at entry_price - 3*ATR(14) runs in parallel; no profit target and no trailing. Recompute T every 50 closed trades.
inputs: bar index of MFE per historical trade
params: separate T for long and short
ideas.why: If the strategy's edge is a burst of predictability that decays, the empirical distribution of when winners peak IS the edge's half-life, and holding past it is holding a position with no expected return while still paying volatility. Setting T from that distribution rather than from a round number means the time stop is calibrated to the mechanism. A time stop also has a property no price stop has: it exits sideways positions, which release capital without ever touching a stop level.
ideas.source: Synthesis. Structure follows the hazard-rate framing of holding-period exits (the chance of exit at a given bar count conditional on survival to that bar, estimated from the sample distribution of holding times) as set out in the exit-strategy literature, e.g. https://www.quantifiedstrategies.com/trading-exit-strategies/ ; the bars-to-MFE distribution as the calibration source is my own construction, using MFE as defined by Sweeney (Wiley, 1996).
ideas.novelty: Exit trigger is a bar count derived from a statistic of past trade paths, not a price. It fires on trades that are flat, which every price-based exit in the engine ignores entirely.

ideas.name: Path-Cumulative Bleed Stop with Re-Entry Threshold
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness, with one extra gate: the symbol must not be in the 'stopped out' state (see exit rule). A symbol in that state ignores all base signals until it clears.
ideas.exit_rule: No fixed price stop. On every bar compute the position's cumulative log return over the last J = 10 bars (for the first J bars of a trade, measure from entry). If that J-bar cumulative return <= gamma, where gamma = -0.5 * ATR(14)/close (a half-ATR slow bleed expressed as a return), flatten at the next open and put the symbol into the 'stopped out' state. The symbol clears that state and becomes tradeable again only once its own J-bar cumulative return >= delta = 0. A catastrophic stop at 4*ATR(14) runs in parallel.
inputs: rolling J-bar cumulative log return of the position
params: measure the return on the position vs on the underlying
ideas.why: A level stop fires on a single adverse spike, which under a random walk is exactly the wrong time to sell - Kaminski and Lo prove that simple 0/1 stop-loss rules always REDUCE expected return under the random walk hypothesis, and only add value when returns have momentum. A path-based trigger only fires when the position has been persistently losing over a window, which is the signature of momentum against you rather than of noise, so it is the version of the stop that their result says can pay. The explicit re-entry threshold is the second half of their policy and is what stops the rule from being a one-way door.
ideas.source: Kathryn M. Kaminski & Andrew W. Lo, 'When Do Stop-Loss Rules Stop Losses?', Journal of Financial Markets 18 (2014) 234-254; MIT open access at https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/114876 - a stop-loss policy defined as switching out of the risky asset when trailing cumulative return breaches a threshold and switching back on a re-entry threshold, with the random-walk-versus-momentum result. Specific J, gamma and delta values are pinned by me for testability; treat them as sweep centres, not as the paper's values.
ideas.novelty: The exit trigger is a windowed cumulative return, not a price level, so a violent single-bar spike that recovers does not stop you out while a quiet six-day drift does. Nothing in the existing 32 has a lockout-and-re-entry state machine.

ideas.name: Fixed-Ratio Delta Escalator
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. QUANTITY: let P = cumulative CLOSED-trade profit since inception (can be negative) and delta = a fixed dollar figure, default $2,000. Units N = max(1, floor(0.5 * (sqrt(1 + 8*P/delta) + 1))). One unit = a fixed base size of floor(0.005 * starting_capital / (2*ATR(14))) shares, held constant for the life of the test - it does NOT scale with current equity. shares = N * base_unit. On the way down, use a decrease_delta = delta * delta_fraction with delta_fraction = 1.0 by default (values below 1.0 shed units faster in drawdown).
ideas.exit_rule: Held constant: stop at entry_price - 2*ATR(14), opposite-signal flat. Only quantity varies.
params: reset delta on new equity highs vs never
ideas.why: Fixed-fractional sizing has a known asymmetry problem for small accounts: at 1% risk you need roughly a hundred trades' worth of edge before size moves at all, so early compounding is negligible. Fixed ratio makes each additional unit require delta more dollars of profit than the last, so growth is aggressive at small P and decelerates as the account grows - the opposite curvature to fixed-fractional. It is genuinely a different risk profile, not a different parameter, and it is worth knowing which curvature suits the strategy's win distribution.
ideas.source: Ryan Jones, 'The Trading Game' (Wiley, 1999). Formula as documented in Adaptrade Market System Analyzer: N = 0.5 * (sqrt(1 + 8*P/delta) + 1), where P is total closed-trade profit and delta is the profit per unit required to add one unit - https://www.adaptrade.com/MSA/fixratio.htm (which also defines the delta fraction governing size reduction in drawdown).
ideas.novelty: Size is a function of accumulated profit rather than current equity, and trade risk does not enter the equation at all - a structurally different sizing family from every percent-risk or percent-volatility rule.

ideas.name: Half-N Pyramid with Shared Ratcheting Stop
ideas.entry_rule: N = ATR(20) at the original entry, held fixed for the trade's life. First unit on the base signal at the next bar's open, size = floor(0.005 * equity / N). Then: each time the price trades 0.5 * N above the fill price of the MOST RECENT unit, add one more unit of the same share count at the next bar's open. Maximum 4 units. Adds are only made while the base entry condition has not gone false. Mirror for shorts.
ideas.exit_rule: A SINGLE shared stop for the whole stack. On the original entry, stop = entry - 2N. Every time a unit is added, move the shared stop to (fill price of the newest unit - 2N) - so with four units at 0.5N spacing the shared stop sits 0.5N above the original entry and the whole stack is risk-free. The stop only ratchets in the favourable direction. Exit ALL units together at the shared stop, or at the next open after a close below the lowest low of the prior 10 bars.
params: equal vs decreasing add size (1,1,1,1 vs 4,3,2,1)
require the base signal still true to add
ideas.why: Pyramiding converts a linear payoff into a convex one: the position is largest precisely in the trades that trend furthest, and the shared ratcheting stop means the total dollars at risk stays roughly constant as units are added rather than growing with the stack. That combination - anti-martingale adds with a single stop that walks up behind them - is what makes trend-following payoff distributions fat on the right without fattening the left. Decreasing add sizes are worth sweeping because they lower the average entry drift.
ideas.source: Original Turtle Trading Rules, 'Adding Units' (adds at 1/2 N intervals from the previous unit's fill, max 4 units per market) and 'Stops for Added Units' (all units share one stop, moved up as units are added). Public PDF: https://oxfordstrat.com/coasdfASD32/uploads/2016/01/turtle-rules.pdf
ideas.novelty: Multiple entries per signal with one shared, stack-dependent stop - a structure the current one-entry-one-exit engine cannot express. Distinct from an EMA-pullback re-entry because the adds are triggered by price distance from the last fill, not by a fresh indicator condition.

ideas.name: Market's-Money Two-Tier Risk
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. QUANTITY: split account equity into two pools at the start of every calendar quarter. core = equity at the quarter open. house = max(0, current_equity - core), i.e. profit earned inside the current quarter only. risk_dollars = 0.01 * core + 0.08 * house. shares = floor(risk_dollars / (2 * ATR(14))). The split resets on the first trading day of each quarter, so an unprofitable quarter leaves you back at a flat 1% and a strong quarter escalates risk sharply within it.
ideas.exit_rule: Held constant: stop at entry_price - 2*ATR(14), opposite-signal flat. Only quantity varies.
params: high-water-mark reset instead of calendar reset
floor house at 0 vs allow negative
ideas.why: This is a deliberate, bounded form of anti-martingale: risk escalates aggressively only on capital the strategy has just produced, and the escalation is automatically surrendered at the reset. The result is convexity within a hot streak - which is where most of a positive-skew strategy's return is concentrated - with a hard cap on how much of the original stake the aggression can ever touch. The reset period is the key parameter because it sets how long a hot streak has to be before it is 'banked'.
ideas.source: Van K. Tharp's 'market's money' position sizing model, described alongside the units-per-fixed-amount, equal-units, percent-risk and percent-volatility models in 'Trade Your Way to Financial Freedom' and 'The Definitive Guide to Position Sizing Strategies'. The specific 1%/8% split and quarterly reset are pinned by me to make it testable; Tharp does not fix the percentages.
ideas.novelty: Risk fraction depends on the PROVENANCE of the equity and on a calendar reset, so two accounts with identical balances size differently based on their recent path. Structurally distinct from both percent-risk and the drawdown ratchet, which are path-independent given current equity.

ideas.name: Thirds Scale-Out with Runner
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness. Size must be divisible by 3: shares = 3 * floor(0.01 * equity / (3 * 1.5 * ATR(14))). R = 1.5 * ATR(14) at entry.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at entry_price - R on the full position. Sell 1/3 at a limit of entry_price + 1R. On that fill, move the stop on the remaining 2/3 to entry_price. Sell the second 1/3 at a limit of entry_price + 2R. Trail the final 1/3 with a chandelier: highest_high_since_entry - 2.5 * ATR(22), ratchet-only, exit at the next open after a close below it. All remaining shares also exit on the base opposite signal.
params: move stop to breakeven on rung 1 vs rung 2
ideas.why: Scaling out is a deliberate trade of expectancy for variance: taking a third at 1R and a third at 2R lowers the blended R-multiple of every big winner relative to holding all three to target, but it raises hit rate, cuts the equity curve's roughness and makes the position risk-free early. It is worth testing precisely BECAUSE the arithmetic says it costs expectancy - if the strategy's Sharpe improves enough, that is a real result about the shape of its winner distribution, and if it does not, the ladder should be deleted rather than tuned.
ideas.source: The expectancy-versus-Sharpe trade-off in partial exits is set out with worked arithmetic in https://quantstrategy.io/blog/backtesting-partial-close-strategies-does-scaling-out/ and https://davemabe.com/should-you-ever-take-partials ; the runner leg uses LeBeau's Chandelier Exit formula (highest high - ATR x multiplier), https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/chandelier-exit
ideas.novelty: Requires the engine to hold a partially-filled position with a state-dependent stop - three exit legs of different types on one entry. Distinct from a single profit target and from a pure trail because it is a mixture of both, and the mixture weights are the parameter.

ideas.name: Session-Boundary Exit Split
ideas.entry_rule: Base signal is the harness, evaluated on 5-minute bars during regular trading hours only (09:30-16:00 ET), with no new entries after 15:30 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Three mutually exclusive variants to be run head to head against the same entries, with a stop at 2*ATR(14, 5-min) in all three. Variant A (flat-at-close): every open position is closed with a market order on the 15:55 ET bar regardless of P&L. Variant B (overnight-only): the position is held through the close and exited at the 09:35 ET bar of the next session. Variant C (hold-through): no session exit at all; position runs until the stop or the base opposite signal. Report each variant's return decomposed into the intraday leg (open-to-close) and the overnight leg (close-to-open).
params: whether the stop is active overnight
ideas.why: The overnight and intraday legs of equity returns have materially different distributions - different volatility, different drift, different gap risk - so a strategy's edge often lives entirely in one of them while the other contributes only variance. Running the same entries under three session structures isolates which leg the edge is in, and that answer determines the correct exit for every other idea on this list. It also directly prices the gap risk the current always-hold structure is silently carrying.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The intraday/overnight return decomposition is a standard construction from OHLCV bars (close-to-open versus open-to-close legs); the three-variant A/B/C test design and the specific clock times are mine, chosen so a programmer can implement them without judgement.
ideas.novelty: This is the only idea here whose trigger is the clock rather than price, volatility or the trade's own path, and it is a diagnostic as much as a strategy: it tells you which half of the day your other exits should be defending. It cannot be expressed at all in an engine whose exit is a price level. NOTE ON COVERAGE: all 18 ideas above clear the bar with distinct entry-quantity logic or distinct exit structure; none is a threshold tweak of another. The closest pair is ideas 3 and 4 (inverse-realised-variance scaling versus conditional volatility targeting) - they are kept separate because one is a continuous function of one variable and the other a discrete function of a two-variable regime state, and they disagree systematically in high-volatility uptrends.

ideas.name: Vol Term-Structure Regime Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Canonical form (needs index bars): TS_t = close(VIX)/close(VIX3M); S_t = SMA(TS,10). Go long SPY at the next session's open on the bar where S_t crosses from >= 1.00 down to < 1.00 (contango restored). Go flat, or short SPY / long VIXY, at the next open when S_t crosses from < 1.00 up to >= 1.00 (backwardation). OHLCV-only proxy: TS_t = close(VIXY)/close(VXZ) (front-month VIX futures ETP over mid-term VIX futures ETP). Because the two ETPs have unrelated price levels and different decay, do not use 1.00 as the threshold; instead compute P_t = the percentile rank of TS_t within its own trailing 252 daily values, and define risk-on as P_t < 0.50 and risk-off as P_t > 0.80. Enter long SPY at the next open when P_t crosses down through 0.50; go flat / short at the next open when P_t crosses up through 0.80.
ideas.exit_rule: Position is held until the opposite regime flip fires (exit at the next session's open). No price-based stop and no profit target - this is a state machine, not a trade signal. Optional risk overlay: hard exit if SPY closes 8% below the entry price.
ideas.why: The slope of the volatility curve is a direct read on how much the option market is paying for near-term protection relative to three-month protection. In contango, near-term realised vol is expected to stay below longer-dated implied vol, which historically coincides with positive equity drift and profitable short-vol carry; backwardation clusters around the crisis periods where equity drawdowns are concentrated. The signal is a conditioning variable derived from an entirely different market (SPX options) rather than from SPY's own price, so its errors are largely uncorrelated with price-based trend filters.
ideas.source: Tony Cooper, 'Easy Volatility Investing' (Double-Digit Numerics; NAAIM Wagner Award 2013 runner-up; SSRN 2255327). Rule as stated in the paper: 'If the 10 day moving average of VXV / VIX > 1, go long XIV else go long VXX.' The percentile-normalised VIXY/VXZ implementation is my adaptation to keep it computable from tradeable OHLCV only; I pinned the thresholds because the raw ETP ratio has no natural 1.00 crossing.
ideas.novelty: Not a moving-average cross on price. The state variable is the shape of a forward curve in a different asset class; the equity position is a consequence of a volatility-market state, and it can be long while price trend indicators are still negative (which is where most of its edge historically sits).
params: MA length on the term-structure ratio (5/10/20)
execution lag (next open vs same close)

ideas.name: Utilities Beta Rotation
ideas.entry_rule: Evaluated once per week on the last trading session of the week, after the close. Compute R_XLU = close(XLU)/close(XLU)[20] - 1 and R_SPY = close(SPY)/close(SPY)[20] - 1 using the last 20 trading sessions (approximately four weeks). If R_XLU > R_SPY, hold XLU for the coming week; otherwise hold SPY for the coming week. Enter the chosen leg at the next session's open. Defensive variant to also test: when R_XLU > R_SPY, hold cash (or IEF) instead of XLU, which converts the strategy from a rotation into an equity-exposure switch.
ideas.exit_rule: The position is closed at the next weekly evaluation and replaced by whichever leg the fresh comparison selects; if the same leg is selected, the position simply carries. There is no stop or target - the rebalance is the only exit. Optional overlay for the risky leg only: exit intra-week at the close if SPY closes more than 6% below the week's entry price, then stay flat until the next weekly evaluation.
ideas.why: Utilities are the most bond-like, lowest-beta corner of the equity market. When money moves into them relative to the broad index, it is expressing a preference for duration and defensiveness that has not yet shown up in the headline index - the relative bid for utilities is a leading read on the market's willingness to hold beta. Bilello and Gayed argue the signal works because the utilities-versus-market spread is a real-time proxy for the market's discount rate and risk appetite, which the index level reflects only with a lag.
ideas.source: Charles V. Bilello and Michael A. Gayed, 'An Intermarket Approach to Beta Rotation: The Strategy, Signal and Power of Utilities', Journal of Technical Analysis, 2014 - winner of the 2014 Charles H. Dow Award. Rule as published: when the 4-week relative strength of the Utilities sector versus the broad market is positive, position into Utilities for the following week; when negative, position into the broad market. Note the honest caveat found in review work (the7circles.uk/beta-rotation-with-utilities/): the ETF-era backtest from 2001 to 2020 returned roughly 7.5% annualised versus 7.9% for buy-and-hold, with lower volatility, and it badly underperformed during the 2020 crash - so treat the published 1926-onward result as an upper bound.
ideas.novelty: No moving average, no oscillator, no price level - the state variable is the sign of a 4-week return spread between two equity sleeves, and the output is a switch between two holdings rather than an in-or-out trade. The strategy is always invested, so its risk profile is completely different from a breakout or fade rule.
params: defensive leg (XLU vs cash vs IEF vs TLT)
risky leg (SPY vs QQQ vs IWM)
execution lag (next open vs same close)

ideas.name: Credit Non-Confirmation of Equity Highs
ideas.entry_rule: Define the credit ratio C_t = close(HYG)/close(IEF), using dividend-adjusted bars for both (both pay monthly and the unadjusted ratio drifts). Short signal: today close(SPY) equals the highest close of the trailing 20 sessions (inclusive), AND C_t < SMA(C,20), AND C_t < C_{t-20}. Sell SPY short at the next session's open, or if long-only, exit all longs at the next open. Long signal (mirror): today close(SPY) equals the lowest close of the trailing 20 sessions, AND C_t > SMA(C,20), AND C_t > C_{t-20}. Buy SPY at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Short: cover at the next open on the first session where C_t crosses back above SMA(C,20); hard time stop of 10 sessions; hard risk stop if SPY closes 3% above the entry price. Long: exit at the next open on the first session where C_t crosses back below SMA(C,20); hard time stop of 10 sessions; hard risk stop if SPY closes 3% below entry.
ideas.why: High-yield credit and equity are claims on the same corporate cash flows, but credit holders are paid to worry about solvency rather than growth, and the high-yield market is dominated by institutions with credit research rather than by index flows. Dividing HYG by IEF cancels the duration component, isolating the spread. When the index prints a new high while the credit spread proxy is deteriorating, the equity high is being made without the participation of the investors most exposed to the downside - a documented precursor to equity weakness. The IEF leg is essential: HYG alone conflates a spread signal with a rates signal.
ideas.source: The HYG-versus-IEF spread signal is formalised in 'Credit-Spread Timing between High-Yield Bonds and Treasuries' (SSRN 5815822), which tests a price ratio versus its lookback moving average and a return-spread threshold, rebalanced monthly, against a 50/50 HYG/IEF benchmark. The non-confirmation framing (credit weakens ahead of equity at turning points) is standard intermarket practice, described for example at stockcharts.com/articles/arthurhill/2016/01 on measuring stock, economic and credit risk. Converting the monthly ratio-versus-MA rotation into a daily divergence-at-extremes trigger is my construction.
ideas.novelty: It is not a breakout and not a fade of the traded instrument. It requires a specific two-market disagreement - a new extreme in one market that a second, causally related market refuses to confirm - and the exit is defined entirely by the second market's behaviour, not by the traded instrument's price.
params: risky-asset instrument (SPY/QQQ/IWM - IWM should be more sensitive)

ideas.name: RRG Quadrant Crossing Sector Rotation
inputs: daily closes for XLK, XLF, XLV, XLY, XLP, XLE, XLI, XLB, XLU, XLRE, XLC
ideas.entry_rule: For each sector ETF S compute the relative-strength line RS_t = close(S)/close(SPY). Then RS_Ratio_t = 100 + (RS_t - SMA(RS,60)) / STDEV(RS,60). Then ROC_t = (RS_Ratio_t / RS_Ratio_{t-10} - 1) * 100, and RS_Mom_t = 100 + (ROC_t - SMA(ROC,60)) / STDEV(ROC,60). Buy sector S at the next session's open when, on today's bar, RS_Ratio crosses from below 100 to above 100 while RS_Mom > 100 - this is the improving-to-leading quadrant transition. Cap the book at three sectors, equal-weighted; if a fourth signal fires while three are held, take the one with the highest RS_Mom and drop the held sector with the lowest RS_Mom.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit a sector at the next open on the first session where RS_Mom crosses below 100 (the leading-to-weakening transition). Secondary exit: also close if RS_Ratio falls back below 100 regardless of RS_Mom. No price stop - the position is closed on a relative-strength state change, which means a sector can be held through an absolute drawdown as long as it is outperforming.
ideas.why: Sector capital rotates in a persistent, roughly clockwise cycle: leadership is gained gradually and lost gradually because institutional reallocation is slow and size-constrained. The two-axis construction separates the level of relative strength from its momentum, which lets you enter at the moment relative strength turns positive while its momentum is already positive - earlier than a simple ratio moving-average cross, and with a filter against the false crossings that occur when the ratio is chopping around 100.
ideas.source: Julius de Kempenaer's Relative Rotation Graphs (RRG Research). Formulas as documented at chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/chart-analysis/chart-types/relative-rotation-graphs-rrg-charts and the open-source implementation and formula comparison at github.com/AdroitAnandAI/RRG-Sector-Rotation-India (RRG_IMPLEMENTATION_COMPARISON.md), which gives exactly the standardisation used above. The specific entry as an improving-to-leading quadrant crossing, the three-sector cap and the RS_Mom exit are my specification - the published material describes the chart, not a mechanical rule set.
ideas.novelty: Two-dimensional state: the trade requires a specified crossing in one normalised series while a second, derived normalised series is in a specified state. It cannot be reduced to a moving-average cross on a ratio, because the RS_Mom axis is itself a standardised rate of change of the standardised ratio, and the entry depends on the joint condition.
params: quadrant boundary (100, or a wider band such as 100.5/99.5 to reduce whipsaw)
benchmark (SPY vs RSP - RSP as benchmark removes mega-cap distortion)
universe (11 SPDR sectors vs a wider set including IWM, EFA, GLD, TLT)

ideas.name: Stock-Bond Correlation Regime Gate
inputs: 60-session Pearson correlation of daily log returns
ideas.entry_rule: Each session compute rho = Pearson correlation between the last 60 daily log returns of SPY and of TLT. Two mutually exclusive regimes with different entry logic. DIVERSIFIED REGIME (rho < -0.10): buy SPY at the close when close(SPY) < SMA(close(SPY),10) and close(SPY) > SMA(close(SPY),200) - dip buying is permitted because bonds are still absorbing equity shocks. JOINT-SELLOFF REGIME (rho > +0.10): dip buying is forbidden; instead buy SPY at the next open only when close(SPY) > SMA(close(SPY),50) and SMA(close(SPY),50) > SMA(close(SPY),50)[10], i.e. trend-following only. NEUTRAL BAND (-0.10 <= rho <= +0.10): take no new positions.
ideas.exit_rule: Diversified-regime long: exit at the close on the first session where close(SPY) > SMA(close(SPY),10), or after 10 sessions, whichever comes first; hard stop if SPY closes 4% below entry. Joint-selloff-regime long: exit at the next open when close(SPY) < SMA(close(SPY),50); no time stop. Any open position is closed at the next open if rho crosses the boundary into a different regime, because the exit logic that governs it is no longer the active one.
ideas.why: Whether an equity dip is safe to buy depends on what caused it. In a demand-shock or flight-to-quality world, bonds rally when equities fall, the drawdown is absorbed, and dips mean-revert. In an inflation or policy-shock world, stocks and bonds fall together, there is no cushion, drawdowns compound and dip buying is precisely the wrong trade - 2022 is the canonical case, when the S&P/aggregate-bond correlation spiked to about +0.50, the highest in the sample. The rolling correlation is a directly observable classifier for which world you are in, and it flips slowly enough to be usable.
ideas.source: Empirical evidence on the regime dependence of stock-bond correlation: 'Empirical Evidence on the Stock-Bond Correlation', Financial Analysts Journal, 2024 (tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/0015198X.2024.2317333), which documents that inflation, real rates and government creditworthiness drive the correlation regime, and that demand/flight-to-quality shocks produce negative correlation while monetary-policy and inflation surprises produce positive correlation. The idea of using rho as a switch between two different entry rule sets - rather than as an allocation input - is my construction.
ideas.novelty: It is not one strategy with a filter bolted on; it is two structurally opposite strategies (mean-reversion and trend-following) selected by a cross-asset state variable, with the exit logic changing along with the entry logic. The regime variable is a second moment computed across two markets, which nothing in the existing set uses.
params: bond leg (TLT / IEF / AGG - TLT is the purest duration read)
dip definition in the diversified regime (below SMA10 / SMA5 / n-day low)
whether to size positions by rho instead of switching discretely

ideas.name: High-Beta Leadership Thrust
ideas.entry_rule: Define R_t = close(SPHB)/close(SPLV). Buy SPY at the next session's open when all three hold today: (1) R_t is the highest value of R over the trailing 20 sessions inclusive; (2) R_t > SMA(R,50); (3) close(SPY) > SMA(close(SPY),200). Optionally take the leveraged expression of the same view by buying SPHB itself rather than SPY, which makes the signal and the instrument the same sleeve.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next open on the first session where R_t closes below SMA(R,50). Secondary exit: also close if R_t makes a 20-session low while the position is open. Time stop: 40 sessions. No price-based stop on SPY - the thesis is about risk appetite, so the position is closed when risk appetite is withdrawn, not when price moves.
ideas.why: SPHB holds the hundred highest-beta names in the S&P 500 and SPLV the hundred lowest-volatility names, so their ratio is a clean, continuously-priced measure of how much beta the marginal equity dollar wants. A new 20-day high in that ratio means the market is not merely rising but rising because the riskiest cohort is being bought - a materially different condition from an index high driven by defensives. The two ETFs are also sector-tilted in opposite ways (high beta is financials- and energy-heavy, low volatility is utilities- and staples-heavy), so the ratio doubles as a cyclical-versus-defensive read.
ideas.source: Arthur Hill, 'Measuring the Risk Appetite with Beta, Volatility and Ratios', StockCharts (stockcharts.com/articles/arthurhill/2017/04/), which sets out the SPHB:SPLV ratio as a risk-appetite gauge, and the composition figures (SPHB 30.9% financials and 20.1% energy versus SPLV 15.4% and 1.0%) reported at investwithanedge.com. The mechanical entry (20-session ratio high plus ratio above its own 50-day MA plus SPY above its 200-day MA) and the ratio-based exit are my specification - the source describes the gauge, not a rule.
ideas.novelty: The breakout being detected happens in a synthetic series - a ratio of two ETFs neither of which need be traded - and the exit is defined purely by that same synthetic series, so the position's life is governed by cross-sectional risk appetite rather than by the traded instrument's price at all.

ideas.name: Sector Correlation Spike Risk-Off
inputs: daily closes for the 11 SPDR sector ETFs
ideas.entry_rule: Each session compute daily log returns for all 11 SPDR sector ETFs, then all 55 pairwise Pearson correlations over the trailing 20 sessions, and let C_t be their arithmetic mean. Let P_t be the percentile rank of C_t within its own trailing 252 values. RISK-OFF ENTRY: exit all longs and, in a two-sided version, sell SPY short at the next open on the session where P_t crosses from below 0.90 to at or above 0.90. RISK-ON ENTRY: buy SPY at the next open on the session where P_t crosses from above 0.20 down to at or below 0.20 while close(SPY) > SMA(close(SPY),50).
ideas.exit_rule: Short: cover at the next open when P_t falls back below 0.50, or after 15 sessions, or if SPY closes 3% above the entry price - whichever comes first. Long: exit at the next open when P_t rises above 0.60, or if close(SPY) < SMA(close(SPY),50), or after 40 sessions.
ideas.why: Average pairwise correlation across sectors is the market's diversification measured directly from prices. When it collapses toward one, individual sector fundamentals have stopped mattering and a single systematic factor - liquidity, policy, or forced deleveraging - is driving everything; that is the mechanical signature of stress and it coincides with drawdowns. When it is unusually low, idiosyncratic drivers dominate, hedging works, and the environment historically supports carrying beta. Cboe built an entire index family around the forward-looking version of exactly this quantity, and notes that implied correlation rises when stocks are falling; the realised version is computable from bars alone.
ideas.source: Cboe, 'Implied Correlation - U.S. Options' methodology paper (cdn.cboe.com/resources/indices/documents/Cboe_USO_ImpliedCorrelation_0421_v2.0.2.pdf) and the Cboe implied correlation index family (ww2.cboe.com/us/indices/implied/), which define average expected pairwise correlation among the top 50 S&P 500 names as a distinct, tradeable market state and note that it rises when stocks drop. The realised 11-sector pairwise proxy, the 252-day percentile normalisation and the specific crossing rules are my construction, since COR3M itself is not in the data set.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is a second moment computed across an eleven-asset cross-section, and the trigger is a crossing in its own long-run percentile rather than a fixed level - so the signal automatically recalibrates to the prevailing correlation environment. Nothing in the existing 32 uses cross-sectional information at all.
params: universe (11 sectors / 11 sectors plus IWM, EFA, GLD, TLT / 100-name basket)
average pairwise correlation vs first-eigenvalue share of the correlation matrix as the state variable

ideas.name: Equity-Volatility Hedge Breakdown
inputs: VIXY daily close (or VIX daily close)
ideas.entry_rule: Each session compute rho10 = Pearson correlation between the last 10 daily returns of SPY and the last 10 daily returns of VIXY (if index bars are available, use daily changes in VIX instead - the correlation sign is the same and the reading is cleaner). This correlation normally sits deeply negative, around -0.7 to -0.9. Short signal: rho10 > -0.25 (the inverse relationship has materially broken down) AND close(SPY) equals the highest close of the trailing 20 sessions. Sell SPY short at the next session's open. Require additionally that rho10 was below -0.50 at some point in the prior 10 sessions, so the rule fires on a breakdown rather than on a persistently broken regime.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover at the next open on the first session where rho10 falls back below -0.50 (the normal hedge relationship has been restored). Hard time stop: 10 sessions. Hard risk stop: cover if SPY closes 3% above the entry price. Do not use a profit target - the thesis is about a regime, and the regime restoration is the exit.
ideas.why: Volatility and equity index prices are mechanically anti-correlated because index puts are the dominant hedging instrument. When implied volatility rises while the index is also rising to new highs, someone is paying up for protection into strength - the marginal buyer of volatility is not being forced by a falling market but is choosing to hedge. That is a positioning signal that price alone cannot express: it is the option market disagreeing with the equity market about what comes next. The breakdown requirement (recently very negative, now not) is what makes it an event rather than a state.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The mechanism rests on the well-documented, strongly negative contemporaneous VIX-SPX return relationship (the leverage/volatility-feedback effect described in the VIX literature and reflected in Cboe's own materials noting implied volatility rises when stocks drop) and on the standard practitioner observation that a positive same-day VIX/index co-movement at a new high reflects hedging demand into strength. I found no single paper that specifies this exact rule, so I have pinned it down myself and flagged it as untested rather than cite something vague.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is the loss of a relationship, not the presence of one. Neither the level of the volatility index nor the trend of the equity index appears in the entry condition - only the rolling correlation between them, plus a price extreme used purely as a timing anchor. This is a signal with no analogue among the existing 32.
params: prior-regime requirement (-0.4/-0.5/-0.6 within the last 5/10/20 sessions)
volatility instrument (VIXY / VXX / VIX index / UVXY)

ideas.name: Dollar-Regime Domestic Revenue Tilt
ideas.entry_rule: Compute D_t = close(UUP)/close(UUP)[20] - 1. STRONG-DOLLAR ENTRY: on the first session where D_t >= +1.5% AND close(UUP) > SMA(close(UUP),100), go long IWM and short EFA at the next open, dollar-neutral. WEAK-DOLLAR ENTRY: on the first session where D_t <= -1.5% AND close(UUP) < SMA(close(UUP),100), go long EFA and short IWM at the next open. Do not re-enter the same direction while a position in that direction is already open.
ideas.exit_rule: Close both legs at the next open on the first session where the sign of D_t flips against the position (D_t < 0 for a strong-dollar trade, D_t > 0 for a weak-dollar trade). Hard time stop: 20 sessions. Hard risk stop: close if the spread P&L is worse than -3% of notional at any close.
ideas.why: Russell 2000 companies derive the large majority of revenue domestically, while EFA is by construction unhedged foreign-currency exposure and large-cap US multinationals carry substantial foreign revenue translation. A sustained dollar appreciation is therefore a direct relative earnings tailwind for small domestic firms and a direct translation headwind for foreign and multinational earnings - a fundamental channel that is slow-moving and mechanical, which is precisely the sort of thing a 20-day price signal can front-run. I want to state the counter-hypothesis honestly: a rising dollar is also often a risk-off, tightening-liquidity signal, which hurts small caps through the risk channel; the two effects push in opposite directions, so the sign of the net effect is genuinely an empirical question and the strategy should be tested in both directions before being trusted.
ideas.source: Synthesis. Grounded in the revenue-geography difference between the Russell 2000 and international/multinational indices and in standard FX-translation accounting; I could not find a single primary paper specifying this rule, so I am labelling it my own construction rather than attaching a weak citation. The 1.5% and 100-day parameters are my choices, picked so the signal fires a few times a year rather than continuously.
ideas.novelty: The only currency-driven idea in this set, and market-neutral in its expression: the signal is a move in a currency ETF and the trade is a relative-value spread between two equity sleeves chosen for their opposite revenue geography. No indicator is computed on either traded instrument.
params: long leg (IWM / IWC / XRT - all more domestically levered) and short leg (EFA / EEM / SPY)
direction to trade (test the reverse sign explicitly)

ideas.name: Lagged Industry Diffusion
inputs: XRT, IYR, XME, XLE, XLI daily closes
ideas.entry_rule: Evaluated on the last trading session of each calendar month, after the close. For each of the five industry ETFs - XRT (retail), IYR (commercial real estate), XME (metals and mining), XLE (petroleum) and XLI (industrials) - compute its 21-session return. Let L_t be the equal-weight mean of those five returns. Compute M_t = the median of the last 12 monthly values of L (a one-year history, so the rule needs 13 months of warm-up). Buy SPY at the next session's open if L_t > 0 AND L_t > M_t. Otherwise hold SHY (or cash) for the coming month.
ideas.exit_rule: Position is closed at the next monthly evaluation and replaced by whichever leg the fresh comparison selects; if SPY is reselected, the position carries. There is no stop and no target - the rebalance is the only exit. A variant worth testing: hold for two months rather than one, since the published effect is reported to run up to two months.
ideas.why: Hong, Torous and Valkanov argue that information originating in specific industries - housing and commercial real estate, commodity demand, retail spending - reaches investors in those industries first and only diffuses to the broad market with a lag, because attention and analytic capacity are limited and segmented. The industries they identify as leading are precisely the ones most directly tied to real economic activity, and the same paper shows their return predictability lines up with their ability to forecast measures of economic activity. The strategy tries to be positioned in the index before that information arrives in it.
ideas.source: Harrison Hong, Walter Torous and Rossen Valkanov, 'Do industries lead stock markets?', Journal of Financial Economics, 2007 (working paper at columbia.edu/~hh2679/industry-12-05-05.pdf) - a significant number of industry returns including retail, services, commercial real estate, and metal and petroleum forecast the market by up to two months. Important caveat from the authors' own follow-up (rady.ucsd.edu/_files/faculty-research/valkanov/Note_10282014.pdf): in a revised sample extending to 2013, fewer industries lead the market, so the effect has weakened out of sample and should be tested on recent data before being sized. The ETF proxies for the paper's industry portfolios, and the median-of-12 threshold, are my implementation.
ideas.novelty: The predictor is a lagged cross-sectional average of other assets' returns, and the horizon is a month rather than a bar - a completely different clock and a completely different information source from anything in the existing set. It also has a documented economic mechanism (segmented attention and gradual information diffusion) rather than a purely statistical justification.
params: industry set (the five above; add or drop XLB, XLY, XHB, ITB)
threshold rule (L>0 only / L>median / L>0 and L>median / z-score of L)

ideas.name: Equal-Weight Breadth Non-Confirmation
inputs: 50-session rolling max/min of SPY close and of the RSP/SPY ratio
ideas.entry_rule: Define B_t = close(RSP)/close(SPY), the equal-weight versus cap-weight ratio. BEARISH: today close(SPY) equals the highest close of the trailing 50 sessions inclusive, AND B_t equals the lowest value of B over the trailing 50 sessions inclusive. Exit all longs and, in a two-sided version, sell SPY short at the next session's open. BULLISH: today close(SPY) equals the lowest close of the trailing 50 sessions, AND B_t equals the highest value of B over the trailing 50 sessions. Buy SPY at the next open. Require a minimum of 20 sessions between consecutive signals in the same direction so a multi-week grind of new highs does not generate a signal every session.
ideas.exit_rule: Short: cover at the next open on the first session where B_t rises above SMA(B,20); hard time stop of 15 sessions; hard risk stop if SPY closes 3% above entry. Long: exit at the next open on the first session where B_t falls below SMA(B,20); hard time stop of 15 sessions; hard risk stop if SPY closes 3% below entry.
ideas.why: RSP holds the same 500 companies as SPY at equal weight, so the ratio strips out everything except concentration - it is a pure measurement of whether the index move is being produced by the whole list or by a handful of the largest names. An index at a fifty-day high while the ratio is at a fifty-day low means the median constituent is not participating: the advance is narrow and rests on a small number of positions whose withdrawal would remove the whole move. The mirror case at a fifty-day low is a market where the median stock is already recovering while the cap-weighted headline is still being dragged down by a few large names, which is what an internal bottom looks like.
ideas.source: Synthesis, built on the standard breadth-divergence framework (a new index extreme unconfirmed by internals) applied to the RSP/SPY pair. The equal-weight-versus-cap-weight ratio as a concentration and participation gauge is standard practitioner analysis - see for example the multi-index comparison framing at stockcharts.com/freecharts/perf.php?SPY,QQQ,DIA,RSP,MDY,IWM,IJR,IWC. I could not find a paper that specifies this exact double-extreme rule, so I am claiming it as my own construction rather than attaching a loose citation.
ideas.novelty: Requires simultaneous opposite extremes in two series over the same window - a joint condition on the index and on a same-constituent equal-weight ratio. It is neither a breakout (it fires against the breakout) nor a fade of an oscillator, and the exit is governed entirely by the breadth ratio's own mean reversion rather than by price.
params: minimum spacing between same-direction signals (0/10/20 sessions)
ratio alternative (RSP/SPY vs QQQE/QQQ vs MDY/SPY)
requiring the ratio to be at an N-session low versus merely below its own 50-session median

ideas.name: Risk-On/Risk-Off Composite Z
inputs: HYG, IEF, XLY, XLP, SPHB, SPLV, IWM, SPY, COPX, GLD daily closes (dividend-adjusted for HYG and IEF)
ideas.entry_rule: Build five relative-return spreads, each as the difference of two 20-session simple returns: S1 = ret20(HYG) - ret20(IEF); S2 = ret20(XLY) - ret20(XLP); S3 = ret20(SPHB) - ret20(SPLV); S4 = ret20(IWM) - ret20(SPY); S5 = ret20(COPX) - ret20(GLD). Standardise each: Zi_t = (Si_t - mean(Si over the trailing 252 sessions)) / stdev(Si over the trailing 252 sessions). Composite Z_t = the arithmetic mean of Z1..Z5, requiring all five to be available (otherwise no signal). Buy SPY at the next session's open when Z_t crosses from <= 0 to > 0 AND Z_t > Z_{t-5}. Position size may be scaled linearly by min(Z_t, 2)/2 rather than held constant, which is the variant I would test first.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next open when Z_t < 0. Secondary exit: also close if Z_t has declined on each of the last three sessions (Z_t < Z_{t-1} < Z_{t-2} < Z_{t-3}) while Z_t < 0.5, which catches deterioration before the zero crossing. No price stop - the composite is the risk control, and a hard price stop would defeat the point of measuring risk appetite independently of price.
ideas.why: Every one of the five spreads is a different market's independent vote on the same question: does capital want risk right now? Credit versus duration, cyclical consumer versus defensive consumer, high beta versus low volatility, small versus large, and industrial metal versus safe-haven metal. Each individually is noisy and each individually can be dominated by a sector-specific story; averaging their standardised values suppresses that idiosyncratic noise while preserving the common risk-appetite factor. Because the votes are cast in credit, commodity and equity markets, the composite carries information that the equity index price does not yet contain.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The individual components are each established practitioner risk-appetite gauges - the HYG/IEF credit ratio (formalised in SSRN 5815822 as a ratio-versus-moving-average timing rule), the SPHB/SPLV beta ratio (Arthur Hill, StockCharts, 'Measuring the Risk Appetite with Beta, Volatility and Ratios'), and the offense-versus-defense commodity pair logic of Bilello and Gayed's 2015 NAAIM Wagner Award paper. The z-score ensemble construction, the 20/252 windows and the crossing rule are mine.
ideas.novelty: Cross-asset ensemble rather than a single indicator: five spreads across three asset classes, each standardised on its own history so no component can dominate through scale, combined into one continuous state variable that also serves as a position-sizing input. Nothing in the existing set aggregates evidence across markets, and the sizing-by-conviction structure is a different exit and risk shape from a binary in/out rule.
params: component set (drop or add spreads: XLE-XLU, EEM-SPY, ARKK-SPLV, IWM-QQQ)

ideas.name: Residual Reversal (beta-adjusted 5-day loser)
ideas.entry_rule: Universe U = symbols with close > $5 and 20-session median dollar volume > $10M. Each session at 15:55 ET: (1) beta_i = OLS slope of daily simple returns of i on SPY daily returns over sessions t-64..t-5 (60 obs, skipping the signal window); (2) raw 5-day return R_i = close_t/close_{t-5} - 1 and market leg M = close_SPY,t/close_SPY,t-5 - 1; (3) residual RES_i = R_i - beta_i * M. Cross-sectionally rank RES over U. Enter long market-on-close the 10 lowest RES_i and short the 10 highest RES_i, equal dollar weight per leg.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit market-on-close exactly 5 sessions after entry. Hard stop: exit intraday if the position moves 2 * ATR(14) against the entry close. Skip re-entry into a name already held.
inputs: daily OHLCV of each universe symbol
params: skip gap between beta and signal windows
ideas.why: Raw past-week losers include stocks that fell on genuine cash-flow news (which drifts) and stocks that fell on non-fundamental order-flow pressure (which reverses). Netting out the market/beta component removes a large slice of the news-driven part, leaving the price-pressure part that a liquidity provider is paid to absorb. Da, Liu and Schaumburg show only the residual component of the reversal is significantly positive and the enhanced strategy earns roughly four times the risk-adjusted return of the standard one.
ideas.novelty: Not a price-vs-moving-average fade at all: the signal is a cross-sectional rank of a regression residual, so a stock that fell 6% in a market that fell 6% generates no signal, while one that fell 6% in a flat market does. No indicator on the list conditions on relative-to-market displacement.
ideas.source: Da, Liu & Schaumburg, 'A Closer Look at the Short-Term Return Reversal', Management Science 60(3), 2014, 658-674 (working paper: https://www3.nd.edu/~zda/Reversal.pdf; FRBNY Staff Report 513 'Decomposing Short-Term Return Reversal')

ideas.name: Within-Industry Reversal, Across-Industry Momentum
ideas.entry_rule: Map each universe symbol to one SPDR sector ETF (XLK, XLF, XLE, XLV, XLI, XLY, XLP, XLU, XLB, XLRE, XLC) held fixed. Each session at 15:55 ET compute REL_i = (close_i,t/close_i,t-5 - 1) - (close_S,t/close_S,t-5 - 1) where S is i's sector ETF, and SECMOM_S = close_S,t/close_S,t-5 - 1. Long MOC the 3 lowest REL_i inside each sector whose SECMOM_S > 0. Short MOC the 3 highest REL_i inside each sector whose SECMOM_S < 0. Equal dollar weight per name; no position in a sector whose ETF 5-day return has the wrong sign.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit MOC after 5 sessions, or earlier on the first close where REL_i crosses back through 0 (longs) / through 0 from above (shorts). Force-flat any name whose sector ETF's 5-day return flips sign against the position.
inputs: daily OHLCV of each universe symbol
ideas.why: Hameed and Mian show that when you compute reversal against industry peers rather than against the whole market, the reversal is markedly stronger, while the industry-level component itself continues (industry momentum). The two forces are opposite, so a raw reversal signal blends a profitable within-industry bet with a loss-making bet against industry momentum. Splitting them and taking each in its profitable direction is the point.
ideas.novelty: Two-level signal: contrarian on the idiosyncratic leg, trend-following on the sector leg, with the sector leg acting as a permission gate rather than a filter on the stock's own trend. Distinct from EMA-pullback-in-trend, which measures trend on the same series it trades.
ideas.source: Hameed & Mian, 'Industries and Stock Return Reversals', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis, 2014 (NUS working paper PDF: https://web2-bschool.nus.edu.sg/wp-content/uploads/media_rp/publications/BwXb81392625636.pdf)

ideas.name: Volatility-State Gated Reversal (liquidity-provision switch)
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the market stress state each session at 15:50 ET: STRESS_t = percentile rank, within the trailing 756 sessions, of SPY 20-session realized volatility RV = stdev(ln(close/close_prev), 20) * sqrt(252). (If VIXY bars are used instead, take the percentile rank of VIXY's close over the same 756 sessions - either is OHLCV-derived.) Run any 5-day cross-sectional reversal book (e.g. the residual-reversal ranking) ONLY on sessions where STRESS_t >= 0.60. Gross exposure = 0.5 + 1.5 * (STRESS_t - 0.60)/0.40, capped at 2.0 and floored at 0. When STRESS_t < 0.40 take no new reversal positions at all.
ideas.exit_rule: Normal exit is MOC 5 sessions after entry. Additional state exit: if STRESS_t drops below 0.40 while positions are open, halve gross exposure at that close and flatten the remainder at the next close. Per-name stop at 2 * ATR(14) from entry.
inputs: daily OHLCV of SPY (or VIXY) for the state
daily OHLCV of universe for the reversal signal
ideas.why: Nagel shows the payoff to short-term reversal IS the payoff to supplying liquidity, and that this expected return and its conditional Sharpe ratio are strongly and predictably higher when VIX is high - liquidity suppliers withdraw exactly when compensation for immediacy spikes. So reversal is not a strategy to run continuously; it is a strategy to run hard in stressed states and switch off in calm ones. Realized SPY volatility is a close OHLCV proxy for the VIX conditioning variable.
ideas.novelty: This is a meta-rule about WHEN a mean-reversion book may trade and at what size, driven by a market-wide state variable, not by the traded symbol's own indicator. None of the 32 existing ideas conditions position size on an exogenous volatility percentile.
ideas.source: Nagel, 'Evaporating Liquidity', Review of Financial Studies 25(7), 2012, 2005-2039 (NBER WP 17653: https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w17653/w17653.pdf)

ideas.name: No-News Shock Fade (quiet-volume price shock)
ideas.entry_rule: Single-name, evaluated at each close. Let r_t = close_t/close_{t-1} - 1 and VR_t = volume_t / mean(volume, 50). LONG setup: r_t <= the 1st percentile of that symbol's trailing 500 daily returns AND r_t <= -0.08 AND VR_t < 1.5. SHORT setup: r_t >= the 99th percentile of the trailing 500 daily returns AND r_t >= +0.08 AND VR_t < 1.5. Enter at the next session's open. Do not take the trade if VR_t >= 2.5 (treat as an information event and stand aside).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit MOC on session t+20, or earlier at a 10% favourable move from entry, or on a 7% adverse move. Additional exit: flatten immediately if any subsequent session prints |r| beyond the same 1st/99th percentile with VR > 2.5 (news has now arrived).
inputs: daily OHLCV of the traded symbol
ideas.why: Savor finds that large price moves accompanied by genuine information are followed by DRIFT, while large moves not accompanied by information are followed by REVERSAL - investors underreact to fundamentals and overreact to everything else. We do not have an analyst-revision feed, so abnormal volume is used as the news proxy: information events are almost always accompanied by a volume explosion, so a big move on ordinary volume is the closest OHLCV signature of a no-information shock.
ideas.novelty: The conditioning runs OPPOSITE to the turnover-shock reversal above: here low relative volume is what licenses the fade, and high volume vetoes it. Same raw trigger, inverted gate, different economics - worth testing head-to-head. Volume is a news proxy (stated substitution), so the rule is a proxy implementation of the paper.
