ideas.source: Savor, 'Stock Returns after Major Price Shocks: The Impact of Information', Journal of Financial Economics 106(3), 2012, 635-659 (https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/10/Stock-Returns-After-Major-Price-Shocks---May-2012---Final.pdf); volume-as-news proxy is my substitution for the paper's analyst-report classification

ideas.name: Attention Gap Fade (intraday unwind of the overnight move)
ideas.entry_rule: At 09:45 ET compute GAP_t = open_t/close_{t-1} - 1 for each universe symbol. SHORT setup: GAP_t >= +2.0% AND GAP_t is above the 95th percentile of that symbol's trailing 250 daily gaps AND the 09:30-09:45 bar closes below its own open. LONG setup: GAP_t <= -2.0% AND below the 5th percentile of trailing 250 gaps AND the 09:30-09:45 bar closes above its own open. Enter at 09:45 with a marketable limit; take at most the 5 largest-|GAP| qualifying names per side per day.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit MOC at 15:55 ET the same session. Stop: for shorts, the high of the 09:30-09:45 bar; for longs, its low. First target: yesterday's close - scale out half there and trail the remainder to the close.
ideas.why: Berkman, Koch, Tuttle and Zhang show that high-attention stocks open at a premium and then give it back over the trading day - the hidden cost of buying at the open. Lou, Polk and Skouras document the same tension systematically: overnight and intraday return components persist within themselves but reverse against each other. Retail and attention-driven orders queue overnight and execute at the open; the resulting price is an inventory price, not a value price.
ideas.novelty: Fades the OVERNIGHT return component specifically, using the gap's own historical percentile rather than a session-range breakout, and requires a failed-follow-through confirmation bar. Distinct from opening range fade, which triggers off the break of a 15-30 minute range regardless of how the market opened relative to yesterday's close.
ideas.source: Berkman, Koch, Tuttle & Zhang, 'Paying Attention: Overnight Returns and the Hidden Cost of Buying at the Open', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 47(4), 2012; Lou, Polk & Skouras, 'A Tug of War: Overnight versus Intraday Expected Returns', Journal of Financial Economics 134(1), 2019 (https://personal.lse.ac.uk/polk/research/TugOfWar.pdf)

ideas.name: Overnight-Only Reversal Harvest
ideas.entry_rule: Each session at 15:55 ET rank U on the 5-session residual reversal score RES_i (as in the Residual Reversal idea: 5-day return minus beta_i times SPY's 5-day return, beta from 60 prior sessions). Buy market-on-close the 10 lowest RES_i and short market-on-close the 10 highest RES_i, equal dollar weight. Positions are opened every session; there is no multi-day carry.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit every position market-on-open the very next session (17.5-hour hold). No intraday holding at all, no stop needed inside the holding window because the position never spans a trading session; if the open is halted, exit at the first print after resumption.
inputs: daily OHLCV of each universe symbol
params: skip nights before known high-gap events (earnings-season blackout by |gap| history)
ideas.why: Lou, Polk and Skouras decompose 14 strategies and find the short-term reversal premium is earned ENTIRELY overnight, with the intraday component contributing nothing or working against it. If the premium accrues between the close and the open, an overnight-only holding period earns the same edge with roughly a quarter of the market exposure hours, and avoids the intraday continuation that drags the standard 5-day version.
ideas.novelty: Same ranking as a standard reversal book, completely different EXIT STRUCTURE - close-to-open only, re-formed daily. The distinctness is in when the risk is held, which is exactly where the published premium lives; it also changes the strategy's risk profile from intraday drawdown to gap risk.
ideas.source: Lou, Polk & Skouras, 'A Tug of War: Overnight versus Intraday Expected Returns', Journal of Financial Economics 134(1), 2019, 192-213 (https://personal.lse.ac.uk/polk/research/TugOfWar.pdf)

ideas.name: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Residual S-Score
ideas.entry_rule: For each symbol i and its sector ETF S, over the trailing 60 sessions regress daily returns r_i on r_S (OLS, no intercept constraint) and form the cumulative residual X_k = SUM of residuals from the start of the window to session k. Fit AR(1): X_{k+1} = a + b * X_k + zeta. Require 0 < b < 1. Derive kappa = -ln(b) * 252, m = a/(1-b), sigma_eq = sqrt( var(zeta) / (1 - b^2) ), and s = (X_last - m)/sigma_eq. Trade only names with kappa > 252/30 (mean-reversion half-life under ~30 calendar days). ENTER LONG when s < -1.25; ENTER SHORT when s > +1.25. Hedge each position with an offsetting dollar amount of S equal to beta_i times the stock notional (or run the book beta-neutral in aggregate).
ideas.exit_rule: Close longs when s > -0.50; close shorts when s < +0.75 (Avellaneda-Lee's asymmetric bands). Force exit if kappa falls below 252/30 at any daily re-estimation, or after 60 sessions in the trade, whichever comes first.
inputs: daily OHLCV of each universe symbol
ideas.why: Avellaneda and Lee formalise mean-reversion trading as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process on the residual of a stock against its factor/ETF exposure: the tradable object is the idiosyncratic deviation, and the s-score is that deviation in units of its own stationary standard deviation. The kappa filter is what stops you from fading a residual that is drifting rather than reverting - it directly measures the speed of reversion instead of assuming it.
ideas.novelty: The z-score is computed on a fitted stochastic process (stationary standard deviation of an OU model), not on a rolling sample standard deviation of price, and entry is gated on an ESTIMATED SPEED OF REVERSION. That kappa gate is the key difference from any band-fade: a wide residual with slow reversion is explicitly not a trade.
ideas.source: Avellaneda & Lee, 'Statistical arbitrage in the US equities market', Quantitative Finance 10(7), 2010, 761-782 (Crossref-confirmed; SSRN 2008 working paper). Entry/exit band values 1.25/1.25/0.75/0.50 are the paper's own.

ideas.name: Variance-Ratio Regime Gate
ideas.entry_rule: For each symbol compute the Lo-MacKinlay variance ratio over the trailing 120 sessions: with x_d = ln(close_d/close_{d-1}), VR(q) = [ Var of overlapping q-period sums of x, using the unbiased m = q(T-q+1)(1-q/T) denominator ] / [ q * Var(x) ], for q = 5. Classify: MEAN-REVERTING if VR(5) < 0.90, RANDOM if 0.90 <= VR(5) <= 1.10, TRENDING if VR(5) > 1.10. Only in the MEAN-REVERTING state, enter long at the close when the 2-session cumulative return close_t/close_{t-2} - 1 <= -1.5 * ATR(14)/close_t, and enter short when it is >= +1.5 * ATR(14)/close_t. Take no mean-reversion trade in the other two states.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close when the 2-session cumulative return has recovered to >= 0 (longs) or <= 0 (shorts), or after 5 sessions, or on a 2 * ATR(14) adverse move. Immediate flatten if VR(5) rises above 1.10 at a daily re-estimate.
inputs: daily OHLCV of the traded symbol
params: heteroskedasticity-robust VR statistic vs raw ratio
ideas.why: Lo and MacKinlay's variance ratio directly measures whether a series' variance grows slower than linearly in time, which is precisely the signature of mean reversion; VR < 1 means negative autocorrelation and VR > 1 positive. Most mean-reversion strategies die because they are run through trending regimes - gating on the estimated autocorrelation structure of the traded series itself is the most direct possible fix, and it costs nothing but OHLCV.
ideas.novelty: The regime filter is the second moment's scaling behaviour, not a trend indicator: ADX, moving-average slope and SuperTrend all measure direction, whereas VR measures whether increments are anti-persistent. A symbol can be in a strong uptrend with VR < 1 (staircase) or flat with VR > 1 (whipsaw regime), and this gate distinguishes them.
ideas.source: Lo & MacKinlay, 'Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test', Review of Financial Studies 1(1), 1988, 41-66; combination with an ATR-scaled displacement trigger is my synthesis

ideas.name: Month-End Dash-for-Cash Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Trade only around month boundaries. On the second-to-last trading session of the calendar month, at 15:55 ET, rank U on R5_i = close_t/close_{t-5} - 1. Enter MOC long the 10 lowest R5_i and short the 10 highest R5_i, equal dollar weight, restricting to names with 20-session median dollar volume > $20M. No positions are opened on any other session.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit MOC on the 3rd trading session of the following calendar month. Hard stop at 2 * ATR(14) from entry close; flatten the whole book early if SPY's cumulative return from entry exceeds -3%/+3% (regime shock).
inputs: daily OHLCV of each universe symbol
params: entry day (-1/-2/-3 sessions to month end)
ideas.why: Etula, Rinne, Suominen and Vaittinen show institutional liquidity needs cluster at month end - funds raise cash for redemptions and payouts - producing predictable month-end price pressure that reverses in the first days of the new month. Because the flow is calendar-driven rather than information-driven, the stocks pushed furthest by it are the ones that snap back hardest, which makes a stale short-term reversal signal unusually informative on exactly those dates.
ideas.novelty: The signal is a date, and the cross-sectional reversal ranking only determines WHICH names to express it in. Nothing in the existing 32 conditions on the calendar; this also has a natural risk advantage - the book is flat ~85% of the time.
ideas.source: Etula, Rinne, Suominen & Vaittinen, 'Dash for Cash: Monthly Market Impact of Institutional Liquidity Needs', Review of Financial Studies 33(1), 2020 (Crossref lists the RFS record under 2019/2020)

ideas.name: Forced-Exit Down Streak
ideas.entry_rule: Single-name. At the close, require ALL of: (a) five consecutive down closes, close_d < close_{d-1} for d = t-4..t; (b) volume_d > mean(volume, 20) measured at d-1, for every one of those five sessions (sustained distribution, not a one-day flush); (c) the cumulative 5-session return <= -6%; (d) the symbol's 20-session median dollar volume > $10M; (e) the 5-session return is at or below the 10th percentile of the symbol's own trailing 250 rolling 5-session returns. Enter long MOC on session t.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit MOC on the first session whose close exceeds the HIGH of the entry session, or after 5 sessions, whichever comes first. Stop: exit MOC if the close falls below the low of the entry session. Do not re-enter the same name for 10 sessions after an exit.
inputs: daily OHLCV of the traded symbol
params: volume condition (all days vs majority of days)
ideas.why: Cheng, Hameed, Subrahmanyam and Titman show that short-term reversals are much stronger for stocks experiencing institutional EXITS - persistent one-sided selling that requires a liquidity provider to be paid to absorb it - and correspondingly weaker where liquidity provision is already efficient. We cannot see institutional ownership, so the OHLCV signature used here is a multi-session down streak on consistently above-average volume, which is what a worked liquidation looks like on a bar chart, as opposed to a single high-volume capitulation bar.
ideas.novelty: The signal is the PERSISTENCE of a volume-backed streak across consecutive sessions rather than a single-bar extreme, and the exit is defined by a specific reference bar (entry-session high/low) instead of an indicator crossing. Distinct from three-bar momentum, which trades continuation of the streak rather than its exhaustion.
ideas.source: Cheng, Hameed, Subrahmanyam & Titman, 'Short-Term Reversals: The Effects of Past Returns and Institutional Exits', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 52(1), 2017 (Crossref-confirmed; earlier SSRN title 'Short-Term Reversals and the Efficiency of Liquidity Provision'). The streak-plus-volume construction is my OHLCV proxy for institutional exits.

ideas.name: Lehmann Continuous Contrarian Weights
ideas.entry_rule: No sorting or thresholds. Each session at 15:55 ET, over universe U of N names compute r_i = close_t/close_{t-5} - 1 and rbar = (1/N) * SUM r_i. Set raw weights w_i = -(r_i - rbar), then normalise so the book is dollar-neutral and has fixed gross exposure G: w_i_final = G * w_i / SUM_j |w_j|. Trade to those target weights MOC every session (trade only the difference from current holdings). Every name in U carries a position whose size is proportional to how far its own 5-day return sits from the cross-sectional average.
ideas.exit_rule: There is no discrete exit: positions decay to zero as the target weights update each session, so a name that has fully reverted is automatically flat. Risk exits: flatten the whole book if its 10-session realized volatility exceeds 3x its 250-session average, and cap any single |w_i_final| at 5% of gross.
inputs: daily OHLCV of each universe symbol
params: rebalance frequency (daily vs every 2-3 sessions to cut turnover)
ideas.why: This is Lehmann's original construction: a self-financing arbitrage portfolio whose weight on each stock is proportional to the negative of its return in excess of the equal-weighted average, rebalanced each period. It earned roughly 1.7% per week gross over 1962-1986. Using continuous weights extracts information from every name instead of throwing away everything between the deciles, and it produces far smoother turnover than a decile sort that flips names in and out.
ideas.novelty: A different portfolio-construction primitive rather than a different indicator: signal strength maps continuously into position size and there is no entry threshold and no explicit exit, only weight decay. It also naturally holds a small contrarian position in every name, which changes the capacity and turnover profile completely versus a top-10 sort.
ideas.source: Lehmann, 'Fads, Martingales, and Market Efficiency', Quarterly Journal of Economics 105(1), 1990, 1-28; Jegadeesh, 'Evidence of Predictable Behavior of Security Returns', Journal of Finance 45(3), 1990 (one-month reversal ~2%/month, 1934-1987)

ideas.name: Closing-Auction Pressure Fade
ideas.entry_rule: At 15:30 ET compute for each universe symbol the intraday move so far, INTRA = close_15:30 / open_09:30 - 1, and its typical scale TYP = mean over the last 20 sessions of |close_15:30/open_09:30 - 1|. Also compute LATE = close_15:30 / close_14:30 - 1. SHORT setup: INTRA >= 2.0 * TYP AND INTRA > 0 AND LATE > 0 (the move is still being pressed into the close). LONG setup: INTRA <= -2.0 * TYP AND LATE < 0. Enter at 15:45 ET with a marketable limit; at most 5 names per side, ranked by |INTRA|/TYP.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit market-on-open the next session (holding the close-to-open window only). Stop: exit MOC the same day at 15:59 if the position is already 1.5 * ATR(14, daily)/close against you at 15:55. Never carry past the next open.
params: exit at next open vs next 10:00
ideas.why: Bogousslavsky's infrequent-rebalancing model implies that investors who rebalance on a fixed schedule concentrate demand into the end of the day, producing price pressure that is mechanically reversed once the demand is satisfied - his paper documents the resulting intraday return autocorrelation and seasonality patterns. Lou, Polk and Skouras independently establish that reversal profits accrue in the close-to-open window, which is exactly the window in which this pressure unwinds, so the two results line up on the same trade.
ideas.novelty: Fades a within-day displacement measured from the OPEN (not from a band or an opening range) and requires the move to still be accelerating in the final hour, then holds only the close-to-open window. Distinct from opening range fade in both the measurement window and the holding period.
ideas.source: Bogousslavsky, 'Infrequent Rebalancing, Return Autocorrelation, and Seasonality', Journal of Finance 71(6), 2016 (Crossref-confirmed) for the mechanism; Lou, Polk & Skouras (JFE 2019) for the close-to-open location of reversal profits. The specific bar-by-bar trigger is my synthesis - the papers give the mechanism and timing, not a trading rule.

ideas.name: BVC-VPIN Toxicity Continuation
ideas.entry_rule: On 5-min bars compute dP_t = C_t - C_{t-1} and sigma_t = stdev(dP, 50). Bulk Volume Classification: buy volume V^B_t = V_t * Phi(dP_t / sigma_t) where Phi is the standard normal CDF; sell volume V^S_t = V_t - V^B_t. Accumulate bar volume into volume buckets of size V* = ADV(20 days)/50, pro-rating a bar's volume (and its buy fraction) across a bucket boundary. On completion of bucket k: VPIN_k = (1/50) * sum_{j=k-49..k} |V^B_j - V^S_j| / V*. Enter LONG at the open of the next 5-min bar when (a) VPIN_k >= the 90th percentile of VPIN over the prior 250 buckets, (b) the bucket's signed imbalance sum(V^B - V^S) > 0, and (c) the bucket's last price > its first price. Mirror exactly for SHORT.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when VPIN falls back below its 50th percentile of the trailing 250 buckets, OR after 3 completed volume buckets, OR on a 1.5 x ATR(14, 5-min) stop from entry - whichever comes first.
inputs: rolling stdev of bar close-to-close price changes
ideas.why: Easley, Lopez de Prado and O'Hara argue that persistently one-sided volume adversely selects market makers, who widen or withdraw. Once liquidity providers step back, the informed side faces less resistance and the move extends rather than reverting. The measure is deliberately built in volume time, not clock time, so it fires when information is arriving fast regardless of the hour.
ideas.source: Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara (2012), 'Flow Toxicity and Liquidity in a High-Frequency World', Review of Financial Studies 25(5); SSRN 1695596 and the NYU Stern working copy at stern.nyu.edu/sites/default/files/assets/documents/con_035928.pdf. BVC buy-fraction f = Phi(dP/sigma_dP) and VPIN = (1/n) sum |V^B - V^S| / V confirmed against the same paper's implementations.
ideas.novelty: Nothing in the existing 32 signs volume. This classifies each bar's volume into buy and sell halves probabilistically and trades the persistence of the imbalance, not the price pattern. It is also the only idea here that runs on a volume clock rather than a time clock.
params: bucket size divisor (25/50/100 buckets per day)
normal CDF vs Student-t CDF with nu = 0.25

ideas.name: BVC Absorption Fade
ideas.entry_rule: Using the same BVC construction, define per-bar signed imbalance OI_t = V_t * (2*Phi(dP_t/sigma_t) - 1). Let SumOI_t = sum of OI over the last 6 bars and R_t = C_t/C_{t-6} - 1. Enter SHORT at the next bar's open when SumOI_t >= the 90th percentile of SumOI over the trailing 500 bars AND |R_t| <= 0.25 * ATR(14)/C_t - i.e. heavy net BUYING that produced almost no net price advance. Enter LONG on the mirror condition (SumOI <= 10th percentile with no net decline).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when the trailing 6-bar SumOI crosses back through its 50th percentile, OR after 8 bars, OR on a 1.0 x ATR(14) stop, OR at a 1.5 x ATR(14) target.
ideas.why: Kyle's lambda says price should move in proportion to signed order flow. When large signed flow produces no price response, lambda has locally collapsed because a large resting counterparty is absorbing the flow - an iceberg, a VWAP seller, a hedger. Once the aggressive side exhausts itself the absorbed side wins and price moves against the flow. This is the classic 'absorption' read from tape trading, made computable without a tape.
ideas.source: Kyle (1985), 'Continuous Auctions and Insider Trading', Econometrica 53(6) for the flow-to-price-impact relation; the absorption interpretation is my own synthesis - the testable formulation is flow in the top decile paired with a price response below a quarter of an ATR.
ideas.novelty: It is a divergence between order flow and price, not between an oscillator and price. RSI divergence compares price to a momentum oscillator; this compares price to classified volume, so a bar can show a large absorption signal with a perfectly neutral RSI.

ideas.name: Kyle Lambda Shock
ideas.entry_rule: Let r_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-1}), s_t = sign(r_t) (skip bars with r_t = 0), and x_t = s_t * sqrt(C_t * V_t) (signed square-root dollar volume). Estimate lambda_t as the OLS slope (with intercept) of r on x over the trailing 60 bars. Compute z_lambda = (lambda_t - mean(lambda, 250)) / stdev(lambda, 250). Enter LONG at the next bar's open when z_lambda >= 2.0 AND lambda_t > lambda_{t-5} (impact still rising) AND |r_t| >= 1.0 * ATR(14)/C_t AND r_t > 0. Mirror for SHORT with r_t < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when z_lambda <= 0, OR after 10 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: Lambda is the slope of the price-impact function - dollars of price move per unit of order flow. A sharp rise means the book has thinned: the same size now moves price further. In a thin book, an initiated move meets less resistance and follows through, and market makers charge more to lean against it. Rising lambda plus a large directional bar is the signature of liquidity withdrawal ahead of a directional repricing.
ideas.source: Kyle (1985), Econometrica 53(6). The estimation form - regressing returns on signed SQUARE-ROOT dollar volume over a rolling window - follows the Office of Financial Research Working Paper 15-11, 'Systemwide Commonalities in Market Liquidity' (financialresearch.gov/working-papers/files/OFRwp-2015-11_Systemwide-Commonalities-in-Market-Liquidity.pdf), and Hasbrouck (2009) on estimating trading costs from daily data.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is a regression coefficient measuring market depth, not a price statistic. ATR expansion breakout keys off realized volatility; lambda can rise while ATR is flat, because it measures volatility PER UNIT OF VOLUME. The two disagree most in exactly the thin-tape conditions that matter.
params: signed sqrt-dollar-volume vs signed raw dollar volume
sign source: return sign vs BVC imbalance sign

ideas.name: Amihud Illiquidity Spike Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: ILLIQ_t = |r_t| / (C_t * V_t) * 1e9 where r_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-1}). Enter LONG at the next bar's open when (a) ILLIQ_t >= the 95th percentile of ILLIQ over the trailing 250 bars, (b) r_t < 0, and (c) the 20-bar MEDIAN of ILLIQ is NOT itself in the top quartile of its own trailing 250 values - the spike must be a one-bar event, not a persistent illiquidity regime. Mirror for SHORT after an ILLIQ spike with r_t > 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when ILLIQ_t falls to or below its 50th percentile of the trailing 250, OR after 5 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: Amihud's ratio is price move per dollar traded. A one-bar spike means the move happened on almost no volume, so it is very unlikely to be information - it is a liquidity air pocket. Nagel shows that the expected return to providing liquidity into exactly these dislocations rises sharply when liquidity evaporates. The regime filter matters: if illiquidity is chronically elevated the stock is simply thin, and the reversal premium is offset by the cost of trading it.
ideas.source: Amihud (2002), 'Illiquidity and stock returns: cross-section and time-series effects', Journal of Financial Markets 5(1); Nagel (2012), 'Evaporating Liquidity', Review of Financial Studies 25(7) / NBER WP 17653 (nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w17653/w17653.pdf), which shows reversal-strategy returns are compensation for liquidity provision and are strongly time-varying.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is return-per-dollar-of-volume, which is orthogonal to both price extremes and raw volume. A bar can spike ILLIQ with a small return on tiny volume - invisible to Bollinger, RSI or any volume-surge rule. The transient-vs-regime median filter is the part that makes it tradeable.

ideas.name: Corwin-Schultz Spread Shock Fade
ideas.entry_rule: For consecutive bars t and t+1 compute beta = [ln(H_t/L_t)]^2 + [ln(H_{t+1}/L_{t+1})]^2; gamma = [ln(max(H_t,H_{t+1}) / min(L_t,L_{t+1}))]^2; alpha = (sqrt(2*beta) - sqrt(beta))/(3 - 2*sqrt(2)) - sqrt(gamma/(3 - 2*sqrt(2))); S_t = 2*(e^alpha - 1)/(1 + e^alpha), setting S_t = 0 when alpha < 0. Let Sbar_t = mean(S, 5). Enter LONG at the next bar's open when Sbar_t >= the 95th percentile of Sbar over the trailing 250 bars AND the cumulative return over the two bars used in the estimate is negative. Mirror for SHORT.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when Sbar_t falls below its 50th percentile of the trailing 250, OR after 5 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
inputs: daily or intraday High and Low only for the spread estimate
ideas.why: Corwin and Schultz show that the daily high is nearly always a buy at the ask and the low nearly always a sell at the bid, so the high-low ratio contains both variance and spread; because variance scales with the return interval and the spread does not, the one-day versus two-day ranges separate them. A spike in the estimated spread means the effective cost of immediacy has jumped - liquidity suppliers have backed away. Prices pushed through a temporarily wide spread revert once it normalises, which is the mechanical part of short-horizon reversal.
ideas.source: Corwin & Schultz (2012), 'A Simple Way to Estimate Bid-Ask Spreads from Daily High and Low Prices', Journal of Finance 67(2):719-759; formula cross-checked against Odegaard's lecture notes (ba-odegaard.no/teach/notes/liquidity_estimators/corwin_schultz_high_low_estimator/) and the intraday application at sites.nd.edu/scorwin/files/2019/11/Application_Intraday_Analysis.pdf.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is an estimated TRANSACTION COST recovered from the geometry of overlapping ranges, not a volatility band. Keltner and Bollinger fades widen with volatility; this estimator explicitly nets volatility out of the range and keeps only the spread component, so it can spike on a day whose ATR is unremarkable.

ideas.name: Abdi-Ranaldo Negative-Product Run
ideas.entry_rule: Work in logs: c_t = ln(C_t), eta_t = (ln(H_t) + ln(L_t))/2 (log mid-range). Define the Abdi-Ranaldo inner product pi_t = (c_t - eta_t) * (c_t - eta_{t+1}); the AR spread estimate is 2*sqrt(max(0, pi_t)). Note pi_t is only known at bar t+1, so act at the open of bar t+2. Enter LONG when pi has been strictly NEGATIVE on at least 4 of the last 5 bars AND the mean of (c_t - eta_t) over those same 5 bars is > 0. Mirror for SHORT (4 of 5 negative pi with mean (c - eta) < 0).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on the first bar where pi_t >= 0, OR when the 5-bar mean of (c - eta) changes sign, OR after 10 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: Abdi and Ranaldo build their estimator on the fact that under a pure bid-ask bounce the close sits randomly above or below the mid-range, so the product of consecutive close-minus-mid deviations is positive in expectation. When that product is persistently NEGATIVE the estimator breaks down - and it breaks down precisely because the close is being pinned to one side of the range by directional pressure rather than bouncing. The failure mode of the spread estimator is itself the informed-trading signal.
ideas.source: Abdi & Ranaldo (2017), 'A Simple Estimation of Bid-Ask Spreads from Daily Close, High, and Low Prices', Review of Financial Studies 30(12):4437-4480 (SSRN 2725981). Closed form AR_t = sqrt(2*(C_t - 0.5(H_t+L_t))*(C_t - 0.5(H_{t+1}+L_{t+1}))) as reproduced in Entropy 22(7):783, 'Do Liquidity Proxies Based on Daily Prices and Quotes Really Measure Liquidity?'.
ideas.novelty: Trades the SIGN of a spread estimator's inner product - the part every implementation throws away by clamping to zero. Nobody publishes this as a signal because in the liquidity literature the negative values are treated as estimation noise to be discarded.
params: mean (c - eta) threshold (0 vs 0.25 x sigma)

ideas.name: Roll Autocovariance Sign Flip
ideas.entry_rule: dp_t = ln(C_t) - ln(C_{t-1}). G_t = sample covariance of (dp_t, dp_{t-1}) over the trailing 60 bars. Under Roll's model G < 0 is the bid-ask bounce regime and the implied spread is 2*sqrt(-G). Enter LONG at the next bar's open when G_t > 0 AND G_{t-1} <= 0 (a fresh flip into positive serial covariance) AND the sum of dp over the last 5 bars > 0. Mirror for SHORT with the 5-bar sum < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when G_t returns below 0, OR after 20 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: Roll's estimator assumes all serial covariance in price changes comes from the bid-ask bounce, which forces it negative. Empirically it turns positive a large fraction of the time, and that is not just noise - positive serial covariance means information is being incorporated gradually, so the bounce is being overwhelmed by directional order flow. The flip from negative to positive is the moment the tape stops being noise-dominated and starts trending, which is a cleaner regime marker than any smoothed price statistic because it is defined on the autocovariance rather than the level.
ideas.source: Roll (1984), 'A Simple Implicit Measure of the Effective Bid-Ask Spread in an Efficient Market', Journal of Finance 39(4):1127-1139; the frequency and interpretation of positive-covariance episodes is discussed in Harris (1990), 'Statistical properties of the Roll serial covariance bid/ask spread estimator', Journal of Finance 45(2), and in the bidask R package documentation (cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bidask/bidask.pdf).
ideas.novelty: The trigger is a change in the SIGN of a second moment, not the level of a first moment. ADX, SuperTrend and Hull slope all measure how far price has travelled; this measures whether consecutive price changes have started reinforcing each other, which can flip while price is still flat.

ideas.name: Excess Reversal Beyond the Bounce
ideas.entry_rule: Compute two spread estimates on the same window. (1) Roll: G_t = Cov(dp_t, dp_{t-1}) over the trailing 100 bars; S_roll = 2*sqrt(-G_t) if G_t < 0, else 0. (2) Corwin-Schultz S_cs as defined above, averaged over the last 20 bars. Ratio R_t = S_roll / max(S_cs, 1e-6). Enter LONG at the next bar's open when R_t >= 3.0 AND r_t <= -1.5 * stdev(r, 60). Mirror for SHORT when R_t >= 3.0 and r_t >= +1.5 * stdev(r, 60).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the FOLLOWING bar (a strict one-bar hold), OR on a 1.0 x ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: If observed negative autocorrelation were purely the bid-ask bounce, the Roll-implied spread and the high-low-implied spread would agree. When Roll implies a spread several times larger than the range-based estimate, the extra reversal cannot be a bounce - it is non-synchronous trading and partial price adjustment, which are genuinely tradeable because they represent stale prices catching up. The recent empirical work makes exactly this point on SPY: Roll implies roughly 28 basis points of half-spread against an actual 1-3 basis points, an order-of-magnitude gap that is real predictability, not microstructure noise.
ideas.source: arXiv 2606.29591, 'The Bounce Has No Direction: Sign, Magnitude, and the Microstructure of Short-Horizon Return Reversal' (arxiv.org/html/2606.29591), which documents the Roll-implied vs actual spread discrepancy and attributes the residual to non-synchronous trading; combined with Roll (1984) and Corwin & Schultz (2012).
ideas.novelty: It is a ratio of two independent estimators of the SAME quantity, traded on their disagreement. That is a different construct from any single-indicator threshold: the signal only fires when two microstructure measurements of spread are inconsistent, which is a condition no price-based indicator can express.

ideas.name: Sign-Autocorrelation z Score
ideas.entry_rule: Let s_t = +1 if r_t > 0 and -1 if r_t < 0, dropping bars with r_t = 0. For lag m, let p_m = the fraction of the last N = 250 valid pairs for which s_t = s_{t-m}, and z_m = (2*p_m - 1) * sqrt(N). Enter at the next bar's open, requiring |r_t| >= 0.5 * stdev(r, 60): if z_m <= -2.0, take the OPPOSITE side to s_t; if z_m >= +2.0, take the SAME side as s_t. No trade when |z_m| < 2.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of bar t+m (so a one-bar hold when m = 1), OR on a 1.5 x ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: Scalar return autocorrelation mixes direction and magnitude, and the recent evidence is that on liquid index ETFs a strongly significant lag-1 autocorrelation can come almost entirely from magnitude while the sign carries no information at all - and the reverse also happens: at lag 3 the sign test is significant while the scalar autocorrelation is not. Since a directional trade only monetises the sign, the sign-continuation frequency is the statistic that actually maps to P&L, and it identifies horizons the ordinary autocorrelation hides.
ideas.source: arXiv 2606.29591, 'The Bounce Has No Direction' - the FRI sign test, rho_sign(m) = 2*p_{m,0} - 1 with p_{m,0} the continuation frequency and 0.5 the random-walk null; the paper reports z_sign = -1.59 at lag 1 (insignificant) alongside rho(1) = -0.081 with z* = -7.39, and z_sign = -2.32 at lag 3 where rho(3) is insignificant.
ideas.novelty: Three-bar momentum hard-codes a fixed sign pattern. This estimates whether sign persistence exists at all, at each lag, and only trades when it is statistically significant - and it explicitly discards magnitude, which is the opposite of every momentum rule in the existing set.

ideas.name: Variance Ratio Term-Structure Inversion
ideas.entry_rule: On 5-min log returns compute the Lo-MacKinlay variance ratio VR(q) = Var(q-bar overlapping sums) / (q * Var(1-bar returns)), with the standard overlapping-sample bias correction, over the trailing 1000 bars, for q = 2, 6 and 24. Enter LONG at the next bar's open on the bar where the term structure INVERTS: VR(2) crosses from >= 1.0 to < 0.95 while VR(24) is >= 1.05 and rising versus 20 bars ago, and the trailing 24-bar return is positive. Mirror for SHORT with a negative 24-bar return.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when VR(24) falls to or below 1.0, OR when VR(2) rises back above 1.0, OR after 24 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
inputs: overlapping variance ratios at three horizons
ideas.why: VR(q) > 1 is positive serial dependence, VR(q) < 1 is mean reversion, and VR(q) = 1 is a random walk. When the short-horizon ratio drops below one while the long-horizon ratio rises above one, the tape has separated into two layers: microstructure noise and stale-quote reversal at the minute scale sitting on top of a genuine drift at the hour scale. That specific shape says a directional flow is being worked into a noisy book, and the drift is the part that persists. The Fejer identity VR(q) = 1 + 2 * sum_{m=1..q-1}(1 - m/q)*rho(m) makes the ratio a weighted sum of autocorrelations, so the inversion is a statement about the whole autocorrelation profile, not one lag.
ideas.source: Lo & MacKinlay (1988), 'Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test', Review of Financial Studies 1(1):41-66; the Fejer/spectral interpretation and the resolution-dependent finding that the random-walk null is rejected below 5 minutes but not at 1 hour is from arXiv 2606.29591; implementation reference: the vrtest R package (cran.r-project.org/web/packages/vrtest/vrtest.pdf).
ideas.novelty: A regime signal built from a formal statistical test at several horizons simultaneously, keyed on the SHAPE of the term structure rather than any single value. It is not a pullback rule - it fires on the inversion event itself, whether or not price has pulled back.

ideas.name: Overnight vs Intraday Amihud Gap Fade
ideas.entry_rule: For each session compute ILLIQ_on = |ln(O_t/C_{t-1})| / (dollar volume in the first 30 minutes of day t) * 1e9, and ILLIQ_id = |ln(C_t/O_t)| / (dollar volume from 10:00 ET to the close) * 1e9. Take z-scores of each over the trailing 250 sessions. At 10:00 ET on day t, enter AGAINST the overnight gap when z(ILLIQ_on, day t) >= 2.0 AND z(ILLIQ_id, day t-1) <= 0.5 AND |ln(O_t/C_{t-1})| >= 0.5 * ATR(14, daily)/C_{t-1}. So a gap UP on thin opening volume with a normally-liquid prior session is a SHORT.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of day t, OR when price has retraced 75% of the gap back toward C_{t-1}, OR on a stop placed one full gap width beyond O_t.
inputs: 1-min or 5-min bars to split first-30-minute volume from rest-of-day volume
ideas.why: Amihud's ratio behaves very differently overnight than intraday - the overnight component is dominated by the opening auction and by a small number of participants, not by continuous price discovery. A gap that is large relative to the volume that produced it, on a stock whose regular-session liquidity is normal, is a repricing done by very few hands, and it tends to be walked back once the full complement of liquidity providers arrives. Requiring the PRIOR session's intraday illiquidity to be normal separates 'thin open' from 'thin stock'.
ideas.source: Bernhardt, Davies and co-authors, 'The Night and Day of Amihud's (2002) Liquidity Measure', University of Warwick Working Paper 1211 (warwick.ac.uk/fac/soc/economics/research/workingpapers/2019/twerp_1211_bernhardt.pdf), which decomposes the measure into overnight and intraday components and shows they carry different information; Amihud (2002), Journal of Financial Markets 5(1).
ideas.novelty: Opening range fade uses the first N minutes of PRICE. This uses the ratio of overnight price move to opening VOLUME, cross-filtered against the prior session's intraday illiquidity - a two-component liquidity decomposition, and it can decline to trade a large gap that came on heavy volume, which a range-based rule cannot.

ideas.name: Bipower Jump-Test Continuation
ideas.entry_rule: For each session with M five-minute log returns r_1..r_M: RV = sum r_i^2; BV = (pi/2) * (M/(M-1)) * sum_{i=2..M} |r_i| * |r_{i-1}|; TQ = M * mu^-3 * (M/(M-2)) * sum_{i=3..M} |r_i|^(4/3) |r_{i-1}|^(4/3) |r_{i-2}|^(4/3) with mu = 2^(2/3) * Gamma(7/6)/Gamma(1/2); RJ = (RV - BV)/RV; z = RJ / sqrt( ((pi/2)^2 + pi - 5) * (1/M) * max(1, TQ/BV^2) ). If z > 3.09 the session contains a statistically significant jump. Let J = the sign of the largest-absolute 5-min return of that session. Enter at the next session's open in the direction of J.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of session t+3, OR on a 1.5 x ATR(14, daily) stop.
ideas.why: Bipower variation is robust to jumps because it multiplies adjacent returns, so RV minus BV isolates the discontinuous part of the day's quadratic variation. A statistically significant jump means the price moved further than the diffusion could account for - it is a repricing to new information rather than an accumulation of noise. The literature ties individual-stock jumps to scheduled announcements and index jumps to macro news, and information-driven repricings do not mean-revert the way diffusive moves do. The test also lets you REFUSE to trade a same-sized move that fails the jump test, which is where the edge sits.
ideas.source: Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard (2004, 2006), 'Econometrics of Testing for Jumps in Financial Economics Using Bipower Variation', Journal of Financial Econometrics (public.econ.duke.edu/~get/browse/courses/883/Spr15/COURSE-MATERIALS/Z_Papers/BNSJFEC2006.pdf); ratio-statistic form and critical values as in Huang & Tauchen (2005); reference implementation BNSjumptest in the R highfrequency package (rdrr.io/rforge/highfrequency/man/BNSjumptest.html).
ideas.novelty: ATR expansion breakout treats all large moves alike. This applies a formal statistical test that separates a jump from a run of large diffusive returns of identical total size, and only trades the former. The decision variable is a test statistic with a known null distribution, not a threshold on a smoothed range.
params: staggered/skip-one-return BV variant to reduce microstructure bias

ideas.name: Range-Path Efficiency Regime
ideas.entry_rule: Per bar compute the Parkinson variance sigma2_P = ln(H_t/L_t)^2 / (4*ln 2) and r_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-1}). Define per-bar efficiency e_t = r_t^2 / max(sigma2_P, 1e-12) and E_t = mean(e, 20). Enter LONG at the next bar's open when E_t >= the 80th percentile of E over the trailing 250 bars AND sum(r) over the last 20 bars > 0. Mirror for SHORT with a negative 20-bar sum.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when E_t falls to or below its 50th percentile of the trailing 250, OR after 20 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
inputs: 20-bar mean of the return-to-range variance ratio
ideas.why: Parkinson's estimator measures how far price travelled inside the bar; the squared close-to-close return measures how far it got. Their ratio is the fraction of path converted into displacement - a direct measure of how much of the tape is microstructure noise versus directional flow. Low ratio means liquidity providers are winning and the bar is churn; high ratio means orders are being filled in one direction with little push-back. This is the noise-to-signal ratio the range-based volatility literature uses to argue the range estimator is up to five times more efficient than close-to-close, turned around and used as the signal rather than as a variance-reduction device.
ideas.source: Parkinson (1980), 'The Extreme Value Method for Estimating the Variance of the Rate of Return', Journal of Business 53(1); Alizadeh, Brandt & Diebold (2002), 'Range-Based Estimation of Stochastic Volatility Models', Journal of Finance 57(3), on the range/return variance relationship. The use of the ratio as a tradeable regime variable is my own synthesis - the reasoning is that the ratio is exactly the signal-to-noise term the range literature exploits for efficiency.
ideas.novelty: It is a ratio of two variance ESTIMATORS of the same underlying quantity that disagree only in the presence of path inefficiency. Unlike ADX or any directional-movement measure, it is scale-free and completely insensitive to trend direction, so it can be computed over a window with zero net return and still say whether the tape is efficient.
params: Parkinson vs Garman-Klass in the denominator

ideas.name: Rogers-Satchell Drift Wedge
ideas.entry_rule: Per bar: sigma2_GK = 0.5*ln(H_t/L_t)^2 - (2*ln2 - 1)*ln(C_t/O_t)^2; sigma2_RS = ln(H_t/C_t)*ln(H_t/O_t) + ln(L_t/C_t)*ln(L_t/O_t). Wedge W_t = sigma2_GK - sigma2_RS, and Wbar_t = mean(W, 10). Enter LONG at the next bar's open when Wbar_t >= the 80th percentile of Wbar over the trailing 250 bars AND sum over the last 10 bars of (ln C_t - ln O_t) > 0. Mirror for SHORT.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when Wbar_t falls below its 50th percentile of the trailing 250 or turns negative, OR after 15 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: Garman-Klass assumes zero drift within the bar; Rogers-Satchell is constructed to be drift-independent. Their difference is therefore an estimate of how much of the measured 'volatility' is actually one-way drift rather than two-way noise. That is a trend detector derived from the estimator bias itself, and it responds to within-bar structure - where the open and close sit relative to the high and low - rather than to a smoothed sequence of closes, so it can flag directional pressure a bar or two before any moving-average construct.
ideas.source: Rogers & Satchell (1991), 'Estimating Variance from High, Low and Closing Prices', Annals of Applied Probability 1(4); Garman & Klass (1980), 'On the Estimation of Security Price Volatilities from Historical Data', Journal of Business 53(1). The GK-minus-RS gap as a drift diagnostic is discussed in Macrosynergy, 'Six ways to estimate realized volatility' (macrosynergy.com/research/six-ways-to-estimate-realized-volatility/); using it as an entry trigger is my synthesis.
ideas.novelty: Direction is inferred from the DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN TWO VARIANCE ESTIMATORS, one drift-sensitive and one drift-immune. No moving average, no oscillator, no price level enters the trigger - only within-bar geometry. Hull MA slope and TRIX both smooth closes; this uses information those discard entirely.

ideas.name: Yang-Zhang Overnight Variance Share
ideas.entry_rule: Over the trailing n = 20 sessions compute sigma2_o = variance of ln(O_t/C_{t-1}); sigma2_c = variance of ln(C_t/O_t); sigma2_RS = mean of the per-session Rogers-Satchell variance; k = 0.34/(1.34 + (n+1)/(n-1)); sigma2_YZ = sigma2_o + k*sigma2_c + (1-k)*sigma2_RS. Overnight share Q = sigma2_o / sigma2_YZ. FADE BRANCH - when Q >= 0.60: on any 5-min bar before 15:00 ET where the session's cumulative move from the open is <= -0.5 * ATR(14, daily)/O_t, enter LONG at that bar's close; mirror for SHORT on a +0.5 ATR move up. BREAKOUT BRANCH - when Q <= 0.30: enter in the DIRECTION of the same 0.5-ATR intraday displacement instead. No intraday trade when 0.30 < Q < 0.60.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the session close, OR on a stop at 0.5 x ATR(14, daily) beyond entry, OR at a target of 0.75 x ATR(14, daily).
ideas.why: Yang-Zhang decomposes total variance into an overnight gap piece, an open-to-close drift piece and a drift-free intraday range piece. When the overnight share is high, price discovery is happening outside the continuous session - the regular session is mostly liquidity providers rebalancing around an already-repriced level, and intraday moves revert. When the overnight share is low, the information is arriving during the session and intraday moves extend. The share, not the level, is what switches the regime, and it is the only OHLC statistic that separates the two.
ideas.source: Yang & Zhang (2000), 'Drift-Independent Volatility Estimation Based on High, Low, Open, and Close Prices', Journal of Business 73(3):477-491, which gives the three-component decomposition and the k weight; regime interpretation of the component shares is my synthesis of that decomposition.
ideas.novelty: A single scalar - the fraction of total variance that arrives between sessions - flips the strategy between fade and follow. That is an exit-and-entry STRUCTURE switch driven by a variance decomposition, not another entry rule. Opening range breakout and fade are two fixed strategies; this decides which of the two the current regime supports.

ideas.name: Temporary vs Permanent Impact Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Define an 'event' bar as one with |r_t| >= 1.5 * stdev(r, 60), r = log return. For the most recent 100 event bars strictly in the past, compute per event the temporary-impact ratio ti = -(sum_{i=1..3} r_{t+i}) / r_t, and let TI = the median of those 100 values. Then, on a new event bar t: if TI >= 0.5 enter AGAINST sign(r_t) at the next bar's open; if TI <= -0.2 enter WITH sign(r_t) at the next bar's open; otherwise no trade.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of bar t+3 - the horizon over which TI is estimated, so the exit structure and the estimator are matched by construction. Hard stop at 1.5 x ATR(14).
ideas.why: The microstructure decomposition of a trade's price impact splits it into a permanent component (information now in the price) and a temporary component (the compensation paid to the liquidity provider, which reverts). The realized spread is precisely the part that reverts within a short horizon. TI is a bar-level estimate of that split, measured from the asset's own history: TI near 1 means large moves are almost entirely liquidity-driven and fully revert, TI near 0 or negative means they are informational and extend. The strategy does not assume which regime holds - it measures it and takes the corresponding side.
ideas.source: Hasbrouck (1991), 'Measuring the Information Content of Stock Trades', Review of Financial Studies 4(1), on permanent vs transitory impact; Huang & Stoll (1996), 'Dealer versus auction markets', Journal of Financial Economics 41(3), for the effective-vs-realized-spread decomposition. The bar-level TI estimator and the sign-switching rule are my synthesis of that decomposition.
ideas.novelty: The strategy's SIDE is not fixed by the rule - the same trigger produces a fade or a follow depending on an estimated impact-decomposition parameter. Every rule in the existing 32 has a hard-coded polarity; this one learns it, and the estimation horizon and the holding horizon are deliberately identical so the estimate is of the exact quantity being traded.

ideas.name: Order-Sign Long-Memory Follow
ideas.entry_rule: Build the BVC signed-imbalance series OI_t = V_t*(2*Phi(dP_t/sigma_t) - 1) on 5-min bars and take u_t = sign(OI_t). Estimate the Hurst exponent H of {u_t} by detrended fluctuation analysis over the trailing 512 bars: for scales n in {8,16,32,64,128}, integrate the mean-centred series, fit and remove a linear trend within each non-overlapping window of length n, compute the RMS residual F(n), and take H as the OLS slope of log F(n) on log n. Enter LONG at the next bar's open when H >= 0.60 AND sum(u) over the last 20 bars >= +8. Mirror for SHORT with sum(u) <= -8.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when H falls below 0.55, OR when sum(u) over the trailing 20 bars changes sign, OR after 30 bars, OR on a 2.0 x ATR(14) stop.
inputs: DFA Hurst estimate of the sign series
ideas.why: Lillo and Farmer showed that order signs are a long-memory process - the autocorrelation decays as a power law with exponent about 0.6, corresponding to H around 0.7 - because large institutional metaorders are split into many small child orders that arrive over hours. Crucially, in normal conditions the resulting sign predictability is offset by anti-correlated liquidity, so returns stay close to a martingale. The trade is on the episodes where H rises above its baseline in one direction: that is a metaorder being worked, and the offsetting liquidity is not always sufficient. Standing aside when H is near 0.5 is as important as entering when it is high.
ideas.source: Lillo & Farmer (2004), 'The Long Memory of the Efficient Market', Studies in Nonlinear Dynamics & Econometrics 8(3); Santa Fe Institute working paper 03-12-066 (sfi-edu.s3.amazonaws.com/sfi-edu/production/uploads/sfi-com/dev/uploads/filer/d0/d9/d0d92e50-17b7-4072-98a7-293ca01b8d89/03-12-066.pdf); the order-splitting mechanism is from Lillo, Mike & Farmer (2005).
ideas.novelty: The state variable is the memory EXPONENT of a signed-flow series, estimated by DFA - a long-range-dependence statistic, not a level, slope or oscillator. It answers 'is someone working a large order right now' rather than 'has price moved'. Nothing in the existing 32 estimates a scaling exponent.
params: R/S vs DFA vs GPH estimator

ideas.name: Volume-Clock Duration Collapse
ideas.entry_rule: Build volume bars by accumulating 1-min bars until cumulative volume reaches V* = ADV(20 days)/100, pro-rating a minute's volume across a boundary and pricing each contributing minute at (H+L+C)/3. Record for volume bar i its open price, close price and its DURATION d_i in clock minutes. Enter LONG at the start of volume bar i+1 when d_i <= the 10th percentile of {d} over the last 200 volume bars AND the close of volume bar i > its open. Mirror for SHORT.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when a subsequent volume bar's duration exceeds the median of the last 200 durations, OR after 5 volume bars, OR on a 1.5 x ATR(14, computed on the volume-bar series) stop.
inputs: 20-day ADV to size the volume bar
ideas.why: Easley and O'Hara's sequential-trade model makes the interval between trades informative: informed traders trade when they have information and are absent when they do not, so short durations signal an information event, not merely activity. Building volume bars converts this into something computable from minute bars - the time taken to absorb a fixed quantity of shares is the inverse of trade intensity. It also normalises the sampling: volume bars have far more Gaussian, less heteroskedastic returns than time bars, so a threshold set on them is stable across the session's U-shape without any time-of-day adjustment.
ideas.source: Easley & O'Hara (1992), 'Time and the Process of Security Price Adjustment', Journal of Finance 47(2); Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara (2012), 'The Volume Clock: Insights into the High-Frequency Paradigm', Journal of Portfolio Management 39(1) (researchgate.net/publication/254199259).
ideas.novelty: The bar itself is redefined. Every one of the existing 32 is computed on fixed-time bars; this one samples in volume time and makes the CLOCK DURATION the signal. That is a different sampling scheme, not a different indicator, and it automatically de-seasonalises the open and close.

ideas.name: Liquidity Vacuum Depth Collapse
ideas.entry_rule: Depth proxy D_t = (C_t * V_t) / max((H_t - L_t)/C_t, 1e-6) - dollar volume per unit of relative range, an inverse of Kyle's lambda. Let z_t = (ln D_t - mean(ln D, 60)) / stdev(ln D, 60). Enter at the next bar's open when z_t <= -2.0 on two CONSECUTIVE bars AND the sum of the BVC signed imbalance OI over those two bars is positive - go LONG; go SHORT when that sum is negative.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when z_t returns to >= 0, OR after 10 bars, OR on a 1.5 x ATR(14) stop.
inputs: log depth proxy and its 60-bar z-score
ideas.why: Depth is the amount of volume the book can absorb per unit of price movement, the reciprocal of price impact. When it collapses for two bars running, the resting size has been pulled and whatever flow arrives next travels much further than usual. The direction is taken from the classified imbalance rather than from price, so the trade is 'thin book plus one-sided flow' rather than 'price broke a level'. The Amivest ratio family - volume divided by absolute return - is the daily ancestor of this measure; using range in the denominator rather than the net return makes it responsive to intrabar liquidity withdrawal that leaves the close unchanged.
ideas.source: Amivest liquidity ratio as introduced in Cooper, Groth & Avera (1985), Journal of Economics and Business 37(1); Kyle (1985) for depth as 1/lambda; the family of volume-to-range and volume-to-return liquidity proxies is surveyed in Fong, Holden & Trzcinka, 'What Are the Best Liquidity Proxies for Global Research?' (cicfconf.org/sites/default/files/paper_337.pdf). The two-bar depth-collapse entry is my synthesis.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is a collapse in a LIQUIDITY measure, with direction supplied by classified flow - price plays no part in the trigger at all. Donchian and ATR-expansion breakouts both require price to have already done something; this fires while price can still be flat, on the disappearance of the resting size.
params: range vs true range in the denominator

ideas.name: Turtle System 1 loser-filtered breakout
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars. N = Wilder 20-period ATR (N_t = (19*N_{t-1} + TR_t)/20). A long breakout event occurs on bar t when High_t > max(High[t-20 .. t-1]); short when Low_t < min(Low[t-20 .. t-1]). Maintain a state variable last_breakout_result. Compute it by phantom-simulating the MOST RECENT prior breakout event b regardless of whether it was traded: phantom entry price = the broken level itself, phantom N = N_b, phantom stop = entry - 2*N_b (long) / entry + 2*N_b (short); walk bars forward from b+1 and mark it LOSER if the stop is touched before the 10-day trailing exit (Low < min(Low[u-10..u-1]) for a long) is touched, else WINNER. RULE: take the current 20-day breakout ONLY if last_breakout_result == LOSER (or no prior breakout exists). If last_breakout_result == WINNER, skip it but keep updating state. OVERRIDE: always take the trade, filter or not, if High_t > max(High[t-55 .. t-1]) (long) or Low_t < min(Low[t-55 .. t-1]) (short) — the documented 55-day failsafe.
ideas.exit_rule: Long: exit on the bar where Low < min(Low[t-10 .. t-1]). Short: exit where High > max(High[t-10 .. t-1]). Hard stop at entry -/+ 2*N measured with N at the entry bar. Whichever comes first.
ideas.why: Donchian breakouts cluster: after a breakout that trends, the next breakout in the same market is disproportionately a late-stage exhaustion move, while a breakout following a failed one occurs after weak hands have been shaken out. The filter is an explicit bet that breakout outcomes are negatively autocorrelated at the event level. Dennis and Eckhardt used it to cut the trade count roughly in half while keeping most of the big trends, with the 55-day failsafe insuring against the one skipped breakout that becomes the year's biggest move.
ideas.source: Original Turtle Trading rules as published by Richard Dennis's students (Curtis Faith, 'The Original Turtle Trading Rules'), rules summary at https://www.theturtletrader.com/turtle-trading-rules/ — System 1 20-day entry with the skip-if-previous-breakout-was-a-winner filter, the 55-day failsafe, N as 20-day EMA of true range, 2N stop, 10-day exit.
ideas.novelty: Plain Donchian breakout is an unconditional rule on price alone. This adds a memory of the previous signal's OUTCOME as a gating variable — the same price bar is tradeable or not depending on trade history. Nothing in the existing 32 conditions entry on the P&L of a prior hypothetical trade.

ideas.name: Half-N pyramid with unified ratcheting stop
ideas.entry_rule: Initial entry can be any breakout trigger (use the 20-day Donchian break as the base case). N = Wilder ATR(20) frozen at the initial entry bar. After the initial 1 unit is filled at price P0, place a resting stop-entry order to ADD one more unit at P0 + 0.5*N (long). Each time an add fills at price Pk, immediately place the next add order at Pk + 0.5*N. Stop adding after 4 total units in the instrument. Adds are triggered intrabar by the resting stop, not on close.
ideas.exit_rule: Single stop for the WHOLE position, not per unit: after every fill, move the stop for all units to (price of the most recent fill) - 2*N (long). The stop only ever ratchets in the trade's favour. Full position exits on the first touch. Independently, exit the whole position if Low < min(Low[t-10 .. t-1]).
inputs: ATR(20) Wilder-smoothed and frozen at initial entry
params: whether N is refrozen at each add or held from entry
ideas.why: Scaling in on volatility-normalised advances means size is largest exactly in the trades that have already proven themselves, so the right tail of the return distribution is levered and the left tail is not. The unified stop at last-fill minus 2N is the key piece: it converts the whole stack into a single position whose risk stays constant in N terms as it grows, so a four-unit position that reverses gives back a bounded amount rather than four separate 2N losses. This is the mechanism that produced the Turtles' documented return profile far more than the entry did.
ideas.source: Original Turtle Trading rules, pyramiding section: 'When a position moved 1/2N in their favor, the Turtles added another unit, and continued adding every 1/2N up to a maximum of 4 units in a single market', with every unit stopped 2N from entry — https://www.theturtletrader.com/turtle-trading-rules/
ideas.novelty: This is an exit and position-sizing structure, not a signal. None of the existing 32 scale into a winner or move a shared stop in volatility units; they are all single-entry, single-exit.

ideas.name: Darvas box with three-day confirmed walls
ideas.entry_rule: Step 1 (candidate): the stock's High_t equals max(High[t-251 .. t]) — a new 52-week high — and Volume_t > 1.5 * SMA(Volume, 50). Record H_box = High_t. Step 2 (ceiling confirmation): if the next 3 consecutive daily bars all satisfy High < H_box, the ceiling is confirmed. If any of those 3 bars exceeds H_box, reset H_box to that bar's high and restart the 3-day count. Step 3 (floor confirmation): after the ceiling is confirmed, take L_candidate = the lowest Low made since the ceiling bar; if the next 3 consecutive bars all satisfy Low > L_candidate, set L_box = L_candidate and the box is complete. If any bar breaks below L_candidate, reset L_candidate to that bar's low and restart the 3-day count. Step 4 (entry): buy on a stop order at H_box + 0.10 once the box is complete.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at L_box - 0.10, placed immediately on entry. When a NEW box completes at a higher level (repeat steps 1-3 from the new high), raise the stop to the new box's L_box - 0.10. Position is exited only by the box-bottom stop; there is no profit target.
ideas.why: The three-day no-violation requirement on both walls converts an arbitrary swing point into a level that supply and demand have actually defended, which filters the single-bar spike highs that make raw Donchian channels noisy. The stop then ratchets in discrete confirmed steps rather than continuously, so it stays out of the way during normal consolidation but is always sitting under real support. Darvas's economic claim was that institutions accumulate in boxes and the box top marks where their bid overwhelms remaining supply.
ideas.source: Nicolas Darvas, 'How I Made $2,000,000 in the Stock Market' (1960); algorithmic box construction with the three-consecutive-day confirmation rule for both ceiling and floor described at https://clickalgo.com/darvas-box-theory and https://investinganswers.com/dictionary/d/darvas-box-theory
ideas.novelty: Donchian breakout uses a raw rolling extreme with no confirmation and a symmetric channel stop. The Darvas box requires a pivot to survive three bars before it counts, builds an asymmetric box whose floor is discovered separately from its ceiling, and ratchets the stop box-by-box rather than bar-by-bar.

ideas.name: Crabel two-day narrow range with noise-scaled stretch
ideas.entry_rule: SETUP on daily bars: R2[i] = max(High[i], High[i-1]) - min(Low[i], Low[i-1]). Require R2[i] <= min(R2[i-1] .. R2[i-19]) — the narrowest two-day range relative to any two-day range in the previous 20 sessions. TRIGGER on the NEXT session: Noise[j] = min(High[j] - Open[j], Open[j] - Low[j]) computed on daily bars; AvgNoise = SMA(Noise, 10) as of the prior session; Stretch = 2.0 * AvgNoise. At the open, place a buy stop at TodayOpen + Stretch and a sell stop at TodayOpen - Stretch. Whichever fills first is the position; the opposite order is left working as the protective stop-and-reverse level.
ideas.exit_rule: Three exits, first to trigger wins: (1) the opposite stretch order at TodayOpen -/+ Stretch, which reverses the position; (2) hard stop at Entry - 6*ATR(20) for longs, Entry + 6*ATR(20) for shorts; (3) time exit at the close of the nth session after entry, default n=1.
ideas.why: Range contraction is serially correlated with range expansion, so a two-day compression identifies sessions where the market has stored energy. The stretch is the clever half: it sets the trigger distance from the average of the SMALLER of the two open-to-extreme excursions, which measures the size of the market's routine noise around the open. A move that exceeds twice typical noise is by construction not routine, so the bracket only fires on genuine directional commitment rather than the usual two-sided churn.
ideas.source: Toby Crabel, 'Day Trading With Short Term Price Patterns and Opening Range Breakout' (1990); exact coding of the 2-bar NR pattern with Noise, Average_Noise, Stretch_Multiple 2.0, Stretch_Length 10, ATR_Stop 6, tested on 42 US futures 1980-2013, at https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/toby-crabel-narrow-range-2/
ideas.novelty: Standard opening range breakout triggers on the high or low of the first N minutes. Here the trigger distance is computed from the prior 10 sessions' average intraday noise and applied to the open price directly, so no opening range is measured at all — and the entry is gated by a two-day compression state that ORB ignores entirely.

ideas.name: NR7 inside-day double compression bracket
ideas.entry_rule: On daily bar i, require BOTH: (a) NR7 — Range[i] = High[i]-Low[i] and Range[i] < Range[i-k] for every k in 1..6; and (b) inside day — High[i] < High[i-1] AND Low[i] > Low[i-1]. On the next session place an OCO bracket: buy stop at High[i] + 0.01, sell stop at Low[i] - 0.01. If neither fills within 2 sessions, cancel both. Optional directional filter to trade one side only: take the long side only if Close[i] > SMA(Close, 50)[i], the short side only if Close[i] < SMA(Close, 50)[i].
ideas.exit_rule: Protective stop at the opposite side of the NR7 bar (Low[i] - 0.01 for a long). Profit exit at the first profitable close — the first daily close above the entry price for a long, below it for a short. Hard time exit at the close of the 3rd session after entry if neither has triggered.
inputs: SMA(close,50) if the filter is used
ideas.why: An inside day and an NR7 occurring on the same session is a rarer, stricter compression than either alone: the range is not only the smallest in a week but is also fully contained by the prior day, meaning neither side managed to extend the previous session's boundaries at all. That is a market where the auction has genuinely stalled and both stop clusters sit immediately outside a very tight bar, so the first side to break gets an order-flow cascade. The first-profitable-close exit is Crabel's own — the edge is a one to three day burst, and holding past it gives the gain back.
ideas.source: Toby Crabel, 'Day Trading With Short Term Price Patterns and Opening Range Breakout' (1990), the IDnr7 / NR7ID double-compression pattern; rules and the first-profitable-close exit documented at https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/trading-strategies-and-models/trading-strategies/narrow-range-day-nr7
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the stretch-based Crabel idea above: different compression definition (single-bar range plus containment rather than two-bar range), the trigger sits at the pattern's own extremes rather than at open plus a noise multiple, and the exit is a close-based first-profit rule rather than a reversal bracket.

ideas.name: Bollinger squeeze head-fake reversal
ideas.entry_rule: BandWidth BW_t = (UpperBB(20,2) - LowerBB(20,2)) / SMA(Close,20). Mark bar s as a squeeze when BW_s == min(BW[s-125 .. s]) — the lowest BandWidth in roughly six months. Then, within the following 10 bars, record the FIRST band break: fake_up if Close > UpperBB(20,2), fake_down if Close < LowerBB(20,2); record the extreme price reached during that break (fake_high or fake_low). Do NOT trade that break. ENTRY: if fake_up occurred and, within the next 10 bars, a bar closes below LowerBB(20,2), enter short at that close. Symmetrically, if fake_down occurred and within 10 bars a bar closes above UpperBB(20,2), enter long at that close. If the 10-bar window elapses with no opposite-band close, the setup is dead and the squeeze state resets.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at fake_high + 0.10 for shorts (fake_low - 0.10 for longs) — the extreme of the failed move. Trailing exit: exit on the first close back above SMA(Close,20) for a short, below it for a long. Hard time exit after 20 bars in the position.
ideas.why: Bollinger's own caution is that a squeeze's first band break is frequently a head fake — the coiled position is crowded, and the initial break runs the stops of everyone positioned for the other side before the real expansion goes the opposite way. That makes the failed break informative: it identifies which side has just been forcibly liquidated, and their re-entry pressure fuels the move the other way. The tight squeeze also means the risk point (the fake extreme) is unusually close, so the reward-to-risk on the reversal is far better than on the first break.
ideas.source: John Bollinger, 'Bollinger on Bollinger Bands' (2001) — the Squeeze and the head fake; head-fake description and the six-month BandWidth low criterion at https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/trading-strategies-and-models/trading-strategies/bollinger-band-squeeze and Bollinger's own rules at https://www.bollingerbands.com/bollinger-band-rules
ideas.novelty: Squeeze release trades the first break. This deliberately refuses the first break, requires it to fail, and trades the opposite band — the entry condition includes a prior failed signal in the opposite direction, which is the inverse of the existing squeeze rule rather than a parameter change to it.

ideas.name: Wilder close-based volatility stop-and-reverse
ideas.entry_rule: Always-in-the-market. Define ARC (Average Range Constant) = c * ATR(7) with c = 3.0. While long, track SIC = the highest CLOSE recorded since the current long position began. Reverse to short on the first bar whose Close < SIC - ARC. While short, track SIC = the lowest CLOSE since the short began; reverse to long on the first bar whose Close > SIC + ARC. Initialise direction by the sign of Close_t - Close_{t-7}. All comparisons use closes only; intrabar highs and lows are ignored except inside the true-range calculation.
ideas.exit_rule: There is no flat state — the exit IS the reversal signal above. The position flips at the close of the triggering bar.
inputs: running highest/lowest close since the last reversal
params: allow-flat variant with a separate re-entry band
ideas.why: Anchoring the trail to the highest CLOSE rather than the highest high makes the system immune to single-bar spikes and stop-run wicks — a violent intraday probe that closes back inside does not move the reference point or trigger the reverse. Wilder's argument was that closes represent settled agreement between buyers and sellers while extremes represent momentary imbalance, so a trend is only broken when settled agreement moves against you by more than three typical daily ranges. The always-in construction means the system pays no re-entry lag when a trend resumes.
ideas.source: J. Welles Wilder Jr., 'New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems' (1978), the Volatility System chapter — ARC = ATR(7) times a constant (Wilder's tested band roughly 2.8-3.1), stop-and-reverse from the significant close (SIC)
ideas.novelty: PSAR is time-accelerating and anchored to extremes; the chandelier is anchored to the highest high and goes flat. This is close-anchored, constant-width in ATR terms, and always-in — three different mechanics. The close-only anchoring in particular is a genuinely different response to wicks, which is exactly what separates it in a backtest.

ideas.name: Elder triple screen with a daily ratcheting entry stop
ideas.category: multi-timeframe trend + pullback with pending-order entry
ideas.entry_rule: SCREEN 1 (tide): resample daily bars to weekly. Compute MACD histogram (12,26,9) on weekly closes. Tide is UP if hist[w] > hist[w-1] on the most recently completed week. SCREEN 2 (wave, must oppose the tide): on daily bars compute Force Index = Volume_t * (Close_t - Close_{t-1}) and its 2-period EMA. Setup arms when tide is UP and EMA2(ForceIndex) < 0. SCREEN 3 (trigger): on the first day after the setup arms, place a buy stop at High[t-1] + 0.01. If it does not fill by that day's close, REPLACE it the next day with a buy stop at the new High[t-1] + 0.01 — so if the market keeps falling the entry order walks DOWN with it, never up. Cancel the order if the weekly histogram slope turns down, or after 5 unfilled days. Mirror all three screens for shorts (tide DOWN, EMA2(ForceIndex) > 0, sell stop at Low[t-1] - 0.01 that walks up).
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at Low[t-1] - 0.01 measured on the bar before the fill. Trail with the ratcheted chandelier: highest high since entry - 3*ATR(22), monotone. Also exit on the first completed week where the weekly MACD histogram slope turns down.
ideas.why: The entry order that ratchets downward is the mechanism, not the filter stack. It refuses to buy strength during a pullback and instead lets the market keep marking down the trigger price for as long as the pullback continues, so the fill price improves the deeper the pullback goes while the trend filter still guarantees direction. The trade is only taken when the falling wave actually turns, and the stop is by construction a fraction of a day's range away, which produces very high reward-to-risk on the trades that do fill and simply no trade on the ones that keep falling.
ideas.source: Alexander Elder, 'Trading for a Living' (1993) and 'Come Into My Trading Room' (2002) — the Triple Screen system; screen-3 trailing buy-stop rule ('place the buy order one tick above the previous day high... the order also moves down, one point above the high, until a buy opens or the main trend reverses') as documented at https://www.mql5.com/en/blogs/post/731016 and https://www.asktraders.com/learn-to-trade/trading-guide/elders-triple-screening-strategy/
ideas.novelty: EMA pullback in trend enters on a signal bar at market. Here the entry is a resting stop order whose price is re-set lower every single day of the pullback, so the fill price and the trade set are both materially different — most EMA-pullback signals never fill under this rule, and the ones that do fill at the exact turn.

ideas.name: Weinstein Stage 2 breakout on weekly bars
ideas.entry_rule: Resample daily bars to weekly. Let MA30 = SMA(weekly Close, 30). Enter long at the close of week w when ALL of: (1) MA30[w] > MA30[w-4] — the 30-week average is rising, not merely flat; (2) Close[w] > MA30[w]; (3) Close[w] > max(Close[w-30 .. w-1]) — a weekly close above the highest weekly close of the prior 30 weeks, which is the Stage 1 resistance ceiling; (4) Volume[w] >= 2.0 * SMA(weekly Volume, 30)[w-1]; (5) relative strength: (Close[w]/Close[w-26] - 1) > (SPY_Close[w]/SPY_Close[w-26] - 1) using SPY's own weekly bars as the index proxy.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on the first weekly close below MA30[w]. Pyramid rule: while the position is open, a weekly close that touches MA30 intra-week (Low[w] <= MA30[w]) but closes above it is a permitted add of a further half unit, up to 2 units total. Hard stop at the low of the breakout week minus 0.5*ATR(14 weekly).
inputs: SPY weekly closes for the relative-strength leg
ideas.why: Weinstein's claim is that institutional accumulation is only complete when a base's ceiling gives way on volume that could not have come from retail, and that the 30-week average is the single best divider between distribution and markup. Requiring the average to be rising rather than merely below price rejects the very common case of price popping above a still-declining long average, which is the main failure mode of simple MA filters. The relative-strength leg forces the buy into names outperforming the index, so the trade is not just long beta at a moment when everything is breaking out.
ideas.source: Stan Weinstein, 'Secrets for Profiting in Bull and Bear Markets' (1988); Stage 2 breakout criteria — price closing above Stage 1 resistance on 2-3x average volume with a rising 30-week MA and relative strength versus the index — codified at https://traderlion.com/trading-strategies/stage-analysis/ and https://www.mql5.com/en/articles/22746
ideas.novelty: Donchian breakout has no moving-average slope condition, no volume-doubling condition, and no cross-asset relative-strength condition, and runs on daily bars. The conjunction of a rising long MA, a 2x volume expansion and index-relative outperformance at the moment of a weekly-close breakout is a different and far more selective event.

ideas.name: Minervini trend template gate with tight quiet pivot
ideas.category: trend regime gate + low-volatility pivot entry
ideas.entry_rule: GATE — all 8 must be true on bar t: (1) Close > SMA(Close,150) and Close > SMA(Close,200); (2) SMA150 > SMA200; (3) SMA200[t] > SMA200[t-21] — the 200-day has risen for at least a month; (4) Close > SMA(Close,50); (5) SMA50 > SMA150 and SMA50 > SMA200; (6) Close >= 1.30 * min(Low[t-251 .. t]); (7) Close >= 0.75 * max(High[t-251 .. t]); (8) relative-strength proxy in place of the IBD RS rank: the stock's 252-day total return ranks in the top 30% of the tradable universe on bar t. TRIGGER — on the first bar where the gate is true AND (High_t - Low_t) == min(High-Low over bars t-9..t) AND Volume_t < 0.7 * SMA(Volume,50): place a buy stop at High_t + 0.05, good for 3 sessions, else cancel.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at Low_t - 0.05 of the pivot bar, or entry * 0.92, whichever is tighter. Exit the remainder on a daily close below SMA(Close,50). Optional: sell half at entry + 2 * (entry - initial stop) and trail the rest with the ratcheted chandelier at 3*ATR(22).
inputs: cross-sectional 252-day return ranks across the traded universe
ideas.why: The template selects for a specific structural shape — stacked and rising averages, already well off the low, still near the high — which is a proxy for sustained institutional sponsorship rather than a bounce. The pivot condition then times entry to the moment of maximum supply exhaustion: the narrowest range in ten days on below-average volume means sellers have simply stopped showing up, so the risk point is unusually close and the breakout that follows meets almost no overhead supply. The combination is why the same entry price behaves very differently inside and outside the template.
ideas.source: Mark Minervini, 'Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard' (2013) and 'Think and Trade Like a Champion' (2016) — the 8-criterion Trend Template and the volatility-contraction pivot; criteria with numeric thresholds at https://deepvue.com/screener/minervini-trend-template/ and https://www.chartmill.com//documentation/stock-screener/fundamental-analysis-investing-strategies/464-Mark-Minervini-Strategy-Think-and-Trade-Like-a-Champion-Part-1
ideas.novelty: I pinned two vague pieces down: the IBD relative-strength rating becomes a 252-day cross-sectional return percentile computed from the bot's own universe, and the qualitative 'VCP pivot' becomes narrowest-range-in-10 with volume under 0.7x its 50-day average. Nothing in the existing 32 combines a multi-MA structural regime gate with a volume-dryup contraction trigger; ATR expansion breakout is the opposite condition.

ideas.name: Dual Thrust cross-extreme range breakout
ideas.entry_rule: From the N=4 most recently COMPLETED daily bars compute HH = max(High), LC = min(Close), HC = max(Close), LL = min(Low), then Range = max(HH - LC, HC - LL). Note the deliberate crossing of highs against closes and closes against lows. At today's session open O, set BuyLine = O + K1 * Range and SellLine = O - K2 * Range with K1 = K2 = 0.5. On 5-minute bars: go long on the first bar that CLOSES above BuyLine; go short on the first bar that CLOSES below SellLine. The system is stop-and-reverse — if long when a 5-minute bar closes below SellLine, close the long and open a short on the same bar, and vice versa. No new entries in the final 15 minutes of the session.
ideas.exit_rule: Flat all positions at the session close (market-on-close). Within the session the only exit is the opposite line reversal. Optional hard stop at 1.0 * ATR(14 daily) from entry.
inputs: daily OHLC for the 4-bar range calculation
ATR(14) daily if the hard stop is used
params: K1 and K2 independently 0.2-1.0 (asymmetric K is the interesting sweep)
ideas.why: Using max(HH-LC, HC-LL) rather than max(High)-min(Low) is the whole point: it measures the largest realised displacement between an extreme and a settlement over the window, which throws away the portion of the raw range that was pure wick noise and never settled. That gives a trigger distance calibrated to how far the market actually travels when it commits, so the band is wide enough to sit outside routine chop but narrow enough to catch the move early. Asymmetric K1 and K2 let the system be structurally biased long in an equity book without adding a separate trend filter.
ideas.source: Dual Thrust by Michael Chalek; range definition Range = max(HH-LC, HC-LL) with UpTrack = Open + K1*Range and DownTrack = Open - K2*Range documented at https://www.quantconnect.com/learning/articles/investment-strategy-library/dual-thrust-trading-algorithm and https://github.com/fmzquant/strategies/blob/master/Dual-Thrust-Trading-Algorithm-ps4.md
