ideas.novelty: Opening range breakout derives its trigger from the current session's own first N minutes. Dual Thrust derives it from a cross-extreme statistic over four prior daily bars and anchors it to the open price, so the bands exist from the first tick of the session — and it reverses rather than going flat, which is a different exit structure as well as a different entry.

ideas.name: Volatility-targeted time-series momentum
ideas.category: trend following / position sizing as the signal
ideas.entry_rule: On the last trading day of each month t, for each instrument compute r_12 = Close_t / Close_{t-252} - 1. Signal s = +1 if r_12 > 0, -1 if r_12 < 0. Compute ex-ante annualised volatility sigma_t = sqrt(261 * EWMA of squared daily returns), where the EWMA uses exponentially decaying weights with a 60-day centre of mass (delta = 60/61, weights proportional to delta^i normalised to sum to 1, applied to (r_{t-i} - rbar)^2). Target position notional = s * (0.40 / sigma_t) * (capital allocated to that instrument), capped at the broker's leverage limit and at 4x. Trade the difference into the new target at the monthly close. Positions are held for one month and re-evaluated only at month end.
ideas.exit_rule: There is no discrete exit — the position size is recomputed monthly and goes to zero-crossing-and-flip when sign(r_12) flips. Size also shrinks automatically as sigma_t rises, so a volatility spike reduces exposure before any price signal changes. Optional overlay: cut the whole position to zero intramonth if the drawdown from the position's high-water mark exceeds 3 * sigma_t / sqrt(12).
inputs: daily returns for the EWMA volatility estimate
params: lookback 252 days (the paper shows 1-12 month lookbacks all work; sweep 21-252)
volatility target 0.40 (scale to the account's risk budget)
ideas.why: The documented result is that the sign of an instrument's own past 12-month return predicts the sign of its next month's return across dozens of futures and equity markets, and that the effect reverses beyond about 12 months — consistent with initial underreaction followed by delayed overreaction. The volatility scaling is what makes it tradeable: it equalises risk contribution across instruments and across time, so a quiet regime gets levered up and a violent one gets cut automatically. In an equity book this means the strategy de-risks into a volatility spike without needing a stop to be hit.
ideas.source: Moskowitz, T.J., Ooi, Y.H., and Pedersen, L.H., 'Time Series Momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), 2012, pp. 228-250 — sign of the past 12-month excess return, one-month holding period, position scaled to a 40% annualised volatility target using an exponentially weighted ex-ante volatility estimate with a 60-day centre of mass. (I could not extract text from the hosted PDF at w4.stern.nyu.edu; the parameters above are the published specification and should be re-checked against the paper before implementation.)
ideas.novelty: EMA cross is a price-versus-price rule with a binary in/out. This uses the sign of a raw 252-day return as the only entry condition and puts all the sophistication in a continuously varying, volatility-inverse position size that is itself the risk control — a different exit structure, since exposure decays on volatility rather than on price.

ideas.name: Month-end 10-month SMA timing
ideas.entry_rule: Resample to monthly bars using the last trading day of each calendar month. Compute SMA10 = simple moving average of the last 10 monthly closes. On the last trading day of month m ONLY, evaluate: if MonthlyClose[m] > SMA10[m], hold a full long position from that close; otherwise hold zero. Execute at that day's close. Price action within the month is explicitly ignored — no intramonth signal, no intramonth stop.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit to cash at the month-end close whenever MonthlyClose[m] <= SMA10[m]. There is no other exit; the position is not stopped out intramonth by design.
params: evaluation cadence monthly vs weekly vs daily (this is the experiment)
buffer band around the MA to cut whipsaw, e.g. require a 1% breach
ideas.why: The deliberate throttling of the sampling rate is the edge, not a limitation. Evaluating once a month makes the rule structurally immune to the whipsaws that dominate a daily 200-day cross — the same underlying trend filter, sampled twelve times a year instead of 252, generates roughly a tenth of the trades and misses most of the false crossings while still exiting every sustained drawdown. It is the cleanest available test of whether a strategy's costs come from its signal or from its sampling frequency, which is a question worth answering for the whole book.
ideas.source: Mebane T. Faber, 'A Quantitative Approach to Tactical Asset Allocation', Journal of Wealth Management, Spring 2007 (SSRN abstract 962461); rules restated by the author at https://mebfaber.com/timing-model/ — 10-month SMA, 'only updated once a month on the last day of the month', with intramonth market action ignored
ideas.novelty: Distinct from EMA cross in two ways that matter to a backtest: it is price against a single average rather than two averages crossing, and the signal is sampled only at month end so the trade set barely overlaps with any daily MA rule. Running it side by side with a daily 200-day equivalent isolates the sampling-frequency effect directly.

ideas.name: Modified Hikkake false-break continuation
ideas.entry_rule: LONG setup: bar i-1 must be an inside bar — High[i-1] < High[i-2] AND Low[i-1] > Low[i-2]. Bar i (the 'fake') must close lower than the inside bar: Close[i] < Close[i-1]. On confirmation of bar i, place a buy stop at max(High[i-1], High[i]) + 0.01. The order is live for a maximum of 3 subsequent bars; if unfilled at the close of bar i+3, cancel it. SHORT setup is the mirror: inside bar at i-1, Close[i] > Close[i-1], sell stop at min(Low[i-1], Low[i]) - 0.01, same 3-bar life. Optional trend filter: take longs only when Close[i] > Close[i-Trend_Index] with Trend_Index around 50.
ideas.exit_rule: Protective stop at the pattern extreme on the opposite side — min(Low[i-1], Low[i]) - 0.01 for a long. Hard volatility stop at Entry - 6*ATR(20) for longs, Entry + 6*ATR(20) for shorts. Time exit at the close of the nth bar after entry, default n = 5.
ideas.why: An inside bar concentrates resting stop orders immediately above and below a very tight range. The fake bar closing against the eventual direction pulls in traders on the wrong side and triggers the breakout stops there; when price then reverses and takes out the combined two-bar extreme, those positions are forced to cover into the move. The three-bar expiry is essential and is what makes it testable — the trapped-trader fuel dissipates quickly, so a fill five bars later is not the same trade and should not be taken.
ideas.source: Dan Chesler, CMT, the Hikkake pattern (Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, 2004); exact coded form — inside bar High[i-1]<High[i-2] and Low[i-1]>Low[i-2], the opposite-close fake bar, buy stop one tick above the two-bar high, signals must be generated within three bars, ATR(20) x 6 stop — at https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/modified-hikkake-pattern/
ideas.novelty: The distinguishing mechanic is the hard 3-bar expiry on a resting stop order after a specific 3-bar inside/fake sequence. Break of structure and change of character are structural swing-based rules with no bar-count expiry and no inside-bar precondition; this fires on an exact bar template or not at all.

ideas.name: ACD A-level breakout with time confirmation and pivot-range gate
ideas.timeframe: 30-minute opening range, 5-minute execution, daily ATR input
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the daily pivot range from the PRIOR session: P = (High + Low + Close)/3; PD = |P - (High + Low)/2|; PivotHigh = P + PD, PivotLow = P - PD. Compute A_value = 0.22 * ATR(30) on daily bars (Fisher's published ES figure; sweep it). Opening range OR = high and low of the first 30 minutes of the session; ORH and ORL. A_up = ORH + A_value, A_down = ORL - A_value. LONG: after the opening range completes, enter long at the close of the first 5-minute bar that both trades above A_up AND CLOSES above A_up, provided the session opened above PivotHigh. The requirement that price close a full bar beyond the level, not merely touch it, is the time confirmation that rejects fake breakouts. SHORT is the mirror using A_down with the session opening below PivotLow. C-POINT REVERSAL: if a long A_up entry is stopped out and price subsequently trades A_value below ORL (the C-down level), reverse and enter short there; symmetric for a stopped short.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at the opposite side of the opening range — ORL for a long, ORH for a short. Move the stop to breakeven once price reaches entry + A_value. Exit all positions market-on-close; carry nothing overnight. Optional target at ORH + 3*A_value.
inputs: prior daily OHLC for the pivot range
params: confirmation = 1 closed 5-min bar (sweep 1-3 bars or a dwell time in minutes)
ideas.why: Two mechanisms that plain ORB lacks. First, the offset scales with the instrument's recent daily ATR, so the same rule adapts across names and volatility regimes instead of using a fixed opening range that is too wide for a quiet stock and too tight for a fast one. Second, the dwell requirement — price must hold beyond the level for a complete bar — is a direct filter on the single most common ORB failure, the one-print stop run that immediately reverts. The pivot range acts as a regime gate: opening outside it means the market has already gapped away from the prior session's value area and is more likely to trend than to rotate.
ideas.source: Mark B. Fisher, 'The Logical Trader: Applying a Method to the Madness' (2002) — the ACD method, A and C levels as an ATR-scaled extension of the opening range with the 22% of 30-day ATR figure for the ES, and the three-day rolling pivot range P = (H+L+C)/3 with pivot differential |P - (H+L)/2|; documented at http://www.dacharts.com/templates/descr/ACDmethod.htm and https://news.cqg.com/workspaces/2016/11/mark-fisher-indicator
ideas.novelty: Opening range breakout triggers on a touch of the OR extreme. This triggers at an ATR-scaled distance BEYOND it, requires a full closed bar of persistence past the level, gates the whole day on where the open sat relative to a prior-session pivot range, and adds a documented reversal entry (C) when the first attempt fails — four separate mechanical differences.

ideas.name: Lunch-Break Reversion
ideas.entry_rule: Build the universe daily as the top 20 US-listed ETFs by prior-day dollar volume. At 12:00 ET exactly, for each symbol compute r = (last trade price at 12:00 / prior session's official close) - 1. Enter SHORT every symbol with r > 0 and LONG every symbol with r < 0, equal dollar weight across all 20 positions. (Rank-selective variant worth sweeping: trade only the 4 highest r as shorts and the 4 lowest r as longs.)
ideas.exit_rule: Liquidate the entire book at 13:00 ET - a fixed 60-minute holding window. No stop or target; the clock is the only exit.
inputs: daily dollar volume for universe ranking
params: optional |r| floor to skip flat names
ideas.why: US intraday volume is J-shaped: the trough sits over the lunch hour. With order flow thinnest, the same size moves price further, so any morning imbalance overshoots and then partially retraces once flow normalises into the afternoon. The strategy is explicitly a liquidity-provision trade conditioned on the known volume trough, not a technical pattern.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Lean, Algorithm.Python/Alphas/MeanReversionLunchBreakAlpha.py - https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/blob/master/Algorithm.Python/Alphas/MeanReversionLunchBreakAlpha.py
ideas.novelty: The signal is anchored to a specific wall-clock hour chosen for a microstructural reason (the volume trough), and the measurement window straddles the overnight gap (prior close to noon). Neither opening-range breakout nor opening-range fade touches midday, and no indicator is computed at all.

ideas.name: Volatility-Normalised Gap Fade
ideas.entry_rule: On each completed 1-minute bar for each symbol in a universe of the top 25 stocks by dollar volume (refreshed weekly), compute jump = (close / close[1] - 1) * 100 (percent). Maintain a rolling 100-bar sample standard deviation of that same percent-return series, call it vol. If abs(jump) > 3 * vol, enter at the next bar's open: SHORT if jump > 0, LONG if jump < 0. Equal dollar weight per open position.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit exactly 5 bars after entry at that bar's close, unconditionally. Pure time stop - no target, no trailing stop, no reversal condition.
ideas.why: A single-bar move that is large relative to that symbol's own recent return dispersion is far more likely to be a liquidity air-pocket - a marketable order sweeping a thin book - than genuine repricing. Normalising by the trailing return standard deviation rather than by a fixed cent or percent amount makes the trigger comparable across a mixed-volatility universe, and the fixed 5-bar exit caps the damage when the move actually was information.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Lean, Algorithm.Python/Alphas/PriceGapMeanReversionAlpha.py - https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/blob/master/Algorithm.Python/Alphas/PriceGapMeanReversionAlpha.py
ideas.novelty: Normalises by the standard deviation of RETURNS, not by ATR (which is a range measure), and fades rather than follows. ATR expansion breakout goes with the move on a range measure; this goes against the move on a return-dispersion measure and exits on a bar count rather than on price.

ideas.name: Leveraged ETF Rebalance Front-Run
ideas.entry_rule: Define underlying/LETF groups, e.g. SPY -> {UPRO long, SPXU inverse}, QQQ -> {TQQQ, SQQQ}, IWM -> {TNA, TZA}, XLF -> {FAS, FAZ}. At 14:15 ET compute r = (underlying's last price / underlying's prior-day close) - 1. If r >= +0.01, BUY the ultra-long LETF of that group. If r <= -0.01, BUY the ultra-short (inverse) LETF of that group. If -0.01 < r < 0.01, take no position in that group. Size by expected rebalance magnitude, proportional to (L^2 - L) * r where L is the stated leverage factor (3 for a 3x fund).
ideas.exit_rule: Market-on-close the same session, i.e. hold approximately 105 minutes from 14:15 to 16:00. No intraday stop in the published version.
inputs: prior daily close of the underlying
ideas.why: A leveraged ETF must rebalance its exposure every day to restore its stated multiple, and the required trade is always in the same direction as the day's move, sized roughly (L^2 - L) times the fund's assets times the day's return. That flow is mechanically forced, publicly predictable, and concentrated into the last hour. When the underlying is already up 1% by early afternoon, a large forced buy is coming - the trade is front-running a rebalance that has to happen regardless of anyone's opinion.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Lean, Algorithm.Python/Alphas/RebalancingLeveragedETFAlpha.py (docstring cites the leveraged-ETF rebalance literature; academic origin is Cheng & Madhavan, 'The Dynamics of Leveraged and Inverse ETFs') - https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/blob/master/Algorithm.Python/Alphas/RebalancingLeveragedETFAlpha.py
ideas.novelty: The edge is not statistical at all - it is a known, dated, sized order that a counterparty is legally obliged to send. Nothing in the existing 32 conditions on another instrument's forced flow, and the entry is a wall-clock time plus a threshold on a DIFFERENT instrument's return than the one traded.

ideas.name: Dual Thrust Asymmetric Range Breakout
ideas.entry_rule: Over the previous N = 20 completed sessions compute four extremes: HH = max(high), LL = min(low), HC = max(close), LC = min(close). Set Range = max(HH - LC, HC - LL). Let O = today's session open. During the session, go LONG when price crosses above O + K1 * Range while not already long; go SHORT when price crosses below O - K2 * Range while not already short. K1 = K2 = 0.63 by default; asymmetric K1 != K2 is the standard tuning knob.
ideas.exit_rule: Reverse on the opposite band cross (stop-and-reverse). Additionally flatten at the session close, or let the position expire after a fixed 5-day horizon if carrying overnight is permitted.
params: consolidation bar size for intraday use
ideas.why: The range is deliberately built from crossed extremes - highest high minus lowest close, and highest close minus lowest low - so it measures the largest displacement between a settlement level and an extreme rather than the plain high-low span. That makes it larger and more stable than a simple range in choppy regimes and prevents the bands from collapsing after a single narrow day. Anchoring to today's open rather than to a rolling average makes the trigger a same-session displacement measure, so the signal resets cleanly every morning.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Lean, Algorithm.Python/Alphas/VIXDualThrustAlpha.py, plus the QuantConnect Strategy Library entry 'Dual Thrust Trading Algorithm' - https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/blob/master/Algorithm.Python/Alphas/VIXDualThrustAlpha.py
ideas.novelty: Donchian breakout triggers on price exceeding a past extreme; Dual Thrust triggers on displacement from TODAY'S OPEN by a fraction of a crossed-extreme range, with independently tunable up and down multipliers. Different anchor, different range construction, and it can fire long before any prior high is taken out.

ideas.name: Dynamic Breakout II (Volatility-Adaptive Lookback)
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain a state variable N, initialised to 20. Each day compute vol_today = stdev(close, 30) using bars through today and vol_yest = stdev(close, 30) using bars through yesterday; deltavol = (vol_today - vol_yest) / vol_today; then N = clip(round(N * (1 + deltavol)), 20, 60). Using the updated N, compute Bollinger Bands on close with period N and k = 2. Go LONG when yesterday's close > upper band AND today's price > the highest high of the last N days. Go SHORT when yesterday's close < lower band AND today's price < the lowest low of the last N days.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit a long when price falls below SMA(close, N) using the current adaptive N; exit a short when price rises above SMA(close, N). Note the exit lookback moves with the entry lookback, so exits tighten as volatility rises.
params: whether deltavol uses stdev of close or of returns
ideas.why: A fixed breakout lookback is implicitly a bet on a fixed holding horizon. When volatility rises, price traverses a given distance faster, so a 20-day channel produces more false breaks; when volatility falls, a 20-day channel becomes too slow to catch a real regime change. Letting N expand with rising volatility and contract with falling volatility keeps the breakout threshold at roughly constant statistical significance, and requiring BOTH a band violation and a channel break filters the single-bar spikes that a channel break alone would take.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Strategy Library, 'The Dynamic Breakout II Strategy' - https://www.quantconnect.com/tutorials/strategy-library/the-dynamic-breakout-ii-strategy
ideas.novelty: The lookback is a state variable updated recursively from realised volatility, so the indicator's own period is path-dependent - two runs from different start dates can carry different N on the same day. That is a structurally different object from any fixed-period Donchian or Bollinger rule, and the exit MA inherits the same moving period.

ideas.name: Market Intraday Momentum (First 30 Minutes Predicts Last 30)
ideas.entry_rule: For each symbol in a small liquid ETF list (SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, EEM, EFA, XLF, IYR, TLT), at 15:30 ET compute r_open = (close of the 10:00 ET bar / today's official open) - 1, i.e. the first-half-hour return. If r_open > 0, enter LONG at 15:30. If r_open < 0, enter SHORT at 15:30. If exactly 0, no trade. Equal dollar weight across symbols traded.
ideas.exit_rule: Market-on-close at 16:00 ET. Fixed 30-minute holding window, no stop, no target.
ideas.why: Gao, Han, Li and Zhou document that the first half-hour return positively predicts the last half-hour return, and attribute it to late-informed investors and to intraday position-rebalancing by traders who must close by the bell. Both mechanisms push the last half hour in the same direction as the morning imbalance. This is the only well-documented case where two non-adjacent intraday windows are linked, which is why the middle of the day is deliberately excluded.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Strategy Library, 'Intraday ETF Momentum', citing Gao, Han, Li and Zhou (2018), 'Market intraday momentum', Journal of Financial Economics - https://www.quantconnect.com/tutorials/strategy-library/intraday-etf-momentum
ideas.novelty: Opening-range breakout and opening-range fade both trade immediately after the opening range forms. This deliberately sits out five and a half hours, then trades the final 30 minutes on the sign of the morning return. The gap between signal and trade is the whole point, and the mechanism (end-of-day rebalancing pressure) is different from the ORB mechanism.

ideas.name: Market-State Gated Momentum
ideas.entry_rule: On the first trading day of each month compute the broad-market state: S = (SPY close / SPY close[252]) - 1, using SPY as an OHLCV proxy for the Wilshire 5000. If S > 0, state = UP; else state = DOWN. When state = UP: rank the universe by 6-month momentum percent MOMP = (close/close[126] - 1) * 100, go LONG the top 20 names and SHORT the bottom 20 names, each leg equal-weighted at 0.5/20 = 2.5% of capital per name. When state = DOWN: take no equity momentum positions at all.
ideas.exit_rule: Rebalance monthly. On a transition to DOWN, liquidate every equity leg immediately and hold TLT (or cash) for the month. On a transition back to UP, re-enter the freshly ranked lists. Within an UP month, exit any name that has dropped out of its list.
ideas.why: Cooper, Gutierrez and Hameed showed that momentum profits are conditional on the market's own prior state: after a rising 12-month market, momentum earns a substantial premium; after a falling market it is roughly zero or negative, because momentum crashes are concentrated in sharp rebounds off market lows when the short leg violently reverses. Gating on the market's own trailing return sidesteps precisely the regime where the strategy's worst drawdowns cluster.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Strategy Library, 'Momentum and State of Market Filters', citing Cooper, Gutierrez and Hameed, 'Market States and Momentum' (SSRN 299927) - https://www.quantconnect.com/tutorials/strategy-library/momentum-and-state-of-market-filters
ideas.novelty: The gate is a slow, market-wide return sign that switches the entire strategy on or off, not a per-instrument trend filter. That is a different object from 'RSI extreme with trend filter' or 'EMA pullback in trend', where the filter is computed on the traded instrument itself.

ideas.name: TD Sequential Nine-Count Buy Setup
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain two counters. seq_buy increments by 1 on each bar where close < close[4] and resets to 0 otherwise; seq_sell increments on each bar where close > close[4] and resets to 0 otherwise. When seq_buy reaches 9, index the setup bars so bar9 = current bar (shift 0), bar8 = shift 1, bar7 = shift 2, bar6 = shift 3. Require the perfection condition: (low[0] < low[2] AND low[0] < low[3]) OR (low[1] < low[2] AND low[1] < low[3]). If seq_buy >= 9 AND that condition holds, enter LONG at the next bar's open. Mirror for shorts using seq_sell >= 9 with (high[0] > high[2] AND high[0] > high[3]) OR (high[1] > high[2] AND high[1] > high[3]).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit a long when EITHER the mirrored sell condition fires (seq_sell >= 9 with high perfection) OR seq_sell simply exceeds 8, whichever comes first. Optional overlay the published code relies on: a fixed take-profit and a hard stop, since the count-based exit can be slow.
params: whether perfection is required or optional
ideas.why: The count measures how many consecutive bars have closed below the close of four bars earlier - a persistence-of-selling measure with no averaging and no smoothing. Nine consecutive such bars is a run so long that it is statistically rare under a random walk, and it typically means a single motivated seller has been working an order to completion. The perfection condition additionally demands that the final bars of the run make a genuine new low relative to bars 6 and 7, which distinguishes real exhaustion from a slow grind.
ideas.source: freqtrade-strategies, user_data/strategies/berlinguyinca/TDSequentialStrategy.py - https://github.com/freqtrade/freqtrade-strategies/blob/main/user_data/strategies/berlinguyinca/TDSequentialStrategy.py (implements Tom DeMark's TD Sequential setup)
ideas.novelty: Purely ordinal - it counts comparisons between closes four bars apart and never computes an average, a band or a ratio. Three-bar momentum counts three bars of same-direction change; this counts nine bars against a fixed four-bar lag and adds a geometric perfection filter on the lows.

ideas.name: Bollinger Break With Candle-Anatomy Filters (BinHV45)
ideas.entry_rule: Compute mid = SMA(close, 40) and lower = mid - 2 * stdev(close, 40). Derive four magnitudes on the current bar: bbdelta = abs(mid - lower); closedelta = abs(close - close[1]); tail = abs(close - low); and require lower[1] > 0. Enter LONG when ALL of: (a) bbdelta > close * 0.007 (band is wide enough in relative terms), (b) closedelta > close * 0.017 (the bar itself moved sharply), (c) tail < bbdelta * 0.025 (the close sits essentially on the low - almost no lower wick), (d) close < lower[1] (closed below the PREVIOUS bar's lower band), and (e) close <= close[1]. Published defaults were tuned on crypto and must be re-swept for equities: treat 0.007 / 0.017 / 0.025 as starting points, not as constants.
ideas.exit_rule: The published code emits no exit signal - it relies on the framework's ROI table and stop-loss. Pinning it down for implementation: exit at the first close back above mid = SMA(close, 40), or after a fixed 20-bar time stop, or on a stop at entry_low - 1.0 * ATR(14), whichever comes first.
ideas.why: A close below the lower band is common and mostly meaningless. The three magnitude filters together demand a specific bar shape: the band must be genuinely wide (so the market is already volatile, not asleep), the bar must have travelled far from the previous close (a real capitulation candle rather than drift), and the close must be pinned to the low with almost no lower wick (no dip-buyers absorbed it yet). That last condition is counter-intuitive - most fade rules want to see a rejection wick - and it identifies the bar BEFORE the reversal rather than after it.
ideas.source: freqtrade-strategies, user_data/strategies/berlinguyinca/BinHV45.py - https://github.com/freqtrade/freqtrade-strategies/blob/main/user_data/strategies/berlinguyinca/BinHV45.py
ideas.novelty: Distinct from plain Bollinger fade because the trigger is a conjunction of three ratios describing the bar's geometry - band width, bar displacement and wick length - each normalised to a different denominator (close, close, bbdelta). It also compares to the PREVIOUS bar's band rather than the current one, avoiding the self-referential problem where a large bar widens the very band it must break.

ideas.name: Micro-Cap Open-to-Close Pump Fade
ideas.entry_rule: Build the daily universe: stocks with close < $5 whose prior-day dollar volume falls between $10,000 and $1,000,000, then take the top 500 by dollar volume. On the completed daily bar compute pump = close/open - 1 for each. Rank descending and SHORT the 10 largest pump values at the next open, equal dollar weight. Long-side variant to avoid borrow constraints entirely: rank ascending and BUY the 10 most negative open-to-close moves.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover (or sell) at the next daily close - a one-session hold. Hard stop at 20% adverse move given the volatility of the cohort.
ideas.why: Thinly traded low-priced stocks that travel a large distance from open to close on a single session are almost never repricing on fundamentals - they are absorbing a promotional or retail-attention shock into a book with almost no depth. Once the attention flow stops, there is no natural holder at the elevated price and the move unwinds. The deliberately narrow dollar-volume band is the key filter: it targets the size range where a modest amount of buying can move price a lot.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Lean, Algorithm.Python/Alphas/SykesShortMicroCapAlpha.py - https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/blob/master/Algorithm.Python/Alphas/SykesShortMicroCapAlpha.py
ideas.novelty: The signal is the open-to-close bar body as a fraction of the open, ranked cross-sectionally, with the universe defined by an unusual two-sided dollar-volume BAND rather than a minimum. Practical caveat for Alpaca: sub-$5 names are frequently hard to borrow or non-shortable, so the long-side variant is the more implementable form.

ideas.name: Dynamic Lead-Lag Partner
ideas.entry_rule: Designate a leader instrument L and a candidate follower set F (e.g. leader = XLE, followers = USO, XOP, OIH, VDE; or leader = SPY, followers = sector ETFs). Every 30 calendar days recompute the 90-day Pearson correlation of daily closes between L and each candidate, and select the single candidate with the highest correlation as the active follower F*. Intraday, on each completed 5-minute bar compute roc_L = (close_L / close_L[5] - 1) * 100. If roc_L > +0.75, BUY F* at the next bar's open. If roc_L < -0.75, SHORT F*. Only one position in F* at a time.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit 5 bars after entry at that bar's close - a pure time stop matched to the ROC lookback. Additionally liquidate any existing follower position immediately when the 30-day correlation refresh selects a different F*.
inputs: 5-minute close of leader and all candidates
ideas.why: Related instruments do not reprice simultaneously. The more liquid or more informationally central instrument absorbs a shock first, and the less liquid related name follows over the next few minutes. Rather than hard-coding a pair, the strategy re-selects the follower every month from realised correlation, which handles the fact that the tightest partner drifts as sector composition and flows change. The ROC threshold ensures only shocks large enough to propagate are traded.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Lean, Algorithm.Python/Alphas/GasAndCrudeOilEnergyCorrelationAlpha.py - https://github.com/QuantConnect/Lean/blob/master/Algorithm.Python/Alphas/GasAndCrudeOilEnergyCorrelationAlpha.py
ideas.novelty: The instrument traded is chosen dynamically by a rolling correlation search, and the trigger is computed on a DIFFERENT instrument entirely. Every one of the existing 32 computes its signal on the instrument it trades.

ideas.name: Volatility-Screened Momentum (Conservative Formula, OHLCV Proxy)
ideas.entry_rule: Monthly, on the first trading day: (1) take a liquid universe (e.g. top 500 by 60-day average dollar volume); (2) for each name compute vol = stdev of the last 36 monthly returns (or, on daily bars, stdev of daily returns over 756 days, annualised); (3) keep only the 50% of the universe with the LOWEST vol; (4) within that surviving half, compute mom = close/close[252] - 1 and rank descending; (5) go LONG the top 10% of the surviving half, equal weight, holding 5% of capital in cash as a buffer against gaps and partial fills. The published formula is (momentum * net payout yield) / volatility; net payout yield is a fundamental field this bot does not have, so the OHLCV proxy drops that factor and keeps the sequential volatility screen followed by the momentum rank - I have pinned this substitution deliberately.
ideas.exit_rule: Rebalance monthly in three ordered steps: first sell every holding that has dropped out of the current selection, then resize surviving holdings to the equal-weight target, then buy the new entrants with the freed capital. Ordering matters - selling first prevents rejected buys from insufficient buying power.
ideas.why: Momentum and low volatility are both robust cross-sectional premia, but they are negatively correlated in practice - the highest-momentum names are usually the most volatile. Screening on volatility FIRST and ranking on momentum SECOND is not the same as ranking on a combined score: the sequential screen hard-excludes the high-volatility tail where momentum crashes originate, then harvests momentum only inside the well-behaved half. That sequencing is why the published construction beats a naive risk-adjusted-momentum ratio.
ideas.source: backtrader blog, 'Rebalancing - Conservative Formula', implementing Blitz and van Vliet, 'The Conservative Formula: Quantitative Investing Made Easy' (SSRN 3145152) - https://www.backtrader.com/blog/2019-07-19-rebalancing-conservative/rebalancing-conservative/
ideas.novelty: A sequential screen-then-rank rather than a composite score, with the volatility measured over a deliberately long 36-month window so it captures regime behaviour rather than recent noise. The three-step rebalance ordering is itself part of the published specification.

ideas.name: Momentum Ranked by Turnover Within Deciles
ideas.entry_rule: Monthly, on the first trading day: (1) rank the universe by 12-month ROC = close/close[252] - 1; (2) take the top 20% as the high-momentum group and the bottom 20% as the low-momentum group; (3) within EACH group, rank by turnover. The published turnover is shares traded divided by shares outstanding, which requires fundamentals; the OHLCV proxy is relative turnover = volume / SMA(volume, 60), or dollar volume / SMA(dollar volume, 60), averaged over the last 21 days; (4) LONG the top 1% by turnover drawn from the high-momentum group, SHORT the top 1% by turnover drawn from the low-momentum group, equal weight within each leg.
ideas.exit_rule: Three-month holding period implemented as overlapping monthly tranches: each month, one third of the book is rolled - liquidate the tranche opened three months ago and deploy that capital into the current month's selection. This staggers turnover and averages out entry timing.
ideas.why: Turnover proxies for investor attention and disagreement. High-turnover winners are the names where the momentum story is being actively debated and re-priced, so the drift has further to run; high-turnover losers are where capitulation selling is still in progress. Conditioning on turnover inside momentum deciles therefore sharpens both legs, and the effect is strongest exactly where volume is abnormal relative to the name's own baseline - which is what the relative-turnover proxy measures.
ideas.source: QuantConnect Strategy Library, 'Combining Momentum Effect with Volume' - https://www.quantconnect.com/tutorials/strategy-library/combining-momentum-effect-with-volume
ideas.novelty: Distinct from 'Bollinger with volume', where volume is a same-bar confirmation gate. Here volume is a second cross-sectional SORT applied inside momentum deciles, and the exit is a three-tranche overlapping roll rather than a single monthly rebalance - the overlapping-tranche exit structure alone makes it a different strategy.

ideas.name: Variance Ratio Onset
ideas.category: volatility regime detection / statistical test as signal
ideas.entry_rule: On daily bars let r_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-1}). Over a rolling window of n=120 returns compute the Lo-MacKinlay overlapping variance ratio at q=5: mu = mean(r); sigma_a^2 = (1/(n-1)) * SUM (r_t - mu)^2; sigma_c^2 = (1/m) * SUM_{t=q..n} (ln(C_t/C_{t-q}) - q*mu)^2 with m = q*(n-q+1)*(1 - q/n); VR = sigma_c^2 / sigma_a^2. Heteroskedasticity-robust statistic z* = (VR - 1)/sqrt(theta), where theta = SUM_{j=1..q-1} ((2*(q-j)/q)^2) * delta_j and delta_j = [SUM_{t=j+1..n} (r_t-mu)^2 (r_{t-j}-mu)^2] / [SUM_{t=1..n} (r_t-mu)^2]^2. LONG at the next open when z* > +1.96 today and z* <= +1.96 on the prior bar, AND the sum of r over the last 20 bars > 0. SHORT on the same z* crossing when the 20-bar return sum < 0. No position while |z*| <= 1.96.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when z* falls below 0 (persistence has died), or on a stop at entry -/+ 2.5*ATR(14), or after 30 bars held - whichever comes first.
ideas.why: The variance ratio measures whether return shocks compound (VR>1, persistence) or cancel (VR<1, reversal). Trading the moment the statistic first becomes significant, rather than trading while it is already significant, targets the birth of a persistence regime - the point at which order flow starts autocorrelating - instead of buying a trend that is already fully priced. The heteroskedasticity-robust denominator matters because equity returns are strongly conditionally heteroskedastic, so the naive z-stat over-rejects and would generate constant false regime calls.
ideas.novelty: Not a moving-average or oscillator signal at all - the trigger is a formal specification test crossing its critical value, and the direction comes from the sign of accumulated drift over the same window. An MA cross fires on price; this fires on a change in the autocorrelation structure of returns.
ideas.source: Lo & MacKinlay (1988), 'Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test', Review of Financial Studies 1(1), 41-66 - the heteroskedasticity-robust z*(q) is their Theorem 2 / equation for M2. Regime-gated trading applications: https://www.algobot.live/variance-ratio-trend-regime-ea-mt5/ and https://quanterlab.com/articles/mr-variance-ratio

ideas.name: Anti-Persistence Fade (DFA Hurst)
ideas.entry_rule: Estimate the Hurst exponent by detrended fluctuation analysis over the last 256 daily log closes. Build the integrated series Y(k) = SUM_{i=1..k} (r_i - mean(r)). For each scale s in {8, 16, 32, 64}: split Y into floor(256/s) non-overlapping boxes, fit a first-order polynomial by OLS inside each box, and set F(s) = sqrt(mean of squared residuals across all boxes). H = OLS slope of ln F(s) on ln s. Separately compute d_t = (C_t - SMA20(C)) / ATR(14). LONG when H < 0.42 AND d_t <= -1.5 AND C_t > C_{t-1} (first up close after the excursion). SHORT when H < 0.42 AND d_t >= +1.5 AND C_t < C_{t-1}. No trade when H >= 0.42.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when d_t crosses 0 (price touches SMA20), or on a stop 1.0*ATR(14) beyond the entry bar's extreme, or after 10 bars - whichever first.
ideas.why: H < 0.5 means the series is anti-persistent: an up move is more likely than chance to be followed by a down move. Fading stretched price only when the estimator says the series currently has anti-memory should remove the losing half of all fade trades - the ones taken inside a persistent trend. Using DFA rather than classical R/S matters because R/S is badly biased when the series has a local drift; DFA detrends inside each box first.
ideas.novelty: Bollinger fade and Keltner fade gate on a volatility band; this gates on an estimate of the series' fractal memory and measures the excursion in ATR units rather than in band widths, so the trigger distance does not shrink when volatility contracts (bands do the opposite, which is why band fades cluster in quiet regimes).
ideas.source: Peng et al. (1994), 'Mosaic organization of DNA nucleotides', Phys. Rev. E 49(2) - the DFA algorithm; regime-filter application to trading described at https://pyquantlab.medium.com/enhancing-trading-strategies-with-a-hurst-based-regime-filter-ac6639be43cf and https://www.mql5.com/en/code/76439 (Hurst Exponent Regime Switch Indicator). Thresholds pinned to H<0.42 / H>0.55 per those write-ups.

ideas.name: Signed Jump Variation Reversal
ideas.timeframe: signal from 5-minute bars, held in daily bars
ideas.entry_rule: From the 78 regular-session 5-minute bars of day t compute r_i = ln(C_i/C_{i-1}). RSplus = SUM r_i^2 over bars where r_i > 0; RSminus = SUM r_i^2 over bars where r_i < 0; RV_t = RSplus + RSminus. Signed jump variation SJ_t = (RSplus - RSminus)/RV_t, bounded in [-1, +1]. LONG at the open of day t+1 when SJ_t <= -0.35 AND RV_t >= 1.5 * median(RV over the prior 20 sessions) AND daily close > SMA200. SHORT at the open of day t+1 when SJ_t >= +0.35 AND RV_t >= 1.5 * median(RV, 20) AND daily close < SMA200.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 5th session after entry; hard stop at 2.0*ATR(14) daily against the position; profit target at 3.0*ATR(14).
ideas.why: Patton & Sheppard show that variance created by negative intraday returns ('bad volatility') and variance created by positive returns ('good volatility') have opposite predictive signs for both future volatility and future returns: bad volatility predicts higher subsequent market returns, good volatility predicts lower ones. A day whose realized variance was overwhelmingly generated by down-ticks is therefore a compensated-risk event, not an information event, and the compensation is paid out over the following week.
ideas.novelty: Splits a single day's realized variance by the sign of the intraday returns that produced it. RSI divergence and other reversal signals use net price change; this uses the composition of variance while holding net price change irrelevant - two days with identical closes can have SJ of +0.6 and -0.6.
ideas.source: Patton & Sheppard (2015), 'Good Volatility, Bad Volatility: Signed Jumps and the Persistence of Volatility', Review of Economics and Statistics 97(3), 683-697. Full text: https://public.econ.duke.edu/~ap172/Patton_Sheppard_REStat_2015.pdf ; realized semivariance definitions originate in Barndorff-Nielsen, Kinnebrock & Shephard (2010).

ideas.name: Realized Skewness Percentile Reversal
ideas.timeframe: 5-minute bars aggregated weekly, held for one week
ideas.entry_rule: Over the last 5 trading sessions collect the n = 390 five-minute log returns r_i. Realized skewness RSk = sqrt(n) * SUM r_i^3 / (SUM r_i^2)^(3/2). Rank RSk against its own trailing 252-session history of weekly values to get a percentile. LONG at the next open when the percentile <= 20. SHORT at the next open when the percentile >= 80. Require median 5-session dollar volume >= the 20-session median dollar volume, so the third moment is not driven by thin prints.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold exactly 5 trading sessions and exit at the close of the 5th. Hard stop at 3.0*ATR(14) daily. No trailing stop - the paper's effect is a fixed one-week horizon and a trailing exit would truncate it.
ideas.why: Amaya, Christoffersen, Jacobs & Vasquez find that stocks in the lowest realized-skewness decile outperform the highest decile by about 19bp the following week (t = 3.70), not captured by Fama-French or Carhart factors. The economic reading is that investors overpay for lottery-like right-tail payoffs, so recently right-skewed names are overpriced and recently left-skewed names are underpriced. Because the effect decays at a weekly frequency, the fixed-horizon exit is part of the idea.
ideas.novelty: The third moment of intraday returns is orthogonal to every mean and second-moment indicator in the existing set - a stock can be flat with normal ATR and still sit in the 5th percentile of realized skew. Ranking against its own history rather than a cross-section makes it runnable on one ticker.
ideas.source: Amaya, Christoffersen, Jacobs & Vasquez (2015), 'Does realized skewness predict the cross-section of equity returns?', Journal of Financial Economics 118(1), 135-167. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0304405X15001257 ; working paper version: https://pure.au.dk/ws/files/67739582/rp13_41.pdf

ideas.name: Lee-Mykland No-News Jump Fade
ideas.entry_rule: On 5-minute bars let r_i = ln(C_i/C_{i-1}). Local bipower spot volatility with K = 270: sigma_i^2 = (1/(K-2)) * SUM_{j=i-K+2..i-1} |r_j| * |r_{j-1}|. Test statistic L_i = r_i / sigma_i. With n = number of bars in the test window, c = sqrt(2/pi) = 0.79788, C_n = (2*ln n)^0.5 / c - (ln(pi) + ln(ln n)) / (2*c*(2*ln n)^0.5), S_n = 1 / (c * (2*ln n)^0.5). Declare a jump on bar i when |L_i| > C_n + S_n * (-ln(-ln(0.99))) (1% Gumbel critical value). FADE it: if a jump is declared with L_i > 0 AND that bar's volume < 2.0 * the 20-session median volume for the same time-of-day bin, SHORT at the close of the jump bar; if L_i < 0 with the same volume condition, LONG at the close of the jump bar. Skip the first 30 minutes and any bar within 10 minutes of the close.
ideas.exit_rule: Target = 60% retracement of the jump bar's range, measured from the jump bar's close. Stop = 1.0 * jump bar range beyond the jump extreme. Time stop at 12 bars (60 minutes) or 15:55 ET, whichever first.
ideas.why: Lee & Mykland's statistic standardises each return by locally-estimated diffusive volatility (bipower variation, which is robust to the jump itself), so it separates a genuine discontinuity from an ordinary large move in a high-vol stretch. The volume condition is the discriminator: a jump on ordinary volume is a liquidity vacuum - a market order sweeping a thin book - and mean-reverts, whereas a jump on heavy volume is information and continues. Fading only the low-volume half is where the edge should live.
ideas.novelty: Liquidity sweep and order-block retests are drawn by eye from structure; this is a distributional test with an explicit false-positive rate, and the volume gate reverses the sign of the trade rather than just filtering it. The null distribution is Gumbel, not normal, because the test is on the maximum of many standardised returns.
ideas.source: Lee & Mykland (2008), 'Jumps in Financial Markets: A New Nonparametric Test and Jump Dynamics', Review of Financial Studies 21(6), 2535-2563. Discussion of the K=270 window at 5-minute sampling and the Gumbel constants: https://www.scheller.gatech.edu/directory/research/finance/lee/pdf/leehannig09.pdf

ideas.name: HAR-RV Forecast Expansion Bracket
ideas.entry_rule: RV_t = SUM of squared 5-minute log returns for session t. On a rolling 500-session window fit by OLS: ln RV_t = c + b1*ln RV_{t-1} + b5*ln(mean RV over t-5..t-1) + b22*ln(mean RV over t-22..t-1). Produce the one-step forecast F_{t+1} = exp(fitted value for t+1). ARM the setup at today's close when F_{t+1}/RV_t >= 1.25 AND today's true range <= 0.7 * ATR(20). On session t+1 place a stop-buy at today's high + 0.10*ATR(20) and a stop-sell at today's low - 0.10*ATR(20); take whichever fills first and cancel the other. If neither fills by the close of t+1, cancel both.
ideas.exit_rule: Trail a stop at 2.0*ATR(20) from the highest close since entry (mirrored for shorts); take profit at 2.5*ATR(20); force flat at the close of session t+3 if neither has triggered.
ideas.why: Corsi's HAR is a cascade of daily, weekly and monthly volatility components; it forecasts realized volatility about as well as far more complex long-memory models and is estimable by plain OLS. The trade takes the one configuration where the model disagrees with the tape: today is unusually quiet but the fitted weekly and monthly components say the volatility level should be higher. That gap resolves by expansion, and since the model forecasts magnitude and not sign, the correct expression is a two-sided bracket rather than a directional bet.
ideas.novelty: ATR expansion breakout fires after volatility has already expanded; this fires before, on a regression forecast of tomorrow's variance. The entry is a symmetric OCO bracket, so it takes no directional view at all - direction is decided by which side the market chooses.
ideas.source: Corsi (2009), 'A Simple Approximate Long-Memory Model of Realized Volatility', Journal of Financial Econometrics 7(2), 174-196. Full text: https://statmath.wu.ac.at/~hauser/LVs/FinEtricsQF/References/Corsi2009JFinEtrics_LMmodelRealizedVola.pdf ; practitioner implementation notes: https://www.garp.org/hubfs/Whitepapers/a2r1W000000iDb0QAE_RiskIntell.6.20.19.Whitepaper.Volatility.pdf

ideas.name: GARCH Conditional Variance Normalization
ideas.entry_rule: Fit GARCH(1,1) by Gaussian QMLE on the last 1000 daily log returns, refitting every 5 sessions: h_t = omega + alpha*e_{t-1}^2 + beta*h_{t-1}. Unconditional variance V = omega/(1 - alpha - beta) (require alpha + beta < 1; skip the ticker if not). Let g_t = h_t / V. LONG at the next open when (a) g_t reached >= 2.0 at some point in the last 10 sessions, (b) g_t < 1.5 today, and (c) today's close > today's open. Long side only.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when g_t < 0.8 (volatility has fully normalised and the compensation is gone), or after 15 sessions held, or on a 2.5*ATR(14) stop - whichever first.
ideas.why: GARCH decomposes today's variance into a persistent level and a mean-reverting deviation from it. Because alpha + beta is typically 0.95-0.99 for equities but strictly below 1, an elevated h_t is a forecast of decline toward V, and the equity risk premium is realised disproportionately during that normalisation window - investors who de-risked into the spike must re-risk. Requiring g_t to have already fallen below 1.5, plus an up-close, avoids catching the spike on the way up, which is the failure mode of every 'buy the fear' rule.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is a fitted latent variance relative to its own model-implied long-run level, not a rolling standard deviation. Two stocks with identical 20-day realized vol can have g_t of 0.7 and 2.5 depending on their estimated persistence, and the exit is defined in variance space rather than price space.
ideas.source: Bollerslev (1986), 'Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity', Journal of Econometrics 31(3), 307-327. Volatility-timing rationale follows Moreira & Muir (2017), Journal of Finance 72(4); survey of GARCH-variant forecasting in trading contexts: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/389181465_Applications_of_GARCH_Models_for_Volatility_Forecasting_in_High-Frequency_Trading_Environments

ideas.name: Vol-of-Vol Collapse
ideas.entry_rule: RV5_t = stdev of the last 5 daily log returns * sqrt(252). VoV_t = stdev of ln(RV5) over the last 20 sessions. Rank VoV_t against its own trailing 504-session distribution to get a percentile P_t. LONG at the next open when P_t crosses down through 50 today AND P_t was >= 90 at some point in the previous 10 sessions.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when P_t rises back above 80, or after 20 sessions held, or on a 3.0*ATR(14) stop.
params: direction (long-on-collapse vs short-on-spike - sweep both signs)
ideas.why: Vol-of-vol measures uncertainty about the level of risk itself, distinct from the level of risk. When it is extreme, position sizing across the market is unstable and risk budgets are being cut mechanically; when it collapses back to normal, that mechanical selling stops and mean-variance investors can re-lever. The entry is deliberately on the collapse, not the spike, because the spike itself carries no timing information - only its resolution does.
ideas.novelty: Second-order volatility: the dispersion of the volatility series, not the dispersion of returns. No indicator in the existing set is a function of the variance of a variance estimate. The sign of the effect is genuinely uncertain in the literature (option-implied vol-of-vol predicts LOW returns cross-sectionally), so both directions should be swept rather than assumed.
ideas.source: Synthesis - a realized-data analogue of the option-implied vol-of-vol effect documented in Baltussen, van Bekkum & van der Grient (2018), 'Unknown Unknowns: Uncertainty About Risk and Stock Returns', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 53(4). Since no option chain is available, the proxy replaces implied vol-of-vol with the standard deviation of log realized vol; the proxy is noisier and its sign is an empirical question, hence the two-sided parameter sweep.

ideas.name: Realized Vol Term Structure Normalization
ideas.entry_rule: TS_t = RV(5)/RV(60) where RV(k) = stdev of the last k daily log returns (no annualisation needed, the ratio cancels it). LONG at the next open when TS_t crosses below 1.00 today AND max(TS) over the previous 10 sessions >= 1.35 AND close > SMA200. SHORT at the next open when TS_t crosses above 1.35 from below AND close < SMA200 AND the 10-session return is negative.
ideas.exit_rule: Long: exit when TS_t > 1.35 again, or after 20 sessions, or on a 2.5*ATR(14) stop. Short: exit when TS_t falls back below 1.00, or after 10 sessions, or on a 2.0*ATR(14) stop (the short side is a stress trade and should be given less rope).
ideas.why: This is the realized-data version of the VIX/VIX3M term structure. TS > 1 (backwardation) means near-term volatility exceeds the regime level - the market is in an event, and equity drift is negative on average while it lasts. TS crossing back below 1 marks the event's resolution, and the bulk of post-stress equity returns accrue in that window. The literature on the implied term structure finds the slope forecasts future realized volatility changes and future option returns, i.e. it measures over- and under-reaction of the volatility level.
ideas.novelty: A ratio of two realized volatilities at different horizons is a shape signal, not a level signal - it fires identically at 15% and 60% absolute vol. Squeeze release fires on absolute compression; this fires on relative compression against the stock's own medium-term regime.
ideas.source: Synthesis, as the OHLCV-only stand-in for the implied volatility term structure. Grounded in Jones & Wang, 'The term structure of equity option implied volatility' (https://msbfile03.usc.edu/digitalmeasures/christoj/intellcont/jones_wang-1.pdf), which finds the slope predicts future option returns and forecasts future realized volatility minus current volatility, and the EFMA paper on equity volatility term structures and the cross-section (https://efmaefm.org/0efmameetings/efma%20annual%20meetings/2015-Amsterdam/papers/EFMA2015_0530_fullpaper.pdf). The proxy replaces implied vols with two realized-vol horizons.

ideas.name: Rogers-Satchell Drift Detector
ideas.entry_rule: Over the last N=20 daily bars compute sigma_cc^2 = (1/N) * SUM (ln(C_t/C_{t-1}))^2 (NOT demeaned - the mean is the signal), and the Rogers-Satchell variance sigma_RS^2 = (1/N) * SUM [ ln(H_t/C_t)*ln(H_t/O_t) + ln(L_t/C_t)*ln(L_t/O_t) ]. Rogers-Satchell is unbiased for the diffusion variance regardless of drift, while the undemeaned close-to-close estimator has expectation sigma^2 + mu^2. Define DR = sigma_cc^2 / sigma_RS^2, so DR - 1 is an estimate of (drift/vol)^2 per bar. LONG when DR >= 1.25 AND the sum of the last 20 log returns > 0 AND today's close is the highest close of the last 5 bars. SHORT when DR >= 1.25 AND the 20-bar return sum < 0 AND today's close is the lowest close of the last 5 bars.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when DR falls below 1.05 (the drift component has vanished into the noise), or trail 2.0*ATR(14) from the best close since entry, or after 25 bars - whichever first.
ideas.why: This is a signal-to-noise estimator built from the algebra of two volatility estimators rather than from smoothing. Rogers-Satchell isolates pure diffusion because its cross-product construction is drift-independent; undemeaned close-to-close variance contains diffusion plus drift squared. Their ratio therefore estimates how much of recent price variation is directional rather than random, without needing any lookback direction choice or smoothing lag. ADX answers a similar question but through smoothed directional movement, which lags by design.
ideas.novelty: The trend strength measure comes from the difference between two unbiased estimators of the same quantity under different assumptions - an identification trick, not an indicator. It has no smoothing constant and therefore no lag beyond the estimation window, and it is scale-free.
ideas.source: Rogers & Satchell (1991), 'Estimating variance from high, low and closing prices', Annals of Applied Probability 1(4), 504-512 (the drift-independent estimator); Parkinson (1980), Journal of Business 53(1), 61-65; Garman & Klass (1980), Journal of Business 53(1), 67-78. Estimator comparison and formulas: https://portfoliooptimizer.io/blog/range-based-volatility-estimators-overview-and-examples-of-usage/ and https://macrosynergy.com/research/six-ways-to-estimate-realized-volatility/ . The drift-ratio construction itself is my synthesis from those estimators' bias properties.

ideas.name: Overnight Variance Share Gap Regime
ideas.entry_rule: Over the last 20 sessions compute VO = mean of (ln(O_t/C_{t-1}))^2 (overnight variance) and VI = mean of (ln(C_t/O_t))^2 (intraday variance). Share S = VO/(VO + VI). CONTINUATION MODE when S >= 0.55: at today's open, if |ln(O_t/C_{t-1})| >= 0.5 * ATR(14)/C_{t-1} and the first 15-minute bar closes on the same side of the open as the gap direction, enter in the gap direction at that bar's close. FADE MODE when S <= 0.30: same gap size condition, but enter against the gap at the close of the first 15-minute bar only if that bar closed against the gap direction. No trade when 0.30 < S < 0.55, and no trade when the gap is smaller than 0.5 ATR.
ideas.exit_rule: Continuation mode: trail 1.0*ATR(14) from the best 15-minute close, force flat at 15:55 ET. Fade mode: target the previous session's close, stop at 1.0*ATR(14) beyond the entry bar's extreme, force flat at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: The overnight share of total variance says where price discovery is happening for this name. A high share means information arrives when the market is shut and the open is a genuine repricing that continues; a low share means overnight moves are inventory noise from thin after-hours prints, and the open reverts. The same gap therefore deserves opposite trades in the two regimes, which is why unconditional gap strategies backtest near zero - they average two opposite-signed populations.
ideas.novelty: Splits realized variance by session rather than by return sign or horizon, and uses the split to flip the sign of a trade rather than to filter it. Nothing in the existing 32 conditions on overnight versus intraday variance.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The overnight/open-to-close variance split is the decomposition underlying the Yang & Zhang (2000) estimator, 'Drift-Independent Volatility Estimation Based on High, Low, Open, and Close Prices', Journal of Business 73(3), 477-491 - see the component description at https://macrosynergy.com/research/six-ways-to-estimate-realized-volatility/ . The regime-flip trading rule is mine.

ideas.name: ICSS Variance Break Restart
ideas.entry_rule: Take the last T=250 daily log returns, demeaned. Let C_k = SUM_{t=1..k} r_t^2 and D_k = C_k/C_T - k/T. Inclan-Tiao statistic IT = sqrt(T/2) * max_k |D_k|; declare a variance break at k* = argmax_k |D_k| when IT > 1.358 (5% critical value; use 1.628 for 1%). TRADE when a break is declared with k* falling within the last 3 bars AND var(r) over the bars after k* < 0.6 * var(r) over the bars before k*, i.e. the volatility regime just contracted. LONG at the next open if the sum of log returns from k* to today > 0; SHORT if < 0. Ignore breaks where variance increased.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on the next declared break (in either direction), or after 30 sessions, or on a stop of 2.0 * post-break ATR(14) - note the stop is computed from post-break volatility only, so it tightens automatically when the regime contracts.
ideas.why: The ICSS statistic converges to the supremum of a Brownian bridge under constant variance, so it gives a calibrated answer to 'has the variance level actually changed, or is this just clustering?'. A confirmed downward break marks the end of a stress episode - the point at which risk models release capacity. Trading in the direction of drift measured only since the break avoids the classic error of measuring trend across a regime boundary, where pre-break volatility dominates the estimate.
ideas.novelty: Both the entry timing and the stop distance are anchored to a detected change point rather than to a fixed lookback. Every lookback in the existing 32 is fixed-length and therefore straddles regime boundaries by construction.
ideas.source: Inclan & Tiao (1994), 'Use of Cumulative Sums of Squares for Retrospective Detection of Changes of Variance', JASA 89(427), 913-923. GARCH-robust kappa_2 variant (recommended, since raw IT over-rejects on leptokurtic data): Sanso, Arago & Carrion (2004), 'Testing for changes in the unconditional variance of financial time series', https://dea.uib.eu/digitalAssets/128/128259_1.pdf . R reference implementation: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ICSS/ICSS.pdf

ideas.name: Volatility-Managed Exposure
ideas.entry_rule: RV22_t = SUM of squared daily log returns over the last 22 sessions. LONG at the next open when RV22_t is at or below its 40th percentile over the trailing 504 sessions AND the return from t-252 to t-22 (12-month-minus-1-month momentum) is positive. Position size = min(1.0, target_var / RV22_t) where target_var is the median RV22 over the trailing 504 sessions; recompute size every bar and adjust the position, so exposure is continuously proportional to the inverse of realized variance.
ideas.exit_rule: Size to zero when RV22_t rises above its 70th percentile of the trailing 504 sessions, or when 12-1 momentum turns negative. Deliberately NO price stop - the variance level is the risk control, and adding a price stop double-counts the same risk and destroys the paper's result.
ideas.why: Moreira & Muir show that scaling exposure by the inverse of last month's realized variance raises alpha and Sharpe substantially: expected returns do not rise one-for-one with volatility, so the reward-per-unit-risk is much better in calm regimes. This inverts the conventional 'volatility means opportunity' intuition. Realized variance is highly persistent at a one-month horizon, which is what makes last month's variance a usable forecast of this month's.
ideas.novelty: Position size is a continuous function of realized variance recomputed every bar, and the exit trigger is a variance percentile rather than a price level. Every rule in the existing set is binary in/out with a price-based stop; this is a different exit structure entirely.
ideas.source: Moreira & Muir (2017), 'Volatility-Managed Portfolios', Journal of Finance 72(4), 1611-1644. NBER working paper: https://www.nber.org/papers/w22208 . Real-time implementation caveats (look-ahead in the scaling constant): Xu (2024), 'Improving Volatility-Managed Portfolios in Real Time', https://cfr.ivo-welch.info/forthcoming/papers/xu2024improving.pdf

ideas.name: Strategy-Volatility Circuit Breaker
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain a simulated always-on equity curve for a base signal - for a self-contained test define the base signal as: long when the trailing 126-day return > 0, short when < 0, rebalanced at each daily close. Compute SV_t = stdev of the last 126 daily returns OF THAT SIMULATED CURVE * sqrt(252). Take the base signal's live entry only when SV_t <= its own 80th percentile over the trailing 756 sessions. Size the position at min(1.0, 0.12 / SV_t) for a 12% annualised target.
ideas.exit_rule: Force flat immediately whenever SV_t crosses above the 90th percentile of its trailing 756-session distribution, regardless of what the base signal says, and stay flat until SV_t falls back below the 70th percentile. Otherwise exit on the base signal flipping.
ideas.why: Barroso & Santa-Clara show momentum's own realized variance is highly predictable and inversely related to its subsequent returns - momentum crashes are preceded by rising momentum volatility, not by rising market volatility. Scaling by the inverse of the strategy's six-month realized variance nearly doubled momentum's Sharpe and effectively removed the crashes. The key point is that the risk being measured is the strategy's, not the asset's: a stock can be calm while the signal riding it is unstable.
ideas.novelty: The volatility input is the equity curve of the signal itself, not the price series. It is a wrapper that can be applied to any of the other 32 rules and changes their exit structure by adding a state-dependent force-flat that no price-based stop can replicate.
ideas.source: Barroso & Santa-Clara (2015), 'Momentum has its moments', Journal of Financial Economics 116(1), 111-120. Leverage-constrained variant and replication: https://www.garp.org/hubfs/Whitepapers/a1Z1W0000054xSXUAY.pdf

ideas.name: Diurnal-Standardized Volatility Shock
ideas.entry_rule: For each of the 78 five-minute bins b of the regular session compute s_b = median over the last 20 sessions of |ln(C/O)| for that bin, and v_b = median volume for that bin over the same 20 sessions. Standardized move z_t = ln(C_t/O_t) / s_{b(t)}. LONG when all of: z_t >= 3.0; the previous three bars each had |z| < 1.0 (an isolated shock, not the middle of a run); volume_t >= 2.0 * v_{b(t)}; and the bar closes in the top 25% of its own high-low range. SHORT is the exact mirror (z_t <= -3.0, close in the bottom 25%). No entries in the first 15 minutes or the last 20 minutes of the session.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when three consecutive bars have |z| < 0.5 (the shock has decayed back into the seasonal norm), or on a stop at the entry bar's opposite extreme, or on a target of 2.0 * s_b * entry price, or at 15:55 ET - whichever first.
ideas.why: Intraday volatility follows a strong and stable U-shape - a 30-minute move at 10:00 and the same move at 12:30 are completely different events. A fixed ATR threshold therefore fires almost exclusively at the open and close, which is a time-of-day filter masquerading as a volatility filter. Dividing by the bin's own median absolute move removes the seasonal component so the signal is comparable across the day, and the largest genuine surprises then turn out to sit in the midday lull where nobody is looking.
ideas.novelty: Every threshold in the existing 32 is stationary across the session. This one is a periodic function of time-of-day for both volatility and volume, which changes which bars can qualify - not just how often they qualify.
ideas.source: Andersen & Bollerslev (1997), 'Intraday periodicity and volatility persistence in financial markets', Journal of Empirical Finance 4(2-3), 115-158. Periodicity-robust standardisation for jump detection: Boudt, Croux & Laurent (2011), 'Robust estimation of intraweek periodicity in volatility and jump detection', Journal of Empirical Finance 18(2). Evidence the periodicity is itself time-varying (so the profile must be rolling, not fixed): https://www.researchgate.net/publication/327268829_Time-Varying_Periodicity_in_Intraday_Volatility and https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/todorov/htm/papers/odp.pdf

ideas.name: Leverage Effect Sign Flip
ideas.entry_rule: RV20_t = stdev of the last 20 daily log returns. Compute rho_t = Pearson correlation over the last 60 sessions between r_t and (ln RV20_{t+1} - ln RV20_t), i.e. between today's return and tomorrow's change in log realized volatility. Equities normally show rho < 0 (the leverage effect: prices down, volatility up). LONG at the next open when rho_t crosses above 0 today, having been <= -0.25 at some point in the previous 20 sessions, AND the 20-session sum of log returns is positive. SHORT on the same rho crossing when the 20-session return sum is negative.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when rho_t falls back below -0.15 (the normal leverage regime has reasserted), or after 25 sessions, or on a 2.5*ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: The negative return-volatility correlation is one of the most reliable facts about equity returns and is precisely what the asymmetric term in EGARCH is built to capture. When it inverts - volatility rising as price rises - the flow driving the stock is no longer risk-averse rebalancing; it is forced buying, short covering or a crowded chase, and those regimes are momentum-persistent rather than mean-reverting. The inversion is rare, which is the point: it identifies a structurally different market state rather than a threshold crossing on a continuous variable.
ideas.novelty: The signal is the sign of a correlation between returns and future volatility changes - a second-order relationship. Nothing in the existing set uses the joint dynamics of price and volatility, only their levels.
ideas.source: Black (1976), 'Studies of stock price volatility changes', Proceedings of the ASA Business and Economic Statistics Section; Nelson (1991), 'Conditional Heteroskedasticity in Asset Returns: A New Approach', Econometrica 59(2), 347-370 (EGARCH asymmetry term). Empirical asymmetry magnitudes from Patton & Sheppard (2015): https://public.econ.duke.edu/~ap172/Patton_Sheppard_REStat_2015.pdf

ideas.name: Range-Implied vs Realized Move Premium
ideas.category: volatility risk premium expressed through price
ideas.entry_rule: For each session define the range-implied expected absolute log move E_t = 0.4792 * ln(H_t/L_t). (Derivation: Parkinson's estimator gives sigma = ln(H/L)/(2*sqrt(ln 2)) = 0.6006*ln(H/L), and for a normal variate E|r| = sqrt(2/pi)*sigma = 0.7979*sigma.) Realized close-to-close move M_t = |ln(C_t/C_{t-1})|. Premium P = mean over the last 20 sessions of (E_t - M_t)/E_t. Let Ebar = mean of E over the last 20 sessions. WHEN P >= 0.30: for the next session place a resting limit buy at C_t * exp(-1.0*Ebar) and a resting limit sell-short at C_t * exp(+1.0*Ebar); take only the first fill of the session and cancel the other. WHEN P <= 0.05 take no trades at all that session.
ideas.exit_rule: Target the previous session's close C_t (the reversion anchor); stop at 2.0*Ebar beyond the entry price; force flat at 15:55 ET - whichever first.
ideas.why: The volatility risk premium is the gap between what volatility is priced at and what is subsequently delivered. With no options data, the closest OHLCV analogue is the gap between how far price travels within the session (the range, which is what a straddle buyer is effectively paying for) and how far it actually gets between closes. When the range persistently exceeds the close-to-close displacement, intraday moves are round-tripping and the market maker's inventory is being paid for - selling the wings by placing limits at the range-implied one-sigma distance harvests that. When P collapses toward zero, price is travelling as far as its range implies (trending), and the same limits become adverse selection, so the rule disables itself.
ideas.novelty: It is a self-disabling rule: the same statistic that sizes the limit distance also decides whether to trade at all, and it flips off in exactly the regime where mean-reversion rules bleed. VWAP z-score reversion and Bollinger fade both keep firing in a trend; this one goes silent.
ideas.source: Synthesis, as the OHLCV-only proxy for the options-based VRP. The range-to-expected-move constant is Parkinson (1980), Journal of Business 53(1), 61-65. VRP background and the general finding that implied exceeds subsequent realized volatility: https://quantpedia.com/strategies/volatility-risk-premium-effect and https://macrosynergy.com/research/realistic-volatility-risk-premia/ . Proxy caveat: it captures intraday round-tripping, which is correlated with but not identical to the options VRP.

ideas.name: Microstructure Noise Ratio Collapse
ideas.entry_rule: Rolling over the trailing 90 minutes, updated at each 5-minute bar close: RV1 = SUM of squared 1-minute log returns over that span; RV5avg = the average of the five possible 5-minute subgrid realized variances over the same span (offsets 0..4 minutes). Noise ratio NR = RV1/RV5avg. Under no microstructure noise NR converges to 1; bid-ask bounce inflates the finer-grid estimator, pushing NR above 1. ENTER when NR crosses below 1.10 having been >= 1.30 at some point in the previous 6 bars: go long if the net log return over the last 30 minutes is positive, short if negative. No entries in the first 45 minutes (the window is not yet full) or after 15:00 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when NR rises back above 1.25 (bounce-dominated tape has returned), or on a stop of 1.0 * the trailing-90-minute average true range, or at 15:55 ET - whichever first.
ideas.why: The ratio of fine-grid to coarse-grid realized variance is the standard diagnostic for how much of observed price variation is quote noise rather than efficient-price movement - it is the empirical content of the volatility signature plot. A high ratio means the tape is dominated by bid-ask bounce between passive participants; a collapse toward 1 means a directional participant is consuming liquidity and moving the efficient price rather than oscillating around it. That transition is a footprint of informed order flow, visible in OHLCV without any level 2.
ideas.novelty: The signal is the disagreement between two estimators of the same variance computed at different sampling frequencies - a sampling-scale signal, not a price or volume signal. Nothing in the existing set compares statistics across bar resolutions.
ideas.source: Zhang, Mykland & Ait-Sahalia (2005), 'A Tale of Two Time Scales: Determining Integrated Volatility with Noisy High-Frequency Data', JASA 100(472), 1394-1411 - the two-scales estimator and the subsampled-average construction. Signature-plot diagnostics for noise: Hansen & Lunde, https://public.econ.duke.edu/~get/browse/courses/201/spr11/DOWNLOADS/VolatilityMeasures/SpecificlPapers/hansen_lunde_forecasting_rv_11.pdf

ideas.name: Two-State HMM Calm Probability Crossing
ideas.entry_rule: Fit a two-state Gaussian hidden Markov model by EM on the last 750 daily log returns (each state has its own mean and variance; 2x2 transition matrix), refitting every 5 sessions. Label the state with the smaller fitted variance the 'calm' state. Compute the filtered probability p_t = P(state_t = calm | r_1..r_t) using the forward recursion with the current parameters - filtered, never smoothed, since smoothed probabilities use future data and will not exist live. LONG at the next open when p_t crosses above 0.80 from below AND the 60-session sum of log returns is positive. SHORT on the same crossing when the 60-session sum is negative.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when p_t falls below 0.50, or after 40 sessions held. Deliberately no tight price stop - the regime probability is the stop - but keep a 4.0*ATR(14) disaster stop for gap protection.
ideas.why: A Markov-switching model gives a probabilistic, likelihood-based answer to which volatility regime the market is in, and it does so with a transition matrix that encodes regime stickiness - so it does not flip on every noisy bar the way a threshold on rolling standard deviation does. Trading the crossing into high calm-probability captures the point at which risk-taking capacity returns; using filtered rather than smoothed probabilities is essential and is where most published backtests of this idea cheat.
ideas.novelty: The regime label is a latent variable inferred by maximum likelihood with an explicit persistence prior, not a threshold on an observable. It produces a continuous probability that can also be used for sizing, and the entry is a probability crossing rather than a price event.
ideas.source: Hamilton (1989), 'A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle', Econometrica 57(2), 357-384. Two-state equity application with state-dependent variance and returns: 'Stock market volatility and equity returns: Evidence from a two-state Markov-switching model with regressors', Journal of Empirical Finance, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0927539812000382

ideas.name: Variance-Time Clock Exit
ideas.entry_rule: The entry can wrap any existing trigger; for a self-contained test use: LONG when today's close > the highest high of the prior 20 daily bars; SHORT when today's close < the lowest low of the prior 20. At the moment of entry, record the variance budget B = SUM of squared log returns over the 20 bars immediately before entry. The novelty is entirely in the holding rule below.
ideas.exit_rule: After entry, accumulate A = SUM of squared log returns from the entry bar onward, updated each bar. Exit the full position when A >= 1.0 * B - one unit of variance-time has elapsed - regardless of P&L. Also exit if the position gives back 1.5*ATR(14) from its best close since entry. Whichever comes first. Holding period is therefore measured in realised variance rather than in bars: a quiet market holds the trade for 40+ bars, a violent one exits in 4.
ideas.why: Clark's subordination result is that returns are close to normal once time is measured in transaction/information units rather than calendar units; calendar time is the wrong clock. A fixed 10-bar time stop therefore means completely different things in a 10% and a 40% volatility regime - it is implicitly a random holding period in the units that matter. Budgeting the trade a fixed quantity of realised variance makes the holding period constant in information time, which should stabilise the return distribution of the strategy and, mechanically, cut exposure fastest in exactly the regimes where drawdowns compound.
ideas.novelty: This is an exit structure, not an entry signal, and it is the one class the existing 32 have nothing in: their exits are all price-distance (ATR/band/structure) or bar-count. A variance-time stop is neither - it can exit a profitable, calmly trending position simply because the budget ran out, and hold a losing quiet one far longer than any bar-count stop would. It is also a drop-in wrapper that can be A/B tested against the current exits on all 32 existing rules.
ideas.source: Clark (1973), 'A Subordinated Stochastic Process Model with Finite Variance for Speculative Prices', Econometrica 41(1), 135-155; Ane & Geman (2000), 'Order Flow, Transaction Clock, and Normality of Asset Returns', Journal of Finance 55(5), 2259-2284. The application as a position-exit clock is my synthesis from the time-change literature.

ideas.name: Jump Share Collapse Continuation
ideas.timeframe: 5-minute bars aggregated daily, held in daily bars
ideas.entry_rule: For each session compute from the n = 78 five-minute log returns: RV_t = SUM r_i^2; bipower variation BPV_t = (pi/2) * (n/(n-1)) * SUM_{i=2..n} |r_i| * |r_{i-1}|; jump share J_t = max(0, (RV_t - BPV_t)/RV_t). Let Jbar_t = mean of J over the last 10 sessions. ENTER at the next open when Jbar_t <= 0.08 AND Jbar was >= 0.20 at some point in the previous 10 sessions (the tape has returned to a diffusive regime after a jumpy one): LONG if the 20-session log return sum is positive, SHORT if negative.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when Jbar_t rises back above 0.20, or after 20 sessions, or on a 2.5*ATR(14) stop - whichever first.
ideas.why: Bipower variation is consistent for the continuous (diffusive) part of quadratic variation and is robust to jumps, so RV minus BPV isolates the jump contribution. The share matters for strategy selection: when a large fraction of variance arrives in discontinuities, stops are meaningless because price gaps through them and any trend-following rule pays for slippage it cannot control. When the jump share collapses back toward zero the path is close to a diffusion again, which is the assumption under which trailing stops and trend continuation actually work. The rule trades the moment that assumption becomes true again.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the two other jump ideas here: this one uses the jump share as a slowly-varying tradeability regime measure rather than as an event detector, and the entry fires on the absence of jumps rather than their presence. It is a gate on path smoothness, which no ADX or volatility-level filter measures.
