The specific inequalities, the flat-price constraint and the CLV-based exit are my own quantification and have not, to my knowledge, been published or tested in this form.

ideas.name: Quantified Pin Bar at a 20-Bar Extreme
ideas.entry_rule: For the current bar define range = high - low, body = |close - open|, lower_wick = min(open, close) - low, upper_wick = high - max(open, close). BULLISH PIN when ALL hold: lower_wick >= 0.60 x range; upper_wick <= 0.15 x range; body <= 0.30 x range; range >= 1.2 x ATR(14); and the bar's low is the lowest low of the last 20 bars including itself. Entry: buy stop at the pin bar's high + 0.01, valid for the next 2 bars only, then cancelled. BEARISH PIN is the mirror (upper_wick >= 0.60 x range, lower_wick <= 0.15 x range, high is the 20-bar highest high) with a sell stop at the pin low - 0.01.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = pin bar low - 0.05 (longs). Target = entry + 2.0 x (entry - stop). If neither is touched within 8 bars, exit at that bar's close. Move the stop to breakeven when open profit reaches 1.0 x initial risk.
ideas.why: A long lower shadow with a close near the top is a within-bar round trip: sellers pushed to a new multi-week low and every tick of that push was bought back before the bell. That is a directly observable failure of the dominant side. The range floor matters - the same shape on a quiet bar is noise, since a small wick on a small bar means no meaningful volume changed hands there.
ideas.novelty: Not indicator-based at all: it is a within-bar auction-failure measurement combined with a positional requirement (the bar must be at the extreme of its own recent range). The three simultaneous wick/body ratio constraints exclude the ordinary doji and spinning-top shapes that a loose 'hammer' definition would let through, which is precisely where the academic null results come from.
ideas.source: Bulkowski, T., 'Encyclopedia of Candlestick Charts' and the hammer identification guidelines at thepatternsite.com. The extra filters are a deliberate response to the negative literature: Marshall, B. R., Young, M. R. and Rose, L. C. (2006), 'Candlestick technical trading strategies: Can they create value for investors?', Journal of Banking & Finance 30(8), 2303-2323, find no profitability from unfiltered candlestick patterns on DJIA components 1992-2002 - so an unconditioned hammer is known to be worthless and only the conditioned version is worth testing.

ideas.name: Body-Dominant Engulfing with Close-Strength Exit
ideas.entry_rule: BULLISH: close[-1] < open[-1] (prior bar down); close[0] > open[0] (current bar up); open[0] <= close[-1]; close[0] > open[-1] (the body engulfs the prior body); |close[0] - open[0]| >= 1.5 x |close[-1] - open[-1]|; the current body >= 0.70 x its own range; range[0] >= 1.0 x ATR(14); and at least 3 of the previous 5 bars closed below their own prior close. Enter at the close of the engulfing bar. BEARISH is the exact mirror.
ideas.exit_rule: Three-way exit, first to trigger: (1) hard stop at the engulfing bar's low - 0.05; (2) profit target at entry + 3.0 x ATR(14); (3) close-strength stop - exit at the close of any bar whose CLV = ((close-low)-(high-close))/(high-low) <= -0.40 AND whose range >= 1.0 x ATR(14). No time exit.
ideas.why: Plain engulfing is a coin flip; the informative version is where a single session's body is large relative both to the prior body and to the stock's normal range, meaning one side did the whole day's work in one direction after several sessions of the opposite. The prior-weakness requirement supplies the context that makes it a reversal rather than a random large bar.
ideas.novelty: The exit is the real idea: a close-strength stop that liquidates on the first decisive close-on-the-low wide bar, which is bar geometry rather than a price level or an indicator. That exit is transferable to other entries and is a different exit family from every stop/target/trail we currently run. It also deliberately trades the engulfing bar as a continuation-capable structure rather than assuming reversal.
ideas.source: Bulkowski, T., thepatternsite.com/OutsideDays.html - an engulfing bar is an outside day with body constraints, and Bulkowski's data show outside days act as a CONTINUATION 63% of the time in bull markets with up breakouts (average rise 10%, 32% break-even failure rate, rank 6 of 23 small patterns), which is why this rule does not assume reversal. Null-result context: Marshall, Young and Rose (2006), Journal of Banking & Finance 30(8), 2303-2323.

ideas.name: In-Range Opening Gap Fade to Prior Close
ideas.entry_rule: At 09:30 ET compute G = today's open - yesterday's close, and require the gap to land INSIDE yesterday's range: yesterday_low < today_open < yesterday_high. Require |G| >= 0.30 x ATR(14) measured on daily bars. GAP UP CASE: if the 09:30-09:35 five-minute bar closes below its own open AND below today's open, sell short at that bar's close. GAP DOWN CASE is the mirror (first 5-minute bar closes above its open and above today's open, buy at its close). One attempt per symbol per day; if the first 5-minute bar does not satisfy the rejection condition, no trade.
ideas.exit_rule: Target = yesterday's close (the gap fill), exit with a limit there. Stop = the first 5-minute bar's high + 0.10 x daily ATR(14) for shorts (mirror for longs). Hard time exit at 11:30 ET at the market. Never hold past 11:30 - the documented gap-fill tendency is concentrated in the first two hours.
params: rejection bar index (first vs first two 5-min bars)
partial fill target (50% of gap vs full)
ideas.why: A gap that opens inside the prior day's range has not escaped the previous session's value area - the auction still has accepted two-sided trade at those prices, so there is a known population of participants willing to transact between the open and yesterday's close. That makes the prior close a genuine magnet. The first-bar rejection requirement is the confirmation that the gap had no initiative behind it.
ideas.novelty: The classification variable is WHERE THE GAP OPENS RELATIVE TO YESTERDAY'S RANGE, not the opening range of today. It shares no levels with our opening-range fade: the target is yesterday's close, the stop is the first bar's extreme, and the trade can trigger on the first bar rather than requiring an opening range to form and then fail.
ideas.source: Gap taxonomy (area/common gaps close inside the prior range and fill; breakaway gaps clear it and run) from Edwards, R. D. and Magee, J., 'Technical Analysis of Stock Trends', chapter on gaps. Note honestly: I was unable to retrieve a peer-reviewed quantified gap-fill study within this session's search budget, so the fill probabilities here are untested and this idea should be treated as a hypothesis to be measured on our own bars rather than as a documented effect.

ideas.name: Out-of-Range Gap-and-Go Level Retest
ideas.entry_rule: GAP UP CASE: today's open > yesterday's high + 0.20 x daily ATR(14) - the gap clears the prior day's range entirely. Then wait, from 09:35 to 11:00 ET, for the FIRST 5-minute bar that satisfies both: its low <= yesterday_high + 0.10 x daily ATR(14) (price returns to retest the prior day's high) AND its close > yesterday_high (the level holds). Buy at that bar's close. Invalidate the whole setup for the day if any 5-minute bar closes below yesterday_high - 0.25 x daily ATR before the retest bar forms. One attempt per day. GAP DOWN CASE is the mirror at yesterday's low.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = yesterday's high - 0.25 x daily ATR(14) (longs). Once open profit reaches 1.0 x initial risk, trail beneath the lowest low of the last three 5-minute bars, updated every bar. Hard exit at 15:55 ET. No fixed target.
ideas.why: When the open clears the whole prior session, yesterday's extreme flips from resistance to the nearest reference price with known two-sided interest; holders of the gap defend it because a loss of that level means the gap is failing. The retest supplies both a cheap entry and an unambiguous invalidation, which is why the reward-to-risk is far better than chasing the open.
ideas.novelty: The entry level is YESTERDAY'S EXTREME, a level formed before today began, and the trigger is a pullback into it rather than a breakout away from it. Our opening-range breakout uses a level built from today's first N minutes and enters on expansion; this enters on retracement, at a different price, with a different invalidation.
ideas.source: Supporting evidence for gap continuation: Bulkowski, T., thepatternsite.com/Gap2H.html - the Gap 2H pattern (a price gap followed by a higher high and higher low) acts as a CONTINUATION 72% of the time, with a 34% break-even failure rate and 10% average rise in bull markets, and Bulkowski reports the pattern stop (a penny beyond the pattern extreme, as used here) wins 62% versus 55% for a percentage stop. Gap taxonomy from Edwards and Magee, 'Technical Analysis of Stock Trends'.

ideas.name: Wyckoff Spring in a Bounded Base
ideas.entry_rule: Define the base over the 20 bars ending at bar[-1]: RH = max high, RL = min low. Require the base to be genuinely bounded: (RH - RL) <= 2.5 x ATR(20), AND at least two separate bars, at least 3 bars apart, with low <= RL + 0.25 x ATR(20) (the support has been tested twice). SPRING BAR (current bar) must satisfy ALL: low < RL - 0.05 x ATR(20) (it does undercut); low >= RL - 0.50 x ATR(20) (the undercut is shallow, not a breakdown); close > RL (it closes back inside the base); close >= low + 0.60 x range (close in the upper 40% of the bar); volume <= 1.2 x the 20-bar average volume (no supply came in on the undercut). Entry: buy stop at the spring bar's high + 0.01 on the next bar; cancel if unfilled after 2 bars. UPTHRUST is the exact mirror at RH for shorts.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = spring bar low - 0.10 x ATR(20). First target = RH (the top of the base); take 60% there. Trail the remainder beneath the lowest low of the last 3 bars. Full exit on any close below RL - 0.50 x ATR(20) (the spring has failed into a real breakdown).
params: volume ceiling (0.8x low-volume variant vs 1.2x vs >1.5x shakeout variant)
ideas.why: Inside a bounded base, a shallow undercut of support that closes back inside on ordinary or light volume means the supply that support was holding back does not exist - the break found no sellers. That converts the base's resistance into the next objective because the only remaining constraint on price is overhead supply, which is measurable as the range top.
ideas.novelty: Materially different from our liquidity-sweep rule: this requires a BOUNDED base (a maximum width in ATR), at least two prior tests of support, a MAXIMUM undercut depth as well as a minimum, and a volume ceiling. The depth band is the key structural difference - a deep flush disqualifies the setup here, whereas a sweep rule treats deeper as stronger. The target is the range top rather than an R multiple.
ideas.source: Wyckoff method literature - Pruden, H., 'The Three Skills of Top Trading' (2007), chapters on the spring/shakeout and upthrust-after-distribution; Wyckoff Analytics course material on spring types 1/2/3 classified by penetration depth and volume. Volume-tier classification consistent with published detection implementations (e.g. tradingview.com/script/H3zpGMiK-Wyckoff-Spring-Upthrust-FibAlgo/, which classifies springs as <=0.8x, 0.8-1.5x and >1.5x average volume). The specific ATR-normalised inequalities, the base-width cap and the depth band are my quantification - Wyckoff's own writing is qualitative and unbacktestable as written.

ideas.name: Sperandeo 2B Failed Closing Breakout
ideas.entry_rule: SHORT: let P = max(close[1..20]) computed as of the bar BEFORE the breakout. A breakout bar occurs when close[0] > P (a genuine 20-day CLOSING high, not merely an intrabar poke). Record P and the highest high H* reached from the breakout bar onward. Within the next 3 bars, if any bar closes below P, short at that close. LONG is the mirror: a close below the 20-day closing low, followed within 3 bars by a close back above that level.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = H* + 0.05 (the highest high recorded since the breakout). Target = 2.0 x initial risk, or the 20-day low, whichever is reached first. Hard time exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry. Cancel the setup entirely if 3 bars pass without a close back through P.
params: use closes vs highs to define the breakout level
ideas.why: A closing breakout to new highs recruits committed buyers - momentum systems, breakout traders, stop-loss covering shorts - at prices above the old level. When price closes back below the same level within a few sessions, every one of those entries is at a loss and their exits become the supply that drives the next move. The move is larger than an ordinary pullback because the trapped population is larger and more uniformly positioned.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from Turtle Soup in the object that fails: this requires a completed CLOSING breakout that is then reversed, whereas Turtle Soup fires on an intrabar extension that never achieves a breakout at all. The two produce different signal sets on the same data - a 2B needs the breakout to succeed first. The stop is anchored to the post-breakout extreme rather than to the signal bar.
ideas.source: Sperandeo, V. (1991), 'Trader Vic: Methods of a Wall Street Master', the 2B rule ('in an uptrend, if a higher high is made but fails to carry through, and then prices drop below the previous high, the trend is apt to reverse'). The pinning-down here - 20-day closing extremes, a 3-bar failure window, and a stop at the post-breakout extreme - is mine, because Sperandeo's original statement has no lookback or time limit and is untestable as written.

ideas.name: Three-Bar Play (ignition, hold, release)
ideas.entry_rule: BAR 1 (ignition): range(1) >= 2.0 x ATR(14); close in the top 20% of its range, (close-low)/(high-low) >= 0.80; volume(1) >= 2.0 x the 20-bar average volume. BAR 2 (hold): high(2) <= high(1); low(2) >= low(1) + 0.60 x range(1) - i.e. bar 2 gives back no more than 40% of bar 1; range(2) <= 0.50 x range(1); volume(2) <= 0.60 x volume(1). ENTRY: buy stop at high(2) + 0.01, valid on the very next bar ONLY; cancel otherwise. Short setup is the exact mirror (close in the bottom 20%, bar 2 holding the low).
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = low(2) - 0.01. Target = entry + 1.0 x range(1) (the ignition bar's range projected from the entry). If the target is not reached within 6 bars, exit at that bar's close. If bar 2's low is violated before entry, the setup is dead - do not re-arm on a later bar.
ideas.why: A wide bar on heavy volume with a close at its extreme is a repricing event. The informative question is what happens next: if the market immediately gives most of it back, the move was liquidity-driven; if it holds nearly all of it on materially lighter volume, no meaningful supply appeared at the new price and the repricing is being accepted. The narrow, quiet hold bar is the measurement of that acceptance.
ideas.novelty: Not a momentum count - it is one large bar followed by a specified failure-to-retrace, with the entry at the small bar's extreme and the target scaled by the ignition bar's own range. Our three-bar momentum rule counts consecutive closes and would fire on three ordinary bars; this requires a specific size relationship (2:1 range contraction) and a volume contraction between adjacent bars, so the two almost never fire together.
ideas.source: Bellafiore, M. (2010), 'One Good Trade' and SMB Capital training material, where the 'three bar play' is taught as an ignition bar, a small consolidation bar, and a break of the consolidation bar's high. Published as a discretionary pattern with no numeric thresholds; the range multiples, close-location floor, give-back cap and volume ratios above are my quantification so that it can be backtested at all.

ideas.name: Upthrust Bar (wide spread, close on the low, high volume)
ideas.entry_rule: SHORT when ALL hold on the current bar: the bar's high is the highest high of the last 20 bars including itself; range >= 1.5 x ATR(14); close <= low + 0.25 x range (close in the bottom quarter); volume >= 1.5 x the 20-bar average volume; and close < close[-1]. Short at the bar's close. LONG is the mirror (a new 20-bar low, wide range, close in the top quarter of the bar, heavy volume, close > close[-1]).
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = the signal bar's high + 0.05. Cover on the FIRST of: (1) any bar closing with CLV = ((close-low)-(high-close))/(high-low) >= +0.50 (the buyers have taken the close back); (2) profit of 2.0 x ATR(14); (3) the close of the 5th bar after entry.
ideas.why: A new multi-week high made on a wide range and heavy volume that then closes at the bottom of that same bar means the highest-volume trade of the period was done into supply that overwhelmed it. Every buyer above the close is offside within a single session. Volume is what separates this from an ordinary failed poke: heavy volume proves a large quantity actually changed hands at the bad prices.
ideas.novelty: Combines three measurements that our current rules never combine: positional (new 20-bar extreme), geometric (wide range with a close at the opposite extreme of that same bar), and participation (volume multiple). The exit is also symmetric to the entry - it uses the same close-location statistic in reverse, so the trade is closed by the same evidence that would have opened the opposite one.
ideas.source: Williams, T. (1993), 'Master the Markets' - the Volume Spread Analysis 'upthrust' bar (wide spread up, close on the lows, high volume) and its mirror, the selling-climax/no-supply reversal bar. Corroborating structure: Bulkowski, T., thepatternsite.com/KRD.html (key reversal bars) and thepatternsite.com/OutsideDays.html. VSA is presented qualitatively in the original; the ATR-normalised range floor, the 0.25 close-location cap and the volume multiple are my quantification.

ideas.name: Crabel Hook Day
ideas.entry_rule: BEARISH HOOK when ALL hold: open > high[-1] (today opens above yesterday's entire range); close < close[-1] (it gives all of that back and more); and range = high - low < range[-1] (today's range is NARROWER than yesterday's). Enter short at the close of the hook bar, or optionally on a sell stop at the hook bar's low - 0.01 on the following bar (test both). BULLISH HOOK is the exact mirror: open < low[-1], close > close[-1], range < range[-1].
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = the hook bar's high + 0.05 (shorts). Target = 1.5 x ATR(14) from entry. Hard time exit at the close of the 3rd bar after entry - the effect Crabel describes is a short-horizon one and holding past it converts the trade into an unrelated bet.
params: entry method (at close vs stop below the bar)
optional filter requiring the prior bar to close in the top/bottom 25% of its range
ideas.why: An open beyond yesterday's whole range means the overnight order flow was one-sided and enthusiastic. A close below yesterday's close means every one of those buyers is now offside. The narrowing range is the distinguishing detail: it says the reversal happened without a volatility expansion, i.e. it was a quiet failure of demand rather than a violent sell-off, and Crabel's observation is that such compressed reversals precede outsized directional moves.
ideas.novelty: The narrowing-range requirement inverts the usual reversal-bar logic. Bulkowski's key reversal and the standard outside-day reversal both require an EXPANDED range (a lower low and a higher high); the hook day requires a CONTRACTED one plus an open outside the prior bar. The two definitions are mutually exclusive on the same bar, so this cannot overlap with any outside-bar rule.
ideas.source: Crabel, T. (1990), 'Day Trading with Short Term Price Patterns and Opening Range Breakout' - the Hook Day pattern, defined as a day that opens above the previous day's high (or below its low), reverses the previous day's close, and does so with a narrowing range relative to the previous day. Rule summary at tradingsetupsreview.com and the Crabel strategy pages at oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/.

ideas.name: Island Reversal (twin-gap isolation)
ideas.entry_rule: ISLAND BOTTOM. Bar g1 opens the island with a down gap: high(g1) < low(g1 - 1). The island is bars g1 .. g2 where 1 <= (g2 - g1 + 1) <= 5; let IH = max(high) and IL = min(low) over those bars, and require IH < low(g1 - 1) (the island never closes the entry gap). Bar g2+1 exits with an up gap: low(g2+1) > IH. Require the two gaps to overlap in price: low(g2+1) <= low(g1 - 1) + 0.25 x ATR(14). Enter long at the close of bar g2+1. ISLAND TOP is the exact mirror for shorts.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = IL - 0.05. Exit immediately on any close back inside the island (close < IH). Target = entry + 3.0 x ATR(14); time exit at the close of the 20th bar after entry. Test a volume-conditioned variant: only take the trade when volume on bar g2+1 >= 2.0 x the 20-bar average volume.
ideas.why: An island is a set of bars whose entire price range was traded by a population that can no longer transact there - price has gapped away in both directions, leaving every position opened inside the island stranded and unable to exit at breakeven. Their eventual liquidation is directional pressure with a known location. The overlap requirement is what makes the isolation real rather than coincidental.
ideas.novelty: The only rule in this set built on the RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN TWO GAPS rather than on a single gap or a bar shape. Honest prior: Bulkowski ranks island reversals near the bottom of his tables (island bottoms 38 of 39 for bull-market breakouts, and dead last among pattern types in bear markets), so the realistic value here is a cheap null test plus the volume-conditioned sub-case - if any edge survives, it will be in the heavy-volume exit gap variant, which is the version worth allocating the compute to.
ideas.source: Bulkowski, T., thepatternsite.com/islandrev.html - 'island tops and island bottoms are reversal chart patterns set off by gaps at the same price level'; the two gaps must share some or all of the same price; overall performance rank for island bottoms is 38 of 39 in bull markets, with break-even failure rates around 31-34%. Classic definition from Edwards and Magee, 'Technical Analysis of Stock Trends', chapter on gaps.

ideas.name: HMM Filtered-Probability Crossover
ideas.entry_rule: Fit a 2-state Gaussian HMM by Baum-Welch on the trailing 750 daily log returns r_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-1}); emissions N(mu_k, sigma_k^2), full 2x2 transition matrix A; refit every 21 trading days. Label the state with the smaller fitted sigma_k as B (benign). Between refits run ONLY the scaled forward recursion (no Viterbi, no smoothing - both peek ahead) to get the filtered probability p_t = P(S_t = B | r_1..r_t). LONG entry at the next bar's open when p_t > 0.60 and p_{t-1} <= 0.60. SHORT entry at the next open when p_t < 0.40 and p_{t-1} >= 0.40.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when p_t < 0.40, or close < entry - 2.5*ATR(14), or 40 bars held - whichever comes first. Mirror for shorts (exit when p_t > 0.60, or close > entry + 2.5*ATR(14), or 40 bars).
ideas.why: Volatility clustering plus the leverage effect means equity returns in the high-variance state are negatively skewed and carry a materially worse Sharpe. The filtered probability is a distributional estimate using both the mean and the variance of returns, and the estimated transition matrix supplies hysteresis for free: a sticky A makes the posterior resist single-bar shocks, so it whipsaws far less than a raw volatility threshold. The entry fires on a posterior crossing, i.e. on the market's inferred state changing, not on price crossing a line.
ideas.novelty: The state is latent and inferred from the full return distribution rather than read off a price-derived indicator. Nothing in the existing 32 uses a probabilistic state estimate, and the forward-only recursion makes it causal where most published HMM regime work uses Viterbi over the whole sample and is therefore look-ahead contaminated.
ideas.source: Hamilton (1989), 'A New Approach to the Economic Analysis of Nonstationary Time Series and the Business Cycle', Econometrica 57(2). Rolling 2-state Gaussian HMM on daily log returns with vol-ordered state labelling is the exact benchmark specification in arXiv:2402.05272, 'Downside Risk Reduction Using Regime-Switching Signals: A Statistical Jump Model Approach'. Implementation walkthrough: quantstart.com/articles/hidden-markov-models-for-regime-detection-using-r/

ideas.name: Jump-Penalised Regime Path (Statistical Jump Model)
inputs: EWM mean / EWM std / EWM downside deviation at 3 half-lives
ideas.entry_rule: Build a 9-column feature matrix from daily log returns r_t: for each half-life h in {5, 21, 63} compute (a) EWM mean of r_t, (b) EWM mean of the downside deviation max(-r_t, 0), (c) EWM standard deviation of r_t. Standardise each column by its trailing 750-bar mean and sd. Over a trailing window of 750 bars fit a K=2 jump model: minimise sum_t ||x_t - mu_{s_t}||^2 + lambda * sum_t 1[s_t != s_{t-1}] by alternating (i) exact dynamic programming over the state path given fixed centroids (Viterbi-style, O(T*K^2)) and (ii) recomputing each centroid as the mean of its assigned rows; initialise with k-means++, 10 restarts, iterate to convergence. Default lambda = 50. Take the last state on the fitted path as today's regime; the centroid with the higher EWM mean and lower EWM sd is 'bull'. LONG entry at the next open when today's state is bull and yesterday's fitted state was bear.
ideas.exit_rule: Go flat at the next open on the first bar whose fitted state is bear. No price stop - the regime path is the sole exit, which is the point of the L0 penalty.
params: lambda jump penalty (10-200, the key knob)
ideas.why: An HMM's persistence comes from a transition matrix whose geometric sojourn times are a modelling artefact; the jump model instead pays an explicit fixed cost lambda for every state change and solves for the globally optimal path by dynamic programming. That is a direct, tunable control on how many regime flips per year you are willing to trade, and it makes no distributional assumption at all. Downside-deviation features specifically target the asymmetry that drives drawdowns, so the bear state is defined by the risk you actually care about.
ideas.novelty: L0 penalty on transitions solved by exact DP, rather than a probability threshold or a smoothing filter. It produces an order of magnitude fewer regime flips than a thresholded HMM posterior on the same data, and lambda is a single interpretable dial where an HMM offers none.
ideas.source: Bemporad, Breschi, Piga & Boyd, 'Fitting jump models', Automatica 96 (2018) - the DP + centroid alternation algorithm. Financial instantiation and the risk/return feature set derived solely from the return series: arXiv:2402.05272, 'Downside Risk Reduction Using Regime-Switching Signals: A Statistical Jump Model Approach' (jump penalty chosen by time-series cross-validation on strategy performance; tested on US, German and Japanese indices 1990-2023).

ideas.name: Volatility-Scaled Symmetric CUSUM Event
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain two accumulators on log returns r_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-1}): S_pos_t = max(0, S_pos_{t-1} + r_t) and S_neg_t = min(0, S_neg_{t-1} + r_t). Threshold h_t = k * sigma_t where sigma_t is the EWM standard deviation of r with span 100 and k = 3. When S_pos_t >= h_t emit an UP event and reset BOTH accumulators to 0; when S_neg_t <= -h_t emit a DOWN event and reset both to 0. LONG entry at the next bar's open on an UP event, but only if it is the second consecutive UP event with no intervening DOWN event. SHORT entry mirrored on a second consecutive DOWN event.
ideas.exit_rule: Triple barrier from the entry price: profit target at +2 * sigma_t * sqrt(10), stop at -1 * sigma_t * sqrt(10), vertical barrier at 10 bars - whichever is touched first. Additionally exit immediately on any opposite-direction CUSUM event.
ideas.why: CUSUM is the classical optimal detector for a shift in the mean of a process, and the reset makes signal spacing endogenous: quiet, drifting periods emit nothing at all, while a persistent drift accumulates and fires. Scaling h by EWM volatility makes the same code work across tickers and across the volatility cycle without re-tuning. Requiring two same-direction events before trading filters the single-shock case and keeps only genuine persistent mean shifts, which is what CUSUM is theoretically good at detecting.
ideas.novelty: Not a level, a crossover, or a channel break - the trigger is cumulative deviation since the last reset, so an identical absolute price move cannot re-trigger and the same move fires or does not depending on what has accumulated. This is a fundamentally different sampling scheme from any fixed-lookback indicator in the existing 32.
ideas.source: Page (1954), 'Continuous Inspection Schemes', Biometrika 41(1-2). Financial form with volatility-scaled threshold and reset: Lopez de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018), section 2.5.2.1 'The CUSUM Filter'. Reference implementation: github.com/muMAJJI/Trading---CUSUM-FILTER

ideas.name: Bayesian Run-Length Collapse
ideas.entry_rule: Run Adams-MacKay Bayesian online change-point detection on log returns with a Gaussian observation model and a conjugate Normal-Inverse-Gamma prior (mu0 = 0, kappa0 = 1, alpha0 = 1, beta0 = variance of the first 100 returns) and constant hazard H = 1/250. At each bar propagate the run-length posterior P(r_t | data) by the standard message-passing recursion (growth probability = predictive * (1-H), changepoint probability = sum of predictive * H), cap run length at 500 and renormalise. Define R_t = argmax_r P(r_t = r). Declare a change point when R_t < R_{t-1} - 1 (the MAP run length collapses instead of incrementing by one) AND P(r_t <= 5) > 0.30. On a declared change point compute m = mean of the last 5 log returns. LONG entry at the next open if m > 0; SHORT if m < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next declared change point, or after 20 bars, or on a stop at 2 * sigma_20 * sqrt(bars_held) adverse from entry - whichever first.
ideas.why: CUSUM asks whether the mean moved; BOCPD asks whether the entire generating distribution changed, and returns a calibrated posterior over how long the current regime has been running. That posterior is a free confidence measure - you can require the model to be genuinely sure a break happened rather than trading every threshold touch. Direction is read from the NEW segment, so the strategy is agnostic about whether a break continues or reverses the prior trend, which is the honest position given that breaks do both.
ideas.novelty: The tradeable object is a posterior over run length, not a statistic crossing a threshold. It gives an explicit probability that we are early in a fresh regime, which no indicator in the existing set can express, and the confidence gate P(r<=5) > 0.30 is a principled abstention that suppresses most marginal breaks.
ideas.source: Adams & MacKay, 'Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection', arXiv:0710.3742 (2007) - run-length posterior, message-passing recursion, hazard function H(tau). Financial evaluation of detection rules and hazard-rate tuning: ACM DL doi 10.1145/3795154.3795291, 'Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection for Financial Time Series'.

ideas.name: FLOSS Arc-Curve Segmentation
ideas.entry_rule: On the trailing n = 1000 bars of close, compute the matrix profile INDEX I with subsequence length m = 30 using MASS (FFT-based z-normalised Euclidean distance) with an exclusion zone of m/2, keeping only arcs that point FORWARD in time (the online FLOSS variant, which is what makes it causal). Build the arc curve AC[i] = the number of pairs (j, I[j]) whose arc spans index i. Divide by the theoretical parabolic arc count 2*i*(n-i)/n to get the corrected arc curve CAC[i], clipped at 1. Declare a regime boundary at the most recent index i that is a local minimum of CAC with CAC[i] < 0.35 and is at least 5*m bars from any previously declared boundary. LONG entry at the next open when a boundary was declared within the last 3 bars AND the mean close over the bars since the boundary exceeds the mean close over the m bars immediately before it; SHORT if lower.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next declared regime boundary, or after 30 bars, or on a 2.5*ATR(14) trailing stop from the best close since entry - whichever first.
ideas.why: Nearest-neighbour pointers between similar subsequences rarely cross a genuine semantic boundary: if the market's shape vocabulary changes at time i, subsequences after i will match each other rather than anything before i, so the arc count over i collapses. This detects a change in the KIND of behaviour - the character of the wiggles - independently of price level, volatility level, or trend. It is the one segmentation method here that will flag a regime change in which volatility and mean are both unchanged.
ideas.novelty: Regime boundaries come from the topology of nearest-neighbour arcs, not from any moment of the return distribution. The only parameter that matters is the subsequence length m. Nothing in the existing 32 or in the other ideas here detects a change in pattern vocabulary at constant mean and variance.
ideas.source: Gharghabi, Ding, Yeh, Kamgar, Ulanova & Keogh, 'Matrix Profile VIII: Domain Agnostic Online Semantic Segmentation at Superhuman Performance Levels', IEEE ICDM 2017 (FLUSS offline, FLOSS online with forward-only arcs). UCR Matrix Profile page: cs.ucr.edu/~eamonn/MatrixProfile.html. Financial application survey: 'Financial Time Series: Market Analysis Techniques Based on Matrix Profiles', MDPI Engineering Proceedings 5(1):45.

ideas.name: Analogue Forecast with Distance Abstention
ideas.entry_rule: Let w_t be the last m = 20 closes z-normalised (subtract window mean, divide by window sd). For every historical index j in the trailing 2000 bars satisfying j <= t - m - H (H = 10, which enforces that the neighbour's forward return was already fully observed) and |j - t| > m (no self-overlap), compute d_j = Euclidean distance between w_t and the z-normalised window ending at j. Take the k = 25 smallest d_j. Let f_j = ln(C_{j+H}/C_j). LONG entry at the next open when ALL of: (a) mean of f_j over the k neighbours > 0.25 * sigma_H, where sigma_H = sd of H-bar log returns over the trailing 250 bars; (b) at least 65% of the k neighbours have f_j > 0; (c) the mean of the k neighbour distances is below its own 20th percentile over the trailing 250 bars. SHORT is the exact mirror.
ideas.exit_rule: Hard time exit after exactly H = 10 bars (matching the forecast horizon the neighbours voted on), plus a stop at 2 * sigma_H adverse.
ideas.why: There is no model - the history IS the model, so it can express any nonlinear shape-to-outcome mapping without a functional form or a fitting step. Condition (c) is the part that matters: standard k-NN always returns k neighbours no matter how far away they are, and so always produces a forecast even when the current shape is unprecedented. Requiring the neighbours to be genuinely close turns k-NN into a system that abstains most of the time and speaks only when the market is repeating itself.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from any indicator: the feature is the whole z-normalised price path shape, and the signal is a vote of historical analogues' realised forward returns. The distance-percentile abstention gate is the substantive addition over textbook k-NN implementations, which have no notion of 'I have never seen this before'.
ideas.source: Yeh, Zhu, Ulanova, Begum, Ding, Dau, Silva, Mueen & Keogh, 'Matrix Profile I: All Pairs Similarity Joins for Time Series', IEEE ICDM 2016 - the z-normalised nearest-neighbour machinery and MASS. Discretised (SAX) variant: Lin, Keogh, Lonardi & Chiu (2003), 'A Symbolic Representation of Time Series, with Implications for Streaming Algorithms', ACM SIGMOD DMKD Workshop. Financial k-NN evidence: Alkhatib & Najadat, 'Stock Price Prediction Using K-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) Algorithm'.

ideas.name: Discord Novelty Breakout
ideas.entry_rule: Using the same m = 20 z-normalised close windows, compute D_t = the minimum over all non-overlapping historical windows j in the trailing 2000 bars of the z-normalised Euclidean distance between w_t and w_j - i.e. the matrix profile VALUE at t, the nearest-neighbour distance. LONG entry at the next open when ALL of: (a) D_t > the 97th percentile of D over the trailing 500 bars (the current shape is a discord - unprecedented in two years of history); (b) the sum of the last m log returns > 0; (c) mean volume over the last 3 bars > 1.5x the 20-bar average volume. SHORT is the mirror with a negative m-bar return sum.
ideas.exit_rule: Trail a stop at 3 * ATR(14) below the highest close since entry (above the lowest for shorts); hard time exit at 25 bars. No profit target - the thesis is that novelty precedes an extended move.
ideas.why: A discord is a bar sequence the market has not produced before. Institutional flow that is large enough to change the shape of the tape - a new participant, a repositioning, an information event - shows up as shape novelty before it shows up as a completed trend, and it tends to persist because the flow driving it takes days to complete. Volume confirmation separates genuine new flow from a single erratic print.
ideas.novelty: This is shape novelty, not range expansion: a sequence can be a discord at perfectly ordinary ATR and ordinary Bollinger width, because the anomaly is in the ORDER and relative geometry of the moves after z-normalisation removes scale. That makes it orthogonal to the ATR expansion breakout and squeeze release already in the set - it fires on different bars.
ideas.source: Lu, Keogh et al., 'Matrix Profile XXIV: Scaling Time Series Anomaly Detection to Trillions of Datapoints and Ultra-fast Arriving Data Streams (DAMP)', KDD 2022 - discord definition and the online discord-aware matrix profile. UCR Matrix Profile page: cs.ucr.edu/~eamonn/MatrixProfile.html

ideas.name: Online Logistic Regression with Dead Band
ideas.entry_rule: Feature vector x_t, every element standardised by an EXPANDING mean/sd using only data up to t-1: x1 = (C_t - EMA20_t)/ATR14_t; x2 = ln(C_t/C_{t-5})/(sigma_20 * sqrt(5)); x3 = RSI(14)/100 - 0.5; x4 = ln(V_t / mean(V,20)); x5 = (C_t - L_t)/(H_t - L_t) - 0.5; x6 = ATR14_t/mean(ATR14,100) - 1; x7 = ln(O_t/C_{t-1})/sigma_20; x8 = 1 (bias). Target y_t = 1 if ln(C_{t+5}/C_t) > 0 else 0. Weights w updated by online SGD ONLY when a label matures - at bar t+5 apply w += eta*(y_t - sigmoid(w.x_t))*x_t - eta*l2*w with eta = 0.01, l2 = 1e-4. Warm up on the first 500 bars with no trading. LONG entry at the next open when sigmoid(w.x_t) > 0.58; SHORT when sigmoid(w.x_t) < 0.42; no trade in between.
ideas.exit_rule: Fixed 5-bar horizon exit matching the label definition, overridden by a 2*ATR(14) stop. If the probability condition still holds at the exit bar, re-enter at the next open, so a persistent signal rolls the position rather than flipping flat.
ideas.why: The weights are never batch-refit, so they drift continuously with the market and the model reinterprets its own features: in a trending regime the coefficient on x2 (5-bar momentum) goes positive, and in a choppy one it goes negative, so one piece of code is a momentum model and a reversion model at different times without any regime classifier bolted on. The dead band around 0.5 means the model is silent when its features disagree, which is most of the time.
ideas.novelty: An adaptive, sign-flipping linear combination of features rather than a fixed rule over one indicator. The delayed-label update (weights only learn from bar t at bar t+5) is the causally honest version that most published implementations get wrong, and the probability dead band is an explicit abstention region no threshold indicator has.
ideas.source: Standard online SGD logistic regression. Finance instantiation with technical-indicator features and a cascaded architecture: Zhang, Zhang et al., 'Cascading logistic regression onto gradient boosted decision trees for forecasting and trading stock indices', Applied Soft Computing 84 (2019). Adaptive online mid-price learning with Hessian-based adaptive rate: PLOS ONE 15(6): e0234107, 'Mid-price prediction based on machine learning methods with technical and quantitative indicators'.

ideas.name: Meta-Labelled Primary Signal
ideas.entry_rule: PRIMARY model sets side in {+1,-1} on bar t (reference implementation: the 20/50 EMA cross, but any of the existing 32 works). Label every historical primary signal by its triple-barrier outcome: upper barrier at C_t * (1 + side * 2 * sigma_t), lower at C_t * (1 - side * 1 * sigma_t), vertical barrier at 10 bars, where sigma_t is the EWM sd of log returns with span 50; meta-label = 1 if the profit-take barrier is touched first, else 0. Train a SECONDARY binary model (logistic regression, or the 50-stump ensemble of idea 10) on features [ADX(14), ATR14/mean(ATR14,100), (C-EMA50)/ATR14, ln(V/mean(V,20)), RSI(14), permutation entropy (d=3) of the last 40 returns, and for intraday the minutes-since-open], using ONLY labels whose vertical barrier closed before bar t, with a 10-bar embargo after the last training label. ENTRY: take the primary signal at the next open only if the secondary model's predicted probability > 0.55; size the position proportional to (p - 0.55)/0.45.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on whichever of the SAME three barriers used to construct the label is touched first: +2*sigma profit-take, -1*sigma stop, 10-bar vertical. Never exit on a primary-model reversal alone - the label the secondary model learned was defined by these barriers, so the live exit must match it exactly or the model is being asked a different question than it was trained on.
ideas.why: Direction and conviction are different problems and a single model forced to do both does neither well. A trend rule has decent recall and terrible precision; the secondary model's only job is to learn the CONDITIONS under which the primary rule's precision is acceptable - which is a much easier, better-conditioned learning problem because the labels come from the primary signal's actual path-dependent P&L rather than a fixed-horizon return. Position sizing falls out of the probability for free.
ideas.novelty: Not a signal at all - an architecture. Side and size are decided by separate models, training labels are path-dependent triple-barrier outcomes, and the purge-plus-embargo scheme prevents the overlapping-label leakage that makes naive versions of this look spectacular in backtest and fail live. It can be wrapped around any of the 32 existing strategies.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018), Ch. 3 (triple-barrier labelling, getEvents/getBins) and section 3.6 (meta-labelling). Empirical evaluation: Hudson & Thames, 'Does Meta Labeling Add to Signal Efficacy?', hudsonthames.org. Method overview: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meta-Labeling

ideas.name: Rolling AdaBoost Stump Margin
ideas.entry_rule: Every 21 bars, on the trailing 1000 bars, train AdaBoost.M1 with T = 50 depth-1 decision stumps. Candidate scalar features per bar: log return over 1, 3, 5, 10 and 20 bars each divided by sigma_20*sqrt(horizon); ATR14/ATR100; ADX(14); RSI(14); ln(V/mean(V,20)); close location value (C-L)/(H-L); overnight gap ln(O/C_prev)/sigma_20; (H_20 - C)/ATR14 and (C - L_20)/ATR14; realised skew of the last 20 returns. Each stump is a (feature, threshold, polarity) triple selected by exhaustive search over 32 within-feature quantile thresholds to minimise weighted error; boosting weight alpha_i = 0.5*ln((1-err_i)/err_i) with err_i clipped to [1e-6, 0.5-1e-6]. Labels y = sign of the triple-barrier outcome (+2*sigma up, -2*sigma down, 10-bar vertical), with vertical-barrier (flat) outcomes DROPPED from training. Define margin M_t = sum(alpha_i * h_i(x_t)) / sum(alpha_i), which lies in [-1,1]. LONG entry at the next open when M_t > +0.20; SHORT when M_t < -0.20.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when M_t crosses back through zero, or on the triple barrier (+/-2*sigma, 10-bar cap) - whichever first.
ideas.why: Depth-1 stumps can only express 'feature > threshold', so every learner is an interpretable threshold rule of exactly the kind traders already use - and boosting discovers WHICH thresholds on WHICH features the current 1000 bars reward, then reweights them. Because it refits on a rolling window, the ensemble composition is itself a regime readout: when the momentum-feature stumps dominate the alpha mass you are in a trending regime. It captures feature interactions a linear model cannot, while needing no library beyond numpy.
ideas.novelty: Different hypothesis class and different aggregation from the online linear model: an additive ensemble of axis-aligned threshold rules, traded on a continuous margin with an explicit abstention band, not on a class label. The stumps' selected thresholds are directly readable, which makes the model auditable in a way a black-box classifier is not.
ideas.source: Freund & Schapire (1997), 'A Decision-Theoretic Generalization of On-Line Learning and an Application to Boosting', Journal of Computer and System Sciences 55(1). Finance instantiation on technical-indicator features (here deliberately simplified to depth-1 stumps so it runs in plain Python/numpy without sklearn): Zhang et al., Applied Soft Computing 84 (2019), 'Cascading logistic regression onto gradient boosted decision trees for forecasting and trading stock indices'. Labels via Lopez de Prado (2018) Ch. 3.

ideas.name: Causal Trend Scanning (max-|t| horizon)
inputs: OLS slope t-statistic over multiple lookbacks
ideas.entry_rule: At each bar t, for every lookback L in {10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55, 60} regress ln(C) on a time index 0..L-1 over the trailing window [t-L+1, t] and record the OLS slope t-statistic t_L = beta_L / se(beta_L), where se(beta_L) = sqrt( (SSE/(L-2)) / sum((i - ibar)^2) ). Choose L* = argmax_L |t_L| and set T_t = t_{L*}. LONG entry at the next open when T_t > 4.0 AND T_{t-1} <= 4.0 AND L* <= 25. SHORT entry when T_t < -4.0 AND T_{t-1} >= -4.0 AND L* <= 25.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when |T_t| < 1.5 (no horizon shows a significant trend any more), or when sign(T_t) flips, or on a 3*ATR(14) trailing stop from the best close since entry - whichever first.
params: maximum winning L* for the freshness gate
ideas.why: A slope tells you how fast price is moving; a t-statistic tells you how much of that move is signal rather than noise, because it divides by the residual scatter around the fitted line. Two stocks with identical 20-day slopes but different path smoothness get different t-values, and the smooth one is the one worth trading. Letting the data choose the horizon per bar means the system finds the scale at which THIS market is currently trending instead of imposing a fixed lookback that is right only some of the time. The L* <= 25 freshness gate buys young trends rather than exhausted ones.
ideas.novelty: The lookback is selected per bar by statistical significance rather than fixed, and the trigger is a t-statistic crossing - which is volatility-normalised by construction, so it fires on clean trends and stays silent on noisy ones of identical slope. That is structurally different from Hull MA slope or any fixed-window momentum measure, both of which are blind to path smoothness.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, Machine Learning for Asset Managers (Cambridge University Press, 2020) - 'trend scanning': fit regressions over multiple horizons and keep the one with maximum |t| for the slope coefficient. Parameter names and output fields (look_forward_window, min_sample_length, step; returns t-value, return, bin) documented at mlfinpy.readthedocs.io/en/latest/Labelling.html. NOTE: the original is a forward-looking LABELLING method; I have converted it to a causal trailing-window SIGNAL, which is my adaptation and is stated explicitly here.

ideas.name: Ordinal-Pattern Continuation under Low Entropy
ideas.entry_rule: Set embedding dimension d = 4, delay 1. Map the last d closes to their ordinal permutation pattern pi_t - the argsort of [C_{t-3}, C_{t-2}, C_{t-1}, C_t], one of d! = 24 patterns, ties broken by index order. Over the trailing N = 500 bars compute the empirical pattern distribution and permutation entropy PE = -sum_i p_i * ln(p_i) / ln(24). Separately maintain, for each of the 24 patterns, the mean forward 5-bar log return mu_pi and its standard error se_pi over the trailing 1000 bars, excluding the last 5 bars (unmatured). LONG entry at the next open when BOTH: (a) PE < its own 20th percentile over the trailing 500 values, and (b) mu_{pi_t} > 0 with mu_{pi_t}/se_{pi_t} > 2.5. SHORT is the mirror (mu < 0 with t-ratio < -2.5).
ideas.exit_rule: Fixed 5-bar exit matching the horizon over which mu_pi was estimated, plus a 1.5*ATR(14) stop.
ideas.why: The ordinal pattern depends only on the RANK ORDER of the last four closes, so it is invariant to scale and to any monotone transform - volatility is stripped out entirely and only the geometry of the sequence remains. Under a genuine random walk all 24 patterns are equiprobable, so a low permutation entropy is direct evidence that the tape is currently non-random and specific sequences carry information. Conditioning entry on both the global non-randomness AND the specific pattern's own measured forward edge means you only trade when there is measurable inefficiency and you know which way it points.
ideas.novelty: Rank-based rather than value-based: no threshold on any price or indicator level appears anywhere in the rule. The gate is an information-theoretic measure of the whole recent tape and the direction comes from a 24-way conditional lookup table, not from a formula. Nothing in the existing 32 uses ordinal/symbolic dynamics.
ideas.source: Bandt & Pompe (2002), 'Permutation Entropy: A Natural Complexity Measure for Time Series', Physical Review Letters 88, 174102. Financial evidence that under-represented and forbidden ordinal patterns index inefficiency: Zunino, Zanin, Tabak, Perez & Rosso, 'Forbidden patterns, permutation entropy and stock market inefficiency', Physica A 388 (2009). Intraday application: 'Applicability of Intraday Entropy for Trading During Regular Market Hours', Computational Economics, doi 10.1007/s10614-026-11347-2.

ideas.name: Entropy-Rate Book Switch
inputs: log returns quantised to a 3-symbol alphabet
ideas.entry_rule: Quantise log returns into a 3-symbol alphabet by their trailing 250-bar terciles: 'd' (bottom), 'f' (middle), 'u' (top). Take the last 250 symbols as a string. Estimate the entropy rate two ways: (i) PLUG-IN on all overlapping 3-grams, H_plug = -sum_w p_w * ln(p_w) / (3 * ln 3); (ii) LEMPEL-ZIV, one-pass LZ76 parse counting distinct phrases c, H_LZ = c * ln(c) / (n * ln 3). Let H = (H_plug + H_LZ)/2 and P = the percentile rank of H among its own trailing 500 values. IF P < 20 the CONTINUATION book is active: LONG at the next open when the last 3 symbols are 'uuu'; SHORT when they are 'ddd'. IF P > 80 the REVERSION book is active: LONG at the next open when the last 2 symbols are 'dd'; SHORT when they are 'uu'. IF 20 <= P <= 80, take no new position in either book.
ideas.exit_rule: Continuation trades: exit on the first 'd' symbol (first 'u' for shorts) or after 10 bars. Reversion trades: exit on the first 'u' symbol (first 'd' for shorts) or after 3 bars. Both books additionally exit at the next open if P leaves the band that authorised the trade.
params: symbol run lengths for each book
ideas.why: Entropy rate measures compressibility - how much of the next symbol is already determined by the ones before it. A low entropy rate means the return string has exploitable higher-order structure, and critically it can be low while linear autocorrelation is exactly zero, because compressibility captures dependence that correlation cannot see. That makes it a regime variable orthogonal to volatility and to ADX. Using it to select WHICH book runs, rather than to filter one, means the system has something to do in both states.
ideas.novelty: One information-theoretic number arbitrates between two opposite entry logics, and the entry itself is a symbol-run pattern on a quantised return string rather than any indicator threshold. Distinct from the ordinal-pattern idea: that one uses rank permutations and a per-pattern lookup table; this one uses tercile symbols, an entropy RATE (a sequence-compressibility measure), and a book switch.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018), Ch. 18 'Entropy Features' - Shannon entropy, the plug-in/maximum-likelihood estimator over n-grams of quantised returns, Lempel-Ziv estimators, encoding schemes, and their use as market-efficiency features. Chapter contents: oreilly.com/library/view/advances-in-financial/9781119482086/c18.xhtml. Underlying estimator: Lempel & Ziv (1976), 'On the Complexity of Finite Sequences', IEEE Trans. Information Theory 22(1).

ideas.name: Variance-Ratio Significance Gate
ideas.entry_rule: On the trailing n = 250 log returns compute the Lo-MacKinlay variance ratio VR(q) with q = 5 using overlapping q-period returns and the unbiased finite-sample corrections, plus its heteroskedasticity-consistent test statistic z(q) = (VR(q) - 1) / sqrt(theta_star(q)), where theta_star(q) = sum_{j=1}^{q-1} [2(q-j)/q]^2 * delta_j and delta_j is the Lo-MacKinlay heteroskedasticity-consistent estimator of the j-th autocovariance-of-squares term. Let D_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-5}) / sd(5-bar log returns over 250 bars). IF z(5) < -1.96 (significant mean reversion): LONG at the next open when D_t < -1.0; SHORT when D_t > +1.0. IF z(5) > +1.96 (significant momentum) the rule INVERTS: LONG when D_t > +1.0; SHORT when D_t < -1.0. IF |z(5)| <= 1.96 take no position.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after exactly 5 bars, or when D_t crosses back through zero, or on a stop at 2.5 * sd(5-bar returns) adverse - whichever first. Also exit at the next open if z(5) crosses out of the significance band that authorised the trade.
params: optional Hurst exponent as an alternative estimator
ideas.why: The variance ratio is the cleanest test of whether q-period variance scales linearly with q, which it does under a random walk. Using the heteroskedasticity-robust z rather than the raw VR matters enormously in equities, because volatility clustering alone pushes VR away from 1 and produces spurious 'mean reversion' readings. Gating on the test statistic means the system is silent in the very common case where the market is statistically indistinguishable from a random walk - which is the honest answer most of the time - and inverts its own logic only when the data significantly says momentum.
ideas.novelty: The switch is on a SIGNIFICANCE TEST, not a point estimate or a threshold on an indicator, so the strategy has three states including a genuine do-nothing state, and the same code runs as a fade or a breakout depending on a hypothesis test outcome. Distinct from ADX gating (which measures trend strength, not the serial-dependence sign) and from the RLS idea below (one-lag, recursive, no window).
ideas.source: Lo & MacKinlay (1988), 'Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test', Review of Financial Studies 1(1):41-66 - VR(q), the finite-sample corrections and the heteroskedasticity-robust z. Regime-switching application of the closely related Hurst exponent: 'Hurst Exponent as a Regime-Switching Indicator', apjm.apacific.org/PDFs/12-109.pdf. Practitioner treatment: quanterlab.com/articles/mr-variance-ratio

ideas.name: k-Means State Prototypes with Edge Test
ideas.entry_rule: Build a 6-dimensional feature vector per bar, each element standardised against its trailing 500-bar mean/sd: f1 = ln(C_t/C_{t-5}); f2 = ln(sd(last 10 returns)/sd(last 60 returns)); f3 = (H_t - L_t)/ATR14_t; f4 = ln(V_t/mean(V,20)); f5 = (C_t - L_20)/(H_20 - L_20); f6 = realised skew of the last 20 returns. Fit k-means with K = 6 (k-means++ init, 20 restarts, 100 max iterations) on the trailing 1000 feature vectors; refit every 63 bars. Assign today's vector to its nearest centroid c. Using only bars strictly before the refit date, compute for each cluster the mean 5-bar forward log return m_c and its t-statistic t_c = m_c / (sd_c / sqrt(n_c)). LONG entry at the next open when today's cluster has m_c > 0 AND t_c > 2.0 AND today's Euclidean distance to its centroid is below that cluster's median member distance. SHORT is the mirror (m_c < 0, t_c < -2.0).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after 5 bars, or immediately at the next open if the new bar is assigned to a cluster whose t_c has the opposite sign, or on a 2*ATR(14) stop - whichever first.
ideas.why: Clustering the STATE (volatility ratio, range, volume, skew, position within range) rather than the price path finds recurring market conditions directly, and unlike an HMM it imposes no transition model, so it reacts on the first bar that enters a state instead of waiting for a posterior to accumulate. The two gates are what make it tradeable: requiring t_c > 2 means you only trade states with a statistically real historical edge, and requiring the bar to be a CENTRAL member of the cluster means you do not trade boundary cases that k-means assigned almost arbitrarily.
ideas.novelty: Prototype-based rather than neighbour-based (unlike the k-NN idea) and memoryless rather than persistent (unlike the HMM and jump model), with an explicit significance test on each cluster's edge and a centrality requirement on membership. The Wasserstein variant swaps the point-feature distance for a distance between the clusters' empirical return DISTRIBUTIONS, which is the published upgrade.
ideas.source: QuantStart, 'K-Means Clustering of Daily OHLC Bar Data', quantstart.com/articles/k-means-clustering-of-daily-ohlc-bar-data/. Distribution-aware upgrade: Horvath, Issa & Muguruza, 'Clustering Market Regimes using the Wasserstein Distance', arXiv:2110.11848, published Journal of Computational Finance 28(1):1-39, 2024 (Wasserstein k-means on empirical measures; reported to outperform all considered alternatives and to be robust to the underlying model).

ideas.name: Page-Hinkley Drift Hibernation
ideas.category: regime detection / concept drift on strategy outcomes
inputs: closed-trade outcome stream of a base strategy
ideas.entry_rule: Overlay on any base signal (reference: 20/50 EMA cross). Score each CLOSED base trade as e_i = 1 if it lost money net of an assumed round-trip cost, 0 if it won. Run the Page-Hinkley test on the sequence e_i: ebar_i = running mean of e through i; m_i = m_{i-1} + (e_i - ebar_i - delta) with delta = 0.005 and m_0 = 0; M_i = min(m_1..m_i); PH_i = m_i - M_i. Declare DRIFT when PH_i > lambda = 5. In the normal state the ENTRY rule is: take the base signal at the next open. On drift, switch to SHADOW mode - stop entering, but keep simulating and scoring the base signal's trades with m and M reset to zero. Resume live entries only after 10 consecutive shadow trades during which PH stays below lambda AND the shadow win rate exceeds 50%.
ideas.exit_rule: Base-signal exits are unchanged (opposite cross, or a 2.5*ATR(14) trailing stop). In addition, any open position is closed at the next open on the bar the drift alarm fires - a dead edge is not a reason to keep risk on.
params: swap Page-Hinkley for ADWIN or DDM
ideas.why: Every strategy's edge eventually decays, and the usual response is discretionary or a crude drawdown cutoff that fires late and restarts on a hunch. Monitoring the strategy's OWN outcome stream with a sequential change detector asks the right question directly - has the loss rate shifted upward beyond what chance explains - and answers it with a formal test. Because the monitored series is trade outcomes rather than price, it fires when the edge dies even if nothing about the price series looks unusual, which is exactly the case a price-based regime filter misses.
ideas.novelty: A distinct exit/allocation structure rather than an entry signal: the input is the strategy's realised P&L stream, not market data, and there is a formal, non-discretionary re-entry criterion via shadow-mode trading. No existing strategy in the set has any concept of turning itself off and proving itself back on.
ideas.source: Page (1954), 'Continuous Inspection Schemes', Biometrika 41 (Page-Hinkley test). ADWIN alternative: Bifet & Gavalda (2007), 'Learning from Time-Changing Data with Adaptive Windowing', SIAM SDM - variable-length window split into sub-windows, drift when the sub-window mean difference exceeds a threshold, no window size to set. Survey and DDM: Gama, Zliobaite, Bifet, Pechenizkiy & Bouchachia, 'A Survey on Concept Drift Adaptation', ACM Computing Surveys 46(4), 2014. Implementations: cran.r-project.org/web/packages/datadriftR/

ideas.name: Duration-Hazard Phase Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Date bull/bear phases causally with a Bry-Boschan / Pagan-Sossounov rule on daily closes using window w = 21: index t is a PEAK if C_t = max(C_{t-w..t+w}) and a TROUGH if C_t = min over the same window; enforce a minimum phase length of 21 bars and a minimum amplitude of 8% between consecutive turning points, alternating peaks and troughs. Apply the rule only to data up to t-w, so the dating is causal; the last w bars are the 'provisional' tail of the current phase. Maintain, over all available history, the empirical distribution of COMPLETED phase durations separately for bull and for bear phases. LONG entry at the next open when ALL of: (a) the current phase is a bear, (b) its age in trading days exceeds the 60th percentile of historical bear durations, (c) the close has risen at least 1.5*ATR(14) off the running minimum of the phase within the last 5 bars. SHORT entry is the mirror at old bull-phase age with a 1.5*ATR fall off the running maximum.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when the phase age exceeds the 90th percentile of historical bull durations (for a long), or on a 2.5*ATR(14) trailing stop below the highest close since entry, or when a new provisional peak is dated - whichever first.
ideas.why: A standard Markov or HMM regime model has geometric sojourn times, which are memoryless: the probability the regime ends today is the same whether it started last week or last year. That is empirically false - stock market phases show positive duration dependence, so the longer a bear has run the higher its termination hazard. Trading the hazard means buying when a downtrend is statistically overdue to end AND price has confirmed with a real move off the low, which is a fundamentally different timing logic from buying a dip or a crossover.
ideas.novelty: Conditions on HOW LONG the current state has lasted - a variable no HMM, no moving average and none of the existing 32 can express. The entry is the empirical termination hazard crossing a percentile, with price confirmation as a secondary trigger, not the other way round.
ideas.source: Pagan & Sossounov (2003), 'A Simple Framework for Analysing Bull and Bear Markets', Journal of Applied Econometrics 18(1):23-46 - the censoring rules (minimum phase length, minimum cycle length, amplitude) for turning-point dating; original monthly calibration is a 6-month window, 4-month minimum phase and 20% amplitude, rescaled here for daily bars. Lunde & Timmermann (2004), 'Duration Dependence in Stock Prices: An Analysis of Bull and Bear Markets', Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 22(3) - positive duration dependence in phase termination. Semi-Markov formalisation: Bulla & Bulla, 'Stylized facts of financial time series and hidden semi-Markov models', Computational Statistics & Data Analysis 51 (2006).

ideas.name: Split-Conformal Zero-Exclusion
ideas.entry_rule: Base predictor: ridge regression (alpha = 1.0, closed-form normal equations in numpy) of the forward 5-bar log return on the standardised 7-feature vector from the online logistic idea. Every 21 bars refit on the trailing 750 bars, split as the OLDER 500 for training and the MOST RECENT 250 as a conformal calibration set (the model never sees the calibration rows). On the calibration set compute normalised nonconformity scores s_i = |y_i - yhat_i| / u_i with the uncertainty proxy u_i = ATR14_i / C_i. Let q = the ceil((250+1)*(1-alpha))/250 empirical quantile of the s_i with alpha = 0.20. For the live bar the 80% prediction interval is yhat_t +/- q*u_t. LONG entry at the next open when the entire interval lies above zero, i.e. yhat_t - q*u_t > 0. SHORT when yhat_t + q*u_t < 0. Otherwise abstain.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after 5 bars (the prediction horizon), or immediately if the live interval straddles zero on 2 consecutive bars, or on a stop placed at q*u_t adverse from entry - the model's own calibrated uncertainty scale rather than an arbitrary ATR multiple.
params: uncertainty proxy u (ATR/C vs EWM return sd)
ideas.why: A point forecast of 0.3% is meaningless without knowing whether the model's typical error is 0.1% or 3%. Split conformal gives a finite-sample, distribution-free coverage guarantee under exchangeability with essentially no assumptions and no extra fitting - just a quantile of held-out residuals. Requiring the whole interval to exclude zero means you trade only when the calibrated uncertainty is small enough that the sign of the move is not in doubt, which automatically stands the strategy down in high-noise periods. Normalising the residual by ATR is the Mondrian/locally-adaptive variant, which keeps interval width proportional to current volatility.
ideas.novelty: The decision comes from an interval, not a point estimate or a probability threshold - so abstention is the default and trading is the exception, and the stop distance is derived from the same calibrated quantile that authorised the trade. Nothing else in the set sizes or gates on a distribution-free uncertainty estimate.
ideas.source: Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer, Algorithmic Learning in a Random World (Springer, 2005); Lei, G'Sell, Rinaldo, Tibshirani & Wasserman (2018) split conformal. Coverage under the non-exchangeability of financial series (the caveat that matters here): Barber, Candes, Ramdas & Tibshirani, 'Conformal prediction beyond exchangeability' and arXiv:2203.15885, 'Split Conformal Prediction and Non-Exchangeable Data'. Time-series conformal sets: arXiv:2206.07851. Financial walkthrough: mql5.com/en/articles/18324, 'Exploring Conformal Forecasting of Financial Time Series'.

ideas.name: RLS Adaptive Autocorrelation Sign
ideas.entry_rule: Standardise log returns as z_t = r_t / sigma_t with sigma_t the EWM sd (span 100). Run recursive least squares with exponential forgetting on z_t = a + b*z_{t-1} + e_t. With x = [1, z_{t-1}]', update: k = P x / (mu + x' P x); theta += k*(z_t - x'theta); P = (P - k x' P)/mu, with forgetting factor mu = 0.97 and P initialised to 1000*I, theta to [0,0]. Let b_t = theta[1]. Track the recursive standard error se_t = sqrt(s2_t * P[1,1]) where s2_t is an EWM estimate of the residual variance (span 100), and define the ratio G_t = b_t/se_t. LONG entry at the next open when EITHER (a) G_t < -2.0 and z_t < -1.0 (significant one-lag mean reversion, and the last bar was a large down bar), OR (b) G_t > +2.0 and z_t > +1.0 (significant one-lag momentum, last bar was a large up bar). SHORT entry mirrors both branches with the sign of z_t reversed.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after 3 bars, or when |G_t| falls below 1.0 (the serial-dependence structure has evaporated), or on a 2 * sigma_t stop - whichever first.
ideas.why: The regime variable here is a model parameter being tracked in real time, so there is no window length to choose and no refit schedule - the forgetting factor mu sets an effective memory of about 1/(1-mu) bars continuously. When b is significantly negative the market is genuinely fading its own moves at the one-bar scale and you should fade with it; when significantly positive it is extending them. The significance ratio, rather than the raw coefficient, keeps you out during the long stretches where b is noise around zero, which for liquid US equities is most of the time.
ideas.novelty: A recursively estimated model coefficient IS the regime indicator, updated every bar with no window. Distinct from the variance-ratio idea, which uses a multi-period ratio over a fixed 250-bar sample and a formal hypothesis test on a 5-bar deviation; this one is one-lag, recursive, memory-weighted, and triggers on a single-bar move. This idea is largely synthesis - the RLS machinery is textbook and the trading application is my own construction, so treat the citation as method provenance rather than published evidence of profitability. NOTE ON COVERAGE: 19 ideas are returned here, comfortably above the 14 requested; the domain yields more than that and the binding constraint was distinctness, not supply.
ideas.source: Synthesis. RLS with exponential forgetting is standard: Ljung, System Identification: Theory for the User (2nd ed., Prentice Hall, 1999), ch. 11 recursive estimation. The pattern of online adaptive-rate learning applied to short-horizon price prediction appears in PLOS ONE 15(6): e0234107, 'Mid-price prediction based on machine learning methods with technical and quantitative indicators' (online learning with adaptive rate for next mid-price move). The specific entry/exit construction above is mine, not taken from a paper.

ideas.name: Phase C Spring-Test Sequence
ideas.timeframe: daily or 15-minute (identical rules, ATR/SMA computed on the working timeframe)
ideas.entry_rule: Let ATR = ATR(14) and AV = SMA(volume,20) on the working timeframe. (1) Trading range: L = min(low) over bars t-60..t-1, H = max(high) over the same window; require (H-L) <= 3.0*ATR, at least 2 bars separated by >=5 bars with low <= L+0.25*ATR, and at least 2 bars separated by >=5 bars with high >= H-0.25*ATR. (2) Climax bar C = the bar in that window with the lowest low; require volume(C) >= 2.0*AV(C). (3) Spring bar S at index s: low(S) < L - 0.05*ATR AND close(S) > L AND volume(S) <= volume(C). (4) Test bar T at index in s+1..s+10: low(T) > low(S) AND low(T) <= L + 0.5*ATR AND volume(T) <= 0.7*AV AND (high(T)-low(T)) <= 0.7*ATR. (5) LONG entry: buy at the close of the first bar after T whose close > high(T). Abort the whole setup if any close < low(S) before entry. SHORT is the exact mirror (upthrust above H with volume(C) at the highest high, penetration bar closing back below H, then a lower-high low-volume test).
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop = low(S) - 0.10*ATR (mirror: high of upthrust + 0.10*ATR). Take half off at H (the trading-range boundary). Trail the remainder at (highest close since entry) - 2.0*ATR. Hard time stop: exit at market if H is not reached within 30 bars.
ideas.why: Wyckoff's Phase C: the composite operator drives price below obvious support to trigger resting stops and measure how much supply is actually available. The information is not in the penetration itself but in the follow-up test - if the second probe of the low comes on materially lower volume and a narrower spread, the supply that produced the original climax has been exhausted. Requiring the spring's volume to be <= the climax volume is the discriminator between a genuine shakeout inside an accumulated range and a real breakdown.
ideas.source: StockCharts ChartSchool, 'The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial' (spring/shakeout, test: 'higher low on lesser volume', SC 'absorbed by larger professional interests'); Wyckoff Analytics, 'Identifying Wyckoff Springs with Algorithmic Trading Strategies' (support lookback 15-25 bars, close must not be at the bar low, penetration must be temporary). Exact thresholds pinned down by me.
ideas.novelty: Not a liquidity sweep: the sweep bar is never the entry. Entry requires a two-stage sequence (penetration, then a separate higher-low low-volume test) plus a volume relation to a previously identified climax bar. A plain sweep strategy fires on the wick; this one fires several bars later and rejects the majority of sweeps because their tests come on equal or higher volume.

ideas.name: LPSY Failed-Rally Short
ideas.entry_rule: ATR = ATR(14), AV = SMA(volume,20). (1) Prior uptrend: close[t-60] > close[t-120] (daily) or close[t-120] > close[t-240] (intraday). (2) Distribution range: H = max(high), L = min(low) over t-60..t-1 with (H-L) <= 3.0*ATR. (3) Sign of Weakness: a bar B with close(B) < L - 0.5*ATR and volume(B) >= 1.5*AV. (4) Failing rally: within 15 bars after B, a sequence of >=2 consecutive bars with rising highs whose highest high stays BELOW L + 0.25*ATR (i.e. the rally never reclaims the broken boundary), and whose final bar has volume <= 0.8*AV and (high-low) <= 0.8*ATR. (5) SHORT entry: sell at the close of the first bar whose close < the prior bar's low. Cancel the setup if any close > L + 0.25*ATR.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = rally high + 0.10*ATR. Target = L - (H - L), i.e. the range width projected down from the broken support; take half there. Trail the remainder at (lowest close since entry) + 2.0*ATR. Abandon after 40 bars.
ideas.why: Phase D of distribution. Once supply has demonstrably overwhelmed demand (the wide-spread, high-volume break of the range low), the remaining rallies are the composite operator's last opportunities to unload. The signature of a Last Point of Supply is that demand cannot lift price back to the broken boundary AND the rally is made on contracting volume and spread - buyers are absent rather than merely outnumbered.
ideas.source: StockCharts ChartSchool, 'The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial' - SOW defined as 'down-move to (or slightly past) the lower boundary of the TR, usually occurring on increased spread and volume'; LPSY as 'a feeble rally showing considerable difficulty advancing'. Thresholds pinned down by me.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from a break-of-structure retest short in two ways: the rally is required to FAIL to reach the broken level (a retest strategy waits for the level to be touched, this one refuses the trade if it is), and the rally must show simultaneous volume AND spread contraction. Those two conditions reject most retests, which is the point.

ideas.name: Effort-versus-Result Absorption Bar
ideas.entry_rule: Per bar compute Effort E = volume / SMA(volume,20) and Result R = (high-low) / ATR(14), and close-location CL = (close-low)/(high-low). LONG absorption bar A requires: E >= 2.0 AND R <= 0.60 AND CL >= 0.65 AND low(A) <= (40-bar lowest low) + 0.30*ATR. Enter long at the close of the next bar if that bar's close > high(A) and its low >= low(A). SHORT mirror: E >= 2.0, R <= 0.60, CL <= 0.35, high(A) >= (40-bar highest high) - 0.30*ATR; enter short at the close of the next bar closing below low(A). Optional regime confirmation: the bar's Amihud ratio |close/close[1]-1| / (close*volume) must sit in the bottom 20th percentile of its own 250-bar history (very low price impact per unit volume = absorption).
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = low(A) - 0.10*ATR (mirror: high(A) + 0.10*ATR). Target = entry + 2.0 * (entry - stop). Time stop: exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry if neither level is touched.
ideas.why: Wyckoff's third law: large effort producing small result means the move is being absorbed by an opposing party. Formalised, that is exactly Amihud's price-impact ratio - a bar where a lot of volume produced almost no price displacement has abnormally low realised impact, which is the microstructure signature of a large passive counterparty filling into the flow. Requiring the close in the upper third says the absorbing side won the bar.
ideas.source: StockCharts ChartSchool, 'The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial' - Law of Effort versus Result: 'High volume with minimal price advance suggests absorption of supply or weakness'. Formalisation via Amihud, Y. (2002), 'Illiquidity and stock returns: cross-section and time-series effects', Journal of Financial Markets: ILLIQ_t = |R_t| / DollarVolume_t.
ideas.novelty: No band, no oscillator, no moving average. The signal is a two-dimensional condition on the SAME bar - volume expansion with range contraction - combined with location at a 40-bar extreme. Bollinger-with-volume fires on volume plus a band touch, which is a range-EXPANSION signal; this one requires range compression, so the two almost never fire on the same bar.

ideas.name: Wyckoff Wave Volume Ratio
ideas.entry_rule: Segment the series into waves with a ZigZag on closes using a reversal threshold of 1.0*ATR(14). For the last 6 completed waves compute UpVol = (total volume in all up-waves)/(total bars in all up-waves) and DnVol = (total volume in all down-waves)/(total bars in all down-waves); WVR = UpVol/DnVol. LONG entry: WVR crosses above 1.50 on the close of a bar, AND the most recent completed down-wave's low >= the previous down-wave's low - 0.10*ATR (equal or higher low), AND price is inside a range: (60-bar high - 60-bar low) <= 3.0*ATR. Buy at that close. SHORT mirror: WVR crosses below 0.667 with the most recent completed up-wave's high <= previous up-wave's high + 0.10*ATR, inside the same range condition.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = the most recent completed wave low - 0.25*ATR (mirror: wave high + 0.25*ATR). Exit the position when WVR crosses back below 1.00 (mirror: above 1.00). Take profit at the 60-bar range high + 1.5*ATR. Abandon after 40 bars if WVR has not held above 1.20.
ideas.why: Wyckoff read tape in waves, not bars: he compared the total volume and duration of each buying wave against each selling wave to judge which side was dominant inside a trading range. When rallies inside a range carry systematically more volume per bar than declines, while the declines stop at successively equal-or-higher lows, supply is being withdrawn and stock is moving into strong hands - accumulation, before any breakout is visible on price alone.
ideas.source: Wyckoff's Wave Chart / buying-and-selling-wave analysis, as described in StockCharts ChartSchool 'The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial' (composite operator, law of supply and demand). The specific ZigZag segmentation and the UpVol/DnVol ratio construction are my synthesis - Wyckoff specified the concept, not a formula.
ideas.novelty: Volume is aggregated per SWING SEGMENT, not per bar. OBV, MFI, Chaikin A/D and every other volume oscillator accumulate bar-by-bar and therefore mix a 1-bar reaction into a 12-bar rally. Segmenting first means the comparison is effort-per-leg-of-auction, which is what the underlying claim actually is. The equal-or-higher-low condition is a structural filter no volume oscillator carries.

ideas.name: Cause-and-Effect Count Sizing
ideas.entry_rule: Build a point-and-figure chart from daily closes with box size = 0.5*ATR(14) measured on the day the congestion begins (fixed thereafter) and a 3-box reversal. Identify the current congestion: the maximal set of consecutive P&F columns whose column highs and column lows all lie inside a band of width <= 6 boxes. Let N = the number of columns in that congestion, CH = congestion high price, CL = congestion low price. LONG entry: buy at the close of the first daily bar whose close > CH + 0.10*ATR, and ONLY IF N >= 8. SHORT mirror: sell at the close of the first daily bar closing < CL - 0.10*ATR with N >= 8.
ideas.exit_rule: Target (this is the whole point of the idea) = CL + N * boxsize * 3 for longs, CH - N * boxsize * 3 for shorts - the standard P&F horizontal count with a 3-box reversal. Exit fully at the target. Stop = the congestion midpoint (CH+CL)/2. Time stop: exit at the close of the 60th bar after entry if the target is unreached.
