Scale position so that (entry - stop) is a fixed fraction of equity, which means wide bases get smaller size and larger targets.
ideas.why: Wyckoff's Law of Cause and Effect states that the horizontal extent of a trading range is the cause and the subsequent vertical move is the effect - the longer the accumulation, the further the markup. That makes the base width simultaneously a trade filter (do not take breakouts from bases too small to have accumulated a cause) and a natural profit objective that is independent of volatility multiples and trailing logic.
ideas.source: StockCharts ChartSchool, 'The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial' - Law of Cause and Effect: 'The horizontal P&F count within a trading range represents the cause, while the subsequent price movement represents the effect.' P&F 3-box-reversal horizontal count is standard Cohen/Wyckoff construction.
ideas.novelty: The distinctive part is the EXIT STRUCTURE, not the entry: the profit target is derived from the width of the base that preceded the trade, so two breakouts of identical price geometry get completely different targets and position sizes. Donchian/squeeze-release breakouts exit on trailing stops or fixed ATR multiples and are blind to base width. The N >= 8 filter also removes most breakouts a Donchian system would take.

ideas.name: Bulk-Volume Imbalance at Range Edge
ideas.entry_rule: Compute Bulk Volume Classification per 5-minute bar: sigma = stdev of the last 50 bar-to-bar close changes; BuyVol_t = Volume_t * Phi((close_t - close_{t-1})/sigma) where Phi is the standard normal CDF (Student-t with low df is the paper's variant); SellVol_t = Volume_t - BuyVol_t. Accumulate bars into equal-volume buckets of size Vb = (median daily volume of the last 20 sessions)/50. Signed imbalance CI = sum over the last 20 completed buckets of (BuyVol - SellVol); z = (CI - mean(CI over last 250 buckets))/stdev(CI over last 250 buckets). LONG entry: (a) 60-bar range width (high-low) <= 3.0*ATR(14); (b) current close within 0.30*ATR of the 60-bar low; (c) z >= +1.50. Buy at the close of the bar where all three hold. SHORT mirror: within 0.30*ATR of the 60-bar high with z <= -1.50.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = 60-bar range low - 0.50*ATR (mirror: range high + 0.50*ATR). Target = the opposite boundary of the 60-bar range. Immediate exit if z crosses back through 0. Time stop: 60 bars.
inputs: bulk volume classification (normal CDF of standardized close change)
ideas.why: This is the composite-operator idea made measurable. Wyckoff asks who is on the other side of the tape; BVC estimates the buy/sell split of each bar's volume from the standardized price change, and the aggregate imbalance over volume-clock buckets estimates informed order flow. Net buying pressure recorded while price sits pinned at the bottom of a range is precisely 'effort without result in the seller's favour' - somebody is filling size without moving the price up yet.
ideas.source: Easley, D., Lopez de Prado, M., O'Hara, M. (2012), 'Flow Toxicity and Liquidity in a High-Frequency World', Review of Financial Studies, and 'An Improved Version of the Volume-Synchronized Probability of Informed Trading' (Critical Finance Review) - BVC classifies bar volume via the CDF of the standardized price change; VPIN averages |Vbuy - Vsell| over n equal-volume buckets.
ideas.novelty: BVC was designed specifically to work on BARS rather than individual trades, so it gives an order-flow imbalance estimate on exactly the data we have - no level 2 needed. The volume clock (equal-volume buckets) is a different sampling scheme from every calendar-time indicator in the existing set, and the entry is a deliberate DISAGREEMENT between flow direction and price location.

ideas.name: No-Demand / No-Supply Bar
ideas.entry_rule: ATR = ATR(14). SHORT (no-demand): bar D with close(D) > close(D-1), (high(D)-low(D)) <= 0.70*ATR, volume(D) < volume(D-1) AND volume(D) < volume(D-2); context: close(D) < SMA(close,50) and SMA(close,50) < SMA(close,50)[5]; and high(D) within 0.50*ATR of the highest high of the last 20 bars. Sell short at the close of the first subsequent bar whose close < low(D). LONG (no-supply): bar D with close(D) < close(D-1), (high-low) <= 0.70*ATR, volume(D) < volume(D-1) AND volume(D) < volume(D-2); context: close(D) > SMA(close,50) and SMA(close,50) > SMA(close,50)[5]; low(D) within 0.50*ATR of the lowest low of the last 20 bars. Buy at the close of the first subsequent bar whose close > high(D). Setup expires if not triggered within 3 bars.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = high(D) + 0.10*ATR for shorts, low(D) - 0.10*ATR for longs. Target = 2.5 * (entry - stop) distance. Trail after +1.5R at (lowest close since entry) + 1.0*ATR for shorts / (highest close since entry) - 1.0*ATR for longs. Time stop 20 bars.
inputs: volume of the two preceding bars
ideas.why: Tom Williams built VSA directly out of Wyckoff's effort-versus-result law. A rally bar that closes up on a narrow spread with volume below BOTH of the two preceding bars is a move nobody participated in - professional money declined to follow it. The two-bar comparison matters: volume below one prior bar is noise, below both on a narrow directional close means the move is demonstrably unaccompanied. Placing it near a swing extreme in an established downtrend is where the absence of demand is most costly to the buyer.
ideas.source: Tom Williams, 'Master the Markets' / TradeGuider VSA system (VSA_System_explained.pdf, tradeguider.com); LuxAlgo concept reference 'No-demand / No-supply bars' which states the rule as up close, narrow spread, volume lower than each of the previous two bars, with the following bar's close in the expected direction as the conventional trigger.
ideas.novelty: The volume test is relative to the two immediately preceding bars, not to a moving average - it is a local participation test, not a volume-regime test. Combined with the requirement that the spread be NARROW on a bar that closed in the trade's adverse direction, it is the inverse of every volume-confirmation rule in the existing set, which look for volume expansion.

ideas.name: Retest Volume Referee
ideas.entry_rule: ATR = ATR(14), AV = SMA(volume,20). Range: H = 40-bar highest high, L = 40-bar lowest low, require (H-L) <= 3.0*ATR. Breakout bar B: close(B) > H + 0.10*ATR with volume(B) >= 1.3*AV. Enter long at the close of B. (Mirror for shorts below L.) The idea's substance is what happens next, in the exit rule.
ideas.exit_rule: This is an exit-structure idea. From entry, track the FIRST pullback: the run of bars beginning when a bar's low < H (price re-enters the old range). Let PBvol = the maximum single-bar volume during that pullback. RULE: (a) if PBvol >= volume(B), close the entire position at the close of that bar - the retest is being met with more effort than the breakout, which Wyckoff calls a failed secondary test; (b) if PBvol <= 0.70*volume(B) and a bar then closes back above H, hold and move the stop to (pullback low - 0.10*ATR); (c) hard stop at all times = H - 1.0*ATR; (d) if no pullback into the range occurs within 15 bars, trail at (highest close) - 2.0*ATR. Target: H + (H-L), exit fully.
inputs: breakout bar volume retained as state
ideas.why: Wyckoff's secondary test says a breakout is validated by a pullback on DIMINISHED volume and spread, and invalidated by one on expanded volume. Most breakout systems exit on price alone and therefore hold through pullbacks that are actually distribution and cut pullbacks that are healthy. Refereeing the exit by the ratio of pullback volume to breakout volume uses the same price path to reach opposite decisions.
ideas.source: StockCharts ChartSchool, 'The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial' - ST: 'volume and spread should be significantly diminished'; Phase D: 'advances on widening spreads and increasing volume; reactions on smaller spreads and diminished volume.'
ideas.novelty: The entry is deliberately ordinary; the distinct claim is an exit gated on a volume RATIO against a remembered bar (the breakout bar), which is stateful in a way ATR trails and fixed stops are not. Two identical price paths produce opposite management. This can also be bolted onto any existing breakout entry as an exit module.

ideas.name: IB First-Extreme Asymmetry
ideas.entry_rule: Using 5-minute RTH bars, define the Initial Balance as 09:30-10:30 ET: IBH = max high, IBL = min low, IBW = IBH-IBL. Record t_high = the start time of the 5-minute bar containing the IB high and t_low likewise for the IB low (if the same bar contains both, skip the day). Filter: require 0.40*ATRd <= IBW <= 1.20*ATRd where ATRd = ATR(14) on daily bars. THEN: if t_high < t_low (the IB high printed first), arm ONLY a sell-stop at IBL - 0.05*IBW. If t_low < t_high, arm ONLY a buy-stop at IBH + 0.05*IBW. The opposite side is never armed. Order is live 10:30-13:00 ET and cancelled at 13:00 if unfilled.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = the IB midpoint (IBH+IBL)/2. Target = entry - 0.60*IBW for shorts, entry + 0.60*IBW for longs (the study's median extension is ~50-75% of IB for normal-width days). Hard time exit at 15:55 ET. Never re-enter the same session.
inputs: session initial balance high/low and their timestamps
ideas.why: The extreme that prints first in the opening hour is usually the one made by the responsive/short-timeframe side reacting to the overnight gap; the other-timeframe participant then works the opposite direction for the rest of the day. Measured on ES 2015-2025, when the IB high formed first the day produced a single downside breakout 44.8% of the time versus a single upside breakout only 24.0%; when the IB low formed first, single-up 52.5% versus single-down 17.0%.
ideas.source: tradingstats.net, 'Initial Balance Breakout Statistics: ES & NQ Futures 2015-2025' - IB Formation Bias section, plus the IB tier table (narrow <0.5x ATR breaks 98.7% with 74.8% median extension; wide >1.0x ATR breaks 93.5% with 39.6%).
ideas.novelty: Same trigger geometry as an opening-range breakout but only ONE side is ever live, and the side is chosen by the CHRONOLOGY of the two IB extremes - information a standard ORB throws away entirely. That is a directional claim, not a parameter: on any given day this system and a two-sided ORB take opposite trades roughly a third of the time.

ideas.name: IB Retracement-Depth Continuation
ideas.entry_rule: IB = 09:30-10:30 ET; IBH, IBL, IBW as above. Wait for the FIRST breakout: a 5-minute bar closing above IBH (up-case) or below IBL (down-case). Record the breakout extreme XE = the highest high since the breakout (up-case). Then track retracement depth r = (XE - lowest low since XE)/IBW, updated per bar. ENTRY (up-case): price must first re-enter the IB (some bar's low < IBH), and while r has never exceeded 0.25, a 5-minute bar closes back above IBH - buy at that close. Down-case is the mirror with r = (lowest low since breakout to highest high since)/IBW and a close back below IBL. Only one entry per session; do not enter after 14:30 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Signal-nullification stop: exit immediately at market on any 5-minute close that pushes r >= 0.50 (deep retracement - per the study, only 24.8% of such days close in the breakout direction and 52.7% become double-breakout days). Hard price stop = IB midpoint. Target = breakout price + 1.00*IBW (up-case) / - 1.00*IBW (down-case). Otherwise exit at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: After an IB break, essentially every day retraces back into the IB (99.9% of ES days), so the retracement itself carries no information - the DEPTH does. Shallow retracements (under 25% of IB width) closed in the breakout direction 93.8% of the time and produced zero double-breakout days; retracements of 50% or more closed in the breakout direction only 24.8% of the time. The trade is a bet on the pullback failing to go deep, entered after that failure is observable.
ideas.source: tradingstats.net, 'Initial Balance Breakout Statistics: ES & NQ Futures 2015-2025' - Retracement Depth Determines Day Type section (shallow <25%: 93.8% close in breakout direction, 0.0% double breakout; deep >=50%: 24.8% / 52.7%). Retrace-into-IB rate 99.9% ES.
ideas.novelty: Entry is on the RE-BREAK after a measured shallow pullback, not on the original breakout, and the primary stop is a normalized structure percentage (retracement as a fraction of IB width) rather than a price or ATR distance. An ORB system is already long before this system evaluates anything, and an ORB fade takes the opposite side.

ideas.name: Neutral-Extreme Day Follow-Through
ideas.timeframe: daily decision executed on intraday bars
ideas.entry_rule: Classify the completed RTH session D: NEUTRAL if the session traded both above IBH and below IBL (range extension on both sides). Given neutral, classify NEUTRAL-EXTREME-UP if close_D >= low_D + 0.90*(high_D - low_D), NEUTRAL-EXTREME-DOWN if close_D <= low_D + 0.10*(high_D - low_D). ENTRY on session D+1: at 09:45 ET, for neutral-extreme-up, buy at the close of the 09:30-09:45 15-minute bar if that bar's close > its open AND close > close_D; for neutral-extreme-down, sell short if that bar's close < its open AND close < close_D. No trade otherwise.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = the midpoint of session D, (high_D+low_D)/2. Target = high_D + 0.50*(high_D - low_D) for longs, low_D - 0.50*(high_D-low_D) for shorts. Exit at 15:55 ET on D+1 if neither is reached. Move stop to breakeven once price exceeds high_D (longs) / low_D (shorts).
inputs: ohlcv (5- or 15-minute intraday for the IB and the 09:45 trigger)
ideas.why: A neutral day means both the other-timeframe buyer and seller showed up and neither could hold their extension - the auction is genuinely two-sided. But when such a day closes on one extreme, the final auction of the day resolved the disagreement late, and that resolution is usually not fully priced by the bell. Dalton treats the neutral-extreme close as the day's most directionally informative feature. Neutral days are roughly 30% of sessions, so the setup is not rare.
ideas.source: Dalton, Jones & Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' (1993) - neutral day and neutral-extreme day classification; day-type frequency statistics as tabulated by Firich and reproduced by ATAS ('How to improve trading using the Market Profile': neutral days 30.21%, trend days 9.54%, non-trend 6.81%).
ideas.novelty: Conditions on a DAY-TYPE classification - a two-sided range extension combined with a one-sided close - which no indicator in the existing set computes. It is explicitly cross-session: the whole signal is generated by yesterday's auction shape and executed on today's first 15 minutes.

ideas.name: Poor High / Poor Low Repair
ideas.entry_rule: Build a TPO profile from the 13 RTH 30-minute bars of a completed session: rows of width w = 0.05*ATRd; a period 'marks' every row between its own low and high; TPO count per row = number of periods marking it. POOR HIGH: the topmost occupied row has TPO count >= 2 AND the top two rows both have TPO count >= 2 AND at least 2 distinct 30-minute periods have a high within 1 row of the session high (a flat, tail-less top). POOR LOW is the mirror at the bottom. ENTRY (poor high recorded within the last 10 sessions and never yet exceeded): when price first trades within 0.20*ATRd BELOW that poor high and the current 15-minute bar closes above its own open, buy at that close. Mirror for a poor low: when price trades within 0.20*ATRd above it and a 15-minute bar closes below its open, sell short.
ideas.exit_rule: Target = poor high + 0.15*ATRd (the repair - the auction must trade through the flat top to complete). Stop = 0.35*ATRd below entry. Abandon the setup and any open position at the close of the 3rd session after entry. Delete a recorded poor high from the register once it has been exceeded by 0.15*ATRd.
inputs: ohlcv (30-minute for the TPO profile, 15-minute for execution)
register of unrepaired poor highs/lows (10 sessions)
ideas.why: A session extreme made by several 30-minute periods stacked at the same price, with no single-print tail, means the auction stopped for lack of interest rather than being rejected by aggressive opposing size. Dalton calls that unfinished business: the market has not yet found the price at which the other side refuses. Such extremes tend to be revisited and exceeded, because the auction still has to complete the job of finding rejection.
ideas.source: Dalton, Jones & Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' (1993). Operational definition as documented by marketcalls.in ('Poor High and Poor Low Market Profile Structure Explained': lack of excess or a single TPO at the tail) and ShadowTrader glossary ('a poor high will have less than two TPOs of excess with at least 2-3 columns of TPOs lining up to form a flat top'); carry-forward tracking of about one month.
ideas.novelty: Requires constructing a TPO (time-at-price) profile, which is a time-count structure no price/volume indicator in the existing set produces, and it trades TOWARD a resistance level rather than away from it - the opposite of every fade and every breakout rule listed, and the opposite of its own companion idea (excess-tail fade) at a superficially identical price geometry.

ideas.name: Excess Tail Fade to POC
ideas.entry_rule: Build the same 30-minute TPO profile for a completed session. EXCESS HIGH: there are >= 2 consecutive topmost rows each with TPO count == 1 (single prints) and those rows together span >= 5% of the session range; the tail base TB = the lowest of those single-print rows. Record TB and that session's POC. ENTRY (within the next 5 sessions, tail not yet erased): if price trades above TB and then a 15-minute bar CLOSES back below TB, sell short at that close. Mirror for an excess low: price trades below the tail base and a 15-minute bar closes back above it - buy at that close. Erase the record if any session closes beyond the excess extreme.
ideas.exit_rule: Target = the POC of the session that produced the excess tail; exit fully there. Stop = the excess extreme (session high for a short, session low for a long) + / - 0.10*ATRd. Exit at 15:55 ET of the 2nd session after entry if the POC is unreached.
inputs: ohlcv (30-minute for the TPO profile, 15-minute for execution)
register of excess tails and their session POCs
params: minimum tail span (5% of session range)
ideas.why: Excess is the auction-theory definition of a COMPLETED auction: a tail of prices touched by only one time period means aggressive opposing size appeared instantly and rejected the level. Where a poor high says 'come back and finish', an excess high says 'this is done'. Re-entering a rejected zone and failing to hold above its base is a re-confirmation of the original rejection, and the natural objective is the price the same session agreed was fair - its POC.
ideas.source: Dalton, Jones & Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets'; excess/tail definitions per the 'Excess + Tails in TPO profile' tear sheet (webflow-hosted, 2020) and the ShadowTrader glossary entries for excess high/excess low ('the minimum number of TPOs necessary to define an excess low is two').
ideas.novelty: Forms a mutually exclusive pair with Poor High/Low Repair: the same TPO machinery classifies a session extreme as either excess (fade it) or poor (trade toward it), producing opposite trades at price structures that look identical on a candlestick chart. The profit target is a prior session's modal price, not a swing level, ratio or ATR multiple.

ideas.name: Value Migration Acceptance Pullback
ideas.entry_rule: Compute daily VAH/VAL as above. HIGHER-VALUE migration on session D: VAL_D > VAH_{D-1} (today's value area sits entirely above yesterday's, with a gap). LOWER-VALUE migration: VAH_D < VAL_{D-1}. ENTRY (higher-value case) on session D+1: if price trades down to within 0.05*ATRd of VAL_D and then a 30-minute bar CLOSES back above VAL_D, buy at that close. Mirror for lower-value: price trades up to within 0.05*ATRd of VAH_D and a 30-minute bar closes back below VAH_D - sell short at that close. One entry per session; no entry after 14:30 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = VAH_{D-1} for longs / VAL_{D-1} for shorts - i.e. the far side of the gap between the two value areas. Falling back into the OLD value area is the definition of rejected migration, so that is the invalidation. Target = VAH_D + 0.50*(VAH_D - VAL_D) for longs, VAL_D - 0.50*(VAH_D-VAL_D) for shorts. Exit at 15:55 ET of session D+2 if unresolved.
inputs: daily VAH/VAL for two consecutive sessions
ideas.why: Value migrating higher with a gap between the old and new value areas means the market did not merely trade higher, it agreed on higher prices - volume was accepted where it previously was not. The unfilled space between the two value areas is the auction's own statement about what it no longer considers fair. Buying the low edge of new value with the stop on the far side of that gap makes the trade a direct bet on acceptance, and the invalidation is a structural event rather than a price distance.
ideas.source: Dalton, Jones & Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' - value-area placement / value migration framework (higher value, lower value, overlapping value, unchanged value) and the distinction between price movement and accepted value.
ideas.novelty: The stop level is the GAP between two value areas - a level that exists only in profile space and has no price-chart analogue (there need be no price gap at all). Trend definition comes from where volume was accepted on consecutive days, not from a moving average, so this fires on days where MA slope is flat and stays out of MA-trending markets whose value areas overlap.

ideas.name: Rotation Factor Midday Continuation
ideas.entry_rule: On RTH 30-minute bars, for each period p from the second onward compute r_p = sign(high_p - high_{p-1}) + sign(low_p - low_{p-1}) with sign(0)=0 (so higher-high-and-higher-low = +2, lower-high-and-lower-low = -2, inside or outside bar = 0). RF = cumulative sum of r_p from the session's second period. Let IBmid = (IBH+IBL)/2 from the 09:30-10:30 initial balance. DECISION at the close of the 12:00-12:30 ET bar: LONG if RF >= +5 AND that close > IBmid AND that close > the 11:00-11:30 close; SHORT if RF <= -5 AND that close < IBmid AND that close < the 11:00-11:30 close. Enter at that close. No other entries that session.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = 1.0 * ATR(14) computed on 30-minute bars. Move the stop to breakeven once the position gains 1.0 * that ATR. Also exit immediately at the close of any subsequent 30-minute bar on which RF falls back below +3 (longs) or rises back above -3 (shorts). Hard exit at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: The rotation factor is Dalton's objective measure of the day's ATTEMPTED direction: it counts how many 30-minute auction periods rotated higher versus lower, independent of how far price actually travelled. A day that has rotated persistently in one direction through the morning has an other-timeframe participant working in that direction, and the afternoon typically extends the same attempt. Because it counts structure rather than distance, it stays valid on days where price has gone nowhere but every period has printed a higher high and higher low.
ideas.source: Dalton, Jones & Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' (1993) - rotation factor; calculation as documented in the mypivots.com dictionary entry 'Rotation Factor' (+1/-1/0 for the high comparison plus the same for the low, summed across TPO periods) and Sierra Chart's support board implementation.
ideas.novelty: A directional score built entirely from the SEQUENCE of higher-highs and higher-lows across auction periods - it is scale-free and ignores magnitude completely, so it is uncorrelated with every distance-based momentum measure. Three-bar momentum looks at closes over three bars; RF looks at the count of rotations over the whole session and is bounded by the number of periods, not by price.

ideas.name: Open-Drive
ideas.entry_rule: Let O = the 09:30:00 ET opening print (open of the first 1-minute RTH bar) and ATRd = ATR(14) daily. OPEN-DRIVE UP requires, over 09:30-09:40 using 1-minute bars: (a) max high - O >= 0.25*ATRd; (b) min low >= O - 0.05*ATRd (price never trades meaningfully back through the opening print); (c) both 5-minute bars 09:30-09:35 and 09:35-09:40 close above their own opens; (d) the 09:40 price is within 0.10*ATRd of the 09:30-09:40 high (still at the extreme, not fading). ENTRY: buy at the close of 09:40. OPEN-DRIVE DOWN is the exact mirror. No entry if the conditions are met in both directions or in neither.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = O - 0.05*ATRd for longs / O + 0.05*ATRd for shorts - the opening print itself, because a drive that returns through the open is by definition no longer a drive. Target = O + 1.00*ATRd (longs) / O - 1.00*ATRd (shorts). Once the position gains 0.50*ATRd, trail at the lowest low of the last three 15-minute bars (longs) / highest high (shorts). Hard exit at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: Dalton ranks the open-drive as the highest-confidence opening type: participants who decided before the bell auction aggressively in one direction from the first print and never let price back through the open, which means the extreme they leave behind is the most reliable of any open type. The economic content is that positioning was decided on information available before the session, so the day's inventory is one-sided from the start.
ideas.source: Dalton, Jones & Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' (1993) - the four opening types (open-drive, open-test-drive, open-rejection-reverse, open-auction) and their confidence ranking; operational summaries at marketcalls.in 'Market Profile Open Type and Confidence' and mypivots.com dictionary 'Open Drive OD'. Numeric thresholds pinned down by me.
ideas.novelty: The defining test is that price never trades back through the OPENING PRINT - a single reference price, not a range boundary - combined with monotone 5-minute closes. An opening-range breakout waits for a high/low of a 15- or 30-minute range to be exceeded and is agnostic about the path; this system requires the path to be one-directional from the first tick and is already flat by the time an ORB would trigger on many days. The stop is also the opening print, which is what makes the risk tiny relative to the target.

ideas.name: Open-Rejection-Reverse
ideas.entry_rule: Let O = the 09:30 opening print, ATRd = ATR(14) daily. BULLISH ORR: (a) between 09:30 and 10:00 the session low reaches <= O - 0.20*ATRd; (b) after that low, price trades back above O and a 5-minute bar CLOSES >= O + 0.05*ATRd, before 10:30 ET. Buy at the close of that 5-minute bar. BEARISH ORR is the mirror (high >= O + 0.20*ATRd, then a 5-minute close <= O - 0.05*ATRd before 10:30). Require the reversal leg to be faster than the rejection leg: the number of 1-minute bars from the extreme back to O must be <= the number from 09:30 to the extreme. One trade per session.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = the session low - 0.05*ATRd (bullish) / session high + 0.05*ATRd (bearish) - the rejected extreme. Target 1 = the prior session's VAH (bullish) / VAL (bearish); if that has already been exceeded, use IBH + 0.5*IBW / IBL - 0.5*IBW. Take half at target 1, trail the remainder at the low of the last two 30-minute bars. Hard exit at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: An open-rejection-reverse is the auction advertising a price, finding aggressive opposition, and reversing: the early participants who pushed one way are trapped on the wrong side of the opening print and must cover, which supplies the fuel for the move back through value. Requiring the return leg to be faster than the rejection leg distinguishes a genuine reversal (opposing size arrived) from a slow drift back (nobody there).
ideas.source: Dalton, Jones & Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' (1993) - open-rejection-reverse: 'opening in one direction, but the early arrival of the opposite activity comes in before a key reference area is hit, which will reverse the development of the direction'; summaries at mypivots.com and marketcalls.in 'Market Profile Open Type and Confidence'. Thresholds and the speed-asymmetry test are my pinning-down.
ideas.novelty: The trigger price is the OPENING PRINT reclaimed from the wrong side - a level strictly INSIDE the opening range - so the entry geometry is the opposite of an opening-range fade, which triggers at the range boundary. The speed-asymmetry condition (reversal leg must take no longer than the rejection leg) is a time-based filter absent from every listed strategy. This idea plus Open-Drive partition the same first-30-minute tape into two mutually exclusive, oppositely-traded classes.

ideas.name: Percentile-Band Spread with Median Exit
ideas.entry_rule: MULTI-SYMBOL. Formation window = 40 bars. Standardize each leg's close over the formation window: z_i(t) = (P_i(t) - mean_40(P_i)) / sd_40(P_i). spread_t = z_i(t) - z_j(t). Build the EMPIRICAL cdf of spread over those 40 formation bars and record its 5th, 15th, 50th, 85th and 95th percentiles (q05, q15, q50, q85, q95). In the following 40-bar trading window: ENTER SHORT the spread (short i, long j, equal dollars) on the first bar where spread_t >= q85. ENTER LONG the spread (long i, short j) on the first bar where spread_t <= q15.
ideas.exit_rule: Close when spread_t reverts to q50 (the formation MEDIAN, not zero) - crossing it from the entry side. Hard stop: close immediately if spread_t >= q95 for a short-spread position or spread_t <= q05 for a long-spread position. Time exit at the end of the 40-bar trading window.
inputs: 40-bar rolling mean and stdev per leg
empirical percentiles of the formation-window spread distribution
ideas.why: Spread distributions are fat-tailed and skewed, so a Gaussian 2-sigma band mis-states how unusual any given divergence actually is: on a leptokurtic spread, 2 sigma is hit far more often than 5% of the time, and the trader systematically over-trades. Percentiles of the realized distribution are calibration-free and adapt to whatever shape the spread actually has. Exiting at the formation median rather than at zero also concedes that the equilibrium level of a standardized spread is rarely exactly zero - two firms can carry a persistent, non-zero relative premium (different leverage, different payout policy) that a zero-exit rule would keep waiting for.
ideas.source: Nath (2003), 'High Frequency Pairs Trading with U.S. Treasury Securities: Risks and Rewards for Hedge Funds', applied to GovPX 1994-2000; rules summarized in Krauss (2015), FAU Discussion Paper 09/2015, section 2.1 (page 8 discussion of Nath's percentile triggers, median reversion exit and stop-loss percentiles).
ideas.novelty: MULTI-SYMBOL. Distinct from idea 1 on both sides of the trade: the entry threshold is a nonparametric quantile rather than a fitted sigma, and the EXIT STRUCTURE is different - reversion to the formation median plus an explicit percentile stop-loss, where GGR has neither. Krauss notes the real hazard this design introduces (a pair already diverging at the end of formation opens immediately at the start of trading), which is exactly what the q95/q05 stop is there to bound.

ideas.name: Sector-ETF Residual S-Score
ideas.entry_rule: SINGLE-SYMBOL, conditioned on one ETF's data. For stock i and its sector ETF E: regress the last 60 daily returns, r_i(t) = alpha + beta*r_E(t) + eps(t), by OLS. Form the cumulative residual X(n) = sum_{k=1..n} eps(k) for n = 1..60. Fit an AR(1) to X: X(n+1) = a + b*X(n) + zeta(n+1). Derive kappa = -log(b)*252, m = a/(1-b), sigma_eq = sqrt( Var(zeta) / (1-b^2) ). Compute the s-score s = (X(60) - m) / sigma_eq. FILTER: trade only if b is in (0,1) and kappa > 8.4 (mean-reversion half-life shorter than half the 60-day estimation window). ENTER LONG stock i when s < -1.25. ENTER SHORT stock i when s > +1.25. Hedge by shorting beta dollars of E per dollar of stock (or trade the stock unhedged as a simpler variant).
ideas.exit_rule: Close the LONG when s > -0.50. Close the SHORT when s < +0.75. Note the deliberate asymmetry - shorts are covered further from zero than longs are sold. Additional stop: exit if the kappa filter fails on a re-estimate (b <= 0 or kappa <= 8.4), i.e. the residual stopped mean-reverting.
inputs: daily close of its sector ETF (XLK, XLF, XLE, XLV, XLI, XLY, XLP, XLU, XLB, XLRE, XLC)
AR(1) fit on the cumulative residual
ideas.why: Decomposing a stock's return into a systematic part explained by its sector and an idiosyncratic residual isolates the component with no risk premium attached to it. A drifting cumulative residual means the stock has moved relative to its sector for reasons that are, by construction, sector-independent - typically single-name order flow. That is precisely the component that should be stationary in equilibrium, so pushing it far from its own mean creates a genuine expected-return edge that does not require taking sector or market risk. The kappa filter is the honest part: it refuses to trade names whose residual is behaving like a random walk rather than an OU process, which is where this family of strategies loses money.
ideas.source: Avellaneda & Lee (2010), 'Statistical Arbitrage in the U.S. Equities Market', Quantitative Finance 10(7), 761-782 - ETF-regression variant; thresholds sbo=sso=1.25, sbc=0.75, ssc=0.50 and the kappa > 8.4 reversion-speed filter confirmed against the Hudson & Thames arbitragelab PCA-approach documentation (github.com/hudson-and-thames/arbitragelab, docs/source/other_approaches/pca_approach.rst).
ideas.novelty: SINGLE-SYMBOL (needs only one extra ETF series). Unlike every mean-reversion entry in the existing 32, the quantity that reverts is not price - it is the cumulated regression residual against a benchmark, so market and sector moves are removed before the signal is computed. The units are also different: s is a distance to an OU equilibrium scaled by the OU's own stationary sigma, not by a rolling sample sd. Critically it carries an explicit no-trade condition (kappa > 8.4), which none of the 32 have.

ideas.name: Bertram Cost-Aware OU Band Optimization
ideas.entry_rule: MULTI-SYMBOL. Build the log-price spread x_t = log(P_A) - beta*log(P_B) with beta from a 252-bar OLS. Fit a zero-mean OU process dx = -theta*x*dt + sigma*dW via the AR(1) regression x_t = c + rho*x_{t-1} + u_t, giving theta = -log(rho)*252, sigma = sd(u)*sqrt(2*theta/(1-rho^2)), and the stationary sd sigma_eq = sigma/sqrt(2*theta). Let c_cost be the round-trip cost in log-return terms (commission + half-spread on both legs). Grid-search entry level a and exit level m over a in [-3, -0.25]*sigma_eq and m in [0, +1.5]*sigma_eq with a < m: the deterministic log return per cycle is r = m - a - c_cost, and using Bertram's first-passage expressions for E[T(a,m)] and Var[T(a,m)] compute the return per unit time mu = r/E[T] and the variance per unit time, then Sharpe = mu/sqrt(variance per unit time). Choose (a*, m*) maximizing Sharpe per unit time. ENTER LONG the spread when x_t <= a*; the mirror rule ENTER SHORT when x_t >= -a*.
ideas.exit_rule: Close the long at x_t >= m* and the short at x_t <= -m*. The exit level is a free optimized parameter, so m* is generally NOT zero - on a fast-reverting, high-cost spread the optimizer pushes m* past the mean to pay for the round trip, and on a slow spread it pulls m* short of the mean to recycle capital faster. Hard time stop at 3 * ln(2)/theta bars (three half-lives) if m* has not been reached.
inputs: AR(1) fit of the spread giving theta and sigma
OU first-passage-time expressions for E[T] and Var[T]
params: objective (return per unit time vs Sharpe per unit time)
half-life multiple for the time stop
ideas.why: Almost every pairs strategy exits at the mean by reflex, which quietly assumes transaction costs are zero and that capital has no opportunity cost. Neither is true. Bertram's insight is to make the objective explicitly a RATE - profit per unit of time, not profit per trade - which forces the optimizer to weigh how long capital sits in the trade against how much it earns. Once costs enter the objective, the optimal exit level moves off the mean, and it moves in a direction that depends on the spread's reversion speed. This is the cleanest available answer to 'where should I actually take profit', and Cummins & Bucca's large-scale test on 861 energy futures spreads, with an explicit data-snooping correction, found daily returns of 0.07-0.55% with Sharpes often above 2.
ideas.source: Bertram (2010), 'Analytic Solutions for Optimal Statistical Arbitrage Trading', Physica A 389(11); large-scale test with data-snooping controls in Cummins & Bucca (2012), 'Quantitative Spread Trading on Crude Oil and Refined Products Markets', Quantitative Finance. Trade-cycle decomposition T = T1 + T2 and the return function r(a,m,c) = m - a - c reproduced from Krauss (2015), FAU Discussion Paper 09/2015, section 4.2 (equations 22-24).
ideas.novelty: MULTI-SYMBOL. This is a distinct EXIT STRUCTURE above all: the take-profit level is jointly optimized with the entry level against a per-unit-TIME objective that includes transaction costs, so exits routinely land away from the mean in either direction. No band strategy in the existing 32, and none of the other pairs ideas here, optimizes entry and exit as a coupled pair or expresses the objective as a rate.

ideas.name: Copula Mispricing-Index Flags
ideas.entry_rule: MULTI-SYMBOL. Training window = 252 bars of daily returns for the two names. Build empirical marginal CDFs F_X, F_Y (ECDF with the standard n/(n+1) plotting position). Fit candidate bivariate copulas - Gaussian, Student-t, Clayton, Gumbel, Frank, Joe, N14 - by maximum likelihood on the pseudo-observations, and select by lowest AIC. Each trading bar, compute the two conditional probabilities MI_X(t) = P(U_X <= u_X | U_Y = u_Y) and MI_Y(t) = P(U_Y <= u_Y | U_X = u_X), each obtained from the fitted copula's partial derivative. Accumulate running flags: FlagX(t) = FlagX(t-1) + (MI_X(t) - 0.5), FlagY(t) = FlagY(t-1) + (MI_Y(t) - 0.5), both starting at 0. ENTER: if FlagX >= +0.6 OR FlagY <= -0.6, short X and long Y in equal dollars. If FlagX <= -0.6 OR FlagY >= +0.6, long X and short Y. (Sweep the stricter AND-OR variant the authors recommend for stability.)
ideas.exit_rule: Close when EITHER flag returns to zero (crosses it from the entry side), OR when either flag reaches +/-2.0, which is the stop-loss. On any exit, reset BOTH FlagX and FlagY to 0 - the accumulator restarts flat, so the next signal is independent of the losing one. Re-fit the copula every 252 bars.
inputs: fitted bivariate copula and its conditional distribution
ideas.why: A z-score on a spread implicitly assumes the joint distribution of the two names is elliptical, so it treats a large joint down-move exactly like a large joint up-move. Equities are not elliptical - they exhibit strong lower-tail dependence, crashing together far more reliably than they rally together. A copula separates the marginal behaviour of each name from the dependence structure linking them, so 'X is unusually weak GIVEN what Y did today' can be evaluated correctly in the tail where a Gaussian spread model is most wrong and where pairs strategies suffer their worst losses. Accumulating the daily conditional-probability surplus rather than reading a level also means a long string of small, persistent one-sided surprises triggers a trade, which a single-day z-score would miss entirely.
ideas.source: Xie, Liew, Wu & Zou (2016), 'Pairs Trading with Copulas', Journal of Trading 11(3), 41-52; and Liew & Wu (2013), 'Pairs Trading: A Copula Approach', Journal of Derivatives & Hedge Funds 19, 12-30. Flag accumulation formula, D=0.6 open threshold, S=2 stop, zero-crossing exit, flag-reset rule and the OR-OR vs AND-OR variants from the Hudson & Thames arbitragelab mispricing-index-strategy documentation.
ideas.novelty: MULTI-SYMBOL. Entirely different entry logic from every band strategy: the state variable is a cumulative sum of conditional-probability deviations from 0.5 under a fitted non-elliptical dependence model, not a standardized price difference. The path-dependent accumulator with a hard reset on exit is also a distinct EXIT STRUCTURE - the same spread level can be a signal or not depending on how the pair got there.

ideas.name: Quasi-Multivariate Synthetic Peer, Single Leg
ideas.entry_rule: SINGLE-SYMBOL TRADED, conditioned on five other symbols' data. Standardize every candidate's close over a 504-bar (two-year) moving window: z_i(t) = (P_i(t) - mean_504(P_i)) / sd_504(P_i). For target stock i, select the m = 5 names with the highest correlation of standardized price to z_i. Form the synthetic peer z_syn(t) = sum_{k=1..5} w_k * z_k(t), with w_k either equal (1/5) or fitted by OLS of z_i on the five z_k; re-estimate the weights every 10 bars on the trailing 504 bars. Define spread_t = z_i(t) - z_syn(t) and sigma_s = sd(spread) over the trailing 504 bars. ENTER LONG stock i ALONE (no short leg, no hedge) when spread_t <= -1.5 * sigma_s. ENTER SHORT stock i alone when spread_t >= +1.5 * sigma_s.
ideas.exit_rule: Close when |spread_t| <= 0.5 * sigma_s, or after 10 bars, whichever comes first. Hard stop at |spread_t| >= 3.0 * sigma_s. The synthetic peer is never traded - it exists only to generate the signal - so there are no short-leg borrow costs and only one commission per round trip.
inputs: daily closes of the target and its candidate peers
correlation ranking of standardized price series
synthetic peer weights (equal or OLS), refreshed every 10 bars
ideas.why: The whole point of a stat-arb hedge leg is to cancel common risk, but on a broker where shorting is expensive, restricted or unavailable, the hedge leg can cost more than the risk it removes. Perlin's construction accepts that trade: use a five-name synthetic peer to decide WHETHER the target is cheap - which is where the information is - then take the exposure in one instrument. The 10-bar time stop is what makes this survivable unhedged, because it caps how long naked market beta can run against you while the signal is wrong. Perlin found the quasi-multivariate version beat the univariate one across a broad range of thresholds, and Chen et al. independently reached the same conclusion with a 50-name basket.
ideas.source: Perlin (2007, 2009), 'Evaluation of Pairs Trading Strategy at the Brazilian Financial Market' and 'M of a Kind: A Multivariate Approach at Pairs Trading', applied to the 57 most liquid Brazilian stocks 2000-2006. Construction (standardize prices over a two-year moving window, m=5 highest-correlation partners, equal/OLS/correlation weighting, weights re-estimated every ten days, and critically 'only the reference component of each pair is traded and not the synthetic asset, in order to avoid high transaction costs') reproduced from Krauss (2015), FAU Discussion Paper 09/2015, section 2.3.
ideas.novelty: THIS IS THE SINGLE-SYMBOL EXPRESSION OF A STAT-ARB SIGNAL - directly usable in a long-only or short-restricted account, which no other idea in this set is. Distinct from the s-score family because the benchmark is a small correlation-selected peer set standardized in PRICE space rather than a factor regression in return space, and distinct from all pairs ideas because only one leg ever trades. The unhedged construction makes the time stop load-bearing rather than cosmetic.

ideas.name: Intraday Sector-ETF Lead-Lag Catch-Up
ideas.entry_rule: SINGLE-SYMBOL TRADED, conditioned on one ETF's data. On 5-minute bars. Estimate beta_i by OLS of stock i's 5-minute returns on its sector ETF's 5-minute returns over the trailing 20 sessions. Each bar after 10:00 ET compute the session-to-date returns from the 09:30 open: R_E = ETF close / ETF session open - 1, and R_S = stock close / stock session open - 1. Gap G = beta_i * R_E - R_S. Estimate sigma_G as the stdev of G measured at the SAME time-of-day bar over the last 20 sessions. ENTER LONG stock i when ALL of: G > +1.0 * sigma_G; |R_E| > 0.30%; the ETF's last three 5-minute bars all closed in the same direction as the sign of R_E (the leader is still moving, not already reverting); and stock i's 5-minute dollar volume over the last three bars is at least 0.7x its 20-session median for that time-of-day. ENTER SHORT on the mirror condition G < -1.0 * sigma_G with the same three confirmations.
ideas.exit_rule: Close when G falls back to within 0.25 * sigma_G of zero (the laggard has caught up), OR at 15:55 ET (no overnight carry - the effect is an intraday information-diffusion effect and the overnight gap is a different process), OR on a stop when |G| widens to 2.5 * sigma_G against you, which means the divergence is real news in the stock rather than slow diffusion.
inputs: session-open anchored cumulative returns for both
time-of-day conditional stdev of the gap
ideas.why: Information does not reach all securities at the same speed. Index and sector ETFs are where informed and macro traders express views first because they are the cheapest, deepest instruments available, and Hasbrouck's price-discovery decomposition confirms the flow runs overwhelmingly from the index vehicle into the sector vehicles and not back. Individual constituents, particularly the thinner ones, then re-price with a lag measured in minutes. Requiring the leader to still be moving is what separates a genuine diffusion lag from a stale quote or a stock that is idiosyncratically weak for its own reasons, and the liquidity floor stops the signal from firing on a name that simply has not printed.
ideas.source: Hasbrouck (2003), 'Intraday Price Formation in U.S. Equity Index Markets', Journal of Finance 58(6) - finds the S&P 500 ETF contributes markedly to price discovery in the sector ETFs with only minor effects in reverse; Hou (2007), 'Industry Information Diffusion and the Lead-Lag Effect in Stock Returns', Review of Financial Studies 20(4) - establishes that big-firm-leads-small-firm predictability is predominantly an INTRA-industry phenomenon, which is why the conditioning series here is the sector ETF rather than SPY.
ideas.novelty: SINGLE-SYMBOL TRADED. This is directional catch-up, not mean reversion: it buys the laggard while the divergence is still opening, whereas every band strategy waits for it to stop. The predictor is another instrument's intraday path, and the signal is anchored to the session open with a time-of-day conditional band, which correctly handles the U-shaped intraday volatility profile that a flat rolling stdev would smear. Distinct from opening-range breakout, which uses only the stock's own first N minutes and no second symbol.

ideas.name: Relative-Strength Resilience Divergence
ideas.entry_rule: SINGLE-SYMBOL TRADED, conditioned on the sector ETF. Define the relative-strength ratio RS_t = P_stock(t) / P_ETF(t). ENTER LONG when ALL FOUR hold on the same bar: (1) the sector ETF closes at a new 20-bar LOW; (2) the stock does NOT close at a new 20-bar low - specifically its close is at least 1.5% above its own 20-bar low; (3) RS_t closes at a new 20-bar HIGH; (4) the stock's 20-bar average dollar volume is at least $5M. ENTER SHORT on the exact mirror: sector ETF at a new 20-bar HIGH, stock not within 1.5% of its own 20-bar high, RS_t at a new 20-bar LOW, same liquidity floor.
ideas.exit_rule: Close the long when RS_t closes below its own 20-bar SMA, OR on a price stop at entry price minus 2.0 * ATR(14) of the stock, OR after 15 bars. Mirror for shorts. Deliberately note the asymmetry from a plain breakout exit: the exit is triggered by the RATIO losing its trend, not by the stock's own price, so a long can be held through a stock drawdown as long as the sector fell further.
inputs: daily close of the sector ETF
20-bar high/low of the ETF, the stock, and the RS ratio
ideas.why: A stock that refuses to make a new low while its whole sector is making one is revealing something the tape does not otherwise show: there is a persistent buyer absorbing the sector-wide selling in this specific name. That is genuine, observable relative demand rather than an artefact of the stock simply having a low beta. The conditioning is what makes the signal informative - if the stock were breaking out on its own price too, the ratio high would tell you nothing new beyond the price high. By requiring the stock NOT to be breaking out while the ratio does, the signal isolates outperformance that is entirely attributable to relative resilience, which is where the information about differential demand lives.
ideas.source: Synthesis. It combines two documented components: the intra-industry lead-lag and relative-performance predictability of Hou (2007), 'Industry Information Diffusion and the Lead-Lag Effect in Stock Returns', RFS 20(4), with the standard practitioner relative-strength ratio line. The specific resilience conjunction - sector at an extreme, stock explicitly not at its own extreme, ratio at an extreme - is my construction, designed to make the signal non-redundant with a plain price breakout. It is the least literature-backed idea here and should be treated as the speculative one in the batch.
ideas.novelty: SINGLE-SYMBOL TRADED. Explicitly built NOT to be a Donchian breakout reskin: condition (2) is a negative condition that forbids the stock's own price breakout, so the signal fires on a disjoint set of bars from any price-channel rule and the two cannot both trigger on the same bar. The exit is on the ratio's trend rather than the stock's price, which is a distinct exit structure. Longs are entered into sector weakness, so this reads as a fade at the sector level and a momentum trade at the relative level simultaneously.

ideas.name: Trend t-Stat Gate
ideas.entry_rule: On each daily close, fit by OLS ln(close_tau) = a + b*tau + e over the last 252 daily bars, where tau = 1..252 is a simple time index. Compute the Newey-West t-statistic of the slope b, t(b), using lag truncation floor(4*(252/100)^(2/9)) = 5. Go long at the next session open if t(b) > +2.0. Go short at the next open if t(b) < -2.0. Take no position while -2.0 <= t(b) <= +2.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Recompute t(b) at every daily close. Close a long when t(b) falls to +0.5 or below; close a short when t(b) rises to -0.5 or above (asymmetric hysteresis: enter at 2.0, exit at 0.5). There is no price stop and no target - the flat dead-zone is the entire exit mechanism, so the position goes flat when the trend stops being statistically distinguishable from noise rather than when price crosses a level.
inputs: OLS regression of log price on a time index
ideas.why: Trend-following bleeds most of its edge in turnover from flipping position on price moves that are statistically meaningless. Testing whether the fitted log-price drift is significantly different from zero, and holding no position when it is not, keeps the strategy out of exactly those conditions. Baltas and Kosowski find the turnover of a time-series momentum book falls by roughly two thirds versus the plain sign-of-past-return rule, with Sharpe ratios of 0.99 vs 1.04 that are not statistically distinguishable (Ledoit-Wolf p-value) - i.e. the same gross edge at a third of the trading cost.
ideas.source: Baltas & Kosowski, 'Demystifying Time-Series Momentum Strategies: Volatility Estimators, Trading Rules and Pairwise Correlations' (SSRN 2140091), equations (23)-(24): fit log(F_tau) = alpha + beta*tau over the past 12 months of daily log prices; TREND = +1 if NW t(beta) > +2, -1 if t(beta) < -2, 0 otherwise. PDF: https://spiral.imperial.ac.uk/server/api/core/bitstreams/93f06c22-150a-4240-8115-912988dd2c67/content
ideas.novelty: Not a crossing event and not an oscillator threshold. It is a hypothesis test on a fitted trend with an explicit third state - flat. A moving-average cross has no representation for 'no trend': it is always either long or short. The dead zone plus asymmetric re-entry hysteresis is the structural difference.

ideas.name: Yang-Zhang Sized TSMOM
ideas.entry_rule: At the last daily close of each calendar month compute R = close_t/close_{t-252} - 1. If R > 0 open a long at the next session open; if R < 0 open a short. Size it so notional = min(0.40/sigma_YZ, leverage_cap) * equity_allocated, where sigma_YZ is the Yang-Zhang OHLC volatility estimator over the last 63 daily bars annualised by sqrt(252): sigma_YZ^2 = V_o + k*V_c + (1-k)*V_RS, with V_o = sample variance of ln(open_i/close_{i-1}), V_c = sample variance of ln(close_i/open_i), V_RS = mean over the window of [ln(high_i/close_i)*ln(high_i/open_i) + ln(low_i/close_i)*ln(low_i/open_i)], and k = 0.34/(1.34 + (n+1)/(n-1)) with n = 63.
ideas.exit_rule: No price-based exit at all. The position is carried to the last close of the following month, when the sign and the size are both recomputed; if the sign is unchanged only the notional is adjusted. Intra-month, resize only if sigma_YZ has moved more than 25% from the level used at entry, which caps rebalancing churn.
inputs: open, high, low, close (63 daily bars) for the Yang-Zhang estimator
ideas.why: The sign of the trailing 12-month return is the canonical time-series momentum signal, but the thing that makes it a tradeable portfolio rather than a raw signal is constant-risk sizing: losses then do not scale with market volatility. The Yang-Zhang estimator uses the high and the low as well as the close, so it is far more efficient per bar than close-to-close volatility and moves less day to day. Baltas and Kosowski find switching to it cuts strategy turnover by about a tenth with no degradation of risk-adjusted performance, and that a three-month volatility estimation window maximises the Sharpe ratio.
ideas.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, 'Time Series Momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 104(2), 2012 - each position sized to an ex-ante annualised volatility of 40%, i.e. position size 40%/sigma_{t-1} (https://w4.stern.nyu.edu/facdir/lpederse/papers/TimeSeriesMomentum.pdf). Range estimator and 3-month window from Baltas & Kosowski (SSRN 2140091), section 4.1, applying Yang & Zhang (2000).
ideas.novelty: The entry is a sign, not a cross. What is genuinely new relative to the existing 32 is the exit and sizing structure: position size is a continuous function of an OHLC range volatility estimate that is recomputed every day, and the exit is a calendar date rather than any price or indicator event. Nothing in the current set uses the high and low to estimate risk, and nothing exits on the clock.

ideas.name: Volatility-Normalized Momentum Rank
ideas.entry_rule: At each daily close compute for every symbol in the universe M = (close_t/close_{t-252} - 1) / sigma, where sigma = stdev of daily log returns over those same 252 bars * sqrt(252). Rank the universe on M. Go long at the next open the top 20% of symbols, short the bottom 20%. Additionally require M > +0.5 for any long and M < -0.5 for any short, so names whose drift is small relative to their own noise are skipped even if they rank well.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 21 trading days in overlapping tranches (one twenty-first of the book re-formed daily), then re-rank. Exit a position early only when the symbol falls out of the top 40% (for longs) or rises out of the bottom 40% (for shorts) - a buffer band, so a name on the boundary does not churn in and out.
inputs: cross-sectional ranking across the traded universe
ideas.why: A 40% twelve-month move in a quiet stock is a much stronger statement about drift than the same move in a noisy one, but a raw return ranking treats them identically and therefore loads the book almost entirely on the highest-volatility names. Dividing by realised volatility converts the signal into something close to a t-statistic of drift, which equalises information content across the universe. Baltas and Kosowski run their entire momentum predictability panel on exactly this volatility-normalised form of returns.
ideas.source: Baltas & Kosowski (SSRN 2140091), equation (25): r_{t-1,t}/sigma_{t-1} = alpha + beta_lambda * r_{t-lambda-1,t-lambda}/sigma_{t-lambda-1}, estimated for lags 1..60 months with two-way clustered standard errors; t-statistics are positive and significant across the first twelve lags.
ideas.novelty: Ranks on drift per unit of risk rather than on raw return, and uses an asymmetric entry/exit band (enter top 20%, exit at 40%) instead of an indicator crossing. It is a different signal, not a different threshold: two stocks with identical 12-month returns get very different ranks.

ideas.name: Long-Horizon Reversal Veto
ideas.entry_rule: Daily, compute R12 = close_t/close_{t-252} - 1 and R36 = close_t/close_{t-756} - 1. Also compute the percentile rank of the current R36 within that symbol's own trailing 1260-bar history of R36 values. Go long at the next open when R12 > 0 AND that R36 percentile is below 80. Go short when R12 < 0 AND the R36 percentile is above 20. If the veto condition is triggered (R36 percentile >= 80 for a long candidate, <= 20 for a short candidate), stay flat regardless of R12.
ideas.exit_rule: Re-check both conditions at every daily close. Close the position when R12 changes sign, or when the R36 veto becomes active, whichever happens first. A veto-triggered exit forces flat rather than reversing - it is a stand-aside, not a counter-trade.
inputs: trailing percentile of the 3-year return within its own history
ideas.why: Return autocorrelation from time-series momentum work is reliably positive out to about twelve months and turns negative beyond it, with reversals regaining statistical significance around a three-year lag. A twelve-month uptrend sitting on top of an already-stretched three-year move is precisely the configuration where continuation is most likely to be the late extension of a move about to mean-revert. The rule keeps the tradeable horizon and uses the untradeable one purely as a filter.
ideas.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012); the lag structure is reproduced in Baltas & Kosowski (SSRN 2140091), Figure 4 and accompanying text: t-statistics positive across the first twelve monthly lags, then 'statistically strong signs of return reversals after the first year ... [that] only seem to gain some significance for a lag of around three years'.
ideas.novelty: Two horizons in a veto relationship rather than blended into a single score. The long horizon never generates a trade; it only cancels one. Every multi-timeframe rule in the existing set either requires agreement or averages the signals.

ideas.name: Frog-in-the-Pan Continuity
ideas.entry_rule: At each month-end compute PRET = close_t/close_{t-252} - 1. Over those same 252 daily bars count the fraction of days with a negative close-to-close return (%neg) and with a positive one (%pos). Compute ID = sign(PRET) * (%neg - %pos), which lies in [-1, +1] and is larger when the cumulative move arrived in a few big jumps. Rank the universe independently on PRET and on ID. Go long at the next open the intersection of the top PRET tercile and the bottom ID tercile; go short the intersection of the bottom PRET tercile and the bottom ID tercile.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 126 trading days (six months), run as six overlapping monthly tranches so one sixth of the book is closed and replaced each month. No price stop and no indicator exit: the hypothesis is about slow information diffusion, so the position needs the full diffusion window to pay off and an early technical exit would truncate the effect being traded.
inputs: count of positive and negative daily returns over the formation window
ideas.why: Investors underreact far more when the same cumulative price move arrives as a long string of small daily changes than when it arrives in a handful of large ones - the frog does not notice the water heating slowly. Continuous-information winners therefore still have unincorporated information left in them and drift further, while discrete-information winners have already had their news noticed and priced.
ideas.source: Da, Gurun & Warachka, 'Frog in the Pan: Continuous Information and Momentum', Review of Financial Studies 27(7). The ID measure is defined exactly as ID = sign(PRET) * (%neg - %pos), where PRET is the formation-period cumulative return and %neg, %pos are the raw fractions of negative and positive daily returns over that period. PDF: https://academicweb.nd.edu/~zda/Frog.pdf
ideas.novelty: Conditions on the shape of the path that produced the return rather than on the return itself. Two stocks with identical 12-month returns are treated in opposite ways depending on how choppy the path was. No rule in the existing 32 measures the distributional character of the daily returns inside the lookback.
params: weighting %neg-%pos by return magnitude instead of counting days

ideas.name: 52-Week-High Proximity
ideas.entry_rule: At each month-end compute NEAR = close_t / max(high over the last 252 daily bars) for every symbol. Rank the universe on NEAR. Go long at the next open the top 30% by NEAR, subject to an absolute floor of NEAR >= 0.90; go short the bottom 30% by NEAR. Note the long is opened while price is still below the 252-day high - no breach of the high is required or wanted.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 126 trading days, run as six overlapping monthly tranches. No stop-loss and no exit on the 52-week high being taken out or on NEAR falling - George and Hwang's effect is a 6-to-12-month holding-period phenomenon and exiting on price action destroys it.
ideas.why: Investors anchor on the 52-week high and are reluctant to bid a price up through it, so good news is impounded slowly in stocks trading near their high, and symmetrically bad news is impounded slowly in stocks far below theirs. The 52-week high proxies for how much of the recent news is already in the price better than the trailing return does; George and Hwang report roughly 0.45%/month raw and 0.85%/month risk-adjusted on a top-30%-minus-bottom-30% book, and find nearness dominates conventional momentum measures in joint regressions.
ideas.source: George & Hwang, 'The 52-Week High and Momentum Investing', Journal of Finance 59(5), 2004, 2145-2176. Long the 30% of stocks closest to their 52-week high, short the 30% furthest from it. PDF: https://www.bauer.uh.edu/tgeorge/papers/gh4-paper.pdf
ideas.novelty: A level signal, not a change signal, and explicitly not a breakout. The position is put on while price sits below the high and the high is never required to be exceeded - the opposite of a Donchian breakout, which needs the extreme taken out to trigger. It is also a cross-sectional ranking of proximity, so a stock that has been quietly sitting 2% below its high for months is a maximal signal here and no signal at all for any breakout rule.

ideas.name: 52-Week-High Recency Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Compute NEAR = close_t / max(high over the last 252 bars) as above, and additionally AGE = the number of trading days between the bar that produced that 252-day high and today. Go long at the next open only symbols with NEAR in the top 30% of the universe AND AGE <= 21 trading days. Go short only symbols with NEAR in the bottom 30% AND whose 252-day low was set within the last 21 trading days.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 126 trading days in overlapping monthly tranches, but additionally force an exit on any position whose AGE exceeds 126 trading days before its tranche matures - the anchor has gone stale and the behavioural mechanism no longer applies.
inputs: bar index of the running 252-day extreme
ideas.why: Anchoring only works if the anchor is salient. A 52-week high set last week is vivid in investors' minds; one set eleven months ago has been forgotten and exerts no pull. Bhootra and Hur report that the nearness-to-high strategy earns about twice as much per month among stocks whose 52-week high is recent as among those whose high is distant, so recency roughly doubles the signal without changing the underlying variable.
ideas.source: Bhootra & Hur, 'The timing of 52-week high price and momentum', Journal of Banking & Finance, 2013 - defines a 'recency ratio' from the number of days since the 52-week high was formed and shows the anchoring effect is far stronger for recent highs.
ideas.novelty: Introduces a time-since-extreme coordinate. Nothing in the existing 32 measures how long ago an extreme was set - Donchian, liquidity sweep and premium/discount all use where price is relative to a range, never when the range boundary was made. The exit is also driven by the age of the anchor rather than by price.
params: whether to require both recency and a rising 252-day high

ideas.name: Fitted Trend Factor
ideas.entry_rule: At each month-end, for every symbol compute normalised moving-average signals A_L = SMA_L(close)/close_t for L in {3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 400} daily bars (division by the current close is what makes the signal stationary and comparable across symbols and price levels). Run a cross-sectional OLS regression across the universe of each symbol's realised return over month t on its A_L vector measured at the end of month t-1, producing eight slope coefficients b_L^t. Maintain an exponentially weighted forecast of each slope: E_t(b_L) = (1 - lambda)*E_{t-1}(b_L) + lambda*b_L^t with lambda = 0.02. Forecast each symbol's expected return as ER = sum over L of E_t(b_L) * A_L(t). Go long at the next open the top 30% by ER, short the bottom 30%.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold one month. At the next month-end, re-run the cross-sectional regression, refresh the coefficient forecasts and recompute ER; a name is closed when its ER drops out of the top tercile (or rises out of the bottom tercile). The forecast is the exit - there is no price stop, and no individual moving average has any authority to close a position on its own.
inputs: simple moving averages at eight lags
ideas.why: Short-, intermediate- and long-term trends carry separate information, and the correct weight on each is not constant across regimes. Instead of picking one lookback and hard-coding a sign, this fits the weights from the recent cross-section and lets the data say whether the market is currently paying for 3-day or 400-day trends - including paying negatively, which is how it absorbs short-term reversal automatically. Han, Zhou and Zhu report it more than doubles the Sharpe ratios of the short-term reversal, momentum and long-term reversal factors combined. Only information up to month t is used, so the forecast is genuinely out-of-sample.
ideas.source: Han, Zhou & Zhu, 'A trend factor: Any economic gains from using information over investment horizons?', Journal of Financial Economics 122(2), 2016, 352-375. Construction reproduced verbatim in Liu & Zhou, 'Trend Factor in China', equations (1)-(2) (MA of the last L closes, normalised by the closing price on the last trading day), (5) (cross-sectional forecasting regression) and (7) (EWMA coefficient forecast, lambda = 0.02, giving a roughly 4-year effective memory). PDF: https://wrds-www.wharton.upenn.edu/documents/1119/WARSP_TrendChina.pdf
ideas.novelty: The moving averages are regressors in a fitted return forecast, not signals. The weight on each horizon is estimated and time-varying, so the identical price path can produce a long in one regime and a short in another. Every MA rule in the existing 32 hard-codes both which average matters and what sign its signal carries.

ideas.name: Volume-Trend Term Structure
ideas.entry_rule: Same machinery as the fitted trend factor but with volume as an additional block of regressors. At each month-end compute price signals A_L = SMA_L(close)/close_t and volume signals W_L = SMA_L(volume)/volume_t for L in {3, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200} (each normalised by the current day's value for stationarity). Run one cross-sectional regression of next-month return on the joint [A_L, W_L] vector, EWMA the coefficients with lambda = 0.02, and forecast ER = sum_L E(bP_L)*A_L + sum_L E(bV_L)*W_L. Go long the top 30% by ER at the next open and short the bottom 30%.
ideas.exit_rule: One-month holding period, re-formed monthly from a refreshed joint forecast; a name is dropped when its combined ER leaves the top (or bottom) tercile. Neither block can close a position independently - the exit is the aggregate forecast falling out of range.
inputs: normalised moving averages of both series at seven lags
ideas.why: The shape of the volume path across horizons tells you whether a price trend is being fed by growing or decaying participation: a rising price sitting on a volume structure that is decaying at every horizon is a trend running out of buyers. Liu and Zhou add exactly these normalised volume moving averages alongside the price ones in the same forecasting regression and find they carry information the price trend does not.
ideas.source: Liu & Zhou, 'Trend Factor in China' (WRDS working paper), equations (3)-(6): MV_{i,L} = mean of the last L days' volume, normalised as MV/V_d, entered jointly with the normalised price MAs in the cross-sectional forecasting regression and forecast with the same EWMA scheme. PDF: https://wrds-www.wharton.upenn.edu/documents/1119/WARSP_TrendChina.pdf
ideas.novelty: Volume enters as a term structure with fitted, time-varying weights rather than as a binary gate. The existing 'Bollinger with volume' and similar rules use volume only as a threshold filter ('volume > 1.5x average'); here the multi-horizon volume shape is itself a return predictor with an estimated sign.
params: whether to orthogonalise volume signals against price signals first

ideas.name: High-Volatility MA Overlay
ideas.entry_rule: At each daily close rank the universe by the standard deviation of daily close-to-close returns over the last 252 bars, and restrict all trading to the top 30% (highest-volatility tercile). Within that subset only, go long at the next open any symbol whose previous close is strictly above its 10-day simple moving average of closes. Symbols outside the high-volatility tercile are never traded regardless of their MA position.
ideas.exit_rule: Long/flat only, never short. Exit to cash at the next open following any close that is at or below the 10-day SMA. Also exit immediately if the symbol drops out of the high-volatility tercile at the monthly volatility re-rank, even if the MA signal is still long.
ideas.why: Han, Yang and Zhou apply exactly this 10-day rule to volatility decile portfolios and find the abnormal returns rise monotonically with the volatility decile, from about 5.17% annualised in the lowest to 18.55% in the highest, with CAPM alphas from 6.17% to 20.56% and betas near zero or negative. The economic story is that when fundamental signals are imprecise - which is when volatility is high - investors lean harder on price and underreact more, so the trend signal has more mispricing to work against. At 25bp per trade the top five deciles still clear about 10%.
ideas.source: Han, Yang & Zhou, 'A New Anomaly: The Cross-Sectional Profitability of Technical Analysis', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis. Rule as stated in the paper: 'buy or continue to hold the portfolio today when yesterday's price is above its 10-day MA price, and to invest the money into the risk-free asset (the 30-day Treasury bill) otherwise', applied to 10 volatility decile portfolios; robustness at L = 20, 50, 100, 200.
ideas.novelty: The innovation is the conditioning variable, not the indicator. The same trivial MA rule is near-worthless on low-volatility names and strongly profitable on high-volatility ones, so a cross-sectional volatility rank becomes the gate that decides which symbols the rule is even allowed to look at. It is also long/flat rather than long/short: the measured effect is a timing overlay against buy-and-hold, and adding a short leg inverts rather than doubles the payoff.
params: realised range (Parkinson) volatility instead of close-to-close
signal on previous close vs current close

ideas.name: Strategy-Vol-Scaled Momentum
ideas.entry_rule: Run the momentum long-short book and record its own daily P&L series. Each day compute sigma_strat = standard deviation of the strategy's daily returns over the last 126 trading days, annualised by sqrt(252). Set the gross exposure multiplier w = min(sigma_target / sigma_strat, leverage_cap) with sigma_target = 0.12. New positions are entered at the next open with notional equal to the normal weight multiplied by w, and w is applied identically to both legs so the book stays balanced.
ideas.exit_rule: Positions still turn over on the normal 21-trading-day momentum schedule, but exposure is rescaled every day as sigma_strat updates: when w falls the whole book is trimmed pro rata rather than closed, and when w rises it is topped up. If w falls below 0.2 the book goes fully flat and stays flat until w recovers. This is a continuous, graduated exit driven by the strategy's own realised risk rather than by any signal about any symbol.
inputs: the momentum strategy's own daily return series (126 bars)
ideas.why: Momentum's own volatility is strongly autocorrelated and therefore forecastable from its recent realised variance, in a way that its mean return emphatically is not. So you can predict when the strategy is dangerous even when you cannot predict when it will pay. Barroso and Santa-Clara show that scaling exposure by the inverse of six-month realised volatility to a constant target nearly doubles the Sharpe ratio and virtually eliminates the crash left tail - the improvement comes entirely from sizing, with the signal untouched.
ideas.source: Barroso & Santa-Clara, 'Momentum has its moments', Journal of Financial Economics 116(1), 2015. Six-month realised volatility computed from the squared previous 126 daily returns of the momentum portfolio itself; constant-volatility target (12% is the figure used in the related time-series momentum literature).
ideas.novelty: The risk input is the strategy's own realised P&L volatility, not the instrument's. Nothing in the existing 32 sizes off the equity curve of the strategy - ATR-based sizing looks only at the traded instrument and is blind to the fact that a book of twenty positions can become dangerous through correlation while every individual ATR stays flat.
params: forecast realised vol with a GARCH/EWMA instead of a rolling window

ideas.name: Market Intraday Momentum
ideas.entry_rule: On SPY or another liquid index ETF, using 5-minute bars. Define r1 = (close of the 10:00 bar / previous session's daily close) - 1, so that r1 deliberately includes the overnight gap and captures all information since the prior close. Define r12 = (close of the 15:30 bar / close of the 15:00 bar) - 1. At the 15:30 bar open, go long if r1 > 0 AND r12 > 0; go short if r1 <= 0 AND r12 <= 0; take no position otherwise. Optional filter that strengthens the effect: trade only on days where the realised volatility of the thirty 1-minute returns inside the first half hour falls in the top tercile of its trailing 252-day distribution.
ideas.exit_rule: Close at the 16:00 session close, unconditionally. Exactly one trade per day, held exactly thirty minutes, with no stop, no target and no trailing logic. Days on which r1 and r12 disagree produce no trade at all.
ideas.why: Most macro news is released before the open, so a large first half-hour move usually reflects real information. Day traders who faded that move must flatten before the close, and the disposition effect makes them procrastinate on their losing side into the final half hour, pushing price the same way a second time; informed traders separately concentrate their execution in the high-volume opening and closing half hours. Gao, Han, Li and Zhou report the first half-hour return predicts the last with a slope of 0.069 significant at 1% and R-squared of 1.6% (rising to 3.7% in 2007-2009), a Sharpe ratio of 1.08 for the r1-only timing rule against -0.18 for always-long in the same window, and a 77% hit rate for the two-signal version. Predictability is monotonically increasing in first-half-hour volatility and in volume.
ideas.source: Gao, Han, Li & Zhou, 'Market Intraday Momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 129(2), 2018 (SSRN 2440866). Equation (5): eta(r1, r12) = r13 if r1 > 0 and r12 > 0; -r13 if r1 <= 0 and r12 <= 0; 0 otherwise. Equation (1) defines the thirteen half-hour returns with p_0,t set to the previous day's 16:00 price. PDF: https://www.smallake.kr/wp-content/uploads/2015/01/SSRN-id2440866.pdf
ideas.novelty: The signal is measured in the morning and the position is not opened until six hours later, for a thirty-minute window. That is the structural opposite of an opening range breakout, which trades the same morning information immediately. The two-signal version also has a genuine no-trade state - it is out of the market on roughly half of days by construction.

ideas.name: Half-Hour Periodicity Momentum
ideas.entry_rule: Divide the session into thirteen 30-minute intervals j = 1..13, built from 5- or 15-minute bars. The interval-j return on day d is r_j,d = (close of interval j / close of interval j-1) - 1, with interval 0 on day d being the previous session's close. For each symbol and each interval j, compute M_j = the arithmetic mean of r_j,d over the previous 20 trading days. At the open of interval j on the current day, rank the universe on M_j and go long the top 10% and short the bottom 10%.
ideas.exit_rule: Close at the end of interval j on the same day. Each of the thirteen intervals is an independent thirty-minute trade with its own independent cross-sectional ranking; nothing is carried between intervals or across days, so there is no overnight exposure at all.
inputs: 5- or 15-minute bars for at least 20 trading days
per-interval return history indexed by time of day
ideas.why: Heston, Korajczyk and Sadka document return continuation at half-hour intervals that are exact multiples of a trading day - a stock's return in a given half-hour interval positively predicts its return in the same interval on subsequent days - and the effect persists for at least 40 trading days. They attribute it to institutional fund flows and systematic trading programs that execute at the same clock time each day, and show that volume, order imbalance, volatility and bid-ask spreads exhibit the same periodicity but do not explain the return pattern.
ideas.source: Heston, Korajczyk & Sadka, 'Intraday Patterns in the Cross-Section of Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 65(4), 2010, 1369-1407. PDF: https://www.bauer.uh.edu/departments/finance/documents/Heston-Korajczyk-Sadka-jf-2010-01-07.pdf
ideas.novelty: Momentum indexed by clock time rather than by elapsed time: the lookback for a 14:00 trade consists only of previous days' 14:00 half-hours, skipping everything in between. Nothing in the existing 32 conditions on time of day beyond the opening range, and none of them compares a bar to the same-numbered bar on previous days.
params: which intervals to trade (all 13, or only high-volume ones)

ideas.name: Band-Filtered MA with Mandatory Hold
ideas.entry_rule: Daily. Compute SMA_L(close) with L = 50 (also test 150 and 200). Generate a buy signal when the close crosses from below to above SMA_L * 1.01, and a sell signal when it crosses from above to below SMA_L * 0.99. The 1% band must be exceeded, so a close that merely touches or marginally pierces the average generates nothing. Enter at the next session open.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold exactly 10 trading days from entry and exit at the close of the tenth day, ignoring every signal generated in the interim - including a full opposite-direction cross. This is Brock, Lakonishok and LeBaron's fixed-length rule, explicitly as distinct from their variable-length rule which holds until the opposite signal appears. Decide up front whether overlapping signals may stack (a second entry while the first is still held) or are suppressed; the two produce materially different books.
inputs: a percentage band around the average
