ideas.why: BLL's fixed-holding-period construction isolates the predictive content of the signal from the path-dependence of the exit, and they find buy signals generate consistently higher returns than sell signals over the following ten days across ninety years of index data. Practically, the mandatory hold caps whipsaw cost in exactly the chop where an exit-on-opposite-cross rule churns itself to death, and the 1% band suppresses signals generated by noise sitting on top of the average. It also gives a clean answer to a question a variable-length rule cannot separate: is the edge in the signal, or in the exit?
ideas.source: Brock, Lakonishok & LeBaron, 'Simple Technical Trading Rules and the Stochastic Properties of Stock Returns', Journal of Finance 47(5), 1992, 1731-1764. Tests MA combinations (1,50), (1,150), (5,150), (1,200) and (2,200) with and without a 1% band, in both variable-length (hold until opposite signal) and fixed-length (mandatory 10-day holding period) versions, on the Dow Jones index 1897-1986.
ideas.novelty: The exit is a clock, and signals are deliberately ignored while a position is open. Both properties are absent from all 32 existing rules, every one of which exits on an indicator or price condition. The band is a second structural difference: it creates a neutral zone around the average within which crossings are simply not signals, which changes the trade count by an order of magnitude, not just the entry price.

ideas.name: Trend Horizon Consensus
ideas.category: time-series trend, multi-horizon agreement with graduated exit
ideas.entry_rule: At each daily close compute three signals from close prices: S1 = sign(close_t/close_{t-21} - 1), S3 = sign(close_t/close_{t-63} - 1), S12 = sign(close_t/close_{t-252} - 1). Let A = S1 + S3 + S12, which takes values in {-3, -1, +1, +3}. Open a full-size long at the next open only when A = +3, and a full-size short only when A = -3. Size at min(0.10/sigma, leverage_cap) * allocated equity, where sigma is the annualised standard deviation of daily returns over the last 63 bars.
ideas.exit_rule: Graduated rather than binary. Recompute A daily: reduce the position to two thirds of full size when |A| falls to 1 with the sign unchanged, and go fully flat when A changes sign or when the shortest-horizon signal S1 and the longest S12 disagree for five consecutive closes. Exposure therefore scales down through the disagreement zone instead of closing on a single condition, so a brief counter-trend bounce trims the position rather than closing it.
ideas.why: Hurst, Ooi and Pedersen show that equally combining 1-, 3- and 12-month time-series momentum signals across markets reproduces the realised returns of the managed futures industry over more than a century, which is strong evidence that this specific combination is what the trend-following industry actually harvests. Requiring all three horizons to agree filters out the configuration where a short-horizon bounce contradicts the primary trend - which is where single-lookback trend rules take most of their whipsaw losses - and scaling out through the disagreement zone converts a binary exit into a proportional one.
ideas.source: Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen, 'A Century of Evidence on Trend-Following Investing' (AQR; Journal of Portfolio Management 2017) - 1-, 3- and 12-month time-series momentum signals equally weighted, each volatility-scaled. Cited as the standard managed-futures specification in Baltas & Kosowski (SSRN 2140091), which notes Hurst et al. (2013) provide statistical evidence that CTA funds do employ such strategies.
ideas.novelty: Consensus across three separate lookback horizons combined with a staged, proportional exit. Distinct from three-bar momentum, which requires three consecutive bars in one direction over a few days; here the horizons span one month to one year and the position size is a function of how many of them agree. Nothing in the existing 32 scales exposure down through an intermediate disagreement state.

ideas.name: Unfilled Order Ledger
ideas.entry_rule: Reference signal S = Donchian(20) upside breakout, i.e. close_t > max(high over t-20..t-1). Hold S fixed and run three separate backtests over the identical set of signal dates. Arm A (market): fill long at open_{t+1}. Arm B (patient limit, cancel): at close_t place a buy limit at L = close_t - k*ATR(14)_t for k in {0.10, 0.25, 0.50}; it fills on the first bar in t+1..t+N whose low <= L, at price L, except that if that bar's open <= L the fill price is that open; N in {1,2,3,5}. If unfilled at the close of bar t+N, cancel and record the trade in a MISSED ledger rather than dropping it. Arm C (patient limit, chase): same limit as Arm B, but if unfilled at the close of bar t+N, fill at open_{t+N+1} at market.
ideas.exit_rule: Identical across all three arms so that entry is the only difference: hard stop at fill_price - 2*ATR(14)_t, profit target at fill_price + 3*ATR(14)_t, unconditional time stop at the close of bar t+40, whichever comes first; stop and target checked on every bar with the stop taking priority if both are touched in one bar. For every MISSED trade in Arm B, compute the return it would have earned under Arm A's fill and exit rules and book it as opportunity cost. Report Arm B's mean per-signal return twice: over filled trades only, and over filled-plus-missed. The second number is the only valid comparison against Arm A.
ideas.why: A resting limit order is a free option written to the market. It fills preferentially when the signal is wrong (price comes back to you) and goes unfilled when the signal is right (price runs away), so the spread it saves is paid for with an adversely selected fill set. Perold's implementation shortfall framework makes the unfilled orders a first-class cost line - opportunity cost - alongside delay cost and execution cost. Naive backtests silently delete that line by simply not recording a trade that never filled, which makes every patient-limit strategy look better than it is. Forcing the missed trades into the ledger is what makes the test honest, and the sign of (Arm B including misses) minus (Arm A) is the actual answer to whether patience pays on this particular signal.
ideas.novelty: Not a signal at all. The signal is frozen and only the order type varies, so the dependent variable is fill quality net of opportunity cost rather than predictive accuracy. Distinct from any of the 32 because none of them specify how the order reaches the market, and the design's entire point is that unfilled trades are recorded rather than discarded.
ideas.source: Perold (1988), 'The Implementation Shortfall: Paper versus Reality', Journal of Portfolio Management 14(3):4-9 - I confirmed the three-way delay/execution/opportunity-cost decomposition via the implementation shortfall literature summary rather than the paywalled original, so treat the decomposition as verified and the page numbers as standard citation. The adverse-selection framing of resting limit orders is standard market microstructure.
params: k, limit offset in ATR units

ideas.name: Tug-of-War Session Split
ideas.entry_rule: Let S be any of the 32 existing signals evaluated on daily bars; reference instantiation S = close_t > EMA(20)_t and ADX(14)_t > 25. On every day for which S is true at the close, take exactly one of two mutually exclusive expressions, run as separate backtests. Arm N (overnight only): buy at close_t, hold through the close, carry zero intraday exposure. Arm D (intraday only): buy at open_{t+1}, carry zero overnight exposure. Re-evaluate S each day; while S stays true the arm re-enters every session, and when S turns false the arm simply stops opening new positions.
ideas.exit_rule: Arm N exits unconditionally at open_{t+1}. Arm D exits unconditionally at close_{t+1}. There are no stops, targets or trailing exits - the session boundary is the exit, which is the whole point. Compute for each of the 32 signals the mean per-day return of Arm N, of Arm D, and of the conventional close-to-close benchmark, and test whether Arm N + Arm D reconstructs the close-to-close number and whether the two components carry opposite signs.
ideas.why: Lou, Polk and Skouras decompose 14 well-known strategies and find that nine of them earn their entire premium intraday, while the five built on past returns - price momentum, industry momentum, earnings momentum, time-series momentum and short-term reversal - earn their entire premium overnight. Critically, wherever a strategy earns a significant premium in one session it tends to earn an economically significant premium of the OPPOSITE sign in the other. A conventional close-to-close backtest therefore nets a positive leg against a negative leg and reports the difference. If our momentum-family signals behave like their momentum-family strategies, holding only the overnight leg should roughly double the realised edge while cutting time-in-market to about a sixth, and the reversion-family signals should show the mirror pattern. That is a sharp, pre-registered, falsifiable prediction: classify each of the 32 as momentum-family or reversion-family before running it, and check the classification predicts which arm wins.
ideas.novelty: Changes neither the signal nor its parameters - only which of the two daily sessions the exposure is held in. No entry in the existing 32 makes any statement about session, and the hypothesis being tested is that the session choice, not the signal, carries the sign of the edge.
ideas.source: Lou, Polk & Skouras (2019), 'A Tug of War: Overnight versus Intraday Expected Returns', Journal of Financial Economics 134:192-213. Read directly from the published PDF at personal.lse.ac.uk/polk/research/tugofwar.pdf; the nine-intraday / five-overnight split and the opposite-sign offsetting components are stated in the paper's own introduction.
params: which of the 32 signals is used as S
optional minimum-liquidity filter on the ticker

ideas.name: Inventory Absorption Overnight
ideas.side: long (the asymmetry predicts the short version fails; test it anyway as a control)
ideas.entry_rule: At the close of day t compute the close location value CLV_t = (close_t - low_t) / (high_t - low_t), setting CLV_t = 0.5 if high_t == low_t, and relative volume RV_t = volume_t / SMA(volume, 20)_t. Enter long at close_t only when CLV_t < 0.25 AND RV_t > 1.2 - a day that closed in the bottom quarter of its own range on above-average volume. Control arm (predicted to be weak): enter short at close_t when CLV_t > 0.75 AND RV_t > 1.2. Apply as a standalone strategy first, then as a gate that decides whether an existing ladder position may be carried overnight.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit unconditionally at open_{t+1}. No stop, no target - the position exists only across the closed-market window, so there is no bar on which a stop could be evaluated. Report the long arm and the short arm separately and test the null that their absolute mean returns are equal; the paper's asymmetry predicts rejection.
ideas.why: Boyarchenko, Larsen and Whelan show US equity index overnight returns are not compensation for news but the price dealers charge for absorbing the order imbalance left over at the US close - risk-averse market makers take the other side of end-of-day flow and demand positive expected return for carrying that inventory until new participants arrive. They document an explicit asymmetry: market selloffs generate robust positive overnight reversals, while reversals following rallies are much more modest, which they attribute to time-varying dealer risk-bearing capacity. We cannot observe signed order imbalance, but the close's position within the day's own high-low range scaled by relative volume is the standard OHLCV proxy for which side won the session and how much stock had to be absorbed. A close pinned to the low on heavy volume is exactly the negative-imbalance state the paper says dealers get paid to absorb.
ideas.novelty: This is a timing gate on the holding window, not a directional signal: it never decides what to buy, only whether the overnight window is worth being exposed in. It is also the rare idea whose source predicts in advance that the long and short versions will NOT be symmetric, which gives the backtest a real falsification condition rather than just a Sharpe ratio.
ideas.source: Boyarchenko, Larsen & Whelan, 'The Overnight Drift', Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Reports no. 917, February 2020, revised August 2022. Read directly from newyorkfed.org; the inventory mechanism, the end-of-day order imbalance link and the selloff/rally asymmetry are all in the abstract and introduction. CLV as an imbalance proxy is my substitution, since the paper uses signed volume we do not have.
params: whether to require a same-direction base signal as well

ideas.name: Confirmation Ladder
ideas.entry_rule: Define the base state S_t = 1 when close_t > EMA(20)_t AND ADX(14)_t > 25, else 0 (swap in any of the 32 as the state function). Enter long at close_t only on the first bar of an N-bar confirmed run, i.e. when S_t = S_{t-1} = ... = S_{t-N+1} = 1 AND S_{t-N} = 0. Sweep N in {1,2,3,5,8}, N=1 being the unmodified base strategy. Each N is a separate backtest over the same underlying state series, and every signal run contributes to at most one entry per N, so the arms are directly comparable on trade count as well as on return.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold exactly H bars and exit at the close of bar t+H, sweeping H in {5,10,20,40} independently of N, with a hard stop at entry - 2*ATR(14)_t checked on every bar. The deliverable is the full N-by-H grid of mean per-trade return, hit rate, trade count and t-statistic - the confirmation curve - not a single best cell. Also report, for each N, the return of the entries that N discarded relative to N=1, which is the direct measurement of what waiting cost you.
inputs: any of the 32 signals as a boolean state
ideas.why: Requiring persistence trades two effects against each other and the point of the ladder is to measure both. False signals are filtered out as N rises, which raises the hit rate; but the signal's remaining edge decays as N rises, which lowers the payoff on the survivors. Because these move in opposite directions the optimum is interior, and it is a property of the strategy rather than of the indicator - which means it is a real parameter worth owning, not a curve-fit. Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen make the underlying methodological argument explicitly: autocorrelation studies examine predictability where the lookback period is forced to equal the holding period, and that restriction masks predictability that only appears once the two are allowed to differ. The same decoupling applies here between confirmation lag and holding horizon, which is why N and H must be swept as a grid and never tied together.
ideas.novelty: The unit of study is the confirmation lag itself, and the output is a two-dimensional response surface rather than a single rule. It is explicitly not a threshold tweak: N=1 and N=3 are different strategies with different trade populations, because N=3 discards a set of trades that N=1 takes, and the ladder measures what that discarded set was worth.
ideas.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012), 'Time Series Momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 104:228-250. Read directly from the published PDF; the argument that forcing lookback to equal holding period masks predictability is in the paper's literature-review section, and the 1-to-12-month persistence with longer-horizon partial reversal is in the abstract.
params: which of the 32 supplies the state function

ideas.name: Alpha Half-Life Surface
ideas.timeframe: any (run separately per timeframe - the half-life is expected to differ)
ideas.entry_rule: When signal S fires at bar t, deliberately do NOT enter at t. Enter at the close of bar t+L, sweeping the entry lag L in {0,1,2,3,5,8,13,21}, provided the signal has not been invalidated by an opposite-direction fire in between (if it has, drop that observation and log it). Run this for each of the 32 signals independently. Reference S for the first pass = the 20-bar Donchian upside breakout, close_t > max(high over t-20..t-1).
ideas.exit_rule: Two passes. Clean pass: hold exactly H bars and exit at the close of bar t+L+H with no stop and no target, sweeping H in {1,2,3,5,8,13,21,34}; this measures the raw conditional expectation without the path-dependence a stop introduces. Dirty pass: identical, plus a hard stop at entry - 2*ATR(14). The deliverable is an L-by-H matrix of mean return, standard error and t-statistic per signal. From it define the signal's half-life tau as the smallest L at which the mean return of the best H column has fallen to half its L=0 value. That tau then feeds the sizing and tranching in the other ideas here, so this is the measurement instrument the rest of the programme depends on.
ideas.why: Every strategy silently assumes an answer to 'how long is this signal good for' and almost none measures it. Mapping the joint lag-by-horizon surface turns that assumption into an estimate, and the shape of the surface is itself diagnostic. A signal whose entire edge sits at L=0, H=1 is not a strategy, it is a latency race we will lose. A signal whose edge is flat in L out to 8 bars is one where entry timing genuinely does not matter and we should stop paying for urgency. A signal whose edge PEAKS at L=2 or L=3 is telling us something specific - the immediate post-signal bars are crowded with other systems reacting to the same pattern, and the durable move begins after they are done. Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen make the case for decoupling lookback from holding horizon, and Garleanu and Pedersen show why the decay rate is the economically relevant quantity: in their optimal policy, predictors with slower mean reversion, that is slower alpha decay, get more weight.
ideas.novelty: It is a measurement programme promoted to a strategy: the tradeable output is the instruction to trade each signal only in its best (L,H) cell, which for some of the 32 will mean entering several bars late on purpose. Nothing in the existing set delays entry deliberately, and the surface is the object being estimated rather than a by-product.
ideas.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012), Journal of Financial Economics 104:228-250, read directly - for the lookback/holding decoupling argument. Garleanu & Pedersen, 'Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs', NBER Working Paper 15205, August 2009 (later Journal of Finance), abstract read directly from the NBER PDF - for alpha decay as the quantity that determines a predictor's weight.
params: stop multiple in the dirty pass

ideas.name: Honest Pullback Test
ideas.entry_rule: Signal S fires at close_t (reference S = close crosses above EMA(20) while ADX(14) > 25). Arm I (immediate): buy at close_t. Arm P (pullback): place a buy limit at the lesser of EMA(20)_t and close_t - 0.5*ATR(14)_t, valid for the next 5 bars, filling on the first bar whose low touches it. The design rule that makes this test valid: Arm P may not drop unfilled signals. Every signal that Arm P fails to fill is carried in a parallel ledger and scored at the return Arm I earned on that same signal.
ideas.exit_rule: Identical for both arms: trail a stop at (highest close since entry) - 2*ATR(14), evaluated at each bar's close, with an unconditional time stop at 30 bars after entry. Report three numbers - Arm I's mean return, Arm P's mean return over filled trades only, and Arm P's mean return over filled-plus-unfilled. The difference between the second and third is the entry-timing alpha, and if the second beats Arm I while the third does not, the pullback edge was pure selection bias.
ideas.why: 'Wait for the pullback' is near-universal folklore and is almost always evaluated only on the trades that actually pulled back, which is survivorship bias in the entry dimension - the signals that never pull back are exactly the ones that ran, and deleting them from the sample deletes the best outcomes. This is Perold's opportunity cost term appearing in a place practitioners do not usually look for it. Once the missed set is scored, the test becomes a clean question about information diffusion: if the signal's information is impounded quickly, the pullback never comes on the good trades and waiting is expensive; if it diffuses slowly, the pullback is a genuine discount on the same move. Different signals among our 32 should fall on different sides of that line, and knowing which is which is directly actionable.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from EMA-pullback-in-trend, which is a signal that requires a pullback as part of its definition. Here the signal is already complete and the pullback is only an execution choice, so the counterfactual - what the unfilled trades did - is well defined and is the actual measurement.
ideas.source: Perold (1988) implementation shortfall opportunity-cost term, framework confirmed via the implementation shortfall literature; the survivorship-in-entries critique and the test design are my own synthesis.

ideas.name: Decay-Matched Scale-In
ideas.entry_rule: Signal S fires at close_t. Split the intended position into M tranches and enter them at the closes of bars t, t+1, ..., t+M-1 unconditionally, at whatever price prevails, cancelling any remaining tranches if the signal fires in the opposite direction. Sweep M in {1,2,3,5}, where M=1 is the single-shot benchmark. Variant B (front-loaded): tranche i receives weight w_i proportional to exp(-i/tau) normalised to sum to one, with tau taken from the measured half-life produced by the Alpha Half-Life Surface for that same signal, so the schedule is not free-fitted but imported from an independent measurement.
ideas.exit_rule: Two exit structures, crossed with the entry arms. Single-shot exit: close the entire accumulated position at the close of bar t+L+H using that signal's best H from the decay surface. Symmetric scale-out: exit in M equal tranches at the closes of the H-th through (H+M-1)-th bars after the final entry tranche. Both carry a portfolio-level stop at (average fill price) - 2*ATR(14)_t.
inputs: measured signal half-life tau from the Alpha Half-Life Surface
ideas.why: Almgren and Chriss frame execution as a trade-off between the market impact of trading fast and the volatility risk of trading slow, with the optimal number of slices emerging endogenously from that balance. For a small retail order in liquid names the impact term is close to zero, which naively implies M=1 - trade it all at once. But a second cost appears that their framework does not model, because they assume a fixed target: the signal itself decays across the slicing window, so late tranches buy into a weaker expected return. That flips the problem from an impact-versus-risk trade-off to a decay-versus-variance-reduction trade-off, and it yields a falsifiable prediction rather than a fitted parameter - M* should be small for signals whose measured decay surface falls off fast and larger for signals whose surface is flat in L. Testing M* against the independently measured tau is the actual experiment.
ideas.novelty: The optimal slice count is predicted in advance from a separately measured quantity rather than swept and selected, which makes it a genuine out-of-sample test of a mechanism rather than another parameter search. Nothing in the existing 32 splits an entry at all.
ideas.source: Almgren & Chriss (2000), 'Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions', Journal of Risk 3(2):5-39 - impact-versus-timing-risk trade-off and endogenous slice count, confirmed by fetching the paper. Garleanu & Pedersen, NBER WP 15205, abstract read directly, for 'trade partially towards the current aim' as the optimal response to costly trading against a decaying signal.
params: tau, decay constant for the front-loaded weights
whether the exit is single-shot or scaled

ideas.name: Fill-Point Attribution
ideas.timeframe: any (the daily version is the informative one)
ideas.entry_rule: For each of the 32 signals, note that a signal computed from bar t's OHLCV is not knowable until bar t has closed. Run three arms over the identical signal dates. Arm C: fill at close_t, the conventional but generally unachievable assumption. Arm O: fill at open_{t+1}. Arm M: fill at (open_{t+1} + high_{t+1} + low_{t+1} + close_{t+1}) / 4, a standard OHLC proxy for a VWAP execution spread across bar t+1. Reference signal for the first pass = close_t > max(high over t-20..t-1).
ideas.exit_rule: Identical across arms so the fill point is the only difference: hold H bars and exit at that bar's close using the same fill convention the arm used for entry, with a hard stop at entry - 2*ATR(14). The quantity of interest is not which arm wins but the per-signal spread Arm C minus Arm O, measured in ATR units and tested against zero. Rank all 32 signals by that spread.
ideas.why: Filling at the close of the bar that defines the signal is the single most common source of overstated backtest performance, but the overstatement is not a constant haircut you can subtract - it is exactly the signal's loading on the overnight and opening-gap return. Lou, Polk and Skouras show that loading is large and, crucially, opposite in sign between momentum-family and reversion-family strategies. So the Arm C minus Arm O spread should be systematically positive for one family and negative for the other, and for some signals Arm O will actually beat Arm C. That converts a piece of backtest hygiene into a diagnostic: the size and sign of the spread tells you what fraction of a signal's apparent edge is really an overnight-gap harvest that you were never positioned to collect.
ideas.novelty: Treats the fill-point assumption as the independent variable and the resulting spread as the measurement, rather than as a correction to apply and forget. It also produces a ranking that feeds directly into the session-split idea - signals with a large positive C-minus-O spread are precisely the ones predicted to pay in the overnight arm.
ideas.source: Synthesis, grounded in Lou, Polk & Skouras (2019), Journal of Financial Economics 134:192-213, read directly from the published PDF - specifically their finding that momentum and reversal strategies earn their premia overnight while nine others earn theirs intraday, with offsetting opposite-signed components.
params: choice of intrabar VWAP proxy formula

ideas.name: Exit Structure Bake-Off
ideas.entry_rule: Entry is held completely fixed and is not the object of study: enter at close_t whenever signal S fires, where S is any of the 32 at its default parameters. Every arm below sees the identical entry list, so all differences in outcome are attributable to the exit alone.
ideas.exit_rule: Four mutually exclusive exit structures plus one crossed variant, each a separate backtest. E1 (decay time stop): exit unconditionally at the close of bar t+H*, where H* is that signal's measured best holding horizon from the Alpha Half-Life Surface, imported rather than fitted. E2 (bracket): stop at entry - 2*ATR(14)_t, target at entry + 3*ATR(14)_t, no time limit, stop taking priority if both are touched in one bar. E3 (ATR trail): exit when close falls below (highest close since entry) - 2.5*ATR(14), evaluated at each bar's close. E4 (signal-off): exit at the close of the first bar on which S is no longer true. E5 (crossed): E1 and E3 together, whichever triggers first. Report per-arm expectancy, average bars held, maximum adverse excursion, and the fraction of total profit given back after the peak.
inputs: measured H* from the Alpha Half-Life Surface
any of the 32 signals as a boolean state
ideas.why: Exit structure is usually inherited by habit and then never tested, yet it determines the shape of the return distribution more than the entry does. E4, exiting when the signal turns off, is the default in most systems and is the arm most likely to be dominated, because a signal turning off is a lagging event relative to the underlying edge decaying - by the time an EMA cross reverses, the expectancy has been zero for many bars. The specific hypothesis worth testing is that E1 beats E4 on expectancy per bar of exposure for every signal whose decay surface has an interior peak. Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen give the reason to expect a finite horizon at all: they document persistence over one to twelve months that then partially reverses, so holding past the horizon does not merely stop earning, it starts giving back. A position held past its half-life carries full volatility with no expectancy, which is the worst possible risk-adjusted state.
ideas.novelty: The exit is the treatment and the entry is the control, which inverts the usual emphasis. E1 is also unusual in that its holding length is imported from an independent measurement rather than swept, making it a real prediction. None of the 32 specifies an exit structure at all, so this is orthogonal to the entire existing set.
ideas.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012), Journal of Financial Economics 104:228-250, read directly - persistence for one to twelve months followed by partial reversal over longer horizons establishes that signal edges have finite useful lives.

ideas.name: Stop-Out Rehabilitation
ideas.entry_rule: A trade on signal S is opened at close_t and is stopped out at bar u at price entry - 2*ATR(14)_t. The re-entry rule: if within R bars of the stop (u+1 .. u+R, with R swept over {3,5,10}) there is a bar whose close is back above the original entry price AND the original signal state S is still true on that bar, re-enter long at that close. Maximum one re-entry per original signal fire; a second stop-out ends the campaign. Control arm: identical entries, no re-entry permitted.
ideas.exit_rule: The re-entered position uses the same exit structure as the original, with the stop re-anchored to the new fill: stop at new_entry - 2*ATR(14) measured at the re-entry bar, and the time stop counted from the re-entry bar rather than the original. Report the campaign-level return - original trade plus re-entry - against the control, and separately report the standalone expectancy of the re-entry leg, since that is the number that says whether stop-outs on live signals are noise or information.
inputs: any of the 32 signals as a boolean state
ideas.why: A stop-out is a statement about volatility, not about the signal. If S is still true after the stop fires, the stop has told you that your stop distance was too tight relative to the instrument's noise - it has not told you the edge is gone. The two possibilities are cleanly separable and the test separates them: if re-entry is profitable, stop-outs on live signals are mostly noise and the real fix is stop placement or sizing; if re-entry loses, the stop was carrying genuine information about regime change and should be treated as a signal invalidation rather than a risk control. Either answer changes how the fleet is configured, which is rare for a backtest. This also matters disproportionately for a DCA ladder, where being knocked out of a still-valid signal and not returning is the specific failure mode that turns a working strategy into a sequence of small losses.
ideas.novelty: The unit of analysis is the campaign rather than the trade, and the treatment is what happens after an exit rather than at entry. It is the only idea here that studies the interaction between the stop and the signal remaining live, which no entry in the existing 32 addresses because none of them specify a stop.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The reasoning follows the maximum adverse excursion framework popularised by John Sweeney ('Campaign Trading: Tactics and Techniques for Exploiting the Markets', Wiley, 1996), which treats the distribution of adverse excursion on eventually-profitable trades as the correct basis for stop placement - the direct implication being that a stop set inside that distribution generates recoverable, not informative, exits.
params: re-entry price threshold relative to original entry

ideas.name: Auction Blackout
ideas.entry_rule: Overlay on any of the 32 intraday signals. A signal firing on a bar whose timestamp falls within the first K minutes after 09:30 ET is not actionable and generates no order; the signal must fire again on a bar at or after 09:30+K to be traded. Sweep K in {0,5,15,30}, where K=0 is the unmodified base strategy. Symmetric closing variant: block signals on bars within the last K minutes before 16:00 ET. Run open-blackout, close-blackout and both-blackout as separate arms so the two windows are attributed separately.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit rules are inherited unchanged from whatever the base strategy uses, and exits are explicitly NOT blocked during the blackout window - only new entries are. This asymmetry is deliberate: the hypothesis is about the reliability of signals formed during the auction, not about the tradability of the window. Report per-arm Sharpe, expectancy per trade and the number of trades removed, and separately report the standalone expectancy of the removed trades, which is what the blackout is actually giving up.
inputs: session open and close times (09:30 and 16:00 ET)
ideas.why: Boyarchenko, Larsen and Whelan document that the opening hour behaves unlike any other part of the day: returns in the 09:00-10:00 window are on average large and negative, but only during recessionary periods, and flat otherwise. That is the signature of a regime-dependent, high-variance, low-unconditional-expectancy window - the worst possible environment for indicator signals, because every moving average, band and oscillator computed on 1 or 5 minute bars is being fed prices that are still resolving the overnight auction rather than reflecting continuous trading. A breakout at 09:32 is measured against a range that does not yet exist. The blackout tests whether the signals we already own are quietly being degraded by a window we never chose to exclude.
ideas.novelty: This is the exact inverse of the opening range breakout and opening range fade strategies we already run: rather than a rule that trades the open, it is a rule that forbids everything else from trading the open. Because it is a pure overlay, it can be applied to all 32 at once and evaluated by whether it raises or lowers each one's Sharpe, which makes it unusually cheap to test relative to its potential fleet-wide effect.
ideas.source: Boyarchenko, Larsen & Whelan, 'The Overnight Drift', Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Reports no. 917, February 2020, revised August 2022. Read directly from newyorkfed.org - the characterisation of the 09:00-10:00 hour as large and negative only in recessions and flat otherwise, in contrast to the consistently significant 02:00-03:00 window, is in the paper's introduction.
params: K, blackout minutes after the open
K, blackout minutes before the close
whether exits are also blocked (default no)
which signals the overlay is applied to

ideas.name: Bar Location Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Signal S fires at bar t. Compute CLV_t = (close_t - low_t) / (high_t - low_t), with CLV_t set to 0.5 when high_t == low_t. For longs, enter at close_t only if CLV_t > 0.7 - the bar closed in the top 30% of its own range. If the gate fails, do not abandon the signal: re-evaluate on bars t+1 and t+2, entering at the close of the first of those bars that satisfies both CLV > 0.7 and S still true; if none of the three bars qualifies, drop the signal. For shorts, mirror with CLV < 0.3. Reference S = close_t > max(high over t-20..t-1).
ideas.exit_rule: Inherited unchanged from the base strategy so the gate is the only manipulated variable; for the reference implementation use a hard stop at entry - 2*ATR(14) and a time stop 30 bars after entry. Report the base strategy, the gated strategy, and - as the diagnostic that matters - the standalone expectancy of the signals the gate rejected outright, which tells you whether the gate is removing losers or removing winners.
ideas.why: Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov show a near-linear relationship between order flow imbalance and price change, with the coefficient inversely related to market depth, and Gould and Bonart show that top-of-book queue imbalance is a statistically strong predictor of the next mid-price move, more so for large-tick stocks. We have no order book, but the close's position within the bar's own high-low range is the standard OHLCV proxy for which side won that bar. The economic content is specific rather than generic: a breakout bar that closes on its low is a breakout that already failed within the bar, and the signal is being generated by the high rather than by any sustained buying. Gating on close location is the cheapest available approximation to 'did the imbalance that triggered this signal survive to the end of the bar'.
ideas.novelty: It is a timing gate, not a filter that changes what is traded - the deferral branch means a signal rejected on bar t can still be taken on bar t+1 or t+2, so the gate mostly shifts entries by a bar or two rather than removing them. Distinct from any volume-confirmed signal in the existing 32, which condition on volume magnitude rather than on where within the bar the price came to rest.
ideas.source: Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov (2014), 'The Price Impact of Order Book Events', Journal of Financial Econometrics 12(1):47-88, arXiv:1011.6402 - fetched and confirmed, linear imbalance-to-price relation with coefficient inverse to depth. Gould & Bonart (2016), 'Queue Imbalance as a One-Tick-Ahead Price Predictor in a Limit Order Book', arXiv:1512.03492 - fetched and confirmed. The CLV substitution for book imbalance is my own proxy, since we have no level 2.
params: whether the deferral requires S to still be true

ideas.name: Depth-Aware Urgency Router
ideas.entry_rule: Signal S fires at close_t. Compute RV_t = volume_t / SMA(volume, 20)_t and route the order into one of three states rather than always using the same order type. If RV_t > 2.0, cross immediately: market order at open_{t+1}. If 1.0 <= RV_t <= 2.0, work the order: buy limit at close_t - 0.25*ATR(14)_t, valid 2 bars, then cancel and cross at market on the third bar's open. If RV_t < 1.0, do not trade this signal at all. The three branches must be logged separately so the routing rule can be evaluated per state, and the control arm is the same signal always routed to market at open_{t+1}.
ideas.exit_rule: Identical across all routed states and the control: hard stop at fill - 2*ATR(14)_t, target at fill + 3*ATR(14)_t, time stop at 40 bars. Report realised slippage against close_t per state alongside per-state expectancy, and test specifically whether the skipped low-volume state would have been profitable had it been traded, since the skip branch is the aggressive part of the rule and needs its own justification.
ideas.why: Two independent literatures point the same way. Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov find the price change per unit of order flow imbalance is inversely proportional to depth, so in a thin bar the same order moves the price further against you. Zarinelli, Treccani, Farmer and Lillo map an impact surface over participation rate and execution duration and find impact grows with participation rate - and in a low-volume bar, a fixed order size IS a higher participation rate. So low relative volume simultaneously predicts a worse fill and, separately, a less trustworthy signal, since a breakout on below-average volume has little flow behind it. The claim being tested is that these two effects are strong enough jointly to justify a discrete three-state routing rule rather than a single order type applied uniformly, and the falsifiable part is that the skipped state should show materially worse net expectancy than the traded states.
ideas.novelty: Relative volume here selects the ORDER TYPE and the decision to trade at all, not the direction or the signal - the same price pattern produces a market order, a worked limit, or nothing, depending purely on execution conditions. That makes it distinct from the volume-confirmed signals in the existing 32, which use volume as a directional filter and always execute the same way once they fire.
ideas.source: Cont, Kukanov & Stoikov (2014), Journal of Financial Econometrics 12(1):47-88, arXiv:1011.6402 - fetched, impact coefficient inversely related to depth. Zarinelli, Treccani, Farmer & Lillo (2015), 'Beyond the square root: Evidence for logarithmic dependence of market impact on size and participation rate', arXiv:1412.2152 - fetched, impact surface over participation rate and duration.

ideas.name: Aim-In-Front Decay Sizing
ideas.entry_rule: Replace binary in-or-out exposure with a continuously decaying weight. Each time signal S fires at bar t, open a new tranche of notional size_max. Every tranche's weight at bar u is w(u) = exp(-(u - t_fire) / tau), where tau is that signal's half-life imported from the Alpha Half-Life Surface. Total position at bar u is size_max * sum of w(u) over all live tranches, capped at cap * size_max with cap in {1,2,3}. Because S firing on consecutive bars creates overlapping tranches, a persistently true signal produces a large position and a signal that fires once produces a decaying one, with no separate entry or exit event required.
ideas.exit_rule: A tranche is retired - its shares sold - when its weight falls below 0.05, which occurs at approximately 3*tau bars after that tranche's fire. Rebalance the actual share count to the target total weight once per bar at the close, with a no-trade band of 10% of size_max to avoid churning on rounding. Overlay a portfolio-level hard stop that liquidates all tranches if the total position's unrealised loss exceeds 2*ATR(14) measured from the weighted-average fill. Benchmark against the binary version of the same signal held for H* bars.
inputs: measured half-life tau from the Alpha Half-Life Surface
ideas.why: A hold-for-H-bars rule applies a rectangular kernel to an alpha that is actually decaying, which over-weights the stale end of the position's life and under-weights the fresh start of it; an exponential kernel is the matched filter for exponential decay. Garleanu and Pedersen derive the closed-form optimal policy when trading is costly and signals mean-revert at different speeds, and it is characterised by two principles - aim in front of the target, and trade partially towards the current aim - with the optimal portfolio being a weighted average of the current Markowitz portfolio and expected future ones, where predictors with slower alpha decay receive more weight. Exponential tranche weighting keyed to a measured half-life is the single-signal implementation of exactly that, and the no-trade band is the 'trade partially' part. It also dissolves the entry-versus-exit distinction: there is no moment of entry or exit, only a target exposure that rises when the signal is fresh and decays when it is not.
ideas.novelty: Reframes the whole entry/exit timing question as a sizing kernel rather than as discrete events, so overlapping signals compound naturally instead of being suppressed by an already-in-a-position flag. Every one of the 32 is binary, and the specific claim - that the decay constant should be the measured half-life rather than a chosen holding period - is directly testable against the binary benchmark.
ideas.source: Garleanu & Pedersen, 'Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs', NBER Working Paper 15205, August 2009, later Journal of Finance. Abstract read directly from the NBER PDF: the 'aim in front of the target' and 'trade partially towards the current aim' principles, and that predictors with slower mean reversion (alpha decay) receive more weight in the aim portfolio, are quoted from that abstract.

ideas.name: Gap Already Paid
ideas.entry_rule: Signal S fires long at close_t on the daily bar. At open_{t+1} compute the normalised gap g = (open_{t+1} - close_t) / ATR(14)_t. Three arms over identical signal dates. Arm A (unconditional): buy at open_{t+1} always. Arm B (gap-capped): buy at open_{t+1} only if g < 0.5, i.e. skip when the move has largely happened overnight. Arm C (adverse-gap only): buy at open_{t+1} only if g < 0, i.e. only when the open has moved against the signal. Mirror all thresholds for short signals. Reference S = close_t > EMA(20)_t with ADX(14)_t > 25.
ideas.exit_rule: Identical across arms so the gap condition is the only difference: exit at close_{t+1}, giving a pure intraday holding period, with a hard stop at entry - 1.5*ATR(14)_t checked intrabar via the day's low. Also run a five-day-hold variant to check whether any effect is a one-day artefact. Report per-arm expectancy and, as the key diagnostic, the expectancy of the trades each arm skipped.
ideas.why: Lou, Polk and Skouras show that momentum-family strategies earn their entire premium overnight and carry an offsetting negative intraday component. Read as an execution rule, that says something concrete and testable about gaps: when a momentum signal fires at the close and the next open gaps strongly in the signal's direction, the overnight premium has already been paid out to whoever was positioned into the close, and what remains for the intraday session is the negative half of their tug of war. Buying that open is buying the losing leg. Conversely an adverse gap means the overnight leg was not paid, so the intraday session is being entered from a better starting point. The prediction is therefore specific and directional - Arm C should beat Arm A for momentum-family signals, and the ordering should reverse or vanish for reversion-family signals. That is a genuine falsification test derived from a published decomposition rather than a threshold discovered by search.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the session-split idea, which chooses which session to hold; this one conditions on what the gap revealed and decides whether to participate at all. The conditioning variable is the realised overnight return, which is observable before the entry decision and is not used by any of the 32.
ideas.source: Lou, Polk & Skouras (2019), 'A Tug of War: Overnight versus Intraday Expected Returns', Journal of Financial Economics 134:192-213. Read directly from the published PDF; the overnight-versus-intraday decomposition and the offsetting opposite-signed components for momentum-family strategies are stated in the abstract and introduction.
params: holding period (one day versus five days)
which signal family is used as S

ideas.name: Dual Thrust Asymmetric Range Projection
inputs: daily OHLC of prior N sessions
ideas.entry_rule: At each session, compute from the prior N completed daily bars: Range1 = max(High over last N days) - min(Close over last N days); Range2 = max(Close over last N days) - min(Low over last N days); Range = max(Range1, Range2). At today's regular-session open O, fix BuyLine = O + K1*Range and SellLine = O - K2*Range. Go long on the first intraday bar whose close > BuyLine; go short on the first intraday bar whose close < SellLine. If already short and price then closes above BuyLine, reverse to long (and vice versa).
ideas.exit_rule: Reverse on the opposite threshold cross, otherwise flatten at a fixed session time (e.g. 15:55 ET) regardless of P&L. No indicator-based exit.
ideas.why: The prior-N-day range measures how much the market has been able to travel; today's open is the market's fresh consensus. Crossing a fixed fraction of that historical travel from the open means today is delivering an above-average move, which is when intraday trends persist. The deliberately cross-wired terms (HighHigh minus LowClose, HighClose minus LowLow) make the range robust to a single gap day, unlike a plain high-low range.
ideas.source: je-suis-tm/quant-trading, file 'Dual Thrust backtest.py' — Range1/Range2/max construction and sigup = param*range + open, siglo = -(1-param)*range + open, with end-of-session flatten
ideas.novelty: Not opening-range breakout: the trigger levels come from prior DAYS' cross-terms, not today's first N minutes, so a level exists from the very first tick. Not Donchian: levels are anchored to today's open and are asymmetric via independent K1/K2, so the long and short triggers sit at different distances.

ideas.name: Awesome Oscillator Saucer
params: number of prior opposite-colour bars required (2)
exit mode: opposite saucer vs AO zero cross
ideas.entry_rule: AO[t] = SMA(5, (High+Low)/2) - SMA(34, (High+Low)/2). LONG at bar t when ALL hold: AO[t] > 0 and AO[t-1] > 0 (oscillator stays on the bull side of zero throughout); AO[t-1] < AO[t-2] (the oscillator dipped on the previous bar); Close[t] > Open[t] (current bar green); Close[t-1] < Open[t-1] and Close[t-2] < Open[t-2] (the two prior bars were red). SHORT at bar t when ALL hold: AO[t] < 0 and AO[t-1] < 0; AO[t-1] > AO[t-2] (the oscillator bounced on the previous bar); Close[t] < Open[t]; Close[t-1] > Open[t-1] and Close[t-2] > Open[t-2].
ideas.exit_rule: Exit and reverse on the opposite saucer signal; also force-exit if AO crosses zero against the position (AO <= 0 while long, AO >= 0 while short).
ideas.why: A saucer is a momentum dip that never reaches zero. It says the pullback happened in price (two counter-colour bars) and in momentum (AO ticked down) but the underlying regime never changed sign. That is a pullback inside a live trend rather than a reversal, so the resumption bar is a cheap entry with a naturally defined invalidation at the zero line.
ideas.source: je-suis-tm/quant-trading, file 'Awesome Oscillator backtest.py' — the bullish/bearish saucer conditional blocks combining open/close colour sequence with AO sign and AO slope
ideas.novelty: Not an oscillator extreme and not a zero-line cross: the trigger explicitly requires the oscillator to STAY on one side of zero while dipping, and couples that to a three-bar candle-colour sequence. It fires mid-trend, where RSI-extreme and MACD-cross rules are silent.

ideas.name: Shaved Heikin-Ashi Body Expansion
inputs: Heikin-Ashi open/high/low/close derived from raw OHLC
params: direction mode (shaved-bottom long vs shaved-top long)
tick tolerance for the shaved test
ideas.entry_rule: Build Heikin-Ashi bars: HAclose = (O+H+L+C)/4; HAopen = (HAopen[t-1] + HAclose[t-1])/2 (seed with (O[0]+C[0])/2); HAhigh = max(H, HAopen, HAclose); HAlow = min(L, HAopen, HAclose). LONG at bar t when ALL hold: HAclose[t] > HAopen[t] (up bar); HAopen[t] == HAlow[t] within one tick (no lower shadow — a shaved bottom); |HAclose[t] - HAopen[t]| > |HAclose[t-1] - HAopen[t-1]| (body strictly larger than the previous bar's body); HAclose[t-1] > HAopen[t-1] (previous bar was also up). SHORT is the exact mirror: HAclose[t] < HAopen[t]; HAopen[t] == HAhigh[t] within one tick; body expanding; HAclose[t-1] < HAopen[t-1].
ideas.exit_rule: Close the long on the first bar where HAclose < HAopen AND HAopen == HAhigh within one tick AND HAclose[t-1] < HAopen[t-1] (the mirror-image shaved-top signal). Mirror for shorts. Positions accumulated on repeated entries are all closed at once on the exit signal.
ideas.why: A shaved Heikin-Ashi bar means that across the whole averaging window price never traded back through the open — every attempt to retrace failed. Pairing that with a strictly larger body and a same-direction predecessor filters out one-off spikes and isolates the segment of a trend where participation is accelerating rather than merely continuing.
ideas.source: je-suis-tm/quant-trading, file 'Heikin-Ashi backtest.py' — the four-condition entry block (HAopen equals HA extreme, body larger than prior body, prior bar same direction) and the three-condition mirror exit
ideas.novelty: Heikin-Ashi is normally used as a colour-flip trend filter. Here the signal is the candle's GEOMETRY — absence of a shadow plus body expansion versus the previous bar — which is a shape condition on the smoothed bar, not a crossover or a threshold on an indicator.

ideas.name: RSRS High-on-Low Regression Beta
inputs: rolling mean and stdev of the slope
ideas.entry_rule: Each day fit an ordinary least squares regression of the daily HIGH on the daily LOW over the trailing N=18 bars: High_i = alpha + beta*Low_i. Record beta and the regression R-squared. Maintain a rolling series of the last M=600 beta values and compute z = (beta[t] - mean(beta, M)) / stdev(beta, M). Optionally weight it: z_w = z * R2[t]. GO LONG when z_w crosses above +S (S = 0.7). GO SHORT when z_w crosses below -S.
ideas.exit_rule: Close the long when z_w falls below 0 (or below a separate exit threshold, default 0.0); close the short when z_w rises above 0. Hard stop at 2*ATR(14) against entry.
ideas.why: Beta is how far the day's high extends for each unit the day's low extends. Beta large means buyers push the ceiling up faster than sellers push the floor down — support is winning and there is room above. Beta small means the high is capped while the low keeps sliding — resistance is winning. Because raw beta drifts with the instrument, standardising it against its own 600-day history turns it into a comparable regime score, and the R-squared weight discounts readings where the high/low relationship was noisy.
ideas.source: whchien/ai-trader, file ai_trader/backtesting/strategies/strategies/indicators.py, classes RSRS and NormRSRS (OLS of high on low, z-score over a long window, R2-weighted variant), used by ai_trader/backtesting/strategies/classic/rsrs.py
ideas.novelty: Uses the high and low series as regressor and regressand against EACH OTHER rather than against time or against price. No moving average, no oscillator — the signal is the slope of a cross-sectional relationship inside the bar range, standardised against its own multi-year distribution.

ideas.name: Dual Contraction Base Breakout (VCP)
ideas.entry_rule: Define, on daily bars: PriceContract[t] = stdev(Close,10) < 0.7 * stdev(Close,60); VolumeContract[t] = SMA(Volume,10) < 0.7 * SMA(Volume,60). GO LONG at bar t when ALL of: (1) there exists at least one bar in the last 5 bars where PriceContract AND VolumeContract were both true simultaneously; (2) Close[t] equals the highest close of the last 100 bars; (3) Volume[t] > 0.8 * SMA(Volume,20); (4) Close[t] > SMA(Close,250); (5) min(Close over last 20 bars) > 0.7 * max(Close over last 20 bars) (the recent channel is narrower than 30%); (6) Volume[t] * Close[t] > 2,000,000 (dollar liquidity floor).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the entire position on the first daily close below SMA(Close,60). No profit target and no ATR stop — the strategy relies on the long trend MA.
ideas.why: A base forms when supply is exhausted: the daily range narrows AND turnover dries up at the same time. When price then prints a fresh multi-month high while volume is at least normal, the remaining float is held by holders who did not sell into the contraction, so there is little overhead resistance. Requiring both contractions simultaneously is what separates a genuine base from a mere quiet drift.
ideas.source: whchien/ai-trader, file ai_trader/backtesting/strategies/strategies/indicators.py class VCPPattern and strategies/classic/vcp.py — the four buy conditions plus the narrow_channel filter (recent_close_min > recent_close_max * 0.7)
ideas.novelty: Squeeze release compares one band to another band at a single instant. This requires TWO independent contractions — return dispersion and turnover — to coincide inside a 5-bar window, and then demands a 100-bar new closing high rather than a band exit. The trigger is the new high, not the volatility expansion.

ideas.name: Prior-Peak Reclaim With Volume Ramp
ideas.entry_rule: At bar t compute FirstTop = max(Close over the 25 bars ending 30 bars ago, i.e. bars t-54..t-30) and PullbackLow = min(Close over bars t-30..t-1). GO LONG when ALL SEVEN hold: (1) Close[t] >= 0.98 * highest Close of the last 60 bars; (2) PullbackLow < 0.95 * FirstTop (a pullback of at least 5% actually occurred); (3) FirstTop >= 0.90 * Close[t] (the old peak is within 10% of today — the two peaks are comparable, not a random old spike); (4) Close[t] >= FirstTop (today reclaims the old peak); (5) Close[t] > SMA(Close,60); (6) Close[t] > SMA(Close,120); (7) SMA(Volume,5) > SMA(Volume,20).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on the first daily close below SMA(Close,60), or on a close below PullbackLow recorded at entry, whichever comes first.
ideas.why: The old peak is where the last cohort of buyers became trapped. A measured pullback and then a reclaim of that exact level on rising short-term volume means the trapped supply has been absorbed rather than merely bypassed. Requiring the two peaks be within 10% of each other is what makes this a genuine double-structure and not an unrelated old high.
ideas.source: whchien/ai-trader, file ai_trader/backtesting/strategies/strategies/indicators.py class DoubleTop — the seven numbered conditions (cond_1 through cond_7) in its next() method
ideas.novelty: Donchian breakout only asks whether today exceeds an N-bar high. This requires a specific three-point geometry — an identified prior peak in a bounded historical window, a quantified trough between them, and a comparability test — plus a volume-MA ramp. Most Donchian breakouts fail all seven tests.

ideas.name: Internal Bar Strength Reversion
params: optional smoothing of IBS over k bars
ideas.entry_rule: IBS[t] = (Close[t] - Low[t]) / (High[t] - Low[t]); skip the bar entirely when High[t] == Low[t]. GO LONG at the next bar's open when IBS[t] < 0.2 (the close landed in the bottom fifth of the day's range). GO SHORT at the next bar's open when IBS[t] > 0.8. Position size may be scaled by conviction: size proportional to (0.2 - IBS) for longs and (IBS - 0.8) for shorts.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long when IBS rises above 0.8 (or after a fixed maximum holding period of 5 bars, whichever is first). Exit the short when IBS falls below 0.2 or on the same time cap.
ideas.why: IBS measures where in the day's own range the market chose to close, which is a pure position-in-range statistic independent of level, trend and volatility. A close pinned at the low means late sellers paid the full spread to get out and the marginal seller is exhausted; the next session typically opens with that pressure gone. It works because it is measured entirely within one bar, so it carries no lookback bias from a trending window.
ideas.source: neurallayer/roboquant.py, file roboquant/strategies/ibsstrategy.py (IBS = (C-L)/(H-L), buy below 0.2, sell above 0.8, rating scaled by distance); the same construction appears as StockSharp/AlgoTrading strategy 1602_Internal_Bar_Strength_IBS_Mean_Reversion
ideas.novelty: No lookback window at all — the entire signal is computed from a single bar's four prices. Unlike RSI, Williams %R or Stochastic, which normalise the close against an N-bar range, IBS normalises against the CURRENT bar's own range, so it is immune to the trend of the lookback window.

ideas.name: Strong Close Into a New Low
ideas.entry_rule: At bar t compute IBS[t] = (Close[t] - Low[t]) / (High[t] - Low[t]) and PriorLowest = min(Low over bars t-N..t-1) with N = 10. GO SHORT at the close of bar t when ALL hold: (1) Low[t] < PriorLowest (the bar made a genuinely new N-bar low); (2) IBS[t] > 0.85 (yet the bar closed in the top 15% of its own range); (3) if the trend filter is enabled, Close[t] < EMA(Close,200); (4) the bar's timestamp falls inside the configured intraday session window.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover the short on the first subsequent bar whose Close < Low[t-1] (a close beneath the previous bar's low). No stop-loss in the reference implementation; add a stop at High[t] + 0.5*ATR(14) for live use.
ideas.why: A bar that breaks to a new low but then closes at its high is a failed flush inside a downtrend — buyers stepped in intrabar, so the bounce is already spent by the close. Short sellers get to enter after the bounce rather than into it. The 200-EMA filter ensures this is a retracement being sold inside a downtrend rather than a genuine bottom.
ideas.source: StockSharp/AlgoTrading, strategy API/1501-1600/1598_10_Bar_Low_Pullback — 'Low breaks the previous LowestPeriod bars lowest low; IBS > IbsThreshold (0.85); optional close below EMA200; exit on close below previous low'
ideas.novelty: Combines a breakdown (new N-bar low) with its own contradiction (a top-of-range close) in the SAME bar, and trades the contradiction. Most breakout systems would take this as a long-side rejection; here the conflicting close is the short trigger. The exit is a close-versus-prior-bar-low test, not an indicator.

ideas.name: Lag-1 Return Autocorrelation Reversion
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain the last W = 20 closes. Form the W-1 first differences d_i = Close_{i+1} - Close_i. Let mbar = mean(d). Compute rho = sum_{i=1..W-2} (d_i - mbar)(d_{i+1} - mbar) / sum_{i=1..W-2} (d_i - mbar)^2 (return 0 if the denominator is zero). GO LONG when rho < -0.3 AND Close[t] < SMA(Close,20). GO SHORT when rho < -0.3 AND Close[t] > SMA(Close,20).
ideas.exit_rule: Close the long when Close[t] > SMA(Close,20) OR rho rises back above -0.3. Close the short when Close[t] < SMA(Close,20) OR rho rises above -0.3. Percent stop-loss at 3% (1.5x the 2% take-profit distance in the reference).
ideas.why: Negative lag-1 autocorrelation in returns is the direct statistical signature of mean reversion: an up tick is more likely than chance to be followed by a down tick. Rather than assume the market is mean-reverting and fade every extreme, this measures whether it is currently mean-reverting and only fades while the measurement says so. When rho climbs back toward zero the microstructure has changed and the position is dropped regardless of P&L.
ideas.source: StockSharp/AlgoTrading, strategy API/0201-0300/0229_Autocorrelation_Reversal — CalculateAutocorrelation() computes lag-1 autocorrelation of first differences over AutoCorrPeriod; entry when autocorr < AutoCorrThreshold (-0.3) combined with the close's position relative to the SMA
ideas.novelty: The signal is a property of the return series (its serial dependence), not a property of price level. The distance from the mean only chooses the direction; whether to trade at all is decided by a statistic that has no notion of overbought or oversold. Exiting when rho normalises is an exit condition no indicator strategy has.

ideas.name: Hurst Exponent Regime Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Estimate the Hurst exponent H over the last 100 closes as follows: for each lag tau in 2..20 compute s(tau) = stdev(Close[i] - Close[i-tau]) across the window; regress log(s(tau)) on log(tau) by OLS; H is the fitted slope. TREND BRANCH: if H > 0.55, go LONG when Close > SMA(Close,20) and SHORT when Close < SMA(Close,20). REVERSION BRANCH: if H < 0.50, go LONG when Close < SMA(Close,20) and SHORT when Close > SMA(Close,20). Take no new position while 0.50 <= H <= 0.55.
ideas.exit_rule: In the trend branch, exit when price crosses back through SMA(Close,20) against the position OR when H drops below 0.55. In the reversion branch, exit when price reaches SMA(Close,20) OR when H rises above 0.50. Percent stop-loss at 2% in both branches.
ideas.why: H > 0.5 means increments are positively persistent, so the same displacement from the mean is more likely to continue; H < 0.5 means they are anti-persistent, so it is more likely to revert. The identical price configuration (close above the 20-MA) therefore carries opposite information depending on H. Estimating H first and letting it pick which of two contradictory rulesets to apply resolves a conflict that fixed-rule systems cannot.
ideas.source: StockSharp/AlgoTrading, strategies API/0201-0300/0227_Hurst_Exponent_Trend and 0228_Hurst_Exponent_Reversion — identical MA structure with opposite entry logic gated on Hurst above/below threshold; the estimator is pinned here to the standard log-lag dispersion regression since the repo does not specify it
ideas.novelty: Not a filter that turns one strategy on and off — it is a switch between two mutually contradictory strategies on the same MA. The banned ADX-gated rules only suppress trades in chop; this one inverts the sign of the trade in chop.

ideas.name: Consecutive Close-Above-Prior-High Exhaustion
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain a counter K. On each completed bar t: if Close[t] > High[t-1], increment K by 1; otherwise reset K to 0. GO SHORT at the close of bar t when K >= 3 (three or more consecutive bars have each closed above the PREVIOUS bar's high) and, if the filter is enabled, Close[t] < EMA(Close,200). Take only one position per streak — do not re-enter until K has reset to 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover on the first subsequent bar whose Close < Low[t-1] (a close beneath the previous bar's low). Optional protective stop at the highest high of the streak plus 0.25*ATR(14).
ideas.why: Closing above the prior bar's high is a much stiffer test than merely closing up — it means the entire prior bar's trading range was engulfed and the marginal buyer paid above every price the previous session offered. Three in a row is a vertical move with no consolidation, which is where late momentum buyers are most crowded and least able to absorb the first pause. The mirrored exit (close below the prior low) is the first bar where that crowd loses the same test.
ideas.source: StockSharp/AlgoTrading, strategy API/1601-1700/1601_Consecutive_Close_High1_Mean_Reversion — 'counts consecutive closes above the prior high and sells once the count reaches a threshold; position exits when price falls below the prior low; optional 200 EMA filter'
ideas.novelty: Three-bar momentum asks for three up bars and buys them. This asks for a strictly stronger condition (each close exceeds the prior bar's HIGH, not its close) and takes the opposite side. Entry and exit are both bar-versus-prior-bar relations with no indicator, no threshold and no lookback window.

ideas.name: Cumulative Delta Extreme Break
inputs: rolling max/min of the cumulative series
params: lookback for the cumulative series' own extreme (20)
reset frequency of the cumulative sum (per session vs continuous)
ideas.entry_rule: For each completed bar compute the close-location-value weighted signed volume: Delta[t] = Volume[t] * ((Close[t]-Low[t]) - (High[t]-Close[t])) / (High[t]-Low[t]), treating a zero range as Delta = 0. Maintain CumDelta[t] = sum of Delta from the session open (reset each session). GO LONG when CumDelta[t] > max(CumDelta over the previous 20 bars). GO SHORT when CumDelta[t] < min(CumDelta over the previous 20 bars).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when CumDelta crosses back through zero (i.e. the session's net signed volume flips sign against the position), or on a 2% stop-loss, whichever comes first. Flatten at session close.
ideas.why: Where a bar closes inside its own range is the best OHLCV-available estimate of whether volume was transacted into bids or into offers. Accumulating that across the session builds a proxy for net aggressive participation. A new extreme in the ACCUMULATED series says buyers (or sellers) have committed more than at any point today, which frequently precedes the price follow-through rather than lagging it. The zero-cross exit means the position lives exactly as long as the session's net flow agrees with it.
ideas.source: StockSharp/AlgoTrading, strategy API/0001-0100/0054_Cumulative_Delta_Breakout — 'Cumulative Delta sums the difference between buy and sell volume... trades when it breaks above its highest value or below its lowest value within the lookback period; exit when delta crosses back through zero'. The repo's own PY file uses a coarse sign(Close-Open)*Volume proxy; the close-location-value weighting specified above is the standard OHLCV refinement.
ideas.ohlcv_only_note: true — real bid/ask delta is unavailable, so the close-location-value weighted volume is the proxy
ideas.novelty: The breakout is taken on a DERIVED accumulator series, not on price. Price may be flat while CumDelta makes a new extreme, and that divergence is the signal. Neither OBV-style rules nor volume-confirmed price breakouts fire on an extreme of the accumulator itself.

ideas.name: Ehlers Voss Predictive Filter Cross
ideas.entry_rule: Stage 1, two-pole bandpass on the close: F1 = cos(2*pi/Period); G1 = cos(Bandwidth*2*pi/Period); S1 = 1/G1 - sqrt(1/G1^2 - 1); Filt[n] = 0.5*(1-S1)*(Close[n] - Close[n-2]) + F1*(1+S1)*Filt[n-1] - S1*Filt[n-2], with Filt clamped to 0 for the first 6 bars. Stage 2, Voss predictor: Order = 3*Predict (=9 by default); SumC = sum over k=0..Order-1 of ((k+1)/Order) * Voss[n-(Order-k)]; Voss[n] = ((3+Order)/2)*Filt[n] - SumC. GO LONG when Voss crosses above Filt (Voss[n] > Filt[n] and Voss[n-1] <= Filt[n-1]). GO SHORT when Voss crosses below Filt.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit and reverse on the opposite Voss/Filt cross. Add a hard stop at 2*ATR(14) since the filter has no built-in invalidation.
ideas.why: The bandpass strips the trend and the noise and leaves only the component of price oscillating near the tuned period. The Voss stage applies a linearly ramped feedback over its own past outputs, which produces genuine negative group delay — it anticipates the bandpass's zero crossings by roughly Predict bars instead of overshooting the way zero-lag averages do. The cross of predictor against filter is therefore an early read on a cycle turn, degrading gracefully back toward the plain bandpass when no dominant cycle exists.
ideas.source: StockSharp/AlgoTrading strategy API/1501-1600/1544_Voss_Predictor (entry on the predictive filter crossing the band-pass output); exact coefficients from mihakralj/QuanTAlib, lib/filters/voss/Voss.md, which documents the two-pole BPF recursion and the Order = 3*Predict weighted-feedback predictor from Ehlers' Aug 2019 TASC article 'A Peek Into the Future'
ideas.novelty: An IIR filter whose output is a function of its OWN past outputs with a linear weight ramp, deliberately engineered for negative group delay. Nothing in the existing set anticipates — every listed indicator is causal-lagging by construction. Also has a real tunable (Bandwidth) that changes selectivity rather than just speed.

ideas.name: Reflex Versus Trendflex
params: signal mode: Reflex/Trendflex cross vs Reflex zero cross
ideas.entry_rule: SuperSmoother the close: a1 = exp(-1.414*pi/k); b1 = 2*a1*cos(1.414*180/k in degrees); c2 = b1; c3 = -a1*a1; c1 = 1 - c2 - c3; F[i] = c1*(Close[i]+Close[i-1])/2 + c2*F[i-1] + c3*F[i-2]. REFLEX: slope = (F[i-n] - F[i]) / n; s = (1/n) * sum over j=1..n-1 of (F[i] - F[i-j] + j*slope); MS[i] = 0.04*s^2 + 0.96*MS[i-1]; Reflex[i] = s / sqrt(MS[i]). TRENDFLEX: identical but with the slope term omitted — s = (1/n) * sum over j=1..n-1 of (F[i] - F[i-j]); same MS recursion; Trendflex[i] = s / sqrt(MS[i]). GO LONG when Reflex crosses above Trendflex while Trendflex > 0. GO SHORT when Reflex crosses below Trendflex while Trendflex < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long when Reflex crosses back below zero; exit the short when Reflex crosses back above zero. Both indicators are self-normalised so the zero line is a stable, instrument-independent exit.
ideas.why: Trendflex measures how far the smoothed price sits above its own recent history — a trend reading. Reflex measures the same quantity after removing the linear slope of that history — a pure cycle reading with the trend subtracted out. Their divergence isolates the moment a cyclical impulse begins that the trend has not yet absorbed. Dividing by the square root of an EWMA of the squared sum auto-scales both to roughly unit variance, so a single threshold works across instruments and volatility regimes.
ideas.source: pandas-ta (fork gopalparashar421/pandas-ta), files pandas_ta/cycle/reflex.py (np_reflex, with the slope-detrended difference sum) and pandas_ta/trend/trendflex.py (nb_trendflex, without it); paired as a crossover system in StockSharp/AlgoTrading API/1501-1600/1587_Reflex_Trendflex. Ehlers, 'Reflex: A New Zero-Lag Indicator', TASC Feb 2020.
ideas.novelty: Two oscillators that differ by exactly one term (the slope correction), traded against each other. Self-normalisation by a running RMS makes the zero line and thresholds portable across tickers without re-tuning — nothing in the existing set is scale-free in that way.

ideas.name: Mass Index Reversal Bulge
ideas.entry_rule: Compute SingleEMA[t] = EMA(High[t]-Low[t], 9); DoubleEMA[t] = EMA(SingleEMA, 9); Ratio[t] = SingleEMA[t] / DoubleEMA[t]; MassIndex[t] = sum of Ratio over the last 25 bars. A 'reversal bulge' completes at bar t when MassIndex rose above 27.0 at some bar within the last 25 bars AND MassIndex[t] < 26.5 for the first time since that peak. On the bar the bulge completes: GO SHORT if EMA(Close,9) is rising (EMA9[t] > EMA9[t-1]); GO LONG if EMA(Close,9) is falling.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when EMA(Close,9) turns back in the direction of the original trend (for a short: exit when EMA9 stops falling, i.e. EMA9[t] > EMA9[t-1] for two consecutive bars), or on a 2.5*ATR(14) stop from entry, or after 15 bars — whichever comes first.
ideas.why: Dorsey's insight is that a trend reverses after its bars WIDEN, not after price reaches an extreme. The ratio of a fast range EMA to a slower EMA of itself rises when daily ranges are expanding relative to their own recent norm; summing 25 of those readings accumulates the evidence. The bulge above 27 and drop back below 26.5 marks the point where range expansion peaked and began to subside — the classic signature of a climax. The 9-EMA slope only supplies the direction, never the timing.
ideas.source: nardew/talipp, file talipp/indicators/MassIndex.py — EMA of (High-Low) over ma_period, EMA of that over ma_ma_period, ratio, summed over ma_ratio_period (canonical defaults 9/9/25). The 27.0/26.5 reversal-bulge thresholds are Dorsey's published interpretation of that output.
ideas.novelty: Uses only the HIGH-LOW range and never the close for its trigger — the close enters solely as a direction tiebreaker. It signals reversal from range EXPANSION, whereas the existing squeeze-release and ATR-expansion rules read the same expansion as a continuation trigger. Opposite interpretation of the same raw quantity.

ideas.name: Chande Kroll Double-Smoothed Stop Exit
inputs: rolling max/min over q of the raw stops
params: entry lookback for the momentum trigger
ideas.entry_rule: Entry trigger (deliberately simple so the exit is what is being tested): GO LONG when Close[t] > max(Close over bars t-20..t-1) AND Close[t] > SMA(Close,100). GO SHORT on the mirror. The distinguishing component is the stop: FirstHighStop[t] = max(High over p bars) - x*ATR(p); FirstLowStop[t] = min(Low over p bars) + x*ATR(p); StopShort[t] = max(FirstHighStop over the last q bars); StopLong[t] = min(FirstLowStop over the last q bars).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long on the first close below StopLong[t]; exit the short on the first close above StopShort[t]. The stop is recomputed every bar but, because of the second-pass max/min over q bars, it does not ratchet monotonically the way a Chandelier or ATR trailing stop does — it can loosen when the recent extreme rolls off, which keeps the position alive through a normal pullback. No profit target and no time stop.
ideas.why: A single-pass ATR stop hung off the running extreme tightens forever and gets picked off by ordinary retracements. Taking the max over q bars of the raw stop levels means the exit level reflects the most generous of the last q candidate stops, so it widens automatically after a volatility spike and only tightens once that spike has aged out of the q-window. That asymmetry is the whole point: it is tolerant of noise immediately after a large bar, which is exactly when noise is largest.
ideas.source: nardew/talipp, file talipp/indicators/ChandeKrollStop.py — first-pass stops from highest-high minus atr_mult*ATR and lowest-low plus atr_mult*ATR, then a second-pass rolling extreme over `period` to produce the long and short stop lines. Canonical defaults p=10, x=1, q=9.
ideas.novelty: This entry is an exit idea. The two-pass construction (extreme-based stop, then a rolling extreme OF THAT STOP) is not a trailing stop — it is non-monotonic by design and can move away from price. No existing entry in the set carries an exit that loosens.

ideas.name: Envelope of Separate High/Low EMAs With Fast Stochastic
ideas.entry_rule: Build three separate 5-period EMAs, one on the HIGH series (ema_high), one on the LOW series (ema_low) and one on the close (ema_close). Compute fast stochastic with fastk_period=5, fastd_period=3, slowing=3, giving fastk and fastd. GO LONG at bar t when ALL hold: (1) Open[t] < ema_low[t] (the bar opened beneath the EMA of lows — outside the lower edge of the envelope); (2) fastk crosses above fastd at bar t; (3) fastk[t] < 25 and fastd[t] < 25; (4) ADX(14)[t] > 25.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when ANY of: Open[t] >= ema_high[t] (the bar opens above the upper envelope edge); OR fastk crosses above 75; OR fastd crosses above 75.
ideas.why: Smoothing the high series and the low series separately produces an envelope whose width is set by the market's own recent range asymmetry rather than by a fixed multiple of ATR or standard deviation — it widens on the side that has been extending. An open below the EMA-of-lows means the gap opened outside the envelope entirely. Requiring ADX above 25 means this is a retracement inside a live trend, and the fast stochastic cross times the turn.
ideas.source: freqtrade/freqtrade-strategies, file user_data/strategies/berlinguyinca/CofiBitStrategy.py — ema_high/ema_close/ema_low each period 5, STOCHF(5,3,0,3,0), entry on open < ema_low with fastk crossing above fastd, both below 25, and ADX > 25; exit on open >= ema_high or either stochastic line crossing 75
ideas.novelty: The channel is built from EMAs of the HIGH and LOW series as separate inputs, not from a centre line plus a symmetric offset — so it is inherently asymmetric and cannot be reproduced by Keltner or Bollinger. The entry also tests the OPEN against the band rather than the close, which fires on the gap rather than after the bar has resolved.

ideas.name: CUSUM Event Sampling With Triple-Barrier Exit
params: threshold h in units of sigma (default 2.0)
ideas.entry_rule: Let r[t] = log(Close[t]/Close[t-1]) and sigma[t] = EWMA standard deviation of r with span 50. Maintain two accumulators, both starting at 0: Sp[t] = max(0, Sp[t-1] + r[t]) and Sn[t] = min(0, Sn[t-1] + r[t]). Fire an UP EVENT and reset Sp to 0 whenever Sp[t] >= h*sigma[t]; fire a DOWN EVENT and reset Sn to 0 whenever Sn[t] <= -h*sigma[t] (h = 2.0). GO LONG on an up event, GO SHORT on a down event. Take no action on any bar that is not an event bar — this deliberately samples bars unevenly, densely in active markets and sparsely in quiet ones.
ideas.exit_rule: Triple barrier, all three set at entry and evaluated every bar until one is touched: (1) profit-take at entry_price * exp(+2.0*sigma[entry]*sqrt(k)) for a long; (2) stop-loss at entry_price * exp(-1.0*sigma[entry]*sqrt(k)) for a long; (3) a vertical time barrier that closes the position at market after k = 10 bars regardless of price. Mirror the price barriers for shorts. Whichever barrier is touched first ends the trade; no barrier is moved after entry.
ideas.why: Fixed-interval sampling wastes most bars on periods where nothing happened and under-samples the bursts that carry the information. The CUSUM accumulator only fires after a sustained run of same-signed returns totalling h sigma, and because it resets on each fire it cannot chatter while price oscillates around a level — the standard failure mode of threshold crossings.
