The triple barrier then sizes both targets in units of the volatility that prevailed at entry, so the risk/reward ratio is constant in risk-adjusted terms rather than in dollars, and the time barrier caps the opportunity cost of trades that go nowhere.
ideas.source: hudson-and-thames/mlfinlab, file mlfinlab/filters/filters.py (symmetric CUSUM filter: cumulative sums of the raw series reset to zero on each event, requiring 'a full run of length threshold' so that 'multiple events are not triggered by raw_time_series hovering around a threshold level'), paired with the triple-barrier labelling scheme in the same library's labeling module
ideas.novelty: Two structural departures at once. Entry: the strategy does not evaluate a rule on every bar — the CUSUM decides WHICH bars are decision points, and its reset-on-fire behaviour makes it immune to the repeated-signal problem that afflicts every threshold rule in the existing set. Exit: three simultaneous barriers, two of them scaled to entry-time volatility and one purely temporal, with none of them trailing.

ideas.name: Range Filter Streak
ideas.entry_rule: Compute smoothrng = ema(ema(abs(close-close[1]), P), 2*P-1) * M with P=100, M=3.0. Maintain a step filter: filt := close > filt[1] ? max(filt[1], close - smoothrng) : min(filt[1], close + smoothrng), seeded filt[0]=close. Maintain streak counters: upward := filt>filt[1] ? upward[1]+1 : filt<filt[1] ? 0 : upward[1]; downward symmetric. Signal a raw long when close > filt AND upward > 0; a raw short when close < filt AND downward > 0. Take the actual LONG entry only on the bar where a raw long occurs and the last non-neutral raw state was short (state machine: CondIni := longRaw ? 1 : shortRaw ? -1 : CondIni[1]; enter long when longRaw and CondIni[1] == -1). Short is the mirror.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long on the opposite entry signal (first bar where shortRaw fires and CondIni[1]==1), or on a hard stop at filt - smoothrng (the lower band). Exit short mirrored at filt + smoothrng.
params: use wicks vs close for the filter update
ideas.why: The filter refuses to move at all until price travels further than a smoothed measure of recent per-bar travel, so it is a genuine dead-band rather than a lag filter. Small oscillations leave the reference level exactly unchanged, which removes the whipsaw mode that kills MA crosses in chop. The streak counter adds a persistence requirement: the level must have already ratcheted at least once in the new direction before an entry is allowed, which filters single-bar spikes. Economically it targets the fact that dealer-driven noise has a characteristic amplitude; only moves that exceed that amplitude carry information.
ideas.novelty: Not a moving average at all - it is a hysteresis/ratchet level with a zero-lag hold, plus a run-length state machine. An MA cross fires whenever two smoothed lines touch; this fires only after price has genuinely displaced the reference by more than the ambient noise amplitude and the reference has confirmed by moving.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Range Filter [DW]' by DonovanWall, https://www.tradingview.com/script/lut7sBgG-Range-Filter-DW/ . The published script emits only a +1/-1 trend value; I pinned the entry down to the standard streak + state-machine formalisation used by the widely-copied derived Buy/Sell variants, and stated the exact defaults.

ideas.name: HalfTrend Extreme Flip
ideas.entry_rule: Let A = amplitude (default 2). highPrice = high[abs(highestbars(high, A))], lowPrice = low[abs(lowestbars(low, A))], highma = sma(high, A), lowma = sma(low, A), atr2 = atr(100)/2. Keep state trend in {0=up,1=down} and nextTrend in {0,1}, plus running maxLowPrice and minHighPrice. If nextTrend==1: maxLowPrice := max(lowPrice, maxLowPrice); if (highma < maxLowPrice AND close < low[1]) then trend:=1, nextTrend:=0, minHighPrice:=highPrice. Else: minHighPrice := min(highPrice, minHighPrice); if (lowma > minHighPrice AND close > high[1]) then trend:=0, nextTrend:=1, maxLowPrice:=lowPrice. ENTER LONG on the bar where trend goes 1 -> 0. ENTER SHORT on the bar where trend goes 0 -> 1.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on the opposite flip. Optional hard stop: for a long, exit if close < (up - channelDeviation*atr2) where up is the HalfTrend line (up := max(maxLowPrice, up[1]) while trend==0); channelDeviation default 2.
ideas.why: A flip requires two independent things at once: the short average of highs must fall entirely below the running maximum of recent swing lows (structure has rolled over), AND the current close must break the prior bar's low (immediate confirmation). Because maxLowPrice/minHighPrice only ratchet in one direction until a flip, the indicator cannot oscillate - it needs a full structural give-up before reversing.
ideas.novelty: Unlike SuperTrend, the reversal level is not an ATR band around price; it is a ratcheting extreme of swing points, and ATR is used only to draw the optional channel. The two-part condition (average-of-highs vs ratcheted low, plus a prior-bar break) has no analogue in ATR-band flips, and the state can sit in a 'pending' nextTrend condition for many bars before committing.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'HalfTrend' by everget (Alex Orekhov), https://www.tradingview.com/script/U1SJ8ubc-HalfTrend/ . Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/trailing_stops/halftrend.pine

ideas.name: NRTR Percentage Ratchet Exit
ideas.entry_rule: Use as a standalone reversal system or as an exit overlay. Standalone: keep trend in {+1,-1}, hp (highest close since the last long flip) and lp (lowest close since the last short flip), and coefficient k (default 0.02 = 2%). If trend >= 0: hp := max(hp, close); nrtr := hp*(1-k); if close <= nrtr then trend := -1, lp := close, nrtr := lp*(1+k). Else: lp := min(lp, close); nrtr := lp*(1+k); if close > nrtr then trend := +1, hp := close, nrtr := hp*(1-k). ENTER LONG on the bar where trend goes -1 -> +1; ENTER SHORT on -1 flip.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long the bar close <= hp*(1-k) (which is simultaneously the short entry); exit short when close > lp*(1+k). Note the reference extreme is RESET to the current close at every flip, so the stop starts tight after a reversal and only loosens as the new extreme extends.
inputs: running max/min of close since last flip
params: optionally make k = c * atr(n)/close to auto-scale by instrument
ideas.why: A stop set as a fixed percentage of the running extreme is scale-invariant, so one parameter transfers across tickers of very different price levels without re-fitting - which an ATR-multiple stop does not do cleanly when volatility regime shifts. The reset-on-flip behaviour means risk is smallest right after a reversal, when the trade thesis is least proven, and widens only as the trade earns it.
ideas.novelty: Distinct exit STRUCTURE rather than a distinct entry: percentage-of-extreme ratchet with a hard reset at every direction change, versus an ATR-band stop that carries its width across the flip. Also unlike a chandelier stop, the anchor is the extreme CLOSE, not the extreme high/low, so intrabar spikes do not loosen the stop.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Nick Rypock Trailing Reverse (NRTR)' by everget. Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/trailing_stops/nrtr_nick_rypock_trailing_reverse.pine

ideas.name: Stiffness Persistence Cross
ideas.entry_rule: bound = sma(close, 100) - 0.2*stdev(close, 100). raw = 100 * count(close > bound over the last 60 bars) / 60. stiffness = ema(raw, 3). ENTER LONG when stiffness crosses above 90 AND close > sma(close, 100) AND sma(close,100) > sma(close,100)[20] (long-term slope is up).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when stiffness crosses below 50, or when close < sma(close, 100) - 0.2*stdev(close, 100) for two consecutive bars, whichever comes first.
inputs: rolling count of bars above a level
ideas.why: This measures how RELIABLY price has held above a slightly-discounted long moving average, not how far above it price is. A stock that spends 57 of the last 60 days above its (mean minus 0.2 sigma) line is being systematically bid on every dip; a stock that is 15% above its MA but only spent 30 of 60 days above it is a single spike. Persistence of support is a different, and more institutional, footprint than displacement.
ideas.novelty: Occupancy statistic rather than a distance or a cross. The signal fires on the fraction of a window spent above a level, so a large one-day move cannot trigger it and a slow, boring, relentless drift can. The 0.2-sigma discount makes the reference adaptive to the stock's own dispersion instead of being a bare MA.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Stiffness Indicator' by everget, https://www.tradingview.com/script/Ds1akUBu-Stiffness-Indicator/ (original concept: Markos Katsanos, Stocks & Commodities V.36:12, Nov 2018). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/stiffness_indicator.pine . The published script plots the oscillator only; I pinned the entry/exit thresholds and the trend filter down to make it testable.

ideas.name: Trend Trigger Factor
ideas.entry_rule: With N = 15: hh = highest(high, N), ll = lowest(low, N). buyPower = hh - ll[N] (current N-bar high minus the N-bar low as it stood N bars ago). sellPower = hh[N] - ll. TTF = 200*(buyPower - sellPower)/(buyPower + sellPower). ENTER LONG when TTF crosses above +100. ENTER SHORT when TTF crosses below -100.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when TTF crosses below -100 (which is also the short entry) or, for a flat-exit variant, when TTF crosses below 0. Exit short mirrored.
ideas.why: It compares the current window's extreme against the PREVIOUS window's opposite extreme, so it measures how much new ground the range has claimed in each direction over a two-window span, normalised to a bounded scale. That is a range-displacement measure, not a smoothed-price measure, so it is insensitive to where price sits inside the range and responds only to the range itself walking.
ideas.novelty: Both channel breakout (Donchian) and MA crosses react to price touching a level. TTF ignores the touch entirely and scores the net migration of the channel's own boundaries between two adjacent windows - it can be strongly positive while price is mid-range, and neutral on a breakout that immediately reverses the channel.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Trend Trigger Factor' by everget (original: M. H. Pee, Stocks & Commodities). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/trend_trigger_factor.pine

ideas.name: Trend Continuation Factor
ideas.entry_rule: Define plusChange = max(close - close[1], 0) and minusChange = max(close[1] - close, 0). Maintain two run-accumulators that RESET to zero the moment their side is quiet: plusCF := plusChange == 0 ? 0 : plusChange + plusCF[1]; minusCF := minusChange == 0 ? 0 : minusChange + minusCF[1]. Then over N = 35 bars: plusTCF = sum(plusChange - minusCF, N) and minusTCF = sum(minusChange - plusCF, N). ENTER LONG when plusTCF > 0 AND minusTCF < 0. ENTER SHORT when minusTCF > 0 AND plusTCF < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when plusTCF crosses below 0 or minusTCF crosses above 0, whichever comes first. Exit short mirrored. Flat when both are positive or both negative (indeterminate regime).
inputs: per-bar up change and down change
params: require a minimum bar count with plusTCF>0 before entering (1-5)
ideas.why: The run-accumulator only grows while a side keeps producing consecutive same-direction bars and is wiped to zero by a single opposing bar. Subtracting the opposing side's uninterrupted run from each bar's raw change therefore penalises the trend precisely by the length of the counter-runs it has to absorb. A trend built of long unbroken up-runs against short down-runs scores high; the same net drift built of alternating bars scores near zero.
ideas.novelty: Consecutive-run structure, not magnitude, is the load-bearing quantity - the reset-to-zero accumulator has no analogue in MACD, ADX or three-bar momentum. It is also a two-sided condition: both plusTCF>0 and minusTCF<0 must hold, so a market that is strong in both directions (high volatility, no net trend) is correctly refused.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Trend Continuation Factor' by everget (original: M. H. Pee, Stocks & Commodities). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/trend_continuation_factor.pine

ideas.name: Random Walk Index Escape
ideas.entry_rule: For each n in 2..N (N = 14): RWIH(n) = (high - low[n]) / (atr(n) * sqrt(n)); RWIL(n) = (high[n] - low) / (atr(n) * sqrt(n)). Take RWIH = max over n of RWIH(n) and RWIL = max over n of RWIL(n). ENTER LONG when RWIH crosses above 1.0 AND RWIH > RWIL. ENTER SHORT when RWIL crosses above 1.0 AND RWIL > RWIH.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when RWIH falls below 1.0 OR RWIL rises above RWIH. Exit short mirrored. Optional stop: exit long if close < low[n*] where n* is the lookback that produced the max RWIH at entry.
params: use close-to-close instead of high/low for the displacement
ideas.why: Under a random walk, expected displacement over n bars grows as sqrt(n) times the per-bar range. Dividing the actual n-bar displacement by atr(n)*sqrt(n) gives a dimensionless ratio that is ~1 for diffusion and >1 only when the move is larger than diffusion can explain. Taking the maximum over all n asks 'is there ANY horizon on which this move is statistically anomalous', which finds trends whose natural scale you did not guess in advance.
ideas.novelty: An explicit null-hypothesis test rather than a threshold on a smoothed series - the sqrt(n) normalisation and the max-over-horizons search are the idea. Unlike ADX it has an absolute, scale-free meaning (1.0 = random walk), and unlike ATR expansion it measures directional displacement per unit of expected diffusion, not raw range.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Random Walk Index' by everget (original: E. Michael Poulos). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/random_walk_index.pine - the published script fixes a single n; I restored the max-over-n = 2..N form from the original definition and pinned the 1.0 trigger.

ideas.name: Intraday vs Overnight Pressure Divergence
ideas.entry_rule: Intraday Momentum Index: gain = (close > open) ? close - open : 0; loss = (close > open) ? 0 : open - close; IMI(14) = 100 * sum(gain,14) / (sum(gain,14) + sum(loss,14)). Standard RSI(14) is computed on close-to-close (so it includes the overnight gap). ENTER LONG when IMI(14) > 55 AND rsi(close,14) < 45 AND close > sma(close,200). ENTER SHORT when IMI(14) < 45 AND rsi(close,14) > 55 AND close < sma(close,200).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when IMI(14) < 50 OR rsi(close,14) > 55 (the divergence has closed), or after 10 bars, whichever comes first. Exit short mirrored.
ideas.why: IMI decomposes the return into its intraday (open-to-close) component only, discarding the gap. RSI on closes carries both. When IMI is high while RSI is low, the security has been sold overnight and bought back every single session - the classic footprint of institutional accumulation absorbing retail/overseas gap supply. The overnight-vs-intraday return split is one of the better-documented decompositions in equity return data, and this is the cheapest OHLCV-only handle on it.
ideas.novelty: Not an RSI extreme. The signal is the SPREAD between two momentum measures computed on different return components of the same bars - it can fire when both are mid-range and stay silent when both are extreme. Neither leg alone is tradeable.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Intraday Momentum Index' by everget (original: Tushar Chande). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/intraday_momentum_index.pine . The IMI-vs-RSI divergence pairing and thresholds are my synthesis on top of the script's exact IMI formula.

ideas.name: Self-Adjusting RSI Bands
ideas.entry_rule: r = rsi(close, 14). adjust = 2.0 * stdev(r, 14) (alternative estimator: 2.0 * sma(abs(r - sma(r,14)), 14)). obLevel = 50 + adjust; osLevel = 50 - adjust. ENTER LONG when r crosses ABOVE obLevel (breakout reading, trend mode) - or, for the fade variant, when r crosses BACK ABOVE osLevel after having been below it. Pick one variant per backtest and sweep it as a mode flag. ENTER SHORT mirrored around obLevel.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when r crosses back below 50, or when r crosses below osLevel. Exit short mirrored. Optional: exit when adjust itself contracts below its own 50-bar median (bands collapsing = no more information in the reading).
params: band estimator (stdev vs mean absolute deviation)
band length independent of RSI length
ideas.why: A fixed 70/30 pair is wrong for any instrument whose RSI dispersion differs from the one Wilder happened to look at. A low-volatility mega-cap may never print 70; a small-cap may print 70 weekly. Standardising the threshold by the RSI's own recent dispersion makes 'extreme' mean the same statistical thing on every ticker, which is exactly what a multi-ticker fleet needs to avoid per-symbol threshold fitting.
ideas.novelty: This is the textbook case of a genuinely different idea rather than a parameter change: the threshold is a statistic of the indicator itself, recomputed every bar, so the same code produces different effective levels per symbol and per regime. It also self-widens in high-dispersion regimes, which suppresses signals exactly when RSI is least informative.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Self-Adjusting RSI (SARSI)' by everget. Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/self_adjusting_rsi.pine

ideas.name: Relative Volatility Index Direction
ideas.entry_rule: Let s = stdev(src, 10). up = ema( (change(src) >= 0 ? s : 0), 14 ); down = ema( (change(src) >= 0 ? 0 : s), 14 ); RVI(src) = 100 * up / (up + down). Compute the refined form: RVI = 0.5*( RVI(high) + RVI(low) ). ENTER LONG when RVI crosses above 60 AND close > ema(close, 50). ENTER SHORT when RVI crosses below 40 AND close < ema(close, 50).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when RVI crosses below 50; exit short when RVI crosses above 50. Hard stop at 2*atr(14) from entry.
params: refined (avg of high and low) vs single-source
ideas.why: RVI runs the RSI machinery over standard deviation instead of price change, so it answers 'is volatility being generated by up bars or down bars'. Healthy uptrends in equities are usually low-volatility drifts punctuated by high-volatility down bars, so RVI > 60 (volatility concentrated in UP bars) is an unusual, information-rich state - typically breakout or short-squeeze conditions rather than ordinary drift.
ideas.novelty: The input series to the RSI-style up/down decomposition is volatility, not price. It can be flat while price momentum is extreme, and extreme while price is flat. It also has no relationship to Bollinger width or ATR expansion, both of which are direction-blind.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Relative Volatility Index' by everget (original: Donald Dorsey, Stocks & Commodities 1993). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/relative_volatility_index.pine

ideas.name: Chord Convexity (Phase Change)
ideas.entry_rule: Over a window of N = 35 bars, define the straight chord from close[N] to close[0]: chord(i) = close[N] + (close[0] - close[N]) * (N - i)/N for i = 0..N (so chord(N) = close[N] and chord(0) = close[0]). For each i compute dev(i) = close[i] - chord(i). Let P = sum of dev(i) where dev(i) > 0 and Q = sum of -dev(i) where dev(i) < 0. CCI_chord = 100 * P / (P + Q). ENTER SHORT when close[0] > close[N] (net up move) AND CCI_chord > 80 (the path spent the window ABOVE its own chord, i.e. concave / decelerating). ENTER LONG when close[0] < close[N] AND CCI_chord < 20 (path below its chord in a down move: concave down / decelerating sell-off).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when CCI_chord crosses back through 50, or after N/2 bars, or at 1.5*atr(14) adverse excursion - whichever comes first.
inputs: rolling loop over the last N closes
ideas.why: Two moves with identical start and end points can have completely different shapes: one that jumps early and grinds sideways (path above the chord, concave) versus one that grinds then accelerates (path below the chord, convex). Concave moves are late-stage - the marginal buyer has already paid - while convex moves are still accelerating. This is a pure path-shape measure that momentum indicators, which only see endpoints and smoothed derivatives, cannot express.
ideas.novelty: Measures the CONVEXITY of the price path relative to the straight line joining the window's endpoints. Nothing in an RSI, MACD or ATR construction contains this - they are all functions of differences, not of the area between the path and its chord. It fires on shape while net momentum is held constant.
ideas.source: Adapted from TradingView open-source 'Phase Change Index' by everget (original: M. H. Pee). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/phase_change_index.pine . The published script's gradient indexing runs the chord in the reverse direction to the price series, which makes its sign convention ambiguous; I re-derived the chord orientation explicitly above so the rule is unambiguous, and set the directional rule from the geometry rather than from the script's plot colours.

ideas.name: Waddah Attar Explosion V2
ideas.entry_rule: macd(x) = ema(x, 20) - ema(x, 40). t1 = ( macd(close) - macd(close)[1] ) * 150. e1 = bbUpper - bbLower where bbUpper/bbLower = sma(close,20) +/- 2.0*stdev(close,20). DEAD_ZONE = rma(tr, 100) * 3.7. trendUp = t1 >= 0 ? t1 : 0; trendDown = t1 < 0 ? -t1 : 0. ENTER LONG when trendUp > trendUp[1] AND trendUp > e1 AND e1 > e1[1] AND trendUp > DEAD_ZONE. ENTER SHORT when trendDown > trendDown[1] AND trendDown > e1 AND e1 > e1[1] AND trendDown > DEAD_ZONE.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when trendUp crosses below e1 (the explosion line). Exit short when trendDown crosses below e1. Hard stop 1.5*atr(14).
ideas.why: t1 is the first difference of the MACD line - i.e. MACD ACCELERATION, not level. It is then required to exceed the current Bollinger band WIDTH, which is a live estimate of how much range the market is currently capable of producing. Requiring acceleration > available range, with the range itself expanding, isolates the moment a move breaks out of the volatility envelope that had been containing it. The ATR-based dead zone kills the whole signal in quiet tape, which is where an acceleration measure is otherwise pure noise.
ideas.novelty: Three genuinely different things stacked: (1) the second derivative of MACD rather than its level or its signal cross; (2) a threshold that is the Bollinger band width, so the momentum measure is compared against a volatility measure in the same units; (3) an absolute ATR floor that mutes everything below it. None of MACD-gated-by-ADX, Bollinger-with-volume, or squeeze-release does any of these.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Waddah Attar Explosion V2 [SHK]' by shayankm, https://www.tradingview.com/script/d9IjcYyS-Waddah-Attar-Explosion-V2-SHK/ (ported to Pine by LazyBear, adapted by ShayanKM). Full original Pine reproduced in github.com/edyatl/waddah-attar-explosion README, from which the exact constants above are taken; entry/exit conditions are the ones stated in that script's own documentation.

ideas.name: Impulse MACD Dead-Zone Band
ideas.entry_rule: L = 34. smma(x) = na(smma[1]) ? sma(x, L) : (smma[1]*(L-1) + x)/L. hi = smma(high); lo = smma(low). zlema(x) = let e1 = ema(x, L), e2 = ema(e1, L), then e1 + (e1 - e2). mi = zlema(hlc3). md = (mi > hi) ? (mi - hi) : (mi < lo) ? (mi - lo) : 0. sb = sma(md, 9); sh = md - sb. ENTER LONG when md crosses above 0 (i.e. mi enters the region above hi from inside the band) AND sh > 0. ENTER SHORT when md crosses below 0 (mi drops below lo) AND sh < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when md returns to exactly 0 (mi re-enters the hi/lo band) or when md crosses below sb. Exit short mirrored.
params: source for the fast line (hlc3 vs close)
require md > k*atr for an entry
ideas.why: The band between the smoothed high and the smoothed low is a structurally defined null zone: while the zero-lag fast line sits inside it, the indicator is EXACTLY zero, not a small number. That eliminates the near-zero chatter that generates most false MACD signals. Only when the fast line escapes the band entirely does the indicator start reading, and its value is then the distance beyond the band - a direct measure of how far price has left its own recent high/low envelope.
ideas.novelty: An MACD-shaped indicator with a hard-coded dead zone built from separate smoothings of high and low, plus a zero-lag EMA as the fast line. It is not a difference of two moving averages of the same series - it is a distance from a two-sided envelope, and it is identically zero (not merely small) in range conditions.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Impulse MACD [LazyBear]' by LazyBear, https://www.tradingview.com/script/qt6xLfLi-Impulse-MACD-LazyBear/ . Full original Pine reproduced in github.com/edyatl/impulse-macd README; formulas above transcribed from it.

ideas.name: Interquartile Range Band Breakout
ideas.entry_rule: Over the last N = 14 closes: q1 = 25th percentile (nearest rank), q3 = 75th percentile, med = 50th percentile, iqr = q3 - q1. upperBand = q3 + 1.5*iqr; lowerBand = q1 - 1.5*iqr. ENTER LONG when close crosses above upperBand AND volume > sma(volume, 20). ENTER SHORT when close crosses below lowerBand AND volume > sma(volume, 20).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when close crosses back below med (the rolling 50th percentile). Exit short when close crosses back above med. Hard stop at q1 for longs, q3 for shorts.
inputs: rolling 25th/50th/75th percentile of close over N
ideas.why: Standard deviation is inflated by the very outlier you are trying to detect - one big bar widens the Bollinger band and hides the next one. Quartiles are order statistics: a single extreme close cannot move q1 or q3 at all. So the IQR band stays tight through the first outlier, which means the breakout threshold does not run away from price during the initial expansion. That is a mechanically different response to the exact regime the strategy is designed to catch.
ideas.novelty: Robust order-statistic channel, not a moment-based one. It is not Bollinger with a different multiplier, and not Donchian (which uses only the two extremes and therefore is entirely determined by outliers); it uses the middle 50% of the distribution to set the scale and the tail only to trigger.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Interquartile Range Bands (IQRB)' by everget. Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/bands_and_channels/interquartile_range_bands.pine . The published script plots bands only; the breakout/volume entry and the median exit are my specification.

ideas.name: Hampel Outlier Impulse Bar
ideas.entry_rule: Over N = 20 bars: med = 50th percentile (nearest rank) of close; mad = 50th percentile of abs(close - med) over the same N. A bar is a Hampel outlier when abs(close - med) > 3.0 * mad. ENTER LONG when (close - med) > 3.0*mad AND close >= low + 0.75*(high - low) (bar closes in the top quartile of its own range) AND volume > 1.5*sma(volume, 20). ENTER SHORT when (med - close) > 3.0*mad AND close <= low + 0.25*(high - low) AND volume > 1.5*sma(volume, 20).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when close crosses back below med (the running median), or when a bar closes in the bottom quartile of its own range, or after 20 bars - whichever comes first. Exit short mirrored.
ideas.why: The median and MAD are computed from the same window that contains the candidate bar, but because both are order statistics the candidate bar cannot bias its own baseline - a mean/stdev baseline is dragged toward the outlier and therefore understates it. Adding the close-location-in-range and volume conditions makes the bar an INFORMED outlier (it closed on its extreme, on heavy volume) rather than a spike-and-fade, which is the standard microstructure distinction between an information event and a liquidity event.
ideas.novelty: Uses median/MAD contamination-resistant statistics to define the outlier, then requires the outlier's own internal structure (close location within the bar's range) to agree. It is not a Bollinger or Keltner break: the reference and the scale are both order statistics, and the trade is entered on the outlier bar itself rather than on a band cross.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Hampel Filter' by everget. Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/movings/hampel_filter.pine - the script uses the median/MAD test to REPLACE outliers; I inverted it into an entry trigger and added the close-location and volume conditions.

ideas.name: FRAMA Fractal-Dimension Gate
ideas.entry_rule: With L = 14 (even) and H = L/2: N1 = (highest(high,H) - lowest(low,H))/H; N2 = (highest(high,H)[H] - lowest(low,H)[H])/H; N3 = (highest(high,L) - lowest(low,L))/L. D = ( log(N1 + N2) - log(N3) ) / log(2). alpha = exp(-4.6*(D - 1)), clamped to [0.01, 1]. frama := alpha*close + (1 - alpha)*frama[1]. ENTER LONG when close crosses above frama AND D < 1.4. ENTER SHORT when close crosses below frama AND D < 1.4.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when close crosses below frama, or when D rises above 1.6 for two consecutive bars (market has reverted to noise) - whichever comes first. Exit short mirrored.
ideas.why: D is an estimate of the fractal dimension of the price path: D near 1 means the path is close to a straight line, D near 2 means it fills the plane like Brownian motion. The smoothing constant is then set FROM the geometry of the path itself, so the filter is fast exactly when the market is trending and nearly frozen when it is noisy. Gating the entry on D < 1.4 adds a second, independent use of the same quantity: only take crosses when the geometry says a line, not a cloud, is being drawn.
ideas.novelty: The lookback is not a parameter you sweep - it is inferred each bar from a box-counting-style dimension estimate, and the SAME estimate is reused as a standalone regime gate on entries and exits. A plain EMA cross has a fixed responsiveness and no notion of whether a cross is geometrically meaningful.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Fractal Adaptive Moving Average (FRAMA)' by everget (original: John Ehlers). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/movings/fractal_adaptive_moving_average.pine . The D-based entry/exit gates are my addition on top of the script's exact D and alpha formulas.

ideas.name: Recursive Median Roofing Oscillator
ideas.entry_rule: PI = 3.14159265. a1 = (cos(2*PI/12) + sin(2*PI/12) - 1)/cos(2*PI/12). rm := a1 * median(close, 5) + (1 - a1)*rm[1], where median(close,5) is the 5-bar 50th percentile (nearest rank). a2 = (cos(w) + sin(w) - 1)/cos(w) with w = (1/sqrt(2)) * 2*PI/30. rmo := (1 - a2/2)^2 * (rm - 2*rm[1] + rm[2]) + 2*(1 - a2)*rmo[1] - (1 - a2)^2 * rmo[2]. ENTER LONG when rmo crosses above 0. ENTER SHORT when rmo crosses below 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on the opposite zero cross, or when abs(rmo) contracts to below its own 50-bar 25th percentile (signal energy has died), whichever comes first.
inputs: two-pole recursive filters (Ehlers super smoother / high-pass)
ideas.why: Taking a rolling MEDIAN before any filtering removes single-bar price spikes entirely - a mean-based pre-filter smears the spike across the whole filter window instead. The two-pole low-pass then removes the remaining high-frequency component and the two-pole high-pass removes the trend, so what is left is a band-limited cycle component that is immune to the print errors, halt reopens and single-tick spikes that plague intraday equity bars. Its zero crossings are therefore cycle turns rather than spike artefacts.
ideas.novelty: A non-linear (median) pre-filter feeding a linear roofing filter - the combination is what matters. Every oscillator in the existing set (RSI, Stoch, CCI, MFI, Williams %R) is built from means, sums or extremes and inherits their spike sensitivity; none has a median stage, and none applies an explicit band-pass to isolate a cycle band.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Recursive Median Oscillator' by everget (original: John Ehlers, 'Recursive Median Filters', Stocks & Commodities). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/recursive_median_oscillator.pine

ideas.name: RocketRSI Fisher Turn
ideas.entry_rule: With rsiLength = 10 and smoothLength = 8: a1 = exp(-1.414*PI/8); b1 = 2*a1*cos(1.414*PI/8); c2 = b1; c3 = -a1*a1; c1 = 1 - c2 - c3. mom = close - close[rsiLength - 1]. ssf := c1*(mom + mom[1])/2 + c2*ssf[1] + c3*ssf[2]. d = ssf - ssf[1]. upSum = sum(max(d,0), 10); downSum = sum(max(-d,0), 10). r = (upSum - downSum)/(upSum + downSum), clamped to [-0.999, 0.999]. rocketRSI = 0.5 * ln((1 + r)/(1 - r)). ENTER LONG when rocketRSI is below -2.0 and turns up (rocketRSI > rocketRSI[1] and rocketRSI[1] <= rocketRSI[2]). ENTER SHORT when rocketRSI is above +2.0 and turns down.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when rocketRSI crosses above +2.0, or when it turns down while above 0, or after 15 bars. Exit short mirrored.
ideas.why: Two mechanisms stack. The super smoother is a two-pole low-pass with a genuinely flat passband, so it removes noise from the momentum series without the phase lag an EMA of the same delay would add. The Fisher transform then maps the bounded ratio onto an unbounded, roughly Gaussian scale, which stretches the tails - readings that RSI compresses into an indistinguishable 95-99 band become clearly separated numbers, so an unusually extreme reading is actually distinguishable from a merely extreme one.
ideas.novelty: Neither the input (super-smoothed momentum rather than price change) nor the output scale (Fisher-transformed, unbounded, thresholded at standard-deviation-like values) matches a standard RSI. Crucially, the entry is a TURN while beyond the threshold, not a cross of it, so it does not fire while a reading keeps extending.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Rocket RSI' by everget (original: John Ehlers, 'RocketRSI - A Solid Propellant for Your Rocket Science Trading', Stocks & Commodities). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/rocket_rsi.pine

ideas.name: Lag-Band Trendscore
ideas.entry_rule: Trendscore = sum over i = 11..20 of ( close >= close[i] ? +1 : -1 ). Range is -10 to +10. ENTER LONG when Trendscore == +10 AND Trendscore[1] < +10 (first bar of unanimous agreement). ENTER SHORT when Trendscore == -10 AND Trendscore[1] > -10.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when Trendscore falls to +4 or below. Exit short when Trendscore rises to -4 or above. Optional additional stop: exit long if close < lowest(low, 10).
ideas.why: Comparing today's close against each of a BAND of past closes and counting agreements is a sign test - it discards magnitude entirely and asks only whether the current price beats the price at every horizon in a range. Unanimity across a 10-horizon band means no lookback choice in that band would disagree about the direction, which is a direct robustness check against the lookback sensitivity that makes single-lookback momentum fragile. Skipping the most recent 10 bars deliberately excludes short-term reversal effects.
ideas.novelty: A non-parametric sign-count over a band of lags, not a smoothed-series comparison. It cannot be moved by a single large bar (each comparison contributes exactly +1 or -1), and the deliberate 11-20 lag window omits the recent bars where short-horizon mean reversion lives - so it is neither a momentum indicator nor a moving average in any conventional sense.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Trendscore' by everget. Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/trendscore.pine (defaults fromIndex=11, toIndex=20 as coded). The unanimity entry and the score-decay exit are my specification.

ideas.name: Trend Detection Index
ideas.entry_rule: With N = 20: mom = close - close[N]. directionalMove = sum(mom, N). totalMoveFar = sum(abs(mom), 2N) - sum(abs(mom), N) (the absolute-momentum total over the OLDER N bars). TDI = abs(directionalMove) - totalMoveFar. ENTER LONG when TDI > 0 AND directionalMove > 0 AND TDI[1] <= 0. ENTER SHORT when TDI > 0 AND directionalMove < 0 AND TDI[1] <= 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when TDI crosses below 0 (trend condition no longer satisfied) or when directionalMove changes sign, whichever comes first.
inputs: rolling sums of momentum and absolute momentum over N and 2N
params: separate lengths for the recent and reference windows
ideas.why: TDI compares the net directional movement of the RECENT window against the total absolute movement of the PRECEDING window. Requiring the recent net move to exceed all the movement the market managed in the prior period is a demanding, self-normalising test: it automatically scales with the instrument's own recent activity, so it does not need a volatility parameter, and it goes negative in ranges where the prior window churned more than the current one has netted.
ideas.novelty: The normaliser is a DIFFERENT, non-overlapping time window rather than the same window - so it is a comparison across epochs, not a ratio within one. ADX normalises directional movement by concurrent true range; this normalises it by the previous period's activity, which makes it a trend-EMERGENCE detector rather than a trend-strength meter.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Trend Detection Index' by everget (original: M. H. Pee / Dreiss). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/trend_detection_index.pine

ideas.name: Accumulative Swing Index Lead
ideas.entry_rule: Compute Wilder's Swing Index per bar with limit T (T = 10000 for equities, effectively removing the limit-move cap): K = max(abs(high - close[1]), abs(low - close[1])); R = if abs(high-close[1]) >= max(abs(low-close[1]), high-low) then abs(high-close[1]) - 0.5*abs(low-close[1]) + 0.25*abs(close[1]-open[1]); else if abs(low-close[1]) >= max(abs(high-close[1]), high-low) then abs(low-close[1]) - 0.5*abs(high-close[1]) + 0.25*abs(close[1]-open[1]); else (high-low) + 0.25*abs(close[1]-open[1]). SI = 50 * ((close - close[1] + 0.5*(close - open) + 0.25*(close[1] - open[1])) / R) * K / T. ASI = cumulative sum of SI. ENTER LONG when ASI > highest(ASI, 20)[1] AND close <= highest(high, 20)[1] (ASI makes a new 20-bar high while price has NOT). ENTER SHORT when ASI < lowest(ASI, 20)[1] AND close >= lowest(low, 20)[1].
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when ASI falls below lowest(ASI, 10)[1], or when price finally makes its 20-bar high and then closes below it (thesis realised), or after 25 bars. Exit short mirrored.
params: swing lookback for the ASI channel (10-50)
ideas.why: The swing index weights each bar by where it closed relative to its own open AND relative to the previous bar's open and close, divided by the largest of the bar-to-bar gaps. It therefore scores the QUALITY of a bar's move (closing on its high after opening weak scores far higher than a gap-and-fade of the same net size). When this quality-weighted accumulation makes a new high while raw price has not, buyers have been winning the bars without yet winning the level - a structural lead that raw price cannot show.
ideas.novelty: Uses the open, which almost nothing in the existing 32 does, and encodes intra-bar and inter-bar relationships into a single quality score. The signal is a divergence between a cumulative quality series and raw price extremes, not a divergence between an oscillator and price, and not a break of structure.
ideas.source: TradingView open-source: 'Accumulative Swing Index' by everget (original: J. Welles Wilder, 'New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems'). Exact Pine read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/oscillators/accumulative_swing_index.pine . The ASI-leads-price entry condition is my specification of Wilder's ASI-breakout concept.

ideas.name: Kendall Tau Monotonic Trend
ideas.entry_rule: Over the last N = 20 bars compute Kendall's tau between close and bar index: tau = ( sum over all pairs i < j of sign(close[i] - close[j]) * sign(j - i) ) / (N*(N-1)/2), where index 0 is the current bar and larger indices are older (so a rising series gives tau > 0). ENTER LONG when tau crosses above +0.5 AND close > close[N]. ENTER SHORT when tau crosses below -0.5 AND close < close[N].
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long when tau falls below +0.2, or when tau falls for three consecutive bars while above +0.2. Exit short mirrored. Hard stop at 2*atr(14).
inputs: pairwise sign comparisons over an N-bar window
ideas.why: Kendall's tau counts concordant minus discordant pairs, so it measures whether the series is monotonically ordered in time without any reference to the SIZE of the moves. One enormous bar in an otherwise flat window barely moves tau, while a relentless one-tick-a-day grind pushes it to near 1. Linear regression slope and R-squared, which are the usual trend-quality measures, are both dominated by large residuals; tau is not. For a DCA-ladder fleet that wants orderly drifts rather than gap-driven jumps, that distinction is exactly the one that matters.
ideas.novelty: A rank-correlation trend measure. It is scale-free, outlier-immune, and bounded in [-1, +1] with a distribution-free interpretation, none of which is true of ADX, MA slope, or regression R-squared. Two symbols with identical ADX can have wildly different tau, and tau is the one that says whether the trend was orderly.
ideas.source: Method taken from TradingView open-source 'Kendall Rank Correlation Coefficient' by everget - exact pairwise-sign implementation read from github.com/everget/tradingview-pinescript-indicators/blob/master/statistics/kendall_rank_correlation_coefficient.pine . The published script correlates two SYMBOLS; applying the same estimator to close-versus-bar-index as a single-symbol trend-quality measure is my synthesis, so no second data feed is required and the idea stays OHLCV-only.

ideas.name: Episodic Pivot (Dormant Gap Continuation)
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Evaluate at 09:35 ET on day D. Require: (a) open[D]/close[D-1] - 1 >= 0.10; (b) dormancy — close[D-1]/close[D-61] - 1 <= 0.10 (stock has NOT rallied over the prior 60 sessions); (c) volume traded in 09:30–10:00 ET on day D >= 1.0 x SMA(daily volume, 50); (d) close[D-1] >= 5.00. Place a buy-stop at the high of the 09:30–09:35 five-minute bar + 0.02, valid until 11:00 ET, then cancel. Short mirror: open[D]/close[D-1] - 1 <= -0.10, close[D-1]/close[D-61] - 1 >= -0.10, same volume condition, sell-stop at the low of the first 5-minute bar.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at the session low as of fill (session high for shorts). After the position reaches +1R, switch to a daily trail: exit at the next open following the first daily close below EMA(10) (above EMA(10) for shorts). Hard invalidation: exit immediately if price trades below the low of day D.
ideas.why: A >10% overnight gap on volume that already equals a full day's average by 10:00 ET is a discrete repricing event, and post-earnings-announcement drift says the repricing continues for weeks. The dormancy filter is the load-bearing part: it selects names where nobody was already positioned, so the gap is information rather than the continuation of a crowded trade. Qullamaggie's stated preference for stocks that 'have not rallied over the past 3-6 months' is exactly this condition.
ideas.source: Qullamaggie (Kristjan Kullamägi), free write-up 'My 3 Timeless Setups That Have Made Me Tens of Millions', qullamaggie.com/my-3-timeless-setups-that-have-made-me-tens-of-millions/ — fetched directly; he states the 10%+ gap, the 'traded their average daily volume in the first 15-30 minutes' volume condition, the opening-range-high entry, the lows-of-day stop and the 10/20-day MA trail verbatim. Same setup taught as 'Episodic Pivot' by Pradeep Bonde at stockbee.blogspot.com. CAVEAT: neither publishes a trade-level backtest or equity curve — the claimed 30-50x R multiples are unverifiable anecdote.
ideas.novelty: Not an opening-range breakout despite sharing the ORH trigger: the ORB on our list fires on any stock any day, whereas here the opening range is only a fill mechanism for a gap-event gate. Critically, the dormancy filter (60-day return CAPPED at +10%) is the inverse of every momentum filter we run — it deliberately excludes strong stocks.

ideas.name: Parabolic Exhaustion Short
ideas.entry_rule: Short. Evaluate at the close of day D-1. Require all of: (a) close[D-1] > close[D-2] > close[D-3] (at least 3 consecutive higher closes); (b) close[D-1] / SMA(close,20)[D-1] - 1 >= 0.30; (c) close[D-1]/close[D-6] - 1 >= 0.50. If armed, on day D place a sell-stop at the low of the 09:30–09:35 five-minute bar - 0.02, valid until 11:00 ET, then cancel. If day D opens more than 15% above close[D-1], skip (do not chase a second gap).
ideas.exit_rule: Stop is the higher of (i) the session high at time of fill, or (ii) a 5-minute close back above session VWAP after entry. Cover at the first touch of SMA(close,10) computed on daily bars, or at the close of day D+3, whichever comes first. No overnight add.
ideas.why: Vertical multi-day runs are sustained by short-covering and momentum chasers, not by new information. Counting consecutive up closes and measuring percentage extension above the 20-day SMA is a direct read on how stretched positioning is — the marginal buyer is nearly gone. The 10-day SMA is the documented magnet these names snap back to, which makes the target a level rather than an arbitrary R multiple.
ideas.source: Qullamaggie, 'Parabolic Short' section of qullamaggie.com/my-3-timeless-setups-that-have-made-me-tens-of-millions/ — fetched directly; he specifies 'up 50-100%+ in a few days or weeks', 'up 3-5+ days in a row', shorting the opening range lows, stop at highs of day or a VWAP reclaim, and 'the target area is the 10- and 20-day moving averages'. CAVEAT: he states 5-10x reward-to-risk with no published sample; unverifiable.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is a COUNT of consecutive up closes plus a percentage distance from a moving average — a positioning-stretch measure, not an oscillator reading. And the exit is a named magnet level (the 10-day SMA) rather than a target multiple or an indicator cross.

ideas.name: Pocket Pivot
ideas.category: volume signature / accumulation inside a base
ideas.entry_rule: Long. On day D require ALL of: (a) close[D] > open[D]; (b) close[D] > SMA(close,10) and close[D] > SMA(close,50); (c) low[D] <= SMA(close,10)[D] * 1.02 (price is bouncing at or from the 10-day SMA, not extended above it); (d) volume[D] > max{ volume[i] : i in the 10 sessions D-10..D-1 where close[i] < close[i-1] } — i.e. it exceeds the largest DOWN-day volume of the prior 10 sessions; (e) still inside a base: max(high, D-10..D-1) / min(low, D-10..D-1) - 1 <= 0.15. Buy at the close of day D, or on a buy-stop at high[D] + 0.02 on day D+1.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at the lower of low[D] or SMA(close,10) * 0.98. Take 50% off at +2.0x the initial risk. Trail the remainder: exit at the next open after the first daily close below SMA(close,10); full exit on any daily close below SMA(close,50).
ideas.why: It asks a question no volume average can: on this single day, did buying conviction exceed the strongest selling of the past two weeks? That is a footprint of institutional accumulation INSIDE the base, so the entry sits at base support with a tight, well-defined stop, rather than at the breakout level every other participant has an alert on.
ideas.source: Gil Morales & Chris Kacher (former internal portfolio managers at William O'Neil + Co.), the pocket pivot concept from 'Trade Like an O'Neil Disciple' and virtueofselfishinvesting.com. Definition corroborated in two independent open sources I fetched: github.com/Fluxus-Trade-Lab/fluxus-dashboard, JeffSun_Wiki/wiki/pocket-pivot-volume.md ('volume exceeds the highest down-volume day over the prior 10 sessions'), and github.com/gigabouy2004-afk/Tools, 05_Stock_MomentumDetector/docs/Pocket Pivot.txt, which spells out the four algorithmic conditions verbatim. CAVEAT: that second doc claims a 50-60% standalone win rate with no source or sample size — treat as unverified.
ideas.novelty: The volume comparison is against a CONDITIONAL SUBSET of the lookback (down-days only), not against a mean or a multiple of a mean. No moving average of volume can express 'greater than the largest recent down-day' — it is an order statistic over a filtered set.

ideas.name: Momentum Burst out of a Tight Base
ideas.category: range expansion with a time-based exit
ideas.entry_rule: Long. On day D require: (a) close[D]/close[D-1] - 1 >= 0.04 OR close[D] - close[D-1] >= 0.90; (b) volume[D] >= 100000 and volume[D] >= 2.0 * SMA(volume,20); (c) close[D] >= 5.00; (d) close[D-1]/close[D-2] - 1 < 0.02 (yesterday was not already running); (e) prior tight base over the 3-20 sessions before D: (max(high) - min(low)) / min(low) <= 0.15 AND the mean of (high-low)/close over that window <= 0.05; (f) close[D] >= low[D] + 0.75*(high[D]-low[D]) (close in the top quartile of the day's range). Enter on a buy-stop at high[D] + 0.02 on day D+1; if not filled that day, cancel.
ideas.exit_rule: Hard time exit at the close of the 3rd trading day after fill. Take profit early at +8% from entry if hit first. Stop at low[D]. No trailing, no extension of the holding period.
ideas.why: Bonde's core empirical claim is that the bulk of tradeable swing movement arrives as 3-5 day, 8-40% 'bursts' that begin with one range-expansion day emerging from a volatility contraction — and that the money is lost by holding past the burst waiting for a trend that usually never forms. The fixed 3-day exit is the strategy: it harvests the documented burst window and refuses to pay for the mean-reverting tail.
ideas.source: Pradeep Bonde, Stockbee — 'Momentum Burst' / '4% breakout' method, taught free at stockbee.blogspot.com and on his YouTube channel. Exact thresholds corroborated by an open-source implementation of his screen that I fetched: github.com/ZihaoGuan/ticker-screener, src/stockbee_momentum_burst_screen.py — FOUR_PCT_THRESHOLD=4.0, DOLLAR_THRESHOLD=0.90, MIN_VOLUME=100_000, MIN_PRICE=5.0, MIN_BASE_DAYS=3, MAX_BASE_DAYS=20, MAX_BASE_WIDTH_PCT=15.0, MAX_PRIOR_AVG_RANGE_PCT=5.0, MAX_PREV_DAY_GAIN_FOR_RANGE=2.0. His own pre-market scan formula '((c/c1>=1.02) or (c-o>=.90)) ... and v>=100000 and c>=1' appears verbatim on the blog. CAVEAT: Bonde publishes no auditable equity curve.
ideas.novelty: The exit is a BAR COUNT. Every one of the 32 existing strategies exits on a price level, an indicator condition, or a stop — a fixed-holding-period exit is a structurally different exit family, and it is the part of this idea most worth testing independently of the entry.

ideas.name: Trend Template Fresh Pass
ideas.entry_rule: Long. On each daily bar evaluate 8 conditions: (1) close > SMA(close,150) AND close > SMA(close,200); (2) SMA(close,150) > SMA(close,200); (3) SMA(close,200) > SMA(close,200) as of 20 sessions ago; (4) SMA(close,50) > SMA(close,150) AND SMA(close,50) > SMA(close,200); (5) close > SMA(close,50); (6) close >= 1.30 * min(low, last 252 sessions); (7) close >= 0.75 * max(high, last 252 sessions); (8) (close/close_SPY) > (close/close_SPY) as of 20 sessions ago. Enter at the next open on the FIRST day all 8 are simultaneously true, provided at least one condition was false on every one of the preceding 20 sessions. Do not re-enter until the template has been false for 20 consecutive sessions again.
ideas.exit_rule: For the first 5 sessions after entry, hard stop at 1.5 * ATR(14) below entry. Thereafter: exit at the next open after any daily close below SMA(close,50), or after 3 consecutive daily closes below SMA(close,21), whichever comes first.
ideas.why: The template describes a state that thousands of stocks occupy for months at a time; buying the state means buying whatever is already crowded. Requiring a 20-session absence turns it into a dated event — the moment a stock completes its transition into a Stage 2 advance. The transition is where the marginal institutional buyer is arriving, not where they have finished arriving.
ideas.source: Mark Minervini's Trend Template, published free in interviews and in 'Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard'. The exact 8-condition encoding used here follows an open-source implementation I fetched: github.com/marco-hui-95/vcp_screener.github.io, vcp_screener.py, function trend_template() — including the literal 1.3x-52-week-low and 0.75x-52-week-high conditions and the RS = Close/SPX slope condition. The 'fresh pass' event framing is stated as a distinct setup in the EasySwing.trading library, github.com/sofus-nl/swing-trading-strategies, strategies/16-trend-template-fresh-pass.md. CAVEAT: Minervini publishes no trade-level backtest; the template is a screen he describes, and the fresh-pass variant is unvalidated.
ideas.novelty: Converts a screen (a persistent state) into an entry (a state transition), by requiring the condition to have been FALSE for 20 sessions first. That edge-triggering is a different signal class from any 'condition is true' rule in the current 32, and it is testable independently against the naive state version.

ideas.name: Larry Williams OOPS Gap Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Both sides, one attempt per day. Long: if open[D] < low[D-1], place a buy-stop at low[D-1] + 0.10 * ATR(14, daily), live only from 09:30 to 11:30 ET. Short: if open[D] > high[D-1], place a sell-stop at high[D-1] - 0.10 * ATR(14, daily), live only 09:30–11:30 ET. The gap must clear the prior day's RANGE EXTREME, not merely the prior close. If not filled by 11:30 ET, cancel for the day and do not re-arm.
ideas.exit_rule: Trail a stop at the running session low for longs (running session high for shorts), updated on every completed 5-minute bar. Immediate exit if price makes a new session low below the opening gap extreme (longs) or a new session high above it (shorts) — the reversal thesis is dead. Flatten unconditionally at 15:55 ET; never hold overnight.
ideas.why: A gap that clears the whole prior day's range is thin-liquidity overnight price discovery. When the full session's participants arrive and price reclaims the range extreme, the overshoot is actively being corrected — and the stop-order entry means you never take the trade on days when the gap simply holds and runs (gap-and-go trend days), which is the failure mode that kills naive gap fades.
ideas.source: Larry Williams, 'Long-Term Secrets to Short-Term Trading' — the OOPS pattern, taught free in his seminars and on YouTube. Fully implementable spec (0.1x ATR entry filter, 2-hour entry window, intraday-extreme trail, session flatten) from an open backtest spec I fetched: github.com/DexWilder/algo-lab, research/specs/TV-Larry-Oops-Gap-Reversal.md. CAVEAT: that same spec records that a simpler generic gap-fill strategy was REJECTED at profit factor 0.68 on the same instrument family — the distinction (gap beyond the RANGE plus a reclaim-confirmation stop order) is exactly what is being tested, and the edge is not assumed.
ideas.novelty: There is no opening range constructed at all — the reference level is yesterday's high or low, and entry is a stop order that only fills on the reclaim. This is the mirror image of an opening-range fade: it fires precisely on the days an ORB strategy would be stopped out.

ideas.name: Connors Double Seven
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Require close > SMA(close,200) AND close[D] == min(close over the last 7 sessions inclusive of D) — i.e. today's close is the lowest close of the last 7 sessions. Buy at the close of day D (or the open of D+1). Short mirror: close < SMA(close,200) AND close[D] == max(close over the last 7 sessions).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the entire position at the close of the first day on which close[D] == max(close over the last 7 sessions inclusive) for longs, or close[D] == min(close over the last 7) for shorts. The exit is the exact mirror of the entry. Optional disaster stop at 2.5 * ATR(14) from entry.
ideas.why: The signal is an ordinal statistic, so it is scale-free and volatility-regime-free: it fires on relative position inside a short window, and automatically becomes more or less selective as ranges compress or expand. A fixed oscillator threshold cannot do that — RSI(2)<10 fires constantly in a quiet tape and almost never in a violent one. The 200-SMA gate restricts it to instruments where the drift is on your side.
ideas.source: Larry Connors & Cesar Alvarez, 'Short Term Trading Strategies That Work' (the 'Double 7's' strategy). Covered with a backtest by Oddmund Groette at quantifiedstrategies.com ('Larry Connors' Double Seven strategy', listed on their public strategies index which I fetched via github.com/taashareef11112/Po3). Reference implementation with the 200-SMA gate and the 7-day rolling extreme at github.com/nathanssantos/marketmind, apps/backend/strategies/builtin/double-seven.pine, which claims 'consistent 80%+ win rate since 1995'. CAVEAT: I could NOT verify that claim — quantifiedstrategies.com blocks automated fetches behind a bot wall, and the Pine file cites no sample. Connors' own published results are vendor-supplied.
ideas.novelty: Entry and exit are both order statistics over the same window, with no indicator and no threshold anywhere in the rule. The exit being the exact symmetric mirror of the entry (lowest-of-7 in, highest-of-7 out) is a distinct exit structure — not a target, not a stop, not a trailing rule.
params: entry on close vs next open

ideas.name: Connors TPS Scale-In Ladder
ideas.entry_rule: Long, gated by close > SMA(close,200). Tranche 1: on the first day RSI(2) < 25, buy 10% of the intended full position at the close. Tranche 2: on any later day where close < the close at which the previous tranche filled AND RSI(2) < 25, add 20%. Tranche 3: same condition again, add 30%. Tranche 4: same condition again, add 40%. Maximum four tranches; each tranche requires a strictly lower close than the previous fill. Abandon the ladder (stop adding) if RSI(2) > 70 at any point, or if close < SMA(close,200).
ideas.exit_rule: Sell the ENTIRE accumulated position — every tranche — at the close of the first day RSI(2) > 70. There are no per-tranche targets and no per-tranche stops; total exposure is capped by the four-tranche schedule, and that cap IS the risk control. If close < SMA(close,200) while holding, liquidate everything at the next close.
ideas.why: Adding on each further oversold day drops the average cost fastest precisely where the mean-reversion edge is strongest, and closing the whole ladder on a single reversion signal means you take profit once — at the reversion — instead of repeatedly at each rung, which is what caps the upside of a conventional grid. The four-tranche ceiling makes the worst case bounded and knowable before the first fill.
ideas.source: Larry Connors' TPS (Time, Price, Scale-in) method from 'High Probability ETF Trading' and 'Short Term Trading Strategies That Work'; listed among his strategies on Oddmund Groette's public index at quantifiedstrategies.com. CAVEAT: Connors' published TPS results are vendor materials with no independent audit, and quantifiedstrategies.com's own backtest pages block automated access, so I could verify the rules but not any performance claim.
ideas.novelty: This is an exit and position structure, not a signal — none of the 32 existing strategies specify how size is added or removed. It is directly comparable to our existing DCA ladder and is worth testing as a drop-in replacement for the rung schedule: geometric tranche weights (10/20/30/40) with a single collective exit, versus equal rungs with per-rung take-profits.

ideas.name: Internal Bar Strength (IBS) Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Compute IBS = (close - low) / (high - low) on each daily bar; skip any bar where high == low. Long: enter at the close when IBS < 0.15 AND close > SMA(close,200). Short: enter at the close when IBS > 0.90 AND close < SMA(close,200).
ideas.exit_rule: Longs: exit at the close of the first subsequent day on which IBS > 0.75, or at the close of the 5th trading day after entry, whichever comes first. Shorts: exit at the close of the first day IBS < 0.25, or after 5 trading days. Optional disaster stop at 2.0 * ATR(14).
ideas.why: IBS answers where the bar SETTLED inside its own range. A close on the low means sellers controlled the entire session and finished the job — the marginal seller has already transacted, and the next session opens with no overhang. Because it is a ratio inside one bar it is completely scale-free and has no lookback, so it does not decay when the volatility regime changes, which is the standard failure mode of fixed oscillator thresholds.
ideas.source: Taught with backtests by Oddmund Groette at quantifiedstrategies.com (their 'S&P 500 mean reversion using IBS and RSI' strategy appears on the public index I fetched). The indicator is a first-class primitive in QuantConnect (Documentation, '01 Supported Indicators / 052 Internal Bar Strength'), in talipp (talipp/indicators/IBS.py) and in bennycode/trading-signals (src/momentum/IBS/IBS.ts) — all fetched. Reference strategy encoding with explicit thresholds at github.com/fmzquant/strategies, Internal-Bar-Strength-Indicator-Reversion-system.md (long when IBS < 5, short when IBS > 99, on a 0-100 scale). CAVEAT: Quantified Strategies' own performance numbers sit behind a bot wall and I could not verify them.
ideas.novelty: A lookback-free, single-bar positional statistic. Every oscillator in the current 32 — RSI, CCI, Stochastic, Williams %R, MFI — requires a window; IBS requires none, so its behaviour under regime change is structurally different and worth measuring against Williams %R(1) as a control.

ideas.name: Turnaround Tuesday
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Identify the first trading day of each calendar week (Monday, or Tuesday when Monday is a market holiday). If that day's close < its own open AND that day's close < the previous session's close, buy at that day's close.
ideas.exit_rule: Sell at the close of the first subsequent session whose close > the previous session's close. If no such day occurs, exit unconditionally at the close of the 5th trading day after entry. No stop (the time exit bounds the hold).
ideas.why: Institutional flow is organised around the weekly cycle. A down first-day-of-week is disproportionately weekend-risk liquidation rather than new information, and the buy-side rebalancing that follows lands early in the week. The signal is a calendar position conditioned on a single price fact, so it is orthogonal to every trend and oscillator signal in the book — which makes it valuable for portfolio diversification even if its standalone edge is modest.
ideas.source: Oddmund Groette / Quantified Strategies, 'The Turnaround Tuesday trading strategy' — listed on their public S&P 500 strategies index (verified via the mirrored index text at github.com/taashareef11112/Po3). Groette runs a YouTube channel and publishes rules plus backtests for each strategy. CAVEAT: the article body and its equity curve are behind a Cloudflare bot wall that blocked my fetch, so I can confirm the strategy name and construction but NOT their reported returns. Test from scratch.
ideas.novelty: The primary entry variable is a calendar position, not a price feature — an entirely different signal family from all 32 existing strategies, none of which reference the trading calendar. Its likely low correlation to the rest of the book is the main reason to test it.
params: exit on first up close vs fixed N days
restrict to close<SMA(200) (dip version) or close>SMA(200)

ideas.name: Overnight-Only Holding (Close-to-Open Capture)
ideas.entry_rule: Long. At 15:55 ET compute today's IBS = (close - low)/(high - low) using the session's running high, low and current price. Buy market-on-close if IBS < 0.40 AND close > SMA(close,200). Position is opened in the final minutes of the regular session only.
ideas.exit_rule: Sell market-on-open at the next regular session open, unconditionally and with no exceptions. The holding period is exactly one overnight gap. No stop is used — the position is not manageable while held, so risk is controlled by size and by never holding through a second session.
ideas.why: US equity returns decompose into a close-to-open component that carries nearly all of the long-run drift and an open-to-close component that contributes close to zero. Restricting exposure to the overnight window keeps the drift and discards the intraday drag, while cutting time-in-market by roughly three quarters. The weak-close gate selects nights that follow forced end-of-day liquidation, where the overnight rebound is largest.
ideas.source: Overnight-edge strategies are a standing published category at quantifiedstrategies.com — their index states the construction directly: 'buying at the close of the stock exchange until the open the next day'. Oddmund Groette publishes several such backtests free and covers them on YouTube. The underlying close-to-open versus open-to-close return decomposition is one of the most widely replicated results in equity microstructure. CAVEAT: their specific equity curves are behind a bot wall and unverified here; also, this strategy is uniquely sensitive to realistic modelling of MOC/MOO fills and gap slippage — backtest it with explicit auction-price assumptions or the result will be fiction.
ideas.novelty: The exit is a SESSION BOUNDARY, not a price, a level, an indicator or a bar count. Holding-period structure is itself the edge, and it is a clean control: run any existing entry signal with an overnight-only hold and compare against the same signal held through the day.
params: skip nights before known holidays yes/no

ideas.name: Frog-in-the-Pan (Smooth-Path Momentum)
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Over the trailing 126 sessions compute: PRET = close/close[126] - 1; neg = fraction of the 126 daily returns that are < 0; pos = fraction that are > 0; ID = sign(PRET) * (neg - pos). Require ALL of: (a) PRET >= 0.20; (b) ID <= -0.10 (a smooth, gradual climb rather than a few jumps); (c) no single daily return in the 126-session window with absolute value > 0.06; (d) close > SMA(close,50) and close > SMA(close,200). Enter on a buy-stop at max(high, last 20 sessions) + 0.02, valid for 10 sessions then cancel.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at 2.0 * ATR(14) below entry. Scale 50% off at +2.5 * ATR(14). Trail the remainder at min(low, last 10 sessions), exiting at the next open when breached. Immediate full exit at the next open if any single day moves more than 6% in either direction — a jump invalidates the continuous-information thesis the position rests on.
ideas.why: Markets under-react to information that arrives in small continuous increments and over-react to discrete jumps. Ranking momentum by the SMOOTHNESS of its path rather than its magnitude isolates the under-reaction: a stock that has climbed 40% via a hundred small green days has been repriced quietly by informed participants and has not yet appeared on any big-gainer screen, while a stock that climbed 40% on three gap days has already been fully noticed.
ideas.source: Da, Z., Gurun, U. & Warachka, M. (2014), 'Frog in the Pan: Continuous Information and Momentum', Review of Financial Studies 27(7), 2171-2218 — the paper that formalises Information Discreteness and shows the low-ID leg of a momentum portfolio substantially outperforms the high-ID leg. Operationalised as a swing setup with the exact ID formula, the ID tercile rule and the 6%-gap filter in the EasySwing.trading strategy library, github.com/sofus-nl/swing-trading-strategies, strategies/20-frog-in-the-pan.md (fetched). CAVEAT: the academic result is cross-sectional and portfolio-level; the single-name swing operationalisation by the educator is NOT independently backtested and is the part that needs proving.
ideas.novelty: The signal is computed from the DISTRIBUTION of daily returns inside the lookback — the share negative versus positive — rather than from the cumulative return, a moving average, or any oscillator. It is a path-quality measure, and it can be bolted onto any existing momentum entry as a filter to test whether path smoothness adds anything.

ideas.name: Anchored VWAP Reclaim from the Highest-Volume Bar
ideas.timeframe: daily (also testable intraday with an event anchor)
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Let A be the session within the last 120 trading days with the highest volume. Compute AVWAP[t] = sum(TP[i]*volume[i], i=A..t) / sum(volume[i], i=A..t), where TP = (high+low+close)/3. Require ALL of: (a) close[t] > AVWAP[t]; (b) close[t-1] <= AVWAP[t-1] (a FRESH reclaim, not a continuation); (c) AVWAP[t] > AVWAP[t-5] (the anchor's average cost is rising); (d) volume[t] > SMA(volume,20); (e) t is at least 10 sessions after A. Enter at the close of t.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next open after any daily close below AVWAP. Take 50% off at +2.0 * ATR(14). Trail the remaining half at AVWAP itself, exiting on the first close below it. Re-anchor and recompute only when a new highest-volume session appears in the trailing 120-day window; if that happens while in a position, exit at the next close and re-evaluate from scratch.
inputs: anchored VWAP from a selected bar
ideas.why: The highest-volume session of the last six months is where the largest single cohort of current holders got positioned. The AVWAP from that bar is that cohort's average cost. Crossing back above it flips the whole cohort from underwater to profitable in one stroke, which removes the dominant supply overhang — every rally into that level had been meeting sellers who were finally getting out flat, and now they are not there.
ideas.source: Brian Shannon, the anchored-VWAP methodology from 'Technical Analysis Using Multiple Timeframes' and his 'Maximum Trading Gains with Anchored VWAP' — taught free on his Alphatrends YouTube channel, where he states the anchoring logic (anchor at a high-volume event, treat the reclaim as a flip in the holder base). Implementation shape (anchor at a selected bar, buffered flip entry, opposite flip as the exit, ATR sizing) from an open engineering plan I fetched: github.com/richkuo/go-trader, docs/superpowers/plans/2026-06-15-anchored-vwap.md. Also specified as a distinct setup at github.com/sofus-nl/swing-trading-strategies, strategies/09-anchored-vwap.md. CAVEAT: Shannon publishes no systematic backtest; the anchor-selection rule here (highest-volume bar in 120 sessions) is my mechanisation of his discretionary anchoring and is the main thing to sweep.
ideas.novelty: The reference level is anchored to a data-SELECTED event bar and is path-dependent from that bar forward — it never resets on a clock and it is different for every instrument. Session VWAP (which we have) resets daily; a rolling VWAP has a fixed window; neither can represent 'the average cost of the cohort that bought on the single biggest day'.
params: anchor rule: highest volume vs highest dollar volume vs 252-day swing low

ideas.name: Up-Volume / Down-Volume Dominance
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Over the trailing 21 daily bars compute UpVol = sum of volume[i] over bars where close[i] > close[i-1], and DownVol = sum of volume[i] over bars where close[i] < close[i-1]. Compute VWAP21 = sum(TP[i]*volume[i], 21 bars) / sum(volume[i], 21 bars) with TP = (high+low+close)/3. Require ALL of: (a) UpVol > 1.5 * DownVol; (b) close > VWAP21; (c) VWAP21 > VWAP21 as of 5 sessions ago; (d) close > SMA(close,50). Enter at the close on the first day all four are simultaneously true; alternatively rest a limit at VWAP21 * 1.005 valid for 5 sessions.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next open after two CONSECUTIVE daily closes below VWAP21. Stop at the tighter of 1.5 * ATR(14) below entry or 0.5% below VWAP21. Scale 50% off at +2.0 * ATR(14) and trail the rest at VWAP21.
ideas.why: It separates accumulation from distribution by asking where the volume actually went, not how much of it there was. A rising 21-day VWAP means the average institutional fill of the past month is in profit and those holders will defend the structure; up-volume dominance at 1.5:1 means that demand was structural across many sessions rather than one spike that a volume average would have smeared over the whole window.
ideas.source: EasySwing.trading strategy library, 'Volume-Weighted Trend' — github.com/sofus-nl/swing-trading-strategies, strategies/17-volume-weighted-trend.md (fetched), which states the 21-day VWAP condition, the rising-slope requirement, the 1.5x up-volume-to-down-volume ratio and the two-consecutive-closes exit verbatim. The multi-day rolling VWAP framing traces to Brian Shannon (2008). CAVEAT: no auditable backtest is published for the 1.5x threshold or for the setup as a whole — treat every number as a starting point for a sweep, not a finding.
ideas.novelty: Volume is PARTITIONED by the sign of the bar and the two sums are compared as a ratio. 'Bollinger with volume' and every other volume condition in the current 32 uses an undirected volume average, which by construction cannot distinguish a month of accumulation from a month of distribution at the same total volume.
params: entry at close vs pullback limit to VWAP21

ideas.name: Relative Strength Line New High Before Price
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Define RS[t] = close_stock[t] / close_SPY[t]. Require ALL of: (a) RS[t] == max(RS over the last 252 sessions) — the ratio series is at a new 52-week high; (b) close_stock[t] < 0.95 * max(high_stock over the last 252 sessions) — the stock's own price is NOT at a new high; (c) close_stock > SMA(close,50); (d) SMA(close,50) > SMA(close,200); (e) volume[t] > SMA(volume,50). Enter on a buy-stop at max(high, last 10 sessions) + 0.02, valid for 10 sessions then cancel.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop below min(low, last 10 sessions) as measured at entry. Exit at the next open after RS closes below SMA(RS,21). Take 50% off at +3.0 * ATR(14) and trail the remainder on the RS-versus-SMA(RS,21) rule.
inputs: RS ratio series and its 252-session max and 21-session SMA
ideas.why: A stock whose ratio to the index sets a new 52-week high while its own price is still 5%+ below its high is one that fell materially less than the market during the last drawdown — a direct measurement of which names are being defended by real buyers. The divergence between the ratio's high and price's high is the leadership signal, and by construction it appears BEFORE the price breakout that everyone else has an alert set on.
ideas.source: The Relative Strength Line new-high concept (IBD's 'blue dot'), taught free by TraderLion on YouTube and in IBD's Investor's Corner column. The RS-line construction is corroborated as condition 8 of the open-source Minervini trend-template screener I fetched: github.com/marco-hui-95/vcp_screener.github.io, vcp_screener.py — df['RS'] = df['Close']/df_spx['Close'] with a slope test. CAVEAT: IBD's and TraderLion's published win-rate claims for the blue dot are marketing collateral with no disclosed methodology or sample; the rule is precise and testable, the claims are not.
ideas.novelty: The signal is a new extreme in a RATIO of two different price series, combined with an explicit requirement that the underlying price series is NOT at an extreme. That is a divergence between two instruments — structurally different from RSI divergence, which compares a price series to an oscillator derived from that same series.

ideas.name: Five-Day SMA Extended Run Reset
ideas.entry_rule: Long. Maintain run[t] = the number of consecutive sessions up to and including t with close > SMA(close,5). ARM the setup on any day where run[t] >= 8 AND SMA(close,5) > SMA(close,20). Once armed, ENTER at the next session's open following the FIRST session that closes below SMA(close,5). Cancel the arm without trading if close falls below SMA(close,20) before that entry triggers, or if 10 sessions elapse after arming with no close below SMA(close,5). Short mirror uses run of closes below SMA(5) with SMA(5) < SMA(20).
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at min(low) over the two sessions immediately preceding entry. Exit at the close of the first day whose close exceeds the highest high recorded during the armed extended run. Hard time exit at the close of the 8th session after entry regardless of outcome.
inputs: highest high during the run window
ideas.why: Raschke uses the 5-day SMA as a persistence gauge rather than a trend line: a market that holds one side of it for eight or more consecutive sessions is in a genuine trend, and the first close on the other side is therefore supply exhaustion inside that trend, not a reversal of it. Counting consecutive closes measures persistence directly, which ADX — an average of directional movement over a window — smears out and cannot report.
ideas.source: Linda Bradford Raschke's 5-day SMA work, taught free in her webinars and articles at lindaraschke.net and in 'Street Smarts' (Raschke & Connors). The eight-consecutive-session encoding comes from the public TradingView strategy '8 Day Extended Runs' by Marcns_, explicitly credited 'Inspired by Linda Bradford Raschke' and noting she 'used the 5 day SMA to determine that large outlier price moves happen in the direction of the trend'; mirrored at github.com/hasnocool/tradingview-pine-scripts, '8 Day Extended Runs.pine' (fetched). CAVEAT: that script reports only a t-statistic of 4.06 on a single instrument (ZN futures) with no equity curve, no sample size and no out-of-sample split — a single t-stat on one market is not a validated result, and this is US equities, a different instrument class.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is a RUN LENGTH — a count of consecutive satisfied conditions — rather than a level, a slope, or an oscillator value. It also inverts the usual reading: eight days above the 5-SMA arms a BUY on the first close below it, where a naive MA-cross system would read that same close as an exit signal.

ideas.name: Prior-Day Value Area Rejection
ideas.entry_rule: Build yesterday's volume-by-price profile from its 5-minute RTH bars: bin prices in increments of 0.05 * ATR(14, daily), assigning each bar's volume to the bin containing its (high+low+close)/3. POC = the bin with the most volume. Expand one bin at a time from the POC toward whichever adjacent side holds more volume until the enclosed bins contain >= 70% of the day's total volume; the extremes of that set are VAL and VAH. Today: if the 09:30–09:35 bar's open is BELOW yesterday's VAL, and price subsequently produces two CONSECUTIVE 5-minute closes above VAL, enter long at the close of the second such bar. Mirror for shorts: open above VAH, then two consecutive 5-minute closes below VAH. One attempt per side per day; no entries after 14:00 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Target the opposite side of yesterday's value area (VAH for longs, VAL for shorts); take 50% off at the POC on the way. Stop at the extreme of the session reached before entry (session low for longs, session high for shorts). Flatten at 15:55 ET; never hold overnight.
