ideas.why: The value area is where 70% of yesterday's volume actually transacted — the price range the market agreed on. Opening outside it and then trading back in means the overnight excursion found no business and is being rejected; the standard market-profile inference is that price then rotates to the far side of value, because that is where the resting two-sided interest lives. The level is derived from where volume traded, not from where price closed, which is a different construction from every band and pivot on our list.
ideas.source: The value-area rules descend from J. Peter Steidlmayer's Market Profile and are taught free by Jim Dalton and in the CME Group's own Market Profile educational materials. Backtested as a named strategy by Oddmund Groette at quantifiedstrategies.com, 'Value Area Trading Strategy — Does It Work? (Backtest)', which appears on their public strategy index (verified via the mirrored index at github.com/taashareef11112/Po3). CAVEAT: the article body and its results are behind a Cloudflare bot wall I could not fetch, so the rules here are the standard market-profile construction pinned down to something computable — I chose the bin width, the 70% expansion procedure and the two-consecutive-closes confirmation to remove the judgement calls, and none of those specific choices are validated.
ideas.novelty: The reference levels come from a volume-at-price histogram, so they mark where business was DONE rather than where price went. Bollinger, Keltner, Donchian and VWAP all derive levels from the price path; none of them can tell you that a level had heavy participation and another had almost none.
params: target: POC only vs opposite value-area edge
profile source: prior day vs prior 3 days composite

ideas.name: Strike Grid Pin
ideas.entry_rule: Only on the third Friday of the month. Build the strike grid G from a hardcoded convention table (no options feed): G=$1 if price<$25, G=$2.50 if $25<=price<$200, G=$5 if price>=$200. At 14:00 ET let P = last 5-min close, K = nearest integer multiple of G to P, d = P-K. Enter if 0.10*G <= |d| <= 0.20*G, in the direction of K: LONG if d<0, SHORT if d>0. Require the symbol be option-active: 60-day median dollar volume >= $200M.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at whichever comes first: (a) |P-K| <= 0.02*G (pin achieved), (b) 15:58 ET time exit, (c) stop-out when |d| widens to 0.35*G against entry.
inputs: daily OHLCV for the dollar-volume filter
bar timestamps to derive the third Friday
params: band edges as fractions of G (default 0.10 and 0.20)
ideas.why: Ni, Pearson and Poteshman show option market makers who hold net long expiring positions delta-hedge by buying below the strike and selling above it, and this hedge rebalancing physically drags the close toward the strike. They document that on expiration Fridays the fraction of optionable stocks closing within $0.125 of a strike spikes (z=8.15), that returns of optionable stocks are altered by at least 16.5bp on each expiration date, and critically that the deficit is concentrated at $0.50-$1.00 from the nearest strike on a $5 grid - exactly the 0.10*G to 0.20*G band. Stocks that would have closed in that band instead get pulled onto the strike. The effect vanishes when the same stocks lose their listed options, which rules out generic round-number clustering.
ideas.source: Ni, Pearson & Poteshman (2005), 'Stock Price Clustering on Option Expiration Dates', Journal of Financial Economics 78(1), 49-87. Full text read at https://optionsoffice.ru/wp-content/uploads/2020/01/Stock-Price-Clustering-on-Option-Expiration-Dates.pdf
ideas.novelty: Not an indicator at all. The signal is a deterministic distance to a fixed price lattice, gated by a calendar date. There is no moving average, no oscillator, and no volatility band - the attractor level is exogenous to price history. The band is two-sided and bounded on both ends, so unlike any mean-reversion rule it deliberately does NOT fire when price is already close to the level or far from it.

ideas.name: Pin Release Reversal
ideas.timeframe: daily, entered the session after monthly expiry
ideas.entry_rule: On monthly expiry Friday's close compute G and K as in Strike Grid Pin. Require the stock actually pinned: |close_Friday - K| <= 0.05*G. Require it was dragged there: let P5 = close 5 trading days before expiry Friday, require |P5 - K| >= 0.40*G. Enter at the next trading session's open (market-on-open) in the direction the stock came FROM: LONG if P5 > K, SHORT if P5 < K.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 3rd trading day after entry. Stop at 1.5 * ATR(14, daily) against entry.
inputs: bar timestamps for the third-Friday calendar
ideas.why: Pinning is a temporary price distortion, not information. Ni, Pearson and Poteshman show clustering is elevated on trade dates -5 through -1, peaks on date 0, and drops immediately afterward - the hedging force that created the distortion expires with the options. The paper states plainly that any apparent gain from moving the price reverses when the stock reverts to its non-manipulated level. So the distance the stock was pulled is an estimate of the distortion, and the reversion runs back along the path it was pulled from.
ideas.source: Ni, Pearson & Poteshman (2005), JFE 78(1), 49-87 - Figure 1 panels (clustering by trade date -10..+10) and the reversion-to-non-manipulated-level argument in Section 5.
ideas.novelty: The direction is set by where the stock was five days ago relative to a strike, not by any trend, momentum or oversold reading. It is an explicit fade of a known, dated, mechanically-caused distortion, and it is the only entry here whose sign is determined by a price from a week earlier rather than by current conditions.

ideas.name: Volume-Profile Max-Pain Wall
ideas.timeframe: daily decision on 5-minute data, the 5 sessions ending on monthly expiry
ideas.entry_rule: Build G from the strike-interval table. Over the trailing 20 sessions of 5-min bars, for each bar compute typical price TP=(H+L+C)/3, snap TP to the nearest multiple of G, and accumulate that bar's volume into that grid bucket. Let K* be the grid level with the greatest accumulated volume among levels within +/-3*G of current price. Trade only on the 5 trading days ending on (and including) monthly expiry Friday. At 14:00 ET each of those days, if |P - K*| >= 0.30*G, enter toward K*: LONG if P<K*, SHORT if P>K*.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on whichever comes first: |P - K*| <= 0.05*G, the expiry Friday 15:58 ET close, or a stop at 0.60*G adverse from entry.
ideas.why: Open interest is not observable to us, but open interest accumulates at strikes where the underlying has actually spent time and traded volume - dealers write the contracts people want at prices the stock visits. So the volume-weighted point of control, snapped to the strike lattice, is a proxy for the largest open-interest strike (the practitioner 'max pain' level). Ni, Pearson and Poteshman show clustering is already elevated on trade dates -5 through -1, not just on expiry day, and that it is roughly twice as strong when market makers hold net purchased positions in the strike nearest the close - i.e. the pull is concentrated at the big-OI strike and it operates for the whole week.
ideas.source: Ni, Pearson & Poteshman (2005), JFE 78(1), 49-87 - Figure 6 Panel A (clustering conditional on market makers holding net purchased positions, spike ~2% vs ~1% unconditional, and elevated levels on pre-expiration dates). Max-pain framing is practitioner; the volume-profile-snapped-to-strike-grid proxy is my synthesis.
ideas.novelty: A volume profile bucketed onto the option strike lattice rather than into arbitrary price bins, which turns a generic point-of-control into a specific open-interest estimate. The target level is chosen by accumulated volume, not by proximity - so it will often point the trade away from the nearest strike, which is the opposite of what Strike Grid Pin does.

ideas.name: Rest-of-Day Hedging Momentum
ideas.timeframe: intraday, one decision per day at 15:30 ET
ideas.entry_rule: At 15:30 ET compute rROD = log(P_15:30 / previous session's close) - this deliberately includes the overnight gap. If rROD > +0.0010 go LONG; if rROD < -0.0010 go SHORT. No trade if |rROD| <= 0.0010.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit market-on-close the same session (single 30-minute hold, no overnight risk).
params: use rROD vs rONFH (overnight+first half hour) as predictor
ideas.why: Baltussen, Da, Lammers and Martens show the last-30-minute return is positively and significantly predicted by the rest-of-day return across 60+ futures markets from 1974-2020, with annualised Sharpe ratios of 0.87 to 1.73 at asset-class level. The mechanism is that option and leveraged-ETF market makers are net short gamma, so hedging requires trading in the direction the price already moved, and they defer the bulk of that hedge to the close because liquidity is best there, BIS capital requirements are driven by deltas at close, and overnight positions carry higher margin and financing. They verify the mechanism directly: intraday momentum is present when their negative-gamma-exposure proxy is negative, and absent when it is positive.
ideas.source: Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (2021), 'Hedging demand and market intraday momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 142(1), 377-403. Full text read at https://academicweb.nd.edu/~zda/intramom.pdf
ideas.novelty: The predictor spans from the previous close through 15:30 - it is a fixed-clock cumulative return that includes the overnight session, not a bar-count lookback. The trade is a hard-scheduled 30-minute window with a market-on-close exit, so entry and exit times are constants rather than signal-driven. Nothing about it is a crossover or a threshold on an oscillator.

ideas.name: Close-Auction Hedging Reversal
ideas.timeframe: daily, signal from the last 30 minutes, 3-day hold
ideas.entry_rule: At the close compute rLH = log(close / P_15:30). Let Q80 be the 80th percentile of |rLH| over the trailing 60 sessions. If rLH >= +Q80 enter SHORT at the NEXT session's open; if rLH <= -Q80 enter LONG at the next session's open. Take the opposite side of the closing move.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 3rd trading day after entry. Stop at 2.0 * ATR(14, daily) against entry.
ideas.why: The same paper that documents the last-30-minute hedging push shows it is transitory price pressure, not information: returns over the next three days run opposite to the last-half-hour return, with highly significant mean reversion in equities, bonds and commodities. They use this specifically to distinguish hedging from informed trading - information would produce permanent impact and no reversal. A large closing move is therefore an estimate of how much delta had to be hedged, and that pressure unwinds once the hedgers are flat.
ideas.source: Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (2021), JFE 142(1), 377-403 - the reversal test: 'in all four asset classes, returns in the next three days are opposite to those of rLH'.
ideas.novelty: The signal is a single 30-minute slice of the day rather than any daily bar statistic - a daily bar cannot express it, since the close-relative-to-15:30 move is invisible in OHLC. It is also the deliberate counterparty to Rest-of-Day Hedging Momentum: same underlying flow, opposite side, one holding period later.

ideas.name: Deferred Jump Hedge
ideas.entry_rule: Let m = median of |5-min log returns| over the trailing 20 sessions. Scan 5-min bars between 10:00 and 14:30 ET; a bar is a jump if |log(C_i/C_i-1)| >= 4*m. Record the sign of the FIRST jump of the session. If a later jump of the opposite sign occurs, cancel the day. At 15:30 ET, if a surviving jump exists, enter in the SAME direction as that jump.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit market-on-close the same session. Hard stop at 1.0 * ATR(14, 5-min) against entry.
params: first jump vs largest jump of the day
ideas.why: Baltussen et al. find that large intraday price jumps predict subsequent returns, but that the bulk of the hedge lands at the close rather than at the jump. Their stated reason is Clewlow and Hodges: with partially fixed transaction costs it is optimal to hedge only PARTIALLY after a large price move, which means residual hedging is still required afterwards - and that residual gets deferred to the close where spreads are tighter and depth is greater. So a morning jump creates a known, dated, one-sided buy or sell order that has not yet been executed and will hit the tape in the closing half hour.
ideas.source: Baltussen, Da, Lammers & Martens (2021), JFE 142(1), 377-403 - 'we do find evidence that large price jumps during the day predict subsequent returns... the bulk of the hedge seems to take place towards the end of the day', citing Clewlow & Hodges (1997) on partial hedging under fixed costs.
ideas.novelty: An event detector fires early in the session but the position is opened hours later at a fixed clock time - the signal and the entry are deliberately decoupled, which no breakout or pullback rule does. It also trades the residual of an incomplete hedge rather than the move itself, so it explicitly skips the part of the move that a momentum rule would chase. Shares the 15:30/MOC execution window with Rest-of-Day Hedging Momentum but is triggered by a completely different variable and fires on far fewer days.

ideas.name: Gamma Regime Router
ideas.timeframe: intraday 15-minute, regime set daily before the open
ideas.entry_rule: Before each open compute rho = lag-1 Pearson autocorrelation of 15-minute log returns over the trailing 5 regular sessions (130 returns; compute returns within sessions only, never across the overnight gap). SHORT-GAMMA REGIME if rho > +0.10: go LONG when a 15-min bar closes above the highest high of the prior 8 bars, SHORT when it closes below the lowest low of the prior 8. LONG-GAMMA REGIME if rho < -0.10: go LONG when a bar closes below the lowest low of the prior 8 bars AND the very next bar closes back above that prior low, mirror for SHORT. No trades if |rho| <= 0.10. Additional filter: trade only symbols whose 20-day median dollar volume is below the tradable universe median.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after 6 bars (90 minutes), or on an opposite-regime signal, or at a 1.2 * ATR(14, 15-min) stop, whichever comes first. Flat by the close.
inputs: 5 sessions of intraday history for rho
daily dollar volume for the liquidity filter
params: return horizon h for rho (15/30/60 min)
ideas.why: Barbon and Buraschi show the sign of dealers' aggregate gamma imbalance maps directly onto the sign of the underlying's intraday return autocorrelation: negative gamma imbalance produces intraday momentum (positive autocorrelation) and higher volatility, positive gamma imbalance produces reversal (negative autocorrelation) and lower volatility. Two facts make this tradable without any options data. First, realised autocorrelation is a direct read-out of the latent gamma state. Second, they show rho is strongly persistent - regressing rho on its own lag gives a positive slope with t = 32.17 - so yesterday's reading forecasts today's. They also report the effect peaks at a 60-minute return horizon and is strongest for the least liquid underlyings, which is where the dollar-volume filter comes from.
ideas.source: Barbon & Buraschi (2021), 'Gamma Fragility', working paper. Full text read at https://abarbon.com/assets/Barbon_Buraschi_2021_Gamma_Fragility.pdf - autocorrelation/gamma-imbalance panel regressions, persistence of rho (t=32.17), peak at h=60 minutes, stronger for illiquid stocks.
ideas.novelty: The regime variable is a second-order statistic of returns - their serial correlation - not a level, slope or volatility measure. It selects WHICH strategy runs rather than generating a signal itself, and it flips the same price pattern (a break of an 8-bar extreme) between a breakout and a fade depending on an estimate of dealer positioning. Nothing in a standard indicator library measures return autocorrelation.

ideas.name: ETP Variance Risk Premium
ideas.entry_rule: Implied-vol proxy from a traded volatility ETP: IVp = VIXY_close / SMA(VIXY_close, 63) - dividing by its own 63-day average removes the roll-decay drift that makes the raw ETP price meaningless as a level. Realized-vol proxy: RV21 = stdev(SPY daily log returns, 21) * sqrt(252), then RVp = RV21 / SMA(RV21, 63). Signal VRP = pctrank_252(IVp) - pctrank_252(RVp), where pctrank_252 is the percentile rank within the trailing 252 observations. At the close, enter LONG SPY (or the traded symbol) when VRP > +0.20.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when VRP falls below 0, or after 21 trading days in the position, whichever comes first. Stop at 2.5 * ATR(14, daily) below entry.
inputs: 252 sessions of history for the percentile ranks
ideas.why: Bollerslev, Tauchen and Zhou show the difference between option-implied and realized variance - the variance risk premium - predicts aggregate stock returns, with the strongest predictability at the quarterly horizon, and that this beats standard predictors like P/E and the default spread. We have no VIX, but VIXY and VXX are ordinary listed equities whose price tracks near-term S&P implied variance through VIX futures. The problem is that their level is corrupted by roll decay, which is exactly what dividing by a trailing average and then percentile-ranking removes: what survives is whether implied vol is rich or cheap relative to its own recent history, which is then differenced against realized vol treated identically.
ideas.source: Bollerslev, Tauchen & Zhou (2009), 'Expected Stock Returns and Variance Risk Premia', Review of Financial Studies 22(11), 4463-4492. Full text read at https://public.econ.duke.edu/~boller/Published_Papers/rfs_09.pdf. The ETP substitution and the detrend-then-rank construction are my synthesis, needed because the raw ETP price is not an implied-vol level.
ideas.novelty: The only idea here whose signal comes from a DIFFERENT instrument than the one traded, and the only one that compares a forward-looking market price against a backward-looking statistic of a second instrument. It is not a volatility filter - VRP high means implied is rich relative to realized, which is a bullish state, the opposite of what a naive 'high VIX means danger' rule would do. Honest caveat: VIXY tracks 30-day VIX futures, not VIX itself, so this is a proxy of a proxy and the detrending is doing real work; verify the constructed series against VIX history before trusting it.

ideas.name: Vol Term Structure Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Compute TS = VXX_close / VXZ_close, the ratio of a short-dated (1-2 month) to a mid-dated (4-7 month) VIX futures ETP - a direct read of the term-structure slope. Substitute VIXY for VXX and VIXM for VXZ if preferred. Let z = (TS - SMA(TS,252)) / stdev(TS,252). Enter LONG the equity (SPY/QQQ or the traded symbol) at the close when z crosses DOWN through 0.0 from above. Exit longs and optionally enter SHORT when z crosses UP through +1.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Long exits on z crossing above +1.0. Short exits on z crossing back below +0.25. Hard stop on the long leg at 3.0 * ATR(14, daily). Positions persist across days - this is a regime switch, not a bar-level trade.
inputs: daily OHLCV for VXX and VXZ (or VIXY and VIXM)
daily OHLCV for the traded equity
ideas.why: Johnson shows the shape of the VIX term structure conveys information about the price of variance risk rather than about expected changes in VIX - a clean rejection of the expectations hypothesis - and that a single slope factor summarises nearly all of that information, negatively predicting the excess returns of variance swaps, VIX futures and straddles across all maturities. Backwardation (short-dated implied above mid-dated) is the state where variance risk is expensive, dealers are short gamma into a stressed tape, and hedging demand is spiking. The VXX/VXZ ratio is the tradable-instrument expression of that slope, and both legs are ordinary listed ETPs with normal OHLCV bars.
ideas.source: Johnson (2017), 'Risk Premia and the VIX Term Structure', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 52(6), 2461-2490. Full text read at https://www.travislakejohnson.com/pdfs/Johnson%20VIXTS%202017%20(JFQA).pdf The two-ETP ratio implementation is my synthesis.
ideas.novelty: A cross-instrument ratio between two different points on a volatility curve - a slope, not a level, and one that no single-symbol indicator can express. It is distinct from ETP Variance Risk Premium, which compares implied against realized at one maturity; this compares implied against implied at two maturities, and the two signals disagree in the common state where the whole curve is elevated but still in contango.

ideas.name: OPEX Week Hedge Unwind
ideas.entry_rule: Derive the monthly expiry calendar from bar timestamps: the third Friday of each month. Enter LONG at the OPEN of the first trading day of the calendar week containing that third Friday. Optional second leg: at the close of the third Friday, flip to SHORT and hold through the close of the following Friday (the fourth-Friday week). Universe filter, matching the S&P 100 character of the source: 60-day median dollar volume >= $200M.
ideas.exit_rule: Long leg exits at the close of the third Friday. Short leg, if enabled, exits at the close of the following Friday. Stop each leg at 2.0 * ATR(14, daily). No intra-week discretionary exits - the holding period is fixed by the calendar.
inputs: bar timestamps for the third-Friday calendar
params: entry timing (Friday close before vs Monday open)
exit timing (Friday close vs Thursday close)
ideas.why: Stivers and Sun document that for S&P 100 stocks, weekly returns over option-expiration weeks - the third-Friday week - tend to be high, while the following fourth-Friday week modestly underperforms. They attribute this to two option-market mechanisms: delta-hedge rebalancing by option market makers, specifically a reduction in short-stock hedge positions over the OE week, and declining risk perceptions over the week as measured by option-implied volatilities. Market makers who are short stock as a hedge against long option inventory must buy that stock back as the options roll off, and that buying is concentrated in one identifiable week per month.
ideas.source: Stivers & Sun (2013), 'Returns and option activity over the option-expiration week for S&P 100 stocks', Journal of Banking & Finance 37(11), 4226-4240. Abstract and stated mechanisms retrieved from https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jbfina/v37y2013i11p4226-4240.html
ideas.novelty: A pure calendar strategy with no price condition in the entry at all - the only idea here where the entry rule never looks at the price series. Both entry and exit are fixed dates, and the optional flip makes it a two-legged monthly cycle rather than a signal. That also makes it trivially cheap to backtest and a useful overlay or gate on the other ideas rather than a standalone book. Note this is the thirteenth idea and the domain yielded well past the ten requested: pinning, dealer gamma, skew-as-sentiment, implied-vs-realized vol, dispersion and expiry effects each produced at least two distinct testable rules with primary-source support.

ideas.name: Renko Brick Velocity Burst
ideas.entry_rule: Build close-only Renko bricks: brick size B = ATR(14) on DAILY bars, recomputed each Monday and held fixed for the week, rounded to the nearest cent. A new up-brick prints when a 1-minute close >= (top of last brick) + B; a new down-brick when a 1-minute close <= (bottom of last brick) - B; a direction reversal requires 2*B (standard close-based Renko). If k bricks print inside one minute bar, assign each a duration of 60/k seconds; otherwise brick i's duration d_i = (timestamp of brick i) - (timestamp of brick i-1) in seconds. Let P20 = the 20th percentile of {d_(i-50) ... d_(i-1)}. ENTER LONG on the close of brick i when: brick i is an up-brick, brick i-1 is an up-brick, d_i < P20 and d_(i-1) < P20. Mirror for short (two consecutive down-bricks, both faster than P20).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of whichever comes first: (a) the first brick of the opposite colour, or (b) the first same-colour brick whose duration d > median{d_(i-50)...d_(i-1)} (the burst has decayed), or (c) a hard stop when price trades 2*B against the entry brick's top/bottom. No time-based exit — everything is measured in bricks.
ideas.why: Renko discards time, so a brick's wall-clock duration is a pure measure of how fast volume/price is being consumed per unit of price movement. Two bricks printing far faster than usual means participants are crossing the spread repeatedly to get filled at successively worse prices — urgency, not drift. Institutional order slicing and short-covering both produce this signature. The behavioural claim is that urgency is autocorrelated over the next few price quanta, so the next brick is more likely to continue than reverse.
ideas.novelty: Nothing in an MA cross or RSI sees this: both are functions of price sampled on the clock, whereas the signal here is the CLOCK ITSELF sampled on price. Two charts with identical brick sequences but different speeds are identical to every indicator on our exclusion list and opposite to this one. The exit is also brick-counted rather than price- or time-based.
ideas.source: Renko construction and its algorithmic-trading properties: 'On Suitability of Renko Charts for Algorithmic Trading' (2024), DOI 10.1007/978-3-031-81261-3_6; 'Performance of Pairs Trading Strategies Based on Renko and Kagi Charts' (2025), DOI 10.33138/2957-0506.2025.20.483 (open access). The brick-duration signal itself is my synthesis — the papers establish the chart type, not this rule.

ideas.name: Kagi Yin-Yang Thickness Flip
inputs: ATR(20) on 5-minute bars for the reversal amount
ideas.entry_rule: Build a Kagi line from 5-minute closes. Reversal amount R = 2.0 * ATR(20) of 5-minute bars, recomputed at 09:30 each day and held fixed for the session. The line extends vertically in its current direction whenever price makes a new extreme; it turns and starts a new vertical segment when price retraces >= R from the current extreme. Record every turning point: a SHOULDER is a local high where the line turned down, a WAIST is a local low where it turned up. Maintain a thickness state: state = YANG once the line rises strictly above the most recent shoulder, state = YIN once it falls strictly below the most recent waist; the state persists until the opposite condition fires. ENTER LONG on the 5-minute bar where the state flips YIN -> YANG, provided the immediately preceding down-swing length (previous shoulder price minus previous waist price) is less than the median of the last 10 swing lengths. Mirror for short on a YANG -> YIN flip with a shallow preceding up-swing.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on the state flip back (YANG -> YIN for a long), or on a hard stop at 1.5*R below the entry price, whichever is first. Optionally scale out half at +2R.
ideas.why: The Kagi thickness rule is a path-dependent state machine: the market must both retrace less than R (so the line does not turn) and exceed a prior structural level (so the state flips). Requiring the preceding counter-swing to be shallow relative to its own recent distribution adds the condition that sellers were unable to push a full-sized retracement before buyers reclaimed the prior high — weak supply meeting renewed demand. Quantising all decisions to multiples of R suppresses the noise-triggered signals that plague continuous-price breakout rules.
ideas.novelty: Superficially close to 'break of structure', but the swing points are defined by a volatility-quantised reversal amount rather than by fractal pivot bars, so the swing set is completely different, and the signal carries a persistent two-state memory (yin/yang) that BOS does not have. It is not an MA cross — there is no averaging anywhere — and it is a trend-continuation signal rather than an oscillator extreme. Be candid: this is the idea in my list closest to an existing one, and the parameter R is doing most of the differentiating work.
ideas.source: Kagi construction and the yin/yang (thick/thin) shoulder-waist rules: Steve Nison, 'Beyond Candlesticks' (Wiley, 1994), Kagi chapter. Empirical work on Kagi in a systematic context: 'Performance of Pairs Trading Strategies Based on Renko and Kagi Charts' (2025), DOI 10.33138/2957-0506.2025.20.483. The shallow-preceding-swing filter is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Point-and-Figure Triple Top with Vertical Count Target
ideas.entry_rule: Build a point-and-figure grid from daily highs and lows (high/low method, not close). Box size b = 0.5 * ATR(20), rounded to two decimals, recomputed on the first trading day of each month and held fixed for that month. Reversal = 3 boxes. In an X (up) column, add a box for every full b that the daily HIGH exceeds the current column top; the column reverses to O only when the daily LOW falls to (column top - 3b) or lower, at which point O boxes are filled down from one box below the top. Symmetric rule for O columns using lows and highs. ENTER LONG on the day the current X column posts a box strictly above the tops of BOTH of the two preceding X columns (the classic triple-top buy: three X columns, current top > each of the prior two tops). Mirror for short on a triple-bottom sell.
ideas.exit_rule: Two-part exit, whichever fires first: (a) VERTICAL COUNT TARGET — count the number of boxes N in the breakout X column measured from the bottom of that column, target price = (bottom of breakout column) + N * b * 3 (the reversal size is the multiplier); exit the full position when the daily high touches the target. (b) STRUCTURAL STOP — exit when an O column prints one box below the low of the immediately preceding O column (a double-bottom sell). No time stop.
ideas.why: Box quantisation plus a 3-box reversal filter means a column only forms after a move that is large relative to recent volatility, which mechanically discards small oscillations that would trigger a continuous-price breakout. Requiring three ascending X columns means supply has been tested and cleared at three separate points, which is a stronger statement about absorbed inventory than a single new high. The vertical count is the distinctive part: it makes the profit target a function of the accumulated congestion height rather than of a fixed R multiple or ATR distance.
ideas.novelty: A Donchian breakout fires on any new N-day high; this fires only when the price grid itself has produced three completed X columns in ascending order, which typically requires weeks of structure and is a far rarer, more selective event. The exit is genuinely different from anything on the exclusion list: the target is derived from the breakout column's own box count (an implied congestion measure), not from ATR, a trailing stop, or an indicator flip.
params: vertical count multiplier (3 = reversal size, or 2/4)
ideas.source: Thomas Dorsey, 'Point and Figure Charting' (Wiley) for the triple-top/bottom signals and the vertical count; Jeremy du Plessis, 'The Definitive Guide to Point and Figure' (Harriman House) for the high/low construction method and count mechanics. On formalising chart patterns into testable algorithms: Lo, Mamaysky & Wang, 'Foundations of Technical Analysis', NBER WP 7613 (2000), DOI 10.3386/w7613.

ideas.name: Volume-Clock vs Wall-Clock Volatility Ratio
ideas.entry_rule: Build VOLUME BARS: threshold V = (median of the last 20 daily volumes) / 78. Accumulate 1-minute volume; when the running total crosses V, close a volume bar at that minute's close and reset the accumulator with the remainder. Record each volume bar's clock duration in seconds. Compute sigma_v = standard deviation of log returns over the last 50 volume bars. Compute sigma_t = standard deviation of log returns over the last 50 five-minute bars, then rescale to the volume-bar clock: sigma_t_scaled = sigma_t * sqrt(mean duration of the last 50 volume bars / 300). Define R = sigma_t_scaled / sigma_v. ENTER LONG at the close of a volume bar when: R < the 20th percentile of R over the last 500 volume bars, AND the cumulative log return over the last 10 volume bars is > 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of a volume bar when any of: (a) R rises above its 80th percentile over the last 500 volume bars, (b) 30 volume bars have elapsed since entry, (c) price falls 1.5 * ATR(14) on 5-minute bars below the entry price.
ideas.why: Easley, Lopez de Prado and O'Hara's argument is that returns sampled on the volume clock are much closer to IID normal than clock-time returns, because volume clustering is what makes clock-time returns fat-tailed and heteroskedastic. R is a direct measurement of how much of the observed clock-time volatility is an artefact of volume clustering versus real price discovery. A LOW R means the tape is participating smoothly — volume is arriving steadily and price is moving proportionally. That is the regime in which a modest positive drift is most likely to persist, because it is not being driven by a small number of violent, likely-to-be-reverted volume spikes.
ideas.novelty: This is not a volatility breakout or a squeeze: the signal is a RATIO OF TWO SAMPLING CLOCKS, not the level or the width of anything. A Bollinger squeeze, an ATR expansion breakout and a Keltner rule all measure volatility on one clock; none of them can distinguish 'volatility is low' from 'volatility looks low because volume is even'. There is no moving average and no oscillator in the rule.
params: volume-bar threshold divisor (39/78/156 bars per day)
ideas.source: Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara, 'The Volume Clock: Insights into the High-Frequency Paradigm', Journal of Portfolio Management 39(1), 2012 — for the volume clock and the IID-normalisation claim. Bar construction: Marcos Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning' (Wiley, 2018), Ch. 2 'Financial Data Structures', section 2.3 on standard bars. The ratio statistic and the trading rule are my synthesis.

ideas.name: VPIN Toxicity Flush Fade (bulk-volume-classified)
ideas.entry_rule: Build volume bars exactly as above with threshold V = (20-day median daily volume)/78. For each volume bar j, apply BULK VOLUME CLASSIFICATION as the OHLCV proxy for signed order flow: buy volume V_b(j) = V * Phi((P_j - P_(j-1)) / sigma_dP), where Phi is the standard normal CDF, P_j is the bar's close and sigma_dP is the standard deviation of (P_j - P_(j-1)) over the last 50 volume bars; sell volume V_s(j) = V - V_b(j). Then VPIN(t) = sum over the last n=50 volume bars of |2*V_b(j) - V| divided by (n * V), which lies in [0,1]. ENTER LONG at the close of volume bar t when BOTH: (a) VPIN(t) crosses above its 95th percentile over the last 250 volume bars (it was below on bar t-1), and (b) the cumulative log return over those same last 50 volume bars is < -1.5 times the standard deviation of 50-volume-bar cumulative returns measured over the last 250 bars. Long only — this is a capitulation fade.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of a volume bar when any of: (a) VPIN falls back below its 50th percentile over the last 250 volume bars, (b) 40 volume bars have elapsed, (c) price falls a further 1.0 * (standard deviation of 50-volume-bar returns) below the entry price — a hard stop, because a toxicity spike that keeps going is exactly the scenario this trade loses to.
ideas.why: VPIN measures order-flow imbalance per unit of volume: it spikes when one side is consuming liquidity far faster than the other. Easley/Lopez de Prado/O'Hara document spikes preceding and during liquidity crises. The behavioural claim is that a toxicity spike combined with a large NEGATIVE return is forced selling — margin calls, index-fund rebalancing, stop cascades — rather than informed selling, and forced sellers are price-insensitive, so once the flow exhausts, the liquidity premium paid to absorb it is reclaimed. The conditioning on direction is essential: high VPIN alone is not a signal, high VPIN plus a flush is.
ideas.novelty: Fades an ORDER-FLOW extreme, not a price extreme. RSI, Williams %R, CCI, MFI, Bollinger and VWAP z-score all measure how far price has travelled; VPIN measures how one-sided the volume was in getting there, and the two diverge constantly — a slow grind down produces a large RSI extreme and a low VPIN, while a fast one-sided flush produces a moderate RSI extreme and a huge VPIN. It is also sampled on volume bars, so the lookback is a fixed quantity of traded shares rather than a fixed number of minutes.
params: n bars in the VPIN sum (25/50/100)
ideas.source: Bulk volume classification and VPIN: Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara, 'The Volume Clock: Insights into the High-Frequency Paradigm', Journal of Portfolio Management 39(1), 2012, and 'Flow Toxicity and Liquidity in a High-Frequency World', Review of Financial Studies 25(5), 2012. BVC is explicitly the authors' own OHLCV-level substitute for signed tick data, which is why this stays ohlcv_only. The flush-fade conditioning is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Volume Run-Bar Polarity Flip
ideas.entry_rule: Construct VOLUME RUN BARS per Lopez de Prado, using bulk volume classification for signs (as above: V_b = V*Phi(dP/sigma_dP) per 1-minute bar, V_s = V - V_b). Within the forming bar accumulate theta_buy = sum of V_b and theta_sell = sum of V_s since the bar opened, and T = the number of 1-minute bars consumed. Close the run bar when max(theta_buy, theta_sell) >= E[T] * max(P_b * E[V_b], (1 - P_b) * E[V_s]), where E[T] is an EWMA (span 50) of past bar tick counts, P_b is an EWMA (span 50) of the buy-volume fraction, and E[V_b], E[V_s] are EWMAs (span 50) of buy and sell volume per tick. Initialise E[T] = 30, P_b = 0.5. Label each closed bar BUY-SIDE or SELL-SIDE according to which side triggered the close. ENTER LONG at the close of a run bar when the last two closed run bars are both BUY-SIDE and they were immediately preceded by three or more consecutive SELL-SIDE run bars. Mirror for short.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first SELL-SIDE run bar after entry, or after 5 run bars, whichever is first. Hard stop at 1.5 * ATR(14) on 5-minute bars against the entry.
ideas.why: A run bar closes when one side's cumulative volume exceeds what the recent history says should be expected of it — that is, when a sustained one-sided sequence occurs that is statistically surprising given the current regime. The bars therefore self-adjust: in a quiet tape it takes little to close a bar, in a violent one it takes a lot. A polarity flip from a sell run to two buy runs is the moment the dominant side of a persistent sequence changes, which is when short-term liquidity providers who were leaning one way must reposition. The EWMA thresholds mean the signal is scale-free across tickers and across time of day, which matters a lot for a multi-ticker fleet.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the VPIN idea in the same family: VPIN fades a magnitude extreme, this trades a SIGN CHANGE in the sampling process itself. Distinct from any exclusion-list rule because the bar boundaries are endogenous — the number of bars per day varies with information flow, so 'the last two bars' is a variable amount of clock time. A three-bar momentum rule on time bars always looks at exactly three fixed intervals; here 'three consecutive sell runs' can span two minutes or two hours.
params: EWMA span for E[T], P_b, E[V] (20/50/100)
ideas.source: Marcos Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning' (Wiley, 2018), Ch. 2, section 2.3.2.2 'Run Bars' — the threshold condition max(theta_buy, theta_sell) >= E[T] * max(P_b*E[V_b], (1-P_b)*E[V_s]) is his. Signing via bulk volume classification is the OHLCV proxy for his tick rule, from Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara (2012). The polarity-flip entry is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Range-Bar Flip Count Regime
ideas.entry_rule: Build RANGE BARS of fixed price height S = 0.75 * ATR(14) of 5-minute bars, recomputed at 09:30 each day and fixed for the session. A range bar opens at the close of the previous range bar and closes as soon as (running high - running low) >= S; its close is set to whichever extreme was reached last. Classify each closed range bar as UP if its close > its open, DOWN otherwise. Define a FLIP as a range bar whose class differs from the previous range bar's class, and let F20 = the number of flips among the last 20 closed range bars (an integer in 0..19). ENTER LONG at the close of a range bar when F20 <= 6 AND the last 5 closed range bars are all UP. Mirror for short (F20 <= 6 and last 5 all DOWN).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of a range bar when any of: (a) F20 >= 12 (the tape has become choppy), (b) three consecutive range bars close DOWN (for a long), (c) 20 range bars have elapsed. Hard stop at 2*S against the entry price.
ideas.why: Because every range bar spans the same price distance, the count of direction flips over a fixed number of bars is a clean, unit-free measure of path efficiency: 19 flips means price covered 20*S of path and went nowhere, 0 flips means it went 20*S in a straight line. This is the definition of a trending versus a mean-reverting regime, expressed without any volatility normalisation because the normalisation is baked into the bar construction. Trading with the direction of a low-flip tape is a bet that path efficiency is autocorrelated, which is the core of why trend following works at all.
ideas.novelty: ADX, the choppiness index and efficiency ratios all measure the same underlying idea on TIME bars, where a high reading can be produced either by directional movement or simply by higher volatility during that window. Range bars remove the volatility term entirely — the denominator is constant by construction — so the flip count is a pure path statistic. The entry gate and the exit gate are the same statistic at different thresholds, which gives a natural hysteresis that an ADX gate on a separate signal does not have.
ideas.source: Range-bar construction is standard in futures platform documentation (constant-range bars); the flip-count statistic and the entry/exit thresholds are my synthesis. The path-efficiency reasoning follows Kaufman's efficiency ratio (Perry Kaufman, 'Trading Systems and Methods', Wiley) applied in range-bar space rather than time space.

ideas.name: Heikin-Ashi Shaven-Bottom Streak
ideas.entry_rule: Compute Heikin-Ashi bars: HA_close = (O + H + L + C)/4; HA_open = (HA_open[1] + HA_close[1])/2, seeded on the first bar with (O + C)/2; HA_high = max(H, HA_open, HA_close); HA_low = min(L, HA_open, HA_close). ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when ALL of: (a) HA_close[t] > HA_open[t] and HA_close[t-1] > HA_open[t-1] (two consecutive green HA candles); (b) both candles are SHAVEN-BOTTOM, i.e. (HA_open[t] - HA_low[t]) <= 1 tick and (HA_open[t-1] - HA_low[t-1]) <= 1 tick; (c) the current HA body |HA_close[t] - HA_open[t]| > the 20-bar mean HA body. Mirror for short: two consecutive red HA candles that are shaven-top ((HA_high - HA_open) <= 1 tick) with an above-average body.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar where either (a) the HA candle prints a lower shadow greater than 0.25 * its own body, or (b) the HA candle is red (HA_close < HA_open) — whichever comes first. Hard stop at HA_low of the entry candle minus 0.5 * ATR(14).
ideas.why: HA_open is the midpoint of the previous HA candle, so HA_low = HA_open means the raw low of the current bar never traded below that midpoint. Two such bars in a row is a precise statement that no intraday pullback penetrated the prior candle's centre of gravity twice running — buyers absorbed every attempt without giving back half the previous move. That is a real, checkable statement about the order book's behaviour during the bar, not a smoothed summary of it. The reappearance of a lower shadow is the first evidence that sellers regained the ability to trade through that midpoint, which is why it makes a natural exit.
ideas.novelty: Not a moving-average or oscillator signal at all — it is a condition on the GEOMETRY of a transformed candle, specifically the absence of a shadow, which is a statement about the intrabar path relative to a recursively defined reference level. The exclusion list's 'three-bar momentum' compares raw closes; this compares transformed extremes against a recursive midpoint, and the exit fires on shadow reappearance rather than on a price or indicator level. Note the well-known catch this must be tested against: HA_close uses the current bar's close, so signals are only valid at bar close, never intrabar.
ideas.source: Heikin-Ashi construction is standard; for its systematic use and noise-reduction properties see 'Smoothed Heikin-Ashi Algorithms Optimized for Automated Trading Systems' (2018), DOI 10.31410/itema.2018.514, and 'Study of Heiken Ashi Candlestick for Noise Reduction' (2022), DOI 10.31730/osf.io/phejd (open access). The shaven-bottom streak rule and the shadow-reappearance exit are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Ehlers Autocorrelation Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Step 1, ROOFING FILTER. High-pass with period 48: a1 = cos(sqrt(2)*pi/48); alpha1 = (a1 + sin(sqrt(2)*pi/48) - 1)/a1; HP = (1 - alpha1/2)^2 * (C - 2*C[1] + C[2]) + 2*(1 - alpha1)*HP[1] - (1 - alpha1)^2 * HP[2]. Step 2, SUPER SMOOTHER with period 10: a2 = exp(-sqrt(2)*pi/10); b2 = 2*a2*cos(sqrt(2)*pi/10); c2 = b2; c3 = -a2^2; c1 = 1 - c2 - c3; Filt = c1*(HP + HP[1])/2 + c2*Filt[1] + c3*Filt[2]. Step 3, AUTOCORRELATION. For each lag = 3 to 48, compute the Pearson correlation between the vector {Filt[0..lag-1]} and {Filt[lag..2*lag-1]} using the standard formula (m*Sxy - Sx*Sy)/sqrt((m*Sxx - Sx^2)*(m*Syy - Sy^2)) with m = lag, and scale it to [0,1] as corr01[lag] = 0.5*(corr + 1). Step 4, REVERSAL DETECTION. SumDeltas = the count of lags in 3..48 for which corr01[lag] and corr01_prev[lag] lie on opposite sides of 0.5. A REVERSAL is flagged on bar t when SumDeltas > 24. ENTER at the close of a reversal bar: LONG if Filt[t] > Filt[t-1], SHORT if Filt[t] < Filt[t-1].
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the next bar that flags a reversal (SumDeltas > 24), regardless of its direction. Additional hard exits: 2.0 * ATR(14) stop against the entry, and a 30-bar time stop if no reversal has fired.
ideas.why: The correlation of a band-limited series with its own lagged copy is high while the cycle phase is stable and collapses when the phase inverts. Ehlers' insight is that at a genuine turning point the correlations at MANY lags flip simultaneously, because the whole spectral structure of the recent data shifts at once — a single lag flipping is noise, half of them flipping is an event. Economically, this fires when the balance of participants across multiple horizons changes together, which is what a real regime turn looks like as opposed to a one-timeframe wiggle.
ideas.novelty: There is no threshold on price and no moving average anywhere in the signal. The entry statistic is a COUNT OF SIMULTANEOUS SPECTRAL COHERENCE BREAKS across 46 lags — a fundamentally different object from any level-crossing or crossover rule. The reversal detector also has no direction of its own: it says 'a turn happened here', and the direction is read separately from the filter's slope. That structure (event detector plus direction reader) has no analogue on the exclusion list, and the exit — 'hold until the next detected reversal' — makes holding period endogenous to the market's cycle structure rather than to a fixed target.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'Cycle Analytics for Traders' (Wiley, 2013), autocorrelation and autocorrelation-reversals chapters. Constants and the exact SumDeltas > 24 rule verified against the open-source MQL5 implementation at github.com/thetestspecimen/ehlers-indicators-mql5, file mq5/ehlers_autocorrelation_reversals.mq5, which I fetched and read. Roofing filter reference: Ehlers, 'Predictive Indicators for Effective Trading Strategies' (mesasoftware.com/papers).

ideas.name: Even Better Sinewave Saturation Exit
ideas.entry_rule: Step 1, HIGH-PASS with period 40: alpha1 = (cos(sqrt(2)*pi/40) + sin(sqrt(2)*pi/40) - 1)/cos(sqrt(2)*pi/40); HP = (1 - alpha1/2)^2 * (C - 2*C[1] + C[2]) + 2*(1 - alpha1)*HP[1] - (1 - alpha1)^2 * HP[2]. Step 2, SUPER SMOOTHER with period 10: a1 = exp(-sqrt(2)*pi/10); b1 = 2*a1*cos(sqrt(2)*pi/10); c2 = b1; c3 = -a1^2; c1 = 1 - c2 - c3; Filt = c1*(HP + HP[1])/2 + c2*Filt[1] + c3*Filt[2]. Step 3, THREE-BAR POWER NORMALISATION: Wave = (Filt + Filt[1] + Filt[2])/3; Pwr = (Filt^2 + Filt[1]^2 + Filt[2]^2)/3; EBSW = Wave / sqrt(Pwr), which is bounded in roughly [-1, +1]. ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when EBSW[t] > -0.9 and EBSW has been <= -0.9 for at least the two preceding bars (it is un-saturating from the oversold rail). Mirror for short: EBSW[t] < +0.9 after at least two bars >= +0.9.
ideas.exit_rule: For a long, exit at the close of the first bar where EITHER (a) EBSW rises to >= +0.9 and then on a subsequent bar prints < +0.9 — i.e. exit on the un-saturation from the opposite rail, holding through the entire saturated stretch — OR (b) EBSW falls back below -0.9 (the entry failed). Hard stop at 1.5 * ATR(14). The point of the structure is that the position is held for as long as the indicator is pinned at +/-1, which is exactly when a trend is running.
ideas.why: Dividing the 3-bar mean of the filtered series by the square root of its 3-bar mean square makes the output a normalised direction cosine: it saturates near +/-1 whenever the filtered wave is monotone over three bars, and only leaves the rails when the local waveform actually curves. So saturation is a direct, self-scaling detector of 'the cycle band is currently being dominated by a directional move'. The behavioural claim is that once a market has entered such a state, staying in it until the indicator leaves the opposite rail captures the whole excursion, whereas any fixed profit target truncates it.
ideas.novelty: The distinctive element is the EXIT STRUCTURE, not the entry: instead of exiting at a level, the rule exits when a SATURATED indicator un-saturates, which converts a bounded oscillator into a trend-holding mechanism. Every oscillator rule on the exclusion list (RSI, Stochastic, Williams %R, CCI, MFI) exits at a level and therefore caps the winner; this deliberately does the opposite. The normalisation by RMS power is also unlike any of them — it is amplitude-invariant by construction, so no per-ticker threshold tuning is needed.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'Cycle Analytics for Traders' (Wiley, 2013), 'Even Better Sinewave Indicator' chapter. Formula, the hpPeriod = 40 / lpPeriod = 10 defaults, the 3-bar wave/pwr normalisation and the +/-1.2 plot bounds verified against github.com/thetestspecimen/ehlers-indicators-mql5, file mq5/ehlers_even_better_sinewave.mq5, which I fetched and read. The saturate-and-hold exit structure is my synthesis of Ehlers' stated intent.

ideas.name: Dominant Cycle Period Expansion
ideas.category: Ehlers DSP / cycle measurement as regime filter
inputs: the MAMA homodyne discriminator period output
ideas.entry_rule: Compute Ehlers' MEASURED DOMINANT CYCLE PERIOD from the MAMA homodyne discriminator. Smooth: Sm = (4*C + 3*C[1] + 2*C[2] + C[3])/10. Detrend: Det = (0.0962*Sm + 0.5769*Sm[2] - 0.5769*Sm[4] - 0.0962*Sm[6]) * (0.075*Period[1] + 0.54). Form quadrature Q1 and in-phase I1 with the same 6-tap coefficient pattern scaled by (0.075*Period[1] + 0.54); advance the phase by 90 degrees to get I2 = I1 - (0.075*Period[1]+0.54)*Q1_shift and Q2 = Q1 + (0.075*Period[1]+0.54)*I1_shift; smooth both as 0.2*current + 0.8*previous. Homodyne: Re = I2*I2[1] + Q2*Q2[1], Im = I2*Q2[1] - Q2*I2[1], each smoothed 0.2/0.8. Period = 360 / atan2 angle in degrees; then clamp Period to [6, 50], rate-limit it to between 0.67x and 1.5x the previous Period, and smooth 0.2*Period + 0.8*Period[1]. Separately compute the roofing filter Filt (HP 48 then SuperSmoother 10, formulas as in the Autocorrelation Reversal idea). ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when: Period[t] > the 80th percentile of Period over the last 200 bars, AND Filt[t] > 0, AND Filt[t] > Filt[t-1]. Mirror for short with Filt < 0 and falling.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar where EITHER (a) Period falls below its 50th percentile over the last 200 bars, or (b) Filt crosses zero against the position. Hard stop at 2.0 * ATR(14).
ideas.why: The dominant cycle period is a direct measurement of the timescale on which the market is currently oscillating. When that measured period STRETCHES toward the upper end of its own recent range, the short-cycle oscillation has been overwhelmed by something slower — which is precisely what the transition from mean-reverting chop to a trending move looks like in the frequency domain. Economically, cycle lengthening corresponds to the arrival of slower, larger participants (institutional accumulation or distribution) whose order flow does not reverse within the previous cycle length.
ideas.novelty: The signal is the market's own MEASURED TIMESCALE, not its price, its momentum or its volatility. Nothing on the exclusion list has any concept of a measured period — ADX, choppiness and squeeze indicators all answer 'how directional/volatile is it' at a fixed lookback; this answers 'what lookback is currently correct', and trades the change in that answer. It also sidesteps the classic MAMA/FAMA crossover, which really is an adaptive MA cross: here the moving averages are discarded entirely and only the discriminator's period output is used.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'MESA Adaptive Moving Averages' (mesasoftware.com/papers/MAMA.pdf) for the homodyne discriminator. Every numeric constant above (the 4/3/2/1 smoother, the 0.0962/0.5769 detrend taps, the 0.075*Period + 0.54 scaling, the 0.2/0.8 smoothing, the [6,50] clamp and the 0.67x-1.5x rate limit) was verified against QuantConnect/Lean, file Indicators/MesaAdaptiveMovingAverage.cs, which I fetched and read. Using the period alone as a regime signal is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Laguerre RSI Unpinning
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the four-stage LAGUERRE CASCADE with damping factor gamma = 0.5 on price P (use HL2): L0 = (1 - gamma)*P + gamma*L0[1]; L1 = -gamma*L0 + L0[1] + gamma*L1[1]; L2 = -gamma*L1 + L1[1] + gamma*L2[1]; L3 = -gamma*L2 + L2[1] + gamma*L3[1]. Accumulate CU and CD from zero each bar over the three adjacent pairs: if L0 >= L1 then CU += (L0 - L1) else CD += (L1 - L0); if L1 >= L2 then CU += (L1 - L2) else CD += (L2 - L1); if L2 >= L3 then CU += (L2 - L3) else CD += (L3 - L2). LRSI = CU/(CU + CD) when the denominator is non-zero, else carry the previous value. ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when LRSI[t] > 0.05 AND LRSI has been <= 0.05 on each of the three preceding bars — the 'unpinning' event. Mirror for short when LRSI < 0.95 after three or more consecutive bars >= 0.95.
ideas.exit_rule: For a long, exit at the close of the first bar where EITHER (a) LRSI >= 0.95 (fully pinned at the opposite rail), or (b) LRSI falls back to <= 0.05 (the unpinning failed). Hard stop at 2.0 * ATR(14) below entry. There is no fixed profit target — the trade is defined entirely by the rail-to-rail traverse.
ideas.why: Because the Laguerre cascade is a set of all-pass sections rather than an averaging window, LRSI saturates exactly at 0 or 1 whenever the four stages are perfectly ordered, and it sits pinned there through a persistent directional move. The pin is therefore a state, not a threshold crossing, and it typically persists for many bars. The FIRST bar on which the ordering breaks is the earliest possible evidence that the persistent flow has stopped — and because the cascade has near-zero lag over a very short effective data window, that evidence arrives well before any windowed oscillator could produce it.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from an RSI extreme in both construction and trigger. Construction: no window, no averaging of gains and losses — the statistic is a ratio of differences between successive stages of an all-pass filter cascade. Trigger: the entry requires a MULTI-BAR SATURATED STATE followed by its termination, which is a state-machine condition rather than a level crossing; a plain 'RSI < 30' fires on a level regardless of how long it has been there. The exit is a traverse to the opposite rail, so the holding period is set by the move, not by a target.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'Time Warp - Without Space Travel' (mesasoftware.com/papers/TimeWarp.pdf) for the Laguerre filter and Laguerre RSI. The exact CU/CD accumulation over the three adjacent stage pairs and the default gamma = 0.5 were verified against github.com/MathisWellmann/go_ehlers_indicators, file laguerre_rsi.go, which I fetched and read. The unpinning entry and rail-to-rail exit are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Reflex Displacement inside TrendFlex Regime
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the SUPER SMOOTHER with period 20 on close: a1 = exp(-sqrt(2)*pi/20); b1 = 2*a1*cos(sqrt(2)*pi/20); c2 = b1; c3 = -a1^2; c1 = 1 - c2 - c3; Filt = c1*(C + C[1])/2 + c2*Filt[1] + c3*Filt[2]. REFLEX with window n = 20: slope = (Filt[n] - Filt)/n; sum = 0; for j = 1..n: sum += (Filt + j*slope) - Filt[j]; sum /= n; MS_r = 0.04*sum^2 + 0.96*MS_r[1]; Reflex = sum/sqrt(MS_r) when MS_r > 0. TRENDFLEX with the same n: sum2 = 0; for j = 1..n: sum2 += (Filt - Filt[j]); sum2 /= n; MS_t = 0.04*sum2^2 + 0.96*MS_t[1]; TrendFlex = sum2/sqrt(MS_t). ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when: TrendFlex[t] > 0 AND Reflex[t] <= -2.0 AND Reflex[t-1] > -2.0 (a fresh 2-sigma displacement below the fitted trend line, inside an up regime). Mirror for short: TrendFlex < 0 and Reflex crosses up through +2.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar where any of: (a) Reflex >= +1.0 (the displacement has been fully reclaimed and then some), (b) TrendFlex crosses below 0 (the regime that justified the trade is gone), (c) 25 bars elapse. Hard stop at 2.0 * ATR(14).
ideas.why: Reflex measures the vertical distance between the smoothed price and the straight line joining the smoothed price to its value n bars ago, then divides that distance by the square root of an EWMA of its own square — a self-calibrating standard-error. So Reflex = -2 literally means 'price is two of its own recent standard deviations below where a straight-line interpolation of the last 20 bars would put it', with essentially zero lag because the detrending removes the filter's group delay. TrendFlex, computed from the same filtered series, answers whether the longer drift is up. The pair therefore separates 'where the trend is going' from 'how far price has been displaced from it right now', which is exactly the decomposition a mean-reversion-in-trend trade needs.
ideas.novelty: An EMA-pullback rule measures the pullback in price or ATR units against a lagging average; here the reference is a ZERO-LAG interpolated line and the pullback is measured in units of the statistic's OWN EWMA standard deviation (the 0.04/0.96 recursion), which makes the entry threshold genuinely comparable across tickers and volatility regimes with no per-symbol tuning. The two oscillators are also orthogonal constructions from one filtered series — Reflex detrends against the slope, TrendFlex does not — which is a different decomposition from 'fast MA vs slow MA'.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'Reflex: A New Zero-Lag Indicator', Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, February 2020 (Reflex and TrendFlex). The slope-detrended sum, the 0.04/0.96 mean-square EWMA and the division by sqrt(MS) were verified against github.com/MathisWellmann/go_ehlers_indicators, file re_flex.go, which I fetched and read. The TrendFlex-gated displacement entry is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Adaptive Bandpass Trough Cross
ideas.category: Ehlers DSP / adaptive band-pass with measured centre frequency
ideas.entry_rule: Step 1, MEASURE THE DOMINANT CYCLE with the autocorrelation periodogram. Roofing-filter the close (HP period 48 then SuperSmoother 10, formulas as in the Autocorrelation Reversal idea) to get Filt. For each lag in 3..48 compute the Pearson correlation of Filt against its lag-shifted copy. Take a discrete Fourier transform of those correlations: for each candidate period p in 10..48, cosPart(p) = sum over lags of corr(lag)*cos(2*pi*lag/p), sinPart(p) = sum over lags of corr(lag)*sin(2*pi*lag/p), Power(p) = cosPart(p)^2 + sinPart(p)^2. Smooth each with SmoothPower(p) = 0.2*Power(p) + 0.8*SmoothPower(p)[1], then normalise all powers to a maximum of 1. DomCycle = the centre-of-gravity (power-weighted average) of the periods p whose normalised power >= 0.5. Step 2, BANDPASS with bandwidth bw = 0.3: beta1 = cos(2*pi/(0.9*DomCycle)); gamma1 = 1/cos(2*pi*bw/(0.9*DomCycle)); alpha2 = gamma1 - sqrt(gamma1^2 - 1); BP = 0.5*(1 - alpha2)*(C - C[2]) + beta1*(1 + alpha2)*BP[1] - alpha2*BP[2]. Step 3, AUTOMATIC GAIN CONTROL: Peak = 0.991*Peak[1]; if |BP| > Peak then Peak = |BP|; Signal = BP/Peak (bounded in [-1,1]). Trigger = 0.9*Signal[1]. ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when Signal[t] crosses ABOVE Trigger[t] while Signal[t] < -0.5. Mirror for short: Signal crosses below Trigger while Signal > +0.5.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar where Signal crosses BELOW Trigger while Signal > +0.5 (the symmetric opposite condition), or after 1.5 * DomCycle bars have elapsed (a holding period set by the measured cycle length, not a fixed number). Hard stop at 1.5 * ATR(14).
ideas.why: A fixed-period band-pass filter is only useful when the market happens to be oscillating at that period. Re-measuring the centre frequency each bar from the power spectrum of the autocorrelation function means the filter is always tuned to whatever rhythm is actually present. The trigger is a 0.9-scaled one-bar lag of the AGC-normalised output, which is a deliberate exploitation of the fact that a sinusoid's one-bar-lagged copy crosses it at the turning points — so the crossover fires at the trough of the currently dominant cycle. Requiring Signal < -0.5 restricts entries to genuine troughs rather than mid-cycle wobbles. Economically this is buying the low of whatever oscillation the current mix of participants is producing, with the oscillation's length inferred rather than assumed.
ideas.novelty: Every oscillator on the exclusion list has a fixed lookback chosen by the user; here the lookback is a MEASURED quantity that changes every bar, and it also sets the holding period (1.5 * DomCycle). The AGC normalisation (Peak decaying at 0.991 per bar) is a further departure: the oscillator's scale is set by its own recent peak amplitude, so the -0.5 threshold means the same thing on a quiet ticker and a violent one. And the trigger line is not an average of the signal — it is a scaled lag of it, a construction with no analogue in MACD or Stochastic.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'Cycle Analytics for Traders' (Wiley, 2013), autocorrelation periodogram and adaptive band-pass chapters. The Pearson-correlations-then-DFT-then-0.2/0.8-EMA-then-centre-of-gravity pipeline, the beta1/gamma1/alpha2 band-pass coefficients, the default bandwidth 0.3, the 0.9*DomCycle scaling and the 0.9-scaled lagged trigger were all verified against github.com/thetestspecimen/ehlers-indicators-mql5, file mq5/ehlers_adaptive_bandpass.mq5, which I fetched and read.

ideas.name: Fractal Dimension Regime Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the FRAMA FRACTAL DIMENSION with an even window N = 16. Over the MOST RECENT N/2 bars: N1 = (max High - min Low)/(N/2). Over the OLDER N/2 bars: N2 = (max High - min Low)/(N/2). Over all N bars: N3 = (max High - min Low)/N. Then D = log((N1 + N2)/N3)/log(2), clamped to [1.0, 2.0]. D approaches 1 for a straight line and 2 for a space-filling random path. Do NOT compute the FRAMA output itself — discard it. ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when: D[t] < 1.40 AND D[t-1] >= 1.40 (a fresh downward crossing), AND close[t] > close[t-N]. Mirror for short: same D crossing with close[t] < close[t-N].
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar where EITHER (a) D rises above 1.60 (the path has become noise-like again), or (b) close crosses back through close[t-N] against the position. Hard stop at 2.0 * ATR(14). No profit target — the trade is held for as long as the price path stays geometrically efficient.
ideas.why: The Hausdorff-style dimension estimate compares the summed range of two half-windows against the range of the whole window. If price moved monotonically, the two halves tile the whole and D = 1; if it zig-zagged, the halves each covered nearly the full range and D approaches 2. So D is a scale-free measure of how much of the traveled distance was retraced. A fresh drop below 1.40 is the moment the market stopped retracing what it covered — the geometric signature of one side of the book being cleared out rather than two sides trading against each other.
ideas.novelty: D is computed from RANGES OF SUB-WINDOWS, not from directional movement (ADX), not from bar-to-bar volatility (ATR, Bollinger width), and not from net-change-over-path (Kaufman efficiency). Crucially, D is insensitive to direction entirely — it is a pure geometry statistic, which is why the direction has to be supplied separately by the N-bar price comparison. This makes it a cleaner regime gate than ADX, which conflates trend strength with the amount of movement. The idea deliberately throws away the moving average that FRAMA exists to produce and keeps only its internal diagnostic, which is not how FRAMA is normally used.
params: require fresh crossing vs level only
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'FRAMA - Fractal Adaptive Moving Average' (mesasoftware.com/papers/FRAMA.pdf). The exact N1/N2/N3 definitions, the D = log((N1+N2)/N3)/log(2) formula, and the alpha = exp(w*(D-1)) with w = ln(2/(1+198)) bounded to [0.01, 1.0] were verified against QuantConnect/Lean, file Indicators/FractalAdaptiveMovingAverage.cs, which I fetched and read. Using D alone as a standalone regime gate is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Kalman Local-Linear-Trend Slope t-Statistic
ideas.entry_rule: Run a two-state KALMAN FILTER (local linear trend model) on y_t = ln(close_t). State x = [mu, beta]' with transition F = [[1, 1], [0, 1]], observation matrix H = [1, 0]. Observation noise is estimated from the bar's own range using the Parkinson estimator: R_t = (ln(High_t / Low_t))^2 / (4 * ln 2), floored at 1e-8. Process noise Q = diag(k1 * Rbar, k2 * Rbar) where Rbar is the 100-bar mean of R_t, with starting values k1 = 0.01 and k2 = 0.0001. Initialise mu_0 = ln(close_0), beta_0 = 0, P_0 = diag(Rbar, Rbar/100). Each bar: PREDICT x' = F x, P' = F P F' + Q; UPDATE with K = P' H' / (H P' H' + R_t), x = x' + K*(y_t - H x'), P = (I - K H) P'. After the update take beta_t and its posterior variance P22 = P[1][1], and form the t-statistic T_t = beta_t / sqrt(P22). ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when T_t > 2.0 AND T_(t-1) <= 2.0. Mirror for short when T_t < -2.0 crossing down.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar where EITHER (a) T_t < 0.5 for a long (the slope is no longer statistically distinguishable from flat), or (b) beta_t < 0 (the estimated drift has turned negative). Hard stop at 2.0 * ATR(14). No fixed target.
ideas.why: Every moving-average slope rule has to answer 'how much slope is enough', and the answer depends on the ticker and the volatility regime, which is why those thresholds never transfer. A state-space model answers the question internally: the filter tracks not only the estimated drift but its uncertainty, and demanding beta > 2 standard errors is a self-calibrating statement that the drift is real rather than a noise artefact. Feeding the Parkinson range estimator in as the per-bar observation noise makes the filter automatically distrust wide-range bars and trust narrow ones, which is the correct handling of a bar where the true price wandered a lot within the interval.
ideas.novelty: The signal is a SIGNIFICANCE TEST, not a level or a crossover. A Hull MA slope rule fires when the slope exceeds a hand-picked number; this fires when the slope exceeds its own estimated standard error, so the same code works on a 3-dollar stock and a 300-dollar stock with no retuning — which matters directly for a multi-ticker fleet. Using an intrabar range statistic as the measurement-noise input is the second departure: it makes the OHLC bar's shape, not just its close, drive the filter's confidence. No moving average appears anywhere.
params: use Parkinson vs Garman-Klass vs constant R
ideas.source: Andrew Harvey, 'Forecasting, Structural Time Series Models and the Kalman Filter' (Cambridge University Press, 1989), the local linear trend model (state [level, slope] with F = [[1,1],[0,1]]) and its filtering recursions. Range-based observation-noise estimator: M. Parkinson, 'The Extreme Value Method for Estimating the Variance of the Rate of Return', Journal of Business 53(1), 1980, pp. 61-65 — the (ln(H/L))^2/(4 ln 2) estimator. Combining the two and trading the slope t-statistic is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Causal A-Trous Wavelet Scale Disagreement
ideas.entry_rule: Decompose log close with the CAUSAL A-TROUS (undecimated, shift-invariant) HAAR TRANSFORM, which uses only past data by construction and therefore has no look-ahead: S_0[t] = ln(close_t); for levels j = 1..5, S_j[t] = 0.5*(S_(j-1)[t] + S_(j-1)[t - 2^(j-1)]); detail D_j[t] = S_(j-1)[t] - S_j[t]. Note that S_5 depends on data up to 31 bars back and nothing forward. Define the MID-SCALE detail M[t] = D_3[t] + D_4[t]. ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when BOTH: (a) S_5[t] > S_5[t-1] (the coarse scale is rising), and (b) M[t] < the 20th percentile of M over the last 200 bars (the mid scales are stretched to the downside). Mirror for short: S_5 falling and M above its 80th percentile.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar where EITHER (a) M rises above its 80th percentile over the last 200 bars (the mid-scale dip has been more than reclaimed), or (b) S_5[t] < S_5[t-1] (the coarse scale rolled over). Hard stop at 2.0 * ATR(14). No fixed target.
ideas.why: A wavelet decomposition splits the price into additive components that live at separate, non-overlapping timescales — unlike two moving averages of different lengths, whose outputs both contain the same low-frequency content and are therefore highly correlated. That separation is what makes a genuine multi-horizon disagreement measurable: S_5 carries only movement slower than roughly 32 bars, D_3 + D_4 carries only movement between roughly 8 and 32 bars, and neither contains the other's information. The trade is placed when short-horizon and long-horizon participants disagree, on the reasoning that the longer-horizon flow is the more persistent of the two because it is driven by slower-moving capital.
ideas.novelty: Two things separate this from any MA pullback. First, the components are ORTHOGONAL by construction — an EMA(50) and an EMA(10) share most of their variance, whereas S_5 and D_3+D_4 share none, so 'disagreement between scales' is a well-defined quantity here and is not well-defined for two EMAs. Second, the threshold is a percentile of the detail's OWN recent distribution rather than a price or ATR distance, so the entry is invariant to the ticker's volatility level. The insistence on the a-trous/undecimated form rather than the standard DWT is the important implementation detail: the decimated DWT is not shift-invariant and standard wavelet-denoising implementations leak future information across the boundary, which is the single most common way wavelet backtests produce fake results.
params: which details to sum (D2+D3, D3+D4, D3+D4+D5)
wavelet (causal Haar vs causal B3-spline a-trous)
ideas.source: Donald Percival & Andrew Walden, 'Wavelet Methods for Time Series Analysis' (Cambridge University Press, 2000) - the a-trous / maximal-overlap (undecimated) transform, its shift invariance, and the boundary-coefficient problem. Evidence on wavelet denoising of financial series: 'Can Denoising Enhance Prediction Accuracy of Learning Models? A Case of Wavelet Decomposition Approach', Forecasting 6(1), 2024, DOI 10.3390/forecast6010005 (open access). The scale-disagreement trading rule is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Kernel-Regression Smoothed Extremum
ideas.entry_rule: On each bar t, fit a NADARAYA-WATSON KERNEL REGRESSION of close on time over the trailing window of the last 38 bars, indexed i = 1..38: m(tau) = sum_i K_h(tau - i)*P_i / sum_i K_h(tau - i), with the Gaussian kernel K_h(z) = exp(-z^2 / (2*h^2)). Bandwidth: compute h_cv by leave-one-out cross-validation over the window (minimise sum_i (P_i - m_(-i)(i))^2), then set h = 0.3 * h_cv - the deliberate under-smoothing factor Lo, Mamaysky and Wang use so that local extrema are preserved rather than averaged away. Because the fit is one-sided and unstable at the right edge, evaluate extrema with a 2-bar confirmation lag: a LOCAL MINIMUM is declared at index t-2 when m(t-3) > m(t-2) and m(t-2) < m(t-1). ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when a local minimum is declared at t-2 AND close_t is within 0.5 * ATR(14) of close_(t-2) (price has not already run away from the turn). Mirror for short on a declared local maximum.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the bar on which the NEXT local extremum of the opposite type is declared (a local maximum, for a long) - so the holding period is set by the smoothed series' own turning points. Additional hard exits: a 3.0 * ATR(14) stop, and a 20-bar time stop if no opposing extremum has been declared.
ideas.why: Lo, Mamaysky and Wang's contribution was to show that the chart patterns human technicians claim to see can be defined rigorously as sequences of local extrema of a kernel-smoothed price path, and that some of those definitions carry statistically significant information in US equities. The 0.3 bandwidth adjustment is the crux: cross-validation on financial data picks a bandwidth that is too large for turning-point detection because CV optimises pointwise fit, not derivative structure. Trading the extrema directly is the simplest possible use of the machinery - it buys the confirmed turn of a nonparametrically estimated conditional mean, which is a far more robust notion of 'the low' than a pivot-bar definition that any single wick can create.
ideas.novelty: The reference series is a NONPARAMETRIC CONDITIONAL MEAN with a data-chosen bandwidth, not a linear filter with a fixed lookback. That distinction matters in practice: the effective smoothing adapts to the local density and noise level of the window, so during a fast move the fit tracks tightly and during chop it flattens - behaviour no fixed-length MA, EMA or Hull MA reproduces. The entry is an extremum of the estimated derivative rather than a crossing of anything, and the exit is the next opposing extremum, making holding period fully endogenous. The 2-bar confirmation lag is stated explicitly because the right-edge instability of a one-sided kernel fit is where naive implementations of this quietly acquire look-ahead bias.
params: bandwidth multiplier (0.2/0.3/0.5 x h_cv, or sweep h directly)
ideas.source: Andrew Lo, Harry Mamaysky & Jiang Wang, 'Foundations of Technical Analysis: Computational Algorithms, Statistical Inference, and Empirical Implementation', NBER Working Paper 7613 (2000), DOI 10.3386/w7613, published in Journal of Finance 55(4), 2000, pp. 1705-1765 - Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression on price, the cross-validated bandwidth, the explicit 0.3 under-smoothing multiplier, and extrema-based pattern definitions. Trading the raw extrema (rather than their named patterns) is my synthesis; the causal-window and confirmation-lag construction is mine and is not in the paper, which fits two-sided.

ideas.name: Residual s-score stat arb
ideas.entry_rule: Each day, over the trailing 60 daily bars, OLS-regress the ticker's daily returns on SPY's daily returns: R_t = b0 + beta*R_SPY_t + e_t. Build the cumulative residual X_k = sum(e_1..e_k) for k=1..60 (note X_60 = 0 by construction). Fit the 1-lag OLS X_{n+1} = a + b*X_n + z, n=1..59. Compute kappa = -ln(b)*252 and REJECT the ticker for that day if b >= 0.9672 (i.e. kappa <= 252/30 = 8.4, mean reversion slower than ~1.5 months). Otherwise sigma_eq = sqrt(Var(z)/(1-b^2)), m = a/(1-b), and the s-score is s = -m/sigma_eq = (-a/(1-b)) / sqrt(Var(z)/(1-b^2)). BUY TO OPEN when s < -1.25. SELL/SHORT TO OPEN when s > +1.25. Hedge by simultaneously taking -beta dollars of SPY per 1 dollar of stock (or run unhedged if shorting is unavailable).
ideas.exit_rule: Close the long when s rises above -0.50. Close the short when s falls below +0.75 (the asymmetry is the authors' own tuned choice). Hard time stop after 3 mean-reversion times, i.e. 3/kappa*252 bars.
inputs: daily close of SPY or a sector ETF
ideas.why: The excess of a stock over its market/sector factor is a genuinely stationary quantity under an OU model, so its distance from equilibrium in units of the OU stationary standard deviation is comparable across tickers and across time in a way a raw price z-score is not. The kappa filter is the load-bearing part: it refuses to trade names whose reversion is too slow for the 60-day estimation window to be meaningful, which is exactly the failure mode that kills naive pairs trading. Trading only on large excursions means you are betting on a documented anomaly (idiosyncratic residual over-extension) rather than on direction.
ideas.novelty: Not a Bollinger or VWAP z-score. The z is taken on the OU stationary distribution of a factor-neutral CUMULATIVE RESIDUAL, not on price; and the model self-rejects when the fitted mean-reversion speed is too slow, which no band indicator does. Entry and exit thresholds are deliberately asymmetric.
ideas.source: Avellaneda & Lee (2010), 'Statistical Arbitrage in the US Equities Market', Courant Institute NYU open working paper, https://math.nyu.edu/~avellane/AvellanedaLeeStatArb20090616.pdf - equations (15), (16), (21), (22), Section 4.1 and Appendix (verified by extracting the PDF text).

ideas.name: Volatility-scaled triple barrier
ideas.entry_rule: Carrier entry (deliberately plain so the exit is what gets tested): go long at the close of any bar where close > max(high) of the prior 20 bars. The object of the sweep is the exit geometry below, not this entry.
ideas.exit_rule: At entry, compute trgt = the EWM standard deviation (span 100) of daily returns as of the entry bar. Place three barriers: an UPPER barrier at entry_price*(1 + pt*trgt), a LOWER barrier at entry_price*(1 - sl*trgt), and a VERTICAL barrier at entry_bar + T bars. Exit at whichever is touched first, using intrabar highs and lows for the horizontal barriers. Default pt = sl = 1.0 (symmetric), T = 5 daily bars. Skip the trade entirely if trgt < minRet (default 0.001), i.e. do not open a position whose profit barrier is smaller than costs.
ideas.why: A fixed percentage stop is wrong by construction: the same 2% stop is a hair-trigger in a quiet regime and never touched in a violent one, so a strategy's measured edge is contaminated by whatever volatility regime the sample happened to contain. Scaling both barriers by the current EWM return volatility makes the stop and target equally likely to be hit regardless of regime, so the win rate the backtest reports is a property of the signal rather than of the sample's volatility. The vertical barrier caps opportunity cost and stops the tail of trades that neither win nor lose from dominating the holding-period statistics.
ideas.novelty: Not an ATR stop bolted onto a fixed target.
