All three barriers are set simultaneously at entry from ONE volatility estimate, the path is evaluated for first touch (so ordering within a bar matters), and the minRet floor refuses trades whose target is below the cost threshold. The pt/sl asymmetry is a first-class tunable rather than a bolt-on.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning', ch.3 snippets 3.1-3.5, reproduced verbatim in the public repo BlackArbsCEO/Adv_Fin_ML_Exercises, src/features/snippets.py (getDailyVol, applyPtSlOnT1, getEvents, addVerticalBarrier, getBins) - source read directly from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BlackArbsCEO/Adv_Fin_ML_Exercises/master/src/features/snippets.py

ideas.name: Symmetric CUSUM event filter
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain two running sums, both starting at 0. On each bar compute d_t = ln(close_t) - ln(close_{t-1}) (SIGNED, not absolute). Update S_pos = max(0, S_pos + d_t) and S_neg = min(0, S_neg + d_t). Set the threshold h = k * (EWM std of d, span 100) evaluated at bar t, with k = 2 by default. If S_pos > h: fire an UP event at bar t and reset S_pos = 0. If S_neg < -h: fire a DOWN event at bar t and reset S_neg = 0. Go long at the close of an UP event bar; go short (or stay flat) at the close of a DOWN event bar.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold for exactly N bars (default N = 10) and exit at that close, OR exit immediately if an opposite-direction event fires first, whichever comes sooner.
ideas.why: Sampling every bar means most observations carry no information and simply dilute whatever edge exists, and it also means a signal can fire on a 0.1% drift in a dead tape. The CUSUM filter only emits an observation once cumulative signed movement since the last reset exceeds a volatility-scaled threshold, so it is invariant to how often you sample and it self-clears after each event. That makes the event stream a set of genuine run-ups and run-downs rather than of arbitrary calendar instants, which is what a directional bet actually wants to condition on.
ideas.novelty: Not a breakout and not a momentum threshold. The state resets to zero after each trigger, so it measures cumulative displacement since the last acknowledged move, not displacement from a fixed lookback window - it fires on a slow 10-bar grind that no N-bar-return rule would catch, and stays silent through a large move already counted. Note the widely-circulated public snippet takes abs(diff), which collapses the two sums; the signed version above matches the book and is what should be tested.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning', snippet 2.5.2.1 (getTEvents), public reproduction at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BlackArbsCEO/Adv_Fin_ML_Exercises/master/src/features/snippets.py lines 18-49 (read directly; the abs() deviation noted above is visible in that file).

ideas.name: Conditional precision meta-gate
ideas.entry_rule: Take any primary signal P (e.g. the CUSUM up-event or the Donchian breakout). Before acting on a new P signal at bar t, classify the current bar into a volatility tercile: compute v_t = EWM std of daily returns (span 100), rank v_t against its own trailing 252-bar distribution, and label LOW if percentile < 33, MID if 33-67, HIGH if > 67. Look back at the last 50 COMPLETED P-trades whose entry bar fell in the SAME tercile and count the fraction f that exited at the profit barrier rather than the stop barrier. Enter long only if f > 0.50 and at least 20 same-tercile trades exist; otherwise skip the signal entirely and record nothing. All completed trades, taken or skipped, are simulated forward and recorded so the statistic keeps updating.
ideas.exit_rule: Triple barrier as in the volatility-scaled triple barrier idea: pt*trgt above, sl*trgt below, T bars, first touch wins.
inputs: rolling ledger of past simulated trade outcomes
params: bucketing variable (vol vs trend strength vs time of day)
ideas.why: A primary signal usually has decent recall and poor precision - it catches the moves but also fires constantly in conditions where it does not work. Rather than degrade the signal by piling on filters, you keep it and learn, from its own realised track record, WHICH conditions it has recently been right in, then bet only there. This is the deterministic, no-machine-learning version of meta-labelling: it converts the primary signal's own history into a take/skip decision, so it adapts when the market regime that suited the signal disappears.
ideas.novelty: The gate is not a market condition at all - it is the strategy's own recent conditional hit rate. Nothing in a standard indicator stack conditions on the historical precision of the signal being fired. It also degrades gracefully: below the minimum sample it simply refuses to trade rather than guessing.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning', ch.3 meta-labelling (getBins case 2: 'bin in (0,1) <- label by pnl (meta-labeling)'), snippet 3.5/3.7 as reproduced at https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BlackArbsCEO/Adv_Fin_ML_Exercises/master/src/features/snippets.py. The ML classifier is replaced here by an explicit bucketed frequency estimate so it is testable without a model - that substitution is mine.

ideas.name: Backward trend-scan max-t
ideas.entry_rule: At each bar t, for every lookback L in {5, 6, 7, ..., 20}: take the trailing L closes, regress them by OLS on the integer time index i = 0..L-1 (design matrix columns [1, i]), and compute the t-statistic of the slope, t(b1) = b1 / sqrt(Var(b1)), where Var(b1) is the (1,1) element of (X'X)^-1 * SSE/(L-2). Let L* = argmax over L of |t(b1)| and let T_t = the SIGNED t(b1) at L*. Go long at the close when T_t > +2.0 and T_{t-1} <= +2.0. Go short when T_t < -2.0 and T_{t-1} >= -2.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when |T_t| falls below 1.0, or immediately when sign(T_t) flips against the position, whichever comes first.
inputs: OLS slope and its standard error over multiple lookbacks
ideas.why: A trend has two properties - slope and consistency - and every moving-average rule throws the second one away. The t-statistic of the OLS slope divides the slope by its own standard error, so a steep but erratic move scores lower than a shallow, orderly one. Searching over lookbacks and keeping the maximum |t| makes the horizon adaptive: it finds the window over which THIS particular trend is most statistically coherent instead of imposing a fixed 20 or 50 bars. The scale-free t-statistic also means the same threshold works across tickers and across volatility regimes.
ideas.novelty: Not an MA slope and not a linear-regression channel. The lookback is selected per-bar by maximising a statistical significance measure, and the entry threshold is on a t-statistic (a signal-to-noise ratio), not on price displacement. Lopez de Prado's published version scans FORWARD (it is a labelling technique and is not tradeable); the causal backward-scanning adaptation above is mine and is stated as such.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, trend-scanning labels, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning: Lecture 3/10' (free Cornell lecture notes, SSRN 3257419); reference implementation read from mlfinlab/labeling/trend_scanning.py and mlfinlab/structural_breaks/sadf.py get_betas in the archived source at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB (mlfinlab-master.zip). Forward-to-backward adaptation is my own.

ideas.name: BSADF explosiveness onset
ideas.entry_rule: Let y = ln(close). For the trailing window of 252 bars ending at t, and for every possible start point r1 from 0 up to (252 - r0) where r0 = 40 bars is the minimum sub-window, run the augmented Dickey-Fuller regression on the sub-sample [r1, t]: dy_s = alpha + beta*y_{s-1} + sum_{i=1..p} gamma_i*dy_{s-i} + trend*s + eps, with p = 1 lag and a linear trend term. Record the t-statistic of beta. Set BSADF_t = max over all r1 of that t-statistic (this is the backward sup-ADF). Go long at the close when BSADF_t > c and BSADF_{t-1} <= c, where c is the right-tailed critical value (start at c = 1.5 and calibrate by simulating the null on shuffled returns).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar after entry for which BSADF_t < c. Optional hard stop: exit if close falls more than 2*ATR(14) below the highest close since entry.
ideas.why: A right-tailed unit-root test asks a question no trend indicator asks: is the price process currently EXPLOSIVE, i.e. locally more than a random walk, with the autoregressive root above one? That is the statistical signature of a self-reinforcing move rather than a drift. Taking the supremum over all sub-sample start points is what makes it work in practice - Phillips, Shi and Yu showed the plain ADF has almost no power against episodes that end in a collapse, because the crash contaminates the full-sample estimate. The date-stamping rule (first crossing up, first crossing back down) gives a mechanical entry and exit with no discretion.
ideas.novelty: An econometric hypothesis test used directly as the trade trigger. It is not a breakout: price can make new highs with BSADF flat (a steady drift is not explosive), and BSADF can fire before any new high on an accelerating base. The exit is the test's own termination date, which is a fundamentally different exit criterion from a stop or a target.
ideas.source: Phillips, Shi & Yu date-stamping strategy, equations (23), (27), (28), (29) in Pavlidis, Yusupova, Paya, Peel, Martinez-Garcia, Mack & Grossman, 'Episodes of Exuberance in Housing Markets', Federal Reserve Bank of Dallas Globalization Institute Working Paper 165 (open access, https://www.dallasfed.org/~/media/documents/institute/wpapers/2013/0165.pdf) - text extracted directly. Implementation cross-checked against AFML snippets 17.2-17.4 in mlfinlab/structural_breaks/sadf.py.

ideas.name: Corwin-Schultz spread spike fade
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the Corwin-Schultz high-low spread estimator each bar. beta_t = rolling mean over W = 20 bars of [ln(H_t/L_t)^2 + ln(H_{t-1}/L_{t-1})^2]. gamma_t = ln( max(H_t, H_{t-1}) / min(L_t, L_{t-1}) )^2. den = 3 - 2*sqrt(2). alpha_t = (sqrt(2) - 1)*sqrt(beta_t)/den - sqrt(gamma_t/den), then floor alpha_t at 0. Spread S_t = 2*(exp(alpha_t) - 1)/(1 + exp(alpha_t)). Go long at the close when S_t is above its own 95th percentile over the trailing 252 bars AND the 5-bar return ln(close_t/close_{t-5}) < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when S_t falls back below its 252-bar median, or after 10 bars, whichever comes first. Stop out at 2*ATR(14) below entry.
ideas.why: The estimator separates the part of the high-low range caused by volatility (which scales with the length of the interval) from the part caused by the bid-ask spread (which does not), by comparing a single two-day range against the sum of two one-day ranges. A spike in the estimated spread while the price is falling is the OHLCV signature of liquidity withdrawal - market makers widening, not information arriving. Prices dislocated by a liquidity shortage rather than by news are the ones that revert, so entering into the widening and exiting on normalisation is a bet on being paid for supplying the liquidity that vanished.
ideas.novelty: Uses high and low to estimate a microstructure quantity (the effective spread), not a volatility band. It is a liquidity-provision trigger, unavailable to any indicator that only reads close prices, and it fires on the WIDENING of the estimated spread rather than on any price level or momentum condition.
ideas.source: Corwin & Schultz high-low spread estimator, implemented as AFML snippet 19.1 (p.285) in mlfinlab/microstructural_features/first_generation.py (_get_beta, _get_gamma, _get_alpha, get_corwin_schultz_estimator) - source read from the archived mlfinlab-master.zip at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB. Also documented in the open-access CRAN package 'bidask' (Ardia, Guidotti & Kroencke, JFE 2024).

ideas.name: Range-to-close vol ratio gate
ideas.entry_rule: Using the same beta_t and gamma_t as the Corwin-Schultz estimator (W = 20), compute the Bekker-Parkinson volatility: k2 = sqrt(8/pi), den = 3 - 2*sqrt(2), sigma_BP = (2^-0.5 - 1)*sqrt(beta_t)/(k2*den) + sqrt(gamma_t/(k2^2*den)), floored at 0. Separately compute sigma_CC = the standard deviation of daily log close-to-close returns over the same 20 bars. Form R_t = sigma_BP / sigma_CC. If R_t is BELOW its 25th percentile over the trailing 252 bars (efficient, directional tape), take the trend branch: go long when close_t > max(high) of the prior 20 bars. If R_t is ABOVE its 75th percentile (choppy, range-churning tape), take the mean-reversion branch: go long when close_t < min(low) of the prior 20 bars. If R_t is between the 25th and 75th percentiles, take no new positions.
ideas.exit_rule: Trend branch: exit when close < the 10-bar low. Mean-reversion branch: exit when close crosses back above the 20-bar simple mean of close, or after 10 bars. Either branch: flatten immediately if R_t crosses out of the percentile band that authorised the entry.
ideas.why: Both numerator and denominator estimate the same volatility, but from different information: sigma_BP is driven by the intrabar range and sigma_CC only by close-to-close displacement. When a market travels efficiently in one direction the two agree, so the ratio is low. When it churns - covering large intrabar range while ending where it started - the range-based estimate blows out relative to the close-based one and the ratio is high. That ratio is therefore a direct, dimensionless measurement of path efficiency, which is exactly the variable that decides whether a trend rule or a fade rule is the right tool.
ideas.novelty: A regime classifier built from the DISAGREEMENT between two volatility estimators, not from ADX, a squeeze, or realised-vol level. It switches which strategy runs rather than gating a single strategy on or off, and unlike ADX it is a ratio of two estimates of the same quantity, so it is scale- and volatility-level free.
ideas.source: Bekker-Parkinson volatility from the Corwin-Schultz beta/gamma, AFML snippet 19.2 (p.286), read from mlfinlab/microstructural_features/first_generation.py (get_bekker_parkinson_vol) in the archived mlfinlab-master.zip at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB. Pairing the two estimators as an efficiency ratio and using it to switch strategy branch is my own synthesis.

ideas.name: Kyle lambda liquidity gate
ideas.entry_rule: Define the bar sign b_t = sign(close_t - close_{t-1}), carrying forward the previous non-zero sign when the difference is exactly zero. Compute the bar-based Kyle lambda as lambda_t = the rolling mean over the last 20 bars of [ (close_t - close_{t-1}) / (b_t * volume_t) ]. Separately compute the signed volume accumulation A_t = sum over the last 20 bars of (b_t * volume_t). Go long at the close when lambda_t is below its 20th percentile over the trailing 252 bars AND A_t > 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when lambda_t rises above its 252-bar median, OR when A_t turns negative, whichever comes first. Hard stop at 1.5*ATR(14) below entry.
ideas.why: Kyle's lambda is the price impact per unit of signed volume - how far the price moves for each share the market has to absorb. When lambda is low, the book is deep and a given amount of buying pressure moves price very little, which means a directional move that occurs anyway is being driven by size rather than by thin conditions. Combining low impact with positive signed-volume accumulation isolates the case of real accumulation into a deep book, which is the OHLCV shadow of institutional participation, as opposed to a move that is just a thin tape being pushed around.
ideas.novelty: Conditions on the price-impact COEFFICIENT rather than on price or on volume level. The trade is authorised by a liquidity-depth measurement and confirmed by cumulative signed volume, a combination no volume-confirmed breakout expresses - a volume spike would in fact push lambda the wrong way and be rejected here.
ideas.source: Bar-based Kyle lambda, AFML pp.286-288, implemented as get_bar_based_kyle_lambda in mlfinlab/microstructural_features/second_generation.py - source read from the archived mlfinlab-master.zip at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB.

ideas.name: Amihud illiquidity reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the bar-based Amihud illiquidity ratio ILLIQ_t = the rolling mean over the last 20 bars of [ |ln(close_t/close_{t-1})| / (close_t * volume_t) ]. Go long at the close when ILLIQ_t is above its 90th percentile over the trailing 252 bars AND close_t is more than 1.0*ATR(14) below the 20-bar simple moving average of close.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when ILLIQ_t falls back below its 252-bar median, OR when close crosses back above the 20-bar simple moving average, OR after 15 bars - whichever comes first.
ideas.why: Amihud's ratio measures how much price movement each dollar of trading buys. When it is extreme, the observed decline was produced by very little actual money changing hands, so most of the move is a liquidity premium demanded by whoever had to take the other side rather than a revision of value. Liquidity premia are transient by construction - they are compensation for immediacy, and they are repaid once the forced seller is done. Requiring the price to also be extended below its own mean ensures you are being paid the premium rather than paying it.
ideas.novelty: Volume enters as a DENOMINATOR normalising the return, not as a confirmation threshold. Low volume is the trigger here, the exact inverse of every volume-confirmed setup; and the exit is on the illiquidity measure normalising, not on a price target.
ideas.source: Bar-based Amihud lambda, AFML pp.288-289, implemented as get_bar_based_amihud_lambda in mlfinlab/microstructural_features/second_generation.py - source read from the archived mlfinlab-master.zip at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB.

ideas.name: BVC-VPIN toxicity flush
ideas.entry_rule: Classify each bar's volume by bulk volume classification: let sigma_dp = the standard deviation of (close_t - close_{t-1}) over the trailing 50 bars, then BuyVol_t = volume_t * Phi( (close_t - close_{t-1}) / sigma_dp ) where Phi is the standard normal CDF, and SellVol_t = volume_t - BuyVol_t. Compute VPIN_t = [ sum over the last 50 bars of |BuyVol - SellVol| ] / [ sum over the last 50 bars of volume ]. Track the 90th and 70th percentiles of VPIN over the trailing 1000 bars. Go long at the close of the first bar on which VPIN_t crosses DOWN through the 70th percentile, provided VPIN reached above the 90th percentile at some point within the previous 30 bars.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after 10 bars, OR immediately if VPIN_t crosses back above its 90th percentile, whichever comes first. Stop out at 1.5*ATR(14) below entry.
ideas.why: VPIN measures order-flow imbalance as a fraction of total volume, and elevated readings mark periods when one side is systematically taking liquidity - the footprint of informed or forced flow, which is when uninformed liquidity providers lose money. The tradeable moment is therefore not the spike but its resolution: once imbalance collapses back toward balance, the informed participant has finished, the liquidity premium that was demanded during the imbalance is still embedded in price, and the risk of trading against someone who knows more has passed. Bulk volume classification lets you estimate the buy/sell split from bar returns alone, so no tick data is needed.
ideas.novelty: Order-flow imbalance reconstructed from OHLCV via a normal-CDF probability weighting rather than a tick rule, and traded on the DECAY of the imbalance rather than its onset. Nothing in a standard indicator set estimates the buy/sell volume split at all.
ideas.source: VPIN, AFML pp.292-293, implemented as get_vpin in mlfinlab/microstructural_features/third_generation.py (whose docstring names bulk volume classification as one of the accepted buy-volume methods) - source read from the archived mlfinlab-master.zip at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB. Original: Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara. The normal-CDF BVC weighting is the standard form and is stated explicitly above so it is implementable as written.

ideas.name: Roll bounce fade regime
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the Roll effective-spread measure Roll_t = 2*sqrt( max(0, -Cov(dp_t, dp_{t-1})) ) where dp_t = close_t - close_{t-1} and the covariance is taken over the trailing 20 bars. (Take max with 0: the Roll model is only defined when the serial covariance is negative; bars where it is positive are excluded from trading.) Form rho_t = Roll_t / ATR(14)_t. Trade only when rho_t is above its 60th percentile over the trailing 252 bars. In that state, go long at the close of any bar where close_t <= close_{t-1} - 1.0*Roll_t.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first subsequent bar whose close >= the close of the bar immediately BEFORE entry (i.e. the bounce has retraced the down-tick), or after 3 bars, whichever comes first.
ideas.why: Roll's measure derives the effective spread from the negative first-order serial covariance of price changes, because transactions alternating between the bid and the ask induce exactly that negative autocorrelation. When the Roll measure is large relative to true volatility, most bar-to-bar movement is bid-ask bounce rather than information, so a one-bar down-tick is mechanically likely to be followed by an up-tick. The regime filter is essential: in an informationally driven tape the serial covariance turns positive, the measure is undefined, and the fade would be trading into a real trend.
ideas.novelty: The fade is triggered and sized by an estimate of the SPREAD itself, and the regime gate is the sign and magnitude of return autocovariance rather than a trend indicator. This is a different mechanism from any oscillator extreme: it identifies when the price series is dominated by microstructure noise, which is a testable statistical property, not a level.
ideas.source: Roll measure, AFML p.282, implemented as get_roll_measure in mlfinlab/microstructural_features/first_generation.py - source read from the archived mlfinlab-master.zip at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB. Note that implementation uses abs(cov); the max(0, -cov) form above respects Roll's derivation and is what should be tested.

ideas.name: Carver continuous breakout forecast
ideas.entry_rule: For a lookback N, compute roll_max = max(close) over the last N bars, roll_min = min(close) over the last N bars, roll_mean = (roll_max + roll_min)/2. Raw signal raw_t = 40.0 * (close_t - roll_mean) / (roll_max - roll_min). Forecast_t = EWMA(raw, span = max(round(N/4), 1)), then clip to [-20, +20]. Target position (in shares) = (Forecast_t / 10) * (annual_cash_risk_target / (annualised price volatility * price)). There is no discrete entry: the position is continuously proportional to Forecast_t and is long whenever Forecast_t > 0, short whenever < 0. Run N in {10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 320} and average the forecasts, or trade a single N.
ideas.exit_rule: No discrete exit. The position shrinks toward zero as Forecast_t decays toward zero and flips sign when it crosses zero. To control turnover, only send an order when the gap between the current and target position exceeds 10% of the average absolute target position (buffering); inside that band, do nothing.
inputs: annualised return volatility for position scaling
ideas.why: A Donchian breakout throws away everything except whether an extreme was touched, so it enters at full size on a marginal new high and holds full size through deterioration. Normalising position within the range instead makes conviction continuous: you are barely long near the middle of the range and fully long near the top, so partial reversals reduce risk automatically without a stop being hit. Smoothing by a quarter of the lookback removes the whipsaw around the boundary, and the buffering band means the continuous position does not translate into continuous trading costs.
ideas.novelty: The exit structure is the idea: position size is a continuous, bounded function of location within the range, so scaling out is automatic and there is no stop-loss at all. That is structurally different from binary Donchian entry plus a separate exit rule, and the buffering band is an explicit cost-control mechanism absent from every threshold rule.
ideas.source: Rob Carver, 'A simple breakout trading rule', qoppac.blogspot.com, 26 May 2016, https://qoppac.blogspot.com/2016/05/a-simple-breakout-trading-rule.html - formula forecast = 40*(price - roll_mean)/(roll_max - roll_min), roll_mean = (roll_max+roll_min)/2, smooth = max(int(lookback/4.0),1), lookbacks 10/20/40/80/160/320, natural forecast range -20 to +20 (fetched and read directly). Buffering is standard pysystemtrade practice.

ideas.name: Saturated tanh trend position
ideas.entry_rule: For a lookback n bars, compute the reference level P_bar = the exponential moving average of close with span n evaluated THROUGH bar t-1 (the current close is excluded from its own reference). Compute sigma_n = the exponential moving average, span n, of |close_t - close_{t-1}|, also through t-1. The normalised trend signal is s_t = (close_{t-1} - P_bar_{t-1}) / sigma_n(t-1). The target position in shares is pos_t = (K / sigma_n(t-1)) * tanh( s_t / s_star ) with s_star = 0.89 and K a constant chosen so the strategy's realised volatility hits the risk target. Long whenever s_t > 0, short whenever s_t < 0; there is no threshold crossing.
ideas.exit_rule: No discrete exit. Rebalance to pos_t every 20 bars (or monthly). The position saturates in magnitude at K/sigma_n regardless of how extreme s_t becomes, and crosses through zero and flips sign as s_t does. Optional: skip the rebalance if the new target is within 10% of the current position.
ideas.why: Lemperiere and co-authors regressed next-period returns on the normalised trend signal across two centuries of futures data and found the relationship is not linear: the payoff rises with signal strength and then flattens, with the empirical saturation point around s_star = 0.89. The economic reading is that a strong trend is simultaneously the best evidence of continuation and the best evidence of over-extension, and the two effects cancel beyond a point. So a position that scales linearly with signal strength systematically over-bets the extremes, which is where trend strategies take their worst losses. tanh imposes the empirically measured payoff shape directly on position size.
ideas.novelty: Position size is a concave saturating function of signal strength calibrated to a measured payoff curve, so bigger signal does NOT mean bigger bet past s_star. This is the opposite of every strength-scaled rule, and it is a different exit structure: you reduce risk into extremes rather than adding to them.
ideas.source:
Lemperiere, Deremble, Seager, Potters & Bouchaud, 'Two centuries of trend following', arXiv:1404.3274 - signal s_n(t) = [p(t-1) -

_{n,t-1}] / sigma_n(t-1) with

an EMA of past prices excluding p(t), sigma_n an EMA of absolute price changes, positions scaling as 1/sigma_n, and the saturation fit Delta(t) = a + b*s_star*tanh(s_n(t)/s_star) with s_star approximately 0.89 (fetched via ar5iv and read directly).

ideas.name: Ehlers Reversion Index
ideas.entry_rule: With Length = 10: DeltaSum = sum over i = 0..9 of (close[i] - close[i+1]); AbsDeltaSum = sum over i = 0..9 of |close[i] - close[i+1]|; Ratio = DeltaSum / AbsDeltaSum (set to 0 if AbsDeltaSum = 0), which lies in [-1, +1]. Define SuperSmoother(x, P) as: Q = exp(-1.414*pi/P), c1 = 2*Q*cos(1.414*pi*180/(180*P)) [i.e. cosine of 1.414*180/P degrees], c2 = Q*Q, a0 = (1 - c1 + c2)/2, SS_t = a0*(x_t + x_{t-1}) + c1*SS_{t-1} - c2*SS_{t-2}. Set Smooth = SuperSmoother(Ratio, 8) and Trigger = SuperSmoother(Ratio, 4). GO LONG at the close when Trigger crosses above Smooth while Smooth < -0.30. GO SHORT (or exit) when Trigger crosses below Smooth while Smooth > +0.30.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long when Trigger crosses below Smooth while Smooth > +0.30; exit the short on the mirror condition. Time stop after 2*Length bars if no crossing occurs.
inputs: two SuperSmoother (2-pole Butterworth) filters of lengths 4 and 8
params: Length (10, ideally half the dominant cycle)
ideas.why: The ratio is a signed efficiency measure: the numerator differentiates and the summation integrates, so the two operations cancel and the index tracks net displacement as a fraction of total path travelled, bounded in [-1,1] and free of price scale. Ehlers' key observation is that the raw ratio over a short window is too noisy to detect turns by rate of change, but two SuperSmoother filters of different lengths have lags proportional to their lengths, so their crossings land almost exactly on the peaks and valleys of the underlying price - the crossing is a lag-difference trick, not a smoothing threshold.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is the crossing of two filters applied to the SAME bounded efficiency series, exploiting the difference in their group delay to locate turning points. That is a different mechanism from a two-moving-average price cross, and the underlying series is a signed path-efficiency ratio rather than price.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'Reversion Index' (2025), free technical paper at https://www.mesasoftware.com/papers/Reversion%20Index.pdf - EasyLanguage Code Listings 1 and 2 transcribed above, including the suggested SuperSmoother lengths of 4 and 8 and the '+/- 0.3' signal thresholds (downloaded and text-extracted directly).

ideas.name: Correlation trend indicator
ideas.entry_rule: For a given Length, take the last Length closes indexed backwards as X[i] = close[i] for i = 0..Length-1, and set Y[i] = -i (a straight line with positive slope in forward time). Compute the ordinary Pearson correlation Corr = (Length*Sxy - Sx*Sy) / sqrt( (Length*Sxx - Sx^2) * (Length*Syy - Sy^2) ), which is bounded in [-1, +1]. (Optionally use rank-ordered values of X for the Spearman variant.) GO LONG at the close when Corr(20) crosses above +0.5 while Corr(60) > 0. GO SHORT when Corr(20) crosses below -0.5 while Corr(60) < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long when Corr(20) crosses below 0. Exit the short when Corr(20) crosses above 0. Optionally shorten Length as a position ages to detect trend failure sooner, as Ehlers suggests.
inputs: Pearson (or Spearman) correlation of price against a time index
ideas.why: Correlating price against a rising straight line measures how monotonically price is advancing, which is a different question from how fast it is advancing. A shallow but perfectly ordered advance scores near +1; a violent but erratic one scores near 0. Because the output is a correlation coefficient it is bounded and dimensionless, so a single threshold works across every ticker and every volatility level without normalisation. Ehlers notes the lag is about half the correlation length, so pairing a short Length for timing with a longer one as a context filter gives early entries without acting on noise.
ideas.novelty: Measures trend QUALITY (monotonicity) rather than trend magnitude, via a correlation coefficient with a deterministic time regressor. It is not a moving-average slope: a stock and its 3x levered version produce identical readings, and the Spearman variant is fully rank-based and therefore immune to outlier bars.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'Correlation as a Trend Indicator' (c) 2013-2019, free technical paper at https://www.mesasoftware.com/papers/CORRELATION%20AS%20A%20TREND%20INDICATOR.pdf - Code Listing 1 with Sx, Sy, Sxx, Sxy, Syy accumulators and the negative-slope Y line, plus the stated 10/20/40-60 bar length guidance (downloaded and text-extracted directly).

ideas.name: Kendall NET rank oscillator
ideas.entry_rule: First compute MyRSI over L bars: CU = sum over i = 0..L-1 of max(0, close[i] - close[i+1]); CD = sum over i = 0..L-1 of max(0, close[i+1] - close[i]); MyRSI = (CU - CD)/(CU + CD), bounded in [-1, +1] (set to 0 if CU + CD = 0). Then apply Noise Elimination Technology over M bars: let X[i] = MyRSI[i] for i = 1..M counting backwards. Because the reference series Y is a straight line counted backwards, sgn(Y[i] - Y[j]) = -1 for every i < j, so the Kendall numerator simplifies to num = - sum over j = 2..M, i = 1..j-1 of sgn(X[i] - X[j]). Denominator = 0.5*M*(M-1). NET = num / denominator, bounded in [-1, +1]. GO LONG at the close when NET crosses above -0.5 from below. GO SHORT when NET crosses below +0.5 from above.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long when NET crosses below +0.5 from above (i.e. the mirror trigger), or after 3*M bars. Exit the short on the mirror condition.
ideas.why: Every conventional way of making a short-window oscillator readable is a linear smoother, which adds lag proportional to its length and therefore delays the decision it was meant to clarify. A Kendall rank correlation against a monotone line is nonlinear: it counts concordant versus discordant pairs, so it responds to the ORDER of the recent oscillator values rather than their magnitudes. Noise that does not change the ordering contributes nothing, so the output is decisive without the lag a filter would impose. Because it is a pure rank statistic it is also immune to a single outlier bar dominating the reading.
ideas.novelty: A rank-concordance statistic used as the noise filter, not a moving average. The signal is 'has this oscillator been ordering itself upward', a monotonicity count, which is a categorically different quantity from an oscillator level - and it deliberately achieves smoothing with no group delay.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers, 'NET - Noise Elimination Technology: Clarify Your Indicators Using Kendall Correlation', free technical paper at https://www.mesasoftware.com/papers/Noise%20Elimination%20Technology.pdf - including the stated simplification that sgn(y_i - y_j) is always negative because Y is a straight line, and the MyRSI construction (CU, CD, ratio of difference to sum) from Stocks & Commodities May 2018 (downloaded and text-extracted directly).

ideas.name: EMD cycle-versus-trend mode switch
ideas.entry_rule: With Price = (high + low)/2, Period = 20 and delta = 0.5: beta = cos(2*pi/Period); gamma = 1/cos(4*pi*delta/Period); alpha = gamma - sqrt(gamma^2 - 1); bandpass BP_t = 0.5*(1 - alpha)*(Price_t - Price_{t-2}) + beta*(1 + alpha)*BP_{t-1} - alpha*BP_{t-2}. Mean = simple moving average of BP over 2*Period bars. Track Peak = the most recent BP_{t-1} that satisfied BP_{t-1} > BP_t and BP_{t-1} > BP_{t-2} (held until replaced), and Valley likewise for local minima. AvgPeak = SMA(Peak, 50), AvgValley = SMA(Valley, 50), Fraction = 0.1. CLASSIFY: UPTREND mode if Mean > Fraction*AvgPeak; DOWNTREND mode if Mean < Fraction*AvgValley; CYCLE mode otherwise. THEN: in UPTREND mode, go long at the close when BP crosses above 0. In CYCLE mode, go long when BP crosses above AvgValley (from below) and go short when BP crosses below AvgPeak (from above). Take no long entries in DOWNTREND mode.
ideas.exit_rule: Trend-mode long: exit when BP crosses below 0 or when the mode leaves UPTREND. Cycle-mode long: exit when BP crosses below AvgPeak from above, or when the mode leaves CYCLE, or after Period bars.
ideas.why: The bandpass filter isolates a specific band of cycle periods, discarding both the low-frequency trend and the high-frequency noise, so the residual is a clean swing component. Ehlers' insight is that the MEAN of that band-limited component over an integer number of cycle periods should be zero in a pure cycle, but becomes positive in an uptrend because uptrends produce higher swing highs and higher swing lows. Comparing that mean against a fraction of the recent average swing amplitude therefore gives an objective, amplitude-calibrated boundary between cycle mode and trend mode - and the two modes demand opposite tactics, which is precisely why applying one rule set unconditionally fails.
ideas.novelty: The regime classifier is derived from the filtered cycle component itself - its mean relative to its own swing envelope - rather than from a separate trend-strength indicator. It also changes the rule set, not just the permission to trade, and both branches read the same bandpass series so there is no indicator disagreement.
ideas.source: John F. Ehlers and Ric Way, 'Empirical Mode Decomposition: A novel approach for cycle and trend mode detection', free technical paper at https://www.mesasoftware.com/papers/EmpiricalModeDecomposition.pdf - Figure 9 EasyLanguage listing (beta/gamma/alpha bandpass recursion, Mean = Average(BP, 2*Period), Peak/Valley detection, AvgPeak/AvgValley = Average(...,50), Fraction thresholds) and the concluding paragraph stating the trend/cycle delineation rule (downloaded and text-extracted directly).

ideas.name: Inverse realized variance timing
ideas.entry_rule: There is no directional signal. Compute RV_t = the sum of squared daily log returns over the trailing 21 bars (realised variance). The target exposure is w_t = c / RV_t, where c is a single constant calibrated once so that the realised standard deviation of the scaled equity curve over the calibration sample equals that of the unscaled buy-and-hold. Cap w_t at w_max (default 1.5) and floor it at 0. Rebalance the position to w_t every 21 bars (or at each month end); the position is always long, only its size varies.
ideas.exit_rule: No discrete exit. Exposure shrinks continuously as RV_t rises and grows as it falls. Add a hard flatten: go to zero if w_t falls below 0.1 * the median of w over the trailing 252 bars, and re-enter at the next rebalance once it recovers above that level.
ideas.why: Moreira and Muir's finding is that volatility is highly variable and strongly persistent, while expected return is not forecastable by volatility - so the mean-variance optimal weight, which is proportional to expected return over variance, is dominated by movement in the denominator. Scaling exposure by the inverse of last month's realised variance therefore captures almost all the available timing benefit using a quantity that IS predictable, and it does so with no return forecast whatsoever. Because volatility spikes cluster with drawdowns, the rule mechanically reduces exposure into the periods that produce the worst losses.
ideas.novelty: Contains no price-direction signal at all - it is a pure risk-timing overlay whose only input is realised variance, and its entire alpha claim rests on the persistence of volatility rather than on any pattern in price. That makes it orthogonal to every other idea here, and it can be layered on top of any of them as a sizing rule.
ideas.source: Moreira & Muir, 'Volatility Managed Portfolios', NBER Working Paper 22208, https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w22208/w22208.pdf, Section 2.2 equation (1): f*_{t+1} = (c / sigma_hat^2_t(f)) * f_{t+1}, with the paper stating it uses 'the previous month realized variance as a proxy' and chooses c so the managed portfolio matches the buy-and-hold unconditional standard deviation (downloaded and text-extracted directly).

ideas.name: Fractionally differenced z-score
ideas.entry_rule: Build the fractional-differencing weight vector by the recursion w_0 = 1, w_k = -w_{k-1} * (d - k + 1)/k, truncating at the first k where |w_k| < 1e-5; let that truncation length be W. The transformed series is FD_t = sum over k = 0..W-1 of w_k * ln(close_{t-k}). Select d by scanning d over {0, 0.05, 0.10, ..., 1.00} on an expanding in-sample window and taking the SMALLEST d at which the augmented Dickey-Fuller test on FD rejects the unit root at the 95% level; hold that d fixed thereafter. Standardise z_t = (FD_t - mean(FD over trailing 252 bars)) / std(FD over trailing 252 bars). GO LONG at the close when z_t < -2.0 and z_{t-1} >= -2.0. GO SHORT when z_t > +2.0 and z_{t-1} <= +2.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long when z_t rises above -0.5; exit the short when z_t falls below +0.5. Hard time stop after 20 bars. Stop out at 2*ATR(14) adverse.
ideas.why: Integer differencing (returns) makes a series stationary but erases essentially all memory of price level, while raw log price retains full memory but is non-stationary, so any threshold calibrated on it is meaningless out of sample. Fractional differencing at the minimum d that achieves stationarity resolves the tension: the series is statistically comparable across time - so a z-score of -2 in 2019 means the same thing as one in 2026 - while still encoding how far price has travelled from its longer history. That is exactly the property a fixed mean-reversion threshold needs and that a price-minus-moving-average spread does not have.
ideas.novelty: The traded series is neither price, nor returns, nor price minus a moving average - it is a long-memory weighted sum of log prices with geometrically decaying, alternating-sign weights, and the differencing order is chosen by a stationarity test rather than assumed. A fixed threshold on it is therefore defensible in a way a fixed threshold on a price-band spread is not.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning', ch.5 sections 5.4.2 and 5.5 (pp.78-83), implemented as FractionalDifferentiation.get_weights and frac_diff in mlfinlab/features/fracdiff.py, with the exact recursion weights_ = -weights[-1]*(diff_amt - k + 1)/k and the threshold-based truncation - source read from the archived mlfinlab-master.zip at https://github.com/mnewls/MLFINLAB. Referenced there to Hosking (1981), https://wwwf.imperial.ac.uk/~ejm/M3S8/Problems/hosking81.pdf

ideas.name: Take-Profit Cluster Rejection
ideas.category: anchoring / limit-order clustering at round numbers
ideas.timeframe: intraday minutes (5-minute primary, 1-minute for entry timing)
ideas.entry_rule: Define the round-number grid G by price tier: G=1.00 if close>=100; G=0.50 if 20<=close<100; G=0.10 if close<20. Let R = the grid level (an exact integer multiple of G) nearest the current bar. SHORT at the close of bar t when ALL hold: (1) high_t >= R; (2) close_{t-1} < R; (3) close_t < R; (4) (close_t - low_t) / (high_t - low_t) <= 0.40; (5) no bar in t-20..t-1 had close >= R. LONG mirror: low_t <= R, close_{t-1} > R, close_t > R, (high_t - close_t)/(high_t - low_t) <= 0.40, and no bar in t-20..t-1 had close <= R.
ideas.exit_rule: Target = min(1.0 * ATR(14) from entry, the next grid level R -/+ G in the profit direction). Stop = 0.6 * ATR(14) beyond R (i.e. above R for shorts, below R for longs). Time stop: exit at market on bar t+12 if neither hit. Flatten all positions 10 minutes before the close.
params: grid size G per price tier
ATR multiples for target and stop (1.0 / 0.6)
ideas.why: Osler documents directly from a dealing bank's order book that take-profit orders cluster far more strongly at exact round numbers than stop-loss orders do, and that exchange rates 'reverse course relatively frequently when they reach take-profit clusters'. Take-profit orders are limit orders, so they supply liquidity against the incoming move and generate negative-feedback trading. A price arriving at an untouched round level walks into a wall of resting contra-side limit orders placed by traders who anchored their exit on the salient number. The rejection is mechanical, not informational.
ideas.source: C. L. Osler, 'Stop-Loss Orders and Price Cascades in Currency Markets', FRBNY Staff Report (June 2002), https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr150.pdf - VERIFIED by reading the PDF. Section III provides 'evidence that rates reverse course relatively frequently when they reach take-profit clusters'; p.7 reports that of 9,655 orders, 'Almost 10 percent of all such orders are placed at rates ending in 00' and 'executed take-profit orders have a stronger tendency to cluster at rates ending in 00 than executed stop-loss orders'. Companion: Osler (2003), 'Currency Orders and Exchange Rate Dynamics', Journal of Finance 58(5).
ideas.novelty: The anchor is a fixed exogenous price grid, not any feature of the price history. Unlike the liquidity-sweep and order-block patterns we already run, this fires at levels that have NEVER been tested - condition (5) explicitly requires the level to be untouched over the lookback, which is the opposite of a swing-high sweep. It is not a Bollinger/Keltner fade either: no volatility band is involved and the reversion target is a discrete number, not a moving average.

ideas.name: Stop-Cascade Band Above Round
ideas.entry_rule: Grid G as in the Take-Profit Cluster Rejection idea. Define the stop band above R as the half-open interval (R, R + 0.10*G] and below R as [R - 0.10*G, R). LONG at the close of bar t when: (1) close_t is inside (R, R + 0.10*G]; (2) close_{t-1} <= R; (3) volume_t >= 2.0 * median(volume over bars t-30..t-1). SHORT at the close of bar t when: (1) close_t is inside [R - 0.10*G, R); (2) close_{t-1} >= R; (3) same volume condition.
ideas.exit_rule: Hard target at R + 0.40*G for longs, R - 0.40*G for shorts (40% of the way to the next grid level). Trailing stop at 0.75 * ATR(14) from the running favourable extreme, armed immediately. Time stop: exit at market on bar t+20. Flatten 10 minutes before the close.
params: stop-band width as a fraction of G (0.10)
ideas.why: Osler's order-book data show a sharp, measured asymmetry: executed stop-loss BUY orders bunch just ABOVE round numbers and executed stop-loss SELL orders just BELOW them, whereas take-profits sit ON the number. Stops are market orders on trigger, so they consume liquidity and produce positive-feedback trading; Osler finds the price response to stop clusters is both larger and longer-lasting than the response to take-profit clusters, producing 'price cascades'. Traders anchor a protective stop to the round number and then place it a few ticks clear of it, which is exactly why the mass sits in the band beside the number rather than on it.
ideas.source: C. L. Osler, 'Stop-Loss Orders and Price Cascades in Currency Markets', FRBNY Staff Report, https://www.newyorkfed.org/medialibrary/media/research/staff_reports/sr150.pdf - VERIFIED. p.7 and Table III: '14.3 percent of executed stop-loss buy orders have requested execution rates ending in the range [01,10], while only 6.9 percent of those orders have requested execution rates ending in the range [90,99]'. Abstract: 'The response to stop-loss orders is larger than the response to take-profit orders' and 'lasts longer'.
ideas.novelty: Pairs with, and takes the opposite side to, the take-profit rejection idea - the two partition the space by exactly where price sits relative to the round number, which no indicator in the existing 32 can express. It is not a Donchian or opening-range breakout: the trigger level is fixed by the price grid rather than by an N-bar extreme or a session window, and no new high is required (the trade often fires well inside the day's range).

ideas.name: Closing-Bell Round Number Pin
ideas.timeframe: intraday minutes (5-minute), one decision per day
ideas.entry_rule: At 15:30 America/New_York: let R = the nearest grid level to the last price (grid G by tier as above). Enter TOWARD R when ALL hold: (1) 0.02*G <= |last_price - R| <= 0.15*G; (2) the realised volatility of the last six 5-minute bars, measured as stdev of log returns, is below its own 20-day median for that same 15:00-15:30 window; (3) the ticker's clustering intensity CI >= 1.3, where CI = (fraction of the last 4000 five-minute bar closes whose final two cents digits fall in {00, 25, 50, 75}) / 0.04. Direction: LONG if last_price < R, SHORT if last_price > R.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at market when price touches R, or at 15:58 America/New_York, whichever comes first. Stop if price moves 0.30*G away from R in the adverse direction (the pin has failed).
inputs: 5-minute bar closes for the digit histogram
ideas.why: Two documented behavioural regularities compound into the close. First, prices cluster on round ticks far above what a uniform digit distribution implies - Harris's classic result on stock price clustering and discreteness. Second, Osler shows resting limit orders bunch at exactly those levels. Late in the session, order flow is dominated by closing-oriented and marking activity rather than by information, so the resting limit-order structure dominates and price is drawn to the salient level. The clustering-intensity gate is the point: it measures, per ticker, how strongly that specific name's own trading is anchored to the grid, so the strategy only fires on names that demonstrably exhibit the bias.
ideas.source: Synthesis. Grounded in two verified/established sources: (a) Osler, FRBNY Staff Report (VERIFIED above) for round-number limit-order clustering; (b) Lawrence Harris, 'Stock Price Clustering and Discreteness', Review of Financial Studies 4(3), 1991, 389-415, for the equity price-clustering evidence - I was NOT able to open this paper in this session, so treat the Harris citation as from background knowledge rather than verified here. The end-of-day timing, the CI statistic and the trade construction are my own synthesis.
ideas.novelty: The signal is a digit histogram of past closes - a distributional property of the price grid, not a function of price levels or returns at all. Nothing in the existing 32 reads the cents digits. Distinct from the round-number rejection idea because it trades TOWARD the level rather than away from it, and is gated by a per-ticker measurement of how anchored that name actually is.

ideas.name: 52-Week High Proximity Level
ideas.category: anchoring to a salient reference price
ideas.entry_rule: Daily, computed on the last session of each month. PH = close_t / max(high over sessions t-251..t). LONG when: (1) PH >= 0.92 and PH < 1.00; (2) close_t is NOT a new 252-session high, and no new 252-session high has been made in the last 5 sessions; (3) across the fleet, PH ranks in the top 30%. SHORT when PH <= 0.55 and PH ranks in the bottom 30% of the fleet.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 126 trading sessions, then exit at the close regardless. Early exit for longs if PH falls below 0.75; early exit for shorts if PH rises above 0.70. Rebalance one-sixth of the book each month so six overlapping cohorts run at once (the George-Hwang overlapping-portfolio construction).
params: exclusion window for fresh highs (5 sessions)
ideas.why: George and Hwang show that a stock's price relative to its 52-week high predicts future returns better than its own past return does, and that these forecasts do not reverse in the long run. Their mechanism is pure anchoring: 'traders use the 52-week high as a reference point against which they evaluate the potential impact of news. When good news has pushed a stock's price near or to a new 52-week high, traders are reluctant to bid the price of the stock higher even if the information warrants it. The information eventually prevails and the price moves up.' Grinblatt and Keloharju's Finnish account data corroborate the price-level effect directly: investors are much more likely to sell a stock near a historical high and to buy one near a historical low.
ideas.source: Thomas J. George and Chuan-Yang Hwang, 'The 52-Week High and Momentum Investing', Journal of Finance 59(5), October 2004, 2145-2176 - VERIFIED by reading the PDF at https://www.bauer.uh.edu/tgeorge/papers/gh4-paper.pdf. p.5: 'stocks are ranked based on P_{i,t-1}/high_{i,t-1}, where P_{i,t-1} is the price of stock i at the end of month t-1 and high_{i,t-1} is the highest price of stock i during the 12-month period that ends on the last day of month t-1'. Table I: winner-minus-loser 0.45% per month (t=2.00), 30% cutoffs, 6-month hold, 1963-2001. Anchoring quote from p.2, Grinblatt-Keloharju corroboration in footnote 1.
ideas.novelty: This is deliberately NOT a breakout, which is what separates it from the Donchian channel we already run. Condition (2) explicitly disqualifies the bar that makes the new high and the five sessions after it: the trade is on stocks sitting just under the anchor, unable to get through it. The signal is a price LEVEL ratio, not a price CHANGE - George and Hwang's own headline finding is that 'price levels are more important determinants of momentum effects than are past price changes'. Holding period is months, not bars.

ideas.name: Turnover-Decayed Capital Gains Overhang
ideas.category: disposition effect / prospect theory reference price
ideas.timeframe: daily signal built from weekly bars
ideas.entry_rule: Aggregate OHLCV to weekly bars. Define a turnover proxy for week s: V_s = volume_s / (sum of volume over the trailing 52 weeks). Build the reference price over N=260 weeks: R_t = (1/k) * SUM over n=1..260 of [ V_{t-n} * PRODUCT over tau=1..n-1 of (1 - V_{t-n+tau}) ] * close_{t-n}, where k is the normalising constant equal to the sum of the bracketed weights so they total 1. Overhang g_t = (close_t - R_t) / close_t. LONG when g_t >= +0.10. SHORT when g_t <= -0.10. Evaluate weekly at the Friday close; enter on the next Monday open.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 21 trading sessions, or exit earlier when |g_t| falls below 0.02 (the reference price has caught up to the market price and the demand perturbation is spent). Hard stop at 3 * ATR(20) from entry.
ideas.why: Grinblatt and Han show analytically and empirically that when a fixed fraction of investors exhibit the disposition effect, 'stocks with aggregate unrealized capital gains tend to outperform stocks with aggregate unrealized capital losses'. Holders sitting on gains supply the stock eagerly, capping the price below fundamental value; holders sitting on losses refuse to sell, so bad news is absorbed slowly. Prices are a weighted average of fundamental value and this reference price, and the predictable convergence IS the momentum. Their striking claim is that the gain variable subsumes past returns: 'in most of our regression specifications, there is no momentum effect once the disposition effect is controlled for with the gain regressor'.
ideas.source: Mark Grinblatt and Bing Han, 'The Disposition Effect and Momentum', NBER Working Paper 8734 (published as 'Prospect theory, mental accounting, and momentum', Journal of Financial Economics 78, 2005) - VERIFIED via https://www.nber.org/papers/w8734 (abstract) and the full PDF. Equation (15): g_t = P_t - R_t. Equation (19) gives the recursive reference price R_t = w*nu_{t-1}*F_{t-1} + (1-w*nu_{t-1})*w*nu_{t-2}*F_{t-2} + ... , the turnover-decayed weighted average my formula implements. p.20: 'Our empirical work utilizes weekly returns, turnover (weekly trading volume divided by the number of outstanding shares)'. Foundational: Shefrin and Statman (1985); Odean (1998).
ideas.novelty: The reference price is not a moving average and cannot be produced by any smoothing filter. The weight on each past price is the probability that a share bought in that week is still held - the product of survival terms (1 - V) makes recent heavy-volume weeks wipe out the weight on everything before them, so a single high-turnover week can reset the anchor entirely. Two stocks with identical price paths but different volume paths get completely different signals, which no price-only indicator in the existing 32 can distinguish. Grinblatt and Han use shares outstanding for turnover; we lack that field, so the volume-share proxy is the substitution and it preserves the ordering of the decay.

ideas.name: V-Shaped Selling Pressure Overhang
ideas.entry_rule: Use the same weekly turnover weights w_{t-n} = V_{t-n} * PRODUCT over tau=1..n-1 of (1 - V_{t-n+tau}), normalised to sum to 1 over n=1..260. Define VSP_t = SUM over n of w_{t-n} * |(close_t - close_{t-n}) / close_t| - the turnover-weighted mean ABSOLUTE unrealised gain. SHORT at the next open when: (1) VSP_t ranks in the top 20% of that ticker's own trailing 250-week history of VSP; AND (2) close_t / close_{t-5 sessions} - 1 >= +0.03 (a rally is running into the overhang). LONG at the next open when: (1) VSP_t ranks in the bottom 20% of its own history; AND (2) the same 5-session rally condition holds.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 10 trading sessions, then exit at the close. Stop at 1.5 * ATR(14) adverse from entry. Take profit at 2.5 * ATR(14).
params: history window for the percentile (250 weeks)
ideas.why: The plain disposition effect predicts investors sell winners and hold losers, but the empirical selling schedule is V-shaped: propensity to sell rises as the position moves away from the reference price in EITHER direction, because large losers get capitulated and tax-harvested while large winners get realised. That means the overhang that actually matters for near-term supply is the unsigned distance of holders' cost bases from the current price. A stock where a large mass of turnover-weighted cost basis sits far from today's price - above or below - has a deep reservoir of investors ready to hit any bid on strength. Rallying into that reservoir meets supply and stalls; rallying with no reservoir meets none and runs.
ideas.source: Synthesis extending the verified Grinblatt-Han construction (NBER w8734, verified above) using the V-shaped selling schedule documented in Itzhak Ben-David and David Hirshleifer, 'Are Investors Really Reluctant to Realize Their Losses? Trading Responses to Past Returns and the Disposition Effect', Review of Financial Studies 25(8), 2012, 2485-2532. I was NOT able to open the Ben-David and Hirshleifer paper in this session - that citation is from background knowledge, not verified here. The VSP statistic and the trade construction are my own. Related: An, Ang, Bali and Cakici on V-shaped net selling propensity.
ideas.novelty: Strictly distinct from the signed capital-gains-overhang idea: this takes the absolute value inside the sum, so a stock with half its holders deep in gains and half deep in losses scores HIGH here and near ZERO on the signed measure. The two can and will disagree, which is the point of running both. Neither is expressible as any moving average, oscillator or band.

ideas.name: Earnings-Like Event Drift
ideas.entry_rule: Flag session t as an earnings-like event when ALL hold: (1) |open_t / close_{t-1} - 1| >= 3 * median(|open_s / close_{s-1} - 1|) over sessions t-60..t-1; (2) volume_t >= 3 * median(volume) over sessions t-60..t-1; (3) no session already flagged in t-40..t-1. On a flagged session compute the 3-day market-adjusted announcement return EAR = (close_t / close_{t-2} - 1) - (SPY_close_t / SPY_close_{t-2} - 1). Enter at the OPEN of session t+2: LONG if EAR >= +0.05, SHORT if EAR <= -0.05, no trade otherwise.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 60 trading sessions, then exit at the close. Hard stop at 3 * ATR(20) adverse from entry. Force exit early if a NEW earnings-like event is flagged before the 60 sessions elapse (the next announcement resets the information set).
ideas.why: Ball and Brown, then Bernard and Thomas, established that prices continue drifting in the direction of an earnings surprise for weeks to months after the announcement - investors underreact because they fail to grasp the implications of current earnings for future earnings. Critically for us, the surprise does not have to be measured from an earnings feed. Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara and Venkatachalam show that the announcement RETURN itself (EAR) is a sufficient surprise proxy and on its own generates about 7.55% abnormal return a year. EAR is pure price data. The only thing an earnings feed supplies is the DATE, and an earnings release is the single most reliable joint producer of an outsized overnight gap and a triple-normal volume day in a liquid equity.
ideas.source: Ball and Brown (1968); Bernard and Thomas (1989, 1990) - mechanism and magnitude VERIFIED via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-earnings-announcement_drift (Bernard and Thomas 1990 zero-investment portfolios ~8-9% abnormal per quarter; magnitude has decayed to <=3% by the late 2010s; Garfinkel et al. 2024 report 5.1% over three months). EAR construction VERIFIED via https://quantpedia.com/strategies/post-earnings-announcement-effect/ citing Brandt, Kishore, Santa-Clara and Venkatachalam, 'Earnings Announcements are Full of Surprises': 'a strategy that buys and sells companies sorted on EAR produces an average abnormal return of 7.55% per year'.
ideas.novelty: The entry is conditioned on an INFERRED corporate event, reconstructed from the joint signature of an abnormal overnight gap, abnormal volume, and roughly quarterly spacing - a detector no indicator in the existing 32 contains. The proxy for the missing earnings feed is explicit: the event date comes from the gap-plus-volume-plus-spacing filter, and the surprise magnitude comes from EAR, which needs no fundamental data at all. Note this is a hold-for-a-quarter drift trade, the opposite structure to the ATR expansion breakout we already run.

ideas.name: Quarterly Reaction Sign Ladder
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain the four most recent earnings-like events e1 (latest) through e4, detected exactly as in the Earnings-Like Event Drift idea, each with its EAR. Let m = median spacing in sessions between consecutive flagged events (expected near 63). Define the anticipated next event date as e1_date + m. Compute S = sign(EAR_e1) + sign(EAR_e2) + sign(EAR_e3) - sign(EAR_e4). Enter at the close 2 sessions BEFORE the anticipated event date: LONG if S >= +2, SHORT if S <= -2, no trade otherwise. Require that all four events were detected and that m lies in [50, 80] sessions, else skip.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 2nd session AFTER a new earnings-like event actually fires. If no event fires within 10 sessions of the anticipated date, exit at the close of that 10th session. Hard stop at 2 * ATR(20) adverse.
ideas.why: Bernard and Thomas's naive-expectations result is that investors price earnings as if they followed a seasonal random walk. The consequence is a distinctive autocorrelation signature in surprises: positive at the first three quarterly lags and NEGATIVE at the fourth. Investors are repeatedly surprised in the same direction three quarters running, then the year-ago comparison base flips and the fourth-lag term works against them. Because we can only observe the market's reaction and not the earnings number, the sign of the announcement reaction is our observable, and the same lag structure should show up in it. The trade is to be positioned before the event in the direction that structure implies.
ideas.source: Bernard and Thomas (1989, 1990). The naive-expectations mechanism - investors fail 'to recognize fully the implications of current earnings for future earnings' - and the seasonal random walk model were VERIFIED via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Post-earnings-announcement_drift and the Quantpedia PEAD page (which specifies SUE 'calculated using a seasonal random walk model with drift'). The specific lags-1-to-3-positive, lag-4-negative sign pattern is from Bernard and Thomas (1990), 'Evidence that stock prices do not fully reflect the implications of current earnings for future earnings', Journal of Accounting and Economics 13 - I did NOT open that paper in this session; that lag detail is from background knowledge. The S-score ladder and the pre-positioning construction are my own.
ideas.novelty: Entry timing is driven by a PREDICTED future event date extrapolated from the observed spacing of past inferred events, and the direction comes from a signed ladder across four such events with the fourth term deliberately inverted. Nothing in the existing 32 has any notion of event periodicity, and no oscillator can produce a term that flips sign at a specific lag.

ideas.name: Attention U-Shape Fade
ideas.entry_rule: AV_t = volume_t / mean(volume over sessions t-252..t-1). R_t = close_t / close_{t-1} - 1. sigma_t = stdev of daily returns over sessions t-60..t-1. Enter SHORT at the OPEN of session t+1 when BOTH: (1) AV_t >= 5.0; (2) |R_t| >= 3 * sigma_t. Note the absolute value - the trade is a short whether the extreme day was up OR down.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover at the close of session t+5. Stop at 1.5 * ATR(14) above entry. Cover early at the close of any session on which AV falls back below 1.2 (attention has dissipated and the edge is gone).
ideas.why: Barber and Odean's central finding is that individual investors are net BUYERS of attention-grabbing stocks - stocks with high abnormal trading volume and stocks with extreme one-day returns - because buying requires searching thousands of candidates while selling only requires looking at what you already own. The search asymmetry means attention determines the choice set on the buy side only. Crucially, their imbalance curve is U-SHAPED in the previous day's return: retail investors pile into yesterday's biggest LOSERS as eagerly as yesterday's biggest winners. That transitory, non-informational buying pressure inflates the price for a few days and then unwinds, so the trade is to supply the liquidity retail is demanding, on both tails.
ideas.source: Brad M. Barber and Terrance Odean, 'All That Glitters: The Effect of Attention and News on the Buying Behavior of Individual and Institutional Investors', Review of Financial Studies 21(2), 2008, 785-818 - VERIFIED by reading the PDF from Odean's Berkeley faculty page. Table 1 note: 'Abnormal volume is calculated as the ratio of the current day's volume ... divided by the average volume over the previous 252 trading days.' p.14: buy-sell imbalance is '+29.5%' for the highest-volume vingtile versus '-18.15%' for the lowest decile. p.16-17: for stocks sorted on the previous day's return, imbalance 'is 29.4% for the vingtile of stocks with the worst return performance on the previous day', drops 'to 1.8% in the eighth return decile' and rises back for the best - the U-shape.
ideas.novelty: The sign-free |R_t| condition is the entire idea and it is what makes this NOT a mean-reversion trade. A conventional reversion rule buys after a large down day; this one shorts after a large down day, because the behavioural claim is about buying PRESSURE arriving on both tails, not about price being cheap. It is also the opposite direction to the ATR expansion breakout already in the book, and the abnormal-volume denominator is a 252-session mean rather than the 20-bar averages used by the existing volume filters.

ideas.name: Lottery MAX Fade
ideas.entry_rule: On the last session of each month compute MAX5 = the arithmetic mean of the 5 largest daily returns over the trailing 21 sessions. Cross-sectional version: rank all fleet tickers by MAX5 and SHORT the top 20%, LONG the bottom 20%, equal weight, entering at the next session's open. Single-ticker version for a per-symbol bot: SHORT when MAX5 exceeds the 90th percentile of that ticker's own trailing 500-session history of MAX5; LONG when MAX5 falls below its own 10th percentile.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 21 trading sessions and exit at the close on the last session of the following month, then re-form. Hard stop at 2 * ATR(20) adverse from entry.
ideas.why: Under cumulative prospect theory investors overweight small probabilities, so they overpay for assets with a chance of a large positive payoff - a lottery preference. Bali, Cakici and Whitelaw show the single largest daily return in the past month is a sufficient statistic for how lottery-like a stock has recently looked, and that stocks scoring highest on it go on to underperform by more than 1% a month. The demand is coming from poorly diversified investors who evaluate the stock in isolation rather than as a portfolio addition, which is exactly why an idiosyncratic feature like a one-day jackpot gets priced at all.
ideas.source: Turan G. Bali, Nusret Cakici and Robert F. Whitelaw, 'Maxing out: Stocks as lotteries and the cross-section of expected returns', Journal of Financial Economics 99(2), 2011, 427-446 - VERIFIED by reading the PDF at http://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~rwhitela/papers/max jfe11.pdf. Abstract: 'a negative and significant relation between the maximum daily return over the past one month (MAX) and expected stock returns. Average raw and risk-adjusted return differences between stocks in the lowest and highest MAX deciles exceed 1% per month.' p.2: value-weighted decile spread is -1.03%, four-factor alpha -1.18%, July 1962 to December 2005, and 'the results are robust to sorting stocks not only on the single maximum daily return during the month, but also the average of the two, three, four, or five highest daily returns within the month'. Underpinning theory: Barberis and Huang (2008) on probability weighting; Kumar (2009) on lottery-type stocks.
ideas.novelty: The statistic is an order statistic of the return distribution - the mean of the top N daily returns - not a moment, a range, or a smoothed average. Two stocks with identical ATR and identical monthly return can have wildly different MAX5 depending on whether the move came in one jump or twenty steps. Nothing in the existing 32 reads the shape of the return distribution's right tail.

ideas.name: Information Discreteness Momentum Gate
ideas.entry_rule: On the last session of each month: PRET = close_{t-21} / close_{t-252} - 1 (twelve-month cumulative return, skipping the most recent month). Over that same t-252..t-21 window, let pos = fraction of daily returns that are positive and neg = fraction that are negative. ID = sgn(PRET) * (neg - pos), where sgn(PRET) is +1 if PRET > 0 and -1 if PRET < 0. LONG when PRET > 0 AND ID ranks in the bottom 20% of the fleet's cross-sectional ID distribution. SHORT when PRET < 0 AND ID ranks in the bottom 20%. Enter at the next session's open.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 126 trading sessions, then exit at the close - deliberately no reversal exit, since the paper finds continuation from continuous information 'does not reverse in the long run'. Hard stop at 3 * ATR(20) adverse from entry. Rebalance one-sixth of the book each month so six overlapping cohorts are live.
params: formation window (252 sessions) and skip (21 sessions)
ideas.why: Da, Gurun and Warachka's frog-in-the-pan hypothesis: a series of frequent small changes attracts less investor attention than a few dramatic ones, so information that arrives gradually is absorbed with a longer delay and produces stronger, more persistent continuation. Their ID statistic separates two stocks that finished the year at the same place by how they got there. Low ID means the return was built from a steady grind of same-signed days - continuous information, little attention, big drift ahead. High ID means it came from a handful of dramatic jumps that everybody noticed - discrete information, attention paid, no drift or outright reversal.
ideas.source: Zhi Da, Umit G. Gurun and Mitch Warachka, 'Frog in the Pan: Continuous Information and Momentum', Review of Financial Studies 27(7), 2014, 2171-2218 - VERIFIED by reading the PDF at https://academicweb.nd.edu/~zda/Frog.pdf. p.7, equation (1): 'ID = sgn(PRET) x [%neg - %pos]', where '%pos and %neg' are 'the percentage of days during the formation period with positive and negative returns' and 'PRET is defined as a firm's cumulative return over the past twelve months after skipping the most recent month'. Abstract: 'Momentum decreases monotonically from 5.94% for stocks with continuous information during their formation period to -2.07% for stocks with discrete information but similar cumulative formation-period returns.'
ideas.novelty: The gate is a property of the PATH, not of the outcome. Two tickers with identical 12-month returns and identical volatility get opposite treatment based purely on the count of up-days versus down-days that produced the return - a statistic that discards magnitude entirely. No moving average, oscillator or channel in the existing 32 can distinguish them, because they all summarise where price went rather than how evenly it got there.

ideas.name: Turn-of-Month Flow Window
ideas.category: calendar flow / salience of the month boundary
ideas.entry_rule: From the bar timestamps, enumerate the trading sessions of each calendar month. Let T be the LAST trading session of the month. Enter LONG at the close of session T-1 (the second-to-last trading session of the month). No indicator condition. Optional volatility gate: skip the window when ATR(14)/close on session T-1 exceeds the 90th percentile of its own trailing 250-session history.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 3rd trading session of the new calendar month. Fixed four-session window (T-1, T, plus sessions 1, 2, 3 of the new month, exiting at the close of session 3). Hard stop at 2.5 * ATR(20) adverse from entry.
params: entry offset (T-1, or T-4 for the wider variant)
which instrument to apply it to (index proxy versus single names)
ideas.why: Salaries, pensions and retirement-plan contributions are paid on a monthly cycle and are mechanically routed into broad equity funds at the month boundary. Ogden's liquidity hypothesis makes this concrete: standardised payment dates concentrate cash inflows at the turn of the month, and that cash has to buy something. The behavioural component is that the month boundary is a salient accounting and evaluation date - portfolios are marked, statements are cut, and both institutional window dressing and household contribution decisions cluster on it. The effect is a pure flow phenomenon with no informational content, which is why it survives being widely known.
ideas.source: John J. McConnell and Wei Xu, 'Equity Returns at the Turn of the Month', Financial Analysts Journal 64(2), 2008 - trading rules and magnitude VERIFIED via https://quantpedia.com/strategies/turn-of-the-month-in-equity-indexes/, which specifies 'Buy SPY ETF 1 day (some papers say 4 days) before the end of the month and sell the 3rd trading day of the new month at the close' and reports that over 1926-2005 'virtually all of the excess market return is accrued during the four-day turn-of-the-month period' while investors received minimal compensation for market risk over the other 16 trading days. Mechanism: Ogden (1990) on standardised payment dates; Lakonishok and Smidt (1988) on calendar anomalies.
ideas.novelty: Zero indicator input - the signal is the calendar alone, derived from bar timestamps. It is completely orthogonal to all 32 existing strategies, which means it diversifies the book at the correlation level rather than just adding another price-based signal. It also gives the fleet a mechanical seasonal overlay that can be combined multiplicatively with any other entry as a position-size tilt.

ideas.name: Semi-Monthly Payday Window
ideas.entry_rule: Enter LONG at the close of the last trading session that falls on or before the 15th calendar day of the month. If the 15th is a weekend or holiday, use the most recent prior trading session. No indicator condition.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first trading session that falls on or after the 17th calendar day of the month. Hard stop at 2.5 * ATR(20) adverse from entry. Skip the window entirely if it overlaps the turn-of-month window, to avoid double-counting the same flow.
params: whether to also trade the 1st-2nd window
ideas.why: A large fraction of US employers run semi-monthly payroll, paying on the 15th and at month end. Payroll-deducted retirement contributions are swept into target-date and index funds a day or two later, and those funds buy the broad market with no price sensitivity whatsoever. This is the cleanest possible example of a non-informational, calendar-locked demand shock, and it is behavioural in the sense that the automation of the contribution - a deliberate self-control device that households adopt precisely because they will not save otherwise - is what makes the flow so mechanically predictable.
ideas.source: Aixin Ma and William Robert Pratt, 'Payday Anomaly', SSRN working paper 3257064 - trading rule, mechanism and performance VERIFIED via https://quantpedia.com/strategies/payday-anomaly/, which gives the rule as 'Buy and hold the S&P 500 index on the 16th day of each month only', reports 2.57% annualised with 4.31% volatility and a 0.6 Sharpe over a 1980-2010 backtest, and quotes the authors that 'the 16th day of the month statistically and economically outperforms all other calendar days except the 1st and 2nd'.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the turn-of-month window in both timing and underlying flow - this one targets the mid-month payroll date, which the turn-of-month window does not span. Like turn-of-month it is indicator-free, but it fires at a different point in the month, so the two together tile the payroll cycle rather than duplicating it. Best deployed as a fleet-wide long tilt on a liquid index proxy rather than per single name, since the flow buys the market, not individual stocks.

ideas.name: Salience-Weighted Overpricing
ideas.category: salience theory / attention to extreme relative outcomes
ideas.entry_rule: Over the trailing 21 sessions, for each session k compute the stock's return r_ik and the benchmark return r_mk (SPY). Salience of session k: sigma_k = |r_ik - r_mk| / (|r_ik| + |r_mk| + theta), with theta = 0.10. Rank the 21 sessions by sigma in DESCENDING order and let j(k) be the rank of session k (j=1 for the most salient). Assign weights w_k = delta^{j(k)} / SUM over all 21 sessions of delta^{j}, with delta = 0.70. Compute ST_i = SUM over k of (w_k - 1/21) * r_ik - the difference between the salience-weighted mean return and the plain mean return. Rank the fleet by ST_i on the last session of each month: SHORT the top 20%, LONG the bottom 20%, entering at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 21 trading sessions and exit at the close on the last session of the following month, then re-form. Hard stop at 2.5 * ATR(20) adverse from entry.
ideas.why: Bordalo, Gennaioli and Shleifer's salience theory holds that a decision maker's attention is drawn to the states in which an option's payoff differs most from the alternatives, and that those salient states get overweighted relative to their true probability. Applied to stocks: an investor recalling the last month overweights the days on which this stock behaved most unlike the market. If those salient days were up days, the stock looks better than its average return warrants and gets bid too high, so subsequent returns are low. ST_i measures exactly that - the gap between how the stock looks under salience-distorted weights and how it actually performed.
ideas.source: Pedro Bordalo, Nicola Gennaioli and Andrei Shleifer, 'Salience Theory of Choice Under Risk', Quarterly Journal of Economics 127(3), 2012, 1243-1285, for the salience function and the rank-based delta weighting; Mathijs Cosemans and Rik Frehen, 'Salience theory and stock prices: Empirical evidence', Journal of Financial Economics 140(2), 2021, 460-483, for the equity application. IMPORTANT: I was NOT able to open either paper in this session - SSRN returned 403 and my web search budget was exhausted. Both citations and the functional form of sigma and the delta-weighting are from background knowledge, not verified here. Confirm theta, delta and the exact ST construction against Cosemans and Frehen before implementing.
ideas.novelty: The weighting scheme is determined by a RANK ordering of how unusual each day was relative to the benchmark, not by recency. The most salient day gets the largest weight regardless of whether it happened yesterday or three weeks ago - the exact inverse of every exponential-decay indicator in the existing 32, all of which weight by how recent a bar is. Distinct from the MAX lottery fade too: MAX looks only at the stock's own largest raw returns, whereas salience is defined relative to the market, so a stock that jumped 6% on a day the market jumped 6% scores as completely unsalient here while scoring maximally on MAX.

ideas.name: Automatic Rally Ratio Secondary Test
ideas.entry_rule: Let ATR=ATR(14) and AV=SMA(volume,20).
