LONG: (1) Selling-climax bar SC at index c requires low(SC)=lowest low of bars c-39..c, volume(SC)>=2.5*AV(c), and (high(SC)-low(SC))>=1.5*ATR(c). (2) Automatic Rally: let AR=max(high) over bars c+1..c+15 occurring at index a; require AR-low(SC)>=2.0*ATR(c). (3) Ratio gate: ARratio=(AR-low(SC))/(high(SC)-low(SC)) must be >=1.5. (4) Secondary Test bar T at some index in a+3..a+30 requires low(T)>=low(SC) AND low(T)<=low(SC)+0.75*ATR AND volume(T)<=0.60*volume(SC) AND (high(T)-low(T))<=0.80*ATR. (5) Buy at the close of the first bar after T whose close>high(T) AND whose volume>=1.2*AV. Abort the whole setup if any close<low(SC) at any point after SC. SHORT is the exact mirror: buying-climax bar BC with high(BC)=40-bar highest high, same volume and spread conditions; Automatic Reaction AR=min(low) over c+1..c+15 with low(SC-analogue) drop>=2.0*ATR; ratio (high(BC)-AR)/(high(BC)-low(BC))>=1.5; secondary test with high(T)<=high(BC) AND high(T)>=high(BC)-0.75*ATR, volume<=0.60*volume(BC), spread<=0.80*ATR; sell at the close of the first bar closing<low(T) with volume>=1.2*AV; abort on any close>high(BC).
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at low(SC)-0.25*ATR (mirror: high(BC)+0.25*ATR). First target = AR + (AR - low(SC)), i.e. a 1x measured move projected from the automatic-rally leg; scale out half there. After +1.5R, trail the remainder on the lowest low of the last 3 bars (highest high for shorts). Hard time stop: exit at market if neither target nor stop is hit within 40 bars of entry.
ideas.why: This is Wyckoff Phase A, not Phase C. The economic claim is about supply exhaustion measured by the SNAP-BACK rather than by a liquidity sweep: after panic selling clears the last motivated sellers, the removal of supply lets a comparatively small amount of demand lift price a long way. A large automatic rally relative to the climax bar's own range is therefore direct evidence that the offer stack is thin. The secondary test on materially lower volume then confirms that supply has not returned at the same prices. The ARratio gate is the discriminating variable: a weak automatic rally after a climax means sellers are still present and the low will be broken.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the previously catalogued Spring-Test sequence because no penetration below the range low is required or permitted - the secondary test must hold ABOVE the climax low. Distinct from Stopping Volume Climax Reversal because the trigger is not the bar after the climax but a two-stage AR-then-ST confirmation gated by the ratio of rally magnitude to climax-bar range. Not a moving-average or oscillator construct at all.
ideas.source: Wyckoff accumulation schematic Phase A (PS, SC, AR, ST) as codified in the StockCharts ChartSchool 'The Wyckoff Method' article and reproduced in the TradingView 'Wyckoff Accumulation Phase Map' (AGProLabs) and 'Wyckoff Pattern Indicator' (Dr_AtulGoswami) script descriptions, which enumerate PS/SC/AR/ST/Spring/LPS/SOS labels. The ARratio gate and all numeric thresholds are my quantification (synthesis) - the source literature states the sequence qualitatively only.

ideas.name: Creek Jump and Back-Up
ideas.entry_rule: ATR=ATR(14), AV=SMA(volume,20). (1) Identify swing highs by a 7-bar fractal: bar i is a swing high if high(i)>high(j) for all j in i-3..i-1 and i+1..i+3. Take the three most recent swing highs inside a 60-bar window at indices i1<i2<i3. (2) Fit an ordinary least-squares line through the three points (i_k, high(i_k)); call it the creek C(t)=m*t+b. Require slope m<=0 and require range containment: (60-bar highest high - 60-bar lowest low)<=3.5*ATR. (3) JUMP bar J (the jump across the creek): close(J)>C(J)+0.10*ATR AND (high(J)-low(J))>=1.3*ATR AND volume(J)>=1.6*AV AND (close(J)-low(J))/(high(J)-low(J))>=0.70. (4) BACK-UP bar B at some index in J+2..J+10: low(B)<=C(B)+0.30*ATR AND close(B)>C(B) AND volume(B)<=0.80*AV AND (high(B)-low(B))<=0.80*ATR. (5) LONG entry: buy at the close of the first bar after B whose close>high(B). Abort the setup if any close<C(t)-0.50*ATR before entry. SHORT mirror: build the 'ice' line by OLS through the three most recent swing LOWS (7-bar fractal lows) with slope m>=0; jump bar closes below C(J)-0.10*ATR with the same spread/volume conditions and close-location<=0.30; back-up bar has high>=C(B)-0.30*ATR, close<C(B), low volume and narrow spread; sell at the first close below low(B).
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at low(B)-0.25*ATR (short: high(B)+0.25*ATR). Target = entry + (C(entry_index) - 60-bar lowest low), i.e. the depth of the trading range projected upward from the creek at the moment of entry. Exit the whole position on any close back below C(t)-0.50*ATR. If the target is not reached within 30 bars, exit at market.
ideas.why: Wyckoff drew the creek as a wavy, usually down-sloping line joining the rally highs INSIDE a trading range, not a horizontal ceiling, precisely because supply is being distributed at successively lower prices as the range matures. Overhead supply is therefore a downward-sloping function of time, and the price at which the market must show demand to prove absorption falls as the base builds. Jumping that sloping line with wide spread and heavy volume is effort spent to clear the remaining offers; the back-up to the near side of the creek on shrunken spread and volume is the test that no new supply appeared at the newly cleared prices. The pair (effort to clear, absence of supply on the retest) is the causal claim.
ideas.novelty: The boundary is a fitted sloping line through interior swing highs, so this fires at prices strictly below a Donchian/horizontal-high breakout and often several bars earlier, or not at all when the range top is flat. Requires a two-bar confirmation pair (expansion bar, then contraction bar) rather than a single breakout close, which is what separates it from the already-held Donchian breakout and the Retest Volume Referee.
ideas.source: Wyckoff's creek / jump-across-the-creek / back-up-to-the-edge-of-the-creek analogy, as taught in the StockCharts ChartSchool Wyckoff Method article and in Hank Pruden's codification of Wyckoff (The Three Skills of Top Trading, Wiley 2007). The OLS three-swing-point construction, slope constraint and all thresholds are my quantification (synthesis) - the creek is drawn by hand in every source I could reach.

ideas.name: Nine Buying Tests Composite Score
ideas.entry_rule: ATR=ATR(14), AV=SMA(volume,20). Evaluate nine boolean tests on every bar; each is worth 1 point. T1 (downside objective met): close<=(120-bar highest high)-3.0*ATR. T2 (climax and secondary test present): there exists a bar c in the last 60 with volume(c)>=2.5*AV(c) and low(c)=lowest low of the last 60 bars, and a later bar t in c+3..c+40 with low(t) in [low(c), low(c)+0.75*ATR] and volume(t)<=0.60*AV. T3 (activity bullish on rallies): over the last 40 bars, mean volume of bars with close>close[1] > mean volume of bars with close<close[1]. T4 (downward stride broken): close > the value at the current index of the straight line through the two most recent 7-bar fractal swing highs, extended forward. T5 (higher supports): the two most recent 7-bar fractal swing lows satisfy L_recent > L_prior. T6 (higher tops): the two most recent 7-bar fractal swing highs satisfy H_recent > H_prior. T7 (stronger than the market): using SPY daily bars over the same 20 bars, (close/close[20]-1) for the symbol > the same quantity for SPY, AND the symbol's 20-bar lowest low > its 60-bar lowest low while SPY's 20-bar lowest low equals its 60-bar lowest low. T8 (base forming): (40-bar highest high - 40-bar lowest low)<=2.5*ATR. T9 (reward at least 3x risk): (60-bar highest high - close) >= 3.0*(close - 60-bar lowest low). LONG entry: buy at the close of the first bar on which the total score transitions from <=6 to >=7. SHORT entry uses the nine selling tests, which are the exact mirrors of T1-T9 (upside objective met, buying climax and secondary test, activity bearish on declines, upward stride broken, lower supports, lower tops, weaker than SPY, base forming, reward>=3x risk measured downward); sell at the close of the first bar on which the selling score transitions from <=6 to >=7.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first bar on which the score falls back to <=4. Hard stop at (60-bar lowest low at entry)-0.25*ATR for longs, (60-bar highest high at entry)+0.25*ATR for shorts. Take profit at the T9 objective: the 60-bar highest high measured at entry (60-bar lowest low for shorts). No time stop - the score exit handles staleness.
ideas.why: Wyckoff explicitly refused to trade a single pattern; he required a battery of independent conditions to line up before committing, and the nine tests are the surviving checklist. Each test proxies a different piece of the same story - the decline has run its course, supply was exhausted in a climax, demand shows up on rallies and dries up on declines, structure has turned, and the stock is being supported when the market is not. As a portfolio of weakly-correlated conditions, the SCORE has a better signal-to-noise ratio than any one condition, and the crossing of the score is a genuinely different trigger from the firing of any component.
ideas.novelty: An ensemble threshold-crossing entry rather than a pattern match: nothing fires unless seven distinct structural conditions hold simultaneously, and the entry bar is the bar on which the seventh arrives. Also the only rule here that uses cross-sectional relative strength against a benchmark's bars, which is Wyckoff's own comparative-strength test and is absent from every idea in the existing set. The exit is score-decay, not price - also unique here.
ideas.source: The nine classic buying tests and nine selling tests are Wyckoff's, codified and published by Hank Pruden in 'The Three Skills of Top Trading: Behavioral Systems Building, Pattern Recognition, and Mental State Management' (Wiley, 2007), and taught in the Wyckoff Analytics / Wyckoff Stock Market Institute course material. The mapping of each qualitative test to a specific computable predicate, and the 7-of-9 threshold, are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Shortening of the Thrust
ideas.entry_rule: ATR=ATR(14). Build a ZigZag on closes with a reversal threshold of 1.2*ATR, producing alternating confirmed swing lows and swing highs. For a SHORT setup take the three most recent completed up-legs: leg k runs from swing low L_k to swing high H_k (L_1/H_1 oldest, L_3/H_3 newest). Define thrust Th_k = H_k - L_k and leg volume V_k = sum of volume over the bars of leg k. Require ALL of: (a) Th_3 < Th_2 < Th_1; (b) Th_3 <= 0.60*Th_1; (c) H_3 > H_2 > H_1 (the market is still making higher highs, so this is not yet a breakdown); (d) V_3 >= 0.90*V_1 (equal or greater effort producing shrinking result); (e) L_3 > L_2 (the sequence is a genuine uptrend, not a broadening top). SHORT entry: sell at the close of the first bar whose close < L_3. LONG setup is the exact mirror on three consecutive down-legs: Dn_k = H_k - L_k measuring the decline from H_k to L_k, require Dn_3 < Dn_2 < Dn_1, Dn_3 <= 0.60*Dn_1, L_3 < L_2 < L_1, V_3 >= 0.90*V_1, H_3 < H_2; buy at the close of the first bar whose close > H_3.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at H_3 + 0.25*ATR for shorts (L_3 - 0.25*ATR for longs). Primary target = L_1 for shorts (H_1 for longs), i.e. the origin of the thrust sequence, on the reasoning that a failed three-push advance retraces the whole advance. Scale out half at the midpoint (L_2). Time stop: exit at market 20 bars after entry if neither level is reached. Invalidate and exit immediately on any close above H_3 (below L_3 for longs).
ideas.why: Shortening of the thrust is the price-side expression of Wyckoff's Law of Effort versus Result over a swing rather than a bar. Each successive advance costs the same or more volume - the same effort - yet buys progressively less ground. Mechanically this happens when the marginal buyer is being met by increasing supply just above the market: the composite operator is distributing into the advance, so each push absorbs more shares per point gained. Because the pattern requires higher highs throughout, it fires while the trend still looks healthy to trend followers, which is exactly when the reward-to-risk of the reversal is best.
ideas.novelty: The already-catalogued Wyckoff Wave Volume Ratio measures the VOLUME asymmetry between up-waves and down-waves. This measures the geometric decay of PRICE thrust across three legs while holding volume constant, and it fires while higher highs are still printing - the opposite of every breakdown rule. It is not a divergence indicator: no oscillator is involved, and the comparison is leg-to-leg thrust distance, not indicator-to-price slope.
ideas.source: Shortening of the Thrust is a core Volume Spread Analysis / Wyckoff concept from Tom Williams, 'Master the Markets' (TradeGuider), and is central to David Weis's wave work. Confirmed in the TradingView Weis Wave script literature, whose 'Weis Wave Renko - Effort vs Result' description defines SOT as 'a continuous decrease in delta price' across waves and frames effort-vs-result as cumulative wave volume divided by wave length. The three-leg predicate, the 0.60 decay ratio, the V3/V1 effort floor and the ZigZag construction are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Composite Operator Anchored VWAP Reclaim
ideas.entry_rule: ATR=ATR(14), AV=SMA(volume,20), typical price TP=(high+low+close)/3. (1) Anchor selection: scan bars t-120..t-20 and choose the anchor bar A that maximises volume/AV, subject to volume(A)>=2.5*AV(A) AND low(A) <= (lowest low of the 60 bars ending at A) + 0.25*ATR(A). If no bar qualifies, there is no setup. (2) Compute the anchored VWAP from A forward: AVWAP(t) = sum_{i=A..t} TP(i)*volume(i) / sum_{i=A..t} volume(i). (3) Require at least 20 bars since A, and require that close(i)<AVWAP(i) for at least 10 of the last 20 bars (the accumulated position is under water). (4) Require AVWAP(t) >= AVWAP(t-10) (the average cost line is flat or rising - the operator is still bidding, not liquidating). (5) LONG entry: buy at the close of the first bar satisfying close>AVWAP AND close>high[1] AND volume>=1.3*AV. SHORT mirror: anchor A is chosen with volume(A)>=2.5*AV and high(A) >= (highest high of the 60 bars ending at A) - 0.25*ATR; require close(i)>AVWAP(i) for at least 10 of the last 20 bars, require AVWAP(t)<=AVWAP(t-10), and sell at the close of the first bar with close<AVWAP AND close<low[1] AND volume>=1.3*AV.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop = lowest low of the 5 bars preceding entry, minus 0.25*ATR (mirror for shorts). Compute sigma = the standard deviation of (TP(i)-AVWAP(i)) over i=A..t; take profit at AVWAP + 2*sigma. Hard invalidation: exit the whole position at the close of any bar closing below AVWAP - 0.50*ATR (above AVWAP + 0.50*ATR for shorts). Re-entry is permitted on a subsequent qualifying reclaim of the SAME anchor; the anchor is discarded once price closes 3.0*ATR beyond the take-profit band or once 250 bars have elapsed since A.
inputs: anchored VWAP from an event bar
ideas.why: Wyckoff's composite operator framing says the large accumulator has an average cost, and that price behaves differently above and below it: below, the operator is still buying and defending; the moment price reclaims that average cost the operator's book turns profitable and its incentive flips from accumulating to marking up, so it stops supplying the bid and steps aside or supports the move. The anchored VWAP from the climax bar is the most direct OHLCV estimate of that average cost, because the climax is the bar on which the bulk of the inventory changed hands. The slope filter distinguishes accumulation from a bag-holder distribution: a falling anchored VWAP means the operator is averaging down into a losing position, which is not the setup.
ideas.novelty: Not session VWAP and not a VWAP band. The anchor is chosen by an EVENT (the highest relative-volume climax bar near a 60-bar extreme), the line is monotone-ish and slow-moving rather than resetting daily, and the trigger is the first reclaim of that line after a sustained period beneath it, gated by the line's own slope. The existing VWAP z-score reversion and VWAP trend ideas both use the intraday session anchor and would produce entirely different signal sets.
ideas.source: Wyckoff's composite operator concept (StockCharts ChartSchool, 'The Wyckoff Method'); anchored VWAP as an event-anchored fair-value line popularised by Brian Shannon (Alphatrends, 'Maximum Trading Gains with Anchored VWAP', 2023). The practice of anchoring specifically to 'climax/exhaustion bars' and trading the reclaim/rejection is documented in the TradingView anchored-VWAP script literature I reviewed. The anchor-selection algorithm, underwater filter, slope filter and sigma exit are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Declining Effort Test Count
ideas.entry_rule: ATR=ATR(14), AV=SMA(volume,20). LONG: (1) Level L = lowest low of the last 60 bars. (2) A bar is a touch bar if low<=L+0.35*ATR AND close>L. (3) Group touch bars into distinct TOUCH EVENTS: two touch bars belong to different events only if separated by at least 4 consecutive bars whose lows are all > L+0.75*ATR. For each event k record its lowest low low_k and the volume V_k of the bar producing that lowest low, in chronological order. (4) Require at least 3 touch events inside the 60-bar window. (5) Require monotone effort decay: V_k <= 0.75*V_{k-1} for every k>=2, and V_last <= 0.60*AV. (6) Require non-decreasing lows: low_k >= low_{k-1} - 0.10*ATR for every k>=2. (7) Entry: buy at the close of the first bar after the last touch event whose close > the highest high recorded between the second-to-last and last touch events. SHORT mirror: level L = highest high of the last 60 bars, touch bars have high>=L-0.35*ATR AND close<L, events separated by 4 bars with highs < L-0.75*ATR, V_k decays by the same factors, high_k <= high_{k-1} + 0.10*ATR, and entry is the first close below the lowest low recorded between the last two touch events.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at low_last - 0.30*ATR (high_last + 0.30*ATR for shorts). First target = the 60-bar highest high measured at entry (lowest low for shorts). After +1R, trail on the lowest low of the last 5 bars. Abandon the whole structure - flat and no re-entry on this level - if any close goes below L - 0.50*ATR (above L + 0.50*ATR for shorts), since that is supply overwhelming the level rather than absorbing at it.
inputs: event grouping / clustering of level touches
ideas.why: Wyckoff read repeated tests of a level as the market asking the same question and getting a quieter answer each time. The economics: each test flushes out the remaining motivated sellers at that price. If the third visit to the same level clears far less volume than the first while the lows stop deepening, the supply at that price has genuinely been consumed rather than merely paused. That is the cleanest available OHLCV evidence for absorption, and it is a SEQUENCE property - no single bar can show it.
ideas.novelty: The signal is a monotone-decay statistic across three or more discrete, temporally separated events, not a single-bar or single-retest condition. The existing Retest Volume Referee judges one breakout retest; the Effort-versus-Result Absorption Bar judges one bar. This one refuses to fire until the market has visited the level at least three times with each visit quieter than the last, which is a different and much rarer event class.
ideas.source: Wyckoff's Law of Effort versus Result applied to successive secondary tests, and the 'testing' concept in Tom Williams' VSA (Master the Markets), where each successive test on lower volume is the confirmation. The event-grouping algorithm, the monotone-decay predicate and all thresholds are my quantification (synthesis) - the source material describes this qualitatively as 'each test on less volume'.

ideas.name: Double Distribution Trend Day
ideas.entry_rule: Use 1-minute RTH bars to build a developing volume-at-price profile and 30-minute bars to time decisions. ATRd = ATR(14) on daily bars; row width w = 0.05*ATRd; each 1-minute bar adds volume/(number of rows it spans) to every row between its low and high inclusive. (1) IB = 09:30-10:30 ET; IBW = IBH-IBL. GATE: IBW must be <= the 30th percentile of IBW over the last 40 sessions. (2) At the close of each 30-minute bar from 11:00 ET onward, on the profile built from 09:30 to that moment: let M1 = the highest-volume row; let M2 = the highest-volume row that is at least 8 rows away from M1. Require volume(M2) >= 0.70*volume(M1). Require a genuine spine: EVERY row strictly between M1 and M2 must hold <= 0.35*volume(M1). (3) LONG entry (M2 priced above M1): buy at the close of that 30-minute bar provided the last price > (price(M1)+price(M2))/2 AND the last price is within 0.35*ATRd of the session high so far. (4) SHORT entry (M2 priced below M1): sell at that close provided the last price < the midpoint AND is within 0.35*ATRd of the session low so far. One entry per session. No entry after 14:30 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at the spine midpoint (price(M1)+price(M2))/2 - if price returns into the vacuum between the two distributions the day was not a double distribution after all. Target = price(M2) + (price(M2)-price(M1)) for longs, price(M2) - (price(M1)-price(M2)) for shorts, i.e. a third distribution one full spacing further on. Trail: once price exceeds price(M2) by 0.5*(M2-M1), move the stop to price(M2). Flat at 15:55 ET regardless.
ideas.why: The double-distribution trend day is auction theory's account of a market that balances, discovers that price is wrong, moves quickly through a zone where nobody wants to transact, and then balances again somewhere else. The vacuum between the two modes is real information: it says the market rejected those prices so fast that almost no volume traded there, which means there is no inventory held in that zone to act as support or resistance on the way back. Consequently the second distribution is unusually stable, and the path of least resistance is further extension rather than a return to the first mode. The narrow-IB gate is the classic precondition: a compressed opening auction is where the biggest range days start.
ideas.novelty: The entry condition is a property of the SHAPE of the intraday volume distribution - the emergence of bimodality with a verified low-volume spine - not a price level, a breakout, or a moving average. Nothing in the existing set tests for bimodality; the Excess Tail Fade uses single prints at a session extreme, and the naked-POC and value-area ideas use single modes.
ideas.source: The double-distribution trend day is one of the classic day types in Peter Steidlmayer's Market Profile work (CBOT Market Profile handbooks) and in James Dalton, Eric Jones & Robert Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' (Wiley). The Wikipedia Market Profile article confirms the day-type taxonomy but supplies no numbers; the CBOT/Dalton material describes the pattern qualitatively. The bimodality test, spine ceiling, IB percentile gate and all thresholds are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: P and b Profile Shape Follow Through
ideas.entry_rule: ATRd = ATR(14) daily. For a COMPLETED RTH session build the volume-at-price profile from 1-minute bars, rows of width w=0.05*ATRd (volume/(rows spanned) added to each row between low and high). Let SH, SL be the session high and low, R = SH-SL, POC = the highest-volume row, POCpos = (POC-SL)/R, UpperVol = share of session volume in rows above SL+0.70*R, LowerVol = share in rows below SL+0.30*R. Classify: P-SHAPE if POCpos<=0.35 AND LowerVol>=0.45 AND UpperVol<=0.18 AND close>=SL+0.60*R. b-SHAPE if POCpos>=0.65 AND UpperVol>=0.45 AND LowerVol<=0.18 AND close<=SL+0.40*R. Otherwise no setup. NEXT SESSION, decided at the close of the 10:00-10:30 ET 30-minute bar, using POCp = the prior session's POC price: (a) P-shape CONFIRMED - if the current session's lowest low so far >= POCp - 0.10*ATRd AND the 10:30 close > the prior session's close, buy at that close. (b) P-shape FAILED - if at any time before 10:30 price has traded <= POCp - 0.50*ATRd, sell short at the 10:30 close. (c) b-shape CONFIRMED - if the current session's highest high so far <= POCp + 0.10*ATRd AND the 10:30 close < the prior close, sell short at that close. (d) b-shape FAILED - if price has traded >= POCp + 0.50*ATRd before 10:30, buy at the 10:30 close. Exactly one trade per session; if both a confirm and a fail branch would trigger, take the fail branch.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop 0.60*ATRd from entry. Confirmed branches target the prior session's extreme away from the bulge: SH_prev for a P-shape long, SL_prev for a b-shape short. Failed branches target the opposite prior extreme (SL_prev for the P-shape short, SH_prev for the b-shape long), on the reasoning that a rejected short-covering bulge unwinds through the whole distribution. Move the stop to breakeven once price has travelled 0.50*ATRd in favour. Flat at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: A P-shaped profile - a thin tail below with a bulge at the top - is auction theory's signature of short covering rather than fresh buying: the volume clustered high in the range is shorts buying back, not new longs initiating. A b-shape is the mirror, long liquidation. The forecast is conditional, which is why the failure branch matters: if the bulge holds on the next session's test, the covering has been converted into real initiative buying and the market continues; if price cuts straight back through the bulge, the entire cohort that transacted in the bulge is instantly under water, and their forced exit fuels the move the other way. Both branches trade the same inventory imbalance, in opposite directions, depending on whether it is defended.
ideas.novelty: Classifies the SHAPE of the completed distribution - single-tailed with the mode displaced toward one extreme - and, critically, contains an explicit failure branch that reverses the direction of the trade. No idea in the existing set conditions on profile skew, and none contains a built-in direction flip on invalidation.
ideas.source: P-shaped and b-shaped profiles as short-covering and long-liquidation signatures are standard in James Dalton, Eric Jones & Robert Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets: Power Trading with Market Generated Information' (Wiley) and in Dalton's 'Markets in Profile'. All numeric thresholds, the POCpos/UpperVol/LowerVol formulation and the failure branch are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: TPO Count Control Ratio
ideas.entry_rule: ATRd = ATR(14) daily; row width w = 0.05*ATRd. Build the intraday TPO profile from RTH 30-minute bars: each 30-minute period 'marks' every row between its own low and high inclusive; TPO(row) = the number of periods marking that row. At the close of the 12:00-12:30 ET period (six periods completed), let POC = the row with the highest TPO count, breaking ties in favour of the row nearest the session's midpoint (SL+SH)/2. Let TPOabove = sum of TPO counts over all rows strictly above the POC row, TPObelow = sum over all rows strictly below. Ratio = TPOabove/TPObelow (treat TPObelow=0 as Ratio=infinity). LONG entry: Ratio >= 1.60 AND the 12:30 close > price(POC) AND the 12:00-12:30 bar's close > its open. Buy at the 12:30 close. SHORT entry: Ratio <= 0.625 AND the 12:30 close < price(POC) AND that bar's close < its open. Sell at the 12:30 close. If 0.625 < Ratio < 1.60, or if the price/POC condition disagrees with the ratio, take no trade that session. One trade per session.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at price(POC) - 0.15*ATRd for longs, price(POC) + 0.15*ATRd for shorts - the POC is the fair-value reference and losing it invalidates the control reading. Target = the session extreme in the trade's direction as of entry, plus 0.50*IBW in that direction (IBW = the 09:30-10:30 initial-balance width). Move the stop to price(POC) once price has travelled 0.50*IBW in favour. Flat at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: The TPO count is auction theory's direct measure of which side is doing the work. Time spent above the point of control is time the market has held prices that only buyers were willing to pay; time below is the mirror. Structurally, a market whose distribution has accumulated far more time-at-price above fair value than below has been repeatedly rejected on its attempts to go lower and has repeatedly found acceptance higher - the responsive sellers are not showing up. Measuring this by counting time marks rather than by looking at the price path filters out the fast, unaccepted excursions that dominate a bar-by-bar reading.
ideas.novelty: A distribution-asymmetry statistic computed on the TPO histogram, evaluated once at a fixed decision time. The already-held Rotation Factor is a path statistic - it compares each period's high and low to the previous period's - and can be strongly positive on a day whose TPO count is balanced, and vice versa. Nothing in the existing set counts time-at-price either side of the POC.
ideas.source: TPO count / 'who is in control' is standard Market Profile teaching from Peter Steidlmayer's CBOT Market Profile handbooks and James Dalton et al., 'Mind Over Markets' (Wiley). The Wikipedia Market Profile article confirms the TPO definition ('opportunity created by the market at a certain price at a certain time') and the 70% value area but gives no thresholds. The 1.60/0.625 ratio thresholds, the 12:30 decision time and the exit structure are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Developing POC Ratchet
ideas.entry_rule: ATRd = ATR(14) daily; row width w = 0.05*ATRd. Build the DEVELOPING volume-at-price profile intraday from 1-minute RTH bars (volume/(rows spanned) into each row between low and high). At the close of every 30-minute period p, record the developing POC price, POC_p = the highest-volume row of the profile built from 09:30 to that moment. LONG entry, evaluated from the 11:00-11:30 period onward: require POC_p > POC_{p-1} AND POC_{p-1} > POC_{p-2} AND (POC_p - POC_{p-2}) >= 0.25*ATRd AND min(POC_1..POC_p) >= POC_{p-2} (the developing POC has never printed below the base of the ratchet at any earlier period today) AND the last price > POC_p. Buy at the close of period p. SHORT entry is the exact mirror: POC_p < POC_{p-1} < POC_{p-2}, (POC_{p-2} - POC_p) >= 0.25*ATRd, max(POC_1..POC_p) <= POC_{p-2}, and the last price < POC_p; sell at the close of period p. One entry per session; no entry after 14:00 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at POC_{p-2}, the base of the ratchet. Then TRAIL THE STOP ON THE DEVELOPING POC ITSELF: at the close of each subsequent 30-minute period, if the new developing POC is higher than the current stop (lower, for shorts), move the stop to the new developing POC. Exit at market if a 30-minute period closes beyond the stop. No fixed price target - the position is held while the volume mode keeps migrating and is exited when the mode stops moving or reverses. Flat at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: Value migration within a single session is the auction accepting new prices in real time. When the developing point of control ratchets monotonically higher period after period, the price at which the most business is being done is moving up and never coming back - which is the definition of acceptance, as opposed to a price excursion that gets rejected and leaves the mode where it was. The monotonicity requirement matters economically: a POC that oscillates is a market rotating around fair value, whereas a POC that only moves one way is a market whose fair value is being repriced, and repricing tends to run to completion within the session because inventory has to be rebuilt at every new level.
ideas.novelty: Both the entry and the exit are defined on the intraday migration of the volume mode. The trailing stop is the developing POC itself, which is a genuinely different exit structure from anything in the existing set - it is a volume-derived, non-monotone-in-price trailing reference that can sit still for hours while price runs. The existing Value Migration Acceptance Pullback compares COMPLETED daily value areas; this operates inside one session and never looks at the prior day.
ideas.source: Developing POC / developing value area is standard Market Profile instrumentation (Steidlmayer, CBOT Market Profile; Dalton et al., 'Mind Over Markets'), and Sierra Chart documents 'Volume Point Of Control For Bars' and developing value-area studies as built-in tools. The monotone-ratchet predicate, the migration-distance gate and the POC-trailing exit are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Overnight Inventory Correction
ideas.entry_rule: ATRd = ATR(14) daily. Using extended-hours 5-minute bars, let ONH = highest high and ONL = lowest low over 04:00-09:29 ET, ONR = ONH-ONL; let PC = the prior RTH session close and O = the open of the 09:30-09:35 RTH bar. GATE: skip the session if ONR >= 1.00*ATRd (that is a genuine overnight trend, not lopsided inventory) or if ONR <= 0.10*ATRd (no overnight participation to be imbalanced). NET-LONG overnight inventory: O >= ONL + 0.70*ONR AND O > PC + 0.15*ATRd. NET-SHORT: O <= ONL + 0.30*ONR AND O < PC - 0.15*ATRd. SHORT entry (net-long inventory): between 09:30 and 10:30 ET, sell at the close of the first 5-minute bar whose close < O - 0.10*ATRd AND whose close < the low of the 09:30-09:35 bar. LONG entry (net-short inventory) is the mirror: buy at the close of the first 5-minute bar with close > O + 0.10*ATRd AND close > the high of the 09:30-09:35 bar. One trade per session; if no trigger by 10:30 the setup is cancelled. PROXY WITHOUT PRE-MARKET BARS: replace the inventory test with |O - PC| >= 0.25*ATRd AND the prior session's close located in the top 25% of its own range (close >= prior low + 0.75*prior range) for the net-long case, or the bottom 25% for the net-short case - the same one-sided-positioning inference from RTH data only; everything else is unchanged.
ideas.exit_rule: Target = whichever is nearer to the entry: PC (the prior RTH close) or ONL + 0.50*ONR (the overnight midpoint). Stop at ONH + 0.10*ATRd for shorts, ONL - 0.10*ATRd for longs. Hard time exit: flat at 11:30 ET whether or not the target is reached - the inventory correction is a first-two-hours phenomenon and holding past it converts the trade into an unrelated bet on the day's direction.
ideas.why: Auction theory treats the overnight session as thin and populated by participants who cannot easily hedge or exit. When the regular session opens with price pinned near the top of the overnight range and well above the prior close, the overnight cohort is net long and sitting on unrealised profit in a market that is about to become liquid. The first thing a liquid open provides is the ability to flatten, so a predictable wave of inventory-clearing supply meets the open. The trade is not a bet on direction; it is a bet that one-sided, illiquid-hours positioning gets corrected once the primary auction reopens. The ONR gate excludes the case where the overnight move was a genuine repricing rather than a drift.
ideas.novelty: The reference frame is the OVERNIGHT range and where the open sits inside it, which no existing idea uses - the opening-range and initial-balance rules all begin at 09:30. The premise is position unwind rather than momentum or value, and the trade is deliberately against the overnight drift. An explicit RTH-only proxy is specified so it remains testable if extended-hours bars are unavailable.
ideas.source: Overnight inventory and inventory adjustment at the open are core teaching in James Dalton, Eric Jones & Robert Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' and Dalton's 'Markets in Profile' (Wiley), where the open's location within the overnight range is used to infer whether the overnight cohort is net long or net short. All thresholds, the ONR gate, the trigger construction and the RTH-only proxy are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Late Session Spike Base Rules
ideas.entry_rule: ATRd = ATR(14) daily. SPIKE DETECTION on a completed session, using 5-minute RTH bars: let C15 = the close of the 14:55-15:00 ET bar and C16 = the session's closing price. SpikeMove = C16 - C15; require |SpikeMove| >= 0.45*ATRd. Require non-rotational travel: for an UP-spike every 5-minute bar from 15:00 to the close must have low >= C15 - 0.05*ATRd; for a DOWN-spike every such bar must have high <= C15 + 0.05*ATRd. Define the spike base SB = C15. NEXT SESSION (5- and 15-minute bars): (a) UP-SPIKE ACCEPTED - if the session's lowest low from 09:30 through 10:00 is >= SB AND the 09:45-10:00 15-minute bar closes > SB + 0.10*ATRd, buy at that close. (b) UP-SPIKE REJECTED - if any 15-minute bar between 09:30 and 11:00 closes < SB - 0.10*ATRd, sell short at that close. (c) DOWN-SPIKE ACCEPTED - if the session's highest high from 09:30 through 10:00 is <= SB AND the 09:45-10:00 bar closes < SB - 0.10*ATRd, sell short at that close. (d) DOWN-SPIKE REJECTED - if any 15-minute bar between 09:30 and 11:00 closes > SB + 0.10*ATRd, buy at that close. Exactly one trade per session; if an accepted and a rejected condition would both fire on the same bar, take neither.
ideas.exit_rule: ACCEPTED branch: stop at SB - 0.20*ATRd (longs) or SB + 0.20*ATRd (shorts); target = the prior session's closing extreme (the spike's far end) plus 0.50*|SpikeMove| in the trade direction. REJECTED branch: stop 0.20*ATRd beyond the session extreme printed so far on the losing side; target = SB - |SpikeMove| for the up-spike-rejected short and SB + |SpikeMove| for the down-spike-rejected long, i.e. a full unwind of the spike, on the reasoning that the entire spike's volume transacted in a thin, one-sided auction and has no support beneath it. Both branches flat at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: A sharp, non-rotational move in the last hour prints a spike on the profile: a price zone traversed with almost no two-sided auctioning and, crucially, with no time for the market to build value there before the bell. The spike base is therefore the last price the market genuinely agreed on, and the next session's open is a referendum on it. Opening above the base and holding means the spike is accepted as new value and the auction continues; cutting back through it means the spike was an end-of-day liquidity artefact and every participant who transacted in it is trapped, which produces a fast unwind because there is no volume shelf inside the spike to slow the return.
ideas.novelty: Uses a reference set no other idea here touches: a late-day, non-rotational leg and the price at which it began. The rule is explicitly two-branched with opposite directions from the same detected structure, and the rejected branch's target is a full retracement of the spike rather than a level or an ATR multiple.
ideas.source: The spike and the associated 'spike rules' for the following session are a named construct in James Dalton, Eric Jones & Robert Dalton, 'Mind Over Markets' and Dalton's 'Markets in Profile' (Wiley), where opening above or below the spike base determines whether the spike is accepted. The magnitude threshold, the non-rotation test, the decision times and the exit targets are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Low Volume Node Acceleration
ideas.entry_rule: ATRd = ATR(14) daily; row width w = 0.05*ATRd. Build a COMPOSITE volume-at-price profile over the last 20 completed RTH sessions from 1-minute bars (volume/(rows spanned) into each row between low and high), then smooth the row-volume vector with a centred 3-row moving average. Let P80 = the 80th percentile of the smoothed row volumes over occupied rows. A row r is a LOW VOLUME NODE if: vol(r) is a local minimum over r-2..r+2; there exists a row within 15 rows ABOVE r with vol >= P80 (call the largest such peak_up) and a row within 15 rows BELOW r with vol >= P80 (peak_down); and vol(r) <= 0.35*min(peak_up, peak_down). Discard any LVN that has another LVN within 8 rows. Let ATR15 = ATR(14) on 15-minute bars and AV15 = SMA(volume,20) on 15-minute bars. LONG entry: a 15-minute RTH bar whose low < price(LVN) AND whose close > price(LVN) + 0.15*ATRd AND whose (high-low) >= 1.30*ATR15 AND whose volume >= 1.50*AV15. Buy at that close. SHORT entry is the mirror: a 15-minute bar whose high > price(LVN), close < price(LVN) - 0.15*ATRd, range >= 1.30*ATR15 and volume >= 1.50*AV15; sell at that close. Recompute the composite profile once per day before the open; do not update it intraday.
ideas.exit_rule: Target = price(HVN_next), the nearest row beyond the LVN in the trade's direction whose smoothed volume >= P80 - the trade is explicitly a traverse from a thin area to the next thick area. Stop on the far side of the LVN: price(LVN) - 0.20*ATRd for longs, price(LVN) + 0.20*ATRd for shorts, because re-entering the vacuum means the acceleration failed. Time stop: exit at market 12 bars (three hours) after entry if neither level is hit. Do not re-enter on the same LVN for the rest of the session after a stop-out.
ideas.why: A low volume node in a multi-session composite is a price band that the market has repeatedly refused to do business in. Because almost no inventory was accumulated there, there is nobody with a position to defend and nobody waiting to get out at breakeven - the usual sources of friction are absent. The auction-theory prediction is therefore asymmetric: price either rejects the node immediately or travels through it quickly to the next high-volume node, where the accumulated inventory does provide friction. Requiring range expansion and above-average volume on the traversing bar separates genuine acceleration from a drift that will stall inside the vacuum.
ideas.novelty: Trades from one structural feature of a multi-session volume distribution to the next, with the target defined by the profile rather than by an ATR multiple or a swing level. Existing ideas use the POC (a single mode), the value area, and naked POCs; none identifies thin zones, and the composite 20-session construction is a different object from any per-session profile in the set.
ideas.source: High volume node / low volume node structure and the 'price moves fast through thin areas, slowly through thick areas' principle are standard volume-profile practitioner material - Dalton et al., 'Mind Over Markets', and Trader Dale's volume-profile writing; confirmed as implemented instrumentation in the TradingView 'MarketMaulers Volume Profile' script description (VPOC, 70% value area, HVN and LVN identification) and in Sierra Chart's Volume by Price studies. The composite construction, the LVN depth and isolation tests, and the acceleration filter are my quantification (synthesis).

ideas.name: Effective-Tick Clustering Tightening
ideas.category: microstructure / spread proxy from price clustering
ideas.timeframe: daily bars, or 5-minute for intraday variant
ideas.entry_rule: Use the tick grid s = (0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 1.00), indexed j = 1..5 finest to coarsest. For each of the trailing N = 200 closes assign it to the COARSEST s_j for which C/s_j is an integer within 1e-9 (so 50.00 -> 1.00, 50.25 -> 0.25, 50.10 -> 0.10, 50.05 -> 0.05, 50.03 -> 0.01). Let F_j = count_j / N. Unconstrained cluster probabilities: U_1 = 2*F_1; U_j = 2*F_j - F_{j-1} for j = 2..4; U_5 = F_5 - F_4. Constrain sequentially: gamma_j = min(max(U_j, 0), 1 - sum_{k<j} gamma_k), then divide all gamma by their sum. Fine-grid weight W_t = gamma_1 + gamma_2 (the 1c and 5c mass). ENTRY: at the next bar's open when W_t - W_{t-20} >= +0.15 (the price grid has visibly tightened over 20 bars, i.e. the effective tick has collapsed and the tape has become continuously quotable) AND |sum of ln(C/C_prev) over the last 10 bars| >= 1.0 * ATR(14)/C_t. Take the side of that 10-bar sum. No trade when the fine-grid weight has not moved by 0.15.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 20th bar after entry, or earlier if W falls back below its value at entry minus 0.10 (the grid re-coarsens, liquidity has withdrawn), or on a stop at 1.5 * ATR(14) against entry.
ideas.why: Holden's estimator infers the effective spread from where prices cluster: when the spread is wide, prices pile up on coarse increments; when it narrows, mass migrates to the penny grid. A rapid migration to the fine grid is a liquidity event - market makers have tightened, more participants are quoting inside, and the stock has moved from a quote-driven to a flow-driven regime. Directional information that could not be expressed while the spread was wide gets expressed once it is cheap to trade, so a displacement occurring simultaneously with a grid tightening is more likely to be real than the same displacement in a wide-spread regime.
ideas.source: Craig W. Holden, 'New low-frequency spread measures', Journal of Financial Markets 12(4), 778-813, 2009 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finmar/v12y2009i4p778-813.html) - the paper builds spread proxies from daily data using price clustering, serial covariance and no-trade days. The clustering-probability construction is Holden's; the tightening-as-a-trigger entry rule is my synthesis.
ideas.novelty: Nothing in the existing set reads the price grid itself. Roll, Corwin-Schultz and Abdi-Ranaldo all infer spread from return or range covariance structure; this infers it from the discreteness of the closing prints, which is an orthogonal source of information and survives on days when the return-based estimators go degenerate.

ideas.name: FHT No-Trade Band Collapse
ideas.entry_rule: On 5-minute bars, over a rolling window of the last 100 bars compute z = the fraction of bars with C_t exactly equal to C_{t-1} (a zero return, meaning no trade crossed the implicit no-trade band) and sigma = the sample standard deviation of the NON-ZERO log returns in that window. The Fong-Holden-Trzcinka spread estimate is S_t = 2 * sigma * PhiInv((1 + z)/2), where PhiInv is the standard normal inverse CDF; set S_t = 0 when z <= 0. ENTRY at the next bar's open when (a) S_t is at or below the 10th percentile of S over the trailing 500 bars, (b) S_{t-20} was at or above the 60th percentile of that same trailing distribution (the band has genuinely collapsed rather than being permanently tight), and (c) |sum of log returns over the last 5 bars| >= 1.0 * ATR(14)/C_t. Take the side of that 5-bar sum.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 12th bar after entry, or earlier if S_t climbs back above its 50th percentile (the band reopens), or on a stop of 1.0 * ATR(14).
inputs: 500-bar rolling percentile of the spread estimate
ideas.why: Lesmond, Ogden and Trzcinka model the observed return as a censored version of the true return: an informed trader only trades when the true signal exceeds the round-trip cost, so a run of zero returns measures the width of the no-trade band directly. FHT gives that band a closed form under a normal latent return. When the band collapses, small pieces of information that were previously suppressed all become tradable at once - the signal-to-price channel reopens - so a displacement made under a newly narrow band carries information that would otherwise have stayed latent. The trigger is the collapse itself, not the level.
ideas.source: David A. Lesmond, Joseph P. Ogden, Charles A. Trzcinka, 'A New Estimate of Transaction Costs', Review of Financial Studies 12(5), 1113-1141, 1999 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v12y1999i5p1113-41.html) for the zero-return censoring model; Kingsley Y. L. Fong, Craig W. Holden, Charles A. Trzcinka, 'What Are the Best Liquidity Proxies for Global Research?', Review of Finance 21(4), 1355-1401, 2017 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/revfin/v21y2017i4p1355-1401..html) for the closed-form FHT estimator. Entry/exit construction is mine.
ideas.novelty: Uses the count of zero returns - information the existing 32 and the prior microstructure pass all discard. Roll/CS/AR all need non-degenerate price movement to estimate anything; this estimator is driven precisely by the bars where nothing happened, and the signal is a state change in that count.

ideas.name: Lee-Mykland Isolated Jump Fade
ideas.entry_rule: On 5-minute bars let r_i = ln(C_i / C_{i-1}). Local bipower volatility: sigmahat_i^2 = (1/(K-2)) * sum_{j=i-K+2}^{i-1} |r_j| * |r_{j-1}| with K = 156 (two trading days of 5-min bars). Test statistic L_i = r_i / sigmahat_i. With n = 390 (the count of returns in one trailing week), c = sqrt(2/pi) = 0.7979, C_n = sqrt(2*ln n)/c - (ln(pi) + ln(ln n)) / (2*c*sqrt(2*ln n)), and S_n = 1 / (c * sqrt(2*ln n)), form Xi_i = (|L_i| - C_n) / S_n. A jump is flagged at the 1% level when Xi_i > 4.6001 (= -ln(-ln(0.99)), the Gumbel critical value). ENTRY at the open of bar i+1, AGAINST sign(r_i), when (a) Xi_i > 4.6001, (b) max(|L_{i-1}|, |L_{i-2}|, |L_{i-3}|) < 1.0 - the jump is isolated, arriving into a quiet tape rather than extending an ongoing move - and (c) bar i starts at or after 10:00 ET and ends at or before 15:30 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of bar i+6, or earlier when price has retraced 100% of bar i's range (target), or on a stop placed 1.0 * |r_i| * C_i beyond bar i's extreme in the jump direction.
ideas.why: Lee and Mykland standardise each return by a LOCAL bipower volatility estimated from neighbouring returns only, then use the extreme-value (Gumbel) distribution of the maximum of many standardised normals to set the threshold. That controls the false-positive rate bar by bar, which a daily jump test cannot do. The economics of fading rather than following: a jump into a quiet tape with no prior build-up is the signature of a single large marketable order sweeping a thin book - a liquidity event, not an information event - and the compensation to the liquidity provider who absorbs it is the subsequent reversion. Requiring the three preceding bars to be quiet is what separates this case from a news jump, which is preceded by rising standardised returns.
ideas.source: Suzanne S. Lee and Per A. Mykland, 'Jumps in Financial Markets: A New Nonparametric Test and Jump Dynamics', Review of Financial Studies 21(6), 2535-2563, 2008 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v21y2008i6p2535-2563.html).
ideas.novelty: The existing bipower idea is the Barndorff-Nielsen/Shephard DAILY test (one z per session, trades the next open in the jump direction). This is a per-bar test with a local volatility window and an extreme-value threshold, it isolates the jump by requiring a quiet lead-in, and it trades the opposite side on a six-bar horizon. Different statistic, different frequency, different side, different exit.

ideas.name: VNET Depth Surprise
ideas.category: microstructure / market depth from price durations
ideas.entry_rule: Define a price event on 5-minute bars. Set P_ref to the first close of the session. Scan forward; the event completes at the first bar t where |ln(C_t / P_ref)| >= h with h = 0.5 * ATR(14, daily) / C_t. Over the bars of that span accumulate the tick-rule signed volume SV = sum over k in the span of sign(C_k - C_{k-1}) * V_k (carry the previous sign forward when C_k = C_{k-1}). VNET = |SV| - the net directional volume required to move price by h. Record also D = the number of bars in the span and Vbar = the mean bar volume over the span. Over the last 200 completed events fit OLS: ln(VNET) = a0 + a1*ln(D) + a2*ln(Vbar) + a3*(hour-of-day bucket dummies, 6 buckets from 09:30 to 16:00 ET). Let e = the current event's residual and z_e = e / stdev(residuals, 200). ENTRY at the open of the bar after the event completes: if z_e <= -1.5 (far LESS net volume than usual was needed to move price by h - the book was hollow), enter AGAINST the event's direction; if z_e >= +1.5 (far MORE volume was absorbed for the same h - the book was deep and demand persisted anyway), enter WITH the event's direction. No trade when |z_e| < 1.5. Reset P_ref to C_t and continue scanning.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when price has moved h in either direction from the entry price (symmetric target and stop at one event-threshold), or at the close of the 20th bar after entry, whichever comes first.
params: event threshold h in daily ATR (0.5)
ideas.why: Engle and Lange invert the usual question. Instead of asking how far price moves for a given quantity (Kyle's lambda), they fix the price move and ask how much net volume it consumed. That is the quantity a liquidity provider actually cares about, and it separates two very different events that produce identical returns: a move on thin flow (nobody was there, the print is not consensus) and a move that chewed through unusual size (real, persistent demand). Conditioning on duration, average volume and time of day strips out the mechanical determinants so the residual isolates the depth surprise. The fade branch is the liquidity-provision trade; the follow branch is the informed-flow trade.
ideas.source: Robert F. Engle and Joe Lange, 'Predicting VNET: A model of the dynamics of market depth', Journal of Financial Markets 4(2), 113-142, 2001 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finmar/v4y2001i2p113-142.html). Bar-level construction of the price-duration and the residual entry rule are my synthesis.
ideas.novelty: Every impact idea in the existing set fixes the time interval (a bar) and measures price per unit volume. This fixes the PRICE MOVE and measures volume per unit move, sampling in a price clock rather than a clock or volume clock. The existing volume-clock idea samples in a volume clock and measures duration; this is its dual and gives a genuinely different event set.

ideas.name: Hasbrouck VAR Flow Forecast
ideas.entry_rule: Let r_t = ln(C_t / C_{t-1}) and let the signed flow proxy be x_t = sign(C_t - C_{t-1}) * ln(1 + V_t / mean(V, 20)) (carry the previous sign forward when C_t = C_{t-1}). Over the trailing 500 bars estimate a bivariate VAR(5) by OLS with x ordered first, so the r equation may include the contemporaneous x_t: r_t = a + b0*x_t + sum_{i=1..5} b_i * r_{t-i} + sum_{i=1..5} c_i * x_{t-i} + u_t, and x_t = d + sum_{i=1..5} e_i * r_{t-i} + sum_{i=1..5} f_i * x_{t-i} + v_t. Produce the one-step forecast by first forecasting xhat_{t+1} from the x equation, then rhat_{t+1} = a + b0*xhat_{t+1} + sum b_i*r_{t+1-i} + sum c_i*x_{t+1-i}. ENTRY at the open of bar t+1 in the sign of rhat_{t+1} when |rhat_{t+1}| >= 0.75 * stdev(r, 500) AND the r-equation's in-sample R-squared over the 500-bar window is >= 0.01 (below that the VAR is fitting noise and no trade is taken).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of bar t+1 - a strict one-bar hold matching the forecast horizon - with an intrabar stop at 2.0 * stdev(r, 500) against entry. Re-estimate and re-enter each bar; consecutive same-side signals hold the position rather than round-tripping it.
ideas.why: Hasbrouck's contribution was to stop treating trades and returns as a one-way regression and model them as a joint system: order flow is autocorrelated, returns feed back into future order flow, and the price impact of a trade is spread over subsequent periods rather than being contemporaneous. A single-equation lambda regression throws all of that away. The VAR captures both the flow persistence and the staggered impact, so its one-step forecast aggregates several small, individually unusable effects into one number. Requiring a minimum R-squared is the honest gate: for most stocks in most windows there is nothing there, and the rule should say so.
ideas.source: Joel Hasbrouck, 'Measuring the Information Content of Stock Trades', Journal of Finance 46(1), 179-207, 1991 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v46y1991i1p179-207.html) - a VAR of trades and quote revisions, with price effects that materialise gradually and impact that rises concavely with size. Using the fitted VAR as a live one-step forecaster is my construction.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the existing temporary-vs-permanent impact idea, which classifies event bars by a median reversal ratio and switches between two fixed behaviours. This fits a full dynamic system every bar and trades its point forecast, so it can produce a signal on ordinary bars with no event at all, and its exit is horizon-matched rather than fixed-count.

ideas.name: Propagator Residual Fade
ideas.entry_rule: Signed trade proxy eps_t = sign(C_t - C_{t-1}) (carry forward on zero returns), size term ln(V_t). Bouchaud's bare propagator is a power law G0(l) = g * l^(-beta); use beta = 0.4, the critical exponent the paper derives as beta_c = (1 - gamma)/2 with sign-autocorrelation exponent gamma ~ 1/5. With L = 50, define the unscaled predicted displacement Z_t = sum_{l=1..L} l^(-0.4) * eps_{t-l+1} * ln(V_{t-l+1}). Over the trailing 500 bars fit the single scale g by OLS (no intercept) of the realised displacement y_t = ln(C_t) - ln(C_{t-L}) on Z_t. Residual u_t = y_t - g*Z_t; z_u = u_t / stdev(u, 500). ENTRY at the next bar's open: SHORT when z_u >= +2.0 (price sits above what the order flow it absorbed can account for); LONG when z_u <= -2.0. No trade when |z_u| < 2.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when z_u returns to within +/-0.5 of zero (the price has re-converged to its flow-implied level), or at the close of the 30th bar after entry, or on a stop at 2.0 * ATR(14) against entry.
ideas.why: Bouchaud, Gefen, Potters and Wyart write the price as the superposition of the impact of every past trade, p_n = sum over n' < n of G0(n - n') * eps_n' * ln(V_n'), and show the bare propagator must itself decay as a power law with an exponent tuned so that the long-memory of trade signs (which would make prices super-diffusive) is exactly offset (which would make them sub-diffusive). The market sits near that critical point. The practical consequence is that a stock's price has a flow-implied fair value that can be computed from bar data, and the cancellation is not exact - the residual is where the small systematic deviations live. Fading the residual is the mean-reversion trade the model's own critical balance implies.
ideas.source: J.-P. Bouchaud, Y. Gefen, M. Potters, M. Wyart, 'Fluctuations and response in financial markets: the subtle nature of random price changes', arXiv:cond-mat/0307332 (https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0307332). I read the full text: Eq. (12) is the trade-superposition price equation, the exponent relation beta_c = (1 - gamma)/2 is derived in section 3.2, and gamma ~ 1/5 (so beta_c ~ 2/5) is their fitted value on France Telecom.
ideas.novelty: This is a multi-lag fitted impact KERNEL, not a single contemporaneous slope. The existing Kyle-lambda idea regresses this bar's return on this bar's signed root-dollar-volume; here fifty lags of flow each contribute with a decaying weight, and the signal is the forecast residual rather than the coefficient's z-score. The exponent is a theory-imposed constant, not a fitted parameter, which makes it far harder to overfit.

ideas.name: Realized Skewness Weekly Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: At the close of the last session of each week, from that week's n intraday 5-minute log returns r_1..r_n compute RV = sum r_i^2 and RSkew = (sqrt(n) * sum r_i^3) / RV^(3/2). Maintain a rolling history of the last 104 weekly RSkew values for the symbol. ENTRY at the open of the first session of the following week: LONG when RSkew for the just-completed week is at or below the 20th percentile of those 104 values; SHORT when it is at or above the 80th percentile. Require n >= 60 valid 5-minute returns in the week (skip holiday-shortened weeks) and RV to be non-zero. No trade when RSkew falls between the 20th and 80th percentiles.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the last session of the holding week - a fixed one-week hold - with a hard stop at 2.0 * (weekly ATR(14) measured on weekly bars) against entry, and no re-entry until the next weekly signal.
ideas.why: Realized skewness computed from intraday returns is a measure of the asymmetry of the week's price path, and it is dominated by whether the week contained a few large same-signed moves against a background of small opposite ones. Amaya and co-authors find the relation to next-week returns is negative: a week with strongly positive realized skewness is followed by weak returns and vice versa. The microstructure reading is that a positively skewed week is one in which a handful of upward liquidity demands were paid for, i.e. the buyer paid the spread repeatedly, and that transitory pressure reverses. It is also consistent with investors overpaying for lottery-like payoffs, which realized skewness proxies at high frequency.
ideas.source: Diego Amaya, Peter Christoffersen, Kris Jacobs, Aurelio Vasquez, 'Does realized skewness predict the cross-section of equity returns?', Journal of Financial Economics 118(1), 135-167, 2015 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v118y2015i1p135-167.html) - the long-lowest-decile / short-highest-decile realized-skewness spread earned 19 bp the following week with t = 3.70. NOTE: their sort is cross-sectional; I have converted it to a per-symbol time-series percentile, which is a weaker but implementable form and should be tested as such.
ideas.novelty: Third moment of intraday returns. Every existing volatility idea uses second moments (Parkinson, Garman-Klass, Rogers-Satchell, Yang-Zhang, bipower) or the first (returns). Nothing in the set touches skewness, and the weekly rebalance horizon is unlike anything else here.

ideas.name: Two-Frequency Noise Share Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Per session compute RV_1 = sum of squared 1-minute log returns (M1 = 390 returns) and RV_15 = sum of squared 15-minute log returns (M15 = 26 returns). Under i.i.d. microstructure noise, E[RV_M] = IV + 2*M*E[eta^2], so estimate the per-observation noise variance as eta2 = max(0, (RV_1 - RV_15) / (2 * (M1 - M15))) and the NOISE SHARE as q = min(1, 2 * M1 * eta2 / RV_1). Let Q = mean(q, 10 sessions) and rank Q against its trailing 250 sessions. FADE BRANCH - when Q >= its 80th percentile AND the first-order autocorrelation of the last 200 one-minute returns is <= -0.05 (confirming bid-ask bounce): on the next session, on any 5-minute bar between 10:00 and 15:30 ET where ln(C_bar / O_session) exceeds +0.75 * ATR(14, daily)/O_session, SHORT at that bar's close; mirror LONG on a -0.75 breach. FOLLOW BRANCH - when Q <= its 20th percentile AND the Lo-MacKinlay variance ratio VR(6) computed on the trailing 500 five-minute returns is >= 1.05: take the same +/-0.75 ATR breach but enter WITH the direction. No trade when Q sits between its 20th and 80th percentiles or when the confirming statistic fails.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the session close, or on a stop at 1.0 * ATR(14, daily) against entry. One trade per session per branch.
ideas.why: The volatility signature plot is the oldest diagnostic in high-frequency econometrics: realized variance computed at ever-finer sampling intervals rises without bound because each observation carries a noise term that gets counted M times. Bandi and Russell make that decomposition explicit and separable. Differencing RV at two frequencies therefore backs out the noise variance itself - a direct estimate of how much of today's tape is bid-ask bounce and how much is real price discovery, using nothing but bars. When noise dominates, an intraday displacement is disproportionately likely to be the accumulation of transitory bounce and reverts; when the tape is clean, the same displacement is price discovery and persists. The autocorrelation and variance-ratio confirmations are there because the noise estimate is itself noisy and can go negative or spike on a single bad print.
ideas.source: Federico M. Bandi and Jeffrey R. Russell, 'Separating microstructure noise from volatility', Journal of Financial Economics 79(3), 655-692, 2006 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/jfinec/v79y2006i3p655-692.html). The identity E[RV_M] = IV + 2*M*E[eta^2] under i.i.d. noise and the two-frequency differencing follow directly from that framework; the trading construction is mine.
ideas.novelty: Estimates NOISE variance rather than price variance, by exploiting the difference between two sampling frequencies - a quantity none of the existing ideas computes. The Yang-Zhang idea also switches between fade and follow but does so on the overnight share of TOTAL variance, which is a property of the session's shape; this switches on how much of the intraday variance is not real at all.

ideas.name: Open-to-Open Noise Ratio Gap Fade
ideas.entry_rule: Over the trailing 60 sessions compute V_oo = the sample variance of ln(O_t / O_{t-1}) and V_cc = the sample variance of ln(C_t / C_{t-1}); the noise ratio is NR = V_oo / V_cc. At 10:00 ET on day t, ENTER AGAINST the sign of the overnight gap g = ln(O_t / C_{t-1}) when ALL of: (a) NR >= 1.20, (b) |g| >= 0.40 * ATR(14, daily) / C_{t-1}, and (c) the first thirty minutes have already begun correcting the gap - specifically ln(P_1000 / O_t) has the OPPOSITE sign to g and |ln(P_1000 / O_t)| >= 0.20 * |g|, where P_1000 is the close of the 09:55-10:00 five-minute bar. No trade when NR < 1.20, when the gap is too small, or when the first thirty minutes extended the gap rather than correcting it.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the earliest of: price trading through C_{t-1} (the gap fully closed, take profit), the session close, or a stop placed at 1.0 * ATR(14, daily) beyond the session's opening extreme in the gap direction.
ideas.why: Amihud and Mendelson compared returns measured open-to-open against close-to-close for the same stocks and found the opening variance is materially larger. Since the underlying fundamental variance cannot depend on which price you measure it at, the excess is attributable to the trading mechanism: the opening print is set by a single call auction with a thin, unbalanced book, while the closing price is the end of a long continuous session. That makes the opening price a noisier estimate of value than the previous close, and NR measures how noisy this particular stock's open is, right now. Fading the gap only when the stock's own opening mechanism is demonstrably noisy - and only after the first half hour has begun voting against the print - is a targeted version of the gap fade rather than a blanket one.
ideas.source: Yakov Amihud and Haim Mendelson, 'Trading Mechanisms and Stock Returns: An Empirical Investigation', Journal of Finance 42(3), 533-553, 1987 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/jfinan/v42y1987i3p533-53.html). The NR gate and the retracement confirmation are my construction.
ideas.novelty: The conditioning variable is a ratio of two variances measured at different points of the trading day, which is a property of the market MECHANISM rather than of the price path. The existing overnight-Amihud idea conditions on opening illiquidity via dollar volume; this conditions on the stock's historical opening-price noisiness and requires an intraday confirmation before acting, so it fires on a different set of days.

ideas.name: Volatility-Conditioned Autocorrelation Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Let r_t be the log return and sigma_t = stdev(r, 20). Rank sigma_t into terciles using its own trailing 250-bar distribution (low tercile = below the 33rd percentile, high = above the 67th). Over the trailing 500 bars run TWO separate no-intercept-free OLS regressions of r_t on r_{t-1}: rho_low using only bars t whose sigma_{t-1} was in the LOW tercile, and rho_high using only bars whose sigma_{t-1} was in the HIGH tercile. Require at least 80 observations in each subsample or no trade. ENTRY at the next bar's open: if sigma_t is in the LOW tercile AND rho_low >= +0.05, take the SAME side as sign(r_t); if sigma_t is in the HIGH tercile AND rho_high <= -0.05, take the OPPOSITE side to sign(r_t). In both cases require |r_t| >= 0.75 * sigma_t. No trade in the middle tercile, and no trade when the relevant rho fails its threshold.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 3rd bar after entry, or on a stop at 1.5 * ATR(14). Reverse immediately if the opposite condition fires before the 3 bars elapse.
ideas.why: LeBaron documented that the serial correlation of stock returns is not a constant - it changes over time and does so systematically with volatility, being higher in quiet periods and falling (often turning negative) in volatile ones. The microstructure reading is that in quiet markets, order flow arrives in small correlated pieces and prices adjust in a drifting, partially-adjusted way, producing positive autocorrelation; in volatile markets, liquidity providers widen and demand compensation, so prices overshoot and revert, producing negative autocorrelation. Rather than picking momentum or reversal globally, the rule estimates each regime's own AR(1) from that regime's own bars and only acts when the estimated sign supports the trade.
ideas.source: Blake LeBaron, 'Some Relations between Volatility and Serial Correlations in Stock Market Returns', Journal of Business 65(2), 199-219, 1992 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/ucp/jnlbus/v65y1992i2p199-219.html) - serial correlations change over time and are related to return volatility. The tercile-conditional estimation and the entry gates are my construction.
ideas.novelty: The existing sign-autocorrelation idea computes ONE unconditional statistic on the signs of returns and trades its z-score. This estimates the AR(1) coefficient of the returns themselves SEPARATELY within volatility regimes and requires the current regime's own coefficient to support the trade, so it can be a momentum system today and a reversal system tomorrow on the same symbol with no parameter change.

ideas.name: Closing-Period Pressure Reversal
ideas.timeframe: daily signal from 5-minute bars, next-session execution
ideas.entry_rule: For session t let CV_t = (volume traded in 5-minute bars from 15:30 to 16:00 ET) / (session total volume), CR_t = ln(C_t / P_1530) where P_1530 is the close of the 15:25-15:30 bar, and DR_t = ln(P_1530 / O_t) the pre-close portion of the day. ENTRY at the open of session t+1, AGAINST sign(CR_t), when ALL of: (a) CV_t is at or above the 90th percentile of CV over the trailing 250 sessions, (b) |CR_t| >= 0.50 * ATR(14, daily) / C_t, and (c) either sign(DR_t) != sign(CR_t), or |DR_t| < 0.5 * |CR_t| - the late move must NOT be the continuation of a whole-day trend, it must be a late, isolated push. No trade otherwise.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the earliest of: price retracing 100% of CR_t (i.e. touching P_1530 from session t), 11:00 ET on session t+1, or a stop at 1.0 * ATR(14, daily) beyond the session t close in the direction of CR_t.
inputs: 250-session percentile of the closing volume share
ideas.why: Cushing and Madhavan study returns and trading at the close and connect end-of-day price behaviour to the concentration of institutional order flow into the closing period. Index funds, rebalancing programmes and benchmark-tracking mandates are indifferent to price and must complete by the bell, so a large closing volume share paired with a directional late move is liquidity DEMAND at any cost, not a revision of value. That demand disappears at 16:00 and the liquidity providers who absorbed it need the price back to be compensated. The trend-exclusion condition is essential: if the late move merely extended a move that had been running all day, it is more plausibly information, and fading it is a different and worse bet.
ideas.source: David Cushing and Ananth Madhavan, 'Stock returns and trading at the close', Journal of Financial Markets 3(1), 45-67, 2000 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/finmar/v3y2000i1p45-67.html). The volume-share percentile trigger and the trend-exclusion filter are my construction.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is the SHARE of the day's volume that arrived in the last half hour - a distributional feature of the session that nothing in the existing set measures. The opening-range ideas operate at the other end of the day and key off price levels; this keys off where the volume was, and holds through the overnight gap into the following morning.

ideas.name: MRR Adverse-Selection Share
ideas.entry_rule: Trade-indicator proxy x_t = sign(C_t - C_{t-1}) with the previous sign carried forward when C_t = C_{t-1}, so x_t is in {-1, +1}. Over the trailing 500 bars estimate rho = the first-order sample autocorrelation of x. The Madhavan-Richardson-Roomans price equation is dp_t = (phi + theta) * x_t - (phi + rho*theta) * x_{t-1} + e_t, where theta is the asymmetric-information component and phi the order-processing/inventory component. Regress dp_t = ln(C_t / C_{t-1}) on x_t and x_{t-1} by OLS with an intercept over the same 500 bars, obtaining coefficients a (on x_t) and b (on x_{t-1}). Solve: theta = (a + b) / (1 - rho) and phi = a - theta, then ASH = clip(theta / (theta + phi), 0, 1); if theta + phi <= 0 take no trade. Let S5 = sum of x over the last 5 bars. ENTRY at the next bar's open, requiring |S5| >= 3: if ASH >= 0.60, take the side of sign(S5); if ASH <= 0.25, take the side OPPOSITE to sign(S5). No trade when 0.25 < ASH < 0.60.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry, or earlier when sign(S5) flips against the position, or on a stop at 1.5 * ATR(14) against entry.
ideas.why: MRR give a structural, estimable decomposition of every price change into three pieces: a permanent revision due to the information in the trade (theta), a transitory cost of providing liquidity (phi), and public news. Crucially, the model accounts for order-flow autocorrelation rho, so the expected component of flow is not double-counted as information - that is what separates it from a naive signed-flow regression. The share theta/(theta+phi) is then a direct read on whether this stock, right now, is trading on information or on inventory. When it is information, a run of same-signed flow is the informed side accumulating and should be followed; when it is inventory and order processing, the same run is a dealer being pushed off balance and it should be faded. The paper's own finding that information asymmetry falls and transaction costs rise across the trading day means the measure genuinely varies rather than sitting at a constant.
ideas.source: Ananth Madhavan, Matthew Richardson, Mark Roomans, 'Why Do Security Prices Change? A Transaction-Level Analysis of NYSE Stocks', Review of Financial Studies 10(4), 1035-1064, 1997 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/rfinst/v10y1997i4p1035-64.html) - the structural model of intraday price formation whose estimates show information asymmetry decreasing and transaction costs increasing over the day. PROXY NOTE: the paper signs trades against quotes; here the tick rule on bar closes is the substitute.
ideas.novelty: A structural two-parameter decomposition solved from a constrained regression, not a single slope or ratio. The prior pass's temporary/permanent switch classifies event bars empirically by a reversal ratio; MRR separates the two components analytically from ALL bars and explicitly de-biases for flow autocorrelation, which nothing in the existing set does. The switch then applies to a flow-run condition rather than to a single large return.

ideas.name: Pastor-Stambaugh Gamma Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Let r_t be the daily log return and DV_t = C_t * V_t (dollar volume). Standardise dollar volume within the estimation window: dv_t = (DV_t - mean(DV, 60)) / stdev(DV, 60). Over a rolling 60-session window fit by OLS: r_{t+1} = alpha + phi * r_t + gamma * sign(r_t) * dv_t + e_{t+1}. Store the daily gamma estimate and maintain 250 trailing values of it. ENTRY at the open of session t+1, AGAINST sign(r_t), when ALL of: (a) the current gamma is at or below the 20th percentile of its trailing 250 values (this stock is in a strong order-flow-reversal regime), (b) gamma < 0 in absolute terms, (c) |r_t| >= 1.0 * ATR(14, daily) / C_t, and (d) dv_t >= +1.0 (the move was accompanied by unusually heavy dollar volume, which is what gamma prices). No trade otherwise.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of session t+2 (a two-session hold), or on a stop at 1.5 * ATR(14, daily) against entry, or immediately at the next open if the position gapped more than 1.0 * ATR against entry.
ideas.why: Pastor and Stambaugh's liquidity measure is explicitly a REVERSAL coefficient, not an impact coefficient: gamma is the loading of tomorrow's return on today's signed dollar volume, and a more negative gamma means order flow pushes price further than fundamentals justify and it comes back. That is a fundamentally different object from Amihud (which is contemporaneous |return| per dollar) or Kyle's lambda (contemporaneous impact) - those measure how much a trade moves price; gamma measures how much of that move is given back. Estimating gamma per symbol and trading only when it is in the stock's own most-negative quintile means the reversal trade is taken when the stock's own recent history says reversals are what happens, and the heavy-volume condition selects the exact days gamma is about.
ideas.source: Lubos Pastor and Robert F. Stambaugh, 'Liquidity Risk and Expected Stock Returns', Journal of Political Economy 111(3), 642-685, 2003 - the liquidity measure is the OLS gamma in a regression of next-period excess return on the current return and signed dollar volume. NOTE: their gamma is estimated monthly from daily data for an aggregate liquidity factor; converting it to a per-symbol rolling timing signal is my adaptation and should be tested as such.
ideas.novelty: A predictive (t to t+1) coefficient rather than a contemporaneous one. Amihud illiquidity and Kyle lambda are both same-bar measures and both already in the set; gamma is the only one of the three that is about what happens NEXT, and its sign is the trading thesis rather than a filter on top of one.

ideas.name: Kalman Efficient-Price Deviation
ideas.entry_rule: Model the observed log price as y_t = ln(C_t) = m_t + c * q_t, where m_t is the unobserved efficient price following a random walk m_t = m_{t-1} + w_t with w ~ N(0, sw2), and q_t is the trade direction in {-1, +1} with unit unconditional variance, so the observation-noise variance is c2 = c^2. Calibrate from the first two moments of dy_t = y_t - y_{t-1} over the trailing 500 bars: c2 = max(1e-12, -Cov(dy_t, dy_{t-1})) (Roll's identity - the negative first autocovariance IS the bounce), and sw2 = max(1e-12, Var(dy) - 2 * c2). Run a scalar Kalman filter: predict mpred = m_prev, Ppred = P_prev + sw2; gain K = Ppred / (Ppred + c2); update m_t = mpred + K * (y_t - mpred), P_t = (1 - K) * Ppred. Deviation d_t = (y_t - m_t) / sqrt(c2). ENTRY at the next bar's open: LONG when d_t <= -2.0 (the print sits more than two noise standard deviations BELOW the filtered efficient price); SHORT when d_t >= +2.0. Require c2 > 0 strictly (if the first autocovariance is positive there is no bounce to trade and no signal is generated).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when |d_t| falls back below 0.5 (the print has re-converged to the filtered efficient price), or at the close of the 10th bar after entry, or on a stop at 1.5 * ATR(14) against entry. Re-estimate sw2 and c2 every 100 bars, not every bar, to keep the filter's parameters stable.
inputs: 500-bar variance and first autocovariance of log returns
ideas.why: Roll's model says the observed price is the efficient price plus a bounce term of fixed magnitude and random sign. Written as a state-space system rather than as a moment condition, it becomes something you can FILTER: the Kalman recursion produces a running estimate of the unobservable efficient price at every bar, with the gain automatically weighting new prints by how much of their variation is signal versus bounce. The deviation of the observed print from the filtered state is then a directly tradable quantity - it says this print is transitory noise, of this magnitude, right now - whereas the moment-based estimators can only report an average spread over a window.
