The gain adapts on its own: in a high-noise regime K falls and the filter trusts prints less, which is exactly the behaviour you want.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The measurement equation and the two-moment calibration are the standard state-space form of Richard Roll's 1984 model (Journal of Finance, 'A simple implicit measure of the effective bid-ask spread in an efficient market'), which underlies the Roll estimator; the Kalman filtering of the efficient price and the deviation-based entry/exit are my construction. Related in spirit to Hasbrouck's Gibbs-sampler estimation of effective costs from daily data, which fits the same latent-price model by Bayesian rather than filtering methods.
ideas.novelty: Roll appears twice in the existing set but only as an ESTIMATOR whose value or sign is the signal (the autocovariance flip, and the ratio of Roll to Corwin-Schultz). Here the same model is inverted to recover the latent efficient price series itself, and the trade is the gap between the observed print and that latent series - a per-bar, self-normalising deviation with a convergence-based exit rather than a fixed hold.

ideas.name: Klinger Volume Force Absorption Spike
ideas.entry_rule: Build the Klinger volume force exactly: T_t = +1 if (high_t+low_t+close_t) > (high_{t-1}+low_{t-1}+close_{t-1}) else -1; dm_t = high_t - low_t; cm_t = cm_{t-1} + dm_t if T_t == T_{t-1}, else cm_t = dm_{t-1} + dm_t; VF_t = volume_t * abs(2*((dm_t/cm_t) - 1)) * T_t * 100. LONG: VF_t <= the 2nd percentile of VF over the trailing 500 bars, AND (close_t - low_t)/(high_t - low_t) <= 0.25, AND close_t is the lowest close of the last 20 bars, AND on the next bar VF_{t+1} >= 0 AND close_{t+1} > close_t. Enter LONG at the close of bar t+1. SHORT: mirror — VF_t >= the 98th percentile, (close_t-low_t)/(high_t-low_t) >= 0.75, close_t the highest close of the last 20 bars, VF_{t+1} <= 0 and close_{t+1} < close_t; enter SHORT at the close of t+1.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry; or immediately if VF prints beyond the 2nd/98th percentile AGAINST the position (a fresh opposing force spike); or on a stop at entry -/+ 1.5 * ATR(14).
ideas.why: Klinger's volume force scales volume by how far the bar's range deviates from the cumulative range of the current trend leg, so a single-bar extreme is a burst of one-sided committed volume rather than merely a big bar. When that burst is immediately neutralised on the following bar - the force flips sign without price following through - the aggressive flow was absorbed by a resting counterparty rather than initiating a move. Absorption at a 20-bar extreme is the classic point at which a liquidation finishes.
ideas.novelty: Uses the single-bar Volume Force as a tail-percentile event with a one-bar neutralisation confirmation, rather than the conventional KVO/signal-line crossover. Nothing here is a moving-average cross: the trigger is an extreme-then-reversal pair in the force series, and the exit is force-based, not price-based.
ideas.source: Klinger Volume Oscillator construction verified from TradingView's indicator documentation (https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000589157-klinger-oscillator/), which gives KO = EMA34(VF) - EMA55(VF), signal = 13, dm = high-low, cm continuation/reset rule, and VF = V x [2 x ((dm/cm) - 1)] x T x 100. Entry/exit logic is my synthesis on top of that construction.

ideas.name: Ease Of Movement Air Pocket
ideas.entry_rule: Compute Arms's Ease of Movement exactly: box ratio BR_t = volume_t / (high_t - low_t); EMV_t = ((high_t - high_{t-1}) + (low_t - low_{t-1})) / 2 * (high_t - low_t) / volume_t, scaled by 1e8; skip any bar with high_t == low_t. LONG at the next bar's open when: BR_t <= the 15th percentile of BR over the trailing 100 bars, AND close_t > open_t, AND close_t is the highest close of the last 20 bars, AND SMA(EMV,14) at t > 0. SHORT at the next open when: BR_t <= the 15th percentile of BR over the trailing 100 bars, AND close_t < open_t, AND close_t is the lowest close of the last 20 bars, AND SMA(EMV,14) at t < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when BR_t >= the 85th percentile of its trailing 100 values (heavy volume per unit range has returned - the pocket has been filled and someone is now defending the price), OR on a trailing stop of 2 * ATR(14) from the best close reached since entry.
ideas.why: Box ratio is volume required per unit of price travel, i.e. the local depth of resting liquidity. A break to a 20-bar extreme achieved on an unusually LOW box ratio means the price level had almost nobody willing to trade there - the book was thin, so continuation is cheap. Arms's own framing is that the indicator rises when prices move easily on relatively low volume. The exit is symmetric: the trade is over the moment liquidity reappears at the price.
ideas.novelty: Treats low volume-per-unit-range as the entry signal itself, the opposite of every volume-confirmation breakout rule and distinct from a volume dry-up setup (which uses quiet volume only as a precondition for a later expansion trigger). Both entry and exit are functions of the box ratio's own percentile, so the volume distribution defines the whole trade lifecycle.
ideas.source: Ease of Movement / box ratio arithmetic verified from the open-source `ta` library source, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bukosabino/ta/master/ta/volume.py (EaseOfMovementIndicator: emv = (high.diff(1) + low.diff(1)) * (high - low) / (2 * volume) * 1e8). Indicator originally Richard W. Arms Jr.; the air-pocket entry/exit is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Adaptive Volume Autocorrelation Sign Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Let r_t = close_t/close_{t-1} - 1. Volume proxy for turnover: v_t = log(volume_t + 1); detrended V_t = v_t - mean(v over the prior 200 days). At each daily close, fit OLS over the last 250 days: r_{t+1} = c0 + c1*r_t + c2*(V_t * r_t) + e, and let t2 = c2 / se(c2). Require the current bar to be a material high-volume move: abs(r_t) >= 1.5 * stdev(r over the last 20 days) AND V_t >= +0.5. Then: if t2 <= -2.0 (this symbol's high-volume moves REVERSE), enter CONTRARIAN at the next open - SHORT if r_t > 0, LONG if r_t < 0. If t2 >= +2.0 (this symbol's high-volume moves CONTINUE), enter WITH the move at the next open - LONG if r_t > 0, SHORT if r_t < 0. If -2.0 < t2 < +2.0, take no trade.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 5th trading day after entry, or earlier on a stop of 2 * ATR(14) from the entry price.
ideas.why: Llorente, Michaely, Saar and Wang show that volume carries opposite information depending on WHY people are trading: returns generated by risk-sharing (hedging) trades reverse, because the mover pays a liquidity premium that is then given back, while returns generated by speculative (informed) trades continue, because the information is only partly impounded. Their paper's abstract states exactly this. The sign of the volume-return interaction coefficient is therefore a per-symbol, time-varying diagnostic of which population dominates - so rather than hard-coding 'high volume means reversal', the strategy measures it and flips its own polarity.
ideas.novelty: The strategy has no fixed direction: an estimated regression coefficient decides whether the same observable event (a big move on big volume) is a fade or a follow. Distinct from any cross-sectional volume-conditioned reversal because the conditioning is a per-symbol time-series coefficient with a significance gate, and it can produce momentum entries on exactly the setups that produce reversal entries elsewhere.
ideas.source: Llorente, Michaely, Saar & Wang, 'Dynamic Volume-Return Relation of Individual Stocks', NBER Working Paper 8312 (May 2001), published Review of Financial Studies 15(4), 2002. I downloaded and text-extracted the working paper from https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w8312/w8312.pdf; the abstract confirms the reversal-versus-continuation split and its link to the extent of informed trading. The 200-day detrending of log turnover and the c0/c1/c2 specification follow the paper's design; the entry gates and holding period are mine.

ideas.name: Synthetic TRIN Breadth Washout
inputs: close and volume for every symbol in the universe
50-day median dollar volume for universe filtering
60-session mean and stdev of log TRIN
ideas.entry_rule: Rebuild the Arms Index from our own universe's OHLCV. Universe: every symbol with 50-day median dollar volume >= $2,000,000. For each session: A = count of universe symbols with close > previous close; D = count with close < previous close; AV = sum of volume over the advancing symbols; DV = sum of volume over the declining symbols. TRIN = (A/D) / (AV/DV); skip the day if D == 0 or DV == 0. Let L = log(TRIN), with mu and sd its mean and standard deviation over the prior 60 sessions. Trade a liquid index proxy (SPY or QQQ). LONG at the close of any day where L >= mu + 2.0*sd AND that instrument's close < SMA(close,20). SHORT at the close of any day where L <= mu - 2.0*sd AND close > SMA(close,20).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 3rd trading day after entry, or earlier on the first day L returns inside mu +/- 0.5*sd (breadth has normalised), whichever comes first.
ideas.why: TRIN compares the breadth of participation to the breadth of volume. A very high TRIN means declining issues are soaking up disproportionately more volume than their count warrants - selling is being dumped into a small number of names at once, the signature of forced or indiscriminate liquidation rather than repricing. Those episodes revert because the flow is supply-driven, not information-driven. Because it is a ratio of ratios, it is scale-free and does not need a time-of-day or level baseline the way raw volume does.
ideas.novelty: None of the existing 54 ideas look across symbols at all except as a cross-sectional ranking; this is the only one that builds a market-wide volume-breadth statistic from the fleet's own bar data and then trades a single instrument off it. The volume enters as a denominator normalising issue counts, not as a level or a z-score.
ideas.source: Arms Index / TRIN, Richard W. Arms Jr. (1967), standard formula TRIN = (advancing issues / declining issues) / (advancing volume / declining volume). I could not open Fidelity's or StockCharts' indicator pages (navigation-only content and an SSL handshake failure respectively), so the formula is stated from the standard definition rather than quoted from a page I fetched. Reconstructing it from a self-built universe instead of NYSE breadth is my OHLCV-only proxy.

ideas.name: Weis Wave Swing Volume Divergence
ideas.category: effort versus result at swing scale
ideas.entry_rule: Segment price into waves with an ATR zigzag on the close: while in an UP wave, track the highest close; the UP wave ends and a DOWN wave begins on the first bar whose close is more than k * ATR(14) below that highest close (k = 2.0), and mirror for DOWN waves. For each completed wave n record its direction, its price travel P_n = abs(close at wave end - close at wave start), and its wave volume W_n = sum of volume over every bar in the wave. SHORT: an UP wave n has just been confirmed complete, AND P_n >= P_{n-2} (this up-leg travelled at least as far as the previous up-leg), AND W_n <= 0.70 * W_{n-2} (it did so on far less committed volume). Enter SHORT at the close of the bar that confirms the reversal. LONG: mirror on DOWN waves - the completed down-leg travelled at least as far as the prior down-leg on <= 0.70x its volume; enter LONG at the confirming bar's close.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the bar that confirms the END of the next completed wave running in the trade's direction (so the holding period is measured in waves, not bars); stop at the extreme price of the wave that generated the signal.
ideas.why: Wyckoff's effort-versus-result is a statement about swings, not bars: a rally that covers the same ground as the last rally while attracting materially less volume shows the supply of willing buyers thinning even as price rises, which is the setup for the leg to fail. Measuring it per wave rather than per bar is the point - a single quiet bar means little, but a whole leg completed on 30% less volume than its predecessor is a participation deficit.
ideas.novelty: The unit of analysis is a price swing of variable length, not a fixed lookback window or a single bar, so neither the bar-level effort/result residual nor any fixed-window accumulation-line divergence can express it. The exit is also wave-structured: the trade ends when the next swing completes, which adapts its holding period to volatility automatically.
ideas.source: David Weis's Weis Wave, a computerisation of the wave charts in Richard Wyckoff's course; see Weis, 'Trades About to Happen' (Wiley, 2013). I could not retrieve a primary page for the construction (my search budget was exhausted and the fallback search endpoint returned a CAPTCHA, which I did not attempt to solve), so I pinned the wave definition myself to an ATR zigzag to make it unambiguous and testable - flagging that the specific 2.0-ATR segmentation is my choice, not Weis's.

ideas.name: Volume Profile Shape Classifier
inputs: volume-weighted mean, stdev and skew of the price distribution
ideas.entry_rule: For each completed RTH session build a volume profile from 1-minute bars: price bins of width 0.05% of that session's open, each bar's volume spread evenly across the bins its [low, high] covers. Let R = session high - session low, POC = midpoint of the highest-volume bin, and S = (POC - session low) / R. Using bin midpoints p_i with bin volumes w_i, compute mu = sum(w_i*p_i)/sum(w_i), sigma = sqrt(sum(w_i*(p_i-mu)^2)/sum(w_i)), skew = sum(w_i*(p_i-mu)^3) / (sum(w_i)*sigma^3). Classify: P-SHAPE if S >= 0.70 AND skew <= -0.5; b-SHAPE if S <= 0.30 AND skew >= +0.5. Next session: after a P-SHAPE session that closed above its own POC, enter SHORT on the first 5-minute bar at or after 10:00 ET that closes below that prior session's POC. After a b-SHAPE session that closed below its own POC, enter LONG on the first 5-minute bar at or after 10:00 ET that closes above that prior session's POC. One trade per day; no entries after 15:00 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Target the opposite extreme of the prior session's range (prior low for a short, prior high for a long); stop beyond the prior session's extreme on the entry side; hard exit at 15:50 ET regardless.
ideas.why: A P-shaped profile - volume piled into a shelf at the top of the range with a thin tail beneath - is the footprint of short covering: the buying that made the move was closing, not initiating, so no new long inventory sits below to defend the shelf. A b-shape is the mirror, long liquidation. Once price loses the shelf that the covering built, there is nothing under it and the whole move unwinds quickly. The shape statistics separate this from an ordinary balanced session where the value shelf is genuinely two-sided.
ideas.novelty: Classifies the SHAPE of the volume distribution using its moments (POC position within the range plus volume-weighted skew) rather than extracting a level from it. Existing profile ideas all trade a price - a naked POC, a value-area edge, a low-volume node - whereas this one takes no level from the profile at all except as a trigger, and conditions the entire trade on the geometry of the distribution.
ideas.source: Profile shape taxonomy (P, b and D distributions) from J. Peter Steidlmayer's Market Profile work at the CBOT; the specific computable statistics (POC position ratio S and volume-weighted skew, with the thresholds given) are my formalisation, since the practitioner literature describes these shapes visually rather than numerically.

ideas.name: Intraday Volume Concentration Herfindahl
inputs: epicentre bar index and its close location
ideas.entry_rule: For each RTH session with its 78 five-minute bars, let s_i = volume_i / total session volume and H = sum(s_i^2) (a perfectly even session gives H = 1/78 ~ 0.0128; all volume in one bar gives H = 1). Let C = log(H), with mu_C and sd_C its mean and stdev over the prior 60 sessions. Record the EPICENTRE = the index of the highest-volume 5-minute bar, and clv_epi = (close-low)/(high-low) of that bar. CONCENTRATED session: C >= mu_C + 1.5*sd_C AND the epicentre is not among the last 3 bars of the session (so it is an intraday event, not closing-auction mechanics). On a concentrated session, enter at the NEXT session's open: LONG if clv_epi >= 0.70 and the epicentre bar's close > its open; SHORT if clv_epi <= 0.30 and its close < its open; no trade otherwise. DIFFUSE session: C <= mu_C - 1.5*sd_C - take no new position, and close any position this system holds at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 3rd session after entry; or on a stop of 1.5 * ATR(14, daily) from entry; or immediately at the next open following any DIFFUSE session (participation has spread out evenly again, so whatever information caused the concentration is fully distributed).
ideas.why: Total daily volume conflates two very different days: one where a hundred thousand shares trade steadily all day, and one where the same total arrives in a single ten-minute burst. Only the second is an information event. The Herfindahl index of the intraday volume shares separates them without needing any external news feed, and the burst bar's close location tells you which side won the event. Under-reaction to genuine single-moment information is what produces the subsequent drift, while an evenly distributed session means the information is already fully shared and there is no edge left to harvest.
ideas.novelty: Measures the CONCENTRATION of the volume distribution across time as a scalar, then uses it as a regime gate for a drift trade, with the diffuse case as an explicit exit trigger. No existing idea looks at the shape of the intraday volume curve as a whole - the relative-volume ideas score individual bars against a time-of-day baseline, and the pace idea integrates the curve, but neither detects whether volume was concentrated or spread.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The Herfindahl-Hirschman index is the standard concentration measure from industrial organisation; applying it to intraday volume shares as an information-event detector, and gating a drift trade on it, is my own construction.

ideas.name: Volume Time Versus Clock Time Volatility Ratio
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain two parallel return series over a rolling window of the last 2 sessions of 1-minute data. CLOCK series: the raw 1-minute closes; RV_clock = sum of (log(close_i/close_{i-1}))^2. VOLUME series: accumulate 1-minute volume into buckets of fixed size V = (median daily volume over the last 50 sessions) / 78, splitting any bar that overfills a bucket pro rata and interpolating that bar's close linearly to the split point; take the most recent N buckets where N = the number of 1-minute bars in the window, ending at the same instant; RV_vol = sum of squared log returns between consecutive bucket closes. Let Q = RV_clock / RV_vol, percentile-ranked against its own trailing 500 observations. ENTRY (fade) when Q's percentile >= 90: price is moving per unit of clock time far more than per unit of volume, i.e. moving without participation. Let r30 = the return over the last 30 minutes. SHORT at the next 5-minute bar's open if r30 > 0; LONG if r30 < 0. Only between 10:00 and 15:00 ET; at most one trade per direction per session. Take NO new positions while Q's percentile <= 10 (every move is fully volume-backed).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when Q's percentile falls back below 50 (participation has caught up with the price move), or after 12 five-minute bars, or on a stop of 1.0 * ATR(14, 5-minute), whichever comes first.
ideas.why: Sampling by volume rather than by the clock is the core argument of the volume-clock literature: information arrives with trade, not with time, so a volume-time series has better statistical behaviour than a clock-time one. The ratio of the two realized variances is therefore a direct effort-versus-result measure at the level of volatility rather than of individual bars: when clock-time variance greatly exceeds volume-time variance, price is being pushed around inside a thin book by very little actual trading, and those excursions revert once real size arrives.
ideas.novelty: Compares two resamplings of the SAME data - one indexed by time, one by volume - and trades their divergence. No indicator is involved and no bar is scored; the signal is the disagreement between two clocks. Distinct from the volume-bar and imbalance-bar ideas, which sample in volume time and then trade the resulting bars directly rather than measuring volume time against clock time.
ideas.source: Motivated by Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara, 'The Volume Clock: Insights into the High Frequency Paradigm', Journal of Portfolio Management 39(1), 2012 (SSRN 2034858). I attempted to fetch the SSRN page and received HTTP 403, so this is a bibliographic citation, not a verified quotation; the RV_clock / RV_vol ratio and the trading rule are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Developing POC Monotonic Migration
inputs: cumulative session volume versus a 20-session same-checkpoint baseline
ideas.entry_rule: At each 30-minute checkpoint (10:00, 10:30, ... 15:30 ET), rebuild the session-TO-DATE volume profile from 1-minute bars, bin width 0.05% of the session open, volume spread evenly across the bins each bar's [low, high] covers, and record the developing POC, dPOC_k = the midpoint of the highest-volume bin so far today. LONG at the close of checkpoint k (k >= 3, so at or after 11:00 ET) when: dPOC_k > dPOC_{k-1} > dPOC_{k-2} (three strictly rising developing POCs), AND dPOC_k - dPOC_{k-2} >= 0.5 * ATR(14, daily), AND the current price is above dPOC_k, AND cumulative session volume through checkpoint k >= 1.1 x the mean cumulative volume at the same checkpoint over the prior 20 sessions. SHORT: mirror - three strictly falling developing POCs, dPOC_{k-2} - dPOC_k >= 0.5 * ATR(14, daily), price below dPOC_k, same volume-pace condition.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the first later checkpoint whose developing POC moves against the position (dPOC_{k+1} < dPOC_k for a long, or > for a short) - a value-based exit rather than a price-based one; or at 15:55 ET; or on a stop at dPOC_k - 1.0 * ATR(14, daily) for a long, mirrored for a short.
ideas.why: On a range day the fair-value shelf stays put and price merely oscillates around it, so the POC barely moves even as the highs and lows extend. On a genuine trend day the shelf itself relocates, because each new price level accumulates more volume than the last. Requiring three consecutive monotonic migrations of a minimum distance, backed by above-baseline participation, is a direct test of which of those two days is happening - and it tests it using where volume is accumulating rather than where price has been.
ideas.novelty: Trades the VELOCITY of the volume-at-price distribution within the live session, not a level extracted from a completed one. The existing profile ideas all use finished profiles: historical naked POCs as magnets, prior-session value-area edges, or a multi-session composite's thin nodes. None tracks how the current session's POC is moving in real time, and none exits on the POC turning.
ideas.source: Synthesis on top of the market-profile 'developing VPOC' construct used by profile traders; the monotonicity test, the ATR-scaled migration distance, the volume-pace gate and the POC-reversal exit are mine.

ideas.name: Volume Price Confirmation Indicator
ideas.entry_rule: With short = 10 and long = 50, define VWMA(n) = sum(close_i * volume_i over the last n) / sum(volume_i over the last n). Then: VPC = VWMA(long) - SMA(close, long); VPR = VWMA(short) / SMA(close, short); VM = SMA(volume, short) / SMA(volume, long); VPCI = VPC * VPR * VM. LONG at the close of day t when VPCI_t > 0 AND VPCI_{t-1} <= 0 AND close_t > SMA(close, 50) AND VM_t > 1.0. SHORT at the close of day t when VPCI_t < 0 AND VPCI_{t-1} >= 0 AND close_t < SMA(close, 50) AND VM_t > 1.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when VPCI crosses back through zero (confirmation has failed - a flow-based exit with no fixed horizon), or on a stop of 2.5 * ATR(14) from entry.
ideas.why: The difference between a volume-weighted moving average and a plain one answers a question no price indicator can: did the heavy volume trade at higher prices than the average price, or lower? A positive VPC means the size printed above the mean - buyers paid up, which is accumulation. The VPR term scales that by how emphatic the short-horizon version of the same comparison is, and the VM term requires that current volume is actually expanding relative to its own longer baseline, so the confirmation is not read off a quiet tape. The product turns three weak signals into one that only fires when all three agree.
ideas.novelty: Compares two averages of the SAME price series that differ only in their weighting - one by volume, one uniformly. That is a different object from any accumulation line, money-flow oscillator or volume-scored bar: it measures where in the price range the volume actually transacted, aggregated over a window, with no signed classification of bars at all.
ideas.source: Buff Pelz Dormeier, 'Investing with Volume Analysis: Identify, Follow, and Profit from Trends' (FT Press, 2011), and his Volume Price Confirmation Indicator articles in Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities. Bibliographic citation - I could not fetch a primary page (search budget exhausted, and Investopedia is blocked in this environment), so verify the exact VPC/VPR/VM composition against the book before committing the implementation.

ideas.name: OBV New Extreme Before Price
ideas.entry_rule: OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} + volume_t if close_t > close_{t-1}; OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} - volume_t if close_t < close_{t-1}; OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} if equal. LONG at the close of bar t when ALL hold: OBV_t is the highest OBV of the last 50 bars; close_t is NOT the highest close of the last 50 bars; close_t >= 0.97 * the highest close of the last 50 bars (price is coiled just under its high, not lagging far behind); and close_t > SMA(close, 50). SHORT at the close of bar t when: OBV_t is the lowest OBV of the last 50 bars; close_t is NOT the lowest close of the last 50 bars; close_t <= 1.03 * the lowest close of the last 50 bars; and close_t < SMA(close, 50).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when OBV falls below its own SMA(OBV, 20) for a long (or rises above it for a short) - the accumulation that justified the trade has stopped; or after 20 bars; or on a stop of 2 * ATR(14) from entry.
ideas.why: Granville's original claim for OBV was that volume precedes price: a position is accumulated across many sessions of unremarkable price action, and the cumulative signed volume registers it before the price breakout prints. Requiring OBV at a 50-bar high while price is still just under its own 50-bar high captures precisely that lead, and the 3% proximity band excludes the degenerate case where OBV is at an extreme only because price has been grinding sideways far below the high.
ideas.novelty: This is a CONFIRMATION-LEAD rule, structurally the inverse of a divergence rule: it requires the flow series and the price series to agree in direction while the flow gets there first, rather than requiring them to disagree. It also uses OBV's raw new-extreme status rather than a regression slope or a t-statistic, and exits on the flow series crossing its own average rather than on price.
ideas.source: Joseph E. Granville, 'New Key to Stock Market Profits' (Prentice-Hall, 1963), which introduces On-Balance Volume together with the 'volume precedes price' thesis. The OBV recursion above matches the standard implementation in the open-source `ta` library (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bukosabino/ta/master/ta/volume.py, OnBalanceVolumeIndicator), which I fetched; the 50-bar-extreme-lead entry and the OBV-versus-its-own-MA exit are my formalisation.

ideas.name: Volume Profile Excess Tail Rejection
params: tail volume threshold (1.0% of session volume)
ideas.entry_rule: For each completed RTH session build the 1-minute volume profile (bins 0.05% of the session open, each bar's volume spread evenly across the bins its [low, high] covers) and let R = high - low. Define the UPPER TAIL as the bins covering the top 7% of R and the LOWER TAIL as the bottom 7%. Flag an EXCESS HIGH if the upper tail holds <= 1.0% of that session's total volume AND the session closed below the midpoint of R. Flag an EXCESS LOW if the lower tail holds <= 1.0% of session volume AND the session closed above the midpoint of R. The flagged zone stays live for the next 3 sessions. ENTRY SHORT: on the first 5-minute bar at or after 09:45 ET whose high enters the upper-tail zone and whose close is back BELOW the zone's lower edge. ENTRY LONG: on the first 5-minute bar at or after 09:45 ET whose low enters the lower-tail zone and whose close is back ABOVE the zone's upper edge. Cancel the setup if any 5-minute bar closes beyond the excess extreme by more than 0.25 * ATR(14, daily), or when 3 sessions elapse.
ideas.exit_rule: Target the POC of the session that created the excess; stop 0.5 * ATR(14, daily) beyond the excess extreme; hard exit at 15:50 ET on the entry day if neither is hit.
ideas.why: An excess is a price at which the auction printed but almost nothing traded - the market went there, found no willing counterparty at all, and left immediately. That is qualitatively different from a low-volume shelf inside the range: it marks the exact boundary where the auction shut off, and the participants who refused to trade there are generally still refusing on a revisit. The volume share in the tail, rather than the price extreme itself, is what identifies it, which is why the same session high can be an excess on one day and a legitimate acceptance area on another.
ideas.novelty: A low-volume node at a session EXTREME is traded as a rejection boundary, whereas a low-volume node inside a composite range is traded as a fast-traverse zone - opposite trade directions from superficially similar volume geometry, distinguished by location within the range and by the closing position of the session that created it. The setup also has an explicit volume-defined invalidation and a multi-session lifetime rather than a fixed entry bar.
ideas.source: The concept of 'excess' (tails, single prints) at auction extremes comes from J. Peter Steidlmayer's Market Profile framework as taught at the CBOT. The numeric definition - a 7%-of-range tail holding under 1% of session volume, plus the close-location requirement - is my formalisation, since the original is described visually.

ideas.name: Twin Volume Node Absorption
ideas.category: volume climax / absorption at a level
ideas.entry_rule: For each 5-minute slot, let VP90 be the 90th percentile of that same bar-of-day slot's volume over the prior 20 sessions; call bar i HEAVY if volume_i >= VP90 for its slot. SHORT setup: find two heavy bars i < j with 2 <= j - i <= 12, such that abs(high_j - high_i) <= 0.15 * ATR(14, 5-minute); both bars closed in the lower half of their own range, (close-low)/(high-low) <= 0.5; and the maximum high over bars i..j equals max(high_i, high_j) (nothing between them exceeded the twin level). ENTER SHORT at the close of the first bar after j that closes below min(low_i, low_j). LONG setup: mirror - two heavy bars whose LOWS are within 0.15 * ATR of each other, both closing in the upper half of their range, with nothing lower between them; ENTER LONG at the close of the first bar after j that closes above max(high_i, high_j). Cancel if 10 bars pass after j without a trigger, or if any close moves beyond the twin level by more than 0.25 * ATR.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop 0.3 * ATR(14, 5-minute) beyond the twin level; target 2x the entry-to-stop distance; hard exit at 15:55 ET.
ideas.why: One heavy bar that fails at a price is ambiguous - it could be a single large order that is now finished. Two heavy bars probing the SAME price within a few bars, both closing rejected, with nothing exceeding that price in between, is the footprint of a resting passive participant absorbing repeatedly at a fixed level. The information is in the repetition: the level survived two separate high-volume tests, so the aggressive side is exhausted and the passive side is not, and price breaks the other way.
ideas.novelty: Requires a PAIR of high-volume events at a matched price with an untouched level between them - a two-point test of the same price, rather than a single bar scored on its own volume and range. It also imposes no narrow-range or N-bar-extreme requirement, so it fires on structures a single-bar churn test cannot see, and the trigger is a break of the pair's joint opposite extreme rather than of one bar.
ideas.source: Synthesis, formalising the absorption concept from Wyckoff and Volume Spread Analysis into a testable twin-bar test at a price tolerance scaled by ATR.

ideas.name: Chaikin Money Flow Sign Run Exhaustion
ideas.entry_rule: CMF(21) = [sum over the last 21 bars of ((close-low)-(high-close))/(high-low) * volume] / [sum over the last 21 bars of volume], with the multiplier set to 0 when high == low. Track the run length n_t = the number of consecutive bars, ending at t, over which CMF has held the same sign. LONG at the close of bar t when: CMF_t > 0 AND CMF_{t-1} <= 0 AND the immediately preceding negative run had length >= 20 bars AND close_t > SMA(close, 50). SHORT at the close of bar t when: CMF_t < 0 AND CMF_{t-1} >= 0 AND the immediately preceding positive run had length >= 20 bars AND close_t < SMA(close, 50).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the first bar whose CMF sign flips back against the position, or after 25 bars, whichever is first; stop at 2 * ATR(14) from entry.
ideas.why: A zero-line cross on its own is noise - money flow wobbles across zero constantly. What carries information is the completion of a full regime: flow that has been persistently one-sided for at least as long as the indicator's own averaging window has genuinely repriced inventory, and its termination marks a handoff between populations. The run-length requirement is what turns a common crossing into a rare event, and pairing it with a trend filter means the trade is taken only when the newly arriving flow agrees with the longer-term price direction.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is the DURATION of the preceding flow state, not its magnitude or its threshold. Two CMF crossings with identical values are treated completely differently depending on how long the prior regime lasted, which is a different selection principle from any level, z-score, percentile or divergence rule.
ideas.source: Chaikin Money Flow formula verified from the open-source `ta` library source, https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bukosabino/ta/master/ta/volume.py (ChaikinMoneyFlowIndicator: mfv = ((close-low)-(high-close))/(high-low), filled with 0, times volume, rolling-summed and divided by rolling-summed volume). Indicator originally Marc Chaikin; the run-length entry condition and the sign-flip exit are my synthesis.

ideas.name: High Volume Decline Liquidity Premium
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars on a liquid instrument. Let r_t = close_t/close_{t-1} - 1 and V_t = log(volume_t) - mean(log(volume) over the prior 100 days). ENTER LONG at the next session's open when ALL hold on day t: r_t <= -1.0 * stdev(r over the last 20 days) (a material decline); V_t >= +0.4 (volume well above its own trend); and (high_t - low_t)/close_t >= the 60th percentile of that ratio over the last 100 days (a real, wide bar, not a thin holiday session). Explicit NO-TRADE: if V_t <= -0.2, take no position regardless of how large the decline was - a decline on below-trend volume carries no liquidity premium to collect. There is no short leg.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 4th trading day after entry, or earlier if the position gains 1.5 * ATR(14), whichever comes first.
ideas.why: Campbell, Grossman and Wang model price declines accompanied by heavy volume as the market absorbing risk-averse sellers who need to shed exposure: liquidity providers take the other side and require compensation, which shows up as a subsequent expected return. The empirical implication is an asymmetric one - the reversal is a payment for absorbing supply, so it applies to high-volume DECLINES rather than symmetrically to rallies, and it disappears entirely when the decline happens on light volume, because then nobody needed absorbing.
ideas.novelty: Deliberately asymmetric and non-adaptive: the direction is hard-coded long and only declines qualify, with light-volume declines excluded by an explicit veto. That is the opposite design choice from the adaptive coefficient-sign strategy above, which estimates whether a symbol reverses or continues and can take either side; running both lets you test whether the fixed asymmetric prior beats the estimated one.
ideas.source: Campbell, Grossman & Wang, 'Trading Volume and Serial Correlation in Stock Returns', Quarterly Journal of Economics 108(4), 1993 (NBER Working Paper 4193). I downloaded w4193 from NBER but it is a scanned-image PDF that would not extract to text, so this is cited from the published result rather than from a passage I read in the file - verify the specification against the paper before relying on the exact form. The detrending window, thresholds and holding period are mine.

ideas.name: Zumbach Trend-Feedback Expansion
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars. r_t = ln(C_t/C_{t-1}); v_t = r_t^2; aggregated returns R_t(k) = ln(C_t/C_{t-k}). On a rolling 750-session window fit by OLS, refitting every 21 sessions: v_{t+1} = a0 + a1*R_t(1)^2 + a5*R_t(5)^2 + a22*R_t(22)^2 + a66*R_t(66)^2. Note the regressors are SQUARED MULTI-PERIOD RETURNS (past trends), not averaged past variances - this is the Zumbach/quadratic-Hawkes feedback, and it is a different model class from HAR-RV. One-step forecast F = a0 + a1*R_t(1)^2 + a5*R_t(5)^2 + a22*R_t(22)^2 + a66*R_t(66)^2. Trend share Z_t = (a5*R_t(5)^2 + a22*R_t(22)^2 + a66*R_t(66)^2) / (F - a0). ENTER at the next open when (a) Z_t >= 0.60, (b) F >= 1.5 * mean(v over the last 22 sessions), (c) a5 > 0 AND a22 > 0. LONG if R_t(22) > 0, SHORT if R_t(22) < 0. No trade otherwise.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the first session on which sign(R(5)) is opposite the position, OR after 10 sessions held, OR on a stop 2.5*ATR(20) from entry - whichever comes first.
ideas.why: The Zumbach effect is the empirically documented time-reversal asymmetry of markets: past squared returns forecast future volatility better than past volatility forecasts future squared returns. When the model attributes most of the forecast expansion to multi-period TREND terms rather than to yesterday's single-bar shock, the coming volatility is endogenous feedback from an existing directional move - so the expansion should arrive with the trend's sign attached, not as a symmetric burst. HAR-RV cannot express this because its regressors are sign-blind averages of past RV.
ideas.novelty: Not a moving-average cross and not an RSI extreme: it is a fitted variance model whose regressors are squared aggregated returns, and the tradeable object is the SHARE of the forecast coming from trend feedback rather than the forecast level. Distinct from HAR-RV forecasting, which is sign-blind and uses averaged realized variances.
ideas.source: Blanc, Donier & Bouchaud, 'Quadratic Hawkes processes for financial prices', arXiv:1509.07710 (opened and verified this session - confirms feedback effects quadratic in past returns produce multiplicative fat-tailed volatility and time-reversal asymmetry). El Euch, Gatheral, Radoicic & Rosenbaum, 'The Zumbach effect under rough Heston', arXiv:1809.02098 (opened and verified this session - states past squared returns forecast future volatilities better than past volatilities forecast future squared returns). Original: Zumbach & Lynch (2001) on volatility cascades. The regression specification above is my pinning-down of the QHawkes diagonal/off-diagonal feedback into an OLS form implementable on daily OHLCV.

ideas.name: Realized Kurtosis Concentration
ideas.timeframe: intraday 5-minute for the statistic, daily for the trade
ideas.entry_rule: From the 78 regular-session 5-minute bars of session t compute r_i = ln(C_i/C_{i-1}), n = 78. Realized variance RV_t = SUM r_i^2. Realized kurtosis RK_t = n * SUM r_i^4 / (SUM r_i^2)^2 (equivalently 3*RQ_t/RV_t^2 with realized quarticity RQ_t = (n/3)*SUM r_i^4). RK = 3 for i.i.d. Gaussian intraday returns; higher means the day's variance was concentrated into a handful of bars. Day's net move M_t = ln(C_t/O_t). Rank RK_t against its own trailing 252-session history to get percentile P. ENTER at the open of session t+1: LONG when P >= 85 AND M_t > 0 AND |M_t| >= 0.8*sqrt(RV_t); SHORT when P >= 85 AND M_t < 0 AND |M_t| >= 0.8*sqrt(RV_t). Take no trade when P <= 15 (variance spread evenly across all bars - a diffusive, uninformative session).
ideas.exit_rule: Stop order at entry_price * exp(-side * 1.5 * sqrt(RV_t)) placed at entry, where side = +1 long / -1 short. If not stopped, exit at the close of session t+1 if the position is profitable, otherwise hold to the close of session t+2 and exit there unconditionally.
ideas.why: Realized quarticity is the fourth-moment analogue of realized variance and governs the sampling error of RV. Its normalized form, realized kurtosis, separates two sessions with identical RV: one where volatility arrived as a steady hum and one where it arrived as three violent bars. The |M_t| >= 0.8*sqrt(RV_t) condition requires those concentrated bars to have pointed the same way rather than cancelling - which is the signature of a single large participant working an order across the session, whose residual demand carries into the next open.
ideas.novelty: Uses the fourth moment of the intraday return distribution, whereas the volatility literature the fleet already covers stops at the second (RV, bipower) and third (realized skewness). Distinct from realized skewness percentile reversal: kurtosis is sign-blind, the direction comes from the separate net-move term, and the trade is continuation rather than reversal.
ideas.source: Barndorff-Nielsen & Shephard (2002), 'Econometric analysis of realised volatility and its use in estimating stochastic volatility models', JRSS-B 64(2) - the realized quarticity estimator RQ = (n/3)*SUM r_i^4 and the asymptotic role of integrated quarticity. The realized-variance asymptotic distribution and the role of integrated quarticity were confirmed against the Wikipedia 'Realized variance' article this session; the normalization into realized kurtosis and the trading rule are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Geary Normality Ratio Regime Switch
ideas.entry_rule: On the last n = 120 daily log returns r_t, set e_t = r_t - mean(r). Compute d = (1/n)*SUM |e_t| and s = sqrt((1/n)*SUM e_t^2). Geary's ratio a = d/s. Under normality E[a] = sqrt(2/pi) = 0.79788 and SD(a) = 0.21227/sqrt(n). Test statistic z_G = (a - 0.79788) / (0.21227/sqrt(n)). BREAKOUT MODE when z_G <= -2.0 (significantly leptokurtic: variance is concentrated in rare large moves): LONG at the close when C_t > the highest close of the prior 20 sessions; SHORT at the close when C_t < the lowest close of the prior 20 sessions. RANGE MODE when z_G >= 0.0 (near-Gaussian or short-tailed): LONG at the close when (C_t - SMA20)/ATR(20) <= -1.5 AND C_t > C_{t-1}; SHORT when (C_t - SMA20)/ATR(20) >= +1.5 AND C_t < C_{t-1}. NO TRADE when -2.0 < z_G < 0.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Breakout mode: trailing stop 3.0*ATR(20) from the most extreme close reached since entry, re-evaluated each close. Range mode: exit at the close on the first touch of SMA20, or on a stop 2.0*ATR(20) from entry, or after 8 sessions.
ideas.why: The mean-absolute-deviation-to-standard-deviation ratio is a direct, low-variance measure of tail weight that needs no fourth moment (and therefore no eighth moment for its own standard error, which is why sample kurtosis is so unstable). When a is far below sqrt(2/pi) the return distribution is a mixture with a fat component - vol-of-vol is high and most of the variance lives in a few jumps, so an extreme close is likely the start of the next jump cluster rather than an overshoot. When a sits at or above sqrt(2/pi) the process is behaving like a bounded, near-Gaussian oscillator and excursions revert.
ideas.novelty: A formal normality test used as the regime switch, not a volatility LEVEL and not an autocorrelation statistic. The two entry triggers are deliberately plain so that what is being tested is the switch itself. Different from a variance-ratio or Hurst switch, both of which measure serial dependence; Geary's a measures distributional shape at a single lag and is insensitive to autocorrelation.
ideas.source: R.C. Geary (1935), 'The ratio of the mean deviation to the standard deviation as a test of normality', Biometrika 27; Geary (1936), Biometrika 28. The Wikipedia 'Normality test' article, opened this session, confirms 'the ratio of the mean absolute deviation to the standard deviation' as an early normality test statistic but gives no formula, so I derived the asymptotic mean sqrt(2/pi)=0.79788 and SD 0.21227/sqrt(n) myself by the delta method (using Var(|x|)=sigma^2(1-2/pi), Var(s)=sigma^2/(2n), Cov(|x|,x^2)=0.7979*sigma^3) and state them as derived, not quoted.

ideas.name: Wald-Wolfowitz Runs Regime Detector
ideas.entry_rule: Over the last n = 60 bars set s_t = sign(C_t - C_{t-1}) and discard zeros. Let Np = count of +1, Nm = count of -1, N = Np + Nm, and R = the observed number of runs (maximal blocks of identical sign). Under randomness mu = 2*Np*Nm/N + 1, sigma^2 = (mu-1)*(mu-2)/(N-1), and z_R = (R - mu)/sigma. TREND ENTRY: when z_R crosses below -2.0 today (z_R > -2.0 on the prior bar) - significantly TOO FEW runs, so signs persist - enter at the next open LONG if the sum of log returns over the last 60 bars > 0, SHORT if < 0. REVERSION ENTRY: when z_R crosses above +2.0 today (z_R < +2.0 on the prior bar) - significantly TOO MANY runs, so signs alternate - enter at the next open AGAINST the current bar: LONG if C_t < C_{t-1}, SHORT if C_t > C_{t-1}. No position while -2.0 <= z_R <= +2.0.
ideas.exit_rule: Trend leg: exit at the close when z_R rises back above -1.0, or on a trailing stop 3.0*ATR(14) from the extreme close since entry. Reversion leg: exit at the first close that closes against the entry bar's direction (i.e. one favourable close), or after 3 bars, or on a stop 1.5*ATR(14) from entry.
ideas.why: A variance ratio is a second-moment statistic and is badly contaminated by volatility clustering - conditional heteroskedasticity alone pushes VR away from 1 with no serial dependence in the conditional mean present at all, which is exactly why Lo-MacKinlay needs the heteroskedasticity-robust correction. The runs test throws away magnitudes entirely and looks only at the sign sequence, so it is distribution-free and completely immune to volatility clustering, fat tails, and outliers. It therefore answers the trend-versus-chop question with an orthogonal error structure to any variance-based detector, and disagreements between the two are themselves informative.
ideas.novelty: A distribution-free, sign-only randomness test as the regime signal, with an exact finite-sample null distribution. Not a variance ratio, not a Hurst exponent, not an autocorrelation - it is invariant to any monotone transformation of the magnitudes, which no second-moment detector is.
ideas.source: Wald & Wolfowitz (1940), 'On a test whether two samples are from the same population', Annals of Mathematical Statistics 11. Formulas for mu, sigma^2 and z verified this session against the Wikipedia 'Wald-Wolfowitz runs test' article (which sources them to the NIST Engineering Statistics Handbook, 'Runs Test for Detecting Non-randomness'). Application to price sign sequences as a chop detector, and the two-sided entry structure, are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Roughness Index of Log-Volatility
ideas.entry_rule: Daily volatility proxy: sigma_t = sqrt(RV_t) where RV_t = SUM of squared 5-minute log returns for session t. Set x_t = ln(sigma_t). Over a trailing window of T = 500 sessions and for each lag D in {1,2,3,4,5,8,12,16,25,40} compute the first absolute moment m(D) = (1/(T-D)) * SUM_t |x_{t+D} - x_t|. Fit H_vol = the OLS slope of ln m(D) on ln D across the ten lags (at q=1 the scaling m(q,D) ~ D^(qH) gives slope = H directly). PERSISTENT-VOL TREND ENTRY: LONG at the next open when H_vol >= 0.25 AND sigma_t >= its 70th percentile over the trailing 252 sessions AND the 20-session sum of daily log returns > 0; SHORT under the exact mirror (H_vol >= 0.25, sigma_t >= 70th percentile, 20-session sum < 0). ROUGH-VOL FADE ENTRY: when H_vol <= 0.08, SHORT at the next open if (C_t - SMA20)/ATR(14) >= +2.0, LONG at the next open if (C_t - SMA20)/ATR(14) <= -2.0. No trade for 0.08 < H_vol < 0.25.
ideas.exit_rule: Trend leg: hold while H_vol >= 0.20 and the sign of the 20-session return sum is unchanged; exit at the close when either fails, or on a trailing stop 3.0*ATR(14) from the extreme close since entry. Fade leg: exit at the close on the first touch of SMA20, or on a stop 2.0*ATR(14) from entry, or after 5 sessions.
ideas.why: Equity log-volatility is empirically a fractional Brownian motion with H of order 0.1 - it is far rougher than a standard diffusion, meaning a volatility shock decays almost immediately. When the rolling estimate of H_vol drifts up toward 0.25-0.35 the volatility process has temporarily become persistent: today's elevated volatility will still be here in a week. High AND persistent volatility with a directional tape is a regime that sustains trends, because the mean-reversion pressure that normally kills them is absent. Conversely at very low H_vol every volatility spike is a one-bar event, so a large ATR-normalized price excursion has no follow-through mechanism and should be faded.
ideas.novelty: The Hurst exponent is estimated on the LOG-VOLATILITY series, not on price. This is a completely different object from a price-based DFA or R/S Hurst: price H hovers near 0.5 and moves little, while vol H sits near 0.1 and its excursions are large and economically meaningful. The estimator is also different - it is the q=1 absolute-increment scaling used in the rough-volatility literature, not a rescaled-range or detrended-fluctuation calculation.
ideas.source: Gatheral, Jaisson & Rosenbaum, 'Volatility is rough', arXiv:1410.3394, published Quantitative Finance 18(6) 2018 - opened and verified this session; confirms 'log-volatility behaves essentially as a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst exponent H of order 0.1, at any reasonable time scale' and the m(q,Delta) ~ Delta^(qH) scaling framework. The rolling-window trading application and the two-branch entry are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Volume-Clock Compression Breakout
ideas.entry_rule: Rebuild the series in volume time. Over the last 20 sessions compute average daily dollar volume ADV$. Set bucket size B = ADV$/50. Walk the 1-minute bars in chronological order accumulating dollar volume, using typical price TP = (H+L+C)/3 so each 1-minute bar contributes TP*V. Each time the accumulator crosses B, close a VOLUME BAR: its open is the open of the first contributing 1-minute bar, its high and low are the extremes over all contributing bars, its close is the close of the bar in which the threshold was crossed; carry the overflow into the next bucket. Recompute B every 20 sessions. On this volume-bar series let u_j = ln(close_j/close_{j-1}) and sigma_V = stdev of the last 50 u_j. ENTER LONG at the close of volume bar j when close_j is the HIGHEST close of the last 50 volume bars AND sigma_V is at or below its 25th percentile over the last 1000 volume bars. ENTER SHORT when close_j is the LOWEST close of the last 50 volume bars under the same sigma_V condition.
ideas.exit_rule: Trailing stop, updated at each volume-bar close, placed 2.5 * sigma_V * (current close) below the highest close since entry for longs and above the lowest close since entry for shorts. Hard time stop: exit at the close of the 200th volume bar after entry. Flatten at the regular-session close (no overnight carry) since bucket accumulation is discontinuous across the gap.
ideas.why: Returns sampled in transaction or volume time are far closer to i.i.d. Gaussian than returns sampled in clock time - the fat tails and volatility clustering of clock-time returns are largely an artifact of the random, autocorrelated arrival of trading activity. Sampling by dollar volume subordinates the clock to the information flow and largely removes it. The consequence for a breakout system is decisive: a '50-bar extreme' in volume time carries the same statistical meaning at 09:45 as at 15:30, whereas in clock time it means two utterly different things, which is why clock-time breakout systems need time-of-day filters bolted on. The compression filter then becomes a genuine measure of information-flow-adjusted quiet.
ideas.novelty: The novelty is the SAMPLING SCHEME, not the trigger. Every excluded strategy operates on fixed clock-time bars; this one changes the clock itself, which changes the null distribution of every statistic computed on it. A clock-time Donchian breakout and a volume-time Donchian breakout fire on different bars, at different frequencies, and with different hit rates - they are not the same system with a different lookback.
ideas.source: Mandelbrot & Taylor (1967), 'On the distribution of stock price differences', Operations Research 15 - subordination of price to transaction time. Ane & Geman (2000), 'Order Flow, Transaction Clock, and Normality of Asset Returns', Journal of Finance 55(5) - the empirical demonstration that transaction-time returns are close to normal. Easley, Lopez de Prado & O'Hara (2012), 'The Volume Clock: Insights into the High Frequency Paradigm', Journal of Portfolio Management 39(1). Cited from knowledge - the web search budget for this session was already exhausted and I could not open these directly; the dollar-volume bucket construction above follows the standard volume-bar recipe.

ideas.name: Ulcer Index Downside Compression
ideas.entry_rule: Over a trailing window of N = 63 sessions, for each bar t in the window let P_t = the highest close from the start of the window through t (running peak) and R_t = 100 * (C_t - P_t) / P_t (a non-positive percentage retracement). Ulcer Index UI = sqrt( (1/N) * SUM R_t^2 ). Separately compute SD = the standard deviation of the last 63 daily log returns. ENTER LONG at the next open when ALL of: (a) UI is at or below its 15th percentile over the trailing 504 sessions; (b) SD is at or ABOVE its 40th percentile over the same 504 sessions; (c) C_t >= 0.97 * the highest close of the last 63 sessions. Long only.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next open when UI rises above its 60th percentile over the trailing 504 sessions. Concurrently hold a stop at the lowest low of the last 10 sessions, re-evaluated each close and only ever raised, never lowered.
ideas.why: Condition (b) is the whole point. Every symmetric volatility estimator - ATR, close-to-close stdev, Bollinger width, Keltner width - treats a 3% up day and a 3% down day identically, so a name grinding up with real daily range but shallow retracements reads as HIGH volatility and gets filtered out by every compression system. The Ulcer Index is a quadratic mean of drawdowns from the running peak, so it charges nothing for upside range and charges quadratically for depth and duration of declines. Low UI with ordinary SD is the precise fingerprint of a persistent uptrend with no distribution in it, and requiring SD to be ordinary excludes the dead low-volatility tape that a naive low-UI screen would otherwise return.
ideas.novelty: Path-dependent, downside-only, peak-referenced volatility used as the compression detector. It is not a variance, not a range, and not a percentile of either - it is a quadratic mean of drawdowns, which no other volatility statistic in the set can express. The requirement that TOTAL volatility be ordinary while DOWNSIDE volatility is at a multi-year low is a two-estimator divergence that a single symmetric estimator cannot produce.
ideas.source: Peter Martin (1987), the Ulcer Index; published in Peter Martin & Byron McCann (1989), 'The Investor's Guide to Fidelity Funds', John Wiley. Formula (R_i = 100*(price_i - max price)/max price; Ulcer = sqrt(mean of R_i^2)) and attribution verified this session against the Wikipedia 'Ulcer index' article. The SD-floor divergence condition and the entry/exit structure are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Extremal Index Cluster Switch
ideas.entry_rule: Over a trailing window of n = 500 daily log returns set the threshold u = the 95th percentile of |r|. Let the exceedance bar indices be S_1 < S_2 < ... < S_N (bars where |r| > u) and the inter-exceedance times T_i = S_{i+1} - S_i for i = 1..N-1. FERRO-SEGERS INTERVALS ESTIMATOR: if max(T_i) <= 2, theta = 2 * (SUM T_i)^2 / ((N-1) * SUM T_i^2); otherwise theta = 2 * (SUM (T_i - 1))^2 / ((N-1) * SUM (T_i - 1)*(T_i - 2)). Clamp theta to (0, 1]. The mean cluster size of extremes is 1/theta. Act only on days where |r_t| > u. CLUSTER MODE (theta <= 0.45, extremes arrive in clusters of 2 or more): on session t+1 place a stop-buy at H_t + 0.1*ATR(14) and a stop-sell at L_t - 0.1*ATR(14); take whichever fills first, cancel the other; if neither fills by the close of t+1 cancel both. ISOLATED MODE (theta >= 0.75, extremes arrive singly): enter AGAINST today's bar at the open of t+1 - SHORT if r_t > 0, LONG if r_t < 0. No trade when 0.45 < theta < 0.75, and no trade on any day that is not an exceedance.
ideas.exit_rule: Cluster mode: trailing stop 2.0*ATR(14) from the extreme close reached since entry, hard time stop 5 sessions. Isolated mode: profit target at C_{t-1} (the close immediately before the shock bar), stop 1.5*ATR(14) from entry, time stop 3 sessions.
ideas.why: Volatility clustering is universally acknowledged and almost never measured as such - GARCH and HAR measure the persistence of the volatility LEVEL, which is a different thing from the tendency of EXTREME moves to arrive in bunches. The extremal index theta is the exact extreme-value-theory parameter for that tendency, and 1/theta is directly interpretable as the expected number of large moves per cluster. It resolves the perennial ambiguity after a big bar: when theta is low the market is in a state where one shock begets another and a bracket is correct; when theta is near 1 the same-sized bar is a genuine isolated outlier and fading it is correct. Nothing in the standard toolkit distinguishes those two cases.
ideas.novelty: Extreme value theory as a live regime signal. Measures clustering of the tail specifically, using inter-exceedance times, rather than persistence of the conditional variance. Distinct from ARCH/GARCH persistence, from ATR expansion, and from every jump test - it is a property of the arrival PROCESS of extremes, not of any single extreme.
ideas.source: Ferro & Segers (2003), 'Inference for clusters of extreme values', Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series B 65(2) - the intervals estimator of the extremal index reproduced above. Leadbetter, Lindgren & Rootzen (1983), 'Extremes and Related Properties of Random Sequences and Processes' - the definition of the extremal index. Cited from knowledge; the web search budget was exhausted before I could open these, so verify the two-branch estimator formula against Ferro-Segers before implementation. The trading application is my synthesis.

ideas.name: ARCH-LM Clustering Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Take the last n = 250 daily log returns, demean to get e_t. Run the auxiliary OLS regression e_t^2 = b0 + b1*e_{t-1}^2 + b2*e_{t-2}^2 + b3*e_{t-3}^2 + b4*e_{t-4}^2 + b5*e_{t-5}^2 over the 245 usable observations, and take its R-squared. ARCH-LM statistic = 245 * R^2, which under the null of no ARCH effects is distributed chi-square with 5 degrees of freedom (5% critical value 11.070, 1% critical value 15.086). STRONG-CLUSTERING MODE when LM >= 15.086: volatility is demonstrably forecastable, so an expansion begets an expansion. Enter at the next open LONG when today's true range >= 2.0*ATR(20) AND C_t > O_t; SHORT when today's true range >= 2.0*ATR(20) AND C_t < O_t. NO-CLUSTERING MODE when LM <= 11.070: today's expansion carries no information about tomorrow's, so a large bar is an outlier to be faded. Enter at the next open AGAINST the bar under the identical true-range condition - SHORT if C_t > O_t, LONG if C_t < O_t. NO TRADE when 11.070 < LM < 15.086.
ideas.exit_rule: Strong-clustering leg: trailing stop 2.5*ATR(20) from the extreme close since entry; hard time stop 8 sessions. No-clustering leg: exit at the close on the first touch of SMA10, or on a stop 1.5*ATR(20) from entry, or after 3 sessions.
ideas.why: Every volatility breakout system in existence assumes volatility clustering is present. It usually is, but not always, and not in every name - and when it is absent, the identical trigger has the opposite correct response. The ARCH-LM test is the formal hypothesis test for exactly that assumption, computed on the very data the system is about to trade, with a known null distribution and a clean critical value. Rather than filtering the trigger, it selects which of two opposite trades to take, so the same setup makes money in both regimes instead of only one.
ideas.novelty: A specification test for the model assumption used as the direction switch, not as a filter. The excluded GARCH strategy uses the FITTED conditional variance (assuming ARCH is there); this uses the TEST for whether ARCH is there at all, and takes the opposite trade when it is not. Distinct from ATR expansion breakout, which fires unconditionally on the same trigger.
ideas.source: Engle (1982), 'Autoregressive Conditional Heteroscedasticity with Estimates of the Variance of United Kingdom Inflation', Econometrica 50(4) - the Lagrange multiplier test for ARCH effects, T*R^2 from the auxiliary regression of squared residuals on their own lags. Cited from knowledge (web search budget exhausted). The two-branch regime switch and the trading rules are my synthesis; chi-square critical values are standard table values.

ideas.name: Systematic Variance Share Regime
inputs: daily close of the traded symbol
ideas.entry_rule: Requires a second symbol from the same OHLCV feed - SPY. Over the last 60 sessions regress the stock's daily log returns r_t on SPY's daily log returns m_t with an intercept: r_t = alpha + beta*m_t + eps_t. Record beta, the residual standard deviation sigma_e, the residual series eps_t, and R^2. R^2 is the systematic variance share; 1 - R^2 is the idiosyncratic share. Rank R^2 against its own trailing 504-session history to get percentile P_R2. IDIOSYNCRATIC MODE when P_R2 <= 25: compute the 5-session cumulative residual CR = SUM of eps over the last 5 sessions. Enter LONG at the next open when CR <= -2.0 * sigma_e * sqrt(5); SHORT at the next open when CR >= +2.0 * sigma_e * sqrt(5). SYSTEMATIC MODE when P_R2 >= 75: enter LONG at the next open when SPY's close > SPY's SMA50 AND beta >= 1.0 AND the stock's close > its own SMA20; enter SHORT when SPY's close < SPY's SMA50 AND beta >= 1.0 AND the stock's close < its own SMA20. No trade when 25 < P_R2 < 75.
ideas.exit_rule: Idiosyncratic leg: exit at the close when CR crosses back through 0, or on a stop 2.0*ATR(14) from entry, or after 10 sessions. Systematic leg: exit at the next open when SPY closes back through its own SMA50 against the position, or on a trailing stop 3.0*ATR(14) from the extreme close since entry.
ideas.why: Total variance decomposes into a systematic part and an idiosyncratic part, and the two have opposite trading implications. When R^2 is high the name is a levered market proxy: fading its excursions means fading the index, which is a losing trade because index moves are the persistent component. When R^2 is low the name is trading on its own story and its excursions are genuinely idiosyncratic supply-demand imbalances, which do revert. The second refinement is that the idiosyncratic leg fades the RESIDUAL excursion, not the raw price excursion - so a stock down 6% in a week when the market is down 6% has a residual of roughly zero and is correctly left alone, while every ATR- or Bollinger-based fade would be screaming at it.
ideas.novelty: Decomposes volatility into systematic and idiosyncratic components and uses the SHARE as the regime switch, then trades the residual rather than the price. Every listed strategy operates on a single symbol in isolation and cannot distinguish a stock-specific dislocation from a market move that the stock merely inherited.
ideas.source: Campbell, Lettau, Malkiel & Xu (2001), 'Have Individual Stocks Become More Volatile? An Empirical Exploration of Idiosyncratic Risk', Journal of Finance 56(1) - the market/industry/idiosyncratic variance decomposition. Ang, Hodrick, Xing & Zhang (2006), 'The Cross-Section of Volatility and Expected Returns', Journal of Finance 61(1) - the idiosyncratic volatility measure from a market-model regression. Cited from knowledge (web search budget exhausted). Both are cross-sectional papers; the time-series regime-switch application and the residual-excursion entry are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Square-Root-of-Time Progress Exit
ideas.entry_rule: The exit is the idea; the entry is deliberately plain so the exit can be tested on its own. Daily bars: LONG at the close when C_t > the highest close of the prior 20 sessions; SHORT at the close when C_t < the lowest close of the prior 20 sessions. At the moment of entry FREEZE two values and never update them: the entry price E, and sigma_0 = the standard deviation of the last 20 daily log returns.
ideas.exit_rule: At the close of each bar k = 1, 2, 3, ... after entry compute: the diffusive benchmark displacement D_k = 0.79788 * sigma_0 * sqrt(k) - this is E|N(0, sigma_0^2 * k)| for a driftless random walk, since E|Z| = sqrt(2/pi) = 0.79788; the achieved signed displacement in the trade's favour A_k = side * ln(C_k / E) with side = +1 for long and -1 for short; and the progress ratio G_k = A_k / D_k. THREE EXITS: (1) EFFICIENCY EXIT - exit at the close if G_k < 0.5 on three consecutive bars with k >= 3. The position is not outrunning noise and has no edge left to justify the risk. (2) SATURATION EXIT - exit at the close the first time G_k >= 2.5. The move has run far ahead of what diffusion supports and is a reversal candidate; immediately re-arm the entry condition. (3) HARD STOP - a resting stop order at E * exp(-side * 1.5 * sigma_0), i.e. a one-and-a-half-sigma single-bar adverse move in log terms, placed at entry and never moved.
ideas.why: Every conventional exit compares the position to a FIXED distance (n ATR) or a FIXED time (n bars), but the correct benchmark for whether a trade is working is neither: a random walk with the same volatility would itself have wandered 0.798*sigma*sqrt(k) away from the entry after k bars by pure chance. A trade that is up half of that after twenty bars has demonstrated nothing and is paying full risk for it. Freezing sigma_0 at entry is essential - if sigma is recomputed live, the threshold widens exactly when the position gets into trouble, which is backwards. The sqrt(k) shape means the bar is lenient early, when noise dominates, and progressively demanding later, which is exactly the profile a fixed-time or fixed-distance stop cannot produce.
ideas.novelty: A pure exit structure benchmarked against the diffusive null rather than against a fixed distance or a fixed clock. It is materially different from a variance-budget clock: a budget exits on variance CONSUMED regardless of direction, so a fast choppy market that is nonetheless delivering displacement gets cut, and a quiet drift-nowhere market that has consumed almost no variance gets held. This rule does the opposite in both cases, because it measures the RATIO of directional displacement to expected diffusive displacement.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The benchmark is the Bachelier/Einstein sqrt(t) scaling of diffusive displacement, and the 0.79788 constant is E|Z| = sqrt(2/pi) for a standard normal - the same constant that converts a Parkinson volatility into an expected absolute move. I know of no published exit rule that uses the diffusive-progress ratio directly; the closest published relatives are Kaufman's Efficiency Ratio (which is a path-length ratio computed on a fixed lookback and is used as an entry filter, not an exit) and the time-stop literature, neither of which scales the threshold as sqrt(k).

ideas.name: Volatility Contraction Pattern (pinned down)
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars, long only. Define a swing high at bar i if H_i is the highest high of bars i-2 through i+2 (a 5-bar fractal, confirmed two bars later); a swing low symmetrically on lows. A CONTRACTION is a confirmed swing high at bar a followed by the next confirmed swing low at bar b > a, with depth D = (H_a - L_b) / H_a. Scan the last 60 sessions for the three most recent completed contractions, oldest first: D1, D2, D3 with swing highs H_a1, H_a2, H_a3 and swing lows L_b1, L_b2, L_b3. SETUP requires ALL of: (a) D1 > D2 > D3; (b) D3 <= 0.5 * D1; (c) D1 <= 0.35; (d) D3 >= 0.03; (e) H_a1 <= 1.02*H_a2 and H_a2 <= 1.02*H_a3 (the highs are not making lower highs); (f) mean volume over the bars of the third contraction (a3 through b3 inclusive) <= 0.65 * mean volume over the bars of the first contraction (a1 through b1 inclusive). When the setup is present let PIV = the highest high of the last 5 sessions. ENTER on a buy-stop at PIV + 0.05*ATR(14), good for 10 sessions, but only accept a fill on a bar whose volume >= 1.5 * the 50-session average volume; if the stop fills on a lower-volume bar, exit at that bar's close and cancel the setup.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at L_b3 (the swing low of the third and tightest contraction). Once price trades at or above PIV + 2*(PIV - L_b3), replace it with a trailing stop at the lowest low of the last 5 sessions, re-evaluated at each close and only ever raised. Cancel the setup entirely if any close falls below L_b3 before the buy-stop fills.
ideas.why: A Bollinger/Keltner squeeze is a single-scale statement: volatility is low right now. A contraction sequence is a multi-scale statement about how supply is being absorbed - each successive pullback is shallower because progressively fewer holders are willing to sell at progressively higher prices, and the volume dry-up on the tightest leg confirms that the remaining supply has actually been exhausted rather than merely deferred. That distinction determines whether the eventual breakout has anything overhead to fight. A single-window volatility statistic is mathematically incapable of expressing the SEQUENCE, because it averages over exactly the interval where the information lives.
ideas.novelty: A structural, multi-scale compression measured by the monotone decrease of successive pullback depths, with a volume-exhaustion confirmation. Not a band-width percentile, not an ATR percentile, not a squeeze indicator - it requires three ordered events with a specific ordering relation between them, which no single-window statistic can encode.
ideas.source: Mark Minervini (2013), 'Trade Like a Stock Market Wizard: How to Achieve Superperformance in Stocks in Any Market', McGraw-Hill - the Volatility Contraction Pattern (VCP), described there in terms of successive contractions of decreasing depth with diminishing volume. Cited from knowledge (web search budget exhausted). Minervini states the pattern qualitatively; the 5-bar fractal pivot definition, the D3 <= 0.5*D1 ratio, the 0.65 volume dry-up threshold, the 1.5x breakout volume requirement, and all numeric bounds above are my pinning-down of it into something a programmer can implement without judgement calls.

ideas.name: Price-Impact Compression (Amihud)
ideas.entry_rule: Daily. ILLIQ_t = (1/20) * SUM over i = t-19..t of |r_i| / (C_i * V_i), where r_i is the daily log return and C_i * V_i is dollar volume; scale by 1e6 for numerical convenience. This is price move per dollar traded - impact per unit of flow. Rank ILLIQ_t against its trailing 252-session history to get percentile P_I. Separately rank ATR(14)/C_t against its trailing 252-session history to get P_V. ARM the setup for the next 5 sessions whenever P_I >= 80 AND P_V <= 60 - high impact with ordinary volatility, meaning the book has thinned without the price having moved yet. On any armed session, at the close: LONG when (C_t - L_t)/(H_t - L_t) >= 0.80 AND volume_t >= 1.5 * the 20-session average volume; SHORT when (C_t - L_t)/(H_t - L_t) <= 0.20 AND volume_t >= 1.5 * the 20-session average volume. Disarm after a fill or after 5 sessions, whichever first.
ideas.exit_rule: Trailing stop 2.0*ATR(14) from the extreme close reached since entry, re-evaluated each close. Hard time stop of 10 sessions. Additionally exit at the next open if P_I falls below 40 - liquidity has returned and the impact edge is gone regardless of the position's P&L.
ideas.why: Amihud's ratio is the only widely-validated liquidity measure computable from daily bars alone, and it is measuring something no price-only estimator can see: the SLOPE of the demand curve, not the amount price has already moved. The distinctive cell is high impact with ordinary volatility. Ordinary ATR says the tape is calm; high ILLIQ says the calm is being produced by an absence of participants rather than an absence of disagreement. In that state the next genuinely sized order travels much further than its size would normally warrant, so the volume-confirmed directional close is a far stronger continuation signal than the same close in a thick book.
ideas.novelty: Volume enters as the DENOMINATOR of the signal, not as a confirmation multiplier. The entry condition is a divergence between two normalized series - impact high, volatility ordinary - which is structurally unavailable to any single-estimator system. Distinct from the microstructure noise ratio, which compares realized variances at two sampling grids and says nothing about size.
ideas.source: Amihud (2002), 'Illiquidity and stock returns: cross-section and time-series effects', Journal of Financial Markets 5(1) - the ILLIQ measure, defined as the daily average of |return| divided by dollar volume. Cited from knowledge; I attempted to fetch a reference page for it this session and got a 404, and the web search budget was already exhausted. The impact-versus-volatility divergence condition and the entry structure are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Semivariance-Asymmetric Bracket
ideas.entry_rule: Over the last N = 60 daily log returns r_i compute the two realized semi-deviations: sigma_up = sqrt( (1/N) * SUM over the r_i > 0 of r_i^2 ) and sigma_dn = sqrt( (1/N) * SUM over the r_i < 0 of r_i^2 ). Asymmetry A = sigma_dn / sigma_up. Entry trigger, deliberately plain so the bracket is what is being tested: LONG at the close when C_t > SMA50 AND (C_t - SMA20)/ATR(14) <= -1.0 AND C_t > C_{t-1}; SHORT at the close when C_t < SMA50 AND (C_t - SMA20)/ATR(14) >= +1.0 AND C_t < C_{t-1}. VETOES: skip the long entry entirely when A >= 1.6, and skip the short entry entirely when A <= 0.7 - the harmful branch of the distribution is so much heavier than the helpful one that no bracket has favourable geometry.
ideas.exit_rule: The idea is the bracket. Instead of a symmetric k*ATR stop and target, set with horizon H = 10 sessions: FOR LONGS - stop at entry_price * exp(-2.0 * sigma_dn * sqrt(H)), target at entry_price * exp(+2.0 * sigma_up * sqrt(H)). FOR SHORTS - stop at entry_price * exp(+2.0 * sigma_up * sqrt(H)), target at entry_price * exp(-2.0 * sigma_dn * sqrt(H)). Both are placed as resting orders at entry and never moved. If neither is touched, exit at the close of session H unconditionally.
ideas.why: Equity returns exhibit the leverage effect, so sigma_dn and sigma_up are systematically different numbers - typically sigma_dn / sigma_up runs 1.1 to 1.4 and can exceed 1.8 in stressed names. Every ATR- or standard-deviation-based bracket implicitly asserts they are equal, which means a symmetric bracket on a long position is simultaneously too tight on the stop and too near on the target. Sizing the stop by the volatility of the moves that can hurt the position and the target by the volatility of the moves that can help it makes the two legs equally probable in the distribution that actually generated the data. The veto is the second half: when the asymmetry is extreme enough, no placement of the two legs produces a favourable geometry, and the correct action is to skip the trade rather than reprice the bracket.
ideas.novelty: An exit structure whose two legs are sized by two DIFFERENT volatility estimators drawn from the same window, plus a distributional veto on the entry itself. Distinct from signed jump variation, which is an intraday entry SIGNAL; this is a daily-frequency bracket construction and a trade-selection filter. Every bracket in the existing set is symmetric in volatility units.
ideas.source: Barndorff-Nielsen, Kinnebrock & Shephard (2010), 'Measuring downside risk: realised semivariance', in Bollerslev, Russell & Watson (eds), 'Volatility and Time Series Econometrics: Essays in Honor of Robert F. Engle', Oxford University Press - the realized semivariance decomposition RV = RS+ + RS-. Cited from knowledge (web search budget exhausted). The asymmetric bracket construction, the sqrt(H) scaling, and the asymmetry veto are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Choppiness Index Regime Transition
ideas.entry_rule: CHOP(14) = 100 * log10( SUM of TR over the last 14 bars / (highest high of the last 14 bars - lowest low of the last 14 bars) ) / log10(14), where TR is the standard true range including gaps. The numerator is the path length walked and the denominator is the net ground covered, so CHOP is a fractal path-efficiency measure: high when price wanders, low when it goes somewhere. ENTER at the close of the bar on which CHOP(14) crosses DOWN through 38.2, provided CHOP(14) was >= 61.8 at some point in the previous 10 bars, AND the expansion gate holds: SUM of TR over the last 14 bars >= 1.2 * SUM of TR over the 14 bars immediately before that. Direction: LONG if C_t > C_{t-14}, SHORT if C_t < C_{t-14}. Note the entry may fire well INSIDE the prior 14-bar range - it is a transition in path efficiency, not a price-level breakout.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close when CHOP(14) rises back above 50, or on a trailing stop 2.5*ATR(14) from the most extreme close reached since entry - whichever comes first.
ideas.why: ADX measures directional movement passed through two layers of Wilder smoothing, so it confirms a trend only well after the turn. The Choppiness Index is an unsmoothed ratio of two quantities computed over the identical 14-bar window, so the moment efficiency improves is dated precisely rather than being spread across a smoothing lag. The expansion gate matters because CHOP can also fall when the denominator quietly widens on low true range, which is a completely different and untradeable state; requiring the summed true range to be growing forces the transition to be expansion-driven. The entry then fires at the point where the market stops retracing its own steps, which is typically inside the range and several bars before any breakout system will see anything.
