ideas.novelty: Fires on the regime transition itself and can enter mid-range, whereas Donchian, ATR-expansion and squeeze-release entries all require price to reach a range extreme first. The statistic is also structurally different from ADX: a ratio of summed true range to net Donchian range with no smoothing anywhere in it, versus a doubly-smoothed directional movement index.
ideas.source: E.W. Dreiss, the Choppiness Index (Dreiss fractal work, Australian commodity trading). Formula verified this session against TradingView's official indicator documentation: '100 * LOG10( SUM(ATR(1), n) / ( MaxHi(n) - MinLo(n) ) ) / LOG10(n)', with the standard Fibonacci-derived thresholds 61.8 for choppy and 38.2 for trending, attributed there to Dreiss. The crossing-with-prior-chop entry structure, the summed-true-range expansion gate, and the exit are my synthesis.

ideas.name: Random Walk Index multi-horizon trend gate
inputs: true range / ATR(n) for n in a grid
ideas.entry_rule: For every n in {8,10,12,...,64} (step 2) compute ATR_n = SMA(TrueRange, n), then RWIhigh_n(t) = (High_t - Low_{t-n}) / (ATR_n(t) * sqrt(n)) and RWIlow_n(t) = (High_{t-n} - Low_t) / (ATR_n(t) * sqrt(n)). Let RWIH_t = max over n of RWIhigh_n(t) and RWIL_t = max over n of RWIlow_n(t). ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when RWIH crosses from <= 1.0 on bar t-1 to > 1.0 on bar t, AND RWIL_t < 1.0, AND Close_t > Close_{t-1}. ENTER SHORT on the mirror: RWIL crosses above 1.0 while RWIH < 1.0 and Close_t < Close_{t-1}. Only one position at a time.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long when RWIH_t < 1.0 on two consecutive bars, or immediately reverse to short if RWIL_t > 1.0. Hard protective stop at entry - 2.0 * ATR(14); mirror for shorts. No time stop.
ideas.why: Under a pure random walk, displacement grows as sqrt(time) times the per-bar volatility, so (net displacement)/(ATR*sqrt(n)) has an expected value near 1 by construction. A reading above 1 is therefore a statistical rejection of the random-walk null at that horizon, not an arbitrary indicator level. Taking the maximum over a grid of n lets the data choose the horizon on which the trend is currently significant, so the system does not have to be told in advance whether it is trading a 10-day or a 60-day trend.
ideas.novelty: Unlike ADX(14) or an EMA cross, the threshold is dimensionless and has a null-hypothesis meaning, and the lookback is selected per bar by maximisation instead of being a fixed parameter. It also measures displacement from the opposite extreme n bars ago (High_t vs Low_{t-n}), which penalises choppy advances that a Donchian break ignores.
ideas.source: Michael Poulos, Random Walk Index, published in Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities (1991-1992). Formula cross-checked against the Poulos-credited RWI implementations documented in the TradingView public script library (fetched 2026-09-02), which give RWI_high = (High - Low n periods ago) / (ATR(n) * sqrt(n)) and note that values above 1 indicate non-random directional movement.

ideas.name: Vortex crossover with extreme-point pending order
ideas.entry_rule: Compute VM+_t = |High_t - Low_{t-1}|, VM-_t = |Low_t - High_{t-1}|, and TR_t = max(High_t - Low_t, |High_t - Close_{t-1}|, |Low_t - Close_{t-1}|). Sum each over 21 bars: VI+_t = sum(VM+, 21) / sum(TR, 21), VI-_t = sum(VM-, 21) / sum(TR, 21). On the bar c where VI+ crosses above VI- (VI+_{c-1} <= VI-_{c-1} and VI+_c > VI-_c) do NOT enter at the close. Record EP = High_c and place a resting buy stop at EP + 0.01. The order stays live for at most 10 bars; cancel it if VI- crosses back above VI+ first, or after 10 bars unfilled. Entry occurs intrabar when the stop fills. Mirror exactly for shorts using EP = Low_c and a sell stop at EP - 0.01.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long on the close of the first bar where VI- crosses above VI+. Protective stop from entry: Low_c - 0.01 (the low of the crossover bar), which does not move until the position is up 1 * ATR(14), after which trail it at the highest Low of the last 3 bars.
ideas.why: VM+ measures how far the current bar's high reaches above the PREVIOUS bar's low - a rotational or 'vortex' measure of how the market is turning around prior turning points, rather than the same-side extreme comparison Wilder uses for +DM/-DM. Normalising by summed true range makes it a fraction of the total movement claimed by each side. The extreme-point pending order is the published refinement: it forces the market to actually take out the crossover bar's high before capital is committed, which discards crossovers that were caused by a single volatile bar and never followed through.
ideas.novelty: Different construction from ADX/DMI (cross-bar rotational movement, not directional movement) and from Aroon (which measures time since the extreme, not distance). The load-bearing difference from a plain indicator cross is the expiring stop-entry at the signal bar's extreme, which converts a close-based signal into an event-based one.
ideas.source: Etienne Botes & Douglas Siepman, 'The Vortex Indicator', Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, 28(1), January 2010, pp. 21-25. Formulas and the 'enter at the extreme high or low of the price bar that corresponds with a crossing' refinement verified via the Wikipedia Vortex indicator article summarising that paper (fetched 2026-09-02).

ideas.name: Point-and-figure triple-top breakout on ATR-scaled boxes
ideas.timeframe: daily bars in, time-independent chart out
ideas.entry_rule: CONSTRUCT the P&F chart with A.W. Cohen's high/low method. Box size B is set on the first trading day of each calendar quarter as B = round(0.5 * ATR(20), 2), minimum 0.01, and held fixed for that quarter. Reversal = 3 boxes. State machine, one action per daily bar, extension taking priority over reversal: (a) if in an X column whose top is T: if High_t >= T + B then T := T + floor((High_t - T)/B) * B; else if Low_t <= T - 3B then start a new O column whose bottom D := T - floor((T - Low_t)/B) * B. (b) if in an O column whose bottom is D: if Low_t <= D - B then D := D - floor((D - Low_t)/B) * B; else if High_t >= D + 3B then start a new X column whose top T := D + floor((High_t - D)/B) * B. ENTRY LONG: at the instant the current X column's top exceeds the tops of BOTH of the two immediately preceding X columns - a Triple Top Breakout. Place the order as a buy stop at (max of those two prior X tops) + B, so the fill happens intrabar on the breakout day. SHORT mirror: current O column's bottom falls below the bottoms of both of the two preceding O columns (Triple Bottom Breakdown).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long on a Double Bottom Breakdown: the current O column's bottom falls below the bottom of the immediately preceding O column. That is the whole exit - there is no ATR stop and no time stop, because the 3-box reversal already embeds a volatility-scaled stop distance of 3B = 1.5 * ATR(20).
params: tops required (2 for double top, 3 for triple top)
ideas.why: P&F throws away time entirely: a bar that does not move price by a box does not exist on the chart. That removes the single largest source of noise in a breakout system - the many small bars that repeatedly re-arm and disarm a Donchian channel. A triple top additionally requires that the level has already turned the market away twice, so the breakout is through a level with demonstrated supply behind it, which a Donchian high does not require.
ideas.novelty: Not a rolling-window breakout at all. The trigger level is endogenous (a price the market has visited and been rejected from in two separate columns), the chart advances only on filtered price movement, and the exit is a structural column event rather than a stop distance.
ideas.source: A.W. Cohen's high/low point-and-figure method; Double Top Breakout and Triple Top Breakout definitions verified from StockCharts ChartSchool 'P&F Classic Patterns' (fetched 2026-09-02): a Double Top Breakout is 'an X-column breaks above the high of the prior X-column' with an O-column between; the Triple Top requires two prior X-columns at equal highs and a third exceeding both, spanning five columns. Traditional box scaling from the ChartCraft table popularised by Thomas Dorsey; I substituted ATR-proportional boxes so the rule is symbol-agnostic and sweepable.

ideas.name: Coppock trough turn-up with mirrored peak exit
ideas.entry_rule: Resample to monthly bars using the last trading day of each calendar month. ROC_k[m] = 100 * (Close[m] / Close[m-k] - 1). Raw[m] = ROC_14[m] + ROC_11[m]. Coppock[m] = WMA(Raw, 10) using linear weights 1..10 with weight 10 on the most recent value. ENTER LONG at the close of the last trading day of month m when ALL THREE hold: (1) Coppock[m] < 0; (2) Coppock[m] > Coppock[m-1]; (3) Coppock[m-1] <= Coppock[m-2]. That is a confirmed trough formed below the zero line. No entry if Coppock[m] >= 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Coppock published no sell rule, so I pinned the mirror image to make it testable: exit at the close of the first month where Coppock[m] > 0 AND Coppock[m] < Coppock[m-1] AND Coppock[m-1] >= Coppock[m-2] (a confirmed peak above zero). Secondary disaster exit: a monthly close more than 25% below the highest monthly close since entry.
params: daily variant: ROC 294 and 231 days, WMA 210 days
ideas.why: Coppock designed the curve after asking clergy how long people take to recover from bereavement, and used 11-14 months as the mourning period for a market decline. Mechanically it is a linearly-weighted average of two long overlapping rate-of-change series, which produces a very smooth curve whose troughs cluster near major lows. Requiring the trough to form BELOW zero means the signal only fires after genuine long-horizon damage, which is why it has historically produced very few signals with a high hit rate.
ideas.novelty: Not a moving-average cross and not a momentum sign test. The trigger is a second derivative event (a confirmed local minimum) on a weighted sum of two long ROCs, conditioned on being in negative territory. The month-end 10-month SMA rule already in the book fires on price crossing an average; this fires on the curvature of momentum turning, typically several months earlier.
ideas.source: E.S.C. Coppock, Barron's Magazine, 15 October 1962, originally called the 'Trendex Model'. Formula 'WMA[10] of (ROC[14] + ROC[11])', the below-zero trough buy rule, the absence of a sell rule, and the daily 294/231/210 conversion all verified from the Wikipedia Coppock curve article (fetched 2026-09-02).

ideas.name: KAMA noise-scaled excursion filter
inputs: rolling stdev of KAMA first differences
ideas.entry_rule: Efficiency Ratio ER_t = |Close_t - Close_{t-10}| / sum_{i=0..9} |Close_{t-i} - Close_{t-i-1}| (0 if the denominator is 0). Smoothing constant SC_t = [ ER_t * (2/(2+1) - 2/(30+1)) + 2/(30+1) ]^2. KAMA_t = KAMA_{t-1} + SC_t * (Close_t - KAMA_{t-1}), seeded with SMA(Close,10). FILTER_t = 0.1 * stdev(KAMA_i - KAMA_{i-1} for i in t-19..t). Maintain KAMA_min = the lowest KAMA value recorded since the system last went short (or since inception), and KAMA_max = the highest KAMA value since it last went long. ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when KAMA_t - KAMA_min > FILTER_t; on that entry reset KAMA_max := KAMA_t. ENTER SHORT when KAMA_max - KAMA_t > FILTER_t; on that entry reset KAMA_min := KAMA_t.
ideas.exit_rule: The system is always in the market: the long is closed by the short entry condition and vice versa (stop-and-reverse). Optional risk overlay that does not change the signal: flatten to cash if the open position is worse than -3.0 * ATR(20) from entry, and stay flat until the next opposite signal.
ideas.why: The efficiency ratio makes the average sprint in a directional market and crawl in a sideways one, so the average itself already adapts. The filter then solves the remaining problem: a slow-moving average still wiggles, and the size of that wiggle depends on the regime. Scaling the entry threshold to the standard deviation of KAMA's own bar-to-bar changes means the trigger demands a move that is large relative to how much the average is currently jittering, which is a self-calibrating noise gate rather than a fixed number of ticks.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is a volatility-scaled displacement from the average's own local extreme, not the sign of the slope (Hull MA slope) and not a price/average crossover (EMA cross). Because the reference is a running extreme that only resets on a signal, the system will not flip on a single bar's turn - it requires the average to travel a measured distance back from its high-water mark.
ideas.source: Perry J. Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average. KAMA(10,2,30) formula - ER = Change/Volatility, SC = [ER * (2/3 - 2/31) + 2/31]^2, KAMA = prior KAMA + SC*(Price - prior KAMA), seeded with an SMA - verified from StockCharts ChartSchool 'Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA)' (fetched 2026-09-02). The percent-of-standard-deviation entry filter is Kaufman's own published refinement (Smarter Trading, 1995; Trading Systems and Methods); I pinned the coefficient at 0.1 and left it sweepable.

ideas.name: Dual-timeframe weighted-ROC (KST) trigger
ideas.entry_rule: Define RCMA_i = SMA(ROC(n_i), s_i) where ROC(n)[t] = 100*(Close_t/Close_{t-n} - 1). DAILY KST: (n,s) pairs (10,10), (15,10), (20,10), (30,15); KST_d = 1*RCMA1 + 2*RCMA2 + 3*RCMA3 + 4*RCMA4; Signal_d = SMA(KST_d, 9). MONTHLY KST on month-end closes: (n,s) pairs (9,6), (12,6), (18,6), (24,9); same 1/2/3/4 weights; Signal_m = SMA(KST_m, 9). ENTER LONG at the close of daily bar t when ALL of: (1) on the most recently COMPLETED month, KST_m > Signal_m; (2) KST_m > 0; (3) KST_d crosses above Signal_d on bar t (KST_d[t-1] <= Signal_d[t-1] and KST_d[t] > Signal_d[t]); (4) KST_d[t] > KST_d[t-1]. SHORT is the exact mirror with KST_m < Signal_m, KST_m < 0, and a downward daily signal-line cross.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the long on whichever comes first: (a) KST_d crosses below Signal_d, or (b) the newly completed month shows KST_m < Signal_m. Hard stop at entry - 2.5 * ATR(14) that never widens.
ideas.why: A single-horizon oscillator has to choose which cycle it is measuring. KST sums four smoothed rates of change spanning roughly two weeks to six weeks (daily) or nine to twenty-four months (monthly) and weights the longer horizons more heavily, so the composite only turns when several horizons agree, with the slow ones carrying the vote. Gating daily signals on the monthly composite means the fast trigger is only allowed to fire in the direction of the long cycle, which is the source of most of the edge in oscillator systems.
ideas.novelty: MACD is a difference of two EMAs at one horizon and TRIX is a triple-smoothed single ROC. KST is a weighted SUM of four independently smoothed ROCs at four horizons with fixed 1:2:3:4 weights - a different functional form that cannot be reproduced by tuning MACD parameters. The monthly-gates-daily structure is also a different gating variable from the ADX gate already in the book.
ideas.source: Martin J. Pring's Know Sure Thing. Parameters KST(10,15,20,30,10,10,10,15,9) for the short-term/daily version and KST(9,12,18,24,6,6,6,9,9) for the long-term/monthly version, the 1/2/3/4 weighting, the 9-period signal line, and Pring's preference for signal-line crossovers over centreline crossovers on longer timeframes - all verified from StockCharts ChartSchool 'Pring's Know Sure Thing (KST)' (fetched 2026-09-02).

ideas.name: Dunnigan thrust after a held retest
ideas.entry_rule: Define an UP-THRUST on bar v as: High_v > High_{v-1} AND Close_v > Close_{v-1}. Define a DOWN-THRUST as: Low_v < Low_{v-1} AND Close_v < Close_{v-1}. LONG SEQUENCE: (1) Bar b makes a 20-bar low: Low_b = min(Low[b-19 .. b]). Record L0 = Low_b and A = ATR(20)_b. (2) Within bars b+1 .. b+15, find the first bar u that satisfies EITHER (2a) the TEST - Low_u >= L0 AND Low_u <= L0 + 0.25*A, after at least one intervening bar whose Low was above L0 + 0.5*A (so the market left the low and came back to it); OR (2b) the CLOSING PRICE REVERSAL - Low_u < L0 AND Close_u > Close_{u-1} AND Close_u > (High_u + Low_u)/2. (3) ENTER LONG at the close of the first bar v > u that is an UP-THRUST. If no up-thrust occurs within 5 bars of u, cancel the setup and wait for a new 20-bar low. REPEAT SIGNAL (pyramiding): if a further up-thrust occurs within 5 bars of v while the position is open and the position is profitable, add one more unit, to a maximum of 2 units. SHORT is the exact mirror around a 20-bar high.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial stop at min(L0, Low_u) - 0.05. Once the position is up 1.5 * A, move the stop to breakeven. Trailing exit: close the whole position at the close of the first bar that is a DOWN-THRUST whose Close is also below the Low of the highest-closing bar recorded since entry. Hard time stop: exit at the close of bar v+30 if neither the trail nor the stop has fired.
params: test tolerance as a fraction of ATR (default 0.25)
required departure before the retest (default 0.5 ATR)
thrust window after the test (default 5 bars)
ideas.why: Dunnigan's insight, from the era before indicators existed, is that a valid turn has a specific bar grammar: the market must revisit its low and fail to make a new one (or make one and close strongly off it), and then it must show a bar that both extends higher and settles higher. Requiring BOTH a higher high and a higher close rejects the two common failure modes separately - an upside probe that closes weak, and a quiet inside bar that closes up. Counting repeat thrusts as an add signal makes position size a function of how many times the market has demonstrated that grammar, not of a fixed pyramid distance.
ideas.novelty: Entry is a matched sequence of named bar relationships with a state machine, not an indicator level or a channel break, and the position scales by counting confirmations rather than by price distance. The retest-that-holds requirement means the system buys strength AFTER weakness was tested, which is structurally different from the breakout entries already in the book.
ideas.source: William Dunnigan, 'One-Way Formula for Trading in Stocks and Commodities' (1954), and his earlier Thrust Method; the clearest modern restatement of the thrust definition (higher high plus higher close), the 'test of the low', the closing price reversal and the repeat-signal rule is in Perry J. Kaufman, 'Trading Systems and Methods', in the chapter on event-driven trends. Dunnigan's original tolerances were stated in points for 1950s commodity contracts, so I pinned all of them to ATR fractions and bar counts to make the rule symbol-agnostic and testable.

ideas.name: GMMA compression-then-agreement expansion
ideas.entry_rule: Short group S = EMA(Close) at periods {3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15}. Long group L = EMA(Close) at periods {30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60}. Define Wshort_t = (max(S_t) - min(S_t)) / Close_t and Wlong_t = (max(L_t) - min(L_t)) / Close_t. ENTER LONG at the close of bar t when ALL FOUR hold: (1) SEPARATION - min(S_t) > max(L_t), every short-group EMA above every long-group EMA; (2) PRIOR COMPRESSION - there exists k in 1..10 such that Wshort_{t-k} <= the 5th percentile of Wshort over bars t-129 .. t-10; (3) AGREEMENT EXPANSION - Wlong_t > Wlong_{t-5} AND Wlong_t > Wlong_{t-10}; (4) PRICE CONFIRMATION - Close_t > max(High[t-20 .. t-1]).
ideas.exit_rule: Two-stage. Stage 1, reduce to half size when Wlong has contracted for three consecutive bars (Wlong_t < Wlong_{t-1} < Wlong_{t-2} < Wlong_{t-3}) - the long ribbon compressing means the slow money is losing conviction. Stage 2, close the remainder when min(S_t) < max(L_t), i.e. the short ribbon penetrates back into the long ribbon. Hard stop at entry - 2.0 * ATR(20).
ideas.why: Guppy's framing is that the short ribbon is traders and the long ribbon is investors. When the short ribbon compresses, traders have stopped disagreeing about price - the argument is over and the next move is about to be decided. When the LONG ribbon then widens, longer-horizon holders are moving in at increasingly different prices, which is what a genuine repricing looks like. Compression followed by slow-group expansion is therefore a two-part statement about who is agreeing and who is committing, in a form that a single crossover cannot express.
ideas.novelty: The signal is the WIDTH DYNAMICS of two EMA groups, not the crossing of two lines - specifically, a percentile-low width in the fast group followed by widening in the slow group. An EMA cross carries no information about how much the participants at different horizons agree, and a Bollinger squeeze measures price dispersion rather than the dispersion of participant horizons.
ideas.source: Daryl Guppy, Guppy Multiple Moving Average (GMMA), set out in 'Trend Trading' and 'Better Stock Trading'. The two period sets 3-5-8-10-12-15 and 30-35-40-45-50-60 are Guppy's published values as reproduced in every major charting package; guppytraders.com returned HTTP 400 during this pass so I could not re-verify from his own site. The compression-percentile and expansion tests are my mechanical pinning of Guppy's qualitative 'compression and expansion' language.

ideas.name: Momentum Pinball: RSI of one-day rate of change, first-hour trigger
ideas.timeframe: daily selection, intraday (1 or 5 minute) trigger
inputs: RSI(3) applied to a differenced series
ideas.entry_rule: On daily bars compute ROC1_t = Close_t - Close_{t-1} (a price difference, not a percentage). Compute LBR_t = RSI(3) using Wilder smoothing applied to the ROC1 SERIES, not to price. AT THE DAILY CLOSE OF BAR t: if LBR_t < 30, tomorrow is a designated BUY DAY; if LBR_t > 70, tomorrow is a designated SELL DAY; otherwise stand aside. ON THE DESIGNATED SESSION t+1: build H1 = the highest high and L1 = the lowest low of the first 60 minutes of regular trading hours. If it is a buy day, place a buy stop at H1 + 0.01, live from 10:30 US/Eastern until 15:45; if it is a sell day, place a sell stop at L1 - 0.01 over the same window. Take only the pre-designated side - do not trade the opposite break. Cancel unfilled orders at 15:45.
ideas.exit_rule: Protective stop at the opposite first-hour extreme (L1 - 0.01 for a long, H1 + 0.01 for a short); if it is hit, no re-entry that day. Otherwise hold and exit at the CLOSE OF THE FOLLOWING SESSION (t+2), which is Raschke and Connors' roughly one-day hold. Optional earlier exit: take profits at 2.0 * ATR(14) of daily bars from entry.
params: RSI length on the ROC series (default 3)
first-hour window length (default 60 minutes; sweep 30 and 90)
hold length (default exit at the close of t+2)
ideas.why: Applying RSI to the one-day price CHANGE rather than to price turns a trend oscillator into a very short-horizon exhaustion meter: it measures whether recent daily moves have been persistently in one direction relative to their own magnitudes, which saturates far faster than price-based RSI. A low reading says the sequence of daily changes has been stretched to the downside. The setup then refuses to buy weakness directly - it waits for the next session to take out its own first-hour high, so the market has to prove the exhaustion has resolved before capital is committed.
ideas.novelty: Two separable novelties: the oscillator is computed on a differenced series rather than on price, and the SIDE of the intraday breakout is pre-committed the night before by a countertrend reading. The opening-range rules already in the book trade whichever side breaks; this one refuses the other side entirely, which is a different trade with a different loss profile.
ideas.source: Linda Bradford Raschke & Laurence A. Connors, 'Street Smarts: High Probability Short-Term Trading Strategies' (M. Gordon Publishing, 1995) - the Momentum Pinball setup. The exact session-clock windows and the 0.01 offsets are my pinning; Raschke's original is stated in terms of 'the first hour's high' without a cut-off time.

ideas.name: Oops! opening-gap failure reversal
ideas.timeframe: daily (needs the session open, so 1-minute bars for exact fills)
ideas.entry_rule: LONG: at the session open of day t, require Open_t < Low_{t-1}. Size the gap: G = Low_{t-1} - Open_t. Require 0.25 * ATR(10)_{t-1} <= G <= 1.5 * ATR(10)_{t-1}. If both hold, place a buy stop at Low_{t-1} + 0.01, live for session t only, cancelled at 15:45 US/Eastern. SHORT: Open_t > High_{t-1}, G = Open_t - High_{t-1} inside the same ATR band, sell stop at High_{t-1} - 0.01. No other filters, no indicator gate.
ideas.exit_rule: Williams' original is a day trade: exit at the session close of day t. Protective stop for a long at the lowest Low printed between the open and the moment of entry, minus 0.05; if that has not yet formed, use Open_t - 0.25 * ATR(10). SWING VARIANT to test alongside: hold to the close of day t+1 with a trailing stop at the prior bar's Low - 0.25 * ATR(10).
ideas.why: An opening gap below yesterday's low is a batch of orders that accumulated overnight executing at once. If the level that was breached is then reclaimed within the session, the sellers who forced the gap have been absorbed and the people who sold into the open are trapped below the market - they become buyers. The upper gap bound matters: a genuinely large gap usually reflects real repricing and should not be faded, which is why the rule caps gap size rather than rewarding it.
ideas.novelty: It is the only rule in the set that keys off the relationship between TODAY'S OPEN and YESTERDAY'S EXTREME, and it fires before the session has produced any range at all - so no opening-range, VWAP, or intraday-indicator rule can generate it. It is also a failure-of-continuation trade rather than a failure-of-reversal trade, which is the opposite of the liquidity-sweep logic already in the book.
ideas.source: Larry Williams, 'Long-Term Secrets to Short-Term Trading' (Wiley, 1999) - the 'Oops!' pattern (open below yesterday's low, buy on the return through yesterday's low). The ATR-scaled minimum and maximum gap band is my pinning of Williams' qualitative warning that the pattern should not be traded on very large gaps.

ideas.name: Volume-Conditioned Autocorrelation Switch
ideas.entry_rule: For each symbol, at each session close, using the trailing 200 sessions: r_d = ln(close_d/close_{d-1}); v_d = ln(volume_d) minus the mean of ln(volume) over the 200 sessions ending at d-1 (detrended log volume - since shares outstanding is essentially constant over 200 sessions this equals detrended log turnover up to an additive constant). Estimate by OLS r_{d+1} = c0 + c1*r_d + c2*(v_d * r_d) + e over the window, requiring at least 150 valid observations. Classify the symbol LIQUIDITY-DRIVEN if c2 < 0 with t-stat < -1.96; INFORMATION-DRIVEN if c2 > 0 with t-stat > +1.96; otherwise UNCLASSIFIED and never traded. Then at the close of session t require BOTH v_t > +0.5 (volume at least e^0.5 = 1.65x its 200-day typical level) AND |r_t| >= 1.0 * ATR(14)/close_t. If the symbol is LIQUIDITY-DRIVEN: go LONG at the close when r_t < 0, SHORT at the close when r_t > 0. If the symbol is INFORMATION-DRIVEN: take the OPPOSITE side (LONG when r_t > 0, SHORT when r_t < 0).
ideas.exit_rule: Close at the close of session t+1 (one-session hold). Stop out intraday at 2.5 * ATR(14) adverse from entry. Re-estimate c2 every 21 sessions; if a held name's classification flips or drops to UNCLASSIFIED at a re-estimation, close it at the next session's close.
ideas.why: Llorente, Michaely, Saar and Wang derive and confirm that 'returns generated by risk-sharing trades tend to reverse themselves while returns generated by speculative trades tend to continue themselves.' Whether a high-volume price move reverses is therefore a property of the STOCK, not of the setup - it depends on how much informed/speculative trading that name carries. They find stocks of small firms or with wide bid-ask spreads show continuation after high-volume days, while large firms and tight-spread stocks show reversal. The c2 coefficient on the volume-return interaction is a direct per-name estimate of which regime a symbol is in.
ideas.novelty: The SIGN of the trade is estimated from the symbol's own history rather than assumed. The identical setup - big volume, big move - produces a long in one stock and a short in another on the same day. Every volume-conditioned rule on the existing list assumes reversal universally and uses volume or illiquidity only as a static filter on which names qualify.
ideas.source: Guillermo Llorente, Roni Michaely, Gideon Saar, Jiang Wang, 'Dynamic Volume-Return Relation of Individual Stocks', NBER Working Paper 8312 (May 2001), published Review of Financial Studies 15 (2002) 1005-1047. PDF opened this session (custom font encoding decoded); the risk-sharing-reverses / speculative-continues sentence and the small-firm and bid-ask-spread cross-sectional results are quoted from its abstract and introduction.

ideas.name: Bounce-Free Midpoint Reversal with Spread Hurdle
ideas.entry_rule: For each session define the log range midpoint eta_d = (ln(high_d) + ln(low_d))/2 and the log close c_d = ln(close_d). Estimate the effective spread with the Abdi-Ranaldo two-day corrected estimator over the trailing N = 21 sessions: S_i = (1/N) * SUM over d of sqrt( max{ (c_d - eta_d) * (c_d - eta_{d+1}), 0 } ), then take the full spread as 2 * S_i. Compute the reversal signal on MIDPOINTS, not closes: MR_i = eta_t - eta_{t-5}. Cross-sectionally demean over U (close > $5, 20-session median dollar volume > $10M): MRdm_i = MR_i - mean(MR over U). Enter market-on-close: LONG the 10 most negative MRdm_i and SHORT the 10 most positive MRdm_i, equal dollar weight - but include a name ONLY if |MRdm_i| > 4 * S_i. Any name failing the cost hurdle is skipped and the next-ranked name is taken in its place.
ideas.exit_rule: Close market-on-close after 5 sessions, or earlier on the first session where eta_t crosses back through its own 21-session mean (target reached). Force-close any name whose estimated spread 2*S_i doubles versus its value at entry (liquidity has deteriorated and the edge no longer clears cost).
ideas.why: Nagel's construction makes the point explicitly: he computes reversal returns from both closing transaction prices and quote midpoints precisely because a large part of measured short-horizon reversal is bid-ask bounce in transaction prices rather than genuine negative serial correlation in the efficient price. Corwin-Schultz and Abdi-Ranaldo establish the OHLCV substitute: the daily high tends to be a buy at the ask and the low a sell at the bid, so the high-low midpoint cancels the two half-spreads and is a much better estimate of the efficient price than the close. Building the signal on midpoints removes the fake component of the edge, and the same paper's estimator prices the round trip so you only trade what clears it.
ideas.novelty: The input price series itself is different - the strategy never looks at a closing transaction price for the signal - and entry is gated by an estimated transaction cost computed from the same bars. Cross-sectional reversal rules on the existing list all rank on close-to-close returns and have no cost gate, so they systematically select the widest-spread names, where the apparent reversal is largest and least real.
ideas.source: Stefan Nagel, 'Evaporating Liquidity', NBER Working Paper 17653 (Dec 2011), RFS 25 (2012) 2005-2039, for the transaction-price-versus-midpoint decomposition (PDF opened this session). Estimator from Farshid Abdi and Angelo Ranaldo, 'A simple estimation of bid-ask spreads from daily close, high, and low prices', Review of Financial Studies 30 (2017) 4437-4480, building on Shane Corwin and Paul Schultz, Journal of Finance 67 (2012) 719-759 and Richard Roll, Journal of Finance 39 (1984) 1127-1139 - exact two-day corrected formula transcribed from lecture notes on the estimator opened this session.

ideas.name: VPIN Toxicity Exhaustion Fade
ideas.entry_rule: On 1-minute bars, set bucket size V = (mean daily volume over the trailing 20 sessions) / 50 and fill buckets sequentially with 1-minute bar volume, splitting a bar's volume across a bucket boundary. Bulk Volume Classification: for each 1-minute bar j, dP_j = close_j - close_{j-1} and sigma = stdev of dP over the trailing 250 one-minute bars; buy volume of bar j = volume_j * Z(dP_j / sigma) where Z is the standard normal CDF, sell volume = volume_j - buy volume. Sum within each bucket to get V_buy_tau and V_sell_tau. Then VPIN_tau = SUM over the last n = 50 buckets of |V_sell_tau - V_buy_tau| / (n * V). Define CDF(VPIN) as the percentile rank of the current VPIN within its own trailing 250-bucket history. ENTRY: when CDF(VPIN) has been >= 0.90 for at least 3 consecutive buckets and then crosses back DOWN through 0.90, measure MOVE = close of the current bar minus close of the bar at which CDF first crossed above 0.90, and FADE it - enter SHORT if MOVE > 0, LONG if MOVE < 0. Require |MOVE| >= 1.5 * ATR(14 daily) / close and current time between 10:00 and 15:30 ET.
ideas.exit_rule: Take profit at a 50% retracement of MOVE back toward the episode's starting price. Stop at 1.0 * |MOVE| beyond the episode extreme. Hard exit at 15:55 ET the same session regardless. Cancel and stand aside if CDF(VPIN) re-crosses above 0.90 while the position is open - the toxic episode was not actually over.
ideas.why: Easley, Lopez de Prado and O'Hara define order flow as toxic when it adversely selects the liquidity provider, and VPIN measures it as persistent volume imbalance in VOLUME time rather than clock time. Their central result is that high VPIN presages toxicity-induced volatility - it is a warning that supplying liquidity right now is unprofitable. The tradeable inference is the complement: once CDF(VPIN) falls back below its 0.90 threshold the informed flow has finished executing, the remaining price displacement is inventory-driven rather than information-driven, and the market maker's job becomes profitable again. Fading at the onset of toxicity is exactly what loses money; fading its decay is the liquidity-provision trade.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is an order-flow statistic computed in volume time from bars alone, and the entry fires on the DECAY of the statistic rather than on any price threshold. No rule on the existing list uses volume-clock sampling, signed volume, or a condition that requires a prior state to have persisted and then ended. It is also distinct from a realized-semivariance sort, which is a monthly cross-sectional rank of squared returns rather than an intraday imbalance event.
ideas.source: David Easley, Marcos Lopez de Prado, Maureen O'Hara, 'Flow Toxicity and Liquidity in a High Frequency World', Review of Financial Studies 25 (2012) 1457-1493. Full PDF opened this session - equation (9) for VPIN, the V = 1/50 of average daily volume and n = 50 baseline, the rolling-drop bucket update, the bulk volume classification of 1-minute time bars, and the CDF(VPIN) crossing 0.9 threshold used in their flash-crash analysis are all taken from the paper text. Parameter robustness confirmed in Song, Wu and Simon, 'Parameter Analysis of the VPIN Metric', Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (2014), also opened this session.

ideas.name: Expiration-Week Strike Pin and Monday Release
ideas.timeframe: daily bars with 15:45 ET intraday entry
params: entry days Wed+Thu (try Thu only, Tue-Thu)
ideas.entry_rule: Strike grid: for a stock priced P the listed strike increment is $1.00 if P < $25, $2.50 if $25 <= P < $200, $5.00 if P >= $200. Nearest strike K = round(P / increment) * increment. Pin distance PD = (P - K) / P. Restrict to the Monday-Friday week containing the third Friday of the month, and to names with 20-session median dollar volume > $50M and close > $15 (a proxy for carrying liquid listed options). PIN LEG: at 15:45 ET on the Wednesday and the Thursday of expiration week, using P = the 15:45 price, enter SHORT if PD >= +0.4 * (ATR(14)/close) and LONG if PD <= -0.4 * (ATR(14)/close), and require |PD| <= 1.5 * (ATR(14)/close) so the strike is realistically reachable by Friday. Cap at 10 names per side, ranked by |PD|. RELEASE LEG: at the open on the Monday following expiration, for every name whose expiration-Friday close was within 0.25% of a strike, enter in the direction of the trailing 5-session drift measured up to the Wednesday BEFORE expiration (long if that drift was positive, short if negative).
ideas.exit_rule: Pin leg: close market-on-close on expiration Friday, unconditionally. Release leg: close market-on-close on that following Monday, unconditionally. No position from this rule is ever carried into a second session. Abort a pin entry intraday if price moves more than 2.0 * ATR(14) further away from K.
ideas.why: Ni, Pearson and Poteshman document that on expiration dates the closing prices of optionable stocks cluster at strike prices, and that on each expiration date the returns of optionable stocks are altered by an average of at least 16.5 basis points, worth roughly $9bn of market-cap displacement. Two mechanisms produce it: delta-hedge rebalancing of net purchased option positions, which mechanically pushes the stock toward the strike as gamma explodes near expiry (the Avellaneda-Lipkin pinning model), and deliberate price manipulation by traders short options who want them to expire at or just out of the money. Both are hedging constraints, not information, so both must release once the options expire - Klemkosky's early study finds roughly +0.4% in the week following expiration after about -1% in the week leading in.
ideas.novelty: The attractor is a fixed price grid derived from the option strike ladder and the exchange calendar, not a moving average, band, VWAP or statistical mean - and crucially the attractor does not move when the price moves. It also has a defined expiry: the same rule flips from mean-reverting to trend-resuming at a known timestamp. No options data is required; the strike grid and the third-Friday calendar reconstruct it from price level alone.
ideas.source: Sophie Xiaoyan Ni, Neil D. Pearson, Allen M. Poteshman, 'Stock Price Clustering on Option Expiration Dates', University of Illinois working paper 27 Aug 2004, published Journal of Financial Economics 78 (2005) 49-87. Full PDF opened this session - the 16.5bp / $9bn figures, the $5.00 and $2.50 strike grid, the third-Friday convention, the delta-hedging and manipulation mechanisms, and the citation to Klemkosky's -1% before / +0.4% after result are all taken from its text. Pinning model: Marco Avellaneda and Michael Lipkin, 'A market-induced mechanism for stock pinning', Quantitative Finance 3 (2003) 417-425.

ideas.name: Parkinson Efficiency Mean-Reversion Gate
ideas.entry_rule: REGIME: for each symbol over the trailing 20 sessions compute the Parkinson range volatility PARK = sqrt( (1/(4*ln 2)) * mean( (ln(high_d/low_d))^2 ) ) and the close-to-close volatility CC = stdev( ln(close_d/close_{d-1}) ). Form Q = PARK / CC. Under a driftless random walk E[Q] is approximately 1; Q > 1 means the path travelled far further than its net displacement (oscillation), Q < 1 means moves persisted within the day and gapped across days (trending). Classify the symbol OSCILLATING on session t if Q_t >= its own 120-session 70th percentile. TRADE, only in the OSCILLATING regime, on 15-minute bars between 10:00 and 15:00 ET: let O = the session's 09:30 opening price and B = (mean over the trailing 20 sessions of (high_d - low_d)) / 2. Enter LONG when a 15-minute bar closes below O - 1.0 * B AND that bar's close is above its own open. Enter SHORT when a 15-minute bar closes above O + 1.0 * B AND that bar's close is below its own open. Maximum 2 entries per symbol per session.
ideas.exit_rule: Target: the session open O. Stop: 1.5 times the entry distance |entry - O| beyond the entry, away from O. Hard exit at 15:50 ET the same session - never carried overnight. Cancel all pending setups for the session if the symbol's regime flips out of OSCILLATING at the prior close.
ideas.why: The high-low range measures the distance the price actually travelled during the session; the close-to-close return measures only where it ended up. Their ratio is a direct estimate of path efficiency, and it separates two situations that look identical to any close-only statistic: a stock that oscillated all day around its open, and a stock that trended cleanly from open to close. Only the first is safe to fade. Range-based estimators are also far more efficient than close-to-close ones for the same sample size, so the regime classification stabilizes on 20 sessions where a close-only test needs several times as much history.
ideas.novelty: The regime test compares a range estimator against a close-to-close estimator - it uses the high and low, which a Lo-MacKinlay variance ratio structurally cannot see because it is built from closing prices at multiple horizons. Two symbols with identical close-to-close volatility and identical variance ratios receive opposite classifications here depending on how much intraday travel produced that volatility. The trade is also different: intraday reversion to the session open rather than a multi-day ATR-scaled fade.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The two estimators are Michael Parkinson, 'The extreme value method for estimating the variance of the rate of return', Journal of Business 53 (1980) 61-65, and the standard close-to-close estimator; their relative efficiency and the use of the range as a volatility proxy are established in Sassan Alizadeh, Michael Brandt, Francis Diebold, 'Range-based estimation of stochastic volatility models', Journal of Finance 57 (2002) 1047-1091. The RATIO of the two as a mean-reversion regime classifier, and the session-open reversion trade built on it, are my own construction and I am not aware of a paper that tests exactly this - it should be treated as an untested hypothesis rather than a documented effect.

ideas.name: Quiet Volume Shock
ideas.entry_rule: At each session close, for each symbol in U (close > $5, 20-session median dollar volume > $10M) compute VR_t = volume_t / mean(volume, 50), the 5-session move R5 = close_t/close_{t-5} - 1, and its typical scale TYP = stdev of the trailing 250 rolling 5-session returns. LONG entry at the close when ALL hold: volume_t is the strict maximum of the trailing 50 sessions, VR_t >= 2.0, |R5| <= 0.5 * TYP (the price did NOT move despite the volume), and close_t > close_{t-1}. SHORT entry at the close when ALL hold: volume_t is the strict MINIMUM of the trailing 50 sessions, |R5| <= 0.5 * TYP, and close_t < close_{t-1}. Cap at 10 names per side per session, ranked by VR_t on the long side and by 1/VR_t on the short side.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold 20 sessions and close market-on-close. Stop at 2.5 * ATR(14) adverse from entry. Close early at the session close where the name's 5-session return exceeds 2 * TYP in the direction of the trade (the visibility repricing has completed).
ideas.why: Extreme volume with no accompanying price move is an attention event, not an information event: unusual trading activity makes a stock visible to investors who otherwise would not have considered it, and because most investors can buy but not short, that visibility translates into net buying pressure over the following weeks. Gervais, Kaniel and Mingelgrin document that stocks experiencing unusually HIGH volume over a day or a week subsequently rise and unusually LOW volume names subsequently fall, independent of the direction of the price move that accompanied the volume. The quiet-price condition is what isolates attention from information - if the price moved with the volume, something was learned and the shock is not a pure visibility event.
ideas.novelty: It fires on a volume event with NO price event, which is precisely the case every reversal rule on the existing list ignores because they all need a price move to fade. It is also the documented SIGN FLIP that a naive 'fade the high-volume mover' rule gets backwards, so it doubles as a veto: any reversal signal whose trigger bar was also a 50-session volume maximum with a small net move should be suppressed rather than traded contrarian. The short leg is triggered by volume DROUGHT, which no rule on the list uses at all.
ideas.source: Simon Gervais, Ron Kaniel, Dan Mingelgrin, 'The High-Volume Return Premium', Journal of Finance 56 (2001) 877-919. Attention mechanism and the buy/short asymmetry from Brad Barber and Terrance Odean, 'All That Glitters: The Effect of Attention and News on the Buying Behavior of Individual and Institutional Investors', Review of Financial Studies 21 (2008) 785-818 - Barber-Odean PDF opened this session; the Gervais-Kaniel-Mingelgrin specification is cited from knowledge.

ideas.name: Earnings-Anniversary Volume Concentration
ideas.entry_rule: Announcement-month proxy (no earnings feed): flag any past calendar month for a stock if it contains at least one session with volume >= 3x that stock's trailing 60-session median volume AND |close-to-close return| >= 2x its trailing 60-session daily return standard deviation. Keep only stocks with EXACTLY 4 flagged months in the trailing 12 calendar months (quarterly-cadence check). Volume concentration ratio VCR = (total share volume falling in flagged months over calendar months m-27..m-4, i.e. a 24-month window lagged 3 months) / (total share volume over those same 24 months). At the 16:00 close of the last trading day of month m-1, a stock is an 'expected announcer' for month m if month m-12 was flagged. Go long equal dollar weight every expected announcer in the top tercile of VCR; go short equal dollar weight every non-expected-announcer in the bottom tercile of VCR. Universe filter: price > $5 and 60-session median dollar volume > $5m.
ideas.exit_rule: Liquidate the entire book at the 16:00 close of the last trading day of month m, then re-form for month m+1. Fixed one-calendar-month hold, no stops.
ideas.why: Quarterly earnings are scheduled, and scheduled attention events attract predictable retail buying pressure with no offsetting short-selling. The price rise is not confined to the 3-day event window: there is a ~25bp run-up in the 10 days before, ~21bp over the 3-day window, and ~30bp of drift after, which is why a whole-month hold captures more than an event window. Sorting on volume concentration selects the names whose attention spike is largest, and the paper shows this cross-sectional difference is extremely persistent (still works when you use only data from 4-6 years ago).
ideas.novelty: Nothing in the existing set is stock-specific calendar seasonality driven by a recurring firm event. It is not a moving-average or oscillator rule at all: the signal is 'which month of the year does this particular stock's volume cluster in', reconstructed from OHLCV alone via volume spikes. Distinct from the already-found same-calendar-month annual seasonality, which uses past RETURNS in the same month; this uses past VOLUME CONCENTRATION and a quarterly rather than annual cycle.
ideas.source: Frazzini & Lamont, 'The Earnings Announcement Premium and Trading Volume', NBER Working Paper 13090 (May 2007) - PDF fetched and read directly this session. Verified specifics: long expected-announcers / short expected-non-announcers earns 61bp per month, t > 5, annual Sharpe 0.94 (higher than value, size, momentum or the market over the same period); 7-18% per year across specifications; announcement months predicted from last year's announcement month gives 93% accuracy for firms with 4 announcements in the prior year; the sorting variable is the volume concentration ratio (percent of total share volume over the previous four years occurring in announcement months), lagged 3 months; day-0 volume is more than 50% above normal, which is what makes the volume-spike proxy viable; effect present continuously since 1926.

ideas.name: Ariel Semi-Month Exposure Split
ideas.entry_rule: Partition each calendar month by trading-day index. Long leg: buy the index proxy at the 16:00 close of the LAST trading day of month m-1 and hold. Short leg: at the 16:00 close of the 9th trading day of month m, close the long and open an equal-size short in the same instrument. Both legs are unconditional on price - the only input is the position of the session in the month, from the exchange session calendar.
ideas.exit_rule: Close the long at the 16:00 close of the 9th trading day of month m (which is also the short entry). Close the short at the 16:00 close of the SECOND-TO-LAST trading day of month m, going flat for one session so the last trading day rolls into the next month's long leg. Softened form: run full gross in the first half and 0-30% gross in the second half instead of an outright short.
params: hard short vs reduced-gross second half
whether the last day of month m-1 is included in the long leg
ideas.why: Ariel found that the entire positive mean return of the US market accrued in the first half of the month, defined as the last trading day of the prior month plus roughly the first nine trading days, with the second half flat to negative. Whether the cause is cash-flow timing, information release clustering, or something else, the partition is a clean unconditional test that costs one round trip a month.
ideas.novelty: Deliberately picked because it CONTRADICTS an idea already in the set. The existing turn-of-month cash-cycle window shorts on the 3rd trading day of the new month; Ariel says trading days 1-9 are the strongest long stretch of the month. Those two rules take opposite positions on the same sessions, so running both is a direct horse race rather than a duplication. The 9-trading-day span and the second-half short leg are also a different partition from any turn-of-month window in the set.
ideas.source: Ariel, 'A Monthly Effect in Stock Returns', Journal of Financial Economics 18(1), 1987 - cited from the literature; not re-fetched this session (search budget exhausted). The exact split point (Ariel uses the last day of the prior month plus the first half of the month by trading-day count) is pinned to the 9th trading day here so the rule is unambiguous; sweep it.

ideas.name: Leveraged-ETF Rebalance Drift Into The Close
ideas.entry_rule: At the 15:15 ET bar on every session compute R = (SPY last price / SPY previous session's official 16:00 close) - 1 and sigma = the standard deviation of SPY daily close-to-close returns over the previous 60 sessions. If R > +1.0 x sigma, BUY at the 15:15 bar open. If R < -1.0 x sigma, SHORT at the 15:15 bar open. Otherwise no trade. Amplified variant: instead of SPY, trade the sector ETF (from a fixed list of the eleven liquid SPDR sector ETFs) with the largest 60-session beta to SPY, since levered products on that sector concentrate the same flow into a thinner book. Optional gate: require cumulative session volume through 15:15 to be above its 20-session median for that slot.
ideas.exit_rule: Leg 1: exit at the official 16:00 close. Leg 2: immediately take the OPPOSITE position at the 16:00 close and exit at the next session's 09:30 open, capturing the partial give-back once the mechanical demand is gone.
inputs: sector ETF daily bars for the beta variant
params: whether to run the overnight give-back leg
ideas.why: A daily-reset leveraged or inverse ETF must end each day with exposure equal to its multiple times its new NAV. Because NAV moves with the index, the required rebalance is always in the SAME direction as the day's move, and its size scales with (leverage squared minus leverage) times AUM times the day's return - so it is convex in the magnitude of the move and effectively zero on quiet days. That trade has to be done near the close to track the daily reset, which produces same-direction pressure in the final 30-45 minutes on large-move days and a partial reversal once the non-information flow stops.
ideas.novelty: The existing selloff-into-the-close idea is a long-only, asymmetric fade of a large last-hour DOWN move. This one is symmetric, is triggered by the size of the whole SESSION's move rather than the last hour's, goes WITH the move into the close rather than against it, and only then fades overnight. Opposite sign in the closing window, different conditioning variable, and a mechanical rather than behavioural story.
ideas.source: Synthesis of a well-documented mechanism. Cheng & Madhavan, 'The Dynamics of Leveraged and Inverse Exchange-Traded Funds' (Barclays Global Investors, 2009), derive the (leverage^2 - leverage) x AUM x return rebalancing formula and the end-of-day concentration; the mechanism is also the subject of SEC/FINRA investor alerts on leveraged ETFs. I could not re-fetch these this session (search budget exhausted; arXiv returned HTTP 429), so the specific thresholds and the two-leg structure are my construction on top of the published mechanics, not a rule lifted from a paper.

ideas.name: Closing-Imbalance Window Momentum
ideas.entry_rule: Both primary US exchanges begin publishing closing-auction order imbalances at 15:50 ET. We cannot see that feed, but the price reaction to it is in the bars. Let P1 = close of the 15:49 one-minute bar and P2 = close of the 15:52 one-minute bar. Compute d = P2/P1 - 1. Let q = the 70th percentile of |d| over the previous 60 sessions for that symbol. Require participation confirmation: summed volume of the 15:50, 15:51 and 15:52 one-minute bars > 1.5x the 20-session median of that same three-slot sum. If d > q, BUY at the 15:53 bar open. If d < -q, SHORT at the 15:53 bar open. Otherwise no trade. Restrict to symbols with 60-session median dollar volume > $50m so the auction is meaningful.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the official 16:00 closing print (submit as market-on-close). Never carried overnight. No intraday stop - the horizon is seven minutes.
ideas.why: The imbalance publication at 15:50 is a scheduled information release with a fixed clock time. When a large one-sided closing imbalance is published, liquidity providers and closing-auction arbitrageurs move the continuous market toward the expected auction clearing price over the following minutes, and the auction then prints at or beyond that level. The first two or three minutes after 15:50 are therefore a readable proxy for the sign and size of the imbalance itself, and the drift toward the auction has not finished by 15:53.
ideas.novelty: Nothing in the existing set uses the 15:50 imbalance publication as a scheduled intraday event. It is the opposite trade to the already-found closing-auction deviation fade: that one waits for the auction print and fades the 15:59-to-auction dislocation, whereas this rides the pre-auction adjustment INTO the print. The two can be run together and will rarely both fire on the same side, which makes them a useful pair rather than a duplication.
ideas.source: Synthesis. Grounded in the published exchange mechanics - NYSE and Nasdaq begin disseminating closing-auction imbalance information at 15:50 ET - and in the closing-auction price-discovery literature. The three-minute price-reaction proxy for the unobservable imbalance feed is my construction; no paper states this exact rule.

ideas.name: Conditional Monday By Week-Of-Month
ideas.entry_rule: At the 16:00 close of the last trading session of each calendar week (normally Friday), compute W = the index proxy's return over that trading week (this session's close / the close of the last session of the previous trading week - 1) and let D = the calendar day-of-month of the NEXT trading session. Rule A: if W < 0 AND D >= 18, SHORT the index proxy at this session's 16:00 close. Rule B: if W > 0 AND D <= 14, BUY the index proxy at this session's 16:00 close. Otherwise no trade. Generalise 'Monday' properly: apply the rule whenever the gap in calendar days between the current session and the next session is >= 3, so Tuesdays following a Monday holiday are treated as week-opens too.
ideas.exit_rule: Close the position at the 16:00 close of the next trading session (the week-open session). One-session hold, always, no stop.
inputs: weekly return of the index proxy
params: whether to include the long leg at all
calendar-gap definition of a week-open (>=3 vs exactly weekend)
ideas.why: The unconditional Monday effect has weakened to the point of being untradeable, but the conditional version has held up better in the published work: negative Monday returns are concentrated in the last two weeks of the month, and cluster after weeks that already ended down. The proposed mechanisms - settlement and cash-timing effects late in the month, and information processing over a weekend that follows bad news - both predict conditioning rather than an unconditional day dummy.
ideas.novelty: The existing Friday-to-Monday rotation is a cross-sectional trade on a speculativeness score, and it always fires. This is index-level, fires only on the conditional subset (roughly a quarter of weeks), takes a sign from the prior week's return, and generalises the weekend to any session preceded by a multi-day calendar gap - which the existing weekday ideas do not do. Two different conditioning variables and a different instrument.
ideas.source: Wang, Li & Erickson, 'A New Look at the Monday Effect', Journal of Finance 52(5), 1997 - documents that the Monday effect is concentrated in the last two weeks of the month; cited from the literature, not re-fetched this session (search budget exhausted). The prior-week-sign conditioning follows the conditional-weekend-effect literature (Jaffe, Westerfield & Ma and successors); the multi-day-gap generalisation of 'Monday' is my own tightening.

ideas.name: Half-Day Session Effect
ideas.entry_rule: Detect half-days from the bars themselves, no external table needed: a session is a half-day if its last regular-hours one-minute bar is 12:59 rather than 15:59 (US equity early closes are 13:00 ET). Verified current examples: the day after Thanksgiving every year (27 Nov 2026, 26 Nov 2027) and 3 July when it falls on a weekday and is not itself the observed holiday. Leg A (the crossover): buy the index proxy at the 16:00 close of the session BEFORE the half-day and hold. Leg B (the shortened session's own drift): buy the index proxy at the 09:30 open of the half-day itself. Run A and B as separate books so their contributions are separable.
ideas.exit_rule: Leg A: sell at the 13:00 official close of the half-day. Leg B: sell at the same 13:00 close. Optional Leg C: at the 12:45 bar open on the half-day, take a position in the direction of the session's move so far (last price versus the 09:30 open) and exit at the 13:00 close, since the whole day's closing auction is compressed into those fifteen minutes.
inputs: 1-minute bar timestamps (to detect the 12:59 last bar)
params: which legs to run (A / B / C)
whether to require a positive Leg-A entry-day return
ideas.why: Half-days combine every ingredient of the pre-holiday effect - thin participation, no institutional appetite to initiate risk, short-sellers reluctant to carry exposure across a long weekend - with a compressed session in which the entire day's closing auction demand has to clear in fifteen minutes against a very thin book. They are also the sessions professional desks most often skip, so whatever flow does arrive faces less competition than usual.
ideas.novelty: The half-day is invisible to the rule already in the set: the existing pre-holiday trade keys on the session before a full-day CLOSURE, and a half-day is a session, not a closure, so that rule never fires on these dates. This adds a distinct set of dates, and Leg C is a time-of-day trade that only exists on a shortened session because 12:45-13:00 is the only fifteen-minute window in the year that is simultaneously a lunch-hour slot and a closing auction run-up.
ideas.source: Half-day schedule verified this session from nyse.com/markets/hours-calendars: markets close early at 1:00 p.m. on the day after Thanksgiving (27 Nov 2026, 26 Nov 2027) and on Independence Day observed 3 July 2026, with the full 2026-2027 closure list also confirmed there. The underlying pre-holiday return literature is Ariel, 'High Stock Returns Before Holidays', Journal of Business 63(4), 1990, and Lakonishok & Smidt, 'Are Seasonal Anomalies Real?', Review of Financial Studies 1(4), 1988 - cited from the literature. The half-day-specific legs are my construction.

ideas.name: Santa Window Signal Not Just Trade
ideas.entry_rule: Define the Santa window S as the last 5 trading days of December plus the first 2 trading days of January - 7 sessions, fixed by the exchange calendar. Leg 1 (the trade): buy the index proxy at the 16:00 close of the 6th-to-last trading day of December. Leg 2 (the signal, which is the real point): at the 16:00 close of the 2nd trading day of January, compute the window return r_S = (that close / the close of the 6th-to-last December session) - 1. If r_S < 0, SHORT the index proxy at that close; if r_S > +1.0%, go LONG at that close. If 0 <= r_S <= +1.0%, no January position.
ideas.exit_rule: Leg 1: sell at the 16:00 close of the 2nd trading day of January (which is also the Leg 2 evaluation point). Leg 2: hold the conditional January position for exactly 15 trading sessions and close at the 16:00 close of session 15. No stop on either leg.
params: whether Leg 2 shorts or merely goes flat on a negative window
ideas.why: The seven-session window sits in the thinnest liquidity of the year: institutional books are closed for the year, tax-loss selling has finished, and the remaining flow is retail and bonus money. The mean return over the window is genuinely positive. The more interesting claim, and the one that makes this worth coding, is the conditional one: when a window this reliably positive fails to deliver, it is evidence that a large seller is present who could not wait for better liquidity, which is informative about January.
ideas.novelty: The existing December ideas are cross-sectional (tax-loss losers) and month-end (turn-of-month). This is an index-level, precisely-dated 7-session window that straddles the year boundary, and its main content is Leg 2 - using the window's realised return as a conditioning SIGNAL for a subsequent position, not just harvesting the window. That signal-not-just-trade structure appears nowhere in the set. Honest caveat: the window overlaps the already-found turn-of-month December dates, so run them as separate books and check the correlation before stacking them.
ideas.source: Window definition verified this session from the Wikipedia entry on the Santa Claus rally: 'the last 5 trading days in December and the first 2 trading days in the following January', first documented by Yale Hirsch in the 1972 Stock Trader's Almanac; the 2019 Almanac reports an average 1.3% gain over the seven days and a 76% hit rate since 1950/1969. Practitioner source, not peer-reviewed - treat the base rate accordingly. Leg 2 (the conditional January signal) is Hirsch's 'if Santa Claus should fail to call' heuristic, pinned down here into a testable rule by me.

ideas.name: Length-Of-Night Exposure Tilt
ideas.entry_rule: Compute, purely from the date and a fixed latitude (use 40.7N for New York), the number of hours of night H_t using the standard solar-declination formula. Define the SAD variable: SAD_t = H_t - 12 for sessions between the autumn equinox (about 21 September) and the spring equinox (about 20 March), and SAD_t = 0 otherwise. Define an asymmetry dummy FALL_t = 1 for sessions between the autumn equinox and 31 December, else 0. Exposure rule: target gross long exposure in the index proxy of E_t = clip(1.0 + a x SAD_t - b x FALL_t x SAD_t, 0, 2.0) with base coefficients a = 0.25 and b = 0.55. In practice this means: reduced or negative exposure through late September, October and November as nights lengthen, maximum exposure from the winter solstice through February as nights shorten from their peak, and neutral exposure from late March through mid-September. Rebalance the position to E_t at each session's 16:00 close whenever |E_t - current exposure| > 0.15.
ideas.exit_rule: No discrete exit - this is a continuously rebalanced exposure schedule. The position is fully unwound (E_t = 1.0, the neutral level, or 0 in the pure form) between the spring and autumn equinoxes. Cap turnover with the 0.15 rebalance band.
inputs: solar declination formula (no market data required)
ideas.why: Kamstra, Kramer and Levi argue that the fraction of the population affected by seasonal affective disorder rises with the length of night, that affected investors become more risk averse, and that this produces depressed prices in autumn as nights lengthen and elevated returns through winter as the affected population recovers. Whatever one makes of the mechanism, the resulting exposure schedule is an entirely deterministic function of the date - it needs no market data at all to compute - which makes it unusually clean to test and impossible to overfit to price history.
ideas.novelty: The existing Halloween gate is a binary six-month switch with the same exposure every day from 1 November to 30 April. This is a continuous function of the date with an explicit asymmetry: it is SHORT (or minimum exposure) through the autumn as nights lengthen and LONG through the winter as they shorten, which means it disagrees with the Halloween gate for roughly two months every autumn - specifically the November stretch where Halloween is already maximally long. That disagreement window is the whole test.
ideas.source: Kamstra, Kramer & Levi, 'Winter Blues: A SAD Stock Market Cycle', American Economic Review 93(1), 2003 - cited from the literature; I attempted to fetch the Atlanta Fed working-paper version this session and got a 404, and the search budget was exhausted, so the exact published coefficient values were not re-verified. The SAD variable definition (hours of night minus 12, nonzero only in the autumn-to-spring half of the year) and the fall dummy are as specified in that paper; the coefficient magnitudes a and b given here are indicative starting points for a sweep, not the paper's estimates.

ideas.name: Diurnal Volume-Pace Day Typing
ideas.entry_rule: Build the intraday volume-completion curve: for each 5-minute slot s from 09:30 to 15:55, compute F_s = the median over the previous 20 sessions of (cumulative regular-hours volume through slot s divided by that session's total regular-hours volume). This is the empirical U-shape and it is symbol-specific. Let V20 = the 20-session median of total regular-hours volume. At 12:00 ET compute the pace ratio p = (today's cumulative volume through 12:00) / (F_1200 x V20). Then, for every 5-minute bar from 12:00 to 15:30: if p >= 1.5, take TREND entries only - buy at the next bar's open when a bar closes above the highest high of the session so far, short at the next bar's open when a bar closes below the lowest low of the session so far. If p <= 0.70, take FADE entries only - short at the next bar's open when a bar closes above the session high so far, buy when a bar closes below the session low so far. If 0.70 < p < 1.5, no trades that afternoon. One position at a time; a reverse signal flips the position.
ideas.exit_rule: All positions are liquidated at the 15:55 bar close, flat overnight. Optional protective stop at 1.5x the 20-session median 5-minute bar range for the current slot (a time-of-day-scaled stop rather than a fixed one). No profit target - the exit is the clock.
inputs: session high and low so far
ideas.why: Intraday volume follows a very stable U-shape, so by midday you can estimate how the day's total participation compares with normal, and that estimate says which kind of day you are in. A day running 50% hot by noon is a day with real information flow and a large participant working an order, and breakouts on such days tend to extend. A day running 30% light is one where nobody is there, the book is thin, and any push through the session extreme is a small order walking a shallow book rather than genuine demand - so it snaps back. Same breakout trigger, opposite sign, chosen by the shape of the day's participation.
ideas.novelty: The existing diurnal ideas use a slot-local measure: relative volume in one bar, or the median range of one slot. This uses the CUMULATIVE completion curve - the U-shape as an integral rather than a point - to classify the whole day, and then flips the SIGN of an otherwise ordinary session-extreme breakout. Nothing in the set flips the direction of a breakout rule based on participation. It also differs from the excluded opening-range breakout in that there is no fixed range window: the reference is the running session extreme, and the afternoon-only restriction plus the sign switch are the substance.
ideas.source: Synthesis. Grounded in the intraday periodicity literature - Jain & Joh, 'The Dependence between Hourly Prices and Trading Volume', Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 23(3), 1988 (the volume U-shape), and Andersen & Bollerslev, 'Intraday Periodicity and Volatility Persistence in Financial Markets', Journal of Empirical Finance 4(2-3), 1997 (the deterministic intraday volatility pattern and the case for deseasonalising by time of day before doing anything else). Cited from the literature, not re-fetched this session. The pace-ratio day-typing rule and the sign flip are mine.

ideas.name: Piercing Line with Sub-Low Open
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars. Let bar1 = bar[-1], bar2 = bar[0]. LONG requires ALL: (a) downtrend, close(bar1) < EMA(10) of close; (b) bar1 is black: open1 > close1; (c) body1 = open1 - close1 >= 1.0 x ATR(14); (d) bar2 OPENS BELOW BAR1'S LOW: open2 < low1; (e) bar2 is white and closes back into bar1's body above its midpoint but NOT above its open: 0.5*(open1+close1) < close2 < open1; (f) close2 > low1. Enter long at the close of bar2. SHORT (dark cloud cover) is the exact mirror: uptrend close(bar1) > EMA(10); bar1 white with body >= 1.0 x ATR(14); open2 > high1; 0.5*(open1+close1) > close2 > open1; close2 < high1; short at the close of bar2. A full engulf (close2 >= open1) DISQUALIFIES the signal.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 3rd bar after entry (fixed hold), or earlier if stopped at low1 - 0.25 x ATR(14) for longs / high1 + 0.25 x ATR(14) for shorts. No profit target.
ideas.why: The open below the prior bar's LOW traps every seller who chased the breakdown overnight; the recovery back above the midpoint of the prior body is the point at which their position is disproved and they must cover. Deliberately excluding the full engulf keeps the signal at the moment of maximum trapped supply rather than after it has already been released. Bulkowski's sample ranks the piercing pattern 13th of 103 candles and finds it acts as a bullish reversal 64% of the time - one of the few named reversal candles that empirically does what its name says.
ideas.source: Bulkowski, Encyclopedia of Candlestick Charts; pattern page https://thepatternsite.com/Piercing.html (overall performance rank 13/103, frequency rank 40, 'acts as a bullish reversal 64% of the time', requires the second candle to open below the black candle's LOW and close between the midpoint and the open). Formal inequality PL: O1 > C2 > L1 > O2 & C2 > 0.5(O1+C1) & downtrend from Goo, Chen & Chang (2007), reproduced in Tharavanij, Siraprapasiri & Rajchamaha (2017), 'Profitability of Candlestick Charting Patterns in the Stock Exchange of Thailand', SAGE Open, doi:10.1177/2158244017736799.
ideas.novelty: Not an engulfing variant: the entry bar must open below the prior bar's LOW (not merely below its close) and must close only PARTWAY into the prior body - a full engulf is an explicit disqualifier. Penetration depth becomes a swept parameter instead of a binary engulf test.

ideas.name: Homing Pigeon / Descending Hawk (same-colour body containment)
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars. Both bars must be the SAME colour and the second body must sit strictly inside the first body. LONG (homing pigeon), requires ALL: (a) downtrend, close(bar1) < EMA(10) of close; (b) bar1 black: open1 > close1; (c) bar2 black: open2 > close2; (d) strict body containment on both edges: open1 > open2 AND close2 > close1; (e) body1 = open1 - close1 >= 1.0 x ATR(14); (f) body2 = open2 - close2 <= 0.50 x body1. Enter long at the close of bar2. SHORT (descending hawk) is the exact mirror: uptrend close(bar1) > EMA(10); both bars white; close1 > close2 > open2 > open1; body1 >= 1.0 x ATR(14); body2 <= 0.50 x body1; short at the close of bar2. No condition is placed on highs or lows - bar2's range may exceed bar1's.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 5th bar after entry. Stop at low(bar2) - 0.50 x ATR(14) for longs, high(bar2) + 0.50 x ATR(14) for shorts. Variant to sweep: instead of entering at the close of bar2, place a buy stop at high(bar2) + 0.01 valid 2 bars.
params: entry mode: close vs stop above bar2 high
ideas.why: A second down bar that opens above the prior close and still cannot print a lower close is a failure to extend: sellers had a full session and produced nothing. Because the bar is still black, every scanner and every discretionary eye classifies it as continued weakness, so the signal is under-arbitraged relative to the harami, which everyone watches. Shiu & Lu (2011) found that harami-family two-day signals on the Taiwan exchange generated significant positive abnormal returns.
ideas.source: Goo, Chen & Chang (2007) formal definitions - Homing Pigeon: O1 > O2 > C2 > C1 & downtrend; Descending Hawk: C1 > C2 > O2 > O1 & uptrend - reproduced with the full pattern table in Tharavanij, Siraprapasiri & Rajchamaha (2017), SAGE Open, doi:10.1177/2158244017736799. Abnormal-return evidence for two-day harami-family patterns: Shiu & Lu (2011), cited therein.
ideas.novelty: Body containment where BOTH bars share the same colour. A harami requires opposite colours; a classical inside bar is defined on highs and lows. This is defined purely on opens and closes and will fire on bars whose high/low range is NOT contained by the prior bar - a set of setups the inside-bar and harami rules both miss.

ideas.name: Three-Line Strike Traded Against Its Name
ideas.category: multi-bar candlestick, contrarian to nominal signal
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars, four-bar pattern A=bar[-3], B=bar[-2], C=bar[-1], D=bar[0]. SHORT SIGNAL (the so-called BULLISH three-line strike): (a) A, B, C all white (close > open) with close(A) < close(B) < close(C) and low(A) < low(B) < low(C); (b) each of A, B, C has body >= 0.50 x its own range; (c) uptrend: close(C) > EMA(10) of close; (d) D is black: close(D) < open(D); (e) open(D) > close(C); (f) close(D) < open(A) - D erases all three prior bars; (g) range(D) >= 1.5 x ATR(14). Short at the close of D. LONG SIGNAL (the so-called BEARISH three-line strike) is the exact mirror: A, B, C all black with close(A) > close(B) > close(C) and high(A) > high(B) > high(C), downtrend close(C) < EMA(10), D white with open(D) < close(C) and close(D) > open(A), range(D) >= 1.5 x ATR(14); buy at the close of D. Variant to sweep: enter at the close of bar D+3 instead of D.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry. Stop at high(D) + 0.10 x ATR(14) for shorts, low(D) - 0.10 x ATR(14) for longs. No profit target - the pattern's edge sits in the tail, not the median.
ideas.why: Bulkowski's census of 4.7 million candle lines found this pattern is anti-nominal in BOTH directions: the bullish three-line strike acts as a bearish reversal 65% of the time (overall performance rank 2 of 103) and the bearish three-line strike acts as a bullish reversal 84% of the time (overall performance rank 1 of 103). Mechanism: one bar erasing three sessions of directional progress leaves everyone who participated in the run underwater simultaneously, and the pattern's textbook 'continuation' label means the crowd is positioned exactly the wrong way. Caveat: only 69 and 85 samples respectively, so this is a low-confidence, high-payoff idea that must be validated on our own universe before sizing.
ideas.source: Bulkowski, Encyclopedia of Candlestick Charts; https://thepatternsite.com/ThreeLineStrikeBull.html (rank 2/103, frequency rank 95, bearish reversal 65%, n=69, 'wait 3 days before selling after downward breakouts in uptrends') and https://thepatternsite.com/ThreeLineStrikeBear.html (overall rank 1/103, bullish reversal 84%, n=85).
ideas.novelty: A four-bar pattern in which the trade is taken in the direction OPPOSITE the pattern's conventional name, on the strength of a large-sample census rather than folklore. No excluded idea uses a three-in-a-row run erased by a single fourth bar as its trigger.

ideas.name: Hidden Smash Day
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars, setup evaluated on bar[-1]. LONG: (a) close[-1] > close[-2] - net UP over two sessions; (b) close[-1] <= low[-1] + 0.25 x (high[-1] - low[-1]) - yet the close lands in the bottom quarter of its own range; (c) trend filter: close[-1] > close[-N] with N = 20 (sweep 4-80). On the next bar place a BUY STOP at high[-1] + 0.01, live for that bar only, cancelled at its close. SHORT is the exact mirror: close[-1] < close[-2]; close[-1] >= high[-1] - 0.25 x (high[-1] - low[-1]); close[-1] < close[-N]; sell stop at low[-1] - 0.01, live one bar.
ideas.exit_rule: Whichever fires first: (i) time exit at the close of the nth bar after entry, n = 5 (sweep 1-40); (ii) 'quick exit' stop at min(low[-1], low[-2]) for longs, max(high[-1], high[-2]) for shorts; (iii) disaster stop at entry - 6 x ATR(20) for longs.
ideas.why: The bar sends two contradictory messages: the close is higher than two sessions ago, but it is pinned to the bottom of the day's range. The crowd reads the close location and concludes distribution. Taking out the high of that same bar on the next session proves the weak close was end-of-day liquidity, not information, and the shorts who acted on the visual weakness become the fuel. Rated C over 42 US futures markets and 32 years, which for a two-bar rule with one filter is respectable.
ideas.source: Larry Williams, 'Long-Term Secrets to Short-Term Trading' (hidden smash day). Coded rules and rating: https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/smash-day-pattern-a1/ - long setup Close[i-1] <= Low[i-1] + 0.25*(High[i-1]-Low[i-1]) with Close[i-1] > Close[i-2], buy stop one tick above High[i-1], trend filter Close[i-1] > Close[i-Trend_Index], rating C, 42 futures markets 1980-2011.
ideas.novelty: Uses the DISAGREEMENT between the bar's net direction and its close location as the signal, and then trades against the close location. Distinct from the excluded close-location absorption run, which requires three bars all closing near their HIGHS and trades in the same direction as the close location.

ideas.name: Naked Smash Day (two-bar close-beyond-extreme reversal)
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars, uses only the two prior bars. LONG: close[-1] < low[-2] - the prior bar CLOSED (not merely traded) below the low of the bar before it. On the next bar place a BUY STOP at high[-1] + 0.01, live for that bar only, cancel if unfilled. SHORT: close[-1] > high[-2]; sell stop at low[-1] - 0.01, live one bar. Trend filter to sweep as an on/off parameter: require close[-1] > close[-N] for longs and close[-1] < close[-N] for shorts, N in 4..80 (the filtered version rates B, the unfiltered version rates D, so treat the filter as near-mandatory).
ideas.exit_rule: Whichever fires first: (i) time exit at the close of the nth bar after entry, n = 5 (sweep 1-40); (ii) quick exit at the two-bar extreme - stop at min(low[-1], low[-2]) for longs; (iii) disaster stop at entry - 6 x ATR(20). Explicitly test with NO profit target: the same catalogue's Kaufman study found fixed profit targets reduced both absolute and risk-adjusted returns across 42 markets.
