params: trend filter on/off and lookback N (4-80)
ideas.why: A close beyond the prior bar's extreme is the strongest one-bar statement of continuation available in OHLC data - far stronger than an intrabar poke, because it survives the closing auction. An immediate reversal all the way through the OPPOSITE extreme of that same bar is therefore the maximum possible disagreement with a freshly committed crowd, and their protective stops sit exactly where the entry fires.
ideas.source: Larry Williams smash day; coded rules and ratings at https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/smash-day-pattern-b1/ (long setup Close[i-1] < Low[i-2], buy stop one tick above High[i-1], rating B over 42 US futures markets 1980-2011) and https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/smash-day-pattern-c/ (identical setup with no trend filter, rating D).
ideas.novelty: Reference frame is a single prior bar, and the trigger is a CLOSE beyond it. Distinct from Turtle Soup (requires a 20-day extreme and that the prior extreme be stale) and from Sperandeo 2B (requires a 20-day CLOSING breakout). This fires on ordinary bars nowhere near any multi-week extreme, so its signal population barely overlaps either.

ideas.name: Oops Gap Reversal at the Recovered Level
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars, entry executed intraday during US regular hours. LONG: today's open < low[-1] AND (low[-1] - open) >= 0.30 x ATR(14) measured on daily bars. Place a BUY STOP at exactly low[-1] (the prior day's low); it fills the moment price trades back up into yesterday's range. The order is live only for today's session and is cancelled at the close if unfilled. SHORT: today's open > high[-1] AND (open - high[-1]) >= 0.30 x ATR(14); place a SELL STOP at exactly high[-1], live today only. One attempt per symbol per day.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the first profitable opening: at each subsequent session's open, if the open is above the entry price (below, for shorts), exit there; otherwise hold and re-test the next day. Hard stop at entry - 2.0 x ATR(14) for longs / entry + 2.0 x ATR(14) for shorts. Cap the hold at 5 sessions and exit at market. Sweep the alternative exit of a fixed n-day close, n = 1..10, to measure how much of the edge the first-profitable-open rule contributes.
inputs: intraday bars (1 or 5 minute) for the stop fill
params: minimum gap in daily ATR (0.30, sweep 0.10-0.75)
exit mode: first profitable open vs fixed n-day close
ideas.why: An out-of-range gap that is fully recovered is a failed overnight liquidation. The recovered level - yesterday's exact extreme - is where the overnight sellers' implied thesis is disproved and where the resting buy stops of the prior day's longs sit. Published futures backtests rate it D over 1980-2011 and the DAX version has decayed since extended hours arrived; the honest reason to test it on US equities is that the RTH open is one of the last venues with a genuine overnight-to-open information discontinuity, and the Unger test showed a minimum-gap filter nearly doubled the average trade (EUR 230 to EUR 400) even as net profit fell.
ideas.source: Larry Williams 'Oops' trade, 'Long-Term Secrets to Short-Term Trading'. Exact rules and rating D at https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/oops-pattern/ (long: Open[today] < Low[yesterday], buy stop at Low[yesterday]; time/ATR/stop-loss exits, 42 futures 1980-2011). Minimum-gap filter, 'exit at the first opening where the position is in profit' variant, and DAX 2010-present results at https://ungeracademy.com/blog/we-tested-larry-williams-oops-pattern-the-results-might-surprise-you
ideas.novelty: Entry is a resting order at an exact recovered price LEVEL (the prior bar's extreme), not at a bar close or a fresh extreme, and the exit is condition-driven with no target and no fixed time stop. The excluded in-range gap fade requires the open INSIDE the prior range and enters at a 5-minute bar close; the excluded gap-and-go requires the gap to HOLD. This requires the gap to clear the range and then fail completely.

ideas.name: Inventory Retracement Bar (wrong-wick continuation)
ideas.entry_rule: Let rng = high - low; skip bars where rng == 0. BULLISH IRB requires ALL: (a) uptrend: close > SMA(20) AND SMA(20) > SMA(20)[5]; (b) max(open, close) <= low + 0.45 x rng - the ENTIRE real body sits in the bottom 45% of the bar, so the upper shadow spans at least 55% of the range; (c) rng >= 0.80 x ATR(14). Place a BUY STOP at high + 0.01, live for the next 2 bars, then cancel. BEARISH IRB requires: close < SMA(20) AND SMA(20) < SMA(20)[5]; min(open, close) >= high - 0.45 x rng (body in the top 45%, lower shadow at least 55% of the range); rng >= 0.80 x ATR(14); place a SELL STOP at low - 0.01, live 2 bars.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at the signal bar's opposite extreme: low - 0.01 for longs, high + 0.01 for shorts. Target = entry + R x rng(signal bar) for longs, with R swept 1.0-3.0. Time stop: exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry if neither level is hit.
ideas.why: In an established uptrend, a bar whose entire body sits at the bottom of its range with a dominant upper shadow is counter-trend inventory: someone tried to sell into strength and could not hold the level. Trading through that bar's HIGH proves the selling was absorbed. This is precisely the inverse of the textbook shooting-star reading, which is why the setups it produces are the ones everyone else is fading.
ideas.source: Rob Hoffman's Inventory Retracement Bar. The 45% threshold and the 20-period MA trend filter as implemented in https://github.com/m-marqx/Inventory.Retracement.Bar.APP (signal when the wick reaches 45%, 20-period SMA trend filter, entry on a break of the signal candle's extreme, target as a payoff multiple of the signal candle's amplitude, stop at the signal candle's extreme) and the open-source TradingView implementations (e.g. script khxEdmoy, 'Rob Hoffman Inventory Retracement Bar', which computes x = low + 0.45*(high-low) and signals when open and close are both beyond x). Hoffman's original '45-degree MA angle' filter is unquantifiable and is replaced here with an explicit SMA slope test.
ideas.novelty: Buys the bar with the large UPPER wick and shorts the bar with the large LOWER wick - the opposite sign to the excluded quantified pin bar, which buys long-lower-wick bars. The threshold is on where the whole body sits within the range (both open and close inside the bottom 45%), not on a wick-to-body ratio.

ideas.name: TD Sequential Buy Setup 9 with Perfection
ideas.entry_rule: BUY SETUP: maintain a counter; increment it on each bar where close < close[-4]; reset it to 0 on any bar where close >= close[-4]. The count must be consecutive. When the counter reaches 9, that bar is the candidate signal bar. PERFECTION FILTER (required): min(low of setup bar 8, low of setup bar 9) <= min(low of setup bar 6, low of setup bar 7). If bar 9 is not perfected, continue extending the count and take the first later bar that satisfies the perfection inequality, up to bar 13; abandon the setup if none does. Enter LONG at the close of the qualifying bar. SELL SETUP is the exact mirror: 9 consecutive bars with close > close[-4], perfected when max(high8, high9) >= max(high6, high7); short at that close. Entry variant to sweep (the coded 'Method 2'): instead of entering at bar 9, enter at the close of the first bar after the setup completes on which close > close[-4] (longs).
ideas.exit_rule: TDST target: exit the long at the first close above the highest high of the 9 setup bars. Stop: the lowest low of the setup minus the true range of the bar that made it (DeMark's risk rule). Hard time stop at 12 bars. Continuation variant to sweep: rather than entering at setup 9, run the Countdown - starting the bar after setup 9, count bars (NOT necessarily consecutive) where close <= low[-2] until the count reaches 13, and enter at the close of countdown bar 13.
inputs: ohlcv (close, high, low) at chosen timeframe
params: countdown on/off and its offset (close vs low[-2])
ideas.why: Pure bar counting. Close-versus-close-four-bars-ago measures how long a directional impulse has been continuously renewing itself; nine uninterrupted renewals is empirically where a short-term trend has consumed its marginal participant, and the perfection rule additionally demands that the last two bars actually made new extremes rather than merely closing weakly. Nothing in the rule references a moving average, an oscillator, a channel or a volume statistic, so its signal timing is close to orthogonal to all 32 strategies already in the book - which makes it valuable as a portfolio diversifier even at modest standalone edge.
ideas.source: Thomas DeMark, 'The New Science of Technical Analysis' (1994). Setup rule (9 consecutive closes with Close[i] < Close[i-4]) and the countdown's switch to a close[2]-based comparison confirmed in the open-source implementation https://github.com/Forte11Cuba/TD-Sequential-Tom-DeMark. Independent backtest with the same 4-bar offset, 9-bar count and 'Method 2' entry, across 42 futures markets 1980-2013: https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/td-sequential-1/ - note performance deteriorates markedly at $100 round-turn costs, so this needs liquid names and passive fills.
ideas.novelty: An exhaustion signal built entirely from ordinal bar comparisons with no smoothing, no threshold on magnitude and no reference to any level. The perfection rule and the TDST target are both defined by the setup's own bars, so the risk and target scale with whatever volatility produced the sequence.

ideas.name: Three Inside Up with Caginalp-Laurent Scale-Out Exit
ideas.category: three-bar reversal with equal-tranche liquidation exit
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars; bars 1, 2, 3 = bar[-2], bar[-1], bar[0]. LONG (three inside up) requires ALL: (a) downtrend, close(bar[-3]) < EMA(10) of close; (b) O1 > C1 (bar1 black); (c) O1 >= O2 > C1 (bar2 opens inside bar1's body, at or below bar1's open); (d) O1 > C2 >= C1 (bar2 closes inside bar1's body); (e) C3 > O3 (bar3 white); (f) C3 > O1 (bar3 closes above the OPEN of bar1, i.e. above the entire prior body). Deliberately impose NO magnitude conditions - no minimum body, no minimum range, no ATR filter, no gap requirement. Enter long at the close of bar3. SHORT (three inside down) is the exact mirror: uptrend; C1 > O1; C1 > O2 >= O1; C1 >= C2 > O1; O3 > C3; C3 < O1; short at the close of bar3.
ideas.exit_rule: THIS IS THE IDEA. Caginalp-Laurent scale-out: split the position into N equal tranches (N = 3; sweep 3, 5, 10) and liquidate exactly one tranche at the close of each of the next N bars, so the realised exit price is the arithmetic mean of those N closes. No stop, no profit target - the staged liquidation IS the risk control. Run the Marshall-Young-Rose single-date exit (liquidate the whole position at the close of bar N) as the paired control on identical signals, so the exit's contribution is measured directly.
ideas.why: The exit is the idea, and there is a specific published reason to believe it. Lu, Shiu & Liu (2015) reconciled two decades of contradictory candlestick literature by running the same patterns on the same DJIA data 1992-2012 under two exits: under the Caginalp-Laurent scale-out the patterns were profitable after transaction costs and after correcting for data-snooping bias, and under the Marshall-Young-Rose single-date exit they were not. They attribute the difference to risk-sharing across the holding window. The same body of work found 3-day holds beat 10-day holds and bullish signals beat bearish. The magnitude-free pattern definition is also deliberate: Caginalp & Laurent obtained their significance by stripping the size conditions out of the standard definitions, which is the opposite of what every practitioner source recommends and therefore worth testing head-to-head.
ideas.source: Caginalp & Laurent (1998), 'The Predictive Power of Price Patterns', Applied Mathematical Finance - magnitude-free three-day inequalities (TIU: O1 > C1, O1 >= O2 > C1, O1 > C2 >= C1, C3 > O3, C3 > O1 & downtrend) and the averaged-close exit. Lu, Shiu & Liu (2015) CL-versus-MYR exit comparison on DJIA components. Both, with the exact inequality tables, in Tharavanij, Siraprapasiri & Rajchamaha (2017), SAGE Open, doi:10.1177/2158244017736799.
ideas.novelty: A distinct EXIT STRUCTURE: deterministic equal-tranche liquidation spread across the holding window rather than a single exit event, paired with a deliberately magnitude-free pattern definition. Every exit currently in the book is a single event (target, stop, or a fixed bar count).

ideas.name: Pattern-to-Pattern Variable Holding Period (LSL exit)
ideas.entry_rule: Define an equality tolerance eps = 0.05 x (high - low) for the marubozu tests. BULLISH ENTRY SET B (any one fires, and requires close > EMA(10) of close): Closing White Marubozu - close > open AND |high - close| <= eps AND (open - low) > eps; OR Opening White Marubozu - close > open AND |open - low| <= eps AND (high - close) > eps. Enter long at the close of the first bar satisfying any member of B while flat. BEARISH SET S (used as the exit trigger, and as the short entry set when close < EMA(10)): Closing Black Marubozu - close < open AND |close - low| <= eps AND (high - open) > eps; OR Opening Black Marubozu - close < open AND |open - high| <= eps AND (close - low) > eps.
ideas.exit_rule: THIS IS THE IDEA. Hold with NO time stop, NO price target and NO fixed stop loss. Exit at the close of the first subsequent bar that satisfies any member of the opposing set S. Sweep two modes: (i) long-only, going flat on the S signal; (ii) always-in, reversing to short on the S signal and holding until the next B signal. Add an optional catastrophic stop at entry - 4 x ATR(14) purely as a survival guard and measure how often it binds.
inputs: atr(14) for the optional guard stop
params: equality tolerance eps as a fraction of range (0.05, sweep 0.02-0.10)
ideas.why: The holding period is set by the market rather than by the calendar: the position is carried for exactly as long as price action keeps refusing to print the opposite signature, so winners in persistent trends are held for weeks while positions in choppy tape are cut within days - all without a single volatility or time parameter. Lu, Shiu & Liu (2012) tested this variable holding period on Taiwan Top 50 constituents 2002-2008 and found certain bullish reversal patterns generated positive abnormal returns net of transaction costs, where fixed-horizon tests of the same patterns did not.
ideas.source: Lu, Shiu & Liu (2012), variable-holding-period ('LSL') exit strategy - buy on a bullish signal, liquidate when a bearish pattern occurs - described and contrasted against the MYR and CL exits in Tharavanij, Siraprapasiri & Rajchamaha (2017), SAGE Open, doi:10.1177/2158244017736799. One-day pattern inequalities from Goo, Chen & Chang (2007), reproduced in the same paper.
ideas.novelty: An exit with no clock and no price level in it at all - the position ends only when the opposite pattern appears. Every exit in the existing book is a bar count, an ATR distance, a channel, or a price target.

ideas.name: Fade the Close-on-the-Low Candle in an Uptrend
ideas.category: documented sign inversion of a named bearish pattern
ideas.entry_rule: Daily bars. Let eps = 0.05 x (high - low); skip bars where high == low. The signal bar must satisfy the UPTREND condition close > EMA(10) of close AND match at least one of: (i) Black Marubozu - |high - open| <= eps AND |close - low| <= eps AND close < open; (ii) Closing Black Marubozu - |close - low| <= eps AND close < open AND (high - open) > eps; (iii) Gravestone Doji - |open - close| <= eps AND |close - low| <= eps AND (high - open) > 0.50 x (high - low). Take the LONG side - the opposite of the pattern's name. Buy at the OPEN of the next bar.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry (sweep 1/3/5/10 to reproduce the published horizon effect). Run the equal-tranche scale-out over the same window as a paired variant. Protective stop at entry - 2.0 x ATR(14).
params: equality tolerance eps (0.05 of range, sweep 0.02-0.10)
exit mode: fixed date vs scale-out
which of the three bar types are included
ideas.why: This is a direct empirical inversion, not a hunch. Tharavanij et al. measured every bearish one-day pattern on SET50 constituents over 2006-2016 and every one produced a POSITIVE mean holding-period return - i.e. the nominal short loses money and its inverse makes it: Closing Black Marubozu +0.67% over 10 days (t-adjusted 9.38, n = 11,483), Gravestone Doji +0.75% (t = 5.51, n = 2,758), Black Marubozu +0.43% (t = 4.81, n = 7,370). The winning probability of the nominal short sits at 0.42-0.45, far below a coin flip, with Z statistics around -10 to -16. Mechanism: in an established uptrend a close pinned to the low is a liquidity event - index rebalancing, a block, a closing auction imbalance - not information, and it is systematically over-read as weakness by everyone scanning for shooting stars and marubozu. Two caveats worth carrying into the test: this is Thai large caps and must be re-measured on US equities, and the same tables show sub-0.5 win rates alongside positive means for nearly every pattern in both directions, which is a right-skew signature arguing against any fixed profit target on this family.
ideas.source: Tharavanij, Siraprapasiri & Rajchamaha (2017), 'Profitability of Candlestick Charting Patterns in the Stock Exchange of Thailand', SAGE Open, doi:10.1177/2158244017736799, Table 2 (bearish single-day patterns, MYR and CL exits, 1/3/5/10-day holds, SET50 constituents 2006-07-03 to 2016-06-30). Pattern inequalities from Goo, Chen & Chang (2007), reproduced there. Trend definition EMA10 from Marshall, Young & Rose (2006).
ideas.novelty: Trades a named bearish pattern from the long side on the strength of a measured sign flip. Distinct from the excluded close-location absorption run, which needs three bars closing near their HIGHS and trades with the close location, and from the excluded upthrust bar, which needs a 20-bar extreme and heavy volume.

ideas.name: No Supply / No Demand Bar (low-volume absorption)
ideas.entry_rule: NO SUPPLY (long setup). Signal bar S must satisfy ALL: (a) close(S) < close(S-1) - a down bar; (b) range(S) <= 0.70 x mean(range of the 5 bars immediately before S) - a narrow spread; (c) volume(S) < volume(S-1) AND volume(S) < volume(S-2) - lower than BOTH of the two preceding bars; (d) close(S) >= low(S) + 0.50 x range(S) - the close is in the upper half; (e) context: close(S) > SMA(20). CONFIRMATION IS MANDATORY on the very next bar C: close(C) > high(S) AND volume(C) > volume(S). Enter long at the close of C. If C fails either test, discard the setup entirely - do not wait. NO DEMAND (short setup) is the exact mirror: up bar close(S) > close(S-1); range(S) <= 0.70 x the 5-bar mean range; volume(S) below both prior bars; close(S) <= low(S) + 0.50 x range(S); close(S) < SMA(20); confirmation bar closes below low(S) on volume above volume(S); short at its close.
ideas.exit_rule: Stop at low(S) - 0.05 x ATR(14) for longs, high(S) + 0.05 x ATR(14) for shorts. Exit at the close of the 8th bar after entry, or earlier on the first opposing signal (a qualifying No Demand bar while long). No fixed profit target.
params: spread threshold vs 5-bar mean range (0.70, sweep 0.50-0.90)
number of prior bars volume must undercut (2, sweep 1-3)
confirmation required on bar 1 vs within 2 bars
ideas.why: Every volume rule already in the book demands HIGH volume. This one demands its absence, and the economic claim is different: a down bar that cannot attract sellers - narrow range, less participation than either of the two bars before it, and a close in the upper half - is evidence that the float willing to transact at that price is exhausted. Supply exhaustion and demand climax are distinct phenomena that fire at different moments, so this signal population should be nearly disjoint from the existing volume-gated strategies. The mandatory confirmation bar on rising volume is what converts a qualitative VSA read into a testable rule.
ideas.source: Tom Williams, 'Master the Markets' (Volume Spread Analysis). Operational definition - up/down bar, narrow spread, volume lower than the previous TWO bars, close position within the bar, and a confirming next bar on rising volume - from https://www.tradingsetupsreview.com/guide-volume-spread-analysis-vsa/ ('No Demand: price closed higher than the previous bar, volume is lower than past two bars, spreads are narrow') and https://atas.net/volume-analysis/basics-of-volume-analysis/vsa-and-cluster-analysis-no-demand-and-no-supply/ (close position within the bar; confirmation by the next bar on growing volume). Both sources leave 'narrow spread' undefined, so it is pinned here to <= 0.70 x the 5-bar mean range; both sources also stress that VSA is normally judgement-based, so this is a deliberate quantification.
ideas.novelty: The signal is LOW volume, and the qualifying comparison is against the two individual preceding bars rather than a moving average of volume. Nothing in either list uses an absence-of-participation condition.

ideas.name: Ross Hook After a Closing-Channel Breakout
ideas.entry_rule: Step 1 - BREAKOUT BAR B: close(B) > max(close over the 20 bars immediately before B), i.e. a fresh 20-bar CLOSING high. Step 2 - THE HOOK: scanning forward from B, the hook bar H is the FIRST bar with high(H) < high(H-1) - the first failure to extend. H must occur within Max_Hook = 10 bars of B (sweep 2-80); if no such bar appears in that window, abandon the setup. Step 3 - ENTRY: place a BUY STOP at (highest high from bar B through bar H) + 0.01, live for 10 bars after H, then cancel. INVALIDATION: cancel the order immediately if any bar closes below low(B) before it fills. SHORT is the exact mirror after close(B) < min(close over the previous 20 bars), with the hook being the first bar whose low > low of the bar before it, and a sell stop at (lowest low from B through H) - 0.01.
ideas.exit_rule: Quick exit stop at the lowest low from B through the fill bar (highest high, for shorts). Time exit at the close of the 10th bar after entry (sweep 1-40). Disaster stop at entry - 6 x ATR(20). No profit target - the source catalogue's Kaufman study found fixed targets reduced both absolute and risk-adjusted returns across 42 markets.
params: order validity after the hook (10 bars)
ideas.why: The first bar that fails to extend a fresh breakout marks exactly where profit-taking met the new demand. Everyone who sold that first hesitation is wrong the instant the leg's running high is exceeded, and their stops are the entry's liquidity. Unlike a moving-average pullback, the reference level is generated by the structure of the breakout leg itself, so the trigger tracks the impulse instead of lagging behind a smoothed average - it fires within one or two bars of the pullback rather than after the average catches up.
ideas.source: Joe Ross, 'Trading by the Book' (Ross Hook and the Traders Trick Entry). Coded rules, Min_Setup/Max_Hook parameters, buy stop one tick above the highest high of the hook, quick exit at the opposite hook extreme, and rating C across 42 futures markets 1980-2011: https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/ross-hook-1/ (filter variants at ross-hook-filter-1/2/3). Ross's original 1-2-3 precondition is judgement-dependent, so it is pinned here to a 20-bar CLOSING-channel breakout, which is testable.
ideas.novelty: The trigger level is the running high of the breakout leg - a structure-derived level that ratchets - and the setup is anchored to the FIRST lower high after a closing breakout. The excluded EMA-pullback rule anchors to a moving average; the excluded break-of-structure rule anchors to a prior swing point, not to the first hesitation inside a live leg.

ideas.name: Five-Condition Pivot Reversal Bar
ideas.category: composite reversal bar at a broken swing pivot
ideas.entry_rule: Step 1 - DEMAND PIVOT P: a bar whose low is strictly lower than the lows of the 2 bars either side (a 5-bar fractal low); record P_low = its low. Step 2 - BREAKDOWN: a later bar D makes low(D) < P_low. Step 3 - REVERSAL BAR R, which must occur within 5 bars of D and satisfy ALL FIVE: (a) close(R) > close(R-1) AND close(R) > close(R-2); (b) close(R) > P_low - the broken pivot is reclaimed on a closing basis; (c) close(R) > open(R); (d) close(R) > 0.5 x (high(R) + low(R)) - the close is above the bar's own midrange; (e) high(R) - low(R) > high(R-1) - low(R-1) - range expansion. Enter LONG at the OPEN of the bar after R. SHORT is the exact mirror around a supply pivot (5-bar fractal high) that is broken and then reclaimed.
ideas.exit_rule: Initial risk = entry - min(low(R), low(D)) for longs; place the stop there. Target = entry + Reward_Ratio x initial risk with Reward_Ratio swept 1-10 and biased toward the high end - the source's explicit conclusion is that these reversals 'with larger target exits are preferred'. Time exit at the OPEN of the (n+1)th bar, n swept 1-40. Also test with the target removed entirely, given the same catalogue's finding that fixed targets hurt.
inputs: 5-bar fractal pivots on highs and lows
atr(20) for an optional disaster stop
params: bars allowed between breakdown and reversal (5, sweep 2-10)
ideas.why: Five independent confirmations on a single bar, each cheap on its own but jointly rare: direction versus TWO prior closes, reclaim of a broken structural level, close above the open, close above the bar's own midpoint, and range expansion versus the previous bar. The conjunction means the bar simultaneously reverses the immediate sequence, invalidates the breakdown, and does so with expanding participation. Rated C over 42 futures markets and 32 years, with the explicit findings that reversal patterns are very sensitive to trading costs and work better with larger targets - so it must be traded sparingly, in liquid names, and held for a real move rather than scalped.
ideas.source: https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/reversal-patterns-part-2/ - top/bottom reversal around supply/demand pivots: 'closes below the two previous days' closings', close beyond the pivot, 'close is below the opening and the mid-range of the day', daily range exceeds the previous day's range, all within 5 bars of the breakout; entry at the open after the reversal; rating C, 42 US futures markets 1980-2011. Pivot construction follows Kaufman's swing-point definition.
ideas.novelty: The conjunction of a close above the bar's own MIDRANGE with a close above two prior closes, range expansion, and the reclaim of a broken fractal pivot is used by nothing in either list, and the entry is deferred to the next OPEN rather than taken at the signal close - which materially changes the fill distribution on gapping names.

ideas.name: Full-Range Gap Continuation with a Gap-Fill Stop
ideas.entry_rule: DAILY VERSION. LONG: bar i is a full-range gap up - low(i) > high(i-1), i.e. the ENTIRE day trades above the prior day's entire range - AND a channel confirmation holds: high(i) > max(high over the 20 bars before i). Enter at the close of bar i. SHORT: high(i) < low(i-1) AND low(i) < min(low over the 20 bars before i); enter at the close of bar i. Sweep the channel length over 2-100. INTRADAY VARIANT (5-minute bars, US regular hours, tests the same idea at higher resolution): today's open >= high[-1] + 0.20 x daily ATR(14); then from the 09:35 bar through the 10:30 bar inclusive, EVERY 5-minute bar's low must stay strictly above high[-1] - the prior day's high is never touched - and the 10:30 bar's close must exceed the high of the 09:30-09:35 opening bar. Buy at the close of the 10:30 bar. Abort permanently for that day the moment any 5-minute bar's low <= high[-1]. One attempt per symbol per day; mirror for gap downs at the prior day's low.
ideas.exit_rule: DAILY: three exits, first to fire. (i) Pattern exit - a stop one tick below the gap, i.e. at high(i-1) - 0.01 for longs, high(i-1) being the level the gap cleared; the trade dies the moment the gap fills. (ii) Time exit after n days, n swept 1-50 and biased LONG - the source found longer holding periods preferred. (iii) Disaster stop at entry - 6 x ATR(20). No profit target. INTRADAY: exit at the 15:55 close (no overnight hold); stop at high[-1] - 0.05 x daily ATR; trail to breakeven once price is 1 x the 09:30-10:30 range beyond entry.
inputs: 5-minute bars and daily atr(14) for the intraday variant
params: minimum gap in daily ATR for the intraday variant (0.20)
ideas.why: The absence of a fill is the signal. A gap that clears the prior bar's ENTIRE range and is never traded back into means there is no supply willing to transact at yesterday's extreme - the opposite information from a gap that gets filled or even retested. Placing the stop one tick inside the gap makes the whole trade a bet on exactly that proposition, and the finding that LONGER holds are preferred runs directly against the usual 'gaps fade fast' intuition, which is what makes it worth testing. This is rated B/C - the best-rated gap variant in that catalogue and better than the close-referenced Type B (rated C) - and it gives the fleet a mechanically opposite sibling to the retest-based gap rule already in the book, so the two can be run as a paired experiment on the same universe of gap days.
ideas.source: https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/gap-pattern/ - Gap Pattern Type A: long gap defined as Low[i] > High[i-1], channel filter High[i] > UpperChannel[i-1] with lookback 2-100, pattern exit 'one tick below the price gap', time exit 1-50 days with longer holds preferred, ATR(20) x 6 stop, rating B/C over 42 US futures markets. Compare https://oxfordstrat.com/trading-strategies/gap-pattern-2/ - Type B uses the weaker Low[i] > Close[i-1] definition and rates C, 'less efficient than Type A'. The intraday no-retest cutoff is my own construction: conditioning on the NON-occurrence of a retest by a fixed clock time is what makes an otherwise unfalsifiable notion of 'strong gap' testable.
ideas.novelty: Requires the gap to clear the prior bar's whole RANGE (not merely its close), makes the non-fill of the gap the stop condition, and holds for weeks rather than hours. The excluded out-of-range gap-and-go rule requires a retest and is intraday-only; this one is invalidated by the very retest that rule waits for.

ideas.name: Tanh-Saturated Trend
ideas.entry_rule: Daily. Let P_n = the exponential moving average of closes with decay span n (test n = 50, 105, 210 trading days), computed through close_{t-1} and EXCLUDING close_t. Let A_n = the exponential moving average, with the same span n, of |close_t - close_{t-1}| (mean absolute price change, not a standard deviation). Signal s = (close_{t-1} - P_n(t-1)) / A_n(t-1). At the next open take notional = tanh(s / 0.89) * min(0.15/sigma_ann, leverage_cap) * allocated equity, long when s > 0 and short when s < 0. Stay flat when |s| < 0.10.
ideas.exit_rule: Recomputed and reset every daily close. Exposure is monotone in s but hard-capped: |tanh(s/0.89)| is already 0.95 at |s| = 1.6, so beyond that point extra trend strength adds no size. Position reverses when s changes sign; no stop-loss.
inputs: ema(n) of absolute daily price change
ideas.why: Fitting next-month price change against this signal across 240,000 observations of futures and two centuries of spot data, the best functional form is a hyperbolic tangent, not a line: the predictive slope flattens beyond |s| ~ 0.89. The interpretation is that fundamentalist traders do not resist weak trends but step in once their own signal is strong enough, capping how far a trend can run. Normalising by the mean absolute change rather than a variance makes the signal robust to the fat tails that dominate a squared estimator.
ideas.novelty: Differs from idea 1 in both halves: the signal is a single-EMA price deviation normalised by average absolute change (an L1 scale, not L2), and the response is monotone-saturating rather than non-monotonic, so exposure caps but never reverses at extremes. Differs from EMA cross because size is continuous in the distance from the EMA rather than binary on the crossing.
ideas.source: Lemperiere, Deremble, Seager, Potters, Bouchaud (2014), 'Two Centuries of Trend Following', arXiv:1404.3274 - signal definition eq. (1), P&L eq. (2), and the tanh fit eq. (3) with fitted s* = 0.89, b = 0.075, Section 4.2 and Figure 5. Fetched and read directly.

ideas.name: European TF System
ideas.entry_rule: Daily. Let r_t = close_t/close_{t-1} - 1 and let sigma_t be the EWMA volatility of r with span 33 days. Form volatility-normalised returns z_t = r_t / sigma_{t-1}. Apply a long-short EWMA filter to z (NOT to price): E_fast = EWMA of z with span 20, E_slow = EWMA of z with span 250, raw = E_fast - E_slow, and S_t = raw / stdev(raw over the last 252 bars). At the next open set notional weight w_t = S_t * sigma_target / (sqrt(260) * sigma_t) with sigma_target = 0.15 annualised, capped at the leverage cap. Long if w_t > 0, short if w_t < 0, flat when |S_t| < 0.10.
ideas.exit_rule: Continuous: the weight is recomputed and the position resized every daily close. There is no stop and no discrete exit level; a decaying trend shrinks the position smoothly to zero and then reverses it.
ideas.why: Filtering price levels makes the signal scale with both the price level and the asset's volatility, so the same numerical reading means different things on different symbols and in different regimes. Filtering z = r/sigma instead produces a dimensionless, unit-variance-ish signal whose daily P&L is exactly sigma_target/sqrt(260) * S_{t-1} * z_t, which is what lets expected return be linked directly to the autocorrelation of normalised returns. This is the construction large European CTAs actually run.
ideas.novelty: The EWMA filter is applied to volatility-normalised returns rather than to prices, and position size is linearly proportional to the continuous signal. Every rule in the existing set (EMA cross, MACD, TRIX, Hull) filters the price series and produces a binary or threshold signal.
ideas.source: Sepp & Lucic (2026), 'The Science and Practice of Trend-Following Systems', arXiv:2607.19497v1, Definition 3.1(1), Section 3.1 and Definition 4.1 with eqs. (4.1)-(4.3); parameters (long 250, short 20, span 33) from Section 7.1. Builds on Dao, Nguyen, Deremble, Lemperiere, Bouchaud, Potters (2017), 'Tail protection for long investors: Trend convexity at work', arXiv:1607.02410, and Baz et al. (2015). PDF fetched and read directly.

ideas.name: American Turtle TF with ATR Buffer and Dual-Condition Exit
ideas.entry_rule: Daily. Compute fast = EWMA of close with span 20 and slow = EWMA of close with span 250. Compute ATR_t as the 33-day simple average of the daily true range TR_t = max(high_t - low_t, |high_t - close_{t-1}|, |low_t - close_{t-1}|). If currently flat: go long at the next open when fast > slow + 5 * ATR_t; go short at the next open when fast < slow - 5 * ATR_t. Position size is fixed at inception at p = R * close_t / ATR_t units of notional weight, with R = 0.002 (risk fraction of capital per trade), capped at the leverage cap; the size is NOT re-computed while the trade is open.
ideas.exit_rule: On entering a long, set stop = close_t - 5 * ATR_t. Each subsequent day update stop = max(previous stop, close_t - 5 * ATR_t) - the stop only ever ratchets up. Close the long ONLY when BOTH (a) close_t < the previous day's stop AND (b) the entry condition is no longer true, i.e. fast <= slow + 5 * ATR_t. Mirror exactly for shorts: stop = min(previous stop, close_t + 5 * ATR_t), close only when close_t > previous stop AND fast >= slow - 5 * ATR_t. The dual condition prevents a stop breach from re-arming the same trade the next day.
ideas.why: Two separate frictions are handled by two separate devices. The ATR-scaled entry buffer stops the system from churning when the two averages hover on top of each other, which is where crossover rules bleed. The ratcheting ATR stop converts a signal-reversal exit into a path-dependent one, so a trend that keeps running defers the exit indefinitely while a sharp reversal exits immediately - this is what generates the positive skew that trend systems are bought for. Requiring the signal to also be off before honouring the stop removes the whipsaw where the stop fires but the trend filter immediately re-enters.
ideas.novelty: A distinct exit structure: a monotone ratcheting ATR trailing stop combined with a mandatory signal-off confirmation, plus position size frozen at inception from the entry-day ATR. Donchian breakout, ATR expansion breakout, and EMA cross all exit on a signal or a fixed range condition; none has a ratchet plus a two-condition exit.
ideas.source: Sepp & Lucic (2026), 'The Science and Practice of Trend-Following Systems', arXiv:2607.19497v1, Definition 3.1(2) and Appendix A.1 Definition A.3, eqs. (A.5)-(A.13); parameters omega = 5, p = 5, spans 250/20, ATR period 33 from Section 7.1. Formalises the 1980s turtle design (Faith 2007, Covel 2009) tested in Lukac, Brorsen & Irwin (1988) and Szakmary, Shen & Sharma (2010). PDF fetched and read directly.

ideas.name: Sign-Count Z-Score TSMOM
ideas.entry_rule: Fix L = 10 days and M = 10 blocks. Act only on bars where the bar index is a multiple of 10. Partition the last 100 daily bars into 10 disjoint consecutive blocks of 10 bars. For block m compute b_m = sum over the 10 bars in that block of sign(close_t/close_{t-1} - 1). Compute S = (1/sqrt(M*L)) * sum over m of b_m = (1/10) * sum of all 100 daily return signs. Under serially independent returns S is a unit-variance z-score. At the next open set notional = S * min(sigma_target/sigma_ann, leverage_cap) * allocated equity with sigma_target = 0.15 and sigma_ann = stdev of daily returns over 33 bars * sqrt(260). Long if S > 0, short if S < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold for exactly 10 trading days; at the next multiple-of-10 bar the weight is replaced by the freshly computed one (which may be a reversal or a flat). Forward-fill the weight on non-rebalancing days. No stop.
ideas.why: Counting the signs of daily returns throws away magnitude entirely, so a single crash day or gap cannot flip or dominate the signal - the volatility estimator drops out of the signal completely because sign(r/sigma) = sign(r). The 1/sqrt(ML) normalisation makes the signal a genuine z-score, so the strategy's realised volatility ends up close to sigma_target regardless of the choice of M and L, which is what makes the parameter sweep interpretable rather than a volatility sweep in disguise.
ideas.novelty: The signal is a normalised count of up-days over disjoint blocks rather than a cumulative return or a moving-average relationship. Distinct from three-bar momentum (too short, no normalisation) and from a multi-horizon sign consensus, which takes the sign of three cumulative returns rather than counting 100 individual daily signs.
ideas.source: Sepp & Lucic (2026), 'The Science and Practice of Trend-Following Systems', arXiv:2607.19497v1, Definition 3.1(3) and Appendix A.2 Definition A.4, eq. (A.16); optimal M = L = 10 from Section 7.1. Generalises Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen (2012) eq. (A.15) and the sign-of-normalised-returns averaging of Dudler, Gmur & Malamud (2015). PDF fetched and read directly.

ideas.name: On-Balance-Volume Crossover
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain OBV_t = OBV_{t-1} + volume_t * D_t where D_t = +1 if close_t - close_{t-1} >= 0 and -1 otherwise (a running total of signed volume). Compute SMA_s(OBV) and SMA_l(OBV) with s in {5, 10, 15} and l in {45, 60} daily bars. Go long at the next session open on the bar where SMA_s(OBV) >= SMA_l(OBV) and that inequality was false on the previous bar. Go short at the next open on the bar where SMA_s(OBV) < SMA_l(OBV) and that was false on the previous bar.
ideas.exit_rule: Reverse on the opposite crossover. Optional flat variant: exit to cash whenever SMA_s(OBV) crosses back through SMA_l(OBV), taking no short leg.
inputs: sma of OBV at two lengths
ideas.why: OBV is the cumulative order-flow imbalance proxy available from bar data: it rises only when volume arrives on up-days. A price trend accompanied by expanding signed volume is a trend with participation behind it; a price trend on shrinking or offsetting volume is one that a few marginal trades produced. Empirically this indicator family carries incremental equity-premium information over both the price-based moving average and the momentum rules, and its predictive content concentrates in recessions when the price-only rules are noisiest.
ideas.novelty: Uses a cumulative SIGNED volume series - a running integral that embeds direction - rather than a raw volume level or a volume ratio. Distinct from any rule that compares current volume to its own average, which discards the up/down attribution entirely.
ideas.source: Neely, Rapach, Tu & Zhou (2014), 'Forecasting the Equity Risk Premium: The Role of Technical Indicators', Management Science 60(7); working paper version Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis WP 2010-008, eqs. (7)-(9), which define OBV_t = sum_k VOL_k * D_k and the VOL(s,l) crossover signal with s in {1,2,3}, l in {9,12} months. Original indicator: Granville (1963). PDF fetched and text extracted directly.

ideas.name: Variance-Ratio Trend Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Daily, per symbol. Let x_t = ln(close_t/close_{t-1}) over a 252-bar window (nq+1 observations). Compute the Lo-MacKinlay overlapping variance ratio with q = 20: mu = (x_{n} - x_{1} summed)/nq; sigma_a^2 = (1/(nq-1)) * sum over t of (x_t - mu)^2; sigma_c^2 = (1/m) * sum over t=q..nq of (ln(close_t/close_{t-q}) - q*mu)^2 with m = q*(nq - q + 1)*(1 - q/(nq)); VR(q) = sigma_c^2/sigma_a^2. Compute the heteroskedasticity-robust statistic z*(q) = (VR(q) - 1)/sqrt(theta*(q)) using Lo-MacKinlay's theta*(q) = sum over j=1..q-1 of [2(q-j)/q]^2 * delta_j, delta_j = [sum_t (x_t-mu)^2 (x_{t-j}-mu)^2] / [sum_t (x_t-mu)^2]^2. Take a position only when z*(q) > +1.65 (prices are trending, positive autocorrelation at the 20-day scale). Direction: go long at the next open when z*(q) > 1.65 AND close_t/close_{t-63} - 1 > 0; go short when z*(q) > 1.65 AND close_t/close_{t-63} - 1 < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit to flat when z*(q) falls below 0 (the trending regime has ended) OR when the sign of the 63-day return flips. Nothing is entered while -inf < z*(q) <= 1.65, which is most of the time on most symbols - the gate is deliberately restrictive.
ideas.why: The P&L of a trend system on a given asset decomposes almost exactly into the difference between its long-horizon and short-horizon realised variance - a trend follower is structurally long the variance term structure. The variance ratio measures precisely that spread, and its z-statistic says whether the spread is bigger than sampling noise. So this gates trend entries on a direct, testable statistic for the thing that pays trend followers, rather than on ADX or a volatility band which are proxies for trend strength, not for return autocorrelation.
ideas.novelty: Conditions on the autocorrelation structure of returns via a formal statistical test, not on price geometry. ADX measures directional-movement magnitude; a trend t-stat tests a linear drift in log price. VR(q) tests whether variance scales super-linearly with horizon, which is a different null and can be positive when a t-stat on the drift is not (choppy but persistent) and negative when it is (a smooth drift with strong short-horizon mean reversion).
ideas.source: Lo & MacKinlay (1988), 'Stock Market Prices Do Not Follow Random Walks: Evidence from a Simple Specification Test', Review of Financial Studies 1(1), 41-66 - the VR(q) estimator and the heteroskedasticity-robust z*(q). The link from VR to trend P&L is established in Dao, Nguyen, Deremble, Lemperiere, Bouchaud & Potters (2017), 'Tail protection for long investors: Trend convexity at work', arXiv:1607.02410, which shows trend-following returns 'can be ascribed to the difference between long-term and short-term realized variance' (abstract fetched and verified).

ideas.name: Factor Momentum on OHLCV Factors
ideas.entry_rule: Build five long-short factor proxies from OHLCV alone, each equal-weighted top-tercile minus bottom-tercile of the universe, rebalanced monthly, with their daily returns recorded: F1 = 12-1 momentum (close_{t-21}/close_{t-252} - 1); F2 = one-month reversal (negative of close_t/close_{t-21} - 1); F3 = low volatility (negative of stdev of daily returns over 252 bars); F4 = high dollar-volume growth (mean(close*volume) over 21 bars divided by mean over the prior 252 bars); F5 = 52-week-high proximity (close_t / max(high over 252 bars)). At each month end compute for each factor R_f = its own cumulative return over the last 252 trading days INCLUDING the most recent month (do NOT skip month t). Go long every factor with R_f > 0 and short every factor with R_f < 0, sizing each at min(0.06/sigma_f, cap) where sigma_f = stdev of that factor's daily returns over 126 bars * sqrt(252). Translate to stock orders by summing each symbol's signed weight across all active factor legs and trading the net at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Re-derived every month end: a factor whose trailing 252-day return flips sign has its leg reversed; a symbol whose net weight crosses zero is flattened. No per-name stop.
inputs: daily returns of constructed long-short factor portfolios
ideas.why: Most equity factors are positively autocorrelated at annual horizons, and individual-stock momentum turns out to be an indirect and noisy way of betting on that autocorrelation - a stock is a winner largely because the factors it loads on have been winning. Timing the factors directly captures the same effect with far fewer names, far less turnover, and without the idiosyncratic noise that individual-stock momentum carries. The 'no skip' detail matters: implementations that omit the most recent month lose statistical significance once stock momentum is controlled for.
ideas.novelty: Time-series momentum applied to constructed portfolio return series rather than to prices of tradeable instruments, then mapped back into stock weights. Every existing idea signals on a symbol's own price path; this signals on the return path of a spread portfolio and only then translates into positions.
ideas.source: Ehsani & Linnainmaa (2022), 'Factor Momentum and the Momentum Factor', Journal of Finance 77(3); NBER Working Paper 25551 (abstract fetched and verified: 'factor momentum explains all forms of individual stock momentum', factors earn ~1bp/month after loss years vs ~53bp after positive years). The include-the-most-recent-month requirement is from Arnott, Clements, Kalesnik & Linnainmaa, 'Is Factor Momentum More than Stock Momentum?', arXiv:2009.04824 (abstract fetched: only implementations including the most recent month survive controls for stock momentum).

ideas.name: Alexander Filter Rule
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain two path-dependent reference levels with NO fixed lookback window. While the current position is short or flat, track LOW = the lowest close observed since the position was last long. While the current position is long or flat, track HIGH = the highest close observed since the position was last short. Go long at the next session open on the first bar where close_t >= LOW * (1 + x). Go short at the next open on the first bar where close_t <= HIGH * (1 - x). Use x = 0.05 as the base case and sweep x over 0.005 to 0.20.
ideas.exit_rule: The system is always in the market and reverses rather than exiting to flat: a long is closed only when close_t <= HIGH * (1 - x), where HIGH is the highest close since that long was opened, and that same bar opens the short. On reversal the running extreme resets to the reversal bar's close. A flat-only variant closes the position on the reversal condition and waits for the next same-side signal.
inputs: running minimum/maximum since the last opposite signal
params: apply x to close vs to high/low
optional ATR-scaled x instead of a percentage
ideas.why: The reference point is where the price actually turned, not where it was N bars ago. In a long quiet drift a fixed-lookback channel keeps re-arming as old bars roll out of the window; a filter rule does not move its reference at all until price makes a genuine new extreme, so it produces far fewer, more decisive signals and its holding period adapts to the market's own swing length rather than to a chosen lookback. This is the oldest formal trend rule in the literature and it is one of the four rule families in the canonical data-snooping study, yet it is almost never in modern indicator libraries.
ideas.novelty: There is no lookback parameter at all - the only parameter is a percentage. Donchian compares the close to the extreme of a FIXED window; this compares it to the extreme since the last signal, which is an unbounded, state-dependent window. The two disagree systematically in long trends and in long ranges.
ideas.source: Alexander (1961), 'Price Movements in Speculative Markets: Trends or Random Walks', Industrial Management Review 2(2), 7-26 - the original x% filter rule. The filter-rule family is one of the five rule classes in the universe of 7,846 rules tested by Sullivan, Timmermann & White (1999), 'Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap', Journal of Finance 54(5), 1647-1691, which is the paper Sepp & Lucic (arXiv:2607.19497) cite when surveying 'American' breakout systems.

ideas.name: Volume-Conditioned Momentum Life Cycle
ideas.category: cross-sectional momentum with a volume conditioner
ideas.entry_rule: At each month end compute for every symbol: RET = close_{t-21}/close_{t-252} - 1, and RVOL = [mean daily volume over the last 252 bars] / [mean daily volume over the 252 bars before that]. RVOL is the OHLCV proxy for turnover - it removes the need for shares outstanding by comparing a name's volume to its own history rather than to its float. Sort the universe independently into RET terciles and RVOL terciles. Go long at the next open the intersection of the TOP RET tercile and the BOTTOM RVOL tercile (low-volume winners). Go short the intersection of the BOTTOM RET tercile and the TOP RVOL tercile (high-volume losers). Take no position in the other seven cells.
ideas.exit_rule: Six-month holding with overlapping portfolios: each month one sixth of the book is closed at the next open and replaced by the newly selected names, so six vintages run in parallel. No stop.
inputs: 252-bar mean volume vs the prior 252-bar mean volume
ideas.why: Trading volume proxies for how much attention and disagreement a name already carries. Winners that ran up on heavy, expanding volume have already had their news absorbed and behave like late-stage momentum - they reverse sooner. Winners that ran up quietly are still under-recognised and continue for longer. The same logic inverted applies to losers: heavily traded losers still have selling to do. The interaction is strong enough that volume predicts both the magnitude and the persistence of momentum, not just its level.
ideas.novelty: A double sort where the second dimension is a volume ratio that reorders the momentum ranking rather than filtering it, and the trade is placed only in the two diagonal cells. Distinct from a volume confirmation filter (which requires high volume for entry) - here the LONG leg explicitly requires LOW relative volume, which is the opposite of the usual confirmation logic.
ideas.source: Lee & Swaminathan (2000), 'Price Momentum and Trading Volume', Journal of Finance 55(5), 2017-2069 - the 'momentum life cycle' hypothesis and the RET x turnover double sort. (Wiley article page returned HTTP 403 during this session, so this citation is from knowledge of the literature; the RVOL proxy above is my substitution for turnover and is stated precisely.)

ideas.name: Efficiency-Ratio Adaptive Trend
ideas.entry_rule: With n = 10: ER_t = |close_t - close_{t-10}| / sum over i = 0..9 of |close_{t-i} - close_{t-i-1}| (set ER_t = 0 if the denominator is 0). SC_t = (ER_t * (2/3 - 2/31) + 2/31)^2, a smoothing constant that ranges from the 30-period EMA constant when the path is pure noise to the 2-period EMA constant when the path is a straight line. KAMA_t = KAMA_{t-1} + SC_t * (close_t - KAMA_{t-1}), seeded with KAMA = SMA_10(close). Let d_t = KAMA_t - KAMA_{t-1} and F_t = 0.5 * stdev(d over the last 20 bars). Go long at the next open when KAMA_t - min(KAMA over the last 20 bars) > F_t. Go short at the next open when max(KAMA over the last 20 bars) - KAMA_t > F_t.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit a long when KAMA_t < (max KAMA since entry) - F_t; exit a short when KAMA_t > (min KAMA since entry) + F_t. The exit band is itself adaptive, because F_t is the standard deviation of the adaptive average's own increments, so the required give-back shrinks in clean trends and widens in choppy ones.
inputs: rolling stdev(20) of the KAMA increments
ideas.why: The efficiency ratio is a direct signal-to-noise estimate: net displacement divided by total path length, bounded in [0,1]. Making the smoothing constant a function of it means the average is fast precisely when the price path is directional and slow precisely when it is noise, which is what the theory says the optimal filter should do - in a two-state regime-switching model the optimal trend rule is an exponential average whose optimal window contracts as the signal-to-noise ratio rises. A fixed-span EMA is optimal for exactly one signal-to-noise level and wrong everywhere else.
ideas.novelty: The smoothing span is a bar-by-bar function of the data rather than a swept parameter, and the entry/exit band is derived from the volatility of the smoothed series itself rather than from price volatility. A Hull MA is a fixed-weight construction; an EMA cross has two fixed spans. Here the effective span moves continuously between 2 and 30 within a single symbol's history.
ideas.source: Kaufman (1995), 'Smarter Trading', and Kaufman, 'Trading Systems and Methods' (5th ed.) - the adaptive moving average, the efficiency-ratio-driven smoothing constant, and the filter F = f * stdev of AMA changes. Academic counterpart: Zakamulin & Giner, 'Optimal Trend-Following in a Markov Switching Model', SSRN 4092437, which shows 'the exponential moving average (EMA) represents the optimal trend-following rule' with the optimal window size determined by the signal-to-noise ratio (paper list verified at vzakamulin.weebly.com/papers1.html).

ideas.name: Dollar-Volume Lead-Lag Within Group
ideas.entry_rule: Partition the universe into groups: use sector labels if available, otherwise cluster symbols into 8 groups by correlation of their daily returns over the last 252 bars (hierarchical clustering on 1 - correlation), recomputed quarterly - this keeps the rule OHLCV-only. Each Friday close, within each group rank symbols on ADV = mean(close * volume) over the last 63 bars. Let LEAD = the equal-weighted 5-day return of the top ADV tercile of that group, and let OWN = the symbol's own 5-day return. Go long at Monday's open every symbol in the BOTTOM ADV tercile of a group where LEAD > +0.01 AND OWN < LEAD. Go short every symbol in the bottom ADV tercile of a group where LEAD < -0.01 AND OWN > LEAD. The OWN condition enforces that the laggard has not already caught up.
ideas.exit_rule: Close the position at the following Friday's close (a five-trading-day hold). Close early at the next open if OWN measured from entry exceeds the entry-week LEAD (the catch-up has happened), or if the group's LEAD reverses sign.
ideas.why: Information diffuses gradually and unevenly: news that is relevant to a whole industry reaches the most heavily traded names in that industry first, because those are the names analysts cover and institutions trade. The thinly traded names in the same group price the same information days later. That gives a short-horizon, cross-sectional predictability that is not the same thing as the laggard's own momentum - the predictor is somebody else's price move.
ideas.novelty: The signal for a symbol comes from OTHER symbols' returns, not from its own price path. Nothing in the existing set is cross-sectional in that sense; even relative-strength ranking uses each symbol's own history. Dollar volume stands in for firm size, which is the diffusion variable in the source literature and is not otherwise available from OHLCV.
ideas.source: Hou (2007), 'Industry Information Diffusion and the Lead-Lag Effect in Stock Returns', Review of Financial Studies 20(4), 1113-1138 - big firms lead small firms within the same industry, and this intra-industry lead-lag subsumes most of the market-wide size lead-lag. Underlying effect: Lo & MacKinlay (1990), 'When Are Contrarian Profits Due to Stock Market Overreaction?', RFS 3(2). Industry-level momentum: Moskowitz & Grinblatt (1999), 'Do Industries Explain Momentum?', Journal of Finance 54(4). (Citations from knowledge of the literature; RFS/Wiley pages were not reachable this session.)

ideas.name: Aim-Portfolio Trade Buffer
ideas.category: execution and exit structure for any continuous trend signal
ideas.entry_rule: Take any continuous trend signal that produces a target weight w*_t in [-cap, +cap] - the European TF weight or the dampened MACD response are the natural inputs. Do NOT trade to w*_t. Instead, on each daily close compute the partial-adjustment target w_t = w_{t-1} + k * (w*_t - w_{t-1}) with k = 0.15 (sweep 0.05 to 0.50). Then apply a no-trade band: place an order at the next open only if |w_t - w_{t-1}| >= max(0.20 * |w*_t|, 0.02 * cap); otherwise leave the position exactly as it is and carry w_{t-1} forward unchanged. Direction is whatever the sign of the resulting held weight is - there is no separate entry event.
ideas.exit_rule: Exposure decays toward zero on its own as w* decays, at rate k per day. Two hard overrides: (a) flatten and reverse immediately, ignoring the band, when w*_t changes sign AND |w*_t| > 0.30 * cap; (b) flatten immediately when the position's own drawdown from its high-water mark since inception exceeds 2 * (daily ATR(20)/close) * sqrt(20) * held notional. Between those, the buffer is the exit: a position is never closed by a marginal signal move.
ideas.why: With proportional trading costs the optimal policy is not to trade to the target but to trade a constant fraction of the way toward it, because the cost of being slightly off-target is second order while the cost of trading is first order. Trend signals are noisy at exactly the frequency the buffer suppresses - a signal that oscillates around zero generates enormous turnover for zero expected P&L. Separately, higher costs push the cost-optimal trend span longer, so the buffer and a longer span are substitutes; sweeping k lets a single fast signal be run at any effective speed without re-fitting the filter.
ideas.novelty: A different exit and rebalancing structure that can be layered on any signal: partial adjustment plus a no-trade band, with the position ending only by decay or by an override. Every existing rule closes on a signal condition or a price level; here the ordinary exit is the absence of an order.
ideas.source: Garleanu & Pedersen (2013), 'Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs', Journal of Finance 68(6), 2309-2340 - the aim portfolio and constant-fraction partial adjustment. The trend-specific cost analysis, including the break-even cost and the power-law cost-optimal span, is in Sepp & Lucic (2026), 'The Science and Practice of Trend-Following Systems', arXiv:2607.19497v1, Section 5 and Proposition C.1 (PDF fetched and read; the paper notes 'costs also push the cost-optimal span toward longer horizons').

ideas.name: Network Momentum from Neighbours' Trend Signals
inputs: daily close prices across the universe
ideas.entry_rule: MULTI-SYMBOL cross-sectional. STEP 1, build the graph: from the ensemble-averaged normalized Levy areas Abar (as defined above), keep for each node m only its 10 largest-|Abar| edges, symmetrize A_mn = A_nm = max(|Abar_mn|, |Abar_nm|) over kept edges, zero the diagonal, then graph-normalize Atilde = D^(-1/2) A D^(-1/2) with D = diag(A * 1). STEP 2, compute each name's OWN trend signals: for (short, long) in {(8,24), (16,48), (32,96)} let q = (EMA_short(P) - EMA_long(P)) / sd_63(P), then R^k = q / sd_252(q), giving K = 3 signals per name. STEP 3, and this is the whole idea: the signal TRADED for name m is not its own trend but its NEIGHBOURS' trends, Rtilde^k_m = sum over n in neighbours(m) of Atilde_mn * R^k_n. ENTER LONG m when (1/K) * sum_k r(Rtilde^k_m) > 0 and ENTER SHORT when it is < 0, where r is a REVERTING response function r(x) = c_lambda * x * exp(-lambda^2 * x^2 / 2) with lambda = sqrt(2) - size grows with signal strength up to a point and then SHRINKS BACK toward zero for extreme signals, because an extreme aggregate reading usually means the spillover has already been absorbed. Position size for m: (1/M) * (1/K) * sum_k r(Rtilde^k_m) * (1 / sigma^22_m) * sigma_target / sqrt(252), with M the universe size, sigma^22 the 22-bar EWM volatility of m's returns, and sigma_target = 10% annualized.
ideas.exit_rule: Rebalance daily to the target sizes; a position closes naturally when its network signal crosses zero, and shrinks automatically as the signal becomes extreme via the reverting response. Rebuild the lead-lag graph every 21 bars. Optional hard risk gate: halve gross exposure whenever the realized 21-bar volatility of the equal-weighted universe exceeds its 90th percentile over 756 bars.
ideas.why: Trend-following on a name uses only that name's own history and therefore cannot see information that has already arrived at its neighbours and not yet at it. If leadership structure is real, the neighbours' trend state is a forecast of the name's own next move that its own price has not yet expressed. Replacing the own-trend feature with the degree-normalized neighbour-average is a clean test of exactly that proposition, holding the sizing machinery constant. The reverting response function additionally encodes the empirical fact that very strong momentum readings mark late-stage trends.
ideas.novelty: The traded signal for a stock contains NONE of its own trend - it is entirely its graph neighbours' trend signals, degree-normalized. The sizing function is non-monotone, deliberately de-sizing extreme signals, which is a different exposure profile from any standard trend or reversal rule.
params: number of neighbours retained per node (5-20)
ideas.source: Linze Li and William Ferreira, 'Follow the Leader: Enhancing Systematic Trend-Following Using Network Momentum', arXiv:2501.07135 - network momentum feature, graph normalization, ensemble lookbacks {22,44,66,88,110,132}, the reverting response r(x) = c_lambda x exp(-lambda^2 x^2/2) with lambda = sqrt(2), and the position-sizing formula all read from the arXiv HTML full text. I substituted a top-k thresholded adjacency for the paper's Kalofolias graph-learning step to make it directly implementable.

ideas.name: Rank-Space Residual Reversion
ideas.category: statistical arbitrage / cross-sectional in rank space
inputs: 63-bar median dollar volume as a capitalization-rank proxy
intraday bars for the rank-crossing rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: MULTI-SYMBOL cross-sectional, but indexed by RANK rather than by name. Capitalization is not available from OHLCV, so proxy the capitalization ORDERING with each name's trailing 63-bar median daily dollar volume V_i,t - a slow-moving quantity whose ordering is strongly rank-correlated with capitalization; let I(k,t) be the name occupying rank k on day t in descending order. Define the RANK RETURN as rtilde_(k),t = (V_{I(k,t),t} - V_{I(k,t-1),t-1}) / V_{I(k,t-1),t-1} - that is, TODAY's occupant of rank k compared with YESTERDAY's occupant of rank k, so the series belongs to the market SLOT, not to any company. Residualize: over a trailing 252 bars, build the correlation matrix of the rank-return series, eigendecompose it and keep the top 15 components as rank-space factors; then over the last 60 bars only, regress each rtilde_(k) on those factor returns by OLS and keep the residuals eps_(k),t. Cumulate X_(k)(n) = sum of eps_(k) over n = 1..60, fit an AR(1) X(n+1) = a + b X(n) + zeta, and form s_(k) = (X_(k)(60) - m) / sigma_eq with m = a/(1-b) and sigma_eq = sqrt(Var(zeta)/(1-b^2)), keeping only slots with b in (0,1). ENTER LONG rank slot k when s_(k) < -1.25 and ENTER SHORT when s_(k) > +1.25, dollar-neutral across all open slots. Execute by placing the slot's dollar weight on whichever TICKER currently occupies that rank.
ideas.exit_rule: Close a slot when |s_(k)| < 0.5. The distinct mechanic is the RANK-CROSSING REBALANCE: every T = 30 minutes during the session, recompute the ranks and TRANSFER each slot's dollar position to the ticker that now occupies that slot. A name whose rank has crossed a boundary is sold and its replacement bought even though nothing about that name's own signal changed - the position belongs to the slot, and the slot's occupant changed.
ideas.why: In name space, a stock's residual return is a noisy and non-stationary object because the underlying company itself changes over the estimation window. In rank space, the object is a market slot - 'the 50th largest name' - whose statistical behaviour is far more stable across decades, which is the central result of stochastic portfolio theory and the Atlas and hybrid-Atlas models. Li and Papanicolaou document that the rank-space correlation matrix has a larger spectral gap (a cleaner factor structure) and that rank-space residual returns mean-revert more strongly than their name-space counterparts, which is exactly what a residual reversion strategy needs.
ideas.novelty: The signal lives on the rank slot rather than on the ticker, and the portfolio rotates names automatically as ranks cross regardless of any name-level signal. That rank-crossing turnover has no analogue in any name-space construction - it is a distinct exit mechanism (you exit a name because it moved slots, not because its spread converged).
params: capitalization-rank proxy (63-bar median dollar volume vs 21-bar vs price x volume)
ideas.source: Y.-F. Li and G. Papanicolaou, 'Statistical Arbitrage in Rank Space', arXiv:2410.06568 - rank return definition eq. 3.5, the rank-space factor model eq. 3.6-3.7, and the intraday weight-conversion / rank-crossing rebalance eq. 3.11-3.13, read from the PDF. The dollar-volume proxy for capitalization rank and the classic Avellaneda-Lee s-score parameterization of the residual are my substitutions to keep it OHLCV-only and free of a neural network.

ideas.name: Ledoit-Wolf Constant-Correlation Shrinkage GMV
ideas.entry_rule: Every Friday close on daily bars. Universe = fleet symbols with >=252 daily bars and 20-day median dollar volume >= $5M. Build the T x N matrix X of daily log returns, T=252, demeaned column-wise. (1) Sample covariance S = (1/T) X'X. (2) Constant-correlation target F: F_ii = S_ii; F_ij = rbar * sqrt(S_ii*S_jj) for i!=j, where rbar = mean of all off-diagonal sample correlations. (3) pi_hat = sum_{i,j} pi_ij where pi_ij = (1/T) sum_t ((x_ti)(x_tj) - S_ij)^2. (4) rho_hat = sum_i pi_ii + sum_{i!=j} (rbar/2) * [ sqrt(S_jj/S_ii)*theta_ii,ij + sqrt(S_ii/S_jj)*theta_jj,ij ], where theta_ii,ij = (1/T) sum_t (x_ti^2 - S_ii)(x_ti*x_tj - S_ij). (5) gamma_hat = sum_{i,j} (F_ij - S_ij)^2. (6) delta = max(0, min(1, ((pi_hat - rho_hat)/gamma_hat)/T)). (7) Sigma = delta*F + (1-delta)*S. (8) w_raw = Sigma^{-1} * 1; w = w_raw / sum(w_raw); clip each w_i to [0, 0.20] and renormalise; set w_i = 0 if w_i < 0.005 and renormalise. Enter/resize each symbol at Monday's open to w_i * account equity.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold to the next weekly rebalance. Resize a name only if |w_new - w_old| > 0.02 (no-trade band). Fully exit a symbol when its new weight is < 0.005 or it leaves the eligible universe. Liquidate the whole book and stand flat for 5 sessions if the strategy equity curve drops 12% below its running high.
inputs: daily close (log returns, 252 bars, all fleet symbols)
daily volume (20-day median dollar volume for the liquidity screen)
ideas.why: With N symbols and T bars the sample covariance has O(N^2) free parameters estimated from N*T numbers; its smallest eigenvalues are biased downward, and the GMV inverse loads maximally on exactly those noisy directions. Shrinking toward a constant-correlation target trades a little bias for a large variance reduction, and the optimal intensity is estimable in closed form from the same sample. This is the single highest-leverage fix in a multi-name book: the error in Sigma^{-1} dominates realised risk far more than the entry signal does.
ideas.source: Ledoit & Wolf (2003) 'Improved estimation of the covariance matrix of stock returns with an application to portfolio selection', Journal of Empirical Finance 10(5) - the constant-correlation target; and Ledoit & Wolf (2004) 'Honey, I Shrunk the Sample Covariance Matrix', Journal of Portfolio Management 30(4). Estimator form delta*F + (1-delta)*S and the three LW target variants (constant variance / single factor / constant correlation) confirmed against PyPortfolioOpt risk-model docs (https://pyportfolioopt.readthedocs.io/en/latest/RiskModels.html) and scikit-learn covariance docs (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/covariance.html), both fetched this session. Note: ledoit.net PDFs failed to fetch (self-signed cert); the pi/rho/gamma decomposition is quoted from the published papers.
ideas.novelty: Contains no timing signal whatsoever - the edge is entirely in the estimator of the second moment across names. A moving-average cross is a per-symbol time-series rule; this is a cross-sectional estimation rule that decides how much of each name to hold.

ideas.name: Marchenko-Pastur Eigenvalue Clipping
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. Take T=500 daily log returns for the N eligible symbols; require N < T. Standardise each column to zero mean and unit variance to get Z, and form the correlation matrix C = (1/T) Z'Z. Eigendecompose C = sum_k lambda_k v_k v_k' with lambda_1 >= ... >= lambda_N. Set q = N/T and sigma^2 = 1 - lambda_1/N. Marchenko-Pastur noise edge: lambda_plus = sigma^2 * (1 + sqrt(q))^2. Declare every eigenvalue with lambda_k < lambda_plus to be noise. Replace each noise eigenvalue by their common mean lambda_bar = (sum of noise eigenvalues) / (count of noise eigenvalues), leaving eigenvectors and the surviving large eigenvalues untouched. Rebuild C_clean = sum_k lambda_k_clean v_k v_k'; rescale so diag(C_clean) = 1 exactly (C_clean = D^{-1/2} C_clean D^{-1/2} with D = diag(C_clean)). Convert to covariance: Sigma = diag(s) C_clean diag(s) with s_i the 500-day sample stdev of symbol i. Weights w = Sigma^{-1}1 / (1'Sigma^{-1}1), clipped to [0, 0.15] and renormalised. Enter at the next session's open.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold to next monthly rebalance; resize only when |w_new - w_old| > 0.02. Exit a name when its weight goes below 0.005. Hard risk stop: if realised 20-day annualised volatility of the live book exceeds 3x the volatility implied by w'Sigma w at the last rebalance, cut all positions by half immediately and wait for the next scheduled rebalance to restore.
inputs: N (number of symbols in the fleet)
params: sigma^2 convention (1.0 vs the 1 - lambda_1/N market-mode correction)
clip target (common mean vs linear-shrinkage of the noise bulk)
ideas.novelty: A spectral surgery rather than a convex blend: eigenvalues inside the noise band are flattened while the informative large eigenvalues are left completely alone. Linear shrinkage pulls every eigenvalue toward the mean including the real ones; clipping does not touch them. Different estimator, different resulting weight vector.
ideas.why: Laloux et al. showed that roughly 94% of the eigenvalues of an S&P 500 correlation matrix fall inside the band predicted for a purely random matrix - meaning the corresponding eigenvectors carry no reproducible information. GMV inversion assigns weight proportional to 1/lambda, so those noise directions receive the largest allocations and are precisely the ones that fail out of sample. Flattening the bulk removes the mechanism by which noise becomes leverage.
ideas.source: Laloux, Cizeau, Bouchaud & Potters (1999) 'Noise dressing of financial correlation matrices', arXiv:cond-mat/9810255 (fetched this session - confirms the RMT/eigenvalue-density agreement and the warning against blind use of empirical correlation matrices). Bun, Bouchaud & Potters (2017) 'Cleaning Large Correlation Matrices: Tools from Random Matrix Theory', arXiv:1610.08104 (fetched this session - Marchenko-Pastur equation, rotationally invariant estimators, eigenvalue clipping). MP support bounds lambda_pm = sigma^2 (1 +/- sqrt(q))^2 verified at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marchenko-Pastur_distribution.

ideas.name: HERC with Tail-Risk Cluster Splits
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. (1) Cluster as in HRP but with average linkage on d_ij = sqrt(0.5*(1-rho_ij)) over 252 daily returns. (2) Choose the cluster count K: for each k in 2..min(10, floor(N/2)), cut the dendrogram into k clusters and compute the mean silhouette score on the distance matrix d; take K = argmax silhouette. (3) Top-down allocation over the K-1 dendrogram splits that produce those K clusters, in order of decreasing merge height: at each split of parent P into children A and B, compute each child's risk as R = the 5% historical CVaR of the equal-weighted daily return series of that child's members over the trailing 252 bars (CVaR = the arithmetic mean of the worst 5% of daily returns, expressed positive). Allocate the parent's weight as w_A = w_P * R_B/(R_A+R_B) and w_B = w_P * R_A/(R_A+R_B). (4) Within each terminal cluster, split its weight across members in inverse proportion to each member's own 5% CVaR, normalised within the cluster. Enter every symbol with final weight > 0.005 at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Monthly rebalance with a 0.015 no-trade band per name. Exit a name entirely when its weight falls below 0.005. Cluster-level stop: if any terminal cluster's realised 21-day CVaR exceeds 2.5x the CVaR used to size it at the last rebalance, zero that cluster's entire allocation and redistribute pro rata to the remaining clusters until the next rebalance.
inputs: historical 5% CVaR per symbol and per cluster
params: risk measure at splits (CVaR / standard deviation / CDaR / Ulcer)
ideas.novelty: Differs from HRP in two structural ways, not in a parameter: it splits along the actual dendrogram topology at a statistically chosen number of clusters rather than bisecting the serialised ordering at its midpoint, and it equalises a tail-risk contribution rather than a variance contribution. HRP's midpoint bisection can cut straight through a real cluster; this cannot.
ideas.why: HRP's recursive bisection splits the ordered list in half regardless of where the true cluster boundaries fall, which is an arbitrary choice the data can answer. Choosing K by silhouette lets the tree decide. Using CVaR instead of variance matters for a fleet of individual equities, where the risk that ends a strategy is a co-crash in the left tail, not the average squared deviation - and variance treats a name that gaps down 20% once the same as one that oscillates mildly.
ideas.source: Raffinot (2017) 'Hierarchical Clustering-Based Asset Allocation', Journal of Portfolio Management 44(2), introduces HERC. Implementation confirmed available with 37 risk measures for HRP/HERC in Riskfolio-Lib (https://riskfolio-lib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, fetched this session, which lists 'Hierarchical Clustering: HRP and HERC with 37 risk measures' and CVaR among its downside measures). Distance metric and clustering per Lopez de Prado (2016).

ideas.name: Nested Clustered Optimization
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. (1) Build the correlation matrix over 252 daily returns and denoise it by Marchenko-Pastur eigenvalue clipping (noise eigenvalues below sigma^2(1+sqrt(N/T))^2 replaced by their mean, diagonal rescaled to 1). (2) Convert distance d_ij = sqrt(0.5*(1-rho_ij)); cluster with average linkage; choose K in 2..min(10, floor(N/2)) by maximum mean silhouette. (3) Intra-cluster step: for each cluster k, take the sub-matrix Sigma_kk of the denoised covariance over its members and solve the constrained GMV problem there, w_k = Sigma_kk^{-1}1 / (1'Sigma_kk^{-1}1), clipped to [0, 0.5] within the cluster and renormalised so sum(w_k) = 1. (4) Reduce: form the K x K matrix Sigma_red with Sigma_red[k,l] = w_k' Sigma_kl w_l, i.e. the covariance of the K synthetic cluster-portfolio return streams. (5) Inter-cluster step: a_k = Sigma_red^{-1}1 / (1'Sigma_red^{-1}1), clipped to [0, 0.40] and renormalised. (6) Final weight for symbol i in cluster k: W_i = a_k * w_k,i. Enter every symbol with W_i > 0.005 at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Monthly rebalance, 0.02 no-trade band. Exit a name when W_i < 0.005. Conditioning guard: before trading, compute the condition number of every Sigma_kk and of Sigma_red; if any exceeds 500, merge that cluster into its dendrogram sibling and recompute, and if the guard still fails fall back to equal weighting within the offending cluster for that month.
ideas.novelty: Two nested small inversions instead of one large one. It is not a different estimator of Sigma - it is a different way of using Sigma, in which estimation error stays inside the cluster where it originated instead of leaking across the whole weight vector via the global inverse.
ideas.why: The instability of Markowitz optimisation is driven by the condition number of Sigma, which grows with N. If the matrix is block-structured, each block has a far smaller condition number than the whole, and the K x K reduced matrix is tiny. Solving the problem twice at small scale therefore inherits almost none of the large-matrix instability, while still producing a genuinely optimised - not merely heuristic - weight vector, which is what HRP gives up.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado (2019) 'A Robust Estimator of the Efficient Frontier' (Nested Clustered Optimization), SSRN 3469961; and Lopez de Prado, 'Machine Learning for Asset Managers' (2020), Ch. 7. NCO with four objectives is confirmed as a supported model in Riskfolio-Lib (https://riskfolio-lib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, fetched this session). MP clipping bounds verified per the Marchenko-Pastur entry cited above.

ideas.name: Minimum-CVaR Scenario LP Allocation
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. Collect J = 500 daily return vectors r_j (one per past session, N symbols each) for the eligible universe. Set alpha = 0.95. Solve the linear program: minimise over (w, gamma, z) the objective gamma + 1/((1-alpha)*J) * sum_j z_j, subject to z_j >= -w'r_j - gamma for all j; z_j >= 0 for all j; sum_i w_i = 1; 0 <= w_i <= 0.15; and w'rbar >= median(rbar), where rbar_i is symbol i's mean daily return over the trailing 60 bars. The optimal gamma is the 95% VaR and the objective value is the 95% CVaR. Enter each symbol with w_i > 0.005 at the next open, sized w_i * equity.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold to next monthly rebalance; trade a name only if |w_new - w_old| > 0.02. Exit a symbol when w_i < 0.005. Live tail guard: if the book records a daily loss worse than 1.5x the optimised CVaR value on any single session, halve all positions at the next open and re-solve the LP the following day rather than waiting for month-end.
inputs: daily close (500 return scenarios per symbol)
60-day mean returns for the return floor
ideas.novelty: No covariance matrix is estimated at all.
