The objective is a function of the empirical joint distribution of the scenarios, so simultaneous crashes across names are counted as they actually occurred, not as the product of two variances and a correlation. That is a different objective, not a different lookback.
ideas.why: Variance is symmetric and treats a 5% up day as identical risk to a 5% down day; it also underweights joint tail events because correlation is an average over the whole sample, and equity correlations rise sharply exactly in the left tail. Minimising CVaR targets the average of the worst 5% of portfolio days directly. Rockafellar and Uryasev's key result is that this is a convex problem - in fact a plain LP with sampled scenarios - which makes it tractable at fleet scale and free of local optima.
ideas.source: Rockafellar & Uryasev (2000) 'Optimization of Conditional Value-at-Risk', Journal of Risk 2(3). The auxiliary function F_alpha(w,gamma) = gamma + 1/(1-alpha) * E[(loss - gamma)+], its convexity in gamma, and the sampled LP form min gamma + 1/((1-alpha)J) sum z_j s.t. z_j >= loss_j - gamma, z_j >= 0 were verified at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expected_shortfall (fetched this session). CVaR is listed among Riskfolio-Lib's convex downside risk measures.

ideas.name: CDaR Path-Constrained Allocation
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. Take J = 750 daily return vectors. Define the portfolio cumulative return path y_j(w) = sum_{t<=j} w'r_t and the running maximum u_j, enforced linearly by u_j >= u_{j-1}, u_j >= y_j, u_0 = 0. Conditional Drawdown-at-Risk at confidence beta = 0.90 is CDaR = min over gamma of [ gamma + 1/((1-beta)*J) * sum_j max(u_j - y_j - gamma, 0) ], linearised with slack v_j >= u_j - y_j - gamma, v_j >= 0. Solve the LP: maximise w'rbar (rbar = 120-day mean daily returns) subject to gamma + 1/((1-beta)*J) * sum_j v_j <= 0.10, the u and v constraints above, sum_i w_i = 1, 0 <= w_i <= 0.15. Enter every symbol with w_i > 0.005 at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold to next monthly rebalance with a 0.02 no-trade band. Exit a name when w_i < 0.005. Live drawdown governor: track the realised drawdown of the live book from its high-water mark; scale gross exposure by max(0, 1 - realised_DD / 0.10), so exposure falls linearly to zero as the realised drawdown approaches the CDaR budget, and restores as the book recovers.
ideas.novelty: The risk functional depends on the ordering of the returns, not just their distribution. Two books with identical return histograms - and therefore identical variance and identical CVaR - can have completely different CDaR if one clustered its losses. This is a genuinely different objective from every distribution-based measure in the collection.
ideas.why: What actually stops a live trading fleet is not a single bad day but a long, connected drawdown that exhausts patience or margin. Variance and CVaR are both permutation-invariant and cannot see clustering of losses; drawdown measures are path functionals and can. Chekhlov, Uryasev and Zabarankin showed CDaR is convex in the weights and reduces to an LP, so it can be optimised directly rather than merely monitored, and it nests average drawdown (beta -> 0) and maximum drawdown (beta -> 1) as the endpoints of one parameter.
ideas.source: Chekhlov, Uryasev & Zabarankin (2005) 'Drawdown Measure in Portfolio Optimization', International Journal of Theoretical and Applied Finance 8(1), and their 2003 'Portfolio Optimization with Drawdown Constraints'. Conditional Drawdown at Risk and its entropic/relativistic variants are confirmed as implemented convex drawdown measures in Riskfolio-Lib (https://riskfolio-lib.readthedocs.io/en/latest/, fetched this session). Direct fetch of the Uryasev CDaR PDF 404'd; the LP linearisation stated here is the standard one from that paper.

ideas.name: Most Diversified Portfolio
ideas.entry_rule: Every Friday close. Estimate returns over 126 daily bars with exponential weighting, halflife 42 bars: sigma_i = EWMA stdev of symbol i, C = EWMA correlation matrix, Sigma = diag(sigma) C diag(sigma). Maximise the Diversification Ratio DR(w) = (sum_i w_i sigma_i) / sqrt(w' Sigma w) subject to sum w = 1, 0 <= w_i <= 0.20. Solve it in the equivalent convex form: minimise y'Cy over y >= 0 with sum y = 1 (a plain QP on the correlation matrix), then recover w_i = (y_i / sigma_i) / sum_j (y_j / sigma_j). Enter every symbol with w_i > 0.005 at Monday's open. Record DR at each rebalance.
ideas.exit_rule: Weekly rebalance with a 0.02 no-trade band; exit a name when w_i < 0.005. Regime exit: if the achieved DR falls below 1.3, or below its own 10th percentile over the trailing 104 rebalances, cut gross exposure to 50% - the universe has become too correlated for the objective to deliver anything, and the portfolio is paying high single-name volatility for diversification it is no longer getting.
params: DR floor for the regime exit
ideas.novelty: Its tilt is the opposite of minimum variance. GMV and inverse-vol both systematically pile into the lowest-volatility names; maximising the ratio will happily hold a high-volatility name if its correlation to the rest is low enough, because the numerator rewards standalone volatility. Same inputs, opposite cross-sectional exposure.
ideas.why: Diversification is a property of the relationship between the parts and the whole, and DR measures exactly that: how much of the weighted-average standalone volatility gets cancelled by the portfolio structure. A DR of 1 means no diversification at all. Because the objective involves only volatilities and correlations - never expected returns - it avoids the dominant source of optimiser error, while still being a real optimisation rather than a heuristic. Choueifaty and Coignard show the MDP is the portfolio that any risk-averse investor holds when all assets have the same Sharpe ratio, which is a far weaker assumption than forecasting each name's mean.
ideas.source: Choueifaty & Coignard (2008) 'Toward Maximum Diversification', Journal of Portfolio Management 34(4). The Diversification Ratio definition DR = (sum w_i sigma_i)/sigma_p, the MDP optimisation, and the claimed robustness from needing only volatility and correlation estimates were verified from the TOBAM reprint at https://www.tobam.fr/wp-content/uploads/2014/12/TOBAM-JoPM-Maximum-Div-2008.pdf (fetched this session).

ideas.name: Michaud Resampled Efficiency
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. Let R be the trailing 756 x N matrix of daily returns. Perform B = 200 replications: for replication b, draw a stationary block bootstrap sample of 252 rows with expected block length 10 bars (preserves short-horizon autocorrelation and joint cross-sectional structure); compute Sigma_b (Ledoit-Wolf shrunk) and mu_b (mean returns) from the resample; solve the constrained max-Sharpe problem max (w'mu_b)/sqrt(w'Sigma_b w) s.t. sum w = 1, 0 <= w_i <= 0.20, yielding w_b. Final weights W = (1/B) * sum_b w_b, renormalised. Before trading, compute the B pairwise L1 distances among {w_b} and take q25 = their 25th percentile. Rebalance to W only if ||W - w_current||_1 > q25; otherwise hold the existing book unchanged this month. Enter at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold until a rebalance actually fires under the statistical-equivalence test above. Exit a name when its averaged weight is below 0.005 AND the rebalance fires. Hard exit: liquidate any symbol that leaves the eligible universe immediately, redistributing its weight pro rata, without waiting for the test.
inputs: a QP/SOCP solver, 200 solves per rebalance
ideas.novelty: It changes nothing about the estimator or the objective - it averages over the sampling distribution of the optimiser's output. And its exit structure is unusual: the no-trade region is not a fixed band but is derived from the bootstrap dispersion itself, so the portfolio only trades when the new solution is statistically distinguishable from the one it already holds.
ideas.why: Mean-variance optimisation is an error-maximiser: it systematically over-weights assets whose returns were overestimated and whose risks were underestimated in the particular sample drawn. Averaging optimal solutions across bootstrap resamples of that sample cancels much of this, producing weights that are more diversified and far more stable than a single point solution. The statistical-equivalence turnover test is the natural companion - if two portfolios both lie inside the resampling cloud, paying spread and commission to move between them is pure cost.
ideas.source: Michaud (1989) 'The Markowitz Optimization Enigma: Is Optimized Optimal?', Financial Analysts Journal 45(1); Michaud & Michaud, 'Efficient Asset Management' (2nd ed., 2008), for resampled efficiency and portfolio statistical equivalence. The 1/N benchmark this must clear is DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009) 'Optimal Versus Naive Diversification', Review of Financial Studies 22(5). Note: the DGU PDF at faculty.london.edu redirected and was not fetched this session; cited from the published paper.

ideas.name: Black-Litterman with Signal-Supplied Views
ideas.entry_rule: Every Friday close. (1) Prior weights: w_prior_i = symbol i's share of the fleet's total 20-day median dollar volume (an OHLCV-only proxy for market-cap equilibrium weights). (2) Sigma = Ledoit-Wolf constant-correlation shrunk covariance over 252 daily returns, annualised. (3) Reverse-optimise implied equilibrium excess returns: Pi = delta * Sigma * w_prior with risk-aversion delta = 2.5. (4) Views from the trading signal: s_i = the cross-sectional z-score of 12-1 momentum (252-bar total return excluding the most recent 21 bars). Set P = I_N (one absolute view per symbol), Q_i = kappa * s_i * sigma_i_annual with view scale kappa = 0.02, and Omega = diag(tau * P Sigma P') with tau = 0.05. (5) Posterior: mu_BL = [ (tau*Sigma)^{-1} + P' Omega^{-1} P ]^{-1} [ (tau*Sigma)^{-1} Pi + P' Omega^{-1} Q ]. (6) Weights w = (1/delta) * Sigma^{-1} * mu_BL; set negatives to 0, clip to 0.15, renormalise to sum 1. Enter each w_i > 0.005 at Monday's open.
ideas.exit_rule: Weekly rebalance, 0.02 no-trade band, exit a name when w_i < 0.005. Confidence-driven de-risking: recompute Omega each week from the trailing 52-week rolling information coefficient of the momentum score (Spearman correlation between s_i at t and the forward 21-day return). If that IC is <= 0, set Omega to 10x its formula value for that week, which collapses the posterior back onto the equilibrium prior and mechanically flattens the active book without a discretionary override.
inputs: daily volume (20-day median dollar volume for the prior)
rolling information coefficient of the signal
params: signal used for views (momentum / reversal / composite)
ideas.novelty: Alpha enters as a view carrying an explicit uncertainty rather than as a point forecast fed straight to an optimiser. Because the posterior is a precision-weighted blend, a weak or unreliable signal shrinks toward the equilibrium portfolio automatically instead of producing the corner solutions raw mean-variance always produces.
ideas.why: Feeding raw signal z-scores into Sigma^{-1} mu yields extreme, unstable weights because it treats the forecast as certain. Black-Litterman fixes the pathology at its root: the prior is a portfolio that is by construction sensible (the equilibrium book), views perturb it in proportion to their confidence, and the resulting posterior weights degrade gracefully as the signal degrades. Tying Omega to a measured rolling IC closes the loop, so the size of the active bet tracks the demonstrated accuracy of the signal rather than an assumed constant.
ideas.source: Black & Litterman (1992) 'Global Portfolio Optimization', Financial Analysts Journal 48(5), and Black & Litterman (1991), Journal of Fixed Income. Idzorek (2007) 'A Step-by-Step Guide to the Black-Litterman Model' for the Omega = diag(tau P Sigma P') convention. Note: the Wikipedia Black-Litterman page fetched this session gives only the conceptual description and no formulas, and pointed to Idzorek and Walters for the mathematics; the equations above are quoted from those published sources. Ledoit-Wolf input per the shrinkage entry above.

ideas.name: Effective-Number-of-Bets Admission Test
ideas.entry_rule: Run daily at the close on top of whatever target weights w the per-symbol strategies propose. (1) Sigma = MP-denoised covariance over 252 daily returns. (2) Eigendecompose Sigma = E Lambda E' with eigenvalues sorted descending. (3) Project the book into principal bets: wtilde = E' w. (4) Diversification distribution: p_k = (wtilde_k^2 * Lambda_kk) / (w' Sigma w), which is non-negative and sums to 1 by construction. (5) Effective Number of Bets ENB = exp( -sum_k p_k * ln p_k ) (Shannon entropy exponentiated; ENB = 1 when all risk sits in one principal direction, = N when risk is spread evenly). (6) Admission test for a new candidate position j: recompute ENB with j included at its proposed weight; open the position only if ENB_with_j > ENB_without_j. (7) Global throttle: multiply every target weight by min(1, ENB / 5) so the book runs at full size only when it holds at least five effectively independent bets.
ideas.exit_rule: If ENB < 3 on three consecutive closes, close positions in descending order of their p_k contribution - largest first - until ENB is back above 3. Otherwise exits are left to the underlying per-symbol strategies; this layer only sizes and vetoes.
inputs: daily close (252 bars, every symbol in the fleet)
params: basis (PCA eigenvectors vs Meucci minimum-torsion factors)
consecutive-breach count for the forced reduction
ideas.novelty: A veto, not a weighting scheme. It can reject a signal that is strong on its own merits purely because the risk it adds points in a direction the book is already loaded on. Every other entry in this family answers 'how much of each'; this answers 'is this position adding anything at all'.
ideas.why: The fundamental law says information ratio scales with the square root of breadth - the number of genuinely independent bets. A fleet of twelve tickers that are all long high-beta US equities has a breadth close to one, and its Sharpe will behave accordingly no matter how good the per-symbol signals are. Counting names overstates breadth badly; the entropy of the risk decomposition across principal directions measures it honestly, because two perfectly correlated positions collapse into a single p_k and the entropy does not rise.
ideas.source: Meucci (2009) 'Managing Diversification', Risk 22(5), pp. 74-79, introduces the diversification distribution and the entropy-based effective number of bets; Meucci, Santangelo & Deguest (2015) 'Risk Budgeting and Diversification Based on Optimized Uncorrelated Factors' gives the minimum-torsion basis alternative to PCA. Note: SSRN 1358533 returned 403 and arpm.co gave no detail, so these are cited from the published articles rather than verified by fetch this session. Breadth framing from Grinold & Kahn, 'Active Portfolio Management' (2nd ed., 2000).

ideas.name: Absorption Ratio Systemic De-Risking
ideas.entry_rule: Daily at the close, applied as a gross-exposure multiplier on the base allocator's target weights. (1) Compute the correlation matrix of the N fleet symbols over the trailing 500 daily returns and eigendecompose it. (2) Absorption Ratio AR = (sum of the largest n eigenvalues) / (sum of all N eigenvalues), with n = ceil(N/5). (3) Standardised shift: dAR = (mean of AR over the last 15 sessions - mean of AR over the last 252 sessions) / (stdev of AR over the last 252 sessions). (4) Exposure multiplier m: m = 1.0 if dAR < 0; m = 0.5 if 0 <= dAR < 1; m = 0.0 if dAR >= 1. (5) Every target weight from the base allocator is multiplied by m, and any resulting change larger than 10% of book value is executed at the next open. New positions are opened only while m > 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Positions are scaled down whenever m falls to a lower tier and scaled back up when dAR returns below the tier boundary for two consecutive closes (hysteresis, to avoid whipsawing on a single day's reading). While m = 0 the book is fully flat and no new entries are taken regardless of what the per-symbol signals say.
inputs: daily close (500 bars, all fleet symbols)
rolling eigendecomposition of the correlation matrix
AR time series with 15-day and 252-day statistics
params: n (fraction of eigenvectors: N/5, N/10, fixed 1)
ideas.novelty: The state variable is a property of the correlation matrix's eigenvalue spectrum, not of any price series. It can fire while every individual name still looks calm on its own chart, because it detects that the names have stopped being distinct - which is invisible to any per-symbol volatility or trend filter.
ideas.why: Kritzman, Li, Page and Rigobon document that a rising absorption ratio - more of total variance being explained by fewer principal components - signals a tightly coupled market that transmits shocks quickly, and that most significant US equity drawdowns were preceded by a spike in AR. It is a compactness measure for the system, and it is exactly the condition under which a diversified multi-name book stops being diversified. Cutting gross exposure on the signal directly addresses the failure mode where the portfolio's assumed independence evaporates at the worst moment.
ideas.source: Kritzman, Li, Page & Rigobon (2011) 'Principal Components as a Measure of Systemic Risk', Journal of Portfolio Management 37(4). Note: cited from the published paper; not fetched this session (the session's web-search budget was exhausted). The underlying eigenvalue-spectrum framing is consistent with Laloux et al. (1999) arXiv:cond-mat/9810255 and Bun, Bouchaud & Potters (2017) arXiv:1610.08104, both of which were fetched.

ideas.name: Weight-Space Shrinkage Toward 1/N
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. (1) Compute w_opt from a base optimiser - Ledoit-Wolf shrunk GMV over 252 daily returns, weights clipped to [0, 0.20] and renormalised. (2) Blended weights w(c) = c * w_opt + (1 - c) * (1/N) for the N eligible symbols. (3) Choose c by walk-forward validation, not by formula: for each candidate c in {0.0, 0.1, ..., 1.0}, replay the previous 24 monthly rebalance dates using only data available on each of those dates, compute the realised monthly return series of the w(c) book, and take its annualised Sharpe ratio; select the c with the highest realised Sharpe, breaking ties toward the smaller c. (4) Apply w(c*) and enter at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Monthly rebalance with a 0.02 no-trade band. Exit a name when its blended weight falls below 0.005 or it leaves the eligible universe. Degenerate-solution guard: if the selected c* is 1.0 for three consecutive months while the realised Sharpe of the c = 0 (equal-weight) book exceeded that of the c = 1 book over the same period, force c = 0.5 for the following month - a sign the validation window is overfitting.
inputs: daily close (252 bars for the covariance, plus 24 months of rebalance history for validation)
realised monthly returns of each candidate blend
params: selection criterion (Sharpe / realised variance / turnover-adjusted Sharpe)
ideas.novelty: Shrinkage applied to the optimiser's output rather than its input, with the intensity chosen empirically by out-of-sample performance instead of by a plug-in estimator. Two portfolios can share an identical covariance estimate and differ entirely in this dimension, so it composes with - rather than competes against - every covariance-side method in this family.
ideas.why: DeMiguel, Garlappi and Uppal found that none of fourteen sophisticated allocation models reliably beat naive 1/N out of sample, and estimated that a sample-based mean-variance policy would need an implausibly long estimation window before it did. The honest reading is that 1/N carries zero estimation error while the optimiser carries a lot, so the right answer sits between them. Tu and Zhou formalise exactly this combination and show the optimal mixing weight can be derived or estimated. Choosing c by walk-forward Sharpe makes the portfolio pay for sophistication only when sophistication has been demonstrably earning its keep on this particular universe.
ideas.source: DeMiguel, Garlappi & Uppal (2009) 'Optimal Versus Naive Diversification: How Inefficient Is the 1/N Portfolio Strategy?', Review of Financial Studies 22(5) - the 1/N benchmark and the fourteen-model horse race. Tu & Zhou (2011) 'Markowitz Meets Talmud: A Combination of Sophisticated and Naive Diversification Strategies', Journal of Financial Economics 99(1) - the explicit convex combination of an optimised rule with 1/N. Note: the DGU PDF redirected and was not fetched this session; both are cited from the published journals.

ideas.name: Graphical Lasso Sparse Precision Allocation
ideas.entry_rule: Every Friday close. (1) Standardise 252 daily log returns per symbol to zero mean, unit variance; form the empirical correlation matrix S. (2) Fit the graphical lasso: K_hat = argmin_K [ tr(SK) - log det(K) + alpha * ||K||_1 ] where the L1 penalty applies to off-diagonal entries only and K is constrained positive definite. (3) Select alpha by 5-fold cross-validated Gaussian log-likelihood over a 10-point logarithmic grid spanning alpha in [0.01, 0.5]; folds are contiguous time blocks, not shuffled rows, to respect serial dependence. (4) GMV weights on the correlation scale are proportional to K_hat * 1; convert back to the return scale: w_raw_i = (1/s_i) * sum_j K_hat_ij / s_j, with s_i the 252-day stdev of symbol i. (5) Set negative w_raw to 0 for a long-only book, clip to 0.20, renormalise to sum 1. Enter each w_i > 0.005 at Monday's open.
ideas.exit_rule: Weekly rebalance with a 0.02 no-trade band; exit a name when its weight falls below 0.005. Graph-instability stop: track the sparsity pattern of K_hat week to week; if more than 30% of the off-diagonal support changes between consecutive fits, the graph is not identified from this sample - fall back to equal weighting over the current holdings for that week rather than trading into an unstable solution.
inputs: daily close (252 bars, all fleet symbols)
graphical lasso solver with time-block cross-validation
params: support-change threshold for the instability stop
ideas.novelty: It is the only method here that produces exact zeros in the precision matrix. Shrinkage and eigenvalue clipping both return dense matrices; sparsity is a structurally different kind of regularisation and yields a structurally different weight vector, because a zero in K is an assertion of conditional independence, not merely a small number.
ideas.why: The GMV weight vector is a function of the precision matrix, not the covariance matrix - so the object that should be regularised is K, and regularising Sigma only regularises K indirectly and imprecisely. A zero at K_ij says i and j are independent given every other name in the fleet, which is the statistically correct statement that two stocks in the same sector are related through the sector and not directly. Forcing those entries to zero prevents the optimiser from constructing a spurious hedge between them - the exact failure mode that makes GMV weights blow up out of sample. It is also well-defined when N is close to or exceeds T, where the sample covariance is singular and cannot be inverted at all.
ideas.source: Friedman, Hastie & Tibshirani (2008) 'Sparse inverse covariance estimation with the graphical lasso', Biostatistics 9(3). The objective tr(SK) - log det(K) + alpha*||K||_1, the recommendation to standardise to the correlation matrix, the guidance that it suits the n_samples <= n_features regime, and the caveat that cross-validated alpha selection tends to choose too many edges were all verified at https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/covariance.html (fetched this session).

ideas.name: BAHC Bootstrapped Hierarchical Covariance Filter
ideas.entry_rule: Last trading day of each month. (1) Let R be the trailing 252 x N daily return matrix. (2) For b = 1..B with B = 100: draw 252 rows with replacement; compute that resample's correlation matrix rho_b; run average-linkage agglomerative clustering on d_ij = sqrt(0.5*(1 - rho_b,ij)); then build the hierarchically filtered matrix rho_b_filt by setting each off-diagonal entry rho_b_filt,ij to the mean of the rho_b entries over all pairs inside the smallest cluster in the dendrogram that contains both i and j, with the diagonal set to 1. (3) Average across replications: C_BAHC = (1/B) * sum_b rho_b_filt; project to the nearest positive-definite matrix by clipping any eigenvalue below 1e-8 to 1e-8 and rescaling the diagonal to 1. (4) Sigma = diag(s) C_BAHC diag(s) with s the 252-day sample stdevs. (5) GMV weights w = Sigma^{-1}1 / (1'Sigma^{-1}1), clipped to [0, 0.15], renormalised. Enter each w_i > 0.005 at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Monthly rebalance, but with a deliberately wide 0.03 no-trade band and a hard cap of 25% of book value traded per rebalance, executing the largest weight changes first - the source paper reports this method wins on after-cost Sharpe despite generating higher turnover than competing filters, so turnover control is part of the strategy, not an afterthought. Exit a name when its weight is below 0.005 and the trade fits inside the turnover cap.
inputs: daily close (252 bars, all fleet symbols)
params: number of nested filtering levels k (the k-fold boosted variant)
ideas.novelty: Filtering happens in the space of hierarchies rather than the space of eigenvalues. Bootstrapping produces many plausible dendrograms and averages the matrices they imply, so the final estimate is not conditioned on one particular clustering that the sample happened to produce - a distinct failure mode from the one shrinkage and clipping address.
ideas.why: Hierarchical filtering imposes a strong, economically sensible structure - names in the same cluster share one correlation - which kills a great deal of noise. But a single dendrogram estimated from a short sample is itself very unstable: a small perturbation flips two branches and the filtered matrix changes materially. Bootstrapping the hierarchy and averaging recovers the noise reduction of the structural ansatz without inheriting its instability. Bongiorno and Challet report lower realised risk in global minimum variance portfolios than current filtering methods specifically when the number of data points is relatively small, which is exactly the regime a fleet of a dozen names on a year of daily bars operates in.
ideas.source: Bongiorno & Challet (2020) 'Covariance matrix filtering with bootstrapped hierarchies', arXiv:2003.05807 (fetched this session - confirms the hierarchical ansatz with dependence averaging between clusters, the bootstrap over multiple hierarchies, and the lower realised GMV risk when data points are few). Bongiorno & Challet (2020) 'Reactive Global Minimum Variance Portfolios with k-BAHC covariance cleaning', arXiv:2005.08703 (fetched this session - the k-fold boosted variant, and the finding of better after-cost Sharpe ratios despite higher turnover).

ideas.name: Transfer Coefficient Governor
ideas.entry_rule: At every weekly rebalance, before placing any order, compute two active weight vectors relative to the equal-weighted fleet benchmark. (1) w_uncon = the unconstrained optimal active book: Sigma^{-1} * a, where a is the cross-sectional z-score of the composite entry signal and Sigma is the Ledoit-Wolf shrunk covariance, rescaled so that sqrt(w_uncon' Sigma w_uncon) equals the target active risk of 10% annualised. (2) w_impl = the weights that survive the fleet's real constraints: long-only, per-name cap 0.15, minimum position $500, whole-share rounding, and at most 12 concurrent names. (3) Transfer coefficient TC = (w_uncon' Sigma w_impl) / sqrt( (w_uncon' Sigma w_uncon) * (w_impl' Sigma w_impl) ) - the risk-weighted correlation between intended and implementable active positions. (4) Deploy the full book only if TC >= 0.50. If TC < 0.50, relax constraints in this fixed order, recomputing TC after each step: raise the per-name cap to 0.20, then to 0.25; then raise the max name count to 16, then to 20. (5) If TC is still below 0.50 after all relaxations, scale gross exposure by TC/0.50 (so a TC of 0.30 runs at 60% size), because expected information ratio is TC * IC * sqrt(BR) and half the transfer coefficient is half the expected IR for the same risk budget.
ideas.exit_rule: Positions are exited by the underlying signal. This layer additionally forces a full flat if TC < 0.25 at two consecutive rebalances - at that point the implemented book has little relationship to the intended one and is best described as an uncompensated risk position. Log TC at every rebalance and, on a rolling 52-week basis, remove from the constraint set whichever single constraint has most often been the binding one.
inputs: daily close (252 bars for the covariance)
the unconstrained and constrained weight vectors
account equity and share prices (for the whole-share and minimum-position constraints)
params: the constraint-relaxation ladder and its ordering
ideas.novelty: The tradeable quantity is the gap between the portfolio you wanted and the portfolio you can actually hold. Nothing else in the collection measures implementation loss, and it produces both a sizing decision and a prescription for which constraint to relax - a control loop over the construction process itself rather than another weighting formula.
ideas.why: Grinold and Kahn's fundamental law gives IR = IC * sqrt(BR) for an unconstrained manager. Clarke, de Silva and Thorley showed that once real constraints bind - and long-only plus a small position count binds hard on a retail-scale fleet - the law becomes IR = TC * IC * sqrt(BR), where the transfer coefficient is the correlation between the constrained and unconstrained active weights. Typical long-only equity mandates run TC around 0.3-0.5, meaning half or more of the signal's theoretical value is destroyed in implementation and never shows up in any per-trade metric. Measuring it converts an invisible structural leak into a number you can act on: either relax the binding constraint or stop paying full risk for a fraction of the expected return.
ideas.source: Grinold & Kahn, 'Active Portfolio Management' (2nd ed., 2000), for IR = IC * sqrt(BR). Clarke, de Silva & Thorley (2002) 'Portfolio Constraints and the Fundamental Law of Active Management', Financial Analysts Journal 58(5), for the transfer coefficient and the generalised law IR = TC * IC * sqrt(BR). Note: the CFA Institute page for this article returned 404 after redirect this session; cited from the published journal article.

ideas.name: Aim-Portfolio Partial Rebalancing
ideas.entry_rule: Daily at the close, replacing scheduled calendar rebalancing entirely. (1) Compute the target Markowitz portfolio on current information: aim_t = (1/delta) * Sigma_t^{-1} * mu_t, with Sigma_t the Ledoit-Wolf shrunk 252-day covariance, mu_t the cross-sectional z-scores of the composite signal scaled to expected daily excess return by multiplying by 0.02 * sigma_i_daily, and delta = 2.5; clip to [0, 0.15] and renormalise. (2) Do NOT trade to aim_t. Instead trade a fixed fraction of the way there: w_t = w_{t-1} + M * (aim_t - w_{t-1}), with trade rate M in (0,1). (3) Set M from the cost/risk trade-off: M = (sqrt(k^2 + 4k) - k)/2 where k = delta * sigma_p^2 / (2*c), c = the per-unit round-trip cost as a fraction (half-spread from the 20-bar average of (high-low)/close divided by 4, plus 5bp slippage), and sigma_p = the current portfolio daily volatility; clamp M to [0.05, 0.60]. (4) Execute only the per-name deltas whose notional exceeds max($200, 0.25 * average daily dollar volume / 1000) - smaller ones are skipped and carried into the next day's delta.
ideas.exit_rule: There is no rebalance date and no fixed no-trade band; positions decay toward zero automatically whenever their aim weight is zero, at rate M per day, which produces a smooth exponential unwind rather than a cliff. Force an immediate full exit of any name that becomes untradeable (halt, delisting, or 20-day median dollar volume below $2M), bypassing the trade-rate smoothing. If realised portfolio volatility exceeds 1.5x target, temporarily double M so the book converges to the (smaller) aim portfolio faster.
inputs: daily close (252 bars for the covariance and signal)
params: M bounds and the cost parameter c
ideas.novelty: The exit structure is the idea: no rebalance calendar, no threshold band, just a constant fractional convergence toward a moving target. Positions are never closed by a rule about the position - they shrink because the aim moved. That is a different exit mechanism from every stop, target, and time-based exit in the collection.
ideas.why: A portfolio with transaction costs should never jump to the current optimum, because that optimum will move tomorrow and the trade will be partly reversed. Garleanu and Pedersen show the optimal policy is to trade a constant fraction of the way toward an aim portfolio - a weighted average of the current Markowitz optimum and future expected optima - with the fraction set by the ratio of risk aversion to trading cost. Slower-decaying signals are worth chasing further. In practice this converts a lumpy, cost-heavy monthly rebalance into a smooth daily drift, which cuts turnover sharply on a fleet where per-name notionals are small and the spread proxy is a real fraction of the expected edge.
ideas.source: Garleanu & Pedersen (2013) 'Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs', Journal of Finance 68(6) (NBER Working Paper 17777). Note: the NBER PDF fetched this session returned unreadable encoded content, so the aim-portfolio and trade-rate formulas above are quoted from the published paper rather than verified by fetch; the trade rate given is the standard quadratic-cost closed form. Covariance input per Ledoit & Wolf as cited above.

ideas.name: Reflexivity Cascade Ride (Hawkes branching ratio)
inputs: 1-minute bars including Alpaca's trade-count field n (number of trades in the bar)
rolling mean and variance of the trade count
1-minute bar closes for the sign sequence
ideas.entry_rule: Alpaca's bar payload carries n, the number of trades in the bar, alongside OHLCV and vw. Over a rolling window of the last 120 one-minute bars compute mu = mean(n) and sigma_sq = variance(n), and the model-free branching-ratio estimate n_hat = 1 - sqrt(mu / sigma_sq). Enter LONG at the close of bar t when: n_hat_t >= 0.90 AND n_hat_(t-10) <= 0.75 (reflexivity is rising sharply) AND the sum of the signs of the last five bar returns is >= +3 with the two most recent both positive. Enter SHORT under the mirror sign condition (sum of last five signs <= -3, last two negative).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the earliest of: n_hat falling below 0.75, 30 bars elapsed, or a 1.5 x ATR(14) 1-minute stop.
ideas.why: The branching ratio is the fraction of events that are endogenously triggered by other events rather than by exogenous news. Filimonov and Sornette find it rose from about 0.30 in 1998 to 0.70-0.80 after 2007 for E-mini S&P futures, spiking to about 0.95 during the May 2010 flash crash. When n_hat is high the trade-arrival process is self-feeding, so an existing directional run is being amplified by the market's own reaction rather than by fresh information - which is precisely when short-horizon continuation is strongest.
ideas.novelty: The regime variable contains no price information whatsoever - it is an estimate of the self-excitation of the trade ARRIVAL process, derived from the over-dispersion (Fano factor) of trade counts. It is not a volatility measure and not a volume measure; a period can be high-volume and low-reflexivity, or the reverse.
ideas.source: Hardiman & Bouchaud (2014) 'Branching-ratio approximation for the self-exciting Hawkes process', arXiv:1403.5227 - formula verified verbatim as n approx 1 - sqrt(mu_W / sigma_W^2), requiring window W much larger than the kernel correlation time; Filimonov & Sornette (2012) 'Quantifying reflexivity in financial markets', arXiv:1201.3572 for the empirical branching-ratio levels and the flash-crash value of about 0.95; Hardiman, Bercot & Bouchaud (2013), arXiv:1302.1405, for the criticality caveat. NOTE the paper's own warning: with power-law kernels the estimate drifts with window size, so the Fano window must be held fixed and treated as a relative regime indicator, not an absolute one.

ideas.name: Reflexivity Exhaustion Fade
inputs: 1-minute bars including the trade-count field n
20-bar VWAP (from the bar vw and volume fields)
ideas.entry_rule: Compute n_hat = 1 - sqrt(mean(n) / var(n)) over a rolling 120 one-minute bars, as above. Enter COUNTER to the preceding move at the close of bar t when ALL hold: (a) n_hat printed >= 0.95 at some bar within the last 10 bars; (b) n_hat_t is now < 0.80; (c) the close is at least 2.5 x ATR(14) away from the volume-weighted average price of the last 20 bars, in the direction the cascade ran. If the cascade ran down, go LONG; if up, go SHORT.
ideas.exit_rule: Target: the 20-bar VWAP measured at entry. Stop: the extreme (low for longs, high for shorts) of the bar on which n_hat peaked, plus 0.25 x ATR beyond it. Time stop: 60 bars.
ideas.why: A branching ratio near 1 is a near-critical state in which activity is almost entirely self-generated. Such states are unsustainable - by definition the cascade is not being fed by information, so when the self-excitation collapses there is nothing holding the price at its extreme and it reverts toward the volume-weighted consensus. The n_hat-crossing-down condition is what separates this from a naive extension fade: it waits for the mechanical driver of the move to switch off.
ideas.novelty: Same regime variable as the cascade ride but fires on the opposite phase of its life-cycle, and the exit is a VWAP target with a stop anchored to a specific historical bar identified by the regime variable rather than by price action. This is a different entry AND a different exit structure from the ride.
ideas.source: Filimonov & Sornette (2012), arXiv:1201.3572 - the flash-crash episode reached n approx 0.95 and was followed by violent mean reversion, whereas an exogenous news event on 27 April 2010 left n stable; Hardiman & Bouchaud (2014), arXiv:1403.5227 for the estimator. The life-cycle fade rule is my synthesis of those two observations.

ideas.name: Distribution Into Strength
inputs: daily open, high, low, close, volume
ideas.entry_rule: Enter SHORT at the next open when ALL of the following hold on bar t: (1) the cumulative return from close[t-6] to close[t-1] is greater than +3.0%; (2) volume[t] > 1.5 * SMA(volume,20)[t-1]; (3) high[t] > high[t-1]; (4) close[t] < open[t]; (5) (close[t] - low[t]) / (high[t] - low[t]) < 0.30, with the bar skipped if high[t] == low[t].
ideas.exit_rule: Cover at the first of: 10 trading days elapsed; close > high[t] of the signal bar (stop); or price reaching close[t] - 1.5*ATR(14)[t] (target).
ideas.why: Diether, Lee & Werner establish that short sellers are CONTRARIAN in the short run - they increase shorting after positive returns - and that their activity correctly predicts negative abnormal returns, with a daily short-selling strategy generating significant profits. We have no short-volume feed, so this is the OHLCV signature that activity leaves: a stock that has advanced for a week, then prints a heavy-volume day that makes a new high, reverses below its open, and closes in the bottom third of its range. That is supply being met into strength. Boehmer, Jones & Zhang independently document that heavily shorted stocks underperform lightly shorted ones by 1.16% over the following 20 trading days.
ideas.source: Diether, Lee & Werner (2009), 'Short-Sale Strategies and Return Predictability', Review of Financial Studies 22(2), 575-607 - full text read at https://scholarsarchive.byu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=10102&context=facpub, where relss_t is defined as shorted shares divided by traded shares on day t and the contrarian-then-predictive pattern is shown in their Table 3. Complementary magnitude from Boehmer, Jones & Zhang (2008), 'Which Shorts Are Informed?', Journal of Finance 63(2) - abstract via the OpenAlex works API. The OHLCV bar signature is my own proxy for their short-volume measure, stated explicitly as a proxy.
ideas.novelty: Conditions jointly on prior-week direction, volume expansion, a new high, an open-to-close reversal AND close location within the range. It is not a reversal oscillator or a wick-through-a-swing-level pattern - the volume expansion plus close-location test is what proxies the short-flow, and the multi-day prior advance is what makes it contrarian in the sense the paper documents.

ideas.name: Sharpe-Loss Deep Momentum Network
ideas.entry_rule: Per symbol, build a daily 8-element feature vector u_t: (a) five volatility-normalised returns r_{t-k,t}/(sigma_t*sqrt(k)) for k in {1,21,63,126,252}, where sigma_t is the exponentially weighted std of daily returns with a 60-day span; (b) three normalised MACD signals for (S,L) in {(8,24),(16,48),(32,96)}, computed as MACD_t = EWMA(close, halflife=ln(0.5)/ln(1-1/S)) - EWMA(close, halflife=ln(0.5)/ln(1-1/L)), then y_t = MACD_t / rolling_std(close,63), then q_t = y_t / rolling_std(y,252). Feed the trailing 63 days of u into an LSTM (hidden size 10-40, dropout 0.3) whose final dense layer uses tanh, giving position X_t in [-1,1]. Train by minimising L = -sqrt(252)*mean(R)/std(R) where R_{t+1} = X_t*(0.15/sigma_t)*r_{t,t+1}. At each daily close, go long if X_t > +0.10 and short if X_t < -0.10.
ideas.exit_rule: Position is re-set every day to X_t*(0.15/sigma_t); go flat when |X_t| <= 0.10 or when sign(X_t) flips. No price stop and no profit target - the tanh magnitude IS the exit, so a decaying |X_t| scales the position down continuously. Refit the network every 6 months on an expanding window.
ideas.why: Classical time-series momentum destroys information twice: it discretises the trend estimate to a sign, and it imposes a position-sizing function rather than learning one. Training a network to maximise the Sharpe ratio of the volatility-scaled return stream makes it learn the entire response function - where it saturates, where it flips sign, how sharply - from the data. Lim et al. report more than double the Sharpe of standard TSMOM across 88 futures contracts, with the advantage surviving 2-3bp costs.
ideas.source: Lim, Zohren & Roberts (2019), 'Enhancing Time Series Momentum Strategies Using Deep Neural Networks', arXiv:1904.04912. Read the full text (ar5iv): feature set (returns over 1d/1m/3m/6m/1y normalised by daily vol; MACD with S in {8,16,32}, L in {24,48,96}; half-life = log(0.5)/log(1-1/S)), the Sharpe loss formula, tanh-bounded direct position output, 15% annualised vol target with 60-day EWM std, and 63-timestep LSTM trajectories.
ideas.novelty: There is no threshold crossing anywhere in the rule. The trading function is learned end-to-end and the objective is risk-adjusted return, not directional accuracy - which is what separates it from the hand-crafted trend transforms (tanh saturation, dampened MACD) it supersedes.

ideas.name: CNN-Transformer Arbitrage on Factor Residuals
ideas.entry_rule: (i) Each day compute the correlation matrix of daily returns over a rolling 252-day window across the universe and take the top K=5 eigenvectors as factor portfolios. (ii) Regress each symbol's last 60 days of returns on those factor returns to get loadings beta_i; the residual is eps_{i,t} = r_{i,t} - beta_i' F_t. (iii) Form the cumulative residual path over the last L=30 days, x_i = (sum of eps over 1 day, over 2 days, ..., over 30 days), divided by the 30-day std of eps_i. (iv) Pass x_i through a two-layer 1-D CNN (D=8 filters, kernel size 2, ReLU), then a 4-head self-attention layer, taking the final-timestep projection h in R^4. (v) Map h through a feedforward net to a raw residual-space weight. (vi) Project residual-space weights back to stock space and scale so that the sum of |w_i| equals 1. Enter every symbol at the close with its weight w_i.
ideas.exit_rule: Fully re-solve the weight vector at every close and trade only the difference. A position exits when its weight reaches zero or flips sign. Train by maximising E[w'R]/sqrt(Var(w'R)) minus c * E[sum_i |delta w_i|] over a rolling 1000-day window, re-estimating network parameters every 125 trading days.
inputs: rolling PCA factors (252-day correlation window, 60-day loading window)
1-D CNN (8 filters, size 2) + 4-head attention + feedforward allocator
params: CNN filter count and kernel size
ideas.why: Mean reversion is only reliable in the part of a stock's return NOT explained by common factors - trading raw prices means fighting the market factor and calling it alpha. Projecting out the factors first makes the series close to stationary and weakly cross-correlated. The CNN then learns local shapes (up-trend, down-trend, up-reversal, down-reversal) and the attention layer decides which local shapes matter given the whole 30-day path, which is strictly more general than fitting an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process and thresholding its z-score.
ideas.source: Guijarro-Ordonez, Pelger & Zanotti, 'Deep Learning Statistical Arbitrage', arXiv:2106.04028. Read the full text (ar5iv) and verified: residual construction via Fama-French / PCA (252-day rolling window) / IPCA factors with 60-day loading estimation, cumulative-residual input of length L=30, benchmark CNN with D=8 filters of size 2, H=4 attention heads, the Sharpe and mean-variance equivalent objectives, L1-normalised weights mapped back through the projection matrix, daily rebalancing, retraining every 125 days on rolling 1000-day windows, and a universe of roughly the 550 largest US stocks.
ideas.novelty: Signal extraction and capital allocation are a single differentiable object trained on a portfolio-level Sharpe ratio - there is no intermediate per-symbol forecast at all - and the network's input is a residual path rather than a price or an indicator.

ideas.name: Momentum Transformer with Variable-Selection Regime Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Use the same 8 features as the Deep Momentum Network but with a 252-day input sequence, fed to a Temporal Fusion Transformer: a Variable Selection Network producing softmax weights over the 8 inputs at each timestep, gated residual network blocks, an LSTM encoder-decoder for local processing, and masked interpretable multi-head attention over the full 252-step history. Final dense layer with tanh gives position X_t in [-1,1]. Train on L = -sqrt(252)*E[R]/sqrt(Var[R]). Take the network's position at each daily close whenever |X_t| > 0.10.
ideas.exit_rule: The position is reset daily. Add an explicit regime gate read off the model itself: let v_t be the VSN weight assigned to the 1-day normalised return feature. When v_t exceeds its own trailing 252-day 80th percentile, the model has shifted into reversion mode - halve the position size and cap the maximum holding period at 5 sessions. When v_t is below its 252-day median, allow full size and no holding cap.
inputs: Temporal Fusion Transformer: VSN + GRN + multi-head attention + LSTM
VSN weight time series (used as a regime variable)
params: VSN percentile cut for the regime gate
ideas.why: An LSTM compresses all history into a fixed hidden state, so a regime change 100 days back is effectively forgotten. Attention keeps a direct path to every past timestep, letting the model recognise 'this configuration resembles early 2020' rather than only 'recent returns are positive'. Wood et al. find it adapts to new regimes such as the 2020 crash without refitting, and - the reason it is tradeable rather than merely accurate - the VSN weights are readable, so the momentum-versus-reversion blend the model has chosen becomes an observable risk variable.
ideas.source: Wood, Giegerich, Roberts & Zohren (2022), 'Trading with the Momentum Transformer: An Intelligent and Interpretable Architecture', arXiv:2112.08534. Read the full text (ar5iv) and verified: TFT foundation with Variable Selection Networks, Gated Residual Networks and Masked Interpretable Multi-Head Attention; five volatility-normalised return horizons plus three MACD timescales plus optional changepoint features; tanh-bounded position in [-1,1]; Sharpe loss -sqrt(252)*E[R]/sqrt(Var[R]); one-year input sequence versus the LSTM baseline's roughly one quarter; and the finding that the VSN raises the weight on daily returns in mean-reverting regimes and on longer horizons in momentum regimes.
ideas.novelty: A single model learns a time-varying blend of trend and reversion, and the blend weight is extracted from the model's own variable-selection layer and used as a position-sizing gate. That feedback from an interpretability output into the trading rule exists nowhere in a hand-crafted indicator.

ideas.name: Changepoint-Severity Augmented Trend Network
ideas.entry_rule: For each lookback window LBW in {21, 126} days, fit two Gaussian-process regressions to the symbol's volatility-normalised return series: a single Matern-3/2 GP over the whole window, and a changepoint GP whose kernel is a sigmoid-weighted mixture of two Matern-3/2 kernels with a learned changepoint location. Define the SEVERITY score nu = 1 - (NLL_changepoint / NLL_single), clipped to [0,1] - the fractional reduction in negative log-likelihood from allowing a break - and the LOCATION score gamma = (changepoint index) / LBW in [0,1]. Append (nu_21, gamma_21, nu_126, gamma_126) to the 8 momentum features, giving a 12-dimensional input, and feed the trailing 63 days to the Sharpe-trained LSTM with tanh output. Enter at the position the network emits when |X_t| > 0.10.
ideas.exit_rule: Daily re-sizing as in the base Deep Momentum Network, plus a hard override: if nu_21 > 0.8 AND gamma_21 > 0.9 - a severe break detected within roughly the last two sessions - close any position whose sign matches the pre-changepoint trend at the next open and stay flat in that symbol for 3 sessions regardless of what the network outputs.
params: severity and location thresholds for the hard override
flat-period length after a severe break
ideas.why: Momentum's characteristic failure mode is the sharp regime turn - the strategy is maximally long precisely when the trend breaks. Feeding the network an explicit, continuously-valued measure of how disequilibrated the recent window is (severity) and how recently the break occurred (location) lets it shorten its effective lookback exactly when trends stop being reliable, instead of learning that adjustment implicitly from sparse crash episodes. Wood et al. report roughly a 33% Sharpe improvement over the plain DMN across 1995-2020 and about 70% over the more turbulent 2015-2020 subperiod.
ideas.source: Wood, Roberts & Zohren (2021), 'Slow Momentum with Fast Reversion: A Trading Strategy Using Deep Learning and Changepoint Detection', arXiv:2105.13727. Read the full text (ar5iv) and verified: Gaussian-process regression with a Matern 3/2 kernel, a sigmoid approximation to the regime shift instead of fitting multiple GPs, the severity score defined from the reduction in negative log-likelihood, the normalised location score within the lookback window, both scores fed to the LSTM alongside momentum indicators, and the reported Sharpe/Sortino/Calmar improvements.
ideas.novelty: An explicit, continuously-valued regime-break feature produced by a Bayesian model and consumed by the trading network - not a binary regime filter and not a volatility proxy. The severity score also drives a distinct hard exit that the position-sizing output alone would never produce.

ideas.name: Turnover-Penalised Sharpe Trainer
ideas.entry_rule: Identical architecture and features to the Deep Momentum Network, but the training objective is the COST-ADJUSTED Sharpe ratio. Define the net return R_{t+1} = (sigma_tgt / N_t) * sum_i [ (X_{i,t}/sigma_{i,t}) * r_{i,t,t+1} - c * | X_{i,t}/sigma_{i,t} - X_{i,t-1}/sigma_{i,t-1} | ] and minimise L = -sqrt(252) * E[R] / sqrt(Var(R)), with c set to the expected round-trip cost as a decimal fraction (start at c = 0.0010, i.e. 10bp, for retail equities rather than the 2-3bp used for futures). Take the position the network outputs at each daily close when |X_t| > 0.05.
ideas.exit_rule: The exit is emergent rather than rule-based: because turnover is priced inside the loss, the network becomes reluctant to change X_t and positions turn sticky - it only reverses when the change in signal is large enough to pay for the round trip. Go flat when |X_t| < 0.05. Sweep c upward across training runs until realised turnover falls to a level the account can actually bear, and select c on out-of-sample net Sharpe.
ideas.why: Every other approach here trains a signal and then discovers that costs eat it. Putting cost inside the loss changes what the model learns rather than what it earns: it learns to ignore small signal fluctuations instead of trading them and losing. Lim et al. introduce exactly this turnover regularisation term and note the DMN advantage survives 2-3bp; at retail equity cost levels the term matters far more, which makes this the variant worth testing first on a live account.
ideas.source: Lim, Zohren & Roberts (2019), arXiv:1904.04912, turnover regularisation section - the cost-adjusted return formula with the c*|X_t/sigma_t - X_{t-1}/sigma_{t-1}| penalty is quoted from the paper's full text (ar5iv). Raising c to retail equity levels and selecting it on net out-of-sample Sharpe is my adaptation.
ideas.novelty: Cost is a training-time constraint that reshapes the position path, not a post-hoc subtraction from a backtest. With features identical to the base Deep Momentum Network, this is purely a different EXIT structure - positions persist through noise that would otherwise flip them.

ideas.name: Joint Cross-Asset Position Network
ideas.category: deep learning / unified time-series and cross-sectional
ideas.entry_rule: At each daily close, build the feature matrix for the entire universe at once: for each of N symbols compute the 8 features (five volatility-normalised returns at k in {1,20,63,126,252}, three volatility-normalised MACD signals), and concatenate into a single input vector of length 8N. Feed it to a single-hidden-layer perceptron (one fully connected hidden layer, then a tanh output layer of width N) that emits the ENTIRE position vector X_t in [-1,1]^N in one forward pass. Train by maximising the annualised Sharpe ratio of sum_i X_{i,t} * (sigma_tgt/sigma_{i,t}) * r_{i,t,t+1}. Take every component whose magnitude exceeds 0.05 as a position, sized by X_{i,t} * (sigma_tgt/sigma_{i,t}).
ideas.exit_rule: The whole vector is replaced daily; a symbol exits when its component crosses zero or falls under the 0.05 deadband. Cross-sectionally demean the output before trading (X_i <- X_i - mean(X)) so the book is dollar-neutral - which changes the exit condition from 'this symbol's own signal turned negative' to 'this symbol fell below the universe average signal'.
inputs: daily OHLCV for all N symbols
volatility-normalised returns at 1/20/63/126/252 days per symbol
single-layer perceptron with width-N tanh output
ideas.why: Time-series momentum treats each symbol in isolation and cross-sectional momentum uses only rank order; neither can express 'go long A because B is doing X'. Letting one network see the whole cross-section in a single input lets it learn lead-lag and hedging relationships directly. Tan et al. find a single-layer perceptron suffices - the gain comes from the joint input geometry, not from depth, which also makes this cheap enough to fit on a small fleet's history.
ideas.source: Tan, Roberts & Zohren (2023), 'Spatio-Temporal Momentum: Jointly Learning Time-Series and Cross-Sectional Strategies', arXiv:2302.10175. Read the full text (ar5iv) and verified: signals for different assets treated as multiple related prediction tasks solved simultaneously; a single-layer perceptron as the simplest effective architecture; volatility-normalised returns at k in {1,20,63,126,252}; volatility-normalised MACD signals; annualised Sharpe as the loss; and direct output of positions X_t in [-1,1]^{N_t} with per-position volatility scaling.
ideas.novelty: One model, one forward pass, produces the entire book. It unifies time-series and cross-sectional momentum rather than choosing between them, and its input dimension scales with the universe - structurally impossible for any per-symbol indicator.

ideas.name: Universal Pooled Model with Zero-Shot Ticker Transfer
ideas.entry_rule: Train ONE model on the pooled 1-minute bars of every symbol in the universe, with no per-symbol parameters and no symbol identifier among the inputs. Features per bar, over a trailing window of 50 bars: (a) log return of the close; (b) a bar-level order-flow proxy, the close location value CLV = ((C - L) - (H - C)) / (H - L), which equals +1 when the bar closes on its high and -1 on its low; (c) signed volume = CLV * volume, standardised by the 50-bar mean absolute signed volume; (d) bar range (H - L) / C, standardised by its own 50-bar mean. Feed the 50x4 window to a 1-D CNN followed by an LSTM with a softmax over {up, flat, down} for the move over the next 20 bars. Go long when P(up) > 0.60 and P(up) - P(down) > 0.25; go short on the mirror condition.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after 20 bars, or earlier if the probability condition reverses (P(down) > 0.60 while long). The load-bearing rule is what does NOT change: the same trained weights and the same numeric thresholds are deployed on symbols that were never in the training set, with no per-symbol refitting and no per-symbol threshold calibration.
inputs: close location value (CLV) as an order-flow proxy
ideas.why: Sirignano & Cont find that a model trained on data from all stocks outperforms asset-specific linear and nonlinear models, and that the result holds for stocks outside the training sample - price formation has universal features that are stationary across instruments and over time. For a small fleet this is decisive: it is the difference between a few thousand bars per ticker and a few thousand times N, which is the only way a deep model gets enough data to train at all. It also answers 'should I run this on a new ticker' for free - yes, with no refit.
ideas.source: Sirignano & Cont (2019), 'Universal features of price formation in financial markets: perspectives from Deep Learning', Quantitative Finance 19(9):1449-1459; arXiv:1803.06917. Verified from the paper: the universal model trained on all stocks beats asset-specific models out of sample, results hold for stocks not in the training sample, including a long price and order-flow history improves accuracy, and standard normalisations (volatility, price level) proved unnecessary. Their inputs are the full limit order book; the CLV and CLV-signed-volume bar features here are my substitution for queue imbalance, since we have no level 2.
ideas.novelty: The modelling unit is the pooled panel and generalisation to unseen tickers is the design goal rather than a side effect. Every other idea in the corpus fits per symbol; this one is a bet that the fitted object is a property of markets, not of a ticker, and it is directly falsifiable by holding out symbols.

ideas.name: Alpha-Threshold Smoothed Labelling
ideas.entry_rule: The distinguishing element is the SUPERVISION TARGET, not the entry threshold. For each 5-minute bar t, compute m_minus(t) = the mean of the previous k closes and m_plus(t) = the mean of the next k closes, then l_t = (m_plus(t) - m_minus(t)) / m_minus(t). Label +1 if l_t > alpha, -1 if l_t < -alpha, and 0 otherwise, with alpha set to the 67th percentile of |l| over the training set so the three classes are roughly balanced, and k in {10, 20, 50}. Train a CNN over the (log return, CLV, CLV-signed volume, normalised range) channels of the last 100 bars, followed by an Inception block with parallel 1x3 and 1x5 convolutions plus max-pooling, then 64 LSTM units and a 3-way softmax. Go long when P(+1) > 0.55 AND a second model trained at the next-longer k also predicts +1.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit after k bars - the exact horizon the label was defined over - or earlier if P(-1) > 0.50. No fixed price stop: alpha already encodes the minimum move worth trading, so any move that fails to reach alpha is by construction a class-0 event and gets closed on the horizon rather than at an arbitrary price level.
inputs: smoothed forward and backward mean closes over k bars
alpha threshold from the training-set |l| distribution
params: alpha (or the percentile that sets it)
ideas.why: Labelling 'next bar up or down' makes the target almost pure microstructure noise and the model dutifully learns the bid-ask bounce. Smoothing BOTH sides - averaging the previous k and the next k prices rather than comparing two single prints - and then requiring the change to exceed alpha before it counts as a signal removes noise from the label itself. That matters more than the architecture: a clean target with a mediocre model beats a noisy target with a good one. Zhang et al. report this labelling produces markedly more consistent signals.
ideas.source: Zhang, Zohren & Roberts (2019), 'DeepLOB: Deep Convolutional Neural Networks for Limit Order Books', IEEE Transactions on Signal Processing 67(11):3001-3012; arXiv:1808.03668. Read the full text (ar5iv) and verified: m_minus(t) as the mean of the previous k mid-prices, m_plus(t) as the mean of the next k, l_t = (m_plus - m_minus)/m_minus, three-class labelling at threshold alpha, horizons k in {20,50,100}, and the architecture (1x2 stride-2 convolutions over price-volume pairs, a 1x10 integrating filter, Inception@32 with 1x3 and 1x5 branches plus max-pooling, then 64 LSTM units). Applied here to OHLCV bars rather than LOB levels.
ideas.novelty: The innovation lives in the label, not the trade trigger: a two-sided smoothed, threshold-gated target. It is distinct from triple-barrier labelling, which is path-dependent and asymmetric, and from plain next-bar direction, which is dominated by noise. It also makes the exit horizon and the label horizon the same object, which most supervised trading setups get wrong.

ideas.name: Adversarial No-Arbitrage SDF Portfolio
ideas.category: deep learning / asset pricing, adversarial objective
ideas.entry_rule: Train two networks against each other on the return panel. SDF network: takes the macro state h_t and the firm state I_{i,t} and outputs weights omega(h_t, I_{i,t}); the stochastic discount factor is M_{t+1} = 1 - sum_i omega(h_t, I_{i,t}) * R^e_{i,t+1}. Conditioning network: outputs test-asset functions g(h_t, I_{i,t}). Train the min-max objective min_omega max_g (1/N) * sum_j || E[ M_{t+1} * R^e_{j,t+1} * g(h_t, I_{j,t}) ] ||^2, weighting each symbol's sample moment by T_i/T for the unbalanced panel. The macro state h_t comes from an LSTM over five OHLCV-derived aggregate series: the equal-weighted universe return, the cross-sectional standard deviation of daily returns across the universe, aggregate 21-day realised volatility, market breadth (fraction of symbols above their own 200-day SMA), and the average pairwise correlation of the universe over 60 days. The firm state I_{i,t} is the OHLCV characteristic set. Trade the SDF tangency portfolio: hold weight omega(h_t, I_{i,t}) in symbol i at each close, L1-normalised so the weights sum to 1 in absolute value.
ideas.exit_rule: Weights are re-solved at every rebalance; a symbol exits when its omega crosses zero. Portfolio-level volatility control: if the realised 21-day volatility of the SDF portfolio exceeds 1.5x its target, scale every weight by target/realised until it is back in band.
inputs: aggregate market-state series: equal-weighted return, cross-sectional return dispersion, realised volatility, breadth, average pairwise correlation
params: number of hidden macro states K_h
ideas.why: Direct return forecasting fails because the signal-to-noise ratio is around one percent. The no-arbitrage condition E[M * R^e * g] = 0 must hold for EVERY conditioning function g, which is a far richer set of constraints than 'predict next month's return', and the adversarial player actively searches for the g where the current model prices worst - so the model is trained on its own hardest cases rather than on an arbitrary menu of test portfolios. Chen, Pelger & Zhu report roughly 2.6x the out-of-sample Sharpe of standard forecasting and linear benchmarks.
ideas.source: Chen, Pelger & Zhu (2024), 'Deep Learning in Asset Pricing', Management Science 70(2); arXiv:1904.00745. Read the full text (ar5iv) and verified: M_{t+1} = 1 - omega_t' R^e_{t+1}, the min-max objective over conditioning functions g, LSTM extraction of K_h hidden macro states from a large set of macro time series, the T_i/T unbalanced-panel weighting in the empirical loss, and the separate feedforward network for loadings on the traded SDF factor. Their macro inputs are 178 FRED series; the five OHLCV-derived aggregate market-state series substituted here are my proxies, since we have no macro feed.
ideas.novelty: The loss is a set of economic moment conditions with an adversarial player choosing which ones to enforce, and no return forecast is ever produced. Nothing else in the corpus trains against a self-generated worst-case test asset.

ideas.name: Direct Softmax Allocation Network
ideas.entry_rule: There is no per-symbol signal at all. Stack the last 50 daily bars of close price and daily return for each of N instruments into a 50 x 2N input tensor; feed it to an LSTM with 64 units; pass the final hidden state through a dense layer with a SOFTMAX of width N, producing long-only weights w_t that sum to 1. Train by gradient ascent on the Sharpe ratio of the realised portfolio return sum_i w_{i,t} * r_{i,t+1}, minus c * sum_i |w_{i,t} - w_{i,t-1}| with c = 0.001. At each close, allocate capital to the resulting weights - any symbol with a non-trivial weight is a position.
ideas.exit_rule: The allocation is fully replaced each day; a symbol exits when its softmax weight falls below 1/(5N), at which point its capital is redistributed by the network itself rather than by a rule. Overlay volatility scaling on the whole book: multiply every weight by sigma_tgt / (realised 63-day portfolio volatility), capped at 2x gross leverage.
inputs: daily close and daily return for N instruments
softmax output layer of width N
Sharpe objective with a turnover penalty
ideas.why: Every forecasting approach optimises a metric - accuracy, MSE, log-loss - that is not the metric the account is paid on, then converts the forecast into a position through a separate, un-optimised step. Optimising the weights directly makes the loss surface the actual objective. It also lets the model learn to hold a diversifier that has a poor standalone forecast but reduces portfolio variance, which no per-symbol signal can ever discover. Zhang et al. beat mean-variance optimisation, maximum diversification and fixed allocation on a four-instrument universe over 2011 to April 2020, with contained drawdowns through the COVID shock.
ideas.source: Zhang, Zohren & Roberts (2020), 'Deep Learning for Portfolio Optimization', The Journal of Financial Data Science 2(4); arXiv:2005.13665. Read the full text (ar5iv) and verified: a single LSTM layer of 64 units over a 50-day lookback of concatenated prices and returns across four ETFs, a softmax output layer producing weights that sum to one, direct gradient ascent on the Sharpe ratio rather than return forecasting, daily rebalancing, transaction costs modelled as the absolute change in scaled positions times a cost rate (tested at 0.01% and 0.1%), and inverse-volatility position scaling.
ideas.novelty: There is no signal and no threshold anywhere - the model's output IS the book, and diversification is learned rather than imposed by a covariance estimate. Long-only by construction of the softmax, which happens to suit a cash equity account with no shorting.

ideas.name: Net-Edge Admission Gate
ideas.entry_rule: On each bar, when a base signal fires, compute three quantities. (1) spread_hat = the EDGE effective-spread estimate (Ardia-Guidotti-Kroencke) over the trailing 60 OHLC bars, as a fraction of price; fallback if EDGE returns NaN is the Roll half-spread c = sqrt(max(0, -Cov(dlnC_t, dlnC_{t+1}))) over 60 bars, with round-trip spread cost = 2c. (2) impact_hat = Y * sigma_d * sqrt(Q / V20), with Y = 1.0, sigma_d = stdev of daily log returns over 20 days, Q = intended share count, V20 = 20-day average daily share volume. (3) roundtrip_cost = spread_hat + 2 * impact_hat. Then compute expected_edge = the median of the forward H-bar log return over all bars in the trailing 500-bar window on which this same signal fired, using only bars at least H bars in the past (strictly walk-forward, no lookahead). Take the trade ONLY IF expected_edge > hurdle * roundtrip_cost with hurdle = 3.0. If the inequality fails, the signal is logged but not traded.
ideas.exit_rule: Close at the close of the H-th bar after entry, or immediately if price touches entry_price - 2*ATR(14) (long) / entry_price + 2*ATR(14) (short), whichever comes first.
ideas.why: Novy-Marx & Velikov find that most published anomalies do not survive realistic effective spreads, and that the survivors are the low-turnover ones. The economic point is that an edge is not an edge until it clears the round trip, and the round trip is ticker-specific and size-specific. The same signal that is profitable on a liquid name is negative-expectancy on an illiquid one at the same dollar size. Gating on net rather than gross edge is the cheapest way to kill the negative-expectancy half of a signal book without touching the signal itself.
ideas.novelty: Every filter in the existing 32 gates on signal strength or trend context (ADX, volume, trend direction). This one gates on a size-dependent cost estimate, so the identical signal is accepted on one ticker and refused on another purely because of estimated spread and the order's participation rate. Cost enters the entry condition, not the P&L accounting.
ideas.source: Ardia, D., Guidotti, E., Kroencke, T.A. (2024), 'Efficient Estimation of Bid-Ask Spreads from Open, High, Low, and Close Prices', Journal of Financial Economics 161:103916 (reference implementation at github.com/eguidotti/bidask, verified); Roll (1984) model as restated verbatim in Novy-Marx & Velikov, 'A Taxonomy of Anomalies and their Trading Costs' (NBER w20721), p.4: 'c = sqrt(-Cov(dP_t, dP_{t+1}))'; Toth et al. (2011) square-root law for the impact term.

ideas.name: Almgren-Chriss Sinh Slice Schedule
ideas.entry_rule: When a signal fires at bar 0 with target size X shares, do not fill at once. Compute per-bar volatility sigma = stdev of per-bar log returns over 20 bars, converted to dollars per share as sigma_$ = sigma * C_t. Set the temporary impact coefficient eta = c_imp * C_t / V_bar, where V_bar = 20-bar average shares per bar and c_imp is a swept constant. Set kappa = sqrt(lambda * sigma_$^2 / eta) with lambda the swept risk-aversion. With tau = 1 bar, N = T bars, execute slice j (j = 1..N) of size n_j = X * [2*sinh(kappa*tau/2) / sinh(kappa*T)] * cosh(kappa * (T - (j - 0.5)*tau)), each as a market order filled at the next bar's (H+L+C)/3. The half-life theta = 1/kappa is the intrinsic time scale; set T = ceil(3*theta) so the schedule is essentially complete.
ideas.exit_rule: On the exit trigger (H bars elapsed, or a 2*ATR(14) stop, or signal reversal), liquidate on the same sinh schedule recomputed with the then-current sigma and V_bar, over T' = ceil(3/kappa') bars. A stop-loss trigger overrides the schedule and liquidates in a single slice.
inputs: ohlc bars at 1 or 5 minute resolution
ideas.why: Almgren and Chriss show that the cost-minimising liquidation of X shares against linear temporary impact and volatility risk is not a straight line but a hyperbolic-sine decay with a characteristic half-life theta = 1/kappa, kappa ~ sqrt(lambda*sigma^2/eta). The economics: trading fast pays impact, trading slow pays volatility risk, and the optimum front-loads exactly enough to balance them. Critically, theta is independent of X and of any externally imposed deadline, so it is a property of the security, not of the order.
ideas.novelty: None of the 32 model a fill as anything but a point event at a bar price. This makes the ENTRY ITSELF a trajectory with a computed shape, and yields a falsifiable prediction the corpus can test directly: a 100-share and a 10,000-share order in the same name should be worked over the same number of bars.
ideas.source: Almgren, R. & Chriss, N. (2000), 'Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions', eq. (17) x_j = [sinh(kappa*(T-t_j))/sinh(kappa*T)]*X, eq. (18) for the trade list n_j, eq. (19) kappa ~ sqrt(lambda*sigma^2/eta), and section 2.3 defining theta = 1/kappa as the trade's half-life.

ideas.name: Drift-Anchored Steady-State Size
ideas.entry_rule: Do not hold a binary position. Each bar, compute a forecast dollar drift alpha_t and hold the target share count x_bar_t = alpha_t / (2 * lambda * sigma_$^2), where sigma_$ = C_t * stdev(log returns, 20) and lambda is a swept risk-aversion constant. Define alpha_t precisely as alpha_t = C_t * beta_hat_t * z_t, where z_t = (C_t - EMA(20)) / ATR(14) and beta_hat_t is the OLS slope from regressing the next-bar log return on z, fitted on the trailing 500 bars ending at bar t-1 (walk-forward, refit every 20 bars). Trade toward x_bar_t only when |x_bar_t - x_{t-1}| exceeds a no-trade band (see the cube-root band idea, or a fixed band of 10% of x_bar_t).
ideas.exit_rule: There is no discrete exit. As alpha_t decays toward zero the target x_bar_t decays with it and the position is unwound automatically at the band-gated rate. Hard overrides only: flatten if unrealised loss exceeds 3 * ATR(14) * |x_t|, and flatten at the last bar of the session for intraday variants.
inputs: rolling OLS of next-bar return on z
ideas.why: Almgren and Chriss show that when the price has a predictable drift alpha, the optimal execution trajectory no longer relaxes to zero: it relaxes to a non-zero steady-state holding x_bar = alpha/(2*lambda*sigma^2), which is the solution to the static portfolio problem. This is the correct cost-aware answer to 'how big': size is proportional to forecast drift and inversely proportional to variance and risk aversion, and it is independent of account size or notional target.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from volatility targeting, which scales only by 1/sigma and ignores the strength of the forecast; and distinct from fixed-fractional sizing, which ignores both. Here the position is a continuous function of a fitted drift forecast, so a weak signal produces a small position rather than no position, and the exit is a decay rather than an event.
ideas.source: Almgren, R. & Chriss, N. (2000), 'Optimal Execution of Portfolio Transactions', section 4.1 and eq. (25): 'x_bar = alpha / (2*lambda*sigma^2) is the optimal level of security holding for a time-independent portfolio optimization problem', with the drift-corrected trajectory given in eqs. (26)-(27).

ideas.name: Cube-Root No-Trade Band
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain a continuous target weight w*_t = clip(z_t / 3, -1, +1), where z_t = (C_t - SMA(50)) / stdev(C - SMA(50), 50). Each bar, estimate the round-trip cost fraction c_t = spread_hat_t + 2 * Y * sigma_d * sqrt(Q/V20), with spread_hat_t the EDGE estimate over 60 bars, Y = 1, sigma_d = 20-day return stdev, V20 the 20-day average volume, Q the shares implied by w*_t. Set the no-trade half-width Delta_t = k * c_t^(1/3), k swept. Trade ONLY when |w_actual - w*_t| > Delta_t. When you trade, move only to the NEAR EDGE of the band, i.e. to w*_t + Delta_t if you were below it, or w*_t - Delta_t if above — never all the way to w*_t.
ideas.exit_rule: Symmetric and automatic: the position is reduced only when w*_t drifts far enough that w_actual exits the band on the other side, and a position is fully closed only when w*_t crosses zero by more than Delta_t. A hard stop at 3*ATR(14) adverse excursion bypasses the band entirely.
ideas.why: Under proportional transaction costs the optimal policy is an impulse-control policy: an inaction region around the target, with rebalancing back to the nearest boundary rather than to the target. The width of that region is not proportional to cost — it scales as the CUBE ROOT of cost, which means even tiny costs justify a surprisingly wide band (the derivative of band width with respect to cost is infinite at zero). Rebalancing to the near edge rather than the target roughly halves turnover again for the same tracking error.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from a fixed percentage rebalance band because the width is recomputed each bar from a live cost estimate and follows a specific non-linear law, and distinct from every entry rule in the 32 because it makes the trade/no-trade decision a function of estimated cost rather than of the signal. The rebalance-to-edge rather than rebalance-to-target detail is itself a separate structural change.
ideas.source: Novy-Marx, R. & Velikov, M., 'A Taxonomy of Anomalies and their Trading Costs' (NBER w20721), footnote 6, which cites Arrow, Harris & Marschak (1951) for the sS inaction region, Davis & Norman (1990) for 'an inaction region and a return to the closer boundary when rebalancing', and Abel & Eberly (1996) which shows 'the size of this region is proportional to the cube-root of the price wedge for small wedges, which makes its derivative with respect to the wedge infinite'.

ideas.name: Garleanu-Pedersen Aim Portfolio
ideas.entry_rule: Run K signals f_{k,t}, each z-scored over 252 bars. (1) For each signal estimate its mean-reversion speed: fit an AR(1) to f_k over the trailing 500 bars to get rho_k, set Phi_k = 1 - rho_k. (2) Estimate B = the matrix of walk-forward OLS loadings of next-bar asset returns on f, refit every 20 bars on a 500-bar window. (3) Sigma = the 60-bar sample covariance of asset returns. (4) Markowitz target M_t = (gamma*Sigma)^-1 * B * f_t. (5) AIM PORTFOLIO: aim_t = (gamma*Sigma)^-1 * B * (I + (a/gamma)*Phi)^-1 * f_t — i.e. each signal k is shrunk by the scalar 1/(1 + (a/gamma)*Phi_k), so fast-decaying signals get systematically less weight. (6) Trading rate: with rho_bar the average signal persistence, a = [ -(gamma*(1-rho_bar) + lambda*rho_bar) + sqrt( (gamma*(1-rho_bar) + lambda*rho_bar)^2 + 4*gamma*lambda*(1-rho_bar)^2 ) ] / (2*(1-rho_bar)). (7) Set the new position x_t = (1 - a/lambda)*x_{t-1} + (a/lambda)*aim_t. Calibrate lambda so that (lambda/2)*dx'*Sigma*dx equals the square-root-law impact cost Y*sigma_d*sqrt(Q/V20)*Q*P at a typical trade size.
ideas.exit_rule: There is no separate exit rule. When aim_t goes to zero the position decays geometrically at rate a/lambda per bar, which is the cost-optimal unwind speed. Overrides: flatten a name entirely if its 20-bar realised volatility exceeds 4x its 252-bar median, and flatten the book if portfolio drawdown from peak exceeds a swept threshold.
ideas.why: Garleanu & Pedersen solve the dynamic problem in closed form and get two principles: trade PARTIALLY toward the target at a fixed rate, and AIM IN FRONT of it. The aim portfolio is an exponentially weighted average of current and expected future Markowitz portfolios, which is algebraically equivalent to shrinking each signal by its own decay speed.
