This is exactly the right answer for a large signal book under costs: a signal that decays in two days is worth almost nothing after costs even if its raw information ratio is high, while a persistent one is worth trading, and the closed form says by precisely how much.
ideas.novelty: The corpus reportedly has one heuristic nod to partial rebalancing but not the closed form. The two structural pieces missing are (a) the trading rate a/lambda derived from cost and risk aversion rather than picked, and (b) the shrinkage factor 1/(1 + (a/gamma)*Phi_k) that downweights signals by measured alpha decay. Neither appears in any of the 32.
ideas.source: Garleanu, N. & Pedersen, L.H. (2013), 'Dynamic Trading with Predictable Returns and Transaction Costs', Journal of Finance 68(6): Proposition 2 eq. (7) and (10) x_t = (1 - a/lambda)*x_{t-1} + (a/lambda)*aim_t; eq. (9) for a; Proposition 3 eqs. (12)-(13); Proposition 4 eq. (14) aim_t = (gamma*Sigma)^-1 * B * (I + (a/gamma)*Phi)^-1 * f_t, 'the aim portfolio is the Markowitz portfolio built as if the signals f were scaled down based on their mean-reversion Phi'. Assumption 1: Lambda = lambda*Sigma.

ideas.name: Alpha Half-Life vs Cost-Recovery Admission
ideas.entry_rule: This is a meta-rule applied to each candidate signal once per week, before any trading. For signal k on ticker i: (1) Fit an AR(1) to the signal's forward-return forecast over the trailing 1000 bars to get rho_k; the alpha half-life is HL_k = ln(2) / (-ln(rho_k)) bars. (2) Compute the cumulative expected edge curve E(h) = the mean forward h-bar log return conditional on the signal firing, for h = 1..200, estimated walk-forward on the trailing 1000 bars using only bars at least 200 bars old. (3) Compute round-trip cost RT = spread_hat (EDGE, 60 bars) + 2*Y*sigma_d*sqrt(Q/V20). (4) Cost-recovery horizon T_BE = the smallest h with E(h) > RT; if no such h <= 200 exists, T_BE = infinity. (5) ADMIT signal k for live trading this week only if HL_k > 2 * T_BE. Non-admitted signals are computed and logged but generate no orders. Entries for admitted signals use the signal's own base rule.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at h = min(HL_k, first bar on which the signal's z-score crosses zero). Additionally, force an exit if the signal is de-admitted at the weekly re-test (its HL has collapsed or costs have widened), unwinding over the next 5 bars.
inputs: AR(1) fit of the signal forecast
ideas.why: Novy-Marx & Velikov's taxonomy sorts anomalies by turnover and finds that most of the high-turnover ones die after costs while the low-turnover ones survive. Garleanu & Pedersen make the same point structurally: under costs the relevant quantity is signal persistence, not raw predictive power. Combining the two gives a direct, testable admission criterion — a signal is only worth trading if its edge persists comfortably longer than the time it takes to earn back the round trip. Otherwise you are paying the spread to chase an edge that has already gone.
ideas.novelty: This filters the SIGNAL BOOK, not the trade. With 578 signals the real question is which ones deserve capital at all, and no rule in the 32 answers it. It is also the only rule here where the decision variable is a measured decay rate compared against a measured cost-recovery time, so it will systematically de-admit the fast intraday signals on illiquid names and keep the slow ones on liquid names.
ideas.source: Synthesis, built on two verified primary results: Novy-Marx & Velikov (RFS 2016, NBER w20721) turnover taxonomy and the finding that 'few of the strategies with higher turnover' survive costs; and Garleanu & Pedersen (2013) Proposition 4, 'the central relevance of signal persistence in the presence of transaction costs is one of the distinguishing features of our analysis'.

ideas.name: Square-Root Law Impact Budget Sizing
ideas.entry_rule: On a signal, do not use fixed-fractional or 1/ATR sizing. Invert the square-root impact law so that expected impact is a fixed fraction phi of the expected edge. The square-root law is Delta(Q) = Y * sigma_d * sqrt(Q / V20). Setting Delta = phi * E_edge and solving gives the share count Q* = V20 * ( phi * E_edge / (Y * sigma_d) )^2, where E_edge = k_edge * ATR(14) / C_t is the expected fractional move over the holding horizon, sigma_d = stdev of daily log returns over 20 days, V20 = 20-day average daily share volume, Y = 1.0, and phi is swept in [0.05, 0.30]. Enter with Q = min(Q*, participation_cap * V_bar, risk_cap), where participation_cap = 0.02 of the entry bar's own volume and risk_cap = (account_risk_fraction * equity) / (2 * ATR(14)).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the first of: (a) price reaches C_entry * (1 + E_edge) for a long, (b) H bars elapsed, (c) price touches C_entry - 2*ATR(14). Size the exit the same way: if Q exceeds participation_cap * V_bar, split the exit across ceil(Q / (participation_cap * V_bar)) consecutive bars.
inputs: volume (20-day average, and current bar volume)
params: k_edge ATR multiple for expected move
ideas.why: The square-root law is the single most robust empirical regularity in market impact — Toth et al. document it across equities, futures and FX, across two decades and many venues, with the exponent between 0.4 and 0.7. Because impact grows as sqrt(Q), the size at which impact eats a fixed fraction of the edge grows as the SQUARE of the edge-to-volatility ratio. That means an edge twice as large justifies four times the size, not twice. Every linear sizing rule is therefore systematically too small on high-conviction trades and too large on marginal ones.
ideas.novelty: Sizing in the corpus is linear (fixed fractional, or notional/ATR). This rule is quadratic in the edge-to-volatility ratio and linear in volume, which is the direct algebraic consequence of a concave impact law. It also produces the participation rate as an output rather than a hard-coded cap.
ideas.source: Toth, B., Lemperiere, Y., Deremble, C., de Lataillade, J., Kockelkoren, J. & Bouchaud, J-P. (2011), 'Anomalous price impact and the critical nature of liquidity in financial markets' (arXiv:1105.1694), eq. (1): 'Delta(Q) = Y * sigma * sqrt(Q/V), where sigma is the daily volatility of the asset, and V the daily traded volume, both quantities measured contemporaneously to the trade. The numerical constant Y is of order unity.' Reported exponent range delta 0.4-0.7; delta = 0.5 for small-tick, 0.6 for large-tick futures.

ideas.name: Three-Fifths Power Execution Horizon
ideas.entry_rule: On a signal with target size X shares, the decision variable is the execution HORIZON T, not the entry price. Using Almgren et al.'s fitted temporary-impact model, expected cost as a function of horizon is Cost(T) = eta * sigma_d * |X / (V20 * T)|^(3/5) + lambda_risk * sigma_d * (X / V20) * sqrt(T), with eta = 0.142 (the fitted universal coefficient), sigma_d = 20-day daily return stdev, V20 = 20-day average daily volume, T measured in trading days, and lambda_risk a swept delay-risk aversion. Grid-search T over {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0} days, pick T* = argmin Cost(T), convert to N = round(T* * bars_per_day) bars, and execute X/N shares per bar as a market order at each bar's (H+L+C)/3. If N < 1, fill in one bar.
ideas.exit_rule: At the exit trigger, recompute T* with the then-current sigma_d and V20 and liquidate over that many bars, again in equal slices. A stop-loss breach overrides and liquidates immediately in one slice. If the signal reverses mid-execution, cancel the unexecuted remainder.
ideas.why: Almgren, Thum, Hauptmann & Li fit permanent and temporary impact directly to 700,000 real US equity orders and reject the square-root exponent at 95% confidence in favour of 3/5 for the temporary term. Their fitted realised cost is J = I/2 + sgn(X)*eta*sigma*|X/(V*T)|^(3/5) with eta = 0.142. This gives a real, empirically calibrated tradeoff: stretching the execution reduces impact as T^(-3/5) but increases the volatility risk of not being filled as sqrt(T). The minimum is interior and depends on size, volume and volatility, so the right horizon is different for every trade.
ideas.novelty: The existing execution-timing family tests fill assumptions at fixed points in time. This makes the DURATION the optimised quantity, from a published, empirically fitted impact model with a non-obvious exponent. Note the permanent-impact term I = gamma*sigma*(X/V)*(Theta/V)^(1/4) needs shares outstanding Theta, which we do not have — but it does not appear in the horizon minimisation at all (permanent impact is independent of execution time), so the rule is fully OHLCV-computable as written.
ideas.source: Almgren, R., Thum, C., Hauptmann, E. & Li, H. (2005), 'Direct Estimation of Equity Market Impact': fitted exponents alpha = 0.891 +/- 0.10 (permanent, linear not rejected), delta = 0.267 +/- 0.22 (liquidity factor ~ 1/4), beta = 0.600 +/- 0.038 (temporary); coefficients gamma = 0.314 +/- 0.041 (t = 7.7) and eta = 0.142 +/- 0.0062 (t = 23); 'At the 95% confidence level, the square-root model beta = 1/2 is rejected.'

ideas.name: Implementation Shortfall Abort
ideas.entry_rule: At the signal bar, record the DECISION PRICE P0 = close of that bar, and the expected edge E_edge = k_edge * ATR(14) / P0. Begin executing X shares in N equal slices over N bars, each filled at that bar's (H+L+C)/3. After each slice j, compute the running realised shortfall IS_j = (VWAP_filled_j - P0) / P0 for a buy (sign-flipped for a sell), where VWAP_filled_j is the share-weighted average of fills so far. Then branch: (a) if IS_j > phi_abort * E_edge, CANCEL the entire unexecuted remainder and keep only what is filled — the trade is now a smaller position, permanently; (b) if IS_j < 0, i.e. price moved in your favour before you finished, ACCELERATE and execute the whole remainder on the next bar; (c) otherwise continue on schedule. phi_abort is swept in [0.3, 0.7].
ideas.exit_rule: Hold the filled quantity to the normal exit (H bars, or 2*ATR stop, or signal reversal). On exit, run the same logic in reverse against a new decision price = the close of the exit-signal bar: if exit shortfall exceeds phi_abort * E_edge, stagger the remaining liquidation over an additional N bars rather than crossing; a stop-loss exit bypasses the abort logic entirely and liquidates at market.
ideas.why: Perold's implementation shortfall is the gap between the paper portfolio (which trades costlessly at the decision price) and the real one, and it decomposes into execution cost on what you filled plus opportunity cost on what you did not. The key insight for a signal book is that these two are substitutes: once the market has already moved most of your expected edge against you before you are done buying, the remaining shares have negative expected value and the correct action is to stop, not to complete the order. A partially filled position at a good price beats a fully filled one at a bad price.
ideas.novelty: Every one of the 32 treats an entry as atomic — either the trade happens or it does not. This rule lets a trade be ABANDONED HALFWAY based on realised slippage against the decision price, producing variable, endogenous position sizes and an explicit opportunity-cost term. It also has an asymmetric accelerate branch, so favourable pre-fill drift is captured rather than surrendered to the schedule.
ideas.source: Perold, A.F. (1988), 'The Implementation Shortfall: Paper versus Reality', Journal of Portfolio Management 14(3), 4-9 — the paper-versus-real-portfolio decomposition into execution cost and opportunity cost. Complemented by Almgren & Chriss (2000), which uses expected shortfall and its variance as the objective throughout.

ideas.name: Own-Footprint Decay Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain a running estimate of your own residual price footprint in the name: Fp_t = SUM over all your own past slices s of G(t - t_s) * sign_s * (q_s / V_bar_s)^psi, with psi = 0.5, decay kernel G(l) = (1 + l)^(-beta), beta = 0.25, l measured in bars, q_s the slice share count, V_bar_s the volume of the bar it traded in, and sign_s = +1 for buys, -1 for sells. Do NOT fire the next slice, pyramid add, or new position in that ticker until |Fp_t| has decayed below theta_foot * sigma_bar, where sigma_bar = stdev of per-bar log returns over 20 bars and theta_foot is swept in [0.1, 0.5]. When the gate opens and the signal is still live, execute the next slice. Slices whose gate never opens before the signal expires are simply never traded.
ideas.exit_rule: Scale out under the same decay gate: each exit slice waits for the footprint to decay below threshold. Two exemptions that bypass the gate entirely: a stop-loss breach (2*ATR(14) adverse), and the final bar of the holding horizon, at which any residual is liquidated in one slice.
inputs: own trade log (slice size, sign, bar index)
ideas.why: In the propagator model, price is the sum of your own and everyone else's past order flow weighted by a decaying kernel, so the impact you paid on your last slice has not vanished — it is still partly in the price you are about to pay for the next one. Adding again before it decays means buying your own footprint. The kernel decays slowly (a power law, not exponentially), which is precisely why the naive fixed-bar cooldown is the wrong shape. Gatheral's no-dynamic-arbitrage argument ties the concavity of impact to the speed of this decay, so the two exponents cannot be chosen independently — sweeping them jointly is itself an informative test.
ideas.novelty: A cooldown between adds whose length is a function of HOW MUCH you traded and HOW LONG AGO, not a fixed bar count. It distinguishes a 100-share add from a 10,000-share add in the same name at the same moment, which no volume filter or cooldown in the 32 does. It is also the only rule here where your own past trading is a state variable in the entry condition.
ideas.source: Bouchaud, J-P. (2009), 'Price Impact' (arXiv:0903.2428): the propagator model p_T = p_{-inf} + lambda * SUM G(N-n) * eps_n * v_n^psi, with G(l) ~ l^(-beta), beta = (1-gamma)/2 and order-flow autocorrelation exponent gamma ~ 0.5 (giving beta ~ 0.25), and the BARRA-style single-trade response R(dt, v) = A*sigma*sqrt(v/V). Motivated by Gatheral, J. (2010), 'No-Dynamic-Arbitrage and Market Impact', Quantitative Finance 10(7), which constrains impact concavity against decay speed. Zarinelli, Treccani, Farmer & Lillo (2014, arXiv:1412.2152) report that impact relaxes to roughly 2/3 of peak impact, which gives a sanity target for the kernel's long-run level.

ideas.name: Net-The-Book Internal Crossing
ideas.entry_rule: This is a portfolio-level pre-trade rule sitting in front of every signal. Each rebalance bar: (1) let d_{k,i} be the desired position change in shares that signal k wants in ticker i; (2) compute the net D_i = SUM_k d_{k,i} and the gross Gr_i = SUM_k |d_{k,i}|; (3) SEND ONLY D_i to the market, never the individual d_{k,i}; (4) suppress the trade entirely unless |D_i| * C_i > max(min_ticket_notional, band_i), where band_i = k_band * c_i^(1/3) * |current position notional| with c_i the estimated round-trip cost fraction (EDGE spread + square-root impact). (5) Apply the margin rule: if D_i < 0 (net sell) but at least one signal in the book independently wants to be LONG ticker i, halve |D_i|; symmetrically for net buys against a standing short view. Log the internalisation ratio 1 - SUM|D| / SUM Gr as a first-class diagnostic.
ideas.exit_rule: Exits net through the same pipe: a signal wanting to exit does not force a trade if another signal wants in, and the position simply persists at the netted level. Two bypasses: a portfolio-level risk breach and a per-ticker stop both liquidate D_i in full, ignoring the band and the margin rule.
inputs: ohlc for EDGE spread per ticker
desired position changes from all K signals
ideas.why: With hundreds of signals on overlapping tickers, most of the gross turnover is signals trading against each other inside your own book — you pay a full round trip twice to end up flat. Netting first makes that free. Novy-Marx & Velikov go further and show that deliberately slowing sales when a second signal is bullish (what the industry calls screens or filters) lets you take a position in a second strategy at effectively NEGATIVE transaction costs, because the trade you skip was going to cost you anyway. This is the single highest-leverage change available to a 578-signal book.
ideas.novelty: Every one of the 32 is specified and tested in isolation, so the marginal cost of adding signal 579 is assumed to be its own standalone cost. Under this rule that marginal cost is near zero when the new signal correlates with the existing book and can be negative when it is anti-correlated with a pending sell. It changes what it even means to evaluate a signal.
ideas.source: Novy-Marx, R. & Velikov, M., 'A Taxonomy of Anomalies and their Trading Costs' (NBER w20721), section 6, 'Alternative Cost Mitigation Strategies': 'an alternative cost mitigation technique that allows investors trading one strategy to opportunistically take small positions in another at effectively negative trading costs. We call this technique trading one strategy on the margin of another, but it is also known in the industry as screens or filters. The screened strategies are enhanced by slowing sales (purchases) and short covers (shorts) when the screening variable is in the top (bottom) x%.'

ideas.name: Turnover Budget Greedy Queue
ideas.entry_rule: Treat daily turnover as a hard constrained resource. Each rebalance: (1) for every candidate trade j, compute expected net edge E_j = the walk-forward conditional expected log return over the signal's holding horizon (estimated on a trailing 500-bar window, using only bars at least H bars old); (2) compute expected cost C_j = spread_hat_j (EDGE, 60 bars) + eta * sigma_d * |Q_j / (V20_j * T_j)|^(3/5) with eta = 0.142; (3) rank all candidates by R_j = E_j / C_j, descending; (4) fill greedily down the ranking until cumulative traded notional reaches the budget B = b * portfolio_equity, with b swept in [0.02, 0.20] per day; (5) every candidate below the cut is DROPPED for the day, not queued, and is re-ranked from scratch tomorrow against the new opportunity set.
ideas.exit_rule: Exits join the same queue and compete for the same budget, but their score is multiplied by a priority factor m > 1 (swept in [1.0, 3.0]) so that risk reduction outranks risk addition at equal edge-per-cost. Two categories bypass the budget entirely and are always filled: stop-loss exits, and any liquidation required by a portfolio-level risk limit.
params: b daily turnover budget (2%-20% of equity)
ideas.why: The literature's core finding is that anomalies do not fail because the signals are wrong, they fail because the aggregate turnover is unaffordable. If turnover is the binding constraint, then the correct object to maximise is not expected return but expected return per unit of trading cost, subject to a budget — a straightforward knapsack. Ranking by E/C rather than by E means a modest edge in a liquid, tight-spread name beats a large edge in an illiquid one, which is exactly the reordering the cost literature says you should make.
ideas.novelty: Nothing in the 32 has any concept of a shared, exhaustible resource across signals; each fires independently. This makes signals compete, so the book self-limits and the composition of what actually gets traded shifts toward liquidity as the budget tightens. Sweeping b traces out the net-of-cost efficient frontier of the entire 578-signal book in one experiment.
ideas.source: Synthesis. Grounded in Novy-Marx & Velikov (RFS 2016) turnover taxonomy and cost-mitigation results, and in the cost-penalised model-comparison objective of Detzel, A., Novy-Marx, R. & Velikov, M. (2023), 'Model Comparison with Transaction Costs', Journal of Finance — which argues that models must be ranked on net-of-cost rather than gross efficient frontiers.

ideas.name: Spread Regime Passive-Aggressive Switch
ideas.entry_rule: On a signal, compute spread_hat_t = the EDGE effective spread over the trailing 60 bars (fraction of price) and its percentile rank pct_s within its own trailing 252 values. Compute participation p = Q / V_bar, where V_bar is the 20-bar average volume per bar. Then branch on BOTH: (a) if pct_s > 70 AND p < 0.02 — the spread is unusually wide and your order is small — post a passive limit buy at C_t * (1 - spread_hat/2) and hold it for up to W bars; model a fill only on a bar whose LOW <= the limit price, filled at the limit. If still unfilled after W bars, CANCEL AND SKIP THE TRADE — do not convert to a market order and do not chase. (b) otherwise — spread is normal or tight, or your order is large relative to bar volume — cross immediately with a market order at the next bar's open. W is swept in [1, 5].
ideas.exit_rule: Mirror the branch. If pct_s > 70 and p < 0.02, post a passive limit sell at C_t * (1 + spread_hat/2), modelling a fill only on a bar whose HIGH >= the limit; if unfilled after W bars, convert to a market order (unlike the entry, exits must complete). Otherwise cross immediately. A stop-loss breach always crosses immediately regardless of the spread regime.
inputs: rolling percentile of the spread over 252 bars
params: limit offset as a fraction of spread_hat (0.25-0.75)
ideas.why: The cost of crossing is the spread, and the spread is not constant — it widens in stressed and thin conditions and narrows otherwise. When it is wide you are paying a lot to demand immediacy, and if your order is small you can afford to supply liquidity instead and earn the spread rather than pay it. When your order is large relative to the bar, posting is pointless because you cannot get filled at size without moving the book anyway, so crossing is correct. The asymmetric skip-on-no-fill for entries and complete-on-no-fill for exits reflects that a missed entry costs only opportunity while a missed exit carries real risk.
ideas.novelty: The existing execution-timing family tests fill assumptions, but the branch here depends jointly on an ESTIMATED spread regime derived from OHLC and on the order's OWN PARTICIPATION RATE, and an unfilled passive entry kills the trade rather than falling back to a market order. Both are structural changes to the entry logic, not fill-model parameters.
ideas.source: Synthesis, grounded in verified primary sources: Ardia, D., Guidotti, E. & Kroencke, T.A. (2024), 'Efficient Estimation of Bid-Ask Spreads from Open, High, Low, and Close Prices', Journal of Financial Economics 161:103916 (OHLC-only spread estimator; official implementation at github.com/eguidotti/bidask, which notes the estimator works best on intraday bars with at least two trades per period); and the Roll (1984)/Hasbrouck (2009) effective-spread framing used as the cost measure in Novy-Marx & Velikov (RFS 2016), which explicitly caveats that the effective spread 'does not account for the price impact of large trades, and should thus be interpreted as the costs faced by a small liquidity demander' — precisely the condition under which posting passively is viable.

ideas.name: Trading Activity Scaled Bet Size
ideas.entry_rule: Compute the ticker's trading activity W_t = C_t * V20_t * sigma_d_t (dollar volume times daily return volatility), where V20 is the 20-day average daily share volume and sigma_d is the 20-day stdev of daily log returns. Gate: SKIP the trade entirely if W_t is below the 20th percentile of its own trailing 252 values. If admitted, size the position in dollars as N_t = kappa * W_t^theta, with theta swept over {0, 1/3, 1/2, 2/3, 1} and kappa chosen so the median position across the fleet equals the target notional (theta = 0 is the flat-sizing control). Additionally cap the per-ticker rebalance frequency: allow at most floor(f0 * (W_t / median_252(W))^(1/3)) trades per ticker per week, f0 swept in [1, 5]; trades beyond the cap are dropped for the week.
ideas.exit_rule: Standard horizon exit (H bars) or a 2*ATR(14) stop, but the exit is also participation-scheduled: liquidate over ceil(Q / (0.02 * V_bar)) consecutive bars so that participation never exceeds 2% of any bar's volume. A stop-loss breach liquidates in a single bar regardless of participation.
inputs: rolling 252-day percentile and median of W
ideas.why: Kyle and Obizhaeva's invariance programme argues that a single trading-activity variable W = P*V*sigma governs the whole microstructure of a security: how large a typical bet is, how often bets arrive, and what a bet costs. If that is right, both position size and rebalancing frequency should be power functions of W rather than constants, and the cost of a bet sized this way is roughly invariant across names. Even if the exact exponents do not hold, W is the natural single-number liquidity state variable available from OHLCV, and it is far better than raw dollar volume because it is volatility-weighted.
ideas.novelty: Two things are new. First, size scales as a swept POWER of a composite liquidity variable rather than linearly with dollar volume or inversely with ATR. Second — and this exists nowhere in the 32 — the REBALANCE FREQUENCY itself varies by ticker as a function of liquidity, so illiquid names are traded less often as well as smaller. Setting theta = 0 gives a clean control arm, so the sweep is a direct test of whether invariance-style scaling beats flat sizing.
ideas.source: Kyle, A.S. & Obizhaeva, A.A. (2016), 'Market Microstructure Invariance: Empirical Hypotheses', Econometrica 84(4), 1345-1404 — the trading activity variable W = P*V*sigma and the hypothesis that bet size and bet arrival rate are power functions of W. Honest caveat: I could not open a primary copy of this paper in this session, so the exponents are deliberately left as SWEPT PARAMETERS rather than asserted as the paper's values. The liquidity-factor intuition is independently corroborated by Almgren, Thum, Hauptmann & Li (2005), whose fitted permanent-impact term carries a (Theta/V)^(1/4) inverse-turnover factor with delta = 0.267 +/- 0.22, i.e. 'very approximately 1/4'.

ideas.name: Effective Bets Book Governor
inputs: daily closes of every currently held position
250-bar correlation matrix of held positions and its eigenvalues
first eigenvector loadings of held positions
sma(20) and sma(200) of each candidate
ideas.entry_rule: Daily, portfolio level. Let the live book hold M positions. Take the correlation matrix of their daily returns over the trailing 250 bars, eigen-decompose it, let p_k = lambda_k / sum(lambda) be the normalised variance contribution of principal portfolio k, and compute the Effective Number of Bets ENB = exp(-sum_k p_k * ln p_k). A candidate that passes its own price signal - specify: close crosses above SMA20(close) while close > SMA200(close) - is entered at the next open ONLY IF the ENB recomputed with that candidate included is >= 0.60 * (M+1). Otherwise the signal is skipped and not queued.
ideas.exit_rule: THE EXIT IS THE IDEA. If on any close the ENB of the live book falls below 0.50 * M, exit at the next open the single held position with the largest absolute loading on the first eigenvector, then re-test and repeat daily until ENB >= 0.50 * M. Positions not selected by that rule exit normally when close < SMA20(close).
ideas.why: A fleet of independently-signalled ladders silently converges on one bet when correlations rise: the book can hold twelve tickers and carry the risk of two. The entropy of the eigenvalue distribution measures how many genuinely independent bets the book actually contains, so gating entries on it prevents concentration accumulating, and shedding the highest PC1-loading name when it breaches is the single trade that most restores independence.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is computed from the BOOK's own holdings rather than from the market, and it governs both admission and forced liquidation. Every other idea in the corpus decides about one symbol in isolation; this one can refuse a perfectly good signal because of what is already held, and can close a profitable position purely because the book has become undiversified.
ideas.source: Meucci (2009), 'Managing Diversification', Risk 22(5):74-79, which introduces the diversification distribution over principal portfolios and the Effective Number of Bets ENB = exp(-sum p_k ln p_k). The eigenvalue-concentration interpretation is the same statistic underlying the absorption ratio of Kritzman, Li, Page & Rigobon (2011). Applying it as a live admission-and-liquidation governor on a multi-ticker fleet is my synthesis; I did not verify the Meucci reference against its primary text in this session.

ideas.name: Deflated Sharpe Arming Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Keep the per-bar P&L series of ALL M candidate rules in the sweep, synchronised to a common daily index. On the first trading bar of each calendar month, using the trailing T=756 daily returns: (a) for each candidate n compute the NON-annualised Sharpe SR_n = mean(r_n)/std(r_n), skewness g3_n and non-excess kurtosis g4_n; (b) compute V = sample variance of {SR_n} across all M candidates; (c) compute rho_bar = mean of the off-diagonal entries of the Pearson correlation matrix of the M daily P&L series, and the effective number of independent trials N_hat = rho_bar + (1 - rho_bar)*M (Bailey & Lopez de Prado eq. 8-9); (d) compute the selection-bias threshold SR_0 = sqrt(V) * ((1-gamma)*Zinv(1 - 1/N_hat) + gamma*Zinv(1 - 1/(N_hat*e))) with gamma = 0.5772156649, e = 2.718281828, Zinv = inverse standard-normal CDF; (e) compute DSR_n = Phi[ (SR_n - SR_0)*sqrt(T-1) / sqrt(1 - g3_n*SR_n + ((g4_n - 1)/4)*SR_n^2) ]. A candidate is ARMED for the coming month iff DSR_n >= 0.95. On every bar, take an entry only if the underlying candidate rule fires AND that candidate is currently armed. Unarmed candidates generate no orders.
ideas.exit_rule: Positions exit on the underlying candidate rule's own exit signal. Additionally, at each monthly recompute any armed candidate whose DSR falls below 0.60 is DISARMED: flatten its open positions at the next bar's open and take no new entries from it until DSR >= 0.95 again. Hysteresis (arm at 0.95, disarm at 0.60) is deliberate to stop the gate itself from becoming a high-frequency overfit switch.
inputs: per-bar P&L series of every candidate rule
ideas.why: With 578 rules swept over parameter grids, the maximum in-sample Sharpe you observe is an extreme order statistic, not an estimate of skill. Under the null of zero true skill, E[max SR] over N independent trials grows like sqrt(2 ln N) in Sharpe units, so a 2+ Sharpe is the EXPECTED outcome of a large enough search, not evidence. DSR raises the rejection threshold by exactly that expected maximum and simultaneously corrects the Sharpe's own standard error for negative skew and fat tails, which is where trend and mean-reversion P&L actually lives. It is the cheapest single gate that converts the corpus size from a liability into an explicit input.
ideas.novelty: Not a price rule at all - it is an arming layer that sits over every other rule and makes the size of the search a first-class parameter. Nothing in the corpus of 32 conditions references the number of trials.
ideas.source: Bailey, D. & Lopez de Prado, M. (2014), 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio: Correcting for Selection Bias, Backtest Overfitting and Non-Normality', Journal of Portfolio Management 40(5), eqs. (1) and (2) and Appendix A.3 (effective N). PDF: https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/deflated-sharpe.pdf . I reproduced the paper's own worked example numerically to confirm the (1 - 1/(N*e)) form: with SR=2.5 annualised, T=1250, skew=-3, kurt=10, V=1/500, the formula gives DSR=0.9004 at N=100 and 0.9505 at N=46, exactly the two figures the paper quotes. Underlying PSR: Bailey & Lopez de Prado (2012), 'The Sharpe Ratio Efficient Frontier', Journal of Risk 15(2).
params: N_hat estimator (mean-correlation vs PCA eigenvalue count)

ideas.name: CSCV Overfit Probability Gate with Median-Rank Parameter Choice
ideas.entry_rule: For each strategy FAMILY (one rule plus its parameter grid of N configurations), build the T x N matrix M of per-bar P&L, one column per configuration, rows synchronous. Partition the rows into S=16 contiguous, disjoint, equal-length blocks. Form all C(16,8)=12,870 combinations c of 8 blocks. For each c: (a) the training set J is the chosen 8 blocks concatenated in original time order, the test set J' is the complementary 8 blocks in original time order; (b) compute the Sharpe of every column on J and let n*(c) = argmax; (c) compute the rank rbar of column n*(c) among all N columns' Sharpes on J'; (d) set omega_c = rbar/(N+1) and logit lambda_c = ln(omega_c/(1-omega_c)). Define PBO = (#{c : lambda_c < 0}) / 12870. The family is TRADEABLE only if PBO < 0.30 AND the median across c of the OOS Sharpe of column n*(c) is > 0. The configuration actually deployed is NOT the full-sample argmax - it is the column with the highest MEDIAN rank across all 12,870 test sets. Enter exactly when that deployed configuration's own rule fires.
ideas.exit_rule: The deployed configuration's own exit. Re-run CSCV every 63 trading days on the trailing window; if PBO rises above 0.50 the family is retired: flatten at the next open and take no further entries from any configuration of that family. Also monitor the 'performance degradation' regression of OOS Sharpe on IS Sharpe across the 12,870 combinations - a negative slope means the optimiser is actively loss-maximising (memory effect) and the family must be retired immediately regardless of PBO.
inputs: per-bar P&L matrix across the whole parameter grid
Sharpe ratio computed on arbitrary row subsets
ideas.why: A holdout split gives you one out-of-sample number, and if you run twenty holdouts you are guaranteed a good one. CSCV is symmetric: every block serves as both training and test set, so it produces a full DISTRIBUTION of in-sample-optimal-versus-out-of-sample-rank outcomes rather than a single draw, and PBO is the mass of that distribution below the median. It is non-parametric, deterministic (re-running gives identical results), respects time order within blocks, and it also answers a question no t-test answers: was the SELECTION PROCEDURE itself harmful? Deploying the median-rank configuration rather than the argmax is the operational payoff - it picks the parameter set that is robustly good instead of the one that best fits one particular slice.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from every Sharpe-threshold gate: it scores the optimiser, not the strategy, and it changes which parameter set gets deployed. Distinct from the Deflated Sharpe gate in being non-parametric and requiring no assumption about the number of independent trials.
ideas.source: Bailey, D., Borwein, J., Lopez de Prado, M. & Zhu, Q. (2017), 'The Probability of Backtest Overfitting', Journal of Computational Finance 20(4), 39-69 - Algorithm 2.3 (CSCV), Definition 2.2 (PBO), and Section 3 (performance degradation, probability of loss, stochastic dominance). Working paper PDF: https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-prob.pdf
params: performance metric (Sharpe / Sortino / return-over-max-drawdown; note order-dependent metrics require J and J' in original order)

ideas.name: CPCV Purged-Path Lower Bound
ideas.entry_rule: Split the bar history into N=6 contiguous groups of equal bar count. Enumerate all C(6,2)=15 splits that hold out k=2 groups as test. For each split: (a) PURGE from the training set every bar whose label window [t_i0, t_i1] overlaps any test-set label window - for a strategy with an average holding period of H bars, drop every training bar within H bars of a test block boundary; (b) EMBARGO an additional h = ceil(0.01*T) bars immediately AFTER each test block from the training set, to kill serial-correlation leakage from the test block into subsequent training bars; (c) fit or select the rule's parameters on the purged, embargoed training portion only, then score on the test blocks. Recombine the 15 sets of test-block results into phi = k*C(N,k)/N = 5 complete, non-overlapping out-of-sample equity paths covering the whole history. Compute the annualised Sharpe of each of the 5 paths. ARM the rule only if min(path Sharpes) > 0 AND the 5th percentile of a 10,000-draw bootstrap over the 5 path Sharpes exceeds 0.5. When armed, take the rule's own entries.
ideas.exit_rule: The rule's own exit. Position size = clip(SR_p05 / SR_median_path, 0, 1) of the normal risk unit, re-derived every quarter from a fresh CPCV run on the expanding sample. If min(path Sharpe) <= 0 at any quarterly re-fit, flatten at the next open and disarm.
inputs: strategy label start/end times (entry bar and exit bar of each trade)
ideas.why: Standard walk-forward gives you exactly ONE out-of-sample path, so its Sharpe has enormous sampling error and you cannot tell a robust rule from a lucky ordering of regimes. CPCV gives 5 (or many more) full-length OOS paths from the same data, so you get a DISTRIBUTION of out-of-sample outcomes and can require the worst one to be positive. Purging and the embargo matter specifically for bar-based trading: a trade opened in the training set that is still open during the test set leaks the test set's information backwards, and serial correlation leaks it forwards - naive K-fold on overlapping trade labels is systematically optimistic.
ideas.novelty: Sizes by the lower bound of a distribution of out-of-sample paths rather than by a point estimate, and gates on the MINIMUM path rather than the mean. Purge-and-embargo is the specific fix for the overlapping-holding-period leak that plain time-series CV does not address.
ideas.source: Lopez de Prado, M. (2018), 'Advances in Financial Machine Learning', Wiley - ch.7 (purged K-fold with embargo, snippets 7.1-7.4) and ch.12 (Combinatorial Purged Cross-Validation, number of paths phi[N,k] = k*C(N,k)/N). Also Lopez de Prado, 'Backtesting II', Cornell ORIE 5256 lecture 6, https://ssrn.com/abstract=3261943
params: purge window as multiple of H

ideas.name: White Reality Check Benchmark Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Fix the benchmark as buy-and-hold of the same ticker over the same n bars (use a flat/zero benchmark if you want an absolute rather than relative test). For each of the l candidate rules k=1..l compute the per-bar performance differential f_{k,t} = (rule k's bar return) - (benchmark's bar return) and f_bar_k = (1/n)*sum_t f_{k,t}. Observed statistic V_l = max_{k=1..l} sqrt(n)*f_bar_k. Generate B=1000 stationary-bootstrap index paths (Politis-Romano): set t=1, draw u(1) uniformly from {1..n}; at each subsequent step draw U~Uniform[0,1] - if U < q draw u(t) uniformly from {1..n}, else set u(t) = u(t-1)+1 wrapping to 1 past n; use q=0.1 for a mean block length of 10 bars. Apply the SAME index path to all l rules so cross-rule dependence is preserved. For resample i compute V*_{l,i} = max_k sqrt(n)*(f_bar*_{k,i} - f_bar_k) - note the recentring by the ORIGINAL sample mean, which is what imposes the null. Sort the V* and find M = #{i : V*_{l,i} <= V_l}; the Reality Check p-value is P_RC = 1 - M/B. Trade the argmax rule's own entries ONLY if P_RC < 0.05; otherwise the whole family is rejected and you hold the benchmark.
ideas.exit_rule: The winning rule's own exit. Re-run the Reality Check every 126 bars on the expanding sample; revert to benchmark-only (flatten all rule-driven positions at the next open) as soon as P_RC >= 0.10. Because the statistic is recursive - V_k = max(sqrt(n)*f_bar_k, V_{k-1}) - you can add new candidate rules to the family later without re-running the whole search, but you MUST carry the running V and V* forward, which is exactly the accounting that stops you from quietly forgetting earlier trials.
inputs: per-bar returns of every candidate rule
uniform RNG with a recorded seed
ideas.why: The right null is not 'this rule has zero edge' but 'the BEST of the l rules I looked at has no edge over the benchmark', and that null's distribution is the distribution of a maximum over correlated series. The stationary bootstrap preserves the autocorrelation and heteroskedasticity of bar returns (an IID bootstrap would understate the null's spread and pass junk), and applying one common index path across all rules preserves their correlation, which is what stops the test being absurdly conservative when 578 rules are near-duplicates of each other. The recursive form is the practical hook: it makes the honest trial count auditable across sessions and researchers.
ideas.novelty: Tests the maximum over the whole family against a dependence-preserving bootstrap null, rather than testing any single rule. Distinct from DSR in being non-parametric and benchmark-relative rather than absolute.
ideas.source: White, H. (2000), 'A Reality Check for Data Snooping', Econometrica 68(5), 1097-1126 - Corollary 2.4 and Section 3 'Implementing the Bootstrap Reality Check' (P_RC = 1 - M/N, the recursive V_k updates, q=0.1, N=500-1000). PDF: https://users.ssc.wisc.edu/~bhansen/718/White2000.pdf . Applied to technical trading rules in Sullivan, R., Timmermann, A. & White, H. (1999), 'Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap', Journal of Finance 54(5), 1647-1691. Bootstrap: Politis, D. & Romano, J. (1994), 'The Stationary Bootstrap', JASA 89(428), 1303-1313.
params: benchmark (buy-and-hold vs flat vs the incumbent live rule)

ideas.name: Hansen Superior Predictive Ability Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Same f_{k,t} differentials and the same shared stationary-bootstrap index paths as the Reality Check. Additionally compute omega_hat_k, a Newey-West HAC estimate of the standard deviation of sqrt(n)*f_bar_k with bandwidth floor(4*(n/100)^(2/9)). Observed statistic T_SPA = max(0, max_k sqrt(n)*f_bar_k / omega_hat_k). For the bootstrap, recentre each rule by g_hat_k = f_bar_k * 1{ f_bar_k >= -sqrt( (omega_hat_k^2 / n) * 2*ln(ln(n)) ) } - i.e. a rule whose mean differential is worse than that threshold is recentred at ZERO instead of at its own mean, so hopeless rules cannot pad out the null distribution. For each of B=1000 resamples compute T*_{SPA,i} = max(0, max_k sqrt(n)*(f_bar*_{k,i} - g_hat_k)/omega_hat_k); p_SPA = #{i : T*_{SPA,i} > T_SPA} / B. ARM the family's best rule only if p_SPA < 0.05, and take its own entries.
ideas.exit_rule: The armed rule's own exit. Re-run the SPA test quarterly on the expanding sample; disarm and flatten at the next open when p_SPA >= 0.10. Always report BOTH the SPA p-value and the White Reality Check p-value from the same bootstrap paths: a family that passes RC but fails SPA is one where the winner is only winning because it is being compared against a lot of noise, and a family that fails RC but passes SPA has been diluted by junk candidates and deserves a rerun with the junk removed.
inputs: per-bar returns of every candidate rule
ideas.why: White's Reality Check is not consistent against the alternative when the candidate set contains many poor models: adding deliberately terrible rules widens the null distribution of the max and makes the p-value LARGER, so a researcher can manipulate the test in either direction just by curating the candidate list. Hansen fixes this two ways - studentising by each rule's own volatility so a high-variance rule cannot dominate the max on scale alone, and recentring clearly-inferior rules at zero via the law-of-the-iterated-logarithm threshold sqrt(2 log log n). For a 578-rule corpus where most rules are genuinely bad, this is the difference between a test with power and one without.
ideas.novelty: Different entry decision from the Reality Check on the same data: studentised max plus selective recentring means the two tests can and routinely do disagree, and the disagreement is itself diagnostic about whether the candidate pool was padded.
ideas.source: Hansen, P. R. (2005), 'A Test for Superior Predictive Ability', Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 23(4), 365-380 - the studentised T^SPA statistic, the g_hat recentring rule with the -sqrt((omega^2/n) 2 log log n) threshold, and the demonstration that White's RC is sensitive to the inclusion of poor alternatives.
params: recentring constant (the 2 log log n multiplier, or Hansen's lower/upper/consistent variants)

ideas.name: Romano-Wolf Stepdown Multi-Rule Book
ideas.entry_rule: Compute studentised statistics t_k = sqrt(n)*f_bar_k / omega_hat_k for all l candidate rules (f and omega defined as in the SPA gate) and sort descending. STEP 1: with the active set S = {all l rules}, use B=1000 shared stationary-bootstrap paths to build the null distribution of max_{k in S} sqrt(n)*(f_bar*_k - f_bar_k)/omega_hat_k; let c_1 be its (1-alpha) quantile, alpha=0.05. REJECT (declare genuine) every rule with t_k > c_1. STEP 2: remove the rejected rules from S and rebuild the max-statistic null over the REMAINING rules only - this gives c_2 <= c_1 - and reject any further rules with t_k > c_2. Iterate until a step produces no new rejections. Let R = number of rejected rules. Allocate 1/R of the risk budget to each rejected rule and take each one's own entry signals at that weight. Rules that were never rejected generate no orders, ever.
ideas.exit_rule: Each rule exits on its own signal. Re-run the full stepdown every 63 bars on a trailing 3-year window. A rule that drops out of the rejected set is flattened at the next open and its weight redistributed equally among the survivors; a newly rejected rule is added at the next open with the book re-weighted to 1/R. If R falls to 0 the entire book goes flat and stays flat until the next re-run produces at least one rejection.
inputs: per-bar returns of every candidate rule
stationary bootstrap with shared index paths across rules
ideas.why: Bonferroni and the Reality Check answer 'is the best one real?'. That is the wrong question for a fleet: you want to identify EVERY rule that is real, and to allocate across them. A single-step max test is badly under-powered for the second, third, and fourth best rules because they are all judged against the null distribution of the maximum over all 578. The stepdown recovers that power - once the obvious winners are removed the critical value drops, so genuinely good but not-best rules can still be found - while still controlling the family-wise error rate at alpha in the strong sense. Because the bootstrap uses a common index path, the procedure automatically exploits the fact that near-duplicate rules in the corpus are highly correlated, which a Bonferroni correction would ignore and be crushed by.
ideas.novelty: Produces a SET of rules and an allocation, not a single winner. Distinct exit structure: capital is continuously reallocated as the rejected set changes, so the book is an explicit function of what is currently statistically defensible.
ideas.source: Romano, J. P. & Wolf, M. (2005), 'Stepwise Multiple Testing as Formalized Data Snooping', Econometrica 73(4), 1237-1282. Also Romano, J. P., Shaikh, A. & Wolf, M. (2008), 'Formalized Data Snooping Based on Generalized Error Rates', Econometric Theory 24(2), 404-447 (k-FWER and FDP-controlling variants that let you tolerate a few false positives in exchange for far more power).
params: stepdown vs k-FWER variant (allow k=1,2,3 false rejections)

ideas.name: Benjamini-Yekutieli False Discovery Allocator
ideas.entry_rule: Every quarter, for each of the M candidate rules compute a one-sided p-value p_k for the null of zero mean bar return, using the stationary bootstrap null (p_k = fraction of bootstrap means at or above the observed mean) or, as a cheaper proxy, p_k = 1 - Phi(t_k) with t_k the Newey-West t of the rule's bar returns. Sort ascending: p_(1) <= p_(2) <= ... <= p_(M). Compute c(M) = sum_{j=1..M} 1/j (the Benjamini-Yekutieli constant, which makes the procedure valid under ARBITRARY dependence - use c(M)=1 for plain Benjamini-Hochberg only if you are willing to assume positive dependence). Find the largest index i such that p_(i) <= (i / (M * c(M))) * q, with target false discovery rate q = 0.10. Rules ranked 1..i are DISCOVERIES; every other rule is silent. Each discovery is allocated 1/i of the risk budget and takes its own entry signals at that weight. If no i satisfies the inequality, the book is flat for the quarter.
ideas.exit_rule: Each discovery exits on its own signal. At the next quarterly recompute, any rule that falls out of the discovery set is flattened at the next open and its capital redistributed equally; newly discovered rules are added at the next open. Track the realised out-of-sample hit rate of the discovery set: if fewer than (1-q) of the discoveries are profitable over two consecutive quarters, tighten q to 0.05 rather than adding more rules.
inputs: per-bar returns of every candidate rule
Newey-West HAC t-statistics or bootstrap p-values
ideas.why: Family-wise error control (Bonferroni, Holm, Reality Check, Romano-Wolf) asks 'what is the chance I make even one false discovery?'. With 578 candidates that is a brutal standard and it will throw away every real but modest edge. FDR asks the question an allocator actually cares about: 'what fraction of the rules I am funding are junk?' Setting q=0.10 means you consciously accept that about one in ten funded rules is noise, which is a rational trade when the funded rules are diversified across 1/i weights and the cost of a false positive is a small drawdown rather than a blown fund. The Yekutieli c(M) correction is essential here because the 578 rules are heavily dependent - many are re-parameterisations of the same idea - and plain BH is only valid under positive dependence.
ideas.novelty: Controls a different error rate from every other gate here (FDR, not FWER), which yields a materially larger and different funded set. The allocation is an explicit function of the discovery count i, so the book automatically concentrates when evidence is thin and diversifies when it is broad.
ideas.source: Benjamini, Y. & Hochberg, Y. (1995), 'Controlling the False Discovery Rate', JRSS-B 57(1), 289-300; Benjamini, Y. & Yekutieli, D. (2001), 'The Control of the False Discovery Rate in Multiple Testing under Dependency', Annals of Statistics 29(4), 1165-1188. Applied to trading and factor discovery in Harvey, C., Liu, Y. & Zhu, H. (2016), '...and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns', Review of Financial Studies 29(1), 5-68 (their BHY-implied t-hurdle is 3.39 at FDR 1% as of 2012, versus 3.78 for Holm/FWER 5%): https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Research/Published_Papers/P118_and_the_cross.PDF

ideas.name: Haircut Sharpe Position Sizing
ideas.entry_rule: For each candidate rule k with T bars of history and non-annualised Sharpe SR_k, form the single-test statistic t_k = SR_k * sqrt(T) and the one-sided single-test p-value p_S,k = 1 - Phi(t_k). Adjust all M of them for multiplicity with Holm: sort ascending, p_Holm(i) = min{ max_{j<=i} [ (M - j + 1) * p_(j) ], 1 }. Invert the adjusted p-value back to a t: t_H,k = Phi^{-1}(1 - p_Holm(k)), and back to a Sharpe: HSR_k = t_H,k / sqrt(T). The haircut is (SR_k - HSR_k)/SR_k. Rule k then trades its OWN entry signals, but at risk fraction w_k = clip( HSR_k / SR_target, 0, w_max ) with SR_target = 1.0/sqrt(252) (a 1.0 annualised Sharpe) and w_max = 0.25 of the book. Rules with HSR_k <= 0 get w_k = 0 and never fire. Run the same computation with Bonferroni (p_Bonf(i) = min[M*p_(i), 1]) and with BHY (start from the LARGEST p-value: p_BHY(M) = p_(M); p_BHY(i) = min[ p_BHY(i+1), (M*c(M)/i)*p_(i) ] with c(M) = sum_{j=1..M} 1/j) and size on the MINIMUM of the three HSRs.
ideas.exit_rule: Each rule exits on its own signal. Recompute the haircut monthly on an expanding window and rescale live position size to the new w_k at the next bar's open - a rule whose haircut deepens is trimmed rather than switched off, and a rule whose haircut lifts is scaled up, both continuously. Close out entirely and permanently retire a rule the first time w_k reaches 0 on two consecutive monthly recomputes.
inputs: per-bar returns of every candidate rule
sample Sharpe and bar count per rule
sorted p-value vector across all M rules
ideas.why: Every other gate in this area is binary: the rule trades or it does not. That throws information away and creates a cliff edge where a rule oscillates on and off as its p-value jitters around a threshold. The haircut Sharpe is naturally continuous - it answers 'what single-test Sharpe should I assign this rule as if there had been no data mining?' - so it maps directly onto a risk fraction. Harvey and Liu's key empirical finding is that the haircut is strongly NON-LINEAR in the reported Sharpe: a marginal 0.5 Sharpe strategy is haircut nearly to nothing after a few hundred trials while a 1.5 Sharpe strategy loses far less than the folk-rule 50%. Sizing on the haircut therefore concentrates capital in exactly the right place automatically.
ideas.novelty: Continuous capital allocation as a function of multiple-testing-adjusted significance, rather than an on/off gate. Taking the minimum across Bonferroni, Holm and BHY is a deliberate belt-and-braces construction that avoids depending on any single error-rate philosophy.
ideas.source: Harvey, C. & Liu, Y. (2015), 'Backtesting', Journal of Portfolio Management 42(1), 13-28 - the haircut Sharpe ratio and the exact Bonferroni / Holm / BHY adjusted p-value formulas, plus the finding that the haircut is non-linear and that the customary 50% haircut is too punitive for high-Sharpe and too lenient for low-Sharpe strategies. PDF: https://people.duke.edu/~charvey/Research/Published_Papers/P120_Backtesting.PDF . Companion: Harvey, C. & Liu, Y. (2014), 'Evaluating Trading Strategies', JPM 40(5), 108-118.
params: M (the honest trial count - sweep 100 / 578 / 5000 to see sensitivity)
adjustment method (Bonferroni / Holm / BHY / min of three)

ideas.name: MinBTL Trial Budget with 1/e Stopping
ideas.entry_rule: BEFORE any sweep, fix S* = the annualised in-sample Sharpe you refuse to be fooled by (use S* = 1.0) and count y = years of usable history for the ticker. The trial budget is the largest integer N satisfying MinBTL(N) <= y, where MinBTL(N) = [ ( (1-gamma)*Zinv(1 - 1/N) + gamma*Zinv(1 - 1/(N*e)) ) / S* ]^2 with gamma = 0.5772156649 (upper-bounded by 2*ln(N)/S*^2). Verified values: y=2 years gives N=7; y=5 years gives N=45; y=6.4 years gives N=100; y=10.6 years gives N=1000. Enumerate the theoretically justified configurations of the rule in RANDOM order and cap the list at N. Evaluate the first floor(N/e) (about 37%) and deploy NONE of them, recording only the best Sharpe seen, S_best. Then continue one configuration at a time and DEPLOY the first one whose in-sample Sharpe exceeds S_best. If none does by configuration N, deploy nothing and stay flat. The deployed configuration then generates entries by its own rule.
ideas.exit_rule: The deployed configuration's own exit. It is retired without replacement after y/2 years of live trading, or immediately if its live Sharpe over the trailing 126 bars is below zero. A NEW sweep on the same ticker may only begin once MinBTL(N_new) years of genuinely unseen data have accumulated since the last sweep - the calendar, not the researcher's impatience, gates the next search. Every configuration ever evaluated is written to an append-only trial log; that log's length is the M fed into every other gate in this collection.
inputs: length of available OHLCV history in years
count of parameter configurations in the grid
ideas.why: Every other idea here is a post-hoc correction applied after the damage is done. This one is ex ante and it is the only lever that actually reduces the amount of overfitting rather than measuring it. The arithmetic is brutal and worth internalising: with 5 years of data, trying more than about 45 independent configurations essentially GUARANTEES you find one with an in-sample Sharpe of 1.0 and a true out-of-sample Sharpe of zero. With 2 years, seven trials suffice. Since financial series exhibit mean-reverting memory, backtest overfitting does not merely dilute the false pattern out of sample - it selects rules positioned to be actively undone, so the expected out-of-sample result is negative, not zero. The 1/e secretary rule is the optimal-stopping answer to 'when do I stop looking?' when every additional trial carries an irreversible false-positive cost.
ideas.novelty: Constrains the SEARCH rather than correcting its output, and gives a hard, computable cap on the number of configurations as a function of available history. Nothing else in the corpus touches the size of the search. It also produces the auditable M that the DSR, haircut, FDR and stepdown gates all require as an input.
ideas.source: Bailey, D., Borwein, J., Lopez de Prado, M. & Zhu, Q. (2014), 'Pseudo-Mathematics and Financial Charlatanism: The Effects of Backtest Overfitting on Out-of-Sample Performance', Notices of the AMS 61(5), 458-471 - Theorem 3.1 (MinBTL) and the explicit '5 years of data, no more than 45 independent configurations' and '7 trials for a 2-year backtest with IS Sharpe 1' results, which I reproduced numerically (my computation gives 5.00 and 1.92 years respectively). PDF: https://www.davidhbailey.com/dhbpapers/backtest-pseudo.pdf . The 1/e stopping rule is recommended in the 'When should we stop testing?' section of Bailey & Lopez de Prado (2014), 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio', JPM 40(5), citing Bruss, F. T. (1984), 'A Unified Approach to a Class of Best Choice Problems', Annals of Probability 12(3), 882-889.
params: exact MinBTL vs the 2 ln N upper bound
sampling fraction for the stopping rule (1/e vs 1/2)

ideas.name: Optimiser Permutation Test on Shuffled Bars
ideas.entry_rule: Convert the ticker's bar series into T tuples: the close-to-close log return r_t, plus the intrabar offsets (open_t - close_{t-1}), (high_t - close_t), (low_t - close_t) expressed in log terms so bar shape travels with the return. Build P=1000 surrogate series by Fisher-Yates shuffling the ORDER of the tuples and re-cumulating from the original starting price - this destroys all serial structure and all regime persistence while preserving the exact marginal return distribution and the realistic bar geometry. On EACH surrogate, re-run the ENTIRE parameter optimisation for the strategy family and record the best in-sample Sharpe found, S*_p. On the real series record S_real, the best in-sample Sharpe from the identical optimisation. The permutation p-value is p = (1 + #{p : S*_p >= S_real}) / (P + 1). ARM the optimised configuration only if p < 0.05. For rules that depend on intraday structure or overnight gaps, permute in WHOLE-DAY BLOCKS (shuffle the order of trading days, keep each day's intraday bars intact and in order) so the null is not made artificially easy by destroying the intraday shape the rule exploits.
ideas.exit_rule: The armed configuration's own exit. Re-run the permutation test annually on the expanding series and disarm (flatten at the next open) if p >= 0.20. Run a SECOND, complementary permutation with the trading SIGNAL held fixed and only the returns permuted: this tests whether the specific rule has edge, whereas the first test prices the optimiser's greed. Arm only if both tests pass; if the signal-fixed test passes but the optimiser test fails, the rule idea may be real but the parameter search was too aggressive - shrink the grid and re-run rather than deploying.
inputs: full parameter grid and the optimisation routine itself
ideas.why: Every parametric gate assumes something - normality, a known number of independent trials, a particular dependence structure. A permutation test assumes none of that: it just asks how good the best result from THIS EXACT SEARCH looks on data with no structure at all. Because it re-runs the whole optimisation on each surrogate, it automatically prices the greediness of the optimiser, the non-independence of neighbouring grid points, and any subtle selection the researcher built into the grid - none of which the trial count N captures. It is the closest thing to an honest answer to 'how much of my 2.4 Sharpe is the search itself?'. The cost is compute: P times the full sweep. That is a bearable price for the one test with no free parameters to fudge.
ideas.novelty: Resamples the DATA and repeats the SEARCH, rather than resampling a fixed set of P&L series. That distinction matters: White's Reality Check conditions on the l P&L series you happened to produce, whereas this prices the whole discovery process including how the grid was chosen. The paired signal-fixed variant separates rule edge from optimiser greed, which no other test here does.
ideas.source: Masters, T. (2018), 'Permutation and Randomization Tests for Trading System Development: Algorithms in C++', and Masters, T. (2018), 'Testing and Tuning Market Trading Systems' - the training-set (optimiser) permutation test versus the selection-bias permutation test. Related published treatment: Aronson, D. (2006), 'Evidence-Based Technical Analysis', ch.6, which applies White's Reality Check and Monte Carlo permutation to 6,402 TA rules and finds none significant after correction.
params: permutation unit (single bar / whole day / stationary block)
statistic (best Sharpe / best profit factor / mean of top decile)

ideas.name: Sequential Probability Ratio Kill Switch
ideas.entry_rule: When a rule is armed by any of the gates above, freeze from its validation sample the per-trade expected log return mu_b and per-trade log-return standard deviation sigma_b. Set L = 0 at arming. After each closed trade i with realised log return x_i, update the cumulative log-likelihood ratio for H1 (edge equals the backtested edge) against H0 (zero edge, same volatility): L <- L + (mu_b * x_i)/sigma_b^2 - mu_b^2/(2*sigma_b^2). Set Wald boundaries A = ln((1-beta)/alpha) and B = ln(beta/(1-alpha)) with alpha = 0.05 (probability of wrongly killing a genuinely good rule) and beta = 0.20 (probability of wrongly keeping a dead one); with these values A = 2.773 and B = -2.944. The rule KEEPS taking its own entry signals while B < L < A. When L >= A the rule is CONFIRMED: size up by a factor of 1.5 (capped at the book limit) and reset L = 0 to begin a fresh test cycle.
ideas.exit_rule: Open positions exit on the rule's own signal. The rule is KILLED - flatten at the next bar's open and take no further entries - the first time L <= B. A killed rule cannot be revived by subsequent live P&L; it must be re-armed by a fresh CPCV or CSCV validation on data that includes the live period. A hard secondary floor also applies: kill immediately if the live cumulative return since arming falls below the 1st percentile of 10,000 stationary-bootstrap resamples of the validation equity curve evaluated at the SAME trade count, which catches the case where the rule fails by drawdown shape rather than by mean.
inputs: mu_b and sigma_b from the validation sample
ideas.why: Fixed-horizon rules like 'review after 100 trades' waste evidence: a rule that is obviously broken after 12 trades keeps bleeding for another 88, and a rule that is obviously working gets no credit until the arbitrary bell rings. The SPRT is the optimal solution to exactly this problem - among all tests with the same error rates it minimises the expected number of observations needed to reach a decision - so it kills bad rules faster and confirms good ones sooner than any fixed-n alternative. It also disciplines the decision in advance: alpha and beta are chosen once, so the shutdown is not a judgement call made in the middle of a drawdown. Crucially, live trades are the only data in this entire programme that is genuinely, un-recyclably out-of-sample, so the test that consumes them should be the most efficient one available.
ideas.novelty: A sequential, evidence-accumulating exit at the STRATEGY level rather than the position level, with an explicit and pre-committed error-rate budget. Every other exit in the corpus is a price or time condition on a single trade.
ideas.source: Wald, A. (1945), 'Sequential Tests of Statistical Hypotheses', Annals of Mathematical Statistics 16(2), 117-186, and Wald (1947), 'Sequential Analysis'; the boundaries A = ln((1-beta)/alpha), B = ln(beta/(1-alpha)) are Wald's approximations. The application to deciding when to stop trading a discovered strategy follows the framing in Harvey, C. & Liu, Y. (2014), 'Evaluating Trading Strategies', JPM 40(5), 108-118. The specific per-trade Gaussian likelihood-ratio construction and the bootstrap equity-path floor are my synthesis.
params: mu_b haircut factor (test against mu_b, or against the more honest 0.5*mu_b)

ideas.name: Clark-West Nested Admission Test
ideas.entry_rule: You run an incumbent ensemble E producing a one-bar-ahead return forecast f_{E,t}. A candidate rule C is NESTED in E if E's forecast equals the E+C forecast with C's weight set to zero - which is the case whenever you are asking 'should I add this rule to my existing book?'. Over an out-of-sample window of n bars, form f_{E,t}, f_{EC,t} and the realised bar return y_t, then compute the Clark-West adjusted differential cw_t = (y_t - f_{E,t})^2 - [ (y_t - f_{EC,t})^2 - (f_{E,t} - f_{EC,t})^2 ]. The statistic is CW = sqrt(n) * mean(cw) / HAC_se(cw) with Newey-West bandwidth floor(4*(n/100)^(2/9)). ADMIT C to the ensemble only if CW > 1.645 (one-sided 5%, standard-normal critical value, valid for the nested case) AND CW exceeds the Holm-adjusted critical value for the M candidates being considered simultaneously (for M=20 that is Phi^{-1}(1 - 0.05/20) = 3.09). For NON-nested comparisons between two independent rules use plain Diebold-Mariano instead: d_t = L(e_{1,t}) - L(e_{2,t}) with L the squared-error loss, DM = mean(d)/HAC_se(d), compared to the standard normal. Once admitted, the ensemble trades the sign of f_{EC,t} with size proportional to |f_{EC,t}| / ATR(14), capped at 1x.
ideas.exit_rule: C is DROPPED from the ensemble - its contribution zeroed and any C-specific position flattened at the next open - when its rolling 252-bar CW statistic falls below 0. The ensemble as a whole exits a position when f_{EC,t} changes sign or when |f_{EC,t}| falls below 0.25 * ATR(14). Re-run the admission test for every pending candidate quarterly, and never admit more than one candidate per quarter regardless of how many pass, so that the trial count grows slowly enough for MinBTL to stay satisfied.
inputs: one-bar-ahead return forecasts from the incumbent ensemble and from ensemble-plus-candidate
ideas.why: Adding a rule to an existing book is a NESTED model comparison, and the standard Diebold-Mariano test is badly mis-sized in that setting: under the null the extra parameter is zero, so the larger model's forecast error is inflated purely by estimation noise, and DM systematically UNDER-rejects, meaning genuinely useful additions get rejected. Clark-West's adjustment term (f_E - f_EC)^2 removes exactly that noise penalty and restores an approximately standard-normal null. This is the correct statistical machinery for the actual decision a fleet operator makes 578 times: not 'is this rule good in isolation?' but 'does this rule add anything my existing book does not already have?' - which is also the only question that controls the corpus's rampant near-duplication.
ideas.novelty: Tests INCREMENTAL contribution against an incumbent rather than absolute performance against zero, which is a fundamentally different admission decision and the one that actually prevents 578 correlated rules from all being funded. The nested-versus-non-nested distinction and its correct critical values appear nowhere in the corpus.
ideas.source: Clark, T. E. & West, K. D. (2007), 'Approximately Normal Tests for Equal Predictive Accuracy in Nested Models', Journal of Econometrics 138(1), 291-311 - the adjusted MSPE statistic. Also Clark, T. E. & West, K. D. (2006), Journal of Econometrics 135(1-2), 155-186; Clark, T. E. & McCracken, M. W. (2001), Journal of Econometrics 105(1), 85-110. Non-nested case: Diebold, F. X. & Mariano, R. S. (1995), 'Comparing Predictive Accuracy', JBES 13(3), 253-263, with the small-sample correction of Harvey, Leybourne & Newbold (1997), International Journal of Forecasting 13(2), 281-291.
params: loss function (squared error / absolute error / direct P&L)
Holm M (how many candidates are in flight)

ideas.name: Frozen-Parameter Holdout Symbol Binomial
ideas.entry_rule: Partition the tradeable universe ONCE, by a fixed rule (e.g. hash of the ticker string), into a TUNE set of 20 liquid symbols and a HOLDOUT set of 40 different liquid symbols, and never swap them. Sweep every parameter of the rule ONLY on the TUNE set, using only tune-set bars. FREEZE the single winning parameter vector. Apply it, unchanged, to each of the 40 holdout symbols over the same calendar period and record the sign of each symbol's realised Sharpe. Under the null that the rule has no edge, each sign is a fair coin, so the count of positive signs K ~ Binomial(40, 0.5). Require the one-sided binomial p-value P(K >= k_obs) < 0.01, which means k_obs >= 27 of 40. ALSO require the median holdout Sharpe > 0.3 and the interquartile range of holdout Sharpes < 1.5 (a rule that works spectacularly on 3 symbols and fails on 37 is not a rule, it is 3 accidents). Only if all three conditions hold does the rule go live, and it goes live ONLY on the HOLDOUT symbols and on symbols never used in either set - never on the tune symbols, whose results are contaminated by the search.
ideas.exit_rule: Each position exits on the rule's own signal. Re-run the holdout binomial test every 6 months on the trailing 2 years of holdout data; if k_obs falls below 20 of 40 (i.e. worse than a coin flip) flatten every position and retire the rule PERMANENTLY. The holdout set must never be re-tuned on - the moment you adjust a parameter using holdout results, that set becomes a tune set and a fresh holdout must be drawn from symbols never previously used, which is why the initial partition should reserve more symbols than you think you need.
inputs: per-symbol out-of-sample Sharpe under one frozen parameter vector
ideas.why: Every other test in this area fights the multiple-testing problem by inflating critical values. This one sidesteps it: it converts an N-trial selection problem into a SINGLE binomial test with 40 near-independent draws, because the parameter vector is frozen before the holdout symbols are ever touched. Cross-sectional replication also tests something no time-series test can - whether the effect is a property of the RULE or a property of one symbol's particular history. That distinction is precisely what a multi-ticker DCA-ladder fleet needs, since the whole premise of the fleet is that a rule generalises across symbols. The IQR condition is what stops a single explosive symbol from carrying the test.
ideas.novelty: Uses cross-sectional replication rather than time-series resampling as the source of independent evidence, so it costs no extra history and no compute, and it directly answers the fleet-relevant question of transferability. The permanent-retirement and never-re-tune clauses are the operational teeth: without them the holdout silently becomes a tune set within two quarters.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The reasoning follows directly from the false-strategy result in Bailey & Lopez de Prado (2014) 'The Deflated Sharpe Ratio' - it is the number of TRIALS that inflates the maximum Sharpe, so adding independent SAMPLES under a frozen parameter vector adds evidence without adding trials. The cross-sectional replication standard is the one urged in Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2016), 'and the Cross-Section of Expected Returns', RFS 29(1), 5-68, and the empirical case for it is Hou, K., Xue, C. & Zhang, L. (2020), 'Replicating Anomalies', RFS 33(5), 2019-2133, which finds 65% of 452 published anomalies fail to replicate.

ideas.name: Novy-Marx Confluence Critical Value
ideas.entry_rule: Applies to any CONFLUENCE or composite rule that requires n component conditions to agree, where each component's DIRECTION was chosen using in-sample data. Do not test the composite against t = 2. Compute the composite's Newey-West t-statistic on the trailing 756 bars, then compare it to the correct null critical value at p = 0.05: (a) if the n components are equal-weighted after each was signed to predict positive in-sample returns, use t* = sqrt(2/pi)*sqrt(n) + sqrt(1 - 2/pi)*Phi^{-1}(1 - n*p/(n+1)) - which gives 2.23 for n=2, 2.46 for n=3, 2.83 for n=5, 3.54 for n=10; (b) if the composite weights components by their in-sample t-statistics (an ex-post mean-variance-efficient combination) use t** = sqrt( chi2inv(1 - p, n) ); (c) if you SELECTED the best k of n candidate components, treat it as selecting the single best of n^k candidates and use t* = Phi^{-1}[ (1 - p/2)^(1/(n^k)) ] - for the best 3 of 10 that is 4.05, not 2.0. ARM the confluence rule only if its t exceeds the applicable critical value, then enter exactly when the composite condition fires.
ideas.exit_rule: The composite's own exit. Recompute the t and the critical value quarterly; disarm and flatten at the next open as soon as t falls below the critical value. Operationally, log the value of n and k that were actually used to build the composite at the moment it was built - retro-fitting a smaller n later is the single easiest way to cheat this gate, and the log is what prevents it.
inputs: per-bar returns of the composite rule
the count n of components and the count k selected
inverse normal CDF and inverse chi-squared CDF
ideas.why: Confluence rules ('enter when RSI, MACD and volume all agree') are the most common way a rule corpus grows, and they are the most severely overfit construction in the whole space - because each component is silently signed to predict positive in-sample returns, the composite is fitted even when no component was individually selected. Novy-Marx's central empirical result is that combining the best k of n candidate signals produces a bias almost as large as selecting the single best of n^k candidates: a 3-of-10 confluence rule faces a 5% critical t of nearly 4, so a t of 2.5 that looks strongly significant is in fact unremarkable. For a 578-rule corpus that surely contains many multi-condition rules, this is the gate that will disqualify the most ideas, and it will disqualify exactly the ones that look best.
ideas.novelty: Supplies critical values specific to composite/confluence construction, which no general multiple-testing correction gets right because the bias comes from signing components in-sample, not only from selecting among them. The n^k equivalence is a concrete, computable number that turns 'be careful with confluence' into a hard threshold.
ideas.source: Novy-Marx, R. (2015), 'Backtesting Strategies Based on Multiple Signals', NBER Working Paper 21329 - eq. (5) for the best 1-of-n critical value, eq. (7) for the signal-weighted n-of-n chi-distribution result, eqs. (9) and (10) for the equal-weighted asymptotic approximation, and Fig. 4 plus the abstract for the 'best k of n is almost as biased as best 1 of n^k' finding and the near-4 critical t for best 3-of-10. https://www.nber.org/papers/w21329 . I verified eq. (10) numerically: it returns 3.54 for n=10 and the n^k equivalence returns 4.05 for 3-of-10, matching the paper's 'almost four'.
params: weighting scheme (equal vs signal-weighted, which changes the formula)
n and k as actually searched

ideas.name: Stationary Bootstrap Lower-Bound Kelly
ideas.entry_rule: For each armed rule, take its per-bar P&L series over the trailing T = 1260 bars. Draw B = 2000 stationary-bootstrap resamples: start at a uniformly random index; at each step, with probability q jump to a new uniform random index, otherwise advance by one, wrapping at the end; the block length is therefore geometric with mean 1/q. Choose q by the Politis-White automatic rule, or as a simple default q = T^(-1/3) (about 1/11 at T=1260, i.e. 11-bar mean blocks). Compute the annualised Sharpe of each resample; let SR_lcb be the 10th percentile of that bootstrap distribution and SR_point the full-sample Sharpe. The rule takes its OWN entry signals at risk fraction w = clip(SR_lcb / SR_point, 0, 1) * f_kelly, with f_kelly = 0.25 (quarter-Kelly on the point estimate). A rule with SR_lcb <= 0 takes no positions at all.
ideas.exit_rule: Each position exits on the rule's own signal. Re-bootstrap monthly and reset w at the next bar's open. Go and stay flat when SR_lcb <= 0 at two consecutive monthly recomputes. Additionally, compute the bootstrap distribution of maximum drawdown across the 2000 resamples and hard-stop the rule for the remainder of the quarter if the live drawdown exceeds the 95th percentile of that distribution - a drawdown deeper than 95% of what the rule's own resampled history can produce is evidence the edge is gone, not evidence of bad luck.
inputs: annualised Sharpe and maximum drawdown of each resample
ideas.why: Full-Kelly on a POINT Sharpe estimate is a well-known route to ruin, because the estimate is itself a random variable and Kelly is convex in it - the loss from over-betting on an over-estimated edge exceeds the gain from under-betting. Sizing on a bootstrapped lower confidence bound makes the position an explicit function of estimation risk: a rule with 1260 clean bars and a stable edge gets nearly full size, a rule with the same point Sharpe but wild path dependence gets a fraction. The stationary bootstrap is the right resampler here specifically because trading P&L is autocorrelated and heteroskedastic - an IID bootstrap would produce far too tight a confidence interval and hand you exactly the over-sizing you were trying to avoid. The geometric (rather than fixed) block length is what keeps the resampled series stationary, which fixed-block methods do not guarantee.
ideas.novelty: Position size is a function of the WIDTH of the Sharpe confidence interval, not just its centre - a sizing law that no rule in the corpus applies. The drawdown-percentile hard stop uses the rule's own resampled distribution as the reference, rather than a fixed dollar or percentage limit.
ideas.source: Politis, D. N. & Romano, J. P. (1994), 'The Stationary Bootstrap', Journal of the American Statistical Association 89(428), 1303-1313. Automatic block-length selection: Politis, D. N. & White, H. (2004), 'Automatic Block-Length Selection for the Dependent Bootstrap', Econometric Reviews 23(1), 53-70 (with the correction in Patton, Politis & White 2009). The under-betting rationale is standard Kelly estimation-risk analysis; combining it with a stationary-bootstrap lower bound and a bootstrap-drawdown stop is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Campbell-Thompson Doubly-Restricted Premium Forecast
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: On the last trading day of month t, using only data through t: (1) Build the predictor x_t = log of Mele/Neely realised volatility, RVOL_t = sqrt(pi/2) * sqrt(12) * (1/12) * sum_{i=0..11} |r_{t-i}|, where r_s is the monthly log excess return of SPY (monthly log return minus the monthly log risk-free return; if no risk-free series is available use 0 and treat r as total return, applied consistently everywhere). (2) Run an expanding-window OLS regression r_{s+1} = a + b*x_s + e over every s from the first available month to t-1 (minimum 240 observations before the first live signal). (3) COEFFICIENT SIGN RESTRICTION: theory (risk-return tradeoff) says b > 0; if b_hat <= 0, discard the regression and set rhat_{t+1} = the prevailing historical mean (1/t)*sum_{s=1..t} r_s. Otherwise rhat_{t+1} = a_hat + b_hat*x_t. (4) FORECAST RESTRICTION: if rhat_{t+1} < 0, set rhat_{t+1} = 0. (5) sigmahat^2_{t+1} = sample variance of the last 60 monthly excess returns.
