(6) Target weight w_t = (1/gamma) * rhat_{t+1} / sigmahat^2_{t+1} with gamma = 3, then clip w_t to [0, 1.5]. Enter/rebalance to w_t at the next session's open.
ideas.exit_rule: No stop and no profit target. The position is held to the last trading day of month t+1, at which point steps (1)-(6) are repeated and the holding is rebalanced to the new w_{t+1}; w = 0 is a full exit. This scheduled-re-optimisation exit (continuous weight, no price-based stop) is itself the exit structure being tested.
inputs: risk-free proxy (optional; can be set to 0)
params: predictor choice from the OHLCV-computable Goyal-Welch set
which restrictions are active: coefficient only, forecast only, both
ideas.why: Campbell and Thompson's point is that a real-world investor would never mechanically trade a raw OLS forecast. Unrestricted recursive regressions produce economically absurd forecasts (negative equity premia, wrong-signed slopes) purely from estimation error in short samples, and those absurd forecasts are exactly where the out-of-sample loss comes from. Imposing two costless priors - the slope must have the theoretically expected sign, and the equity premium cannot be negative - shrinks the forecast toward the prevailing mean precisely when the data are uninformative. In their Table 1 this flips the count of predictors beating the historical average from a minority to 5 of 7, and they show the resulting out-of-sample R-squared, though tiny in absolute terms, must be judged against the squared Sharpe ratio S^2 (0.012 monthly): an R-squared of 0.25% against S^2 of 1.2% is a ~21% proportional increase in the mean-variance investor's portfolio return.
ideas.novelty: Nothing in the existing 32 is a forecasting model at all - they are all threshold rules on an indicator. Here the traded object is the fitted value of a recursively re-estimated regression, and the distinctive machinery is the restriction layer (wrong-sign fallback to the prevailing mean, truncation at zero) plus continuous mean-variance position sizing with a leverage cap. The prevailing historical mean is the benchmark, not cash.
ideas.source: Campbell, J.Y. and Thompson, S.B., 'Predicting the Equity Premium Out of Sample: Can Anything Beat the Historical Average?', NBER Working Paper 11468 (June 2005), published RFS 2008 - read directly at https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w11468/w11468.pdf. Restrictions described on pp.2-3 and Table 1 panels B/C/D; the R-squared vs S^2 argument and the [0,150%] weight constraint with 5-year rolling variance are on pp.9-10. RVOL definition from Neely, Rapach, Tu & Zhou, FRB St. Louis WP 2010-008 (Aug 2013 revision), eqs. (2)-(3).

ideas.name: Technical Signal Principal Components Premium Regression
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: On the last trading day of month t, from SPY monthly closes P and monthly volume VOL, compute 14 binary signals, each 1 (buy) or 0 (sell): (a) SIX moving-average signals MA(s,l) for s in {1,2,3} and l in {9,12}: S = 1 if MA_s,t >= MA_l,t else 0, where MA_j,t = (1/j)*sum_{i=0..j-1} P_{t-i}. (b) TWO momentum signals MOM(m) for m in {9,12}: S = 1 if P_t >= P_{t-m} else 0. (c) SIX on-balance-volume signals VOL(s,l) for s in {1,2,3} and l in {9,12}: first OBV_t = sum_{k=1..t} VOL_k * D_k with D_k = +1 if P_k - P_{k-1} >= 0 else -1; then S = 1 if MAOBV_s,t >= MAOBV_l,t else 0, where MAOBV_j,t = (1/j)*sum_{i=0..j-1} OBV_{t-i}. Stack the 14 signals into a vector; standardise each column to zero mean and unit variance using only data through t; extract the first K = 3 principal components F1,F2,F3 (K chosen each month by adjusted R-squared over K in {1,2,3}). Run an expanding-window OLS r_{s+1} = a + c1*F1_s + c2*F2_s + c3*F3_s + e through s = t-1 and form rhat_{t+1} = a_hat + c1_hat*F1_t + c2_hat*F2_t + c3_hat*F3_t. Truncate rhat at 0 from below. Rebalance at the next open to w_t = clip((1/5) * rhat_{t+1} / sigmahat^2_{t+1}, 0, 1.5), with sigmahat^2 the variance of the last 60 monthly excess returns.
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Hold to the last trading day of the next month, recompute the 14 signals, re-extract the PCs on the extended sample, re-estimate the regression, and rebalance to the new w. w = 0 exits fully.
ideas.why: Neely, Rapach, Tu and Zhou show that the in-sample R-squared of a regression on PCs of macro variables plus PCs of technical signals equals the SUM of the two separate R-squareds - the information is additive and orthogonal. Technical signals are not a worse version of macro predictors, they capture a different thing: they lead sentiment changes and detect the decline in the realised premium near business-cycle peaks, while macro variables pick up the rise near troughs. Extracting PCs from a panel of 14 correlated binary rules filters the idiosyncratic noise that makes any single crossover rule fragile, which is why the PC forecast survives out-of-sample where individual rules do not. Their reported figures: PC-TECH out-of-sample R-squared 0.65%, PC-ALL 1.79%, both significant by the Clark-West MSFE-adjusted statistic against the very stringent prevailing-mean benchmark. Goyal, Welch and Zafirov's 2024 audit independently found this 'tchi' variable to be one of only four post-2008 predictors that still passes both in-sample and Campbell-Thompson out-of-sample tests through 2021.
ideas.novelty: The corpus already has EMA cross and similar rules, but they trade the crossover event. Here the crossovers are never traded. Fourteen crossover states are used only as inputs to a factor model, and what is traded is the sign and magnitude of a regression fitted value. Two indicators can both be on 'buy' and produce a bearish forecast if the loading pattern is unusual; that behaviour is impossible for any threshold rule.
ideas.source: Neely, C.J., Rapach, D.E., Tu, J. and Zhou, G., 'Forecasting the Equity Risk Premium: The Role of Technical Indicators', Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis Working Paper 2010-008 (Aug 2013 revision), published Management Science 60(7), 2014 - read directly at https://s3.amazonaws.com/real.stlouisfed.org/wp/2010/2010-008.pdf. Indicator definitions eqs. (4)-(9) and pp.7-8; PC regression eq. (12) and eq. (25); out-of-sample results Table 4. Survivorship confirmation: Goyal, Welch and Zafirov, 'A Comprehensive 2022 Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction', RFS 37(11), 2024, p.3492.

ideas.name: Kitchen-Sink Forecast Combination Timer
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain N = 14 separate univariate predictive regressions of the next monthly SPY log excess return on a single OHLCV-derived predictor each: x1 = log RVOL (sqrt(pi/2)*sqrt(12)*(1/12)*sum_{i=0..11}|r_{t-i}|); x2 = 12-month total return; x3 = 1-month return; x4 = log(P_t / 120-month moving average of P); x5 = 60-month realised skewness of monthly returns; x6 = log(current month volume / 12-month average volume); x7 = the value-weighted average pairwise correlation of the top-500 names (see the Average Pairwise Correlation idea); x8 = the cross-sectional Hill tail measure (see the Hill Tail Risk idea); x9 = log aggregate Amihud illiquidity; x10 = the fraction of the top-500 names above their own 200-day moving average; x11 = the cross-sectional standard deviation of trailing 12-month stock returns; x12 = realised monthly variance from daily returns; x13 = the 12-month change in x12; x14 = drawdown depth, log(P_t / max P over the trailing 36 months). On the last trading day of month t, for each i estimate r_{s+1} = a_i + b_i*x_i,s by expanding-window OLS through s = t-1, form rhat_i,t+1, and apply the Campbell-Thompson zero truncation to each individual forecast. Combine: rhat_C = sum_i w_i,t * rhat_i,t+1. Under EQUAL WEIGHTING w_i,t = 1/N. Under DMSPE weighting w_i,t = (phi_i,t)^-1 / sum_j (phi_j,t)^-1 with phi_i,t = sum_{s=s0..t-1} theta^(t-1-s) * (r_{s+1} - rhat_i,s+1)^2 and theta in {1.0, 0.9}. Rebalance at the next open to w_t = clip((1/5)*rhat_C/sigmahat^2, 0, 1.5).
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Hold one month; at the next month-end recompute all 14 forecasts, recompute the combining weights from the updated forecast-error history, and rebalance to the new w_t. w = 0 exits fully.
inputs: running discounted squared-forecast-error accumulator per model
params: N and the membership of the predictor panel
weighting scheme: equal / median / 10%-trimmed mean / DMSPE
holdout length s0 before weights go live
whether the CT truncation is applied per-model or only to the combination
ideas.why: Individual predictive regressions fail out of sample not because there is no signal but because each carries a large, largely independent estimation-error component. Averaging cancels that component while retaining the common signal, which is why combination survives where its members do not - it is a shrinkage device with a variance-reduction interpretation, and it also hedges against model instability, since a predictor that breaks down simply drifts toward zero weight rather than dominating. Neely et al. verify this directly on the Goyal-Welch panel: the simple mean of their 14 bivariate forecasts has an out-of-sample R-squared of 1.16%, versus positive values for only three of the 14 individual macro regressions taken alone. Pettenuzzo, Timmermann and Valkanov independently report an equal-weighted combination of unconstrained forecasts reaching 0.62% against -0.53% for the average individual model.
ideas.novelty: This is a portfolio of forecasts, not a portfolio of trades. Every one of the 32 existing ideas is a single rule with a single opinion; here 14 disagreeing models are reconciled into one continuous exposure, and the combining weights themselves adapt from realised forecast error rather than from price. Nothing in the corpus has a meta-layer that reweights its own components.
ideas.source: Rapach, D.E., Strauss, J.K. and Zhou, G., 'Out-of-Sample Equity Premium Prediction: Combination Forecasts and Links to the Real Economy', Review of Financial Studies 23(2), 2010, 821-862 - the paper is paywalled and I could not open it; its method and the 1.16% figure for the simple mean of 14 bivariate forecasts are verified from Neely et al. (FRB St. Louis WP 2010-008, Aug 2013), footnote 29 and surrounding text, which I read directly. The DMSPE weighting formula follows Stock and Watson (2004) as adopted by RSZ; I state it from standard practice rather than from the primary text, which I could not open - treat theta and the exact phi accumulator as the part to sanity-check against a reference implementation. Combination benchmark figure of 0.62% from Pettenuzzo, Timmermann and Valkanov, Brandeis WP 57 (2013), which I read directly.

ideas.name: Sharpe-Ratio-Bounded Premium Forecast
ideas.category: return predictability econometrics / economically motivated constraints
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: On the last trading day of month t: (1) form any base forecast rhat_raw of next month's log excess return (e.g. the expanding-window univariate regression of the Campbell-Thompson idea, before its truncation). (2) Estimate conditional monthly volatility sigmahat_{t+1} as the square root of an EWMA of daily squared SPY log returns with decay lambda = 0.97, scaled to monthly by multiplying by sqrt(21). (3) Convert to an annualised conditional Sharpe ratio SR_{t+1} = sqrt(12) * rhat_raw / sigmahat_{t+1}. (4) IMPOSE THE DOUBLE BOUND: if SR_{t+1} < SR_l set SR_{t+1} = SR_l; if SR_{t+1} > SR_u set SR_{t+1} = SR_u; with SR_l = 0 and SR_u = 1.0. (5) Map back: rhat_final = SR_{t+1} * sigmahat_{t+1} / sqrt(12). (6) Rebalance at the next open to w_t = clip((1/5) * rhat_final / sigmahat_{t+1}^2, 0, 1.5). Note the upper bound is the active ingredient: it makes the maximum admissible expected return PROPORTIONAL to current conditional volatility, so in a calm tape the model is forbidden from forecasting a large premium no matter what the regression says, and in a violent tape a large premium becomes admissible.
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Hold one month, then recompute sigmahat, re-estimate the base forecast, re-apply both bounds, and rebalance. w = 0 exits fully. A distinct feature versus the Campbell-Thompson version is that the position can be cut purely because volatility fell, with no change in the base forecast at all.
params: SR_l (0 or a small negative value to permit shorts)
EWMA decay lambda (0.94, 0.97) or a stochastic-volatility / GARCH(1,1) alternative
ideas.why: Campbell-Thompson truncation is a one-sided, one-shot fix: it removes negative forecasts but does nothing about implausibly LARGE ones, which is where the damaging leverage comes from. Pettenuzzo, Timmermann and Valkanov show the binding economic prior is a bound on the price of risk, not on the premium itself. Annualised market Sharpe ratios around 0.5 are normal and above 1.0 are essentially impossible for an unlevered market portfolio, so any forecast implying a higher conditional Sharpe ratio is diagnostic of estimation error rather than opportunity. Because the bound is expressed in Sharpe units, it translates into a time-varying premium ceiling proportional to conditional volatility - a genuinely different object from a fixed cap. Their reported results: average out-of-sample R-squared across the Goyal-Welch predictors improves from -0.53% unconstrained to 0.18% under the SR constraint monthly, from -0.23% to 1.02% quarterly, and from -5.27% to 3.86% annually, with the SR constraint beating the simpler non-negativity constraint at every horizon beyond monthly.
ideas.novelty: Every volatility-aware idea in the corpus uses volatility as a filter or a stop distance (ATR expansion, squeeze release, Keltner). Here volatility sets a CEILING ON BELIEF - it caps how bullish the model is allowed to be - and the position can shrink to zero because the tape got calm while the raw forecast stayed constant. The two-sided nature is also new: existing rules clip losses, none clip optimism.
ideas.source: Pettenuzzo, D., Timmermann, A. and Valkanov, R., 'Forecasting Stock Returns under Economic Constraints', Brandeis University Working Paper Series 2013|57, published JFE 114(3), 2014 - read directly at https://www.brandeis.edu/economics/RePEc/brd/doc/Brandeis_WP57.pdf. Sharpe ratio definition eq. (7), the bound SR_l <= SR <= SR_u eq. (8), the choice SR_l = 0 and SR_u = 1 with its justification on p.9, and the out-of-sample R-squared improvements on p.4-5.

ideas.name: Rolling CumSSE Model Confidence Gate
ideas.category: return predictability econometrics / real-time model validation
ideas.timeframe: any; evaluated at the model's own rebalance frequency
ideas.entry_rule: Wrap ANY forecast-based timing model (rhat_t) in a live self-audit. At each rebalance date t, having recorded for every past date s the model's forecast rhat_s and the prevailing-mean benchmark forecast rbar_s = (1/s)*sum_{u<=s} r_u, compute the running difference of cumulative squared prediction errors over a trailing window of L periods: DeltaCumSSE_t = sum_{s = t-L+1 .. t} [ (r_s - rbar_{s-1})^2 - (r_s - rhat_{s-1})^2 ]. This is positive exactly when the model has beaten the naive prevailing mean over that window, and is the same running statistic on which the Diebold-Mariano standard error is built. GATE: if DeltaCumSSE_t > 0, take the model's target weight w_model,t in full. If DeltaCumSSE_t <= 0, override it and hold the benchmark weight w_bench,t = clip((1/gamma)*max(rbar_t, 0)/sigmahat^2, 0, 1.5) instead - i.e. fall back to the prevailing-mean allocation and stop trading the model. Optionally ramp rather than switch: scale the model's deviation from benchmark by g_t = clip(DeltaCumSSE_t / (2*SE_t), 0, 1), with SE_t the standard deviation of the L per-period squared-error differences times sqrt(L), so w_t = w_bench,t + g_t*(w_model,t - w_bench,t).
ideas.exit_rule: The gate itself is the exit: when the trailing DeltaCumSSE turns negative, the model's position is unwound to the benchmark weight regardless of price action, and stays there until the running statistic recovers above zero. There is no price-based stop anywhere in this rule - the position is cut on FORECAST QUALITY, not on drawdown, and the two can diverge (a model can be making money and still be gated off for losing to the prevailing mean).
params: window L (60, 120, 240 periods, or expanding from inception)
gate form: hard on/off vs the g_t ramp
the significance multiple in the ramp denominator (1, 2, 3 standard errors)
hysteresis: require k consecutive positive readings to re-enable
benchmark choice: prevailing mean vs fixed buy-and-hold
ideas.why: Goyal and Welch's central empirical finding is not that predictors are useless on average but that their usefulness is concentrated in a handful of episodes and is otherwise absent or negative - the dividend-price ratio's entire statistical case rests on 1973-74 and 2002, the T-bill rate worked consistently until roughly 1973 and consistently failed afterwards, and the equity-share predictor's edge from the 1973-75 oil shock was almost exactly undone by 1999-2002. The cumulative-squared-error difference plot is how they detect this: an upward-sloping line means the model is earning its keep, a downward-sloping one means the naive average is winning. Turning that diagnostic from a post-hoc chart into a live position gate is the direct trading translation - it stops a decayed model from being traded on faith for the years it takes for a full-sample t-statistic to notice. It also answers the standard objection to every idea in this list: you do not need to know in advance which regime a predictor works in if you have a rule that turns it off when it stops working.
ideas.novelty: This is a meta-rule with a non-price exit. Nothing in the 32 exits a position based on the forecasting model's own out-of-sample loss relative to a naive benchmark - all existing exits are price, time or indicator based. It is also the only rule here whose 'flat' state is an explicit benchmark allocation rather than cash.
ideas.source: Goyal, A. and Welch, I., 'A Comprehensive Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction', NBER Working Paper 10483 (May 2004), published RFS 21(4), 2008 - read directly at https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w10483/w10483.pdf. The diagnostic is defined on p.12 ('the cumulative squared prediction errors of the prevailing mean minus the cumulative squared prediction error of the predictive variable... This is also the running statistic on which the Diebold-Mariano standard error is computed'), and the per-predictor episode-by-episode readings quoted above are on pp.13-14. Converting it into a live gate is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Stambaugh-Corrected Augmented Predictive Regression
ideas.category: return predictability econometrics / small-sample bias correction
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: For any persistent OHLCV-derived predictor x (log aggregate illiquidity, log RVOL, avgcor, the Hill tail measure, log(P/200dma) - all have first-order autocorrelation above 0.7): at each month-end t, using only data through t: (1) Fit the predictor's own AR(1): x_s = mu + rho*x_{s-1} + v_s by OLS. (2) Apply Kendall's small-sample bias correction to the persistence estimate: rho_c = rho_hat + (1 + 3*rho_hat)/T + 3*(1 + 3*rho_hat)/T^2, where T is the number of observations in that AR(1) fit. Adjust the intercept to mu_c = mean(x)*(1 - rho_c). (3) Recompute the corrected innovations vhat_c,s = x_s - mu_c - rho_c*x_{s-1}. (4) Estimate the AUGMENTED predictive regression r_{s+1} = alpha + beta*x_s + phi*vhat_c,s+1 + e_{s+1}, including the CONTEMPORANEOUS corrected predictor innovation as an extra regressor. Because the bias in beta arises entirely from the correlation between the return shock and the predictor shock, projecting that shock out leaves beta_hat unbiased; the raw regression without the vhat term is upward-biased whenever cov(e, v) is non-zero, which it is for every valuation-like or liquidity-like predictor. (5) Form the forecast for trading as rhat_{t+1} = alpha_hat + beta_hat*x_t (the phi term is dropped - vhat_{t+1} is not knowable at t; its only job is to de-bias beta). (6) TRADE GATE: enter only if beta_hat has the theoretically expected sign AND its Newey-West t-statistic with 12 lags exceeds 2.0 in that direction. Otherwise set rhat to the prevailing mean. (7) Truncate rhat at 0 and rebalance at the next open to w_t = clip((1/5)*rhat/sigmahat^2, 0, 1.5).
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Hold one month; at the next month-end refit the AR(1), re-apply Kendall's correction on the now-longer sample, re-estimate the augmented regression, re-check the gate, and rebalance. A position is cut to the prevailing-mean allocation the moment the bias-corrected slope loses significance - so the exit is driven by the predictor's econometric standing, not by price.
inputs: augmented OLS with Newey-West standard errors
params: whether to use Kendall's correction or a wild bootstrap of the null instead
ideas.why: Stambaugh's bias is not a technicality - it is the single largest reason persistent predictors look better in sample than they are. When a predictor is highly autocorrelated and its innovation is correlated with the return innovation (which it always is for price-based ratios: a price move changes both the return and the ratio), the downward bias in the estimated AR root feeds through into an UPWARD bias in the predictive slope and inflates the t-statistic. Trading a signal on that inflated slope is a systematic error, not an unlucky one. Amihud implements exactly this fix in the aggregate-illiquidity setting: he notes that his g1 coefficient is upward biased by Stambaugh's argument, corrects the AR(1) slope with Kendall's method (his 0.764 becomes 0.869, which I verified reproduces exactly from the formula above with T = 34), adds the corrected residual to the right-hand side, and reports only the augmented model. Neely et al. address the same concern with a wild bootstrap and confirm the bias-correction literature (Amihud-Hurvich, Lewellen, Campbell-Yogo) gives qualitatively similar inferences, so either route is defensible.
ideas.novelty: The entry condition is a property of the ESTIMATOR, not of the price. The same predictor at the same level can be tradeable one month and not the next purely because the bias-corrected slope crossed a significance threshold. No indicator rule in the corpus has a gate of this kind, and the augmented-regression construction (adding a contemporaneous innovation you will never observe at trade time, purely to de-bias a coefficient you will use) has no analogue anywhere in it.
ideas.source: Stambaugh, R.F., 'Predictive regressions', Journal of Financial Economics 54, 1999 - the canonical statement of the bias; I did not open the original. The implementation I specify is verified from Amihud, Y., 'Illiquidity and Stock Returns: Cross-Section and Time-Series Effects', NYU working paper FIN-00-041, published JFM 5, 2002 - read directly at http://archive.nyu.edu/bitstream/2451/26706/2/FIN-00-041.pdf, pp.19-20, where the Kendall (1954) correction, the explicit appeal to Stambaugh (1999), and the augmented model (11) with the AR residual on the right-hand side are all set out; I checked Kendall's formula reproduces his reported 0.869 from rho_hat = 0.764 and T = 34. The alternative bias-correction routes (Amihud-Hurvich 2004, Lewellen 2004, Campbell-Yogo 2006) and the wild-bootstrap substitute are named in Neely et al., FRB St. Louis WP 2010-008, p.5 and footnote 3.

ideas.name: Campbell-Yogo Bonferroni Q Predictor Gate
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly re-evaluation
ideas.entry_rule: A licensing test that decides, each month, whether a persistent predictor x is allowed to drive exposure at all. At month-end t, on data through t: (1) Estimate the AR(1) x_s = mu + rho*x_{s-1} + v_s and compute the DF-GLS unit-root t-statistic on x. (2) Build a 90% confidence interval for rho by INVERTING that statistic through simulation: for each candidate rho_g on a grid from 0.80 to 1.02 in steps of 0.002, simulate 5,000 AR(1) paths of length T with intercept and Gaussian innovations, record the DF-GLS t-statistic distribution, and retain rho_g if the observed DF-GLS t lies between that distribution's 5th and 95th percentiles. Call the retained set C_rho. (3) Estimate delta = corr(e_s, v_s), the correlation between the predictive-regression residual and the AR innovation, and sigma_e, sigma_v. (4) For each rho_g in C_rho and each candidate slope beta0 on a grid, compute the Q-statistic Q(beta0, rho_g) = sum_s xdm_{s-1} * [ r_s - beta0*x_{s-1} - (delta*sigma_e/sigma_v)*(x_s - rho_g*x_{s-1}) ] / ( sigma_e * sqrt(1 - delta^2) * sqrt(sum_s xdm_{s-1}^2) ), where xdm is the de-meaned predictor. Retain beta0 if |Q| < 1.645 (one-sided 5% after the Bonferroni split). (5) The Bonferroni confidence interval for beta is the union of retained beta0 across all rho_g in C_rho. (6) TRADE GATE: enter the market-timing position from this predictor only if that entire interval lies strictly on the theoretically expected side of zero. If it straddles zero, the predictor is not licensed this month and exposure falls back to the prevailing-mean benchmark weight.
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Re-run the licensing test every month on the extended sample. The position is unwound to the benchmark weight the month the Bonferroni interval first admits zero. Exposure is therefore governed by the width of a confidence interval, and can be cut in a rising market and restored in a falling one.
inputs: simulated DF-GLS null distributions over a rho grid
params: Bonferroni split (alpha1 for rho, alpha2 for beta; 0.10/0.00, 0.05/0.05)
whether to use the Q-statistic or the simpler Bonferroni t-test
ideas.why: Conventional t-tests on persistent predictors are size-distorted: when the predictor's largest autoregressive root is near unity and its innovation is correlated with the return innovation, the null is rejected far too often, so a nominal 5% test is really a 15-20% test. Campbell and Yogo's fix is to stop pretending rho is known: get a confidence set for the local-to-unity parameter first via DF-GLS, then invert a test statistic that is uniformly most powerful CONDITIONAL on rho, and combine the two intervals by Bonferroni. The Q-statistic achieves this by subtracting the projection of the return on the predictor's contemporaneous innovation, which is exactly the same de-biasing idea as the augmented regression but delivered as an interval rather than a point estimate. In practice their test disqualifies several predictors that pass a naive t-test, which is the whole point: it prevents the bot from committing capital to a signal whose apparent significance is an artefact of persistence.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the Stambaugh/Kendall idea in both machinery and output: that one produces a bias-corrected POINT estimate and gates on its t-statistic; this one abandons point estimation, produces a joint confidence REGION over (rho, beta), and gates on whether the whole region excludes zero. The two disagree in exactly the cases that matter - a predictor can have a significant bias-corrected slope and still fail the Bonferroni test if rho is poorly pinned down. No rule in the corpus conditions on parameter uncertainty at all.
ideas.source: Campbell, J.Y. and Yogo, M., 'Efficient Tests of Stock Return Predictability', NBER Working Paper 10026 (Oct 2003), published JFE 81, 2006 - read directly at https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w10026/w10026.pdf. The Q-statistic is eq. (9) on p.8; the local-to-unity framework is section 3.1; the use of DF-GLS (Elliott, Rothenberg and Stock) rather than ADF to build the confidence interval for c, and the reason for it, are on pp.523-527 of the text; the Bonferroni construction and the choice of the Q-test over the Bonferroni t-test of Cavanagh, Elliott and Stock (1995) are in section 3.3. The simulation-based inversion of the DF-GLS statistic over a rho grid is my pinning-down of a step the paper implements via published lookup tables.

ideas.name: PLS Supervised Predictor Alignment
ideas.category: return predictability econometrics / supervised dimension reduction
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: Take the same N-predictor OHLCV panel as the combination idea, standardised to zero mean and unit variance using data through t. At each month-end t: (1) FIRST PASS - N time-series regressions. For each predictor i, regress the predictor on the CONTEMPORANEOUSLY-FOLLOWING realised return: x_i,s = pi_i0 + pi_i*r_{s+1} + u_i,s, over all s from the start to t-1. Keep the slope pi_i_hat. This is the step that makes the method supervised: the loading of each predictor is estimated by how it co-moves with the return it is meant to forecast, not by how it co-moves with the other predictors. (2) SECOND PASS - one cross-sectional regression per date. For each date s <= t, regress the N standardised predictor values at that date on the N first-pass loadings: x_i,s = c_s + F_s*pi_i_hat + e_i,s, running the regression ACROSS the N predictors with the loadings as the single regressor. The slope F_s is the aligned factor at date s. (3) THIRD PASS - run the expanding-window predictive regression r_{s+1} = a + b*F_s + e through s = t-1 and form rhat_{t+1} = a_hat + b_hat*F_t. (4) Apply the Campbell-Thompson wrong-sign fallback and zero truncation, then rebalance at the next open to w_t = clip((1/5)*rhat/sigmahat^2, 0, 1.5). CRITICAL BACKTEST CONSTRAINT: the first-pass regressions use r_{s+1}, so they must be re-estimated recursively using ONLY returns realised on or before t; using the full sample here is look-ahead and will manufacture spectacular fake results.
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Hold one month; re-run all three passes on the extended sample and rebalance. w = 0 exits fully.
inputs: N first-pass time-series regressions on future returns
T second-pass cross-sectional regressions on the loadings
params: whether the first pass regresses on r_{s+1} or on a multi-month forward return
ideas.why: Principal components are unsupervised: they extract whatever explains the most variance among the predictors, which is not necessarily what forecasts returns. If the dominant common factor in a predictor panel is a nuisance factor - a common measurement artefact, a shared exposure to something unpriced - PCA will hand you that nuisance factor as the first component and throw away the weak signal. Partial least squares, in Kelly and Pruitt's three-pass form, fixes this by using future returns to discipline the dimension reduction: the first pass instruments each predictor's loading with the very thing being forecast, so the second pass's cross-sectional slope isolates the return-relevant common component and discards common and idiosyncratic pieces that are irrelevant for forecasting. Huang, Jiang, Tu and Zhou demonstrate the size of the difference by rebuilding the Baker-Wurgler sentiment index this way from the same six raw proxies and getting a far stronger predictor from identical inputs.
ideas.novelty: Explicitly distinct from the PC-TECH idea in this same list, and that distinction is the point: same panel, same regression frontend, but PCA maximises explained predictor variance while PLS maximises covariance with the forecast target. They select different linear combinations and will disagree. Beyond that, nothing in the 32 involves any dimension reduction, supervised or otherwise.
ideas.source: Huang, D., Jiang, F., Tu, J. and Zhou, G., 'Investor Sentiment Aligned: A Powerful Predictor of Stock Returns', Review of Financial Studies 28(3), 2015 - read directly at the open working-paper copy https://down.aefweb.net/WorkingPapers/w676.pdf. The two-step OLS implementation of PLS is set out on pp.265-300 of that text: first-pass time-series regression eq. (4), second-pass cross-sectional regression eq. (5), and the closed form eq. (6). The method is attributed there to Wold (1966, 1975) and extended by Kelly and Pruitt (2013, 2014); I did not open the Kelly-Pruitt originals.

ideas.name: Sum-of-the-Parts Multiple Reversion
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: PROXY NOTE UP FRONT: the original method decomposes the index return into dividend yield, earnings growth and price-earnings multiple growth. This bot has no dividends or earnings, so the fundamental anchor is replaced by a long moving average of price - a smoothed-price 'multiple' in the spirit of Campbell-Shiller's smoothed earnings-price ratio, where the 10-year average is doing the work of removing cyclical noise. At each month-end t: (1) Define the multiple m_t = ln(P_t) - ln( (1/120)*sum_{i=0..119} P_{t-i} ), the log ratio of the index level to its 120-month moving average. (2) Define the long-run drift component gd_t = the mean monthly log return of the 120-month moving average series itself over the trailing 240 months - this stands in for expected earnings growth and is assumed near-unforecastable. (3) CONTEMPORANEOUS ANCHOR REGRESSION: regress the multiple on a state variable available at the same time, m_s = a + b*z_s + u_s, where z is an OHLCV-computable state variable (use log RVOL as the base case). Both sides are known at s; this is not a predictive regression. The fitted value says what multiple historically prevailed when the economy looked like this. (4) The residual gives the expected multiple growth: -uhat_t = (a_hat + b_hat*z_t) - m_t. If the index sits above the multiple its state variable historically justified, expect the multiple to fall, and vice versa. (5) REVERSION-SPEED REGRESSION: reversion is slow and does not happen in one month, so regress realised multiple growth on the lagged residual, gm_{s+1} = c + d*uhat_s + v_s, and shrink the slope as d_shrunk = (s/(s+i))*d_hat with the shrinkage factor increasing with sample length (equivalently, set c = -d_shrunk * mean(gm) so the unconditional expected multiple growth is zero). (6) Expected multiple growth E[gm_{t+1}] = c + d_shrunk*uhat_t. (7) SUM THE PARTS: rhat_{t+1} = E[gm_{t+1}] + gd_t. (8) Truncate at zero and rebalance at the next open to w_t = clip((1/5)*rhat/sigmahat^2, 0, 1.5).
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Hold one month; recompute the multiple, refit both regressions, rebalance. w = 0 exits fully. The position decays as the multiple reverts toward its state-conditional anchor rather than on any price trigger.
inputs: a contemporaneous state variable z (log RVOL base case)
params: smoothing window for the anchor (60, 120, 180 months)
choice of state variable z (log RVOL, aggregate illiquidity, avgcor, the Hill tail measure)
shrinkage schedule (the s/(s+i) form, or a fixed factor)
direct multiple-growth predictive regression as an alternative to the reversion route
ideas.why: Ferreira and Santa-Clara's argument is that the standard predictive regression estimates ONE coefficient on ONE noisy left-hand side - the total return, which is dominated by an unforecastable component - and so throws away most of the available structure. Decomposing the return into parts and forecasting each with the method best suited to it uses far more prior information: the near-unforecastable growth term gets a long moving average (no estimation risk), the carry term gets a random walk, and only the genuinely predictable multiple-growth term gets a regression. That means far fewer estimated parameters attached to the noisy part of the return, which is precisely where out-of-sample gains in this literature come from. The multiple-reversion variant adds the further idea that the anchor should be state-conditional: an elevated multiple is not automatically bearish if the current state historically justified an elevated multiple. Their reported result is substantial certainty-equivalent gains over the historical mean on the Goyal-Welch data.
ideas.novelty: The 32 contain mean-reversion rules (Bollinger fade, VWAP z-score) but they all revert to a FIXED statistical band. Here the reversion target is itself a regression fitted value that moves with a state variable, so the same distance above the moving average is bearish in one volatility regime and neutral in another - and the expected reversion is deliberately slowed by an estimated, shrunk speed coefficient rather than assumed to complete in one bar. The additive decomposition of the forecast into a drift part and a reversion part has no analogue in the corpus.
ideas.source: Ferreira, M.A. and Santa-Clara, P., 'Forecasting Stock Market Returns: The Sum of the Parts is More than the Whole', NBER Working Paper 14571 (Dec 2008), published JFE 100(3), 2011 - read directly at https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w14571/w14571.pdf. The decomposition is eqs. (13)-(15), the 20-year moving average for expected earnings growth and the random-walk treatment of the dividend-price ratio are on pp.6-7, and the multiple-reversion route with its contemporaneous anchor regression eq. (17), residual eq. (19), reversion-speed regression eq. (20) and shrinkage eqs. (21)-(23) are on p.7. The substitution of a 120-month moving average of price for the earnings-based multiple is my proxy, flagged as such - it is what makes the rule OHLCV-only, and it is the part most in need of validation.

ideas.name: Live OOS-R-Squared Survivorship Ensemble
ideas.category: return predictability econometrics / real-time predictor selection
ideas.timeframe: daily bars aggregated to monthly; monthly rebalance
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain the same N-predictor OHLCV panel and N recursive univariate predictive regressions as the combination idea. At each month-end t, for each predictor i compute two admission statistics using only data through t: (A) its TRAILING OUT-OF-SAMPLE R-SQUARED under the Campbell-Thompson restrictions, R2CT_i = 1 - sum_{s=t-119..t}(r_s - rhatCT_i,s-1)^2 / sum_{s=t-119..t}(r_s - rbar_{s-1})^2, where rhatCT is that predictor's zero-truncated, wrong-sign-corrected recursive forecast and rbar is the prevailing mean; and (B) the absolute Newey-West t-statistic (12 lags) of its slope over the full sample through t. ADMISSION RULE: predictor i enters this month's ensemble only if R2CT_i > 0 AND |t_i| > 3.0. The 3.0 threshold, rather than the conventional 2.0, is deliberate - a higher bar is what separates predictors that survive out of sample from those that do not. Form rhat_ENS = the equal-weighted mean of the admitted predictors' rhatCT_i,t+1. If NO predictor is admitted, set rhat_ENS = max(prevailing mean, 0) and hold the benchmark allocation. Rebalance at the next open to w_t = clip((1/5)*rhat_ENS/sigmahat^2, 0, 1.5).
ideas.exit_rule: No stop, no target. Hold one month; recompute both admission statistics for every predictor, re-form the admitted set, and rebalance. A predictor is silently dropped from the ensemble the month its trailing out-of-sample R-squared turns negative or its t-statistic falls below the threshold, and re-admitted when both recover - so exposure changes because the composition of the committee changed, with no price trigger involved.
params: admission logic: both conditions vs either
whether to equal-weight or DMSPE-weight the admitted set
ideas.why: Goyal, Welch and Zafirov re-tested 29 predictors published after 2008 with data extended to 2021 and found more than a third had lost in-sample significance entirely; of the 10 that survived a common homologous specification, only 4 also showed good Campbell-Thompson out-of-sample performance. Their diagnostic on threshold choice is the operative finding: of all 29 variables only 31% improved their t-statistic with more data, but restricting to those with original t above 3.0 raises that to 40%, above 3.5 to 43%, and at 4.0 two of three improved. A higher admission bar genuinely predicts forward survival. Combining that with the demand for a positive trailing out-of-sample R-squared gives a selection rule that is a live re-run of the audit rather than a one-time backtest choice - which matters because the alternative, freezing a predictor set chosen on a full-sample backtest, is exactly the selection bias the whole literature is warning about.
ideas.novelty: Distinct from the CumSSE gate, which switches one model on and off wholesale; here the model's MEMBERSHIP changes continuously and the surviving members are re-averaged, so exposure can move while every individual predictor's reading is unchanged. Distinct from the plain combination idea, which never drops anyone. No rule in the corpus has a candidate pool with admission and expulsion criteria based on the candidates' own forecast track records.
ideas.source: Goyal, A., Welch, I. and Zafirov, A., 'A Comprehensive 2022 Look at the Empirical Performance of Equity Premium Prediction', Review of Financial Studies 37(11), 2024, 3490-3557 - read directly at the copy posted on Amit Goyal's site. The survivor counts and the four post-2008 variables passing both in-sample and OOSCT tests (tchi, shtint, accrul, gpce) plus tby, i/k, eqis and the forward-only ogap, tail, avgcor are on pp.3491-3492; the t-statistic threshold diagnostic (31% / 36% / 39% / 40% / 43% at thresholds of none / 2.0 / 2.5 / 3.0 / 3.5) is on p.3492, citing Harvey, Liu and Zhu (2016) for the higher-threshold recommendation. The OOSCT restriction is Campbell and Thompson (2008), read directly as cited above. Converting the audit into a live admission rule is my synthesis.

ideas.name: Patell Standardized Residual Reversion
inputs: daily OHLCV of SPY as market proxy
ideas.entry_rule: Fit OLS market model r_i,s = a + b*r_SPY,s over the estimation window of the 250 daily sessions ending 21 sessions before today (window [-270,-21], disjoint from the event window). Record s = residual standard error, M = 250, Rm_bar = mean SPY return in the window, SS = sum of squared deviations of SPY return in the window, and R2 = regression R-squared. Today's abnormal return AR = r_i,today - (a + b*r_SPY,today). Patell prediction-error standard deviation S = s * sqrt(1 + 1/M + (r_SPY,today - Rm_bar)^2 / SS). Standardized abnormal return SAR = AR / S. LONG at the next session's open when SAR <= -3.0 AND |r_SPY,today| <= 0.010 AND R2 >= 0.05. SHORT at the next session's open when SAR >= +3.0 under the same two side conditions.
ideas.exit_rule: Freeze a and b at entry. Each subsequent session accumulate CAR = sum of daily AR since entry. Exit at the next open after the first session on which CAR crosses back through 0 in the favourable direction (CAR >= 0 for longs, CAR <= 0 for shorts). Hard time exit at the close of the 10th session held. Hard stop when CAR reaches -8% (longs) or +8% (shorts).
ideas.why: Patell's standardization divides by the FORECAST error, not the fitted residual sd: the (r_m - Rm_bar)^2/SS term inflates the denominator on days when the market itself is far from its estimation-window mean, so the same raw move counts as a smaller surprise on a wild market day. What survives a -3 SAR filter is therefore genuinely idiosyncratic, not a beta-driven or vol-regime artefact. Idiosyncratic price shocks that carry no market component are largely liquidity events - a forced seller paying for immediacy - and the compensation to the immediacy provider is the reversion over the following days.
ideas.source: Kothari & Warner, 'Econometrics of Event Studies', Handbook of Corporate Finance vol. A ch.1 (2006) - read the full PDF directly (bu.edu/econ/files/2011/01/KothariWarner2.pdf); return decomposition eqs (1)-(2), CAR eq (4), test statistic eqs (5)-(6). Patell (1976) standardized-residual formula S^2_AR = s^2[1 + 1/M + (Rm0-Rm_bar)^2/sum(Rmt-Rm_bar)^2] as documented at https://eventstudytools.com/significance-tests.
ideas.novelty: The trigger is a regression residual standardized by the prediction error, not a price z-score or an oscillator: it removes the market component AND widens the bar when the market itself was extreme. The exit is also stated in abnormal-return space (CAR crossing zero with beta frozen at entry), so the position closes when the event has been undone relative to the market, not when a price level is touched.

ideas.name: Corrado Rank Event Trigger
inputs: rank of residual within trailing window
ideas.entry_rule: Each day compute the market-model abnormal return AR_s over a rolling 250-session estimation window ending yesterday, then form the 251-value series {AR of the 250 estimation sessions, AR of today}. Rank today's AR within that series ascending (rank 1 = most negative) and set the Corrado rank score K_t = rank_t / 252. LONG at tomorrow's open when K_t <= 1/252 (today is the single most negative abnormal return of the last 251 sessions) AND today's volume >= 2x the 50-session median volume. SHORT at tomorrow's open when K_t >= 251/252 under the same volume condition.
ideas.exit_rule: Recompute K_t each session for the held name. Exit at the next open after K_t has been inside [0.25, 0.75] for two consecutive sessions (the symbol has returned to its own normal-return regime). Hard time exit at 15 sessions. No price stop - the rank state is the stop, since a further extreme in the adverse direction keeps K outside the band and is handled by the time exit.
ideas.why: The Corrado rank statistic is distribution-free: it assumes only exchangeability under the null, requires no normality and no symmetry, and is not distorted by event-induced variance - precisely the three failure modes that make a fixed sigma threshold misfire. 'Most extreme day in a year' is a scale-free event definition that self-calibrates to each symbol's own volatility regime, so the same rule works on a 15%-vol utility and a 90%-vol biotech without re-tuning. Kothari & Warner explicitly recommend the non-parametric route when event-period uncertainty inflates variance.
ideas.source: Corrado (1989) rank test, K_i,t = rank(AR_i,t)/(1 + M_i + L_2), z = (K_bar_0 - 0.5)/S_Kbar, documented with the full formula at https://eventstudytools.com/significance-tests. Recommended in Kothari & Warner (2006) footnote 6: non-parametric tests as in Corrado (1989) may be effective for well-specified tests under increased event-period uncertainty.
ideas.novelty: Both the entry and the exit are expressed as rank percentiles of the residual distribution rather than as sigma multiples or price levels, so the strategy has no volatility-scaling parameter at all. It is a different statistic from the Patell trigger, not a different threshold on the same statistic: rank is invariant to the shape of the residual distribution.

ideas.name: Beaver Dual-Criterion Information Event
ideas.entry_rule: Over the 250-session estimation window ending 21 sessions ago, fit the market model and record residual standard error s, the median volume med_V and the median absolute deviation MAD_V of volume. For today compute (a) Beaver's variance U-statistic U_t = AR_t^2 / s^2 and (b) robust abnormal volume V_t = (volume_t - med_V) / (1.4826 * MAD_V). Declare an information event when U_t >= 9.0 (equivalently |AR_t| >= 3s) AND V_t >= 5.0. Enter at the next session's open in the SIGN of AR_t: long if AR_t > 0, short if AR_t < 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold for 40 sessions. Exit early at the next open after the cumulative abnormal return since the event day retraces 50% of the event-day AR against the position (for a long, CAR_since_event <= 0.5 * AR_0; for a short, CAR_since_event >= 0.5 * AR_0). Otherwise exit at the close of session +40.
ideas.why: Beaver (1968) established that the information content of an announcement shows up in BOTH the return variance and trading volume, and that the two carry different information: price moves without volume are noise or a single uninformed print, volume without price is disagreement, and the conjunction is the signature of a genuine information release that a heterogeneous investor base is still absorbing. Requiring both raises the true-event rate sharply, and post-event drift is documented for real information events but not for noise shocks. Directional sign comes from the residual, so the trade is a drift trade on a verified event rather than a momentum trade on any move.
ideas.source: Beaver (1968) 'The Information Content of Annual Earnings Announcements' - the variance and volume U-statistics; cited in Kothari & Warner (2006) footnote 1 as the origin of event studies on return variances and trading volume (alongside Patell 1976 and Campbell & Wasley 1996). Variance-ratio adjustment for event-period volatility discussed in Kothari & Warner sec. 3.3.
ideas.novelty: A two-dimensional event definition - a residual-variance ratio AND a robust (median/MAD) volume z, both measured against the same regression estimation window - and a trade direction taken from the sign of the regression residual rather than from any trend, channel or oscillator state. The exit is a retracement of the abnormal return, measured in units of the event-day residual.

ideas.name: Silent Accumulation: Abnormal Volume with Zero Abnormal Return
inputs: daily OHLCV of SPY (price and volume)
OLS regression on log volume with day-of-week dummies
ideas.entry_rule: Fit a volume market model by OLS over the trailing 250 sessions: ln(1 + volume_i,s) = c + d*ln(1 + volume_SPY,s) + g1*Mon + g2*Tue + g3*Thu + g4*Fri + e_s. Abnormal log volume AV_s = e_s / (residual standard error of that regression). Separately compute SAR_s from the return market model (as in the Patell rule). Enter LONG at the next open when AV_t >= 2.5 AND AV_{t-1} >= 2.5 AND AV_{t-2} >= 2.5 AND max(|SAR_t|, |SAR_{t-1}|, |SAR_{t-2}|) <= 0.5 AND the trailing 20-session total return is between -5% and +5%.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next open after the first session with |SAR| >= 2.0 in either direction (the information has printed - book the move either way). Otherwise exit at the close of the 30th session held. Hard stop at -6% from the entry fill.
ideas.why: Volume carries information that price does not. Sustained abnormal volume with essentially zero abnormal return is the footprint of a patient, size-constrained buyer working an order over days with explicit instructions not to move the price - a VWAP/participation programme, an index pre-position, or an accumulating block. The price impact is being deliberately suppressed, not absent; when the programme completes or the underlying news is released, the suppressed impact is realised. Removing market-wide volume (which is highly seasonal and macro-driven) and day-of-week effects is what makes a three-day run of +2.5 sigma volume meaningful rather than a Friday-expiry artefact.
ideas.source: Volume market-model approach of Ajinkya & Jain and Campbell & Wasley (1996), cited in Kothari & Warner (2006) footnote 1 as the standard for trading-volume event studies; the log-volume specification with calendar dummies follows the same normal-return decomposition as Kothari & Warner eq. (1), applied to volume instead of return. Stephens & Weisbach (1998) (abstract via OpenAlex) document that firm buying is price-insensitive and concentrated after declines, one concrete instance of such a programme.
ideas.novelty: The entry requires HIGH abnormal volume together with LOW abnormal return - the conjunction is the whole signal, and it is the exact inverse of every volume rule in the existing set, all of which pair high volume with a price move. It also uses a regression-residual definition of abnormal volume (net of market volume and day-of-week) rather than a ratio to a moving average.

ideas.name: Cross-Sectional Clustering Gate
inputs: daily OHLCV of the whole tradable universe
ideas.entry_rule: Each session compute SAR_i,t (Patell-standardized market-model residual, 250-session estimation window ending 21 sessions back) for EVERY symbol in the tradable universe. Let f_neg,t = fraction of the universe with SAR_i,t <= -2.0 and f_pos,t = fraction with SAR_i,t >= +2.0. Take a long reversion entry in symbol i at the next open only when SAR_i,t <= -2.5 AND f_neg,t <= 0.10; take a short reversion entry only when SAR_i,t >= +2.5 AND f_pos,t <= 0.10. On any session where the relevant fraction exceeds 0.10, open no new positions on that side at all, regardless of how extreme the individual SAR is.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the next open after CAR since entry (beta frozen at entry) crosses zero in the favourable direction, or at the close of the 10th session held, whichever first. Additionally, force-flatten every open position on the first session where the same-sign fraction f exceeds 0.25 - the regime has become macro and the idiosyncratic thesis is void.
ideas.why: Kothari & Warner devote a section to exactly this problem: event-time clustering breaks the cross-sectional independence assumption, biases the standard-error estimate downward and the test statistic upward, so a clustered sample produces spurious significance. Kolari & Pynnonen's correction multiplies the statistic by sqrt((1-rbar)/(1+(N-1)rbar)), which collapses toward zero as cross-correlation rises. Economically the same point: a -3 sigma day when 40% of the universe is also down 2 sigma is a factor move that will not revert idiosyncratically; a -3 sigma day when nothing else moved is a firm-specific liquidity event that will. The gate converts an econometric correction into a trade filter.
ideas.source: Kothari & Warner (2006) sec. 3.3 on event-time clustering, cross-sectional dependence and the downward-biased standard error (citing Collins & Dent 1984, Bernard 1987, Petersen 2005) - read directly from the PDF. Kolari & Pynnonen (2010) adjusted Patell Z, z_adj = z*sqrt((1-rbar)/(1+(N-1)rbar)), documented at https://eventstudytools.com/significance-tests.
ideas.novelty: The gate is a cross-sectional census of the entire universe on that session, not a single-symbol indicator - the same bar in the same symbol is tradable or not depending on what the other several hundred symbols did that day. Nothing in the existing set conditions on how many other names fired the same signal simultaneously, and it also supplies a portfolio-level force-flatten rule.

ideas.name: Clean-Event Isolation Drift
ideas.entry_rule: Flag an event day 0 when |SAR_0| >= 2.5 (Patell-standardized market-model residual, 250-session estimation window ending 21 sessions back). The event qualifies as CLEAN only if BOTH: (a) no session in [-60,-1] had |SAR| >= 2.0, and (b) the symbol's count of |SAR| >= 2.5 sessions over the trailing 250 sessions is <= 3. On a clean event, enter at the OPEN of session +2 - deliberately skipping session +1 - in the direction of the sign of AR_0 (long if AR_0 > 0, short if AR_0 < 0).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of session +60 relative to the event day. Exit early and immediately at the next open if a second event with |SAR| >= 2.5 of the OPPOSITE sign to AR_0 occurs while the position is open (a confounding event voids the thesis). Hard stop at 15% adverse from the entry fill.
ideas.why: An event study is only interpretable when the event window is uncontaminated: a sample in which half the firms had another announcement inside the window washes out whatever drift exists in the clean half. Trading only the clean subset concentrates the drift instead of averaging it away. The rarity condition (at most 3 big days a year) further selects names whose returns are normally quiet, so a 2.5-sigma day is far more likely to be a genuine one-off corporate event than a routine feature of a habitually jumpy stock. Skipping session +1 handles the event-date uncertainty Kothari & Warner discuss - the release may land after the close, so which session is 'day 0' is ambiguous by one - and also avoids the bid-ask bounce that dominates the session immediately after a shock.
ideas.source: Kothari & Warner (2006), section 3 on confounding events and event-date uncertainty, and the discussion of why multi-day windows such as (-1,+1) or (0,+1) are the convention when the announcement timestamp is uncertain; window conventions also documented at https://eventstudytools.com/expected-return-models (estimation window 120-250 days, disjoint from the event window, with a buffer gap to prevent pre-event leakage).
ideas.novelty: The entry requires an ABSENCE of other events over a two-month lookback plus a low annual event count - a rarity condition on the symbol's own event history, which is the opposite of the usual 'more signal is better' construction. The deliberate one-session entry delay is part of the rule rather than a slippage assumption.

ideas.name: Calendar-Time Event Cohort Portfolio
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain a fixed-size rolling cohort of N = 20 slots. On any session, every symbol whose SAR <= -3.0 (or, for the short book, SAR >= +3.0) becomes a candidate. Fill empty slots with candidates ranked by |SAR| descending, one slot each, entering at the next open with a target weight of 1/N of the sleeve's capital. If no slot is free, evict the member whose own event date is oldest and take the new candidate in its place. Every Friday at the close, rebalance all current members back to exactly 1/N of current sleeve equity (trim winners, add to losers).
ideas.exit_rule: A member leaves the cohort exactly T = 60 sessions after ITS OWN event date, at that session's close, regardless of price, P&L or any indicator. There is no price stop and no profit target at the position level. The only position-level exit is the elapsed-time clock; risk is controlled at the sleeve level by the equal-weight cap and the fixed slot count.
ideas.why: This is the Jensen-alpha / calendar-time portfolio design turned into a live trading rule. The literature adopted it precisely because averaging CARs across firms whose event windows overlap in calendar time produces cross-sectionally correlated observations and inflated test statistics; forming one portfolio per calendar day and studying its time series instead makes the dependence disappear into the portfolio return. The practical consequence is that this sleeve's own realised equity curve IS the alpha estimate - there is no separate statistical step and no way to fool yourself with overlapping windows. The Friday equal-weight rebalance additionally harvests dispersion between cohort members mechanically.
ideas.source: Kothari & Warner (2006), sec. 4.3.2 'Jensen-alpha approach (calendar-time portfolio)': in each calendar month a portfolio is formed of all firms experiencing the event within the previous T months, rebalanced as firms enter and exit, and the time series is regressed as Rpt - Rft = ap + bp(Rmt-Rft) + sp*SMB + hp*HML + mp*UMD + ept (eq. 8). Introduced by Jaffe (1974) and Mandelker (1974); advocated by Fama (1998) and Mitchell & Stafford (2000).
ideas.novelty: A position-level exit driven purely by an elapsed-time clock anchored to that position's own event date, with overlapping cohorts and a periodic equal-weight rebalance at the sleeve level. Every strategy in the existing set exits on a price condition or an indicator flip; none has a portfolio-level, calendar-only exit with slot eviction.

ideas.name: Constant-Notional CAR Replication
ideas.entry_rule: On any event trigger - use SAR <= -3.0 for the long book and SAR >= +3.0 for the short book as the reference trigger - open a position of a FIXED notional X at the next session's open (shares = round(X / open price)).
ideas.exit_rule: This is the whole point of the idea: at every subsequent session's close, rebalance the position back to exactly X of notional - sell shares if the position has appreciated, buy shares if it has depreciated - so the dollar exposure is held constant instead of being allowed to compound. Continue for T = 40 sessions and then close out entirely at the close of session T. Abort the whole position, no rebalance, if cumulative realised-plus-unrealised loss on the sleeve reaches 0.25X.
ideas.why: Barber & Lyon (1997) and Kothari & Warner make the point that CAR (the sum of daily abnormal returns) and BHAR (the compounded product) are not two estimators of one number - they are the payoffs to two different trading rules. CAR is what a constant-dollar, daily-rebalanced position earns; BHAR is what a buy-and-hold earns. When post-event returns are positively skewed - which the long-horizon literature says they are - the buy-and-hold payoff is dominated by a handful of outliers and the median outcome is poor, whereas the constant-dollar version captures the mean drift and, by selling into strength and buying into weakness daily, additionally harvests path noise. Turning the CAR/BHAR distinction into a position-management choice is a directly testable question: which of the two payoffs is actually bigger for our events, after costs.
ideas.source: Kothari & Warner (2006) sec. 4.3.1, BHAR definition eq. (7): BHAR_i(t,T) = product(1+R_i,t) - product(1+R_B,t), and their explicit statement (sec. 3.2, following eq. 4) that the CAR measure equals the return to a trading rule that buys at the start of the first period and holds to the end of the last, versus the periodic (monthly) rebalancing entailed in the alternative approaches. Barber & Lyon (1997) and Lyon, Barber & Tsai (1999) 'Measuring long-horizon security price performance' (abstract via OpenAlex) on the misspecification of the compounded version.
ideas.novelty: The exit is a daily notional-reset schedule rather than a price level, an indicator state or a trailing stop - the position is continuously resized against its own P&L. It converts an econometric distinction (CAR vs BHAR) into an executable position-management rule, and it can be layered on top of any event trigger in the corpus as an A/B against plain buy-and-hold.
params: rebalance deadband (0% / 2% / 5% of X before trading)

ideas.name: Deal-Pinned Target Spread Convergence
ideas.entry_rule: Day-0 candidate: open_0/close_-1 - 1 >= +0.12 AND volume_0 >= 5x the median volume of sessions -50..-1 AND close_0 >= 0.95*high_0. Set the implied deal ceiling P* = max(high) over sessions 0..+5. Confirm the PINNED STATE over sessions +1..+20, requiring all three: (a) realised volatility of daily log closes over +1..+20 <= 0.35x the realised volatility over -60..-1; (b) |OLS beta of daily returns to SPY estimated over +1..+20| <= 0.15; (c) every close in +1..+20 lies inside [0.85*P*, 1.02*P*]. If the pinned state holds, enter LONG at the first close on or after session +21 at which close <= 0.97*P*.
ideas.exit_rule: Take profit when close >= 0.995*P*. Deal-break stop: exit at the next open after any session whose close < 0.90*P* AND whose volume >= 3x its 50-session median. Time exit after 180 sessions in the position (deals that drag past that are regulatory hostages). Re-arm the setup only after a fresh day-0 candidate.
ideas.why: Once a cash acquisition is announced the target detaches from the market: its price is a claim on a fixed cash amount contingent on closing, so its idiosyncratic volatility collapses, its market beta collapses toward zero, and it trades in a narrow band capped by the offer. The residual spread is compensation for deal-break risk and for the arbitrageur's capital being tied up, and it converges mechanically as the closing date approaches. Mitchell & Pulvino, over 4,750 mergers from 1963 to 1998, find risk-arbitrage returns are uncorrelated with the market in flat and rising tapes but correlated in severely falling ones - a written-put payoff - and estimate roughly 4% per year of excess return after transaction costs. The bar signature used here (huge gap on huge volume, closing at the high, then a joint collapse of variance AND beta with the price capped) is the observable fingerprint of exactly that state, so no news feed is required.
ideas.source: Mitchell & Pulvino (2001) 'Characteristics of Risk and Return in Risk Arbitrage', Journal of Finance - abstract retrieved verbatim via the OpenAlex API (4,750 mergers 1963-1998; returns like selling uncovered index puts; ~4% per year excess after transaction costs). Deal-break base rates from Baker & Savasoglu (2002) - 22.7% break rate over 1,901 mergers 1981-1996 - and the 8.0% break rate over 2,182 mergers 1990-2007, both as summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk_arbitrage, which also documents the hostile (38%) versus friendly (82%) completion split.
ideas.novelty: Identifies an announced acquisition target from OHLCV alone through a JOINT variance-and-beta collapse underneath a reconstructed price ceiling, then trades the convergence of a bounded, capped payoff. There is nothing directional about it - it is the first capped-payoff convergence trade in the corpus, and the reference level (P*) is a reconstructed deal price rather than a moving average, channel or pivot.

ideas.name: Deal-Break Breakdown Short
inputs: true range and ATR over the pinned window
ideas.entry_rule: Take any symbol currently in the PINNED STATE defined in the deal-spread rule (realised-vol ratio to the pre-event window <= 0.35, |beta to SPY| <= 0.15, and all closes inside [0.85*P*, 1.02*P*] for at least 15 consecutive sessions, where P* is the post-announcement ceiling). Enter SHORT at the next session's open after the first session that satisfies ALL of: close < 0.93*P*; volume >= 3x its 50-session median; true range >= 3x the average true range measured over the pinned window only.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover at whichever comes first: (a) close <= 0.70*P*; (b) 20 sessions elapsed; (c) stop-out at the next open after any close > 0.97*P* (the deal has been re-affirmed or a competing bid has appeared and the short is on the wrong side of a capped-upside instrument).
ideas.why: The negatively skewed, put-like payoff that Mitchell & Pulvino document has a left tail with a specific mechanism: when a deal breaks, the target must reprice from the offer back to its standalone value in one or two sessions, and the entire arbitrage community - which is levered and mandated to exit on a break - unwinds into the same tape. The pinned state makes the break unusually clean to detect because the volatility was artificially suppressed by the deal, not by genuine calm: an ATR measured inside the pinned window is a very low bar, so a 3x-ATR range day with 3x volume is a decisive regime change rather than ordinary noise. Break rates in the literature are material - 8% to 22.7% depending on sample and era, and far higher for hostile deals - so the setup recurs.
ideas.source: Mitchell & Pulvino (2001) on the put-like, negatively skewed return profile of risk arbitrage (maximum monthly gains ~2.9% against losses beyond -6.5%), as summarised at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risk_arbitrage; Baker & Savasoglu (2002) 22.7% break rate over 1,901 mergers 1981-1996; hostile deals complete only 38% of the time versus 82% for friendly.
ideas.novelty: Shorts a break out of an ARTIFICIALLY compressed volatility regime whose cause of compression has been positively identified, with the reference level a reconstructed deal price and the range threshold calibrated on the compressed window itself. It is the mirror of the convergence trade but with a completely different exit structure - a target defined as a fraction of the deal price, and a stop that fires on the price going UP, which is unusual for a short.

ideas.name: Forward-Split Ex-Date Continuation
ideas.entry_rule: Request the same symbol's daily bars twice from the same OHLCV endpoint - once raw and once split-adjusted - and form the split adjustment factor F_s = raw_close_s / split_adjusted_close_s. Let k_t = F_t / F_{t-1}; the implied forward-split ratio is R = 1/k_t (verified algebraically: a 2:1 split gives k = 0.5 and R = 2; a 3:1 gives k = 0.3333 and R = 3). A forward-split ex-date is any session with k_t <= 0.70 (R >= 1.43). Require additionally: the symbol's trailing 250-session return >= +30% AND its split-adjusted close on the ex-date >= its 200-session moving average. Enter LONG at the close of the ex-date session.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 60th session after the ex-date. Exit early on a -10% stop from the entry fill, or when the split-adjusted close is below the 50-session moving average for two consecutive sessions.
ideas.why: A split is a discretionary management action taken only after a large run-up and only when management is confident the price will not fall straight back through the pre-split range - which is why it is the canonical signalling event and why Fama, Fisher, Jensen & Roll chose it for the first modern event study. The documented post-split abnormal drift, plus the mechanical improvements in retail accessibility, round-lot affordability and option-strike granularity that follow a split, give a continuation edge over the following quarter. The run-up and 200-day filters restrict the sample to the confident-management case rather than the mechanical-price-level case.
ideas.source: Fama, Fisher, Jensen & Roll (1969) - the founding split event study, whose table layout Kothari & Warner (2006, sec. 2.2) note that every event study still copies. Ikenberry, Rankine & Stice (1996) 'What Do Stock Splits Really Signal?', JFQA, on post-split-announcement drift. Detection method is a synthesis: derived from the Alpaca bars `adjustment` parameter and verified numerically (see algebra above).
ideas.novelty: Derives an exact corporate-action calendar - date AND ratio - from the divergence between two adjustment versions of the same bar series, so no corporate-action feed is needed at all. Nothing in the existing set uses the adjustment factor as an input, and the trade is conditioned on the prior-state variables that make the signal informative rather than on the split alone.

ideas.name: Reverse-Split Ex-Date Delayed Short
ideas.entry_rule: Using the same factor F_s = raw_close_s / split_adjusted_close_s and k_t = F_t/F_{t-1}, a reverse-split ex-date is any session with k_t >= 1.40 (the implied reverse ratio is k_t itself: a 1-for-10 reverse gives k = 10). Require additionally: the symbol's trailing 250-session split-adjusted return <= -50% AND the median RAW close over the 20 sessions preceding the ex-date < $5.00. Enter SHORT at the close of the session AFTER the ex-date - one full session of delay is part of the rule.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover at the close of the 60th session after entry. Cover early on a +25% stop from the entry fill, or immediately at the next open if the split-adjusted close exceeds the ex-date session's split-adjusted high.
ideas.why: A reverse split is almost never a discretionary signal of confidence: it is a listing-compliance action taken by a company whose share price has fallen below an exchange minimum, and it is very often the precursor to further dilutive issuance because the higher nominal price restores the ability to issue. Multiplying the price by ten changes nothing about the dilution path, and documented post-reverse-split returns are strongly negative. The deliberate one-session delay is the crux: reverse-split day itself frequently produces a sharp squeeze, because shares outstanding drop by the split factor overnight, existing borrow is recalled and re-established, and short interest as a percentage of float is mechanically distorted. Waiting one session lets that mechanical squeeze exhaust.
ideas.source: Ikenberry, Rankine & Stice (1996) on the signalling content of splits (the reverse-split literature is its mirror image); Kim, Klein & Rosenfeld (2008) 'Return Performance Surrounding Reverse Stock Splits' on post-reverse-split underperformance. Detection method is a synthesis from the Alpaca bars `adjustment` parameter, verified numerically.
ideas.novelty: Same raw-versus-adjusted detection primitive as the forward-split rule but with the opposite sign, a different qualifying population (sub-$5 raw price, heavy prior decline) and an explicit one-session entry delay written into the rule to sidestep a known mechanical squeeze - a distinct entry-timing structure, not a threshold flip.

ideas.name: Ex-Dividend Overshoot Reversal
inputs: 1-minute bars on the ex-date for the intraday stop
ideas.entry_rule: Form the cash-distribution factor F_s = split_adjusted_close_s / fully_adjusted_close_s (using split-adjusted as the numerator isolates cash distributions from splits). Let k_t = F_t/F_{t-1}. An ex-dividend session is any session with 0.9800 <= k_t < 0.9995, and the implied dividend per share is D = split_adjusted_close_{t-1} * (1 - k_t) (verified: a $0.50 dividend on a $100 prior close gives k = 0.9950 and D = 0.50). Require D / split_adjusted_close_{t-1} >= 0.004. On the ex-date, BUY at the open when open_t <= close_{t-1} - 1.5*D.
ideas.exit_rule: Sell at the close of the same ex-date session. Intraday hard stop: exit immediately if the price trades at or below close_{t-1} - 4.0*D (monitored on 1-minute bars). No overnight hold under any circumstance.
ideas.why: The theoretical ex-day price drop is exactly the dividend, but the empirical drop is systematically SMALLER. Bali & Hite show that because prices move in discrete ticks while dividends are essentially continuous, the expected price drop is strictly less than the dividend though within one tick of it, producing a price-drop-to-dividend ratio below one with a characteristic sawtooth in the data; the tax-clientele literature (Elton & Gruber) reaches the same sign by a different route. An opening print already down 1.5x the dividend is therefore a mechanical overshoot by ex-date liquidity-driven sellers rather than an efficient reprice, and the documented tendency is for it to be recovered within the session. Measuring the entry threshold in units of D rather than in ATR or percent is what makes the rule scale-correct across yields.
ideas.source: Bali & Hite (1998) 'Ex dividend day stock price behavior: discreteness or tax-induced clienteles?', JFE - abstract retrieved verbatim via the OpenAlex API: the expected price drop is strictly less than the dividend but within one tick, the price-drop-to-dividend ratio is less than one and shows a sawtooth pattern. Elton & Gruber tax-clientele literature on the same ratio. Ex-date and dividend-amount detection is a synthesis using the Alpaca bars `adjustment` parameter, verified numerically.
ideas.novelty: Reconstructs the exact ex-date AND the exact dividend amount from the divergence between two adjustment versions of the same bars, then trades a same-day mean reversion whose entry threshold, stop and target are all denominated in multiples of the dividend rather than in ATR, percent or standard deviations. No existing rule uses a corporate-action quantity as its unit of measurement.
params: overshoot multiple for entry (1.2/1.5/2.0 x D)

ideas.name: IPO Lockup-Expiration Supply Shock
inputs: the date of the symbol's FIRST available daily bar
ideas.entry_rule: Let L0 be the calendar date of the symbol's first available daily bar, and require that the symbol's total bar history is fewer than 400 sessions (so the first bar really is the listing, not the start of the data vendor's coverage). Compute the lockup date LD = L0 + 180 calendar days, mapped forward to the next trading session if it falls on a holiday or weekend. Require: total return from L0's close to the close 10 sessions before LD >= +20%; 20-session average dollar volume >= $5,000,000. Enter SHORT at the close of the 3rd trading session before LD.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover at the close of the 1st trading session after LD (a five-session window in total). Hard stop at +8% from the entry fill. No re-entry on the same symbol.
ideas.why: Lockup expiration is the cleanest supply shock in equities: the date is fully known in advance from the prospectus, nothing is learned on the day, and yet the price falls and volume jumps. Bradley, Jordan, Roten & Yi document a 1%-3% drop in the stock price and a 40% increase in volume when the lockup ends, and note the event is completely anticipated and observable - a downward-sloping demand curve for shares, not an information event. Field & Hanka reach the same conclusion and find the effect concentrated where insiders have the largest realised gains, which is why the run-up filter is used: the prior return is the OHLCV-observable proxy for insider incentive to sell.
ideas.source: Field & Hanka (2001) 'The Expiration of IPO Share Lockups', Journal of Finance. Bradley, Jordan, Roten & Yi (2001) 'The IPO Lock-Up Period: Implications for Market Efficiency and Downward Sloping Demand Curves' - abstract retrieved verbatim via the OpenAlex API: 'even though the event is totally anticipated, there is a 1%-3% drop in the stock price, and a 40% increase in volume, when the lock-up ends'.
ideas.novelty: The entire event calendar is derived from the LENGTH AND START of the price history itself - the date of the first bar - with no listing feed, prospectus or corporate-action data. Nothing in the existing set uses the age of the series as an input, and this is the only rule in the corpus that trades a date known with certainty in advance rather than a price condition.

ideas.name: Post-Lockup High-Flyer Fade
inputs: date of the first available daily bar
ideas.entry_rule: Using the same construction (L0 = date of first daily bar, history < 400 sessions, LD = L0 + 180 calendar days mapped to the next trading session), require the cumulative return from L0's close to LD's close >= +100%. Enter SHORT at the close of the 5th trading session AFTER LD - deliberately letting the mechanical expiration-window drop pass first.
ideas.exit_rule: Cover at the close of the 120th session after entry. Hard stop at +30% from the entry fill. Exit early if the price closes below 40% of the LD close (target reached, no reason to hold the residual).
ideas.why: Different mechanism and different horizon from the expiration-window trade. Ofek & Richardson argue that before the lockup expires, short-sale constraints plus heterogeneous beliefs let the most optimistic holders set the price with no offsetting supply from pessimists; the expiration is a loosening of that constraint, and they document average long-run excess returns as low as -33% for the high-flyer cohort post-lockup. This is a slow repricing over months, not a one-day supply shock, so the entry deliberately skips the expiration window and the horizon is a full two quarters. The +100% run-up filter is the OHLCV-observable proxy for exactly the high-dispersion, constraint-binding population their mechanism describes.
ideas.source: Ofek & Richardson (2003) 'DotCom Mania: The Rise and Fall of Internet Stock Prices', Journal of Finance - abstract retrieved verbatim via the OpenAlex API: 'arguing that lockup expirations are a loosening of the short sale constraint, we document average, long-run excess returns as low as -33 percent for Internet stocks postlockup'. Field & Hanka (2001) for the lockup-date convention.
ideas.novelty: Same event-date derivation as the supply-shock rule but a completely different economic mechanism (belief-dispersion repricing rather than order-flow pressure), a deliberately delayed entry that skips the window the other rule trades, and a horizon two orders of magnitude longer. The two rules can be run simultaneously on the same symbol without being the same bet.

ideas.name: Index-Rebalance Effective-Close Pressure Reversal
ideas.entry_rule: Define rebalance-effective sessions from the calendar alone: the third Friday of March, June, September and December (S&P quarterly share-count and float rebalance, effective at that close) and the last Friday of June (Russell annual reconstitution, effective at that close).
