On such a session t compute RV = volume_t / median(volume over t-50..t-1), the session return r_t = close_t/close_{t-1} - 1, and CLV = (close_t - low_t)/(high_t - low_t). ADDITION leg: SHORT at the open of t+1 when RV >= 4 AND r_t >= +0.03 AND CLV >= 0.90. DELETION leg: LONG at the open of t+1 when RV >= 4 AND r_t <= -0.03 AND CLV <= 0.10.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of session t+10. Exit early when the price has retraced 80% of |r_t| in the favourable direction. Hard stop at 6% adverse from the entry fill. The two legs are sized independently - the deletion leg carries the larger size per the asymmetry finding.
ideas.why: Harris & Gurel found the S&P-change price and volume effects to be pure price pressure, essentially fully reversed within about two weeks - index funds must buy at the effective close regardless of price, and the liquidity providers who accommodate them are paid by the subsequent reversion. Shleifer read the same event as evidence of a permanently downward-sloping demand curve. Chen, Noronha & Singal reconciled the two with an asymmetry: additions' gains are largely permanent while deletions' losses reverse, which is a sharp, testable prediction - the deletion (long) leg should be the stronger of the two, and if it is not, the asymmetry has decayed and the sleeve should be retired. The CLV >= 0.90 condition captures the specific footprint of a non-discretionary buyer executing at the closing cross.
ideas.source: Harris & Gurel (1986) 'Price and Volume Effects Associated with Changes in the S&P 500 List: New Evidence for the Existence of Price Pressures', Journal of Finance 41(4) 815-829 - record confirmed via the OpenAlex API. Shleifer (1986) 'Do Demand Curves for Stocks Slope Down?'. Chen, Noronha & Singal (2004) 'The Price Response to S&P 500 Index Additions and Deletions: Evidence of Asymmetry and a New Explanation', cited at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Index_fund, which also describes index funds' predictable rebalancing and the resulting demand and supply shocks.
ideas.novelty: The event is a fixed CALENDAR date combined with the shape of a single bar (relative volume plus close-location value) - an index membership change inferred from the closing print rather than from any index-membership feed. It also encodes a falsifiable asymmetry between its two legs, so the backtest tests a specific published prediction rather than just a pattern.
params: rebalance dates (S&P quarterly only / plus Russell recon / plus MSCI May-Nov)

ideas.name: Closing-Auction Concentration Reversal
ideas.timeframe: intraday minutes for the signal, daily for the hold
ideas.entry_rule: From 1-minute bars build AS_t = (volume in the final 1-minute bar of the regular session, which contains the closing-cross print) / (total regular-session volume of that day). For a typical liquid US equity AS runs 2%-5%. Compute the day's return r_t = close_t/close_{t-1} - 1. SHORT at the next session's open when AS_t >= 0.20 AND AS_t >= 4x the 50-session median AS AND r_t >= +0.025. LONG at the next session's open when AS_t >= 0.20 AND AS_t >= 4x the 50-session median AS AND r_t <= -0.025.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 5th session held. Exit early when the price has retraced 70% of |r_t| in the favourable direction. Hard stop at 5% adverse from the entry fill. Skip the setup entirely if the following session is itself a scheduled rebalance date (do not fight a second day of the same flow).
ideas.why: A closing auction that takes 20%+ of the day's volume is not price discovery - it is a non-discretionary participant with a benchmark obligation to trade AT the official close: an index fund tracking a rebalance, an ETF creation/redemption, a portfolio-transition mandate or a large market-on-close order. Because the executing party is indifferent to price on that print, the print is displaced from the equilibrium the continuous session was discovering, and the displacement is paid back over the following days as the temporary imbalance clears. This is the same price-pressure mechanism Harris & Gurel identified for index changes, but detected microstructurally rather than by calendar, so it catches unscheduled additions, deletions, ETF flows and transitions that no calendar rule can anticipate.
ideas.source: Harris & Gurel (1986) on index-change price pressure and its ~two-week reversal (record via OpenAlex); the auction-share detection metric is a synthesis - it is the direct microstructural observable of the non-discretionary closing flow that Harris & Gurel infer indirectly from daily volume, and it is computable from the 1-minute bars available on this feed.
ideas.novelty: Uses the intra-session DISTRIBUTION of volume - specifically the share landing in the closing cross - as the event detector, rather than any daily aggregate. Nothing in the existing set looks at where within the session the volume occurred, and this metric identifies the identity of the marginal trader rather than the size of the move.

ideas.name: Open-Market Buyback Execution Footprint
ideas.entry_rule: Over a rolling 20-session window count the sessions B that satisfy ALL THREE: (a) close_s < close_{s-1} (a down session); (b) CLV_s = (close_s - low_s)/(high_s - low_s) >= 0.70 (it nonetheless closed in the top third of its range); (c) volume_s >= 1.2x the 50-session median volume. Enter LONG at the next session's open when B >= 8 AND the symbol's trailing 120-session return <= -0.15 AND its 20-session realised volatility is below its own 250-session median realised volatility.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 60th session held. Exit early at the next open after B has fallen below 3 for five consecutive sessions (the standing bid has been withdrawn - the reason for the position no longer exists). Hard stop at -12% from the entry fill.
ideas.why: An open-market repurchase programme executes as a price-insensitive standing bid, and because 10b-18 safe-harbour conditions cap participation and discourage buying at the high print, the programme's characteristic footprint is buying weakness and lifting the stock off its low into the close, on modestly elevated volume, without chasing. Stephens & Weisbach show firms actually acquire 74%-82% of announced shares within three years and that repurchases are negatively related to prior price performance - the buying really is concentrated after declines. Ikenberry, Lakonishok & Vermaelen document large positive abnormal drift for up to four years after open-market repurchase announcements, concentrated in beaten-down value names - exactly the population this footprint selects. The low-volatility condition separates an absorbing bid from a panic bounce.
ideas.source: Ikenberry, Lakonishok & Vermaelen (1995) 'Market Underreaction to Open Market Share Repurchases', Journal of Financial Economics 39, on the multi-year post-announcement drift concentrated in value firms. Stephens & Weisbach (1998) 'Actual Share Reacquisitions in Open-Market Repurchase Programs', Journal of Finance - abstract retrieved verbatim via the OpenAlex API: firms acquire 74 to 82 percent of announced shares within three years, and 'share repurchases are negatively related to prior stock price performance'. Wikipedia's share-repurchase entry corroborates that the short-term price increase after buybacks does not reverse on average.
ideas.novelty: Counts the CONDITIONAL SHAPE of down-days - close near the high on elevated volume - as evidence of a specific, identifiable non-discretionary buyer, and makes the disappearance of that buyer the exit. It is a 'who is on the bid' detector rather than an oscillator, trend or channel rule, and the exit condition is the decay of the same count that formed the entry.

ideas.name: Gap-Cadence Earnings Calendar and Pre-Announcement Premium
ideas.entry_rule: CALENDAR RECONSTRUCTION: take the 12 sessions with the largest |overnight gap| = |open_t/close_{t-1} - 1| in the trailing 750 sessions. Sort their dates and keep the maximal subset whose consecutive spacings, measured in trading sessions, all lie in [55, 70]. If at least 6 dates survive, declare a quarterly announcement cadence with median spacing m and most recent announcement date A; the predicted next announcement is session A + m. Discard the symbol if the last two observed spacings differ by more than 8 sessions (the cadence has drifted and the forecast is unreliable). TRADE: enter LONG at the close of session A + m - 6.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of session A + m - 1. The position is ALWAYS flat before the predicted announcement - never hold through it, and never re-enter after it. Hard stop at -6% from the entry fill. If the predicted date passes without a gap of at least 1.5x the symbol's 250-session median |gap|, mark the cadence stale and skip the symbol until it re-qualifies.
ideas.why: There is a documented positive average return in the days running into a scheduled earnings announcement - the earnings-announcement premium - attributed to attention-driven retail buying and to a premium for bearing announcement risk. The whole point of exiting the session before the print is that this is precisely where Beaver showed the return VARIANCE explodes: the premium is earned in the run-in, and the variance is incurred in the print, so the two can be separated by a date-based exit. Reconstructing the announcement calendar from the periodicity of the symbol's own overnight gaps solves the problem that we have no earnings feed - quarterly reporting produces a strongly periodic gap signature with roughly 63 trading sessions between reports, and the four largest gaps of a year are overwhelmingly the four reports.
ideas.source: Beaver (1968) on announcement-period return variance and trading volume, cited in Kothari & Warner (2006) footnote 1. Frazzini & Lamont (2007) 'The Earnings Announcement Premium and Trading Volume' (NBER WP 13090) for the run-in premium. The gap-cadence reconstruction device itself is a synthesis - no earnings calendar is available on this feed, so the event dates are inferred from the periodicity of the symbol's own overnight gaps, and the estimator is falsifiable (the predicted date either does or does not produce an outsized gap).
ideas.novelty: Forecasts a FUTURE event date from the periodicity of the symbol's own bars and defines both the entry and the exit by offsets from that predicted date, with no price condition on either side. Nothing in the existing set predicts when an event will occur; and the rule is self-validating - a missed prediction retires the symbol until the cadence re-establishes. The reconstructed calendar is also reusable as an exclusion filter by every other event rule.
params: entry offset before predicted date (3/6/10 sessions)

ideas.name: Special-Distribution Spinoff Parent Hold
ideas.entry_rule: Form F_s = split_adjusted_close_s / fully_adjusted_close_s and k_t = F_t/F_{t-1}, so the implied one-off distribution as a fraction of the prior close is (1 - k_t) (verified: an 8%-of-value distribution gives k = 0.92). Flag a SPECIAL DISTRIBUTION when ALL of: 0.75 <= k_t <= 0.97 (a distribution worth 3%-25% of price, far too large for a regular dividend); no session in the prior 200 had k <= 0.99 with an implied distribution above 2% (this is a genuine one-off, not a habitual large payer); and 1/k_t is NOT within 1% of 1.5, 2, 3, 4 or 5 (so it is not a forward split leaking through the wrong adjustment channel). Enter LONG the parent at the close of the ex-distribution session.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of the 250th session after entry. Trailing exit: close the position when the close falls more than 20% below the highest close recorded since entry. Hard stop at -25% from the entry fill.
ideas.why: Cusatis, Miles & Woolridge document significant positive abnormal returns for up to three years for both spun-off subsidiaries and their parent companies, attributing the gains to the removal of a conglomerate discount, to sharper managerial incentives in the separated units, and to a markedly elevated rate of subsequent takeover activity among restructured entities. A spinoff or large special distribution is unmistakable in the adjustment factor: a regular dividend is far too small (under 2% of price), and a split produces a clean round ratio, so an irregular one-off distribution worth 3%-25% of value with no precedent in the prior year is a restructuring event. The 250-session horizon with a trailing stop matches the documented multi-year drift while capping the downside of the long-horizon methods that Lyon, Barber & Tsai warn are treacherous.
ideas.source: Cusatis, Miles & Woolridge (1993) 'Restructuring through spinoffs: The stock market evidence', Journal of Financial Economics 33, on positive abnormal returns to parents and subsidiaries for up to three years and elevated subsequent takeover activity. Lyon, Barber & Tsai (1999) 'Measuring long-horizon security price performance' - abstract via OpenAlex, on the severe misspecification of long-horizon tests and the need for extreme caution, which is why this rule carries a trailing stop rather than a pure buy-and-hold. Distribution-detection method is a synthesis from the Alpaca bars `adjustment` parameter, verified numerically.
ideas.novelty: Performs a three-way CLASSIFICATION of corporate actions - forward/reverse split versus regular dividend versus irregular special distribution - purely from the size and roundness of the adjustment-factor ratio, then trades the least-covered leg of the event literature over a one-year horizon with a trailing stop. No existing rule classifies corporate actions at all, let alone from bar data alone.

ideas.name: Characteristic Pure Play (trade the regression slope itself)
inputs: matrix algebra: X_t = [1, zhat_1 ... zhat_K] of shape N x (K+1)
ideas.entry_rule: At each month-end t build X_t = [column of ones, then the K cross-sectionally winsorised-and-z-scored characteristics] over the N eligible stocks (60-day median dollar volume > $2,000,000). Compute W_t = (X_t' X_t)^{-1} X_t', an (K+1) x N matrix. Row k of W_t is a vector of portfolio weights with three exact properties: it has unit cross-sectional exposure to characteristic k, exactly zero exposure to every other characteristic, and its weights sum to zero. Pick one target characteristic k (e.g. MOM12-1). Take w = row k of W_t, scale it so sum|w_i| = 2 (i.e. 100% gross long, 100% gross short), and enter position w_i * capital in every stock i. Optionally estimate W_t by weighted least squares, W_t = (X_t' D_t X_t)^{-1} X_t' D_t with D_t = diag(sqrt(60-day median dollar volume rank / N)), to stop microcaps dominating the slope.
ideas.exit_rule: Hold to the next month-end, then recompute W_t and trade to the new w (trade only the difference). Close the entire book and stay flat for one month if the realised 21-day volatility of the pure-play return exceeds 3x its trailing 3-year value, which signals X_t' X_t has become near-singular.
ideas.why: An OLS slope is mechanically the return on a portfolio: lambda_k,t+1 = (row k of W_t) . r_{t+1}. So the multivariate momentum slope IS a tradable portfolio that is long momentum and hedged, by construction and to first order exactly, against size, beta, volatility, illiquidity and every other characteristic in X. A decile sort cannot do this - it can only neutralise what you happen to double-sort on.
ideas.novelty: The position vector is the generalised inverse of the characteristic matrix, not a rank cut. Weights are continuous, sum to zero, and can be negative for a high-characteristic stock if that stock's other characteristics make it a bad hedge - something no sort can produce.
ideas.source: Back, Kapadia & Ostdiek, 'Slopes as Factors: Characteristic Pure Plays', SSRN 2295993 (2013), later in Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis. The slope-as-portfolio-return algebra originates in Fama (1976), Foundations of Finance, ch. 9, and underlies Fama & MacBeth (1973).
params: which characteristic to make the pure play
ridge term added to X'X for conditioning (0 / 0.01 / 0.1 of trace/N)

ideas.name: Shrunk-SDF Weights on Characteristic-Managed Portfolios
inputs: H characteristics from the CHARS block (H = 15-25)
rank transform and leverage normalisation per Kozak-Nagel-Santosh eqs (31)-(32)
5-year rolling covariance matrix Sigma and mean vector mu_bar of the H managed-portfolio daily returns
ideas.entry_rule: Step 1, build H managed portfolios. For characteristic j at date t: rank all n_t eligible stocks on c_j (average ranks for ties); rc_{i,j,t} = rank / (n_t + 1); then z_{i,j,t} = (rc_{i,j,t} - mean_i rc) / sum_i |rc_{i,j,t} - mean_i rc|. Factor return F_{j,t+1} = sum_i z_{i,j,t} * r_{i,t+1}. Rescale each F_j so its in-sample daily stdev equals SPY's, and subtract beta_j * SPY return with beta_j from a full-sample regression. Step 2, estimate SDF coefficients. Over a trailing 1260-session window compute mu_bar (H-vector of mean F) and Sigma (H x H covariance of F). Set bhat = (Sigma + gamma * I)^{-1} mu_bar, where gamma = 1/(kappa^2 * T) and kappa is chosen by 3-fold cross-validation over the trailing window, split chronologically into 3 blocks, maximising the average out-of-sample R2 = 1 - (mu_bar_2 - Sigma_2 bhat)'(mu_bar_2 - Sigma_2 bhat) / (mu_bar_2' mu_bar_2) on the withheld block. Step 3, trade. Stock weight w_{i,t} = sum_j bhat_j * z_{i,j,t}. Scale so sum|w| = 2. Enter every stock with |w_i| >= 0.05% of gross.
ideas.exit_rule: Recompute bhat and w monthly and trade the difference. Drop any name whose new |w_i| falls below 0.05% of gross. Halve gross exposure for the following month whenever the cross-validated out-of-sample R2 at the last re-estimation is negative, and go flat if it is negative twice in a row.
ideas.why: With H correlated signals the sample mean vector is mostly noise and the unregularised solution Sigma^{-1} mu_bar loads enormously on low-variance directions where the mean is least reliably estimated. Penalising the Hansen-Jagannathan distance with an L2 term shrinks exactly those low-eigenvalue directions, because shrinking them costs little pricing accuracy and buys a lot of penalty relief - which is an economically motivated prior, not an arbitrary regulariser.
ideas.novelty: This is the missing 'how do 578 signals become one book' step. The output is a single continuous stock-level weight vector derived from all signals jointly with a principled shrinkage, rather than 578 separate sleeves or an equal-weight blend.
ideas.source: Kozak, Nagel & Santosh, 'Shrinking the Cross Section', NBER Working Paper 24070 (Nov 2017), equations (27) [HJ-distance with L2 penalty], (28) [dual L1+L2], (30) [cross-validated OOS R2], (31)-(32) [rank transform and leverage normalisation]; published Journal of Financial Economics 135(2):271-292 (2019). They use K=3 folds and interpret gamma via the prior root expected maximum squared Sharpe ratio kappa.
params: daily vs weekly return frequency for Sigma
whether to add an L1 term (see the PC-sparse variant)

ideas.name: Principal-Component SDF (trade the eigenvectors of the signal set)
inputs: the same H rank-transformed characteristic-managed portfolio return series F_j
eigen-decomposition of the H x H covariance of F
ideas.entry_rule: Build the H managed portfolios exactly as in the shrunk-SDF idea. On a trailing 1260-session window compute Sigma = cov(F) and its eigen-decomposition Sigma = Q D Q'. Form PC return series P = F Q. Solve the dual-penalty problem bhat = argmin_b (mu_bar_P - D b)' D^{-1} (mu_bar_P - D b) + gamma_2 b'b + gamma_1 sum_j |b_j| by LARS-EN, choosing (gamma_1, gamma_2) on the 3-fold chronological cross-validated OOS R2 grid, with gamma_1 pushed until at most k PCs retain non-zero coefficients (start k = 5). The stock weight is w_{i,t} = sum over retained PCs p of bhat_p * (sum_j Q_{j,p} * z_{i,j,t}). Enter every stock with |w_i| >= 0.05% of gross, sized so sum|w| = 2.
ideas.exit_rule: Re-estimate monthly and trade the difference. Force a full re-estimation of Q (not just b) if the correlation between this month's top eigenvector and last month's falls below 0.8, and skip trading that month. Go flat if the retained PCs' combined trailing 12-month Sharpe is below -0.5.
ideas.why: Signals are massively collinear. A handful of principal components of the signal set carries almost all the priceable variation, and the remaining components are dominated by estimation noise. Selecting in PC space rather than in characteristic space is also better behaved for L1: lasso applied to highly correlated raw predictors arbitrarily picks one and discards the rest, whereas the PCs are orthogonal by construction.
ideas.novelty: The traded object is an eigenvector of the signal covariance matrix - a linear combination of every signal in the corpus - not any individual signal. Distinct from the ridge-SDF idea because sparsity is imposed in PC space and only k factors survive, which makes the live book small and cheap to trade.
ideas.source: Kozak, Nagel & Santosh, 'Shrinking the Cross Section', NBER WP 24070, section 3.2 and Figures 1b/3b; JFE 135(2):271-292 (2019). Their finding on Fama-French test assets: 'even one PC is already sufficient to get close to the maximum OOS R2 and two PCs are sufficient to attain the maximum', while unregularised models with all factors 'perform extremely poorly'. Solver: Zou & Hastie (2005) LARS-EN.
params: whether PCs come from covariance or correlation matrix
sign convention / stability filter for eigenvectors

ideas.name: Risk-Premium PCA (mean-tilted factor extraction)
inputs: T x H matrix X of daily returns on the H characteristic-managed portfolios
X_bar = H-vector of column means of X
eigen-decomposition of (1/T) X'X + gamma * X_bar X_bar'
ideas.entry_rule: Build the H managed portfolios as above and standardise each column of X to unit standard deviation. Over a trailing 1260-session window form M = (1/T) X'X + gamma * X_bar X_bar', with gamma = 10. Take the first K = 4 eigenvectors of M as the loading matrix Lambda_hat (H x K). Factor returns Fhat = X Lambda_hat (Lambda_hat' Lambda_hat)^{-1}. Compute the tangency weights v = cov(Fhat)^{-1} mean(Fhat) on the same window, clip each element to +/- 3 standard deviations of its own history, and set the stock weight w_{i,t} = sum_p v_p * sum_j Lambda_hat[j,p] * z_{i,j,t}. Scale so sum|w| = 2 and enter every stock with |w_i| >= 0.05% of gross.
ideas.exit_rule: Rebalance monthly to the new w. If any single retained factor's trailing 252-day Sharpe is below -0.3, set its v_p to zero for the next month and renormalise. Go flat if all K factors are suppressed.
ideas.why: Ordinary PCA of a covariance matrix uses only the second moment and is blind to the first: a low-variance direction with a large mean - exactly what an arbitrageur wants - gets discarded as the last principal component. Adding gamma * X_bar X_bar' to the second-moment matrix makes the eigen-decomposition trade variance explained against mean return, so the extracted factors are simultaneously the ones that explain the panel and the ones that pay.
ideas.novelty: A single tuning constant gamma turns dimension reduction into a Sharpe-aware operation; gamma = 0 recovers plain PCA and gamma = -1 recovers correlation-matrix PCA, so it nests the naive versions and can be swept against them directly. No corpus idea extracts latent factors at all, let alone with a pricing penalty.
ideas.source: Lettau & Pelger, 'Estimating Latent Asset-Pricing Factors', NBER Working Paper 24618 (2018), Journal of Econometrics 218(1):1-31 (2020). The estimator is stated there as PCA of (1/T) X'X + gamma * X_bar X_bar' (with an optional weighting matrix Q, in their empirics the inverse diagonal matrix of return standard deviations), reporting 'Sharpe ratios more than twice as large as those based on conventional PCA'. Companion: Lettau & Pelger, 'Factors That Fit the Time Series and Cross-Section of Stock Returns', Review of Financial Studies (2020).
params: tangency vs equal-weight combination of the K factors

ideas.name: Time-Series Spanning-Alpha Residual Portfolio
inputs: daily return series F_k of each of the H characteristic-managed portfolios
rolling 756-session multivariate time-series regression of each F_k on the other H-1 (or on the K retained principal components)
ideas.entry_rule: For each characteristic portfolio F_k, run a rolling 756-session daily time-series regression F_k = alpha_k + sum_{j != k} b_{kj} F_j + e_k (or on the K retained PCs, to keep the right-hand side well conditioned). Compute the Newey-West t-statistic on alpha_k with 21 lags. Admit characteristic k only if its t(alpha_k) > 2.5. Trade the residual, not the raw portfolio: hold the stock-level weights z_{i,k,t} for the admitted characteristic and simultaneously hold minus sum_{j != k} b_{kj} * z_{i,j,t}, so the net book is F_k hedged by its own fitted combination of the other signals. Aggregate across all admitted k with weights proportional to alpha_k / stdev(e_k), scale to sum|w| = 2.
ideas.exit_rule: Re-estimate the spanning regressions and re-admit monthly. Drop any characteristic the month its t(alpha_k) falls below 1.5; a dropped characteristic must clear 2.5 again to return. Close the whole book for a month if fewer than two characteristics are admitted. Rehedge weekly if any |b_{kj}| has moved by more than 0.5 since the last rebalance.
ideas.why: Cross-sectional orthogonalisation removes the confound from the characteristic; time-series orthogonalisation removes it from the return stream. A signal can look distinct in characteristic space and still be a linear combination of other signals' returns - that is exactly what a spanning regression alpha detects. Holding the residual rather than the raw portfolio means you are paid only for the part of the signal nobody else in the book already owns.
ideas.novelty: The hedge is a basket of other signal portfolios with regression-estimated betas, refitted on a rolling window, rather than a static market or sector hedge. It is the dual of cross-sectional residualisation and picks up redundancies that the cross-sectional version cannot see.
ideas.source: The spanning-regression standard comes from Fama & French (1993, 2015). Formalised for model comparison in Barillas & Shanken, 'Which Alpha?', Review of Financial Studies (2017). The redundancy problem it addresses is documented in Green, Hand & Zhang (2017), RFS 30(12):4389-4436, and in Feng, Giglio & Xiu (2020), Journal of Finance 75(3):1327-1370.
params: right-hand side: all other H-1 portfolios vs K principal components

ideas.name: GARCH-POT Conditional-EVT Shortfall Budget
ideas.entry_rule: Every day after the close, per ticker: fit AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) to the trailing 1000 daily log returns, take standardised residuals z_t = (r_t - mu_t)/sigma_t, set u = the 10th percentile of z (so T_u = 100 exceedances out of T = 1000) and fit GPD(xi, beta) by maximum likelihood to the excesses (u - z) over that threshold. Forecast one step ahead: VaR_a = mu_{t+1} + sigma_{t+1} * ( u + (beta/xi) * [ 1 - ( a / (T_u/T) )^(-xi) ] ) and ES_a = mu_{t+1} + sigma_{t+1} * ( VaR_a/(1-xi) - (beta + xi*u)/(1-xi) ), with a = 0.025. Take whatever base long entry the ladder already generates, but size it so that shares * |ES_0.025| * price = 0.75% of account equity. Skip the entry entirely if the GPD fit returns xi >= 0.5 (infinite-variance tail, sizing is meaningless).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit the full position when either (a) the ticker's realised daily return breaches its own forecast VaR_0.01 on two days within any rolling 10-day window, or (b) the forecast ES_0.025 rises above 2.0x its own trailing 250-day median. Re-enter only after ES_0.025 has been below its 250-day median for 5 consecutive closes.
ideas.why: McNeil and Frey's two-stage estimator separates the two things that make a tail forecast wrong: the VOLATILITY DYNAMIC (handled by the GARCH filter, so a quiet period does not get a crisis-sized risk number) and the TAIL SHAPE of the innovations (handled by fitting a generalized Pareto to the residual exceedances, per the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan theorem). Unconditional EVT gets stuck at the average tail over the whole sample; plain GARCH-normal underestimates how bad the bad days are. Sizing off a conditional ES rather than a stop distance means every position carries the same expected loss GIVEN a bad day, which is the number that actually kills a levered book.
ideas.source: McNeil & Frey (2000), 'Estimation of tail-related risk measures for heteroscedastic financial time series: an extreme value approach', J. Empirical Finance 7. Exact VaR/ES closed forms and the two-step procedure as restated in Nieto & Ruiz, 'Backtesting extreme value theory models of expected shortfall', UCM working paper (https://docta.ucm.es/bitstreams/661963d3-b3ca-44e1-b46c-ad300c907b79/download), Section 3. Threshold in the 8-10% quantile range follows Chavez-Demoulin & McGill (2012) and Herrera (2013) as cited there.
ideas.novelty: The exit is triggered by a MODEL FORECAST breaking down, not by price. Two positions with identical charts get different sizes because their residual tails have different GPD shape parameters.

ideas.name: Hill-vs-EPD Bias Gap Reliability Gate
inputs: Hill estimator across a range of k
ideas.entry_rule: Every day per ticker, form losses X_t = -r_t over the trailing 1000 daily bars and sort ascending X_(1) <= ... <= X_(n). For each k in {25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150} compute the Hill estimate H_k = (1/k) * sum_{j=1..k} ln( X_(n-j+1) / X_(n-k) ). Separately, for each k fit the extended Pareto distribution to the excess ratios Y_j = X_(n-j+1)/X_(n-k), j = 1..k, by maximum likelihood on the survival function Gbar(y) = { y * (1 + delta - delta*y^rho) }^(-1/xi) with rho fixed at -1, giving (xi_k, delta_k). Define BIASGAP = mean over k of | H_k - xi_k | / xi_k, and HILLDISP = stdev(H_k over the six k) / mean(H_k). Take the base long entry ONLY when BIASGAP < 0.20 AND HILLDISP < 0.15 (i.e. the simple Pareto tail model is both stable in k and close to its bias-corrected version).
ideas.exit_rule: Cut the position to half size on the first close where BIASGAP >= 0.20 or HILLDISP >= 0.15, and flatten completely if either condition persists for 3 consecutive closes. Restore full size only after 10 consecutive closes with both back under their thresholds.
ideas.why: Beirlant and co-authors point out that in practice the Hill plot is almost never horizontal in k, and that this non-stability is a symptom of second-order slow variation - the true tail is Cx^(-1/xi)(1 + xi^(-1) delta(x)) rather than a clean power law, so any single-k Hill number is contaminated by observations from the middle of the distribution. The EPD adds exactly one parameter to absorb that deviation, so the GAP between the naive Hill and the bias-corrected EPD estimate is a direct, computable measure of how badly the tail model is misspecified for this name right now. Trading only when the tail model is trustworthy is a filter no price-based indicator can supply, and it is precisely the failure mode that blows up a levered book (the tail turns out to be heavier than the estimate said).
ideas.source: Maribe, Verster & Beirlant, 'Reducing bias and MSE in estimation of heavy tails: a Bayesian approach', arXiv:1606.05687 - Hill estimator eq. (3), Weissman tail-probability estimator eq. (4), extended Pareto survival function eq. (6) and the EPD-ML bias-reduced estimator; the observation that Hill stability 'is not visible' in most cases motivates the dispersion term. Hill (1975) for the base estimator; Beirlant et al. (2009) for the EPD subclass F(xi, tau).
ideas.novelty: The signal is the DISAGREEMENT BETWEEN TWO ESTIMATORS OF THE SAME QUANTITY, used as a confidence gate. Nothing in the existing 32 uses estimator instability as a tradeable state.

ideas.name: Conditional-Coverage Break Detector
ideas.entry_rule: For SPY (and separately per ticker if desired), maintain a rolling one-day-ahead VaR_0.05 forecast as mu = 0 and sigma_t from EWMA with lambda = 0.94, VaR_t = -1.645 * sigma_t. Over the trailing T = 250 closes form I_t = 1{r_t < VaR_t}, with T1 = sum I_t and T0 = T - T1, pi_hat = T1/T. Compute LR_uc = -2*ln[ ((1-0.05)^T0 * 0.05^T1) / ((1-pi_hat)^T0 * pi_hat^T1) ]. Build the 2x2 Markov transition counts T00, T01, T10, T11 with pi01 = T01/(T00+T01), pi11 = T11/(T10+T11), and LR_ind = -2*ln[ ((1-pi_hat)^T0 * pi_hat^T1) / ((1-pi01)^T00 * pi01^T01 * (1-pi11)^T10 * pi11^T11) ]. Set LR_cc = LR_uc + LR_ind, which is chi-square with 2 d.f. Take the fleet's base long entries only while LR_cc < 5.99 (the 5% critical value).
ideas.exit_rule: When LR_cc >= 9.21 (the 1% critical value), exit all positions at the next open and stay flat. Re-enable entries only after LR_cc has been below 5.99 for 10 consecutive closes. While 5.99 <= LR_cc < 9.21, hold existing positions but open no new ones.
params: EWMA lambda (0.94, 0.97) or historical-simulation VaR instead
critical values used for the two gates
ideas.why: Kupiec's unconditional-coverage test asks whether you got the RIGHT NUMBER of tail breaches; Christoffersen's independence test asks whether those breaches ARRIVED INDEPENDENTLY. Their sum is the conditional-coverage test, and it is a clean detector of a distributional regime change: exceptions clustering in time means the volatility model has stopped tracking, which is exactly the state in which every trend and mean-reversion rule in the fleet degrades simultaneously. Unlike a drawdown stop, this fires on the STATISTICAL STRUCTURE of the losses, so it can trip before the drawdown arrives (many small clustered breaches) and can stay quiet through a large but well-forecast loss.
ideas.source: Kupiec (1995), 'Techniques for verifying the accuracy of risk measurement models', J. Derivatives 3; Christoffersen (1998), 'Evaluating interval forecasts', International Economic Review 39, 841-862. Exact LR_uc, LR_ind, LR_cc formulas and the Markov-chain construction as restated in Nieto & Ruiz, 'Backtesting extreme value theory models of expected shortfall', UCM working paper Section 4.1 (https://docta.ucm.es/bitstreams/661963d3-b3ca-44e1-b46c-ad300c907b79/download).
ideas.novelty: Uses the SERIAL STRUCTURE of tail-model failures as the state variable. A 250-day window can have exactly the right count of breaches (LR_uc tiny) and still trip on LR_ind because they all arrived in one week - no volatility or drawdown filter can see that distinction.

ideas.name: Cumulative-Violation Severity Clustering
inputs: conditional CDF from a GARCH-t or EWMA-normal model
ideas.entry_rule: Fit a GARCH(1,1) with standardised Student-t innovations to the trailing 1000 daily returns of SPY and produce the probability integral transform u_t = F(r_t | Omega_{t-1}) each day. With alpha = 0.05 form the cumulative violation H_t = (1/alpha) * (alpha - u_t) * 1{u_t <= alpha}, which is 0 on non-violation days and rises toward 1 the deeper the violation. Over the trailing 250 days compute (a) the unconditional statistic U_ES = sqrt(250) * (mean(H_t) - alpha/2) / sqrt( alpha*(1/3 - alpha/4) ), asymptotically N(0,1), and (b) the Box-Pierce statistic BP = 250 * sum_{j=1..5} rho_j^2 on the sample autocorrelations rho_j of the series {H_t - alpha/2}, asymptotically chi-square with 5 d.f. Take the fleet's base long entries only while U_ES < 1.645 AND BP < 11.07 (5% chi-square_5).
ideas.exit_rule: Halve every position on the first close where BP >= 11.07 (tail SEVERITY is autocorrelated, so the next violation is likely to be a deep one). Flatten entirely if U_ES >= 2.33 (the model is systematically under-stating expected shortfall). Restore full size after 10 consecutive closes with both statistics back inside their thresholds.
params: GARCH innovation distribution (t vs skew-t vs normal)
half-size vs quarter-size on the BP trip
ideas.why: Violations of a VaR level are binary - they throw away how bad the bad day was. The cumulative violation H_t integrates the hit function over ALL quantile levels below alpha, so it inherits ES's severity-awareness while remaining distribution-free (H_t has mean alpha/2 and variance alpha*(1/3 - alpha/4) under the null, since u_t is uniform). Du and Escanciano show {H_t - alpha/2} is a martingale difference sequence under a correct model, so autocorrelation in it is direct evidence that DEEP losses cluster - a different and more dangerous failure than the count-clustering that Christoffersen's independence test detects. For a levered ladder that adds on the way down, severity clustering is the exact mechanism that turns a normal drawdown into a wipe-out.
ideas.source: Du & Escanciano (2017), 'Backtesting expected shortfall: accounting for tail risk', Management Science 63(4), building on Costanzino & Curran (2015). Cumulative violation definition H_t(alpha) = (1/alpha)(alpha - u_t)1{u_t <= alpha}, the moments E[H_t] = alpha/2 and Var = alpha(1/3 - alpha/4), the U_ES t-statistic and the Box-Pierce conditional test as set out in Nieto & Ruiz, UCM working paper Section 4.2.4 (https://docta.ucm.es/bitstreams/661963d3-b3ca-44e1-b46c-ad300c907b79/download); open access at https://caepr.indiana.edu/RePEc/inu/caeprp/caepr2015-001.pdf.
ideas.novelty: Trades on the autocorrelation of a continuous severity measure rather than on a violation count. Two return series with identical exception counts, identical volatility and identical Christoffersen statistics can differ completely here.

ideas.name: Acerbi-Szekely Z2 Exposure Dial
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain daily one-day-ahead forecasts VaR_t and ES_t at alpha = 0.05 for the fleet's aggregate P&L (GARCH-POT is the natural source; historical simulation also works). Each Friday close, over the trailing T = 250 days with I_t = 1{r_t < VaR_t}, compute Z2 = (1/(T*alpha)) * sum_t ( I_t * r_t / ES_t ) - 1, using the sign convention that ES_t and r_t are both negative in a loss, so Z2 > 0 means realised tail losses exceeded the ES forecast. Set next week's gross exposure multiplier to G = clip(1 - 2*Z2, 0.25, 1.00) and scale every position (existing and new) to G times its target size at Monday's open. Take base long entries normally while G > 0.25.
ideas.exit_rule: Flatten the entire book and take no new entries for the following week whenever Z2 > 0.50. Resume at G computed from the refreshed statistic once Z2 falls back below 0.25. Establish significance by Monte Carlo: simulate 10,000 paths of length 250 from the assumed predictive distribution, take the empirical 95th percentile of Z2 as an alternative hard cutoff instead of the fixed 0.50.
params: fixed cutoff vs Monte Carlo critical value
ideas.why: Acerbi and Szekely's Z2 divides the sum of realised breach returns by the EXPECTED number of breaches (T*alpha) rather than the realised number, so unlike Z1 it is sensitive both to too many breaches and to breaches that are too deep - rejecting Z2's null includes rejecting the VaR specification itself. That makes it a single scalar summarising 'by how much is my risk model currently wrong, in ES units'. Because it is already a ratio in ES units, it maps naturally onto a leverage multiplier: if your ES forecast is understating by 25%, run 50% less gross. The two statistics are linked by Z2 = (1 + Z1) * N_T/(T*alpha), which is why Z2 and not Z1 is the right dial. Both are model-free and calibrated by simulation rather than asymptotics, so they work at the 250-day sample sizes a real fleet actually has.
ideas.source: Acerbi & Szekely (2014), 'Back-testing Expected Shortfall', Risk Magazine. Exact Z1 and Z2 definitions, null and alternative hypotheses, the identity Z2 = (1+Z1)*N_T/(T*alpha), and the Monte Carlo calibration procedure (10,000 simulated processes of length 1,000) as restated in Nieto & Ruiz, UCM working paper Section 4.2.2 (https://docta.ucm.es/bitstreams/661963d3-b3ca-44e1-b46c-ad300c907b79/download).
ideas.novelty: A backtest statistic used as a CONTINUOUS position-size multiplier rather than a binary pass/fail. Exposure becomes a smooth function of measured risk-model error.

ideas.name: Multinomial Four-Level VaR Shape Monitor
inputs: 250 trailing daily portfolio or index returns
ideas.entry_rule: Set N = 4 and the base level alpha = 0.975, giving levels alpha_j = alpha + (j-1)/N * (1 - alpha) for j = 1..4, i.e. 0.9750, 0.98125, 0.98750, 0.99375. Each day forecast VaR at all four levels from the same model (GARCH-t or GARCH-POT). Define I_t,j = 1{L_t > VaR_alpha_j,t} and X_t = sum_j I_t,j (how many levels today's loss pierced, 0 to 4). Over the trailing n = 250 days form cell counts O_j = #{t : X_t = j} for j = 0..4 and the Pearson statistic S_N = sum_{j=0..4} (O_j - n*(alpha_{j+1} - alpha_j))^2 / (n*(alpha_{j+1} - alpha_j)) with alpha_0 = 0 and alpha_5 = 1; apply the Nass correction cS_N ~ chi-square_nu with c = 2*E[S_N]/Var(S_N), nu = c*E[S_N], E[S_N] = N, Var(S_N) = 2N - (N^2+4N+1)/n + (1/n)*sum_j 1/(alpha_{j+1}-alpha_j). Run the fleet at full size while cS_N < chi-square_nu(0.95). If the test rejects AND O_4 alone exceeds 2x its expected count while O_1 is within 1.5x expectation, classify as DEEP-TAIL MISFIT: cut gross exposure to 50%, widen all ladder rung spacing by 1.5x, and take no new adds. If the test rejects AND O_1 exceeds 2x expectation while O_4 is within 1.5x, classify as VOL-MODEL MISFIT: keep gross exposure but shorten all volatility lookbacks by half and tighten stops to 1.5*ATR(14).
ideas.exit_rule: Return to the default configuration once cS_N falls back below chi-square_nu(0.95) for 10 consecutive closes. Independently, flatten if the deep-tail classification persists for more than 15 consecutive trading days.
params: Pearson vs Nass vs likelihood-ratio test
ideas.why: Emmer, Kratz and Tasche show ES_alpha is well approximated by the average of four quantiles, ES_alpha ~ (1/4)[q(alpha) + q(0.75alpha+0.25) + q(0.5alpha+0.5) + q(0.25alpha+0.75)], which means simultaneously backtesting VaR at four levels IS an implicit ES backtest. Kratz, Lok and McNeil show in simulation that multinomial tests with N >= 4 are far more powerful at detecting trading-book model misspecification than the standard binomial exception test, with Nass robust in size across N. The trading value is not the pass/fail but WHICH CELL is over-populated: too many deep piercings with a normal count of shallow ones means the tail shape is wrong (leverage is the problem); too many shallow piercings with a normal deep count means the volatility scale is wrong (lookback is the problem). Those two failures call for opposite responses, and a single-level backtest cannot tell them apart.
ideas.source: Kratz, Lok & McNeil (2018), 'Multinomial VaR backtests: a simple implicit approach to backtesting expected shortfall', J. Banking & Finance 88; arXiv:1611.04851 - level construction eq. (2.1), Pearson statistic eq. (2.4), the Nass correction with c and nu, and the finding that N >= 4 dominates binomial tests. The ES approximation eq. (1.1) is from Emmer, Kratz & Tasche (2015).
ideas.novelty: Diagnostic rather than binary: the cell histogram of 'how many VaR levels did today pierce' tells you which part of the model broke, and the strategy takes a different action for each diagnosis.

ideas.name: Extreme Expectile-to-Quantile Tail Heaviness
ideas.category: extreme value theory / coherent risk measures
ideas.entry_rule: Each day for SPY (and per ticker for the cross-sectional variant), over the trailing 1000 daily returns with losses Y_t = -r_t: (a) compute the intermediate expectile at tau = 0.95 by asymmetric least squares, xi_tau = argmin_theta sum_t |1{Y_t - theta <= 0} - tau| * (Y_t - theta)^2, solved by iteratively reweighted least squares; (b) compute the Hill estimate gamma_hat with k = 50 upper order statistics; (c) extrapolate to the extreme level tau' = 0.999 by the Weissman-type formula xi_tau' = ((1-tau')/(1-tau))^(-gamma_hat) * xi_tau; (d) compute the empirical 99.9th-percentile loss q_0.999 over the same window; (e) form the heaviness ratio G = xi_tau' / q_0.999. Take the fleet's base long entries only when G is below its own trailing 750-day 80th percentile.
ideas.exit_rule: Halve every position on the first close where G rises above its trailing 750-day 80th percentile; flatten entirely above the 95th percentile. Restore full size after G has been below the 80th percentile for 5 consecutive closes.
ideas.why: Expectiles are the ONLY law-invariant risk measure that is both coherent and elicitable - VaR is elicitable but not coherent, ES is coherent but not elicitable. An expectile therefore has a natural scoring function (asymmetric squared loss) so it can be backtested directly, and unlike a quantile it depends on the MAGNITUDES of the losses beyond the threshold, not only their frequency. The ratio of an extrapolated extreme expectile to the matching empirical quantile is consequently a clean, self-normalising measure of how much mass sits deep in the tail: under a light tail the two nearly coincide, and the ratio grows with the tail index gamma. Because the Weissman extrapolation is explicitly powered by gamma_hat, the signal is a tail-shape reading rather than a volatility reading, so it can rise while realised volatility is flat - which is precisely the pre-crash configuration that a volatility-targeted book walks into.
ideas.source: Padoan & Stupfler, 'Tail risk inference via expectiles in heavy-tailed time series', arXiv:2004.04078 - expectile definition eq. (1) with eta_tau(u) = |1(u<=0) - tau| u^2 (Newey & Powell 1987), the heavy-tail model with index gamma, and the Weissman-type extrapolation eq. (3) xi_tau'/xi_tau ~ ((1-tau')/(1-tau))^(-gamma). Coherence-and-elicitability uniqueness from Bellini & Bignozzi, 'Risk measures with the CxLS property' (arXiv:1411.0426) and Ziegel, 'Coherence and elicitability' (arXiv:1303.1690).
ideas.novelty: A magnitude-weighted tail statistic compared against a frequency-based one; the RATIO is the signal. This is not a volatility measure, not a quantile, and not an ES - it is the divergence between two different notions of 'how bad the tail is'.

ideas.name: FZ-Loss GAS Tail-Only State Machine
inputs: one-factor GAS recursion for joint VaR and ES
ideas.entry_rule: Fit the one-factor GAS model for joint VaR and ES to the trailing 1500 daily returns Y_t of SPY at alpha = 0.05. Specification: v_t = a*exp(kappa_t), e_t = b*exp(kappa_t) with b < a < 0, and kappa_t = omega + beta*kappa_{t-1} + gamma * (1/(b*exp(kappa_{t-1}))) * ( (1/alpha)*1{Y_{t-1} <= a*exp(kappa_{t-1})}*Y_{t-1} - b*exp(kappa_{t-1}) ). Estimate (a, b, beta, gamma) by minimising the FZ0 loss sum_t L(Y_t, v_t, e_t) with L(Y,v,e) = -(1/(alpha*e))*1{Y<=v}*(v-Y) + v/e + log(-e) - 1 (fix omega = 0; it is not separately identified). Update kappa_t daily with the fitted parameters. Take base long entries when kappa_t < the median of the trailing 250 kappa values AND kappa_t < kappa_{t-1} (tail risk is both low and falling).
ideas.exit_rule: Exit all positions when kappa_t rises above the 80th percentile of the trailing 250 kappa values, or when kappa_t > kappa_{t-1} on three consecutive closes. Re-estimate the four parameters every 63 trading days by re-minimising FZ0 loss over the trailing 1500 bars. Optionally run the hybrid variant kappa_t = omega + beta*kappa_{t-1} + gamma*(forcing term) + delta*log|Y_{t-1}| and switch to whichever of the two has the lower average out-of-sample FZ0 loss over the last 250 days.
params: one-factor GAS vs hybrid GAS/GARCH vs GARCH-FZ
ideas.why: The forcing variable in this recursion is derived from the FZ0 loss and, crucially, the term 1{Y_{t-1} <= v_{t-1}}*Y_{t-1} is ZERO on any day the return did not breach VaR - the news impact curve is flat above the VaR threshold and linear below it. So kappa_t is a persistent risk state that updates ONLY on tail days, in contrast to GARCH which updates on every squared return and is therefore dragged around by ordinary large-but-not-extreme moves. The FZ0 loss is the unique zero-homogeneous strictly consistent loss for the (VaR, ES) pair, so parameters fitted by minimising it are tuned to produce the best joint tail forecast rather than the best variance forecast - which is a different and, for a levered book, more relevant objective. Patton, Ziegel and Chen find the one-factor GAS and the hybrid GAS/GARCH beat rolling-window and GARCH-based alternatives on out-of-sample FZ0 loss across major equity indices.
ideas.source: Patton, Ziegel & Chen (2019), 'Dynamic semiparametric models for expected shortfall (and Value-at-Risk)', Journal of Econometrics 211(2), 388-413 (https://public.econ.duke.edu/~ap172/Patton_Ziegel_Chen_JoE_2019.pdf) - FZ0 loss eq. (6), one-factor GAS eqs. (17)-(20), hybrid GAS/GARCH eq. (27), and the finding that omega is unidentified in the one-factor specifications.
ideas.novelty: A latent risk state whose update equation IGNORES every non-tail observation. Its news impact curve is flat above VaR and linear below it - structurally different from any GARCH, ATR, or realised-volatility state variable in the existing 32.

ideas.name: SHAR Forecast-Drop Dip Buy
ideas.category: semivariance HAR volatility forecasting / time-series mean reversion
ideas.entry_rule: Each day t, from 5-minute log returns compute RV_t, RS_plus_t, RS_minus_t. Let RV_w = mean of RV over lags 2..5 and RV_m = mean of RV over lags 6..22. On a rolling 500-day window estimate by OLS two models: (a) plain HAR: RV_{t+1} = b0 + b1*RV_t + bw*RV_w + bm*RV_m; (b) SHAR: RV_{t+1} = c0 + c_plus*RS_plus_t + c_minus*RS_minus_t + cw*RV_w + cm*RV_m. Produce both one-day-ahead forecasts F_HAR and F_SHAR. Go LONG at the next open when ALL of: (i) today's close-to-close log return <= -1.0 * sqrt(RV_t); (ii) F_SHAR <= 0.90 * F_HAR; (iii) RS_plus_t / RV_t >= 0.50, i.e. despite the negative close, at least half of today's variance came from positive 5-minute returns.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of day t+3. Exit earlier if cumulative return from entry reaches +1.0*sqrt(RV_t) (take profit) or -1.0*sqrt(RV_t) (stop). Never hold across an entry re-signal; one position per symbol.
ideas.why: Patton and Sheppard show that the HAR coefficient on negative semivariance is far larger and more significant than on positive semivariance at every horizon from 1 to 66 days: for the S&P 500 ETF the positive-semivariance coefficient is statistically zero at h = 1, 5 and 22 while the negative coefficient is strongly positive, and splitting RV this way raises explained variation in future volatility by 10-20%. The gap F_HAR - F_SHAR is therefore a direct read on whether today's variance carries bad-volatility information. A one-sigma down day whose variance was mostly built out of positive 5-minute moves is a liquidity/mechanical sell-off, not a repricing, and the semivariance model says tomorrow's volatility will fall rather than persist.
ideas.source: Patton & Sheppard (2015), 'Good Volatility, Bad Volatility: Signed Jumps and the Persistence of Volatility', Review of Economics and Statistics 97(3), 683-697. HAR reparameterisation Eq. (12), semivariance HAR Eq. (16), coefficient estimates Tables 2A and 2B. PDF: https://public.econ.duke.edu/~ap172/Patton_Sheppard_REStat_2015.pdf
params: OLS vs WLS with weights = 1/fitted (as in the paper)
ideas.novelty: Not an oscillator threshold and not a volatility-level filter: the entry condition is a disagreement between two nested forecasting models, which fires only when the composition of today's variance contradicts its level.

ideas.name: Realized Quarticity Signal-Precision Gate
ideas.entry_rule: Each day, from the M 5-minute log returns of the session compute RV_t = sum(r_i^2) and the realized quarticity RQ_t = (M/3) * sum(r_i^4). Track the 250-day percentile rank of RQ_t^(1/2), call it q_t. Go LONG at the next open when ALL of: (a) today's close is the highest close of the last 20 trading days; (b) RV_t >= 1.5 * mean(RV over days t-22..t-1); and (c) q_t <= 0.33. If (c) fails, discard the signal entirely - do not take it and do not queue it. Mirror for shorts on a 20-day low with the same RQ gate.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit long on a close below the minimum close of the previous 10 trading days, or after 15 trading days, whichever comes first. Mirror for shorts. Additionally exit immediately if q_t rises above 0.90 while in the trade - the volatility state has become unmeasurable.
ideas.why: The asymptotic theory of Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard gives RV_t = IV_t + eta_t with eta_t ~ MN(0, 2*Delta*IQ_t), so the variance of the measurement error in RV is proportional to integrated quarticity, consistently estimated by RQ. Bollerslev, Patton and Quaedvlieg show the OLS autoregressive coefficient on RV is attenuated by exactly this factor, beta1 = phi1 * (1 + 2*Delta*IQ/Var(IV))^-1, and that letting the daily HAR coefficient vary as (b1 + b1Q * RQ^(1/2)) with b1Q < 0 materially improves forecasts. A volatility-expansion breakout on a high-RQ day is very likely an artefact of two or three outlier 5-minute bars rather than a real regime change; on a low-RQ day the same RV expansion is a precisely measured fact. RQ is close to orthogonal to the level of RV, so this is a genuinely new axis of filtering.
ideas.source: Bollerslev, Patton & Quaedvlieg (2016), 'Exploiting the errors: A simple approach for improved volatility forecasting', Journal of Econometrics 192, 1-18. RQ definition Eq. (5), attenuation Eq. (9), ARQ Eq. (10), HARQ Eq. (12). PDF: https://public.econ.duke.edu/~ap172/BPQ_Exploiting_Errors_JoE_2016.pdf
params: use RQ^(1/2) vs RQ vs 1/RQ (the paper prefers the square root for robustness)
substitute jump-robust quarticity (tri-power, MedRQ) for RQ
ideas.novelty: Every existing volatility filter conditions on the second moment (ATR, RV, Bollinger width). This conditions on the fourth moment, which measures how trustworthy the second moment is today. High-RQ days and high-RV days are different sets of days.

ideas.name: MedRV Jump-Fraction Split for Breakouts
ideas.category: jump-robust realized measure / breakout regime split
ideas.entry_rule: Each day compute from the M 5-minute log returns: RV_t = sum(r_i^2); the nearest-neighbour-truncation estimator MedRV_t = [pi / (6 - 4*sqrt(3) + pi)] * (M/(M-2)) * sum_{i=2..M-1} med(|r_{i-1}|, |r_i|, |r_{i+1}|)^2; bipower variation BV_t = (pi/2) * sum_{i=2..M} |r_i| * |r_{i-1}|; and tri-power quarticity TQ_t = M * (M/(M-2)) * (Gamma(0.5)/(2^(2/3)*Gamma(7/6)))^3 * sum_{i=3..M} |r_i|^(4/3)*|r_{i-1}|^(4/3)*|r_{i-2}|^(4/3). Form the Andersen-Bollerslev-Diebold jump statistic z_t = ((RV_t - BV_t)/RV_t) / sqrt(((pi/2)^2 + pi - 5) * (1/M) * max(1, TQ_t / BV_t^2)), which is asymptotically N(0,1), and the jump fraction JF_t = max(0, RV_t - MedRV_t)/RV_t. CONTINUOUS BRANCH: go LONG at the next open when today's close is the highest close of the last 20 days AND z_t < 1.96 AND JF_t <= 0.10. JUMP BRANCH: when today's close is the highest close of the last 20 days AND z_t > 2.58 AND JF_t >= 0.30, go SHORT at the next open instead.
ideas.exit_rule: Long: exit on a close below the 10-day low, or after 10 trading days. Short (jump-fade branch): exit on a close above the entry-day high, or when JF over the following days drops below 0.10 for two consecutive sessions, or after 5 trading days - jump fades are shorter-lived than continuous trends, so the two branches deliberately have different exit structures.
ideas.why: MinRV and MedRV estimate integrated variance using the minimum or median of adjacent absolute returns, so a single jump contaminates at most one of the three neighbours and is truncated away. Unlike bipower variation they degrade gracefully with zero returns and are far better behaved in finite samples. The RV minus MedRV difference is therefore a clean estimate of jump variation. The economic split: a 20-day breakout assembled out of continuous diffusive trading is a sustained order-flow imbalance and tends to persist, whereas a breakout produced by one discrete jump is a repricing that is already complete the moment it prints, so the marginal buyer arriving after it is the one who gets faded.
ideas.source: Andersen, Dobrev & Schaumburg (2012), 'Jump-robust volatility estimation using nearest neighbor truncation', Journal of Econometrics 169, 75-93. MedRV/MinRV constants and tri-power quarticity exactly as implemented in the R highfrequency package (rMedRVar, rMinRVar, rTPQuar, BNSjumpTest), CRAN reference manual pp. 16-17 and 92-96: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/highfrequency/highfrequency.pdf. Jump statistic form from Andersen, Bollerslev & Diebold (2007), 'Roughing it up', Review of Economics and Statistics 89, 701-720.
params: whether to require the jump be signed in the breakout direction using RS_plus - RS_minus
ideas.novelty: Existing ATR-expansion breakouts treat all variance as one thing. This asks whether the move was continuous or discontinuous and takes opposite sides in the two cases, so it is two entry logics and two exit structures out of one estimator, not a threshold tweak.

ideas.name: First-Order Autocovariance Sign Switch
ideas.timeframe: intraday, decided on daily statistics from 1-minute bars
ideas.entry_rule: Each day compute from the session's 1-minute log returns the empirical autocovariances gamma0 = sum(r_i^2) and gamma1 = sum_{i>=2} r_i * r_{i-1}, and the ratio rho1_t = gamma1_t / gamma0_t. Take the 20-day mean rho1bar_t. MOMENTUM REGIME (rho1bar_t > +0.02): at 10:30 ET on day t+1, buy at market if the 09:30-to-10:30 log return is in the top 30% of that symbol's last 60 days of 09:30-to-10:30 returns; sell short if it is in the bottom 30%. REVERSION REGIME (rho1bar_t < -0.05): at 10:30 ET on day t+1, buy at market if the 09:30-to-10:30 log return is in the BOTTOM 30% of the same 60-day distribution; sell short if it is in the top 30%. If -0.05 <= rho1bar_t <= +0.02, take no intraday position in that name that day.
ideas.exit_rule: Flat at 15:55 ET on the same day, unconditionally. Intraday hard stop at 1.5 * sqrt(gamma0_t * (5/390)) (roughly a five-minute one-sigma move) against the entry. No overnight carry ever.
ideas.why: The realized-kernel estimator gamma0 + 2*sum_{h=1..H} k((h-1)/H)*gamma_h exists precisely because gamma0 alone is contaminated: under i.i.d. microstructure noise the first-order autocovariance of finely sampled returns converges to -omega^2, so gamma1 mixes the noise term with the genuine serial dependence of the efficient price. That makes gamma1/gamma0 a signed diagnostic. Strongly negative means bid-ask bounce dominates and the observed intraday path over-shoots and comes back, favouring reversion. Turning positive means genuine order-flow persistence has swamped the bounce, favouring continuation. Same statistic, opposite trade.
ideas.source: Barndorff-Nielsen, Hansen, Lunde & Shephard (2008), 'Designing realized kernels to measure the ex post variation of equity prices in the presence of noise', Econometrica 76, 1481-1536; kernel form gamma0 + 2*sum k((h-1)/H) gamma_h and the empirical autocovariance definition as documented for rKernelCov in the R highfrequency CRAN manual p. 87. Hansen & Lunde (2006), 'Realized variance and market microstructure noise', Journal of Business and Economic Statistics 24, 127-218, for the gamma1 / noise relationship.
params: bar size for gamma computation (1-min vs 2-min vs 5-min)
rho1 thresholds (+0.02/-0.05, or symbol-specific percentiles of its own rho1 history)
use the full Parzen-kernel estimate with H = floor(sqrt(M)) instead of just gamma1
ideas.novelty: Uses the nuisance parameter of a noise-robust estimator as the trading signal rather than the estimator itself, and it selects between momentum and mean reversion instead of applying one of them everywhere.

ideas.name: HEAVY Two-Component Divergence Gate
ideas.category: high-frequency-based volatility model / breakout-vs-fade regime switch
ideas.entry_rule: For each symbol estimate, on a 1000-day rolling window by separate quasi-maximum likelihood, the two HEAVY equations of Shephard and Sheppard on demeaned daily returns r_t and a daily realized measure RM_t (use MedRV or bipower variation from 5-minute returns, in the same units as squared daily returns): return-variance equation h_t = omega + alpha * RM_{t-1} + beta * h_{t-1}; realized-measure equation mu_t = omega_R + alpha_R * RM_{t-1} + beta_R * mu_{t-1}. Define the divergence D_t = log(mu_t) - log(h_t). BREAKOUT BRANCH: go LONG at the next open when today's close is the highest close of the last 20 trading days AND D_t > 0. FADE BRANCH: when today's close is the highest close of the last 20 days AND D_t < -0.15, go SHORT at the next open instead. Mirror both branches for 20-day lows. Take no position when -0.15 <= D_t <= 0.
ideas.exit_rule: Breakout longs: exit on a close below the 10-day low, or after 10 trading days, or immediately if D_t turns negative for two consecutive sessions. Fade shorts: exit on a close above the entry bar's high, or after 5 trading days - the two branches deliberately carry different holding structures because the fade is a short-lived overshoot and the breakout is a trend.
inputs: QML estimation of two GARCH-type recursions
ideas.why: HEAVY's design point is that the realized-measure equation absorbs new information faster than the return-variance equation, which is a slow-moving GARCH-type recursion on squared returns. The gap between the two conditional variances is therefore a state variable for the MOMENTUM OF VOLATILITY rather than its level: D_t > 0 means the high-frequency measure is signalling more variation than the return-based component has yet priced in, so volatility is still expanding. Trend breaks that occur while volatility is expanding follow through; breaks that occur while the fast component has already rolled over below the slow one are exhaustion.
ideas.source: Shephard & Sheppard (2010), 'Realising the future: forecasting with high frequency based volatility (HEAVY) models', Journal of Applied Econometrics 25, 197-231. The two-equation specification and the separate-estimation convention exactly as documented for HEAVYmodel in the R highfrequency CRAN manual p. 36: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/highfrequency/highfrequency.pdf
params: realized measure fed to HEAVY (RV5, BV5, MedRV, realized kernel, pre-averaged MRC)
D_t thresholds (0 / +0.10 for the breakout branch; -0.10 / -0.15 / -0.25 for the fade branch)
ideas.novelty: Trades the gap between two conditional-variance recursions rather than the level of either. A squeeze-release rule fires on volatility being LOW; this fires on the fast volatility component leading the slow one, which can happen at any volatility level.

ideas.name: Realized GARCH Measurement-Equation Surprise
ideas.entry_rule: For each symbol fit the Realized GARCH(1,1) of Hansen, Huang and Shek on a 1000-day rolling window using daily log returns y_t and the daily realized measure x_t = RV from 5-minute returns: y_t = mu + sigma_t * z_t with z_t i.i.d. mean 0 variance 1; log(sigma_t^2) = w + a * log(x_{t-1}) + b * log(sigma_{t-1}^2); measurement equation log(x_t) = xi + d * log(sigma_t^2) + tau(z_t) + u_t with the leverage function tau(z) = e1*z + e2*(z^2 - 1) and u_t ~ N(0, lam). Each day compute z_hat_t = (y_t - mu_hat)/sigma_hat_t, the measurement residual u_hat_t = log(x_t) - xi_hat - d_hat*log(sigma_hat_t^2) - tau_hat(z_hat_t), and its standardised value utilde_t = u_hat_t / sqrt(lam_hat). QUIET-CHURN LONG: buy at the next open when utilde_t >= +2.0 AND |z_hat_t| <= 0.5. BAD-NEWS SHORT: sell short at the next open when utilde_t >= +2.0 AND z_hat_t <= -1.5.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of day t+5. Exit earlier if the position moves +/- 1.5 * sigma_hat_{t+1} from entry (symmetric take-profit and stop). If a fresh utilde_t >= +2.0 signal in the same direction arrives while in the trade, reset the 5-day clock but do not add size.
inputs: QML estimation of the joint return + measurement likelihood
ideas.why: tau(z) is the news-impact curve: it is exactly the part of today's realized volatility that today's own return direction and magnitude account for, including the leverage asymmetry through e1 < 0. What is left, u_t, is realized variation the price move cannot explain. A day with a huge positive u_t and a near-zero standardised return churned far more variance than either its own conditional volatility level or its direction justify: heavy two-sided flow with no net price change, the classic signature of institutional accumulation or distribution that resolves directionally within a week. The same large u_t alongside a strongly negative z is instead a genuine bad-news repricing where the volatility overshoot confirms rather than contradicts the direction.
ideas.source: Hansen, Huang & Shek (2012), 'Realized GARCH: a joint model for returns and realized measures of volatility', Journal of Applied Econometrics 27, 877-906. Model equations, quadratic Hermite leverage function tau(z) = e1*z + e2*(z^2 - 1), news impact curve nu(z) = d*tau(z), and the factorised joint likelihood as reproduced in the rugarch package vignette 'Introduction to the rugarch package', Section 2.2.9, Eqs. (46)-(53): https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/rugarch/vignettes/Introduction_to_the_rugarch_package.pdf
params: realized measure x_t (RV5, BV, MedRV, realized kernel, pre-averaged MRC)
z threshold for the bad-news branch (-1.0 / -1.5 / -2.0)
ideas.novelty: Trades the RESIDUAL of a volatility measurement equation, not the volatility level or its change. By construction the signal is orthogonal to the day's return, so it cannot be a reskin of any return-based oscillator, and it is orthogonal to the conditional volatility level, so it cannot be a reskin of a squeeze or ATR-expansion rule.

ideas.name: Model Confidence Set Volatility Ensemble
ideas.category: meta-strategy: statistical model selection as the signal
ideas.timeframe: daily, multiple realized measures from 1- and 5-minute bars
ideas.entry_rule: Maintain K = 8 one-day-ahead volatility forecasts per symbol, each a HAR regression RV_{t+1} = b0 + b1*M_t + bw*mean(M over lags 2..5) + bm*mean(M over lags 6..22) fitted on a rolling 500-day window, where M is a different realized measure per model: (1) RV from 5-minute returns; (2) subsampled RV from 1-minute returns averaged over 5 offset grids; (3) MedRV; (4) MinRV; (5) bipower variation; (6) the pre-averaged MRC of Idea 6; (7) a Parzen realized kernel with H = floor(sqrt(M)); (8) SHAR with the RS_plus/RS_minus split of Idea 3. Each day score every model against the realised RV(5-min) with QLIKE loss L = RV/f - log(RV/f) - 1. Over a rolling 250-day window of these loss series run the Hansen-Lunde-Nason Model Confidence Set at alpha = 0.10 using the T_max statistic with 1000 block-bootstrap replications, block length chosen from the maximum number of significant AR(p) coefficients fitted to the loss differentials (minimum 3). Let S_t be the surviving set and f*_t = mean of the forecasts in S_t. RULE: open a new long only when f*_t <= the 60th percentile of f* over the last 250 days. Size the position at target_daily_risk / sqrt(f*_t). If |S_t| = 1, halve that size.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit on a close below the 10-day low, OR when f*_t rises above its 250-day 90th percentile (volatility regime break), OR when the model that was in S_t at entry has been eliminated from S_t for three consecutive days - i.e. the exit is partly governed by the collapse of the forecast that justified the entry, which no fixed-rule exit can express.
ideas.why: Liu, Patton and Sheppard compared over 400 realized measures on 31 assets across five asset classes over 11 years and found that with 5-minute RV as the stated benchmark almost nothing beats it, but under benchmark-free inference some sophisticated measures do win - i.e. which estimator is best is regime-dependent and unknowable ex ante. The Model Confidence Set answers exactly that question with a size-controlled sequential elimination test rather than a beauty contest, and returns a SET rather than a winner. Averaging over the survivors hedges estimator choice, and the width of the set is itself informative: a set that has collapsed to one model means the loss surface has become sharply regime-specific and is likely to shift, which is when a volatility-scaled position is most fragile.
ideas.source: Hansen, Lunde & Nason (2011), 'The Model Confidence Set', Econometrica 79(2), 453-497 - T_max and T_R statistics, block bootstrap, elimination rule; implementation defaults (alpha, B = 1000, statistic, AR-based block length) as in the CRAN MCS package, MCSprocedure and LossVol(QLIKE): https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/MCS/MCS.pdf. Motivation and the estimator comparison from Liu, Patton & Sheppard (2015), 'Does anything beat 5-minute RV? A comparison of realized measures across multiple asset classes', Journal of Econometrics 187, 293-311: https://public.econ.duke.edu/~ap172/Liu_Patton_Sheppard_JoE_2015.pdf
params: loss function (QLIKE vs squared error vs R2LOG)
ideas.novelty: The strategy's own model-selection step is the signal generator. Nothing in the existing 32 makes the identity and cardinality of the surviving forecast set part of the entry, sizing and exit logic.

ideas.name: Pre-Averaged Drift Burst Entry
ideas.entry_rule: Intraday on 1-minute bars, every 60 seconds from 09:45 ET, compute the Christensen-Oomen-Reno drift burst statistic on pre-averaged log returns. Pre-average with g(x) = min(x, 1-x) and horizon k_n = 5: rbar_i = sum_{j=1..k_n-1} g(j/k_n) * r_{i+j}. Spot drift muhat_t = (1/h_n) * sum_i K((t_{i-1} - t)/h_n) * rbar_{i-1} with K a left-sided exponential kernel and h_n = 300 seconds. Spot variance sigmahat_t^2 = (1/h'_n) * [ sum_i (K((t_{i-1} - t)/h'_n) * rbar_{i-1})^2 + 2 * sum_{L=1..L_n} w(L/L_n) * sum_i K((t_{i-1}-t)/h'_n) * K((t_{i+L-1}-t)/h'_n) * rbar_{i-1} * rbar_{i-1+L} ] with w the Parzen kernel, h'_n = 900 seconds, and L_n the Newey-West automatic lag plus 2*(k_n - 1). Statistic Tbar_t = sqrt(h_n / K2) * muhat_t / sigmahat_t, with K2 the squared-kernel constant of the chosen exponential kernel. ENTER LONG at market when Tbar_t exceeds the 99% critical value of the Christensen-Oomen-Reno Appendix B distribution for the number of tests per day (approximately 4.6 for 390 tests) AND the symbol's cumulative volume since the open is at least 1.2x its 20-day average at the same clock time. Mirror for shorts on Tbar_t below the negative critical value.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit when Tbar_t falls back below the 90% critical value (approximately 3.9), or at 15:55 ET, whichever comes first. Hard stop at 1.5 * sigmahat_t * sqrt(1800/h_n) against the entry. Never carry overnight, and never re-enter the same symbol in the same direction on the same day.
ideas.why: The drift burst hypothesis is that flash-crash and flash-rally episodes are locally explosive DRIFTS rather than jumps: the drift-to-volatility ratio diverges over a window of minutes, and the price path is continuous but transiently deterministic. Because the statistic is built from pre-averaged returns with a HAC (Parzen-kernel) long-run variance, it is robust both to microstructure noise and to the serial correlation the pre-averaging itself induces, so it does not fire on bid-ask bounce the way a naive z-score of cumulative return would. The volume confirmation separates genuine flow-driven bursts from thin-book drifts.
ideas.source: Christensen, Oomen & Reno (2022), 'The drift burst hypothesis', Journal of Econometrics 227, 461-497. Test statistic, pre-averaging, HAC variance, default bandwidths and Appendix B critical values exactly as implemented in driftBursts and getCriticalValues in the R highfrequency package, CRAN reference manual pp. 20-22 and 26: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/highfrequency/highfrequency.pdf
ideas.novelty: Not an ATR expansion and not an opening-range break: this is a formal hypothesis test with a nonstandard critical-value distribution on whether the local drift is exploding relative to the local, noise-robust volatility, and the exit is governed by the statistic decaying rather than by price.

ideas.name: Realized Semicorrelation Downside-Concordance Gate
ideas.category: portfolio-level regime gate from realized semicovariance matrices
ideas.entry_rule: Each day, from 15-minute log return vectors over the last 20 trading days across the fleet's N-symbol universe, form the three semicovariance matrices with p(x) = max(x,0) and n(x) = min(x,0): Phat = sum_i p(dX_i) p(dX_i)'; Nhat = sum_i n(dX_i) n(dX_i)'; Mhat = sum_i [ p(dX_i) n(dX_i)' + n(dX_i) p(dX_i)' ]. Note Phat + Nhat + Mhat equals the realized covariance matrix. Scale each into a semicorrelation matrix R = dg(vhat)^-1 * (.) * dg(vhat)^-1 where vhat is the vector of realized volatilities (square roots of the diagonal of the realized covariance matrix), giving R_P, R_N, R_M. Define the downside-concordance index C_t = mean of the off-diagonal entries of R_N minus the mean of the off-diagonal entries of R_P. GATE: allow new long entries from any other strategy in the book only when C_t is below its 250-day 80th percentile.
ideas.exit_rule: When C_t crosses above its 250-day 90th percentile, close half of all long exposure at the next open and place no new longs until C_t falls back below its 250-day 70th percentile. This is a book-level exit that overrides per-name exits; per-name rules continue to govern the remaining half.
inputs: 15-minute OHLCV for every symbol in the universe
ideas.why: Bollerslev, Li, Patton and Quaedvlieg show that the concordant NEGATIVE component of the realized covariance matrix - all names falling together within the same 15-minute window - is the component that spikes in crises and that carries information for forecasting realized covariance beyond total RV. Bollerslev, Patton and Zhang show that clustering S&P 100 names on their realized semicorrelation profiles picks 31 January 2020 as the optimal structural break date, before the price collapse, and produces clusters that cut across conventional industry classifications and differ from clusters built on ordinary realized correlations. A rising R_N relative to R_P is diversification failing specifically in the down direction, which is exactly the state in which a many-name ladder's implicit assumption of independent positions is false and gross exposure needs to come down before any individual name's stop fires.
ideas.source: Bollerslev, Li, Patton & Quaedvlieg (2020), 'Realized Semicovariances', Econometrica 88(4), 1515-1551 (semicovariance matrices, in-fill asymptotics, forecasting content); and Bollerslev, Patton & Zhang (2022), 'Equity clusters through the lens of realized semicorrelations', Economics Letters 211, 110245, Eq. (1) and Sections 2-4 for the semicorrelation scaling and the clustering/break-date evidence. PDF: https://public.econ.duke.edu/~ap172/BPZ_2022_EconLetters.pdf
params: index variant: mean(R_N) - mean(R_P), mean(|R_M|)/mean(R_P + R_N), or the largest eigenvalue of R_N
ideas.novelty: A market-regime gate built from the SIGN STRUCTURE of a covariance matrix rather than from a price index, an index moving average, or a volatility level. It can fire while the index is still making highs, because it measures the direction in which co-movement is concentrating, not the level of co-movement or of price.

ideas.name: Carry Downturn Drawdown Gate
inputs: daily return series of the global carry composite
running maximum of its cumulative return
params: recovery rule (new 21-day high vs fixed fraction of drawdown recovered)
optional exposure ladder rather than binary on/off
ideas.entry_rule: Let r_s be the daily return of the global carry composite (the equal-risk blend of the four carry sleeves). Compute its running drawdown exactly as in the paper: D_t = sum_{s=1..t} r_s - max_{u<=t} sum_{s=1..u} r_s, i.e. cumulative log return minus its own running peak. Maintain the empirical distribution of D over an expanding window starting at least 500 trading days back. The regime is DOWNTURN on day t if D_t is in the worst 20% of that distribution, otherwise EXPANSION. Rule: hold the full carry composite at target risk only while the regime is EXPANSION. On the first close where the regime turns DOWNTURN, cut every carry sleeve to zero at the next open. Optionally, instead of binary, scale exposure linearly from 1.0 at the 50th percentile of D down to 0.0 at the 10th percentile.
ideas.exit_rule: Re-enter at full size at the next open after the regime returns to EXPANSION, defined as D_t rising back above its 20th percentile AND the composite's cumulative return making a new 21-day high (the second condition prevents whipsawing in and out at the threshold). No profit target - this is a gate, not a trade.
ideas.why: Koijen et al identify three 'carry downturns' - Sep-Dec 1992, May 1997-Sep 1998, Nov 2007-Jan 2009 - using precisely this drawdown definition, and show that returns were below average in 23 of 24 sleeve-by-downturn cases. Carry drawdowns are shared across all four asset classes at once and coincide with global recessions and low global liquidity. That means the risk is not diversifiable across sleeves and must instead be timed. The gate converts an unhedgeable common factor into a state variable computed from the strategy's own P&L.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is the strategy's own drawdown percentile, not the price of any traded asset. None of the 32 ideas condition on the equity curve of the strategy itself, and none use a drawdown percentile as a regime switch. This is an exit structure, which the brief explicitly counts as a distinct idea.
ideas.source: Koijen, Moskowitz, Pedersen & Vrugt, 'Carry' (JFE 2018), Section 4: the drawdown is defined as D_t = sum r_s - max_u sum r_s over the global carry1-12 strategy, and the paper documents the three downturns, the 23-of-24 result, and the link to a global recession indicator (mean 0.41 in downturns vs 0.17 in expansions) and to low global liquidity.

ideas.name: Betting Against Beta, Rank-Weighted
inputs: 1-day log returns of each ETF and of the market proxy SPY
ideas.entry_rule: For each asset i in a broad ETF universe (sector SPDRs, size and style ETFs, country ETFs, bond and credit ETFs - at least 25 names), estimate beta the way Frazzini and Pedersen do, estimating volatility and correlation on DIFFERENT windows because correlations move more slowly than volatilities: sigma_i = standard deviation of 1-day log returns over the trailing 252 days; sigma_m = the same for SPY; rho_i = correlation between the asset's and SPY's OVERLAPPING 3-day log returns r3_t = sum_{k=0..2} ln(1+r_{t-k}) over the trailing 1250 days (the 3-day overlap corrects for non-synchronous trading). Then beta_TS_i = rho_i * sigma_i / sigma_m. Shrink toward the cross-sectional mean of 1: beta_i = 0.6 * beta_TS_i + 0.4 * 1.0. Require at least 120 non-missing days for volatility and 750 for correlation, else drop the asset. At each month end rank all N assets ascending by beta_i, let z_i = rank(beta_i) and zbar = mean rank. Weights: w_L = k * (z - zbar)^-, w_H = k * (z - zbar)^+, with k = 2 / sum|z_i - zbar| so each leg's weights sum to 1. Go long the low-beta leg scaled by 1/beta_L and short the high-beta leg scaled by 1/beta_H, where beta_L and beta_H are the weighted-average betas of the two legs, so the book has zero net beta at formation. Enter at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Rebalance every calendar month end to fresh ranks and fresh leg scalings; assets crossing the median beta switch legs. Because the long leg is levered above 1x, apply a hard risk stop: if the book's trailing 21-day realised volatility exceeds 2x its trailing 252-day median, halve both legs until it falls back below 1.5x.
ideas.why: Investors who want more return but face leverage constraints or a leverage aversion bid up high-beta assets instead of levering low-beta ones.
