That bids high-beta prices above fair value and leaves low-beta assets cheap, so the security market line is flatter than CAPM predicts. Levering the cheap low-beta leg and shorting the expensive high-beta leg harvests the difference. The strategy is a bet on the slope of the security market line, not on the market's direction, which is why the legs are explicitly beta-neutralised.
ideas.novelty: The corpus has no risk-based or defensive signal at all, and no cross-sectional ranking construction. The distinctive mechanics here are the split estimation windows (1-year vol, 5-year correlation on 3-day overlapped returns), Vasicek shrinkage toward 1, rank-proportional weights, and per-leg beta scaling - none of which resemble a moving-average or oscillator rule.
ideas.source: Frazzini & Pedersen, 'Betting Against Beta' (JFE 2014; PDF fetched from https://w4.stern.nyu.edu/facdir/lpederse/papers/BettingAgainstBeta.pdf). Equation (14) gives beta = rho * sigma_i / sigma_m; the text specifies 1-year rolling volatility on 1-day log returns, 5-year correlation on overlapping 3-day log returns, minima of 120 and 750 observations. Equation (15) sets shrinkage w = 0.6 toward a cross-sectional mean of 1. Equation (16) gives the rank weights and the text states both legs are rescaled to a beta of one at formation, rebalanced every calendar month.

ideas.name: Betting Against Correlation
inputs: 1-day log returns of each ETF and SPY
params: number of volatility buckets for the neutralising sort (3 or 5)
ideas.entry_rule: Use the Frazzini-Pedersen identity beta_i = rho_i * (sigma_i / sigma_m) and trade ONLY the correlation term. Estimate rho_i as the correlation between asset i's and SPY's overlapping 3-day log returns over the trailing 1250 days, and sigma_i as the 252-day standard deviation of 1-day log returns. At each month end, first sort the ETF universe into 3 equal-count buckets by sigma_i. WITHIN each volatility bucket, rank assets by rho_i and form rank weights w = k*(rank(rho) - mean rank) with the negative part as the long leg and the positive part as the short leg, each summing to 1. Aggregate the three buckets by equal weight, so the resulting book is long low-correlation assets and short high-correlation assets while being neutral to volatility by construction. Scale the long and short legs by 1/beta_L and 1/beta_H (betas computed as in the BAB idea) so the book is beta-neutral at formation. Enter at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Full rebalance every 21 trading days to fresh within-bucket ranks and fresh leg scalings. Flatten the book if realised correlation dispersion collapses - specifically, if the cross-sectional standard deviation of rho_i across the universe falls below its own 20th percentile over the trailing 750 days, since the signal then has no cross-sectional content; re-enter when it rises back above the 40th percentile.
ideas.why: Asness, Frazzini, Gormsen and Pedersen argue the beta anomaly is not one effect but two, because beta is mechanically the product of correlation and relative volatility. The correlation component and the volatility component have different economic drivers: low-correlation assets are the ones a leverage-constrained investor should hold most of and cannot, so leverage constraints bite hardest there, whereas the volatility component is contaminated by lottery-seeking demand for high-volatility assets. Isolating correlation therefore isolates the leverage-constraint channel, which is the one with a coherent theory behind it.
ideas.novelty: Sorting on the correlation half of beta while holding volatility fixed is a genuinely different entry rule from sorting on beta or on volatility. It will hold high-volatility assets long whenever they are also low-correlation, which a low-volatility or low-beta screen would never do. The corpus has no correlation-based cross-sectional signal of any kind.
ideas.source: Concept from Asness, Frazzini, Gormsen & Pedersen, 'Betting Against Correlation: Testing Theories of the Low-Risk Effect' (Journal of Financial Economics 2020). I could NOT open the full text of this paper - the Pedersen, AQR and Wiley copies all returned 403/404 - so the construction above is my reconstruction of the BAC factor from the beta decomposition and estimation windows that I did verify in the Frazzini-Pedersen BAB paper (https://w4.stern.nyu.edu/facdir/lpederse/papers/BettingAgainstBeta.pdf, equation 14). Treat the within-volatility-bucket sort as my specification rather than a verbatim replication.

ideas.name: Correlation-Volatility Corner Portfolio
inputs: 1250-day correlation of overlapping 3-day log returns vs SPY
params: equal-weight vs inverse-volatility weighting within corners
ideas.entry_rule: At each month end, independently double-sort the ETF universe into a 3x3 grid on rho_i (1250-day correlation with SPY using overlapping 3-day log returns) and sigma_i (252-day standard deviation of 1-day log returns). Go long the LOW-correlation / HIGH-volatility corner and short the HIGH-correlation / LOW-volatility corner, equal-weighting within each corner. Note that both corners contain assets with roughly the SAME beta, because beta = rho * sigma/sigma_m and the two sorts move in opposite directions - so this book is close to beta-neutral without any explicit scaling, and it is a pure bet on which half of beta carries the premium. Enter at the next open with equal dollars long and short.
ideas.exit_rule: Full rebalance every 21 trading days. Additionally, verify the neutrality assumption each rebalance: compute the weighted-average shrunk beta of each corner, and if they differ by more than 0.15, scale the higher-beta corner down by the ratio of the two betas before entering. Flatten entirely if fewer than 3 assets populate either corner.
ideas.why: If the low-risk effect is driven by leverage constraints then correlation is what matters and this book should make money; if it is driven by lottery demand for volatile assets then volatility is what matters and this book should lose money. Because the two corners are beta-matched, the trade is a clean horse race between the two competing explanations rather than another way of buying safety. That makes it informative even when it does not pay, which is unusual for a trading rule.
ideas.novelty: A double sort producing a beta-neutral corner portfolio is an entry structure the corpus does not contain. Critically, it deliberately buys high-volatility assets, which is the opposite of what every defensive rule does, and is only sensible once beta is decomposed.
ideas.source: Constructed from the beta decomposition beta = rho * sigma_i/sigma_m in Frazzini & Pedersen, 'Betting Against Beta' (JFE 2014), equation (14), applied to the research question posed by Asness, Frazzini, Gormsen & Pedersen, 'Betting Against Correlation' (JFE 2020), which separates the beta anomaly into correlation and volatility components. The specific corner-portfolio implementation is my own synthesis - I could not open the BAC paper's full text to check whether they use this exact form.

ideas.name: Five-Year Reversal Value Everywhere
inputs: daily closes going back at least 1400 trading days
params: averaging window endpoints (1134 and 1386 trading days, i.e. 4.5-5.5 years)
ideas.entry_rule: For every asset i in a cross-asset ETF universe (equity country and sector ETFs, bond and credit ETFs, commodity ETFs, currency ETFs - at least 20 names), compute the value signal exactly as Asness, Moskowitz and Pedersen define it for asset classes that have no book value: V_i,t = ln( mean(close_i over trading days t-1386 to t-1134) / close_i,t ). That is the log of the average price 4.5 to 5.5 years ago divided by today's price, which is essentially the negative of the 5-year return, and the 12-month averaging window smooths out the endpoint. A high V_i means the asset is cheap. At each month end rank all N assets by V_i and set weights w_i = c_t * (rank(V_i) - mean rank), with c_t scaling the portfolio to one dollar long and one dollar short. Enter at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Full rebalance to fresh rank weights every 21 trading days; positions whose rank crosses the cross-sectional mean flip sign. No individual stop - the signal is deliberately slow and a stop would cut exactly the losers the strategy is designed to accumulate. Portfolio-level circuit breaker: halve exposure if the book's 63-day return is below its own 5th percentile over the trailing 1250 days.
ideas.why: Book-to-market does not exist for commodities, currencies or bonds, so AMP needed a value measure computable from prices alone, and the negative of the 5-year return turns out to be an excellent stand-in - in US stocks a value factor built from negative 5-year returns has a 0.83 correlation with one built from book-to-market sorts. Economically it is long-horizon overreaction: assets that have underperformed for half a decade have had their discount rates pushed up and subsequently mean-revert. Crucially the 5-year horizon is long enough that it does not collide with 1-12 month momentum; the two are negatively correlated.
ideas.novelty: This is not a mean-reversion oscillator. The lookback is 4.5 to 5.5 years, it deliberately excludes the recent past, it is applied cross-sectionally across asset classes rather than to a single instrument, and it is rank-weighted. No existing idea in the 32 uses a lookback longer than a year or ranks across a universe.
ideas.source: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen, 'Value and Momentum Everywhere' (Journal of Finance 2013; PDF fetched from https://w4.stern.nyu.edu/facdir/lpederse/papers/ValMomEverywhere.pdf), p. 938: for commodities value is 'the log of the spot price 5 years ago (actually, the average spot price from 4.5 to 5.5 years ago), divided by the most recent spot price'; the paper reports a 0.83 correlation between US stock portfolios formed on negative 5-year returns and those formed on BE/ME. Equation (1) gives the rank-weighting w_it = c_t(rank(S_it) - mean rank).

ideas.name: Netted Value-Momentum Combination
inputs: daily closes back to 1400 trading days
ideas.entry_rule: On the SAME cross-asset ETF universe, compute two rank-weight vectors each month end. VALUE: V_i = ln( mean(close_i over days t-1386 to t-1134) / close_i,t ), weights w_V,i = c_t*(rank(V_i) - mean rank) scaled to $1 long / $1 short. MOMENTUM: M_i = ln(close_i,t-21 / close_i,t-252), the 2-to-12-month return skipping the most recent month, weights w_M,i = c_t*(rank(M_i) - mean rank) scaled the same way. Final position in asset i is w_i = 0.5*w_V,i + 0.5*w_M,i, computed BEFORE any trade is placed so the two books net against each other at the position level rather than being run as two separate portfolios. An asset that is both cheap and rising gets roughly double weight; an asset that is cheap but still falling nets to approximately zero and is not traded at all. Enter the netted target at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Recompute the netted target every 21 trading days and trade only the difference from the current book, which materially cuts turnover versus running the two sleeves separately. A position exits naturally when the two signals disagree enough to net it to below 0.2% of capital. Portfolio-level gate: cut the momentum half of the blend to zero whenever the Factor Autocorrelation Regime Gate (separate idea) is negative, leaving value running alone.
ideas.why: AMP's central result is not that value works or that momentum works but that they are strongly negatively correlated everywhere, so a 50/50 blend has a much higher Sharpe ratio than either alone and the blend is what should be traded. Netting at the position level rather than the portfolio level is what captures this: the negative correlation shows up as offsetting orders that never get placed, so the investor gets the diversification without paying the turnover for it. The economics are that value is long-horizon overreaction correcting and momentum is short-horizon underreaction continuing - opposite behavioural errors at opposite horizons, so their errors offset.
ideas.novelty: The distinct element is the netting structure and the deliberately opposite horizons (4.5-5.5 years against 2-12 months) applied to one universe. The corpus has no multi-signal netted portfolio and no construction where two signals cancel into a no-trade.
ideas.source: Asness, Moskowitz & Pedersen, 'Value and Momentum Everywhere' (Journal of Finance 2013), equation (3): r_COMBO = 0.5*r_VALUE + 0.5*r_MOM; equation (1) for rank weights; p. 938 for the 5-year value proxy and the choice of MOM2-12 as the momentum measure (the paper explicitly defends 2-12 over 7-12, citing Novy-Marx 2012 and Goyal & Wahal 2012).

ideas.name: Volatility-Scaled Time-Series Momentum
inputs: exponentially weighted variance with 60-day centre of mass
params: holding period h (1 month default, sweep 1-12)
annual volatility target (40% per instrument default)
ideas.entry_rule: For each instrument, estimate ex ante annualised variance with the exact Moskowitz-Ooi-Pedersen model: sigma_t^2 = 261 * sum_{i>=0} (1-d) * d^i * (r_{t-1-i} - rbar_t)^2, where r are 1-day log returns, rbar_t is the exponentially weighted mean computed with the same weights, and d is set so the centre of mass d/(1-d) = 60 days, i.e. d = 60/61 = 0.98361. Use sigma_{t-1} against day-t returns so there is no look-ahead. At each month end (every 21st trading day), take the sign of the trailing 12-month cumulative excess return, S_i = sign(ln(close_t/close_{t-252}) - 252*rf_daily), where rf_daily comes from the BIL ex-dividend gap yield. Position size in dollars is N_i = (target_vol / sigma_i,t-1) * S_i * capital, with target_vol = 40% annualised. Enter at the next open. To avoid a single monthly rebalance date dominating results, run h overlapping sub-portfolios: the position held on any day is the average of the positions implied by formation dates t-21, t-42, ... t-21h.
ideas.exit_rule: Each sub-portfolio is held exactly h months and then replaced by a freshly formed one, so the aggregate position turns over gradually rather than all at once - a sign flip therefore scales the book out over h months instead of reversing it in a day. Between rebalances the dollar position is re-sized daily as sigma_i changes, so a volatility spike automatically shrinks the position without any stop being hit. Hard exit: close a sub-portfolio early only if the instrument stops trading or fails a liquidity screen.
ideas.why: Moskowitz, Ooi and Pedersen document significant return continuation at every lag from 1 to 12 months across 58 futures markets and reversal thereafter, which they attribute to initial under-reaction followed by delayed over-reaction, plus the position flows of hedgers and speculators. The reason to specify this as a separate idea from any moving-average rule is the risk model: sizing at a constant ex ante volatility target is what makes the returns aggregate sensibly across instruments with wildly different volatilities, and it produces automatic de-risking in crises that a fixed-size trend rule does not have.
ideas.novelty: The entry is the sign of a 12-month return, not a crossover, and there is no smoothing of price at all. The genuinely new element for this corpus is the exit and sizing structure: an EWMA-variance-targeted dollar position that is re-sized daily, plus overlapping sub-portfolios so entries and exits are staggered rather than binary. That is a different exit structure, which the brief counts as a distinct idea.
ideas.source: Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen, 'Time Series Momentum' (Journal of Financial Economics 104, 2012, 228-250; PDF fetched from https://w4.stern.nyu.edu/facdir/lpederse/papers/TimeSeriesMomentum.pdf). Section 2.4 equation (1) gives the ex ante volatility model with the 261 annualisation scalar and the centre-of-mass 60-day weighting; Section 3.2 specifies the sign rule, the position size inversely proportional to sigma_{t-1}, and the Jegadeesh-Titman overlapping-portfolio averaging used to avoid overlapping observations.

ideas.name: Factor Autocorrelation Regime Gate
inputs: monthly returns of K factor ETF spreads
expanding-window mean and standard deviation per factor
params: expanding vs rolling window for mu and sigma
ideas.entry_rule: Using the same K factor ETF spread series as the Time-Series Factor Momentum idea, compute for each factor f at each month end: r_t = factor f's return this month; r_minus_t = the mean of factor f's monthly returns from month t-12 to t-1; mu_f and sigma_f = factor f's mean and standard deviation of monthly returns over an expanding window of at least 60 months. Then rho_auto,f,t = (r_minus_t * r_t - mu_f^2) / (sigma_f^2 / sqrt(12)). The aggregate factor autocorrelation index A_t is the cross-sectional average of rho_auto,f,t over all K factors. A_t > 0 means the average factor moved this month in the same direction it moved over the prior year. Rule: run all momentum-family strategies at full size only while A_t > 0. When A_t <= 0 at a month end, cut every momentum-family position to zero at the next open. The gate applies to time-series factor momentum, cross-sectional momentum, and the momentum half of any value-momentum blend; it does NOT gate value or carry.
ideas.exit_rule: Re-enter momentum exposure at full size at the next open after A_t turns positive at a month end. Optional linear form instead of binary: scale momentum exposure by clip(A_t / A_90, 0, 1) where A_90 is the 90th percentile of A over the expanding history, which avoids all-or-nothing switching. As a gate it has no profit target of its own.
ideas.why: Ehsani and Linnainmaa show that momentum crashes are not random: splitting their 1964-2015 sample on the sign of this index, UMD averaged +2.4% per month with 3.3% volatility in the positive-autocorrelation regime and -1.6% per month with 4.4% volatility in the negative regime, and the 5th percentile of UMD returns was -1.9% in the positive regime against -8.8% in the negative one. Almost the entire left tail of momentum concentrates in negative-index months, and they report that a one-unit increase in the index lowers the probability of a momentum crash by 15% (z = -6.78). The mechanism is that momentum is an accumulation of factor autocorrelations, so when factors collectively turn against their own past, every momentum expression breaks at once.
ideas.novelty: The state variable is the cross-sectional average autocorrelation of a set of long-short factor returns - a quantity that is not a price, a volatility, or a trend of any traded asset. Nothing in the 32 conditions on anything like it, and unlike a volatility filter it specifically anticipates the direction-reversal risk that kills momentum rather than the variance risk.
ideas.source: Ehsani & Linnainmaa, 'Factor Momentum and the Momentum Factor' (Journal of Finance 2022; NBER WP 25551). Equation (11) defines a factor's monthly autocorrelation as (r_minus_t * r_t - mu^2)/(sigma^2/sqrt(12)) with the formation period running from t-12 to t-1, and the aggregate index as the cross-sectional average. Figure 4 and the surrounding text report the +2.4%/-1.6% conditional means, the 3.3%/4.4% volatilities, the -1.9%/-8.8% fifth percentiles, and Appendix A.5 the 15% crash-probability result.

ideas.name: Factor Valuation Percentile Timing
inputs: daily closes of paired factor ETFs
params: overlay strength (full tilt vs half tilt)
ideas.entry_rule: Using the same K factor ETF spread series, proxy each factor's relative valuation with the quantity Arnott et al call the factor's relative price, measured from bars alone: P_f,t = sum of factor f's daily log returns over the trailing 1260 trading days (5 years). A factor whose long leg has strongly outperformed its short leg over five years has seen its value spread compress and is therefore expensive; the reverse means cheap. Convert to a percentile: q_f,t = the rank of P_f,t within factor f's OWN history of P over an expanding window starting at least 1260 days after inception, expressed in [0,1]. Rule: at each month end, go long the factor spreads in the bottom tercile of q (cheap factors, q < 1/3) and short those in the top tercile (expensive factors, q > 2/3), equal-weighted, each sized to equal dollar risk by its own 252-day volatility. Factors in the middle tercile are not traded. Enter at the next open. Run the honest null alongside it: the same book with the sign flipped is factor momentum, so a single backtest adjudicates the Arnott-versus-Asness dispute on our data.
ideas.exit_rule: Rebalance monthly to fresh terciles; a factor exits when q moves into the middle tercile. Because valuation signals are extremely slow, impose a minimum holding period of 6 months per factor to stop the tercile boundary generating churn. Portfolio stop: flatten if the book's trailing 252-day return is below its own 10th percentile since inception, since a sustained loss here is the signature of the momentum-dominates-valuation world in which the trade is simply wrong.
ideas.why: Arnott, Beck, Kalesnik and West argue that most of the historical return to smart-beta factors came from rising valuations rather than from the factor premium, and that buying factors when they are cheap relative to their own history and avoiding them when expensive should therefore add value. Asness, Ilmanen and Maloney counter that this timing is far weaker than advertised and is largely redundant with simply owning value, and Asness's 'Siren Song of Factor Timing' argues the whole exercise is close to a value trade in disguise. Haddad, Kozak and Santosh sit in between: they find factor returns genuinely are predictable by their own valuations. The corpus contains dozens of factor-like signals and no layer that decides how much of each to run, so this is worth resolving empirically even though the literature disagrees.
ideas.novelty: The signal is the percentile of a factor's own 5-year cumulative spread return within its own full history - a valuation-style measure applied to a strategy rather than to an asset. That is a different object from anything in the 32, all of which signal on asset prices. Note this is deliberately the OPPOSITE sign to the 12-month factor momentum idea, at a much longer horizon, which is exactly the value-versus-momentum horizon split.
ideas.source: Arnott, Beck, Kalesnik & West, 'How Can Smart Beta Go Horribly Wrong?' (Research Affiliates, 2016) versus Asness, Ilmanen & Maloney, 'Market Timing: Sin a Little' (Journal of Investment Management 2017) and Asness, 'The Siren Song of Factor Timing' (Journal of Portfolio Management 2016). I could not open the Research Affiliates article - the URL now redirects to a dead page - so the relative-price percentile proxy for the factor value spread is my own OHLCV-only substitute for the book-to-market spread those papers use; the direction of the proposed trade follows their stated argument. Haddad, Kozak & Santosh, 'Factor Timing' (RFS 2020; NBER WP 26708) independently confirms that anomaly portfolios are predictable by their own valuation ratios.

ideas.name: Principal-Component Factor Timing
inputs: monthly returns of K factor ETF spreads
params: number of PCs retained (5 default, sweep 3-8)
valuation lookback for each PC (60 months)
ideas.entry_rule: Take the K factor ETF spread series as monthly return vectors. At each month end, using an expanding window of at least 60 months, standardise each factor's returns to unit variance, compute the covariance matrix, and extract the first 5 principal components; fix each eigenvector's sign so its largest-magnitude loading is positive, and carry the previous month's eigenvectors forward by aligning each new one to its predecessor by maximum absolute correlation so the PCs do not arbitrarily flip month to month. Each PC p has a return series r_p,t = e_p' * r_t. Predict each PC's next-month return with its OWN valuation proxy: x_p,t = the z-score, over the expanding history, of minus the trailing 60-month cumulative return of PC p (so a PC that has run up a long way scores negative, i.e. expensive). Estimate b_p by expanding-window OLS of r_p,t+1 on x_p,t, and form the predicted return mu_p,t = b_p * x_p,t. Hold PC p with weight proportional to mu_p,t / var(r_p), i.e. a mean-variance weight across the 5 PCs, then map back to factor positions via w = sum_p weight_p * e_p, and scale the whole book to a 10% annualised volatility target. Enter at the next open.
ideas.exit_rule: Rebalance monthly, recomputing eigenvectors, regressions and weights. Because the PC definitions themselves drift, force a full liquidation and re-entry rather than incremental trading whenever the correlation between this month's and last month's leading eigenvector falls below 0.8, which signals the factor structure has genuinely changed. Cut the book to zero if the realised out-of-sample R-squared of the predictions, tracked on a 36-month rolling basis, turns negative.
ideas.why: Haddad, Kozak and Santosh's key argument is that expected returns must load mostly on the LARGEST sources of return variation, because otherwise small, near-arbitrage components would be wildly predictable and generate implausible Sharpe ratios. Restricting attention to the first five PCs, which explain about 60% of the variation in their 50 anomaly portfolios, is therefore not just a statistical convenience but an economic restriction that stabilises estimation. Empirically it works: they find the first and fourth PCs are predictable by their own valuation ratios with out-of-sample R-squared around 4% per month, roughly four times that of predicting the aggregate market, and that predicting each anomaly separately with its own valuation captures only half as much. Their pure factor timing portfolio achieves a Sharpe ratio of 0.71.
ideas.novelty: The traded objects are principal components of a set of long-short factor spreads, and the dimension reduction is the source of the edge rather than an efficiency measure. Nothing in the corpus performs an eigendecomposition or trades a latent combination of strategies, and the entry logic - regress each component on its own valuation, then mean-variance weight the components - has no analogue among the 32.
ideas.source: Haddad, Kozak & Santosh, 'Factor Timing' (Review of Financial Studies 2020; NBER Working Paper 26708, fetched from https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w26708/w26708.pdf). The paper restricts attention to the first five PCs of 50 anomaly portfolios explaining about 60% of realised return variation, uses only each portfolio's own book-to-market ratio as the predictor, reports out-of-sample monthly R-squared around 4% for the first and fourth PCs and about 1% in total, notes that predicting each anomaly separately yields only half the predictability, and reports a 0.71 Sharpe ratio for the pure factor timing portfolio. The 5-year cumulative PC return substitutes for the book-to-market spread, which we cannot observe.

ideas.name: Two-Speed Wald Sentinel
ideas.timeframe: any (test runs on daily aggregation of the base signal's P&L; base signal may be 1/5/15-min or daily)
ideas.entry_rule: For each sub-strategy s, build its per-bar realised return series r_t (mark-to-market P&L of s's positions divided by capital at risk) over a rolling window of T = 750 bars. Regress r_t on a constant only. For every candidate break index tau in [0.15T, 0.85T] (Andrews' recommended symmetric 15% trimming) compute the Chow/Wald statistic W(tau) for equality of the pre- and post-tau means, using a Newey-West HAC variance with lag = floor(4*(T/100)^(2/9)). Form TWO statistics: supW = max_tau W(tau), and avgW = mean_tau W(tau) over the same trimmed grid. Convert each to a p-value by the Hansen (1997) approximate-asymptotic method (as Stata's estat sbsingle does), or equivalently by stationary bootstrap of r_t with 500 draws and mean block length 20. State machine, evaluated once per day at the close: s is HEALTHY if p(avgW) > 0.10 and p(supW) > 0.05; s is DECAYING if p(avgW) <= 0.10 and p(supW) > 0.05; s is BROKEN if p(supW) <= 0.05 AND mean(r_t) after the argmax break tau_hat is <= 0. New entries: take s's own entry signal at the next bar's open at 100% of base size when HEALTHY, at 40% of base size when DECAYING, and take no new entries when BROKEN.
ideas.exit_rule: Use s's own exit rule normally. Additionally: on the bar s first transitions to BROKEN, flatten every position belonging to s at the next open regardless of its own exit. Re-arming requires 60 consecutive daily evaluations with p(supW) > 0.05 and post-break mean > 0, after which s resumes at 40% size and steps to 100% after a further 60 HEALTHY days.
inputs: OHLCV bars of the traded symbols (to reconstruct the sub-strategy's own P&L series)
rolling per-bar strategy return series r_t
Hansen (1997) p-value approximation or a stationary bootstrap
params: supW p-value threshold for the kill (0.01 / 0.05)
ideas.why: Published anomalies do not usually die with a bang; they bleed. Stata's own documentation of the Andrews (1993) family notes that supremum tests have much less power than average and exponential tests, and that the average test is optimal when the alternative is a SMALL change in parameter values while the exponential/supremum test is optimal for a LARGE break. Gradual crowding-driven alpha decay is precisely the small-change alternative, so a single sup-test will keep passing a strategy all the way down to zero alpha. Running both tests and giving them different jobs - the average test governs position size, the supremum test governs the kill switch - matches the test's power profile to the failure mode it is best at catching.
ideas.source: Andrews, D.W.K. (1993), 'Tests for parameter instability and structural change with unknown change point', Econometrica 61:821-856; Andrews & Ploberger (1994) Econometrica 62:1383-1414; Hansen, B.E. (1997) JBES 15:60-67 for the p-value approximation. Implementation conventions (15% default trimming, avg/exp/sup variants, Hansen p-values) taken verbatim from the Stata manual entry estat sbsingle, https://www.stata.com/manuals/tsestatsbsingle.pdf
ideas.novelty: Not a moving-average cross or an oscillator at all - it is a parameter-stability test on the strategy's own P&L with an unknown break location, and it deliberately runs two tests with different power profiles and wires them to two different actions (size vs kill). Distinct from the corpus's single Page-Hinkley overlay, which is a one-sided sequential CUSUM with a fixed drift parameter and no break-location search or calibrated p-value.

ideas.name: Bai-Perron Last-Segment Allocator
ideas.timeframe: daily evaluation; base signal any timeframe
ideas.entry_rule: Once per month, for each sub-strategy s, fit a Bai-Perron multiple-mean-shift model to s's daily return series over the last 2000 bars: minimum segment length h = 60 bars, maximum number of breaks m = 5. Select the number of breaks m* by sequential sup-F(l+1|l) tests at the 5% level, confirmed by BIC (take the smaller of the two answers). This partitions the history into m*+1 segments. Compute the annualised Sharpe ratio of ONLY the most recent segment, SR_last = mean(r)/std(r) * sqrt(252), using just the bars since the last estimated break date. Set s's risk weight w_s = clip(SR_last / 1.0, 0, 1). If the last segment has fewer than 60 bars, use the pooled mean of the last two segments instead. Take s's own entry signal at the next bar's open, sized at w_s * base size. If w_s = 0, take no entries for s that month.
ideas.exit_rule: s's own exit rule. Additionally, re-run the break detection daily on the last 500 bars only; if a NEW break is detected whose break date falls within the last 5 bars and whose post-break segment mean is negative, flatten all of s's positions at the next open and set w_s = 0 until the next monthly rebalance.
inputs: Bai-Perron dynamic-programming break estimator with sequential sup-F(l+1|l) and BIC
ideas.why: Every allocation decision in a 578-idea corpus defaults to using full-sample backtest Sharpe. If anomalies really lose a third to a half of their return after they become known, the full-sample number is a weighted average of a dead regime and a live one, and it systematically overweights the ideas whose alpha is furthest in the past. Estimating where the breaks actually are and then throwing away everything before the most recent one gives an allocation statistic that is unbiased for the regime the capital will actually be deployed in. Alexander & Fabozzi's split dates for factors such as Debt Issuance (2016), Seasonality (2016) and Momentum (2022) show these breaks are locatable and recent.
ideas.source: Bai, J. & Perron, P. (1998) Econometrica 66:47-78 and (2003) Journal of Applied Econometrics 18:1-22, sequential sup-F(l+1|l) testing for multiple unknown breaks; empirical motivation from Alexander, N. & Fabozzi, F.J., 'Measuring Strategy-Decay Risk: Minimum Regime Performance and the Durability of Systematic Investing', arXiv:2604.08356, Exhibit 3 (per-factor split dates and left/right Sharpe ratios).
ideas.novelty: Uses only the post-final-break sample to size the strategy, rather than a rolling window of arbitrary fixed length. A rolling window blends across breaks by construction; this one refuses to. It is also multiple-break rather than single-break, so a strategy that already died and partly recovered is not evaluated against its pre-death mean.

ideas.name: Minimum Regime Performance Gate
ideas.timeframe: daily evaluation; base signal any timeframe
ideas.entry_rule: For sub-strategy s with daily return series r_1..r_T (use the longest available history, backtest plus live concatenated), compute MRP with one split: define d = 500 bars as the minimum segment length, and MRP1(s) = min over tau in [d, T-d] of min( SR(r_1..r_tau), SR(r_{tau+1}..r_T) ), where SR is the annualised Sharpe ratio of the segment. This is Alexander & Fabozzi's Eq. 3-4 with s = 1 split. Recompute on the first trading day of each month. A sub-strategy is ELIGIBLE if MRP1(s) >= -0.10. Take s's own entry signal at the next bar's open, sized at base * clip((MRP1(s) + 0.5) / 1.0, 0.2, 1.0). Ineligible strategies take no new entries.
ideas.exit_rule: s's own exit rule. Additionally, flatten all of s's positions and retire s for 63 trading days whenever the current month's MRP1(s) has fallen by more than 0.25 Sharpe points relative to MRP1(s) measured three months earlier - a worsening worst regime, which is the paper's stated early-warning signal.
inputs: per-strategy daily return series (backtest and live concatenated)
annualised Sharpe ratio over arbitrary sub-samples
params: history lookback (10 / 20 / 40 years, or max available)
month-over-month MRP deterioration trigger (0.15 / 0.25 / 0.40 Sharpe points)
ideas.why: MRP is the worst Sharpe ratio a strategy has ever realised over ANY admissible partition of its history - the authors call it the expected shortfall of model efficacy. It answers the question the corpus cannot currently answer: not 'did this make money on average' but 'how bad does it get when the supporting relationship weakens'. Their headline empirical result is directly relevant to allocating across 578 ideas: high full-sample Sharpe does not imply high MRP, and several factors with the best full-sample numbers (Debt Issuance SR 1.14, MRP -0.05; Investment SR 0.45, MRP -1.01) are strictly dominated on the decay-risk frontier. Ranking a large corpus by backtest Sharpe therefore systematically buys fragility.
ideas.source: Alexander, N. & Fabozzi, F.J., 'Measuring Strategy-Decay Risk: Minimum Regime Performance and the Durability of Systematic Investing', arXiv:2604.08356, Eqs. 3-4 and Exhibits 3-4 (decay-risk frontier). Code repository cited by the authors: github.com/nolanalexander/minimum_regime_performance
ideas.novelty: The gate statistic is a minimax over split points, not a mean or a rolling window. Unlike a structural-break test it does not ask whether a break is statistically significant - it just reports how bad the worst half was, which makes it robust when the number of observations is too small for a break test to have power. The deterioration-of-the-minimum trigger is a second-order signal no level-based monitor produces.

ideas.name: MinTRL Probation Sizing
ideas.entry_rule: For each sub-strategy s, using ONLY its live (post-deployment) per-bar return series, compute the per-bar Sharpe SR = mean(r)/std(r), the sample skewness g3 and the RAW kurtosis g4 (excess kurtosis + 3). Compute the Minimum Track Record Length: MinTRL = 1 + [ 1 - g3*SR + ((g4 - 1)/4)*SR^2 ] * ( Phi^{-1}(1 - alpha) / SR )^2 with alpha = 0.05 so Phi^{-1}(0.95) = 1.645. Let T_live be the number of live bars observed so far. Sizing rule, recomputed at each day's close: if SR <= 0, s takes no new entries; if SR > 0 and T_live < MinTRL, s is on PROBATION and takes its own entry signal at 25% of base size; if T_live >= MinTRL, s takes its own entry signal at 100% of base size. Entries execute at the next bar's open on s's own trigger.
ideas.exit_rule: s's own exit rule. Additionally: retire s permanently (no re-entry) if it is still on probation after 3 * MinTRL_initial bars, where MinTRL_initial is the value computed at the end of the first 60 live bars - i.e. the strategy has had three times the length of evidence it needed and still cannot clear the bar. Flatten immediately at the next open if live SR turns negative while on probation.
params: benchmark Sharpe SR* (0 or the strategy's costed break-even)
ideas.why: The corpus has 578 ideas and will inevitably deploy many of them on short live histories. MinTRL answers exactly the right question - how many bars of live track record are needed before an observed Sharpe is statistically distinguishable from zero at a stated confidence - and it does so accounting for skewness and fat tails, which matters enormously for the corpus's many stop-loss-heavy and breakout strategies whose returns are strongly negatively skewed. Negative skew and high kurtosis inflate MinTRL sharply, so a strategy that makes many small wins and occasional large losses is correctly forced to earn a much longer probation than a symmetric one before it gets full capital.
ideas.source: Bailey, D.H. & Lopez de Prado, M. (2012), 'The Sharpe Ratio Efficient Frontier' (Minimum Track Record Length). Formula reproduced verbatim as Eq. (1) in Santoni, M.L., Jouanne, V. & Scullin, M.L., 'Equity Strategy Backtesting: Luck or Edge? The MinervaScore as a Statistical Robustness Grade', arXiv:2608.23808, which also notes MinTRL depends only on the single strategy and must not be confused with Minimum Backtest Length MinBTL ~= 2*ln(N)/E[max]^2.
ideas.novelty: Sizes by how much EVIDENCE exists, not by how good the performance looks. It is monotone in track length and in the moments of the return distribution, so it automatically penalises the negatively-skewed strategies in the corpus. Nothing in a Sharpe-threshold or drawdown-threshold monitor has this property.

ideas.name: Regime Composite Rho Gate
ideas.timeframe: daily evaluation; base signal any timeframe
ideas.entry_rule: For sub-strategy s, partition its most recent 252 daily returns into K = 12 consecutive non-overlapping windows of 21 bars each. Compute the annualised Sharpe ratio SR_k of each window. Then compute the three components: p_plus = (number of windows with SR_k > 0)/K; s_SR = sample standard deviation of {SR_1..SR_K}; SR_min = min_k SR_k. Form rho = 0.5*p_plus + 0.3*clip_[0,1](1 - s_SR/2) + 0.2*logistic(SR_min), where logistic(x) = 1/(1+exp(-x)) and the final rho is clipped to [0,1] (this is Eq. 3 of the MinervaScore paper, with the reference dispersion scale sigma_ref = 2). Recompute daily. s may take new entries only when rho >= 0.60 (the paper's tau_rho gate). Size = base * clip((rho - 0.60)/0.30, 0.25, 1.0). Entries fire on s's own trigger at the next bar's open.
ideas.exit_rule: s's own exit rule. Additionally: flatten all of s's positions at the next open when rho falls below 0.50, and keep s flat until rho has been >= 0.65 for 21 consecutive trading days.
ideas.why: A strategy whose whole year of alpha came from three good weeks and nine flat ones has the same annual Sharpe as one that earned steadily, but a completely different survival probability. Rho decomposes that into three observable things - how OFTEN the strategy works (p_plus), how CONSISTENTLY (1 - dispersion), and how bad the worst window was (SR_min) - and combines them on a bounded 0-1 scale that can be thresholded and compared across the whole corpus. It is the one component of the MinervaScore that directly targets the failure mode this gap is about: evidence concentrated in a single regime. The paper's own honesty about this gate being its most heuristic component is a reason to sweep the weights, not to skip it.
ideas.source: Santoni, M.L., Jouanne, V. & Scullin, M.L., 'Equity Strategy Backtesting: Luck or Edge? The MinervaScore as a Statistical Robustness Grade', arXiv:2608.23808, Eq. (2) Seal definition and Eq. (3) regime composite; gate thresholds tau_DSR = 0.95, tau_PBO = 0.50, tau_SPA = 0.10, tau_rho = 0.60.
ideas.novelty: A bounded composite of breadth, consistency and worst case rather than a single moment of the return distribution. It fires on concentration of alpha in time even when the mean and the drawdown both look acceptable, which is exactly the state a decaying strategy passes through before its P&L level ever breaks a threshold.

ideas.name: Signal Horizon Migration Detector
ideas.timeframe: daily signal computation; entries at daily or intraday bars
ideas.entry_rule: For signal S (any of the corpus's entry rules, expressed as a continuous score rather than a binary trigger), each trading day compute the cross-sectional Spearman rank information coefficient IC(h) between the signal score on bar t and the forward return from bar t+1 to bar t+h, for h in {1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 20}, across the full tradable universe (require at least 30 names with 20-day median dollar volume > $5m). Maintain a 250-day rolling mean of each, meanIC(h). Define h* = argmax_h meanIC(h) - the horizon at which the signal's alpha actually lives. Compute the migration M = position of h* in the grid today minus its position 250 trading days ago (negative M means alpha has moved EARLIER). Trading rule: if M >= -1 (horizon stable), take S's entry at the NEXT bar's open at 100% of base size; if M <= -2 (alpha has migrated at least two grid steps earlier, i.e. the trade is being anticipated), execute instead at the CLOSE of the signal bar itself and cut size to 50%.
ideas.exit_rule: Exit at the close of bar t + h*, using the CURRENT value of h* - the holding period contracts automatically as the signal's alpha migrates earlier. Overlay a hard stop at 2 * ATR(14) adverse from entry. Retire S entirely when max_h meanIC(h) <= 0 for 60 consecutive trading days.
inputs: OHLCV bars for the full tradable universe
params: migration threshold for the execution switch (-1 / -2 / -3 grid steps)
ideas.why: When a signal becomes crowded, other participants trade it earlier, so its alpha migrates toward shorter horizons and eventually into the bar on which the signal is computed - at which point a next-open execution captures nothing and pays the full spread. This is decay you can see BEFORE it shows up in P&L, because the total IC can still be positive while the horizon at which it is realised has collapsed. Volpati et al. establish that this crowding is real and growing in exactly the mechanical signals the corpus is full of: momentum portfolio rebalancing alone accounts for 1-2% of total US equity order flow, a share that has grown substantially. The rule does two things with the detection - it moves execution earlier to stay ahead, and it shrinks the holding period to match where the alpha now is.
ideas.source: Volpati, V., Benzaquen, M., Eisler, Z., Mastromatteo, I., Toth, B. & Bouchaud, J.-P., 'Zooming In on Equity Factor Crowding', arXiv:2001.04185 (crowding measured from trade-imbalance fluctuations; momentum rebalancing = 1-2% of order flow and rising). The IC-term-structure migration statistic and the execution/holding-period response are my own synthesis - Volpati et al. use signed order flow, which we do not have, so the horizon shift is the OHLCV-observable consequence of the same mechanism.
ideas.novelty: Detects decay from WHERE IN TIME the alpha sits rather than from the level of P&L, and the response is a change in execution timing plus an adaptive holding period rather than a de-size or a kill. No level- or variance-based monitor can see this.

ideas.name: Volume Share Arbitrage Capital Brake
ideas.entry_rule: Each trading day, for signal S, identify the extreme deciles the signal would trade (top 10% and bottom 10% of the score distribution across the liquid universe). Compute A_t = [ sum of 20-day average dollar volume across the names in those two deciles ] / [ sum of 20-day average dollar volume across the whole universe ], then z_t = (A_t - mean(A over last 750 days)) / std(A over last 750 days). Trading rule: take S's own entry signal at the next bar's open sized at 100% of base when z_t < 1.0; at 50% of base when 1.0 <= z_t < 2.0; take no new entries when z_t >= 2.0. Additionally require the individual name's own 20-day dollar volume z-score (against its own 250-day history) to be below 3.0, to avoid entering a name in the middle of a volume shock.
ideas.exit_rule: S's own exit rule. Additionally, flatten all of S's positions at the next open when z_t >= 2.0 AND S's own trailing 20-day P&L is negative - the combination of unusually heavy trading in exactly the names the signal picks and the signal not working is the observable signature of the trade being crowded and unwinding. Re-enable entries when z_t falls back below 1.0.
inputs: OHLCV bars for the full tradable universe
750-day rolling mean and standard deviation of the volume share
ideas.why: Hanson and Sunderam's central move is to use short interest as an observable measure of how much arbitrage capital is currently deployed against a given strategy, and to show that strategy returns are lower when that capital is high. We have no short-interest feed, but the same economics has an OHLCV shadow: capital deployed against a signal has to trade, and it trades disproportionately in the names at the extremes of that signal. An abnormally high share of total market dollar volume concentrated in the signal's own extreme deciles means the trade is getting crowded. Using it as a capacity throttle rather than a directional signal keeps the claim modest - we are not predicting returns from it, we are refusing to add size to a trade that a lot of other capital has just arrived in.
ideas.source: Motivating result: Hanson, S.G. & Sunderam, A. (2014), 'The Growth and Limits of Arbitrage: Evidence from Short Interest', Review of Financial Studies 27(4) - short interest measures the arbitrage capital devoted to a quantitative strategy and predicts lower subsequent strategy returns. The volume-share proxy and the specific z-score thresholds are my own synthesis; I was unable to obtain the paper's full text, so the proxy should be validated against the paper's stated direction before being trusted.

ideas.name: BOCPD Run Length Sizing
ideas.entry_rule: Run Adams and MacKay's Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection on sub-strategy s's per-bar return series r_t, with a Gaussian observation model with unknown mean and variance (Normal-Inverse-Gamma conjugate prior, mu_0 = 0, kappa_0 = 1, alpha_0 = 2, beta_0 = var(r) over the first 250 bars) and a constant hazard function H(r) = 1/250. At each bar propagate the run-length posterior P(r_t | x_{1:t}) by the message-passing recursion, and record: R_t = E[run length], p_break_t = P(run length < 5), and mu_hat_t = the posterior predictive mean of the current-run return parameter, computed as the run-length-weighted average of the per-run posterior means. Trading rule: s may take new entries only when p_break_t < 0.20 AND mu_hat_t > 0. Size = base * clip(R_t / 250, 0.2, 1.0), so conviction grows with an uninterrupted run and resets after a break. Entries fire on s's own trigger at the next bar's open.
ideas.exit_rule: s's own exit rule. Additionally: flatten every position belonging to s at the next open on any bar where p_break_t > 0.50 - a changepoint has probably just occurred and the parameters governing s are no longer the ones it was sized on. Stay flat until BOTH R_t >= 20 (the new run has accumulated 20 bars) AND mu_hat_t > 0. Note that BOCPD needs no manual reset: the posterior re-initialises the parameter estimate on the new run automatically.
ideas.why: Page-Hinkley - the corpus's one existing overlay - is a one-sided sequential CUSUM: it needs a hand-set drift parameter and a hand-set threshold, it gives a binary alarm with no confidence attached, and after it fires a human has to decide when to reset it. BOCPD gives a full posterior over how long the current regime has lasted, which turns into three things Page-Hinkley cannot give: a graded position size that grows with regime age, a calibrated probability that a break just happened, and an automatic parameter re-estimation on the new regime with no reset step. That last property is what makes it usable unattended across hundreds of strategies. The hazard rate is a genuine prior about decay speed - 1/250 encodes 'expect a regime to last about a year', which is roughly the timescale the publication-effect literature implies.
ideas.source: Adams, R.P. & MacKay, D.J.C. (2007), 'Bayesian Online Changepoint Detection', arXiv:0710.3742 - exact online inference of the run-length posterior via a message-passing recursion with a hazard function; demonstrated on financial, biometric and robotic data.
ideas.novelty: Probabilistic and self-resetting rather than a threshold alarm, and it produces a continuous sizing signal (expected run length) in addition to a kill signal (break probability). Distinct from Page-Hinkley in its output type, not just its formula: PH emits a binary alarm, BOCPD emits a distribution.

ideas.name: Live Deflated Sharpe Re-Gate
ideas.timeframe: monthly evaluation; base signals any timeframe
ideas.entry_rule: Once per month, build the matrix of daily return series for all N candidate ideas in the corpus (backtest history and live history concatenated per idea). Compute N_eff, the effective number of independent trials, by eigen-decomposing the correlation matrix of those series and taking N_eff = the number of leading eigenvalues required to explain 95% of total variance. Compute sigma_SR = the cross-sectional standard deviation of the candidates' Sharpe ratios. Expected maximum Sharpe under the null: E[maxSR] = sigma_SR * [ (1 - g) * Phi^{-1}(1 - 1/N_eff) + g * Phi^{-1}(1 - 1/(N_eff * e)) ] with g = 0.5772 (Euler-Mascheroni). For each idea i with per-bar Sharpe SR_i over T_i bars, skewness g3_i and raw kurtosis g4_i on the COMBINED series, compute DSR_i = Phi[ (SR_i - E[maxSR]) * sqrt(T_i - 1) / sqrt(1 - g3_i*SR_i + ((g4_i - 1)/4) * SR_i^2) ]. Idea i is ADMITTED and may place trades at full base size for the coming month only if DSR_i >= 0.95; otherwise it is paper-only and places no orders.
ideas.exit_rule: Each admitted idea uses its own exit rule for individual trades. At the gate level: an idea demoted to paper-only has all of its open positions flattened at the next open on the rebalance day. An idea that has been paper-only for 12 consecutive monthly evaluations is deleted from the corpus. Because live returns are appended to the combined series each month, the gate is a live monitor: an idea whose live returns are weak will see DSR fall below 0.95 and be demoted without any separate decay test.
inputs: per-idea daily return series (backtest + live concatenated)
cross-idea correlation matrix and its eigenvalues
skewness and raw kurtosis of each idea's returns
params: whether N_eff uses eigenvalues or raw trial count
ideas.why: With 578 ideas the corpus IS a multiple-testing problem, and the single largest reason a backtested edge fails live is that it was the maximum of many noisy draws rather than a real effect. The Deflated Sharpe Ratio corrects for exactly this by comparing the observed Sharpe against the expected MAXIMUM under the null over the number of trials, with a skew/kurtosis correction. The two design choices that make it a decay monitor rather than a one-off screen are: computing it on the backtest-plus-live series so accumulating live data can either confirm or condemn each idea month by month, and using N_eff from eigenvalue decorrelation rather than the raw count of 578, because a corpus of highly correlated trend-following variants is nowhere near 578 independent trials and treating it as such would deflate every idea to nothing.
ideas.source: Bailey, D.H. & Lopez de Prado, M. (2014), the Deflated Sharpe Ratio. Implementation details taken from Santoni, M.L., Jouanne, V. & Scullin, M.L., arXiv:2608.23808 sections 3-4: the tau_DSR = 0.95 gate, the Mertens i.i.d. skew/kurtosis variance correction, and the effective-number-of-independent-trials construction obtained by decorrelating the searched parameter vectors with an eigenvalue-based approach. The paper also reports the sobering result that its full five-gate composite showed no significant forward relationship on unseen real market data (Spearman rho = 0.013, p = 0.40) - so this gate should be read as a floor on statistical support, not a predictor of profit.
ideas.novelty: Turns a one-shot backtest screen into a recurring live gate by appending live returns to the evaluated series, and uses eigenvalue-based N_eff so a large correlated corpus is not over-penalised. Distinct from every other idea here in what it tests: not whether the strategy changed, but whether it was ever real given how many things were tried.

ideas.name: Pre-Registered Revival Trial
ideas.entry_rule: When any decay monitor retires sub-strategy s, do not delete it. Instead open a REVIVAL TRIAL with hard, pre-registered terms fixed at the moment of retirement: trial length exactly 250 bars, trial size exactly 10% of s's normal base size, and success hurdle a running t-statistic of the trial's mean per-bar return, t_k = mean(r_1..r_k) / (std(r_1..r_k)/sqrt(k)), reaching 1.8. During the trial, s takes its own entry signals at the next bar's open at 10% size. Compute t_k at the close of each trial bar. If t_k >= 1.8 at any point with k >= 40, promote s immediately: size steps to 50% of base for the next 60 bars, then to 100%. If bar 250 of the trial is reached without t_k ever having touched 1.8 with k >= 40, retire s permanently - it is deleted from the corpus and never re-trialled.
ideas.exit_rule: s's own exit rule governs trades throughout. Trial-level exits: on promotion, the trial ends and normal sizing resumes; on reaching bar 250 without success, flatten all of s's positions at the next open and delete s. Hard abort: if the trial's cumulative return reaches -3% of the trial's allocated capital before bar 250, terminate the trial early and delete s. A given strategy is allowed exactly one revival trial in its lifetime.
inputs: per-strategy per-bar return series during the trial
params: minimum k before the hurdle can be claimed (20 / 40 / 100)
number of trials allowed per strategy (1 / 2)
ideas.why: Every monitor in this list produces false positives - a strategy is killed by a break test during a run of ordinary bad luck. The usual responses are both wrong: kill permanently (you lose real strategies to noise) or re-arm after an arbitrary cooldown (you keep resurrecting dead ones forever, and the cooldown becomes a tuned parameter that guarantees eventual re-entry). A bounded trial with a pre-registered hurdle, a hard deadline and a one-shot limit converts the resurrection decision into a proper sequential test with a known cost ceiling: at most 10% size for at most 250 bars, once. The 1.8 hurdle is not arbitrary - Chen and Zimmermann find that among predictors that survive journal review, a t-stat hurdle of 1.8 is sufficient to control for multiple testing, because the dispersion of true returns is large enough that each t-stat is genuinely informative. That is the right hurdle for an idea that already has a prior of having worked.
ideas.source: t-stat hurdle of 1.8 from Chen, A.Y. & Zimmermann, T. (2018), 'Publication Bias and the Cross-Section of Stock Returns', FEDS 2018-033 - among predictors that survive journal review, a low t-stat hurdle of 1.8 controls for multiple testing using the statistics of Harvey, Liu & Zhu (2015). The bounded one-shot trial protocol itself is my own synthesis.

ideas.name: Correlated Cohort Decay Contagion
ideas.timeframe: daily evaluation; base signals any timeframe
ideas.entry_rule: Once per quarter, cluster all live ideas by hierarchical clustering with average linkage on the distance d_ij = 1 - corr(r_i, r_j), using the last 750 days of daily strategy returns, cutting the dendrogram at correlation 0.5 (distance 0.5). This produces cohorts of ideas that are economically the same trade. Then daily, for each cohort c with n_c >= 4 members: compute each member's trailing 60-day annualised Sharpe, and let f_c = the fraction of members whose 60-day Sharpe is currently below that member's own 10th percentile of 60-day Sharpe measured over the last 750 days. Declare cohort c DEAD on any day when f_c >= 0.60. Trading rule: an idea may take its own entry signal at the next bar's open only if its cohort is not DEAD - INCLUDING ideas that individually still look healthy. Size = base * clip(1 - f_c, 0.3, 1.0).
ideas.exit_rule: Each idea's own exit governs its trades. Cohort-level: on the bar a cohort is declared DEAD, flatten every position held by every member of that cohort at the next open. The cohort revives - and members resume at 50% size for 20 bars, then full size - once at least 60% of its members have had a 60-day Sharpe above their own 750-day median on each of 20 consecutive trading days. Singleton and small cohorts (n_c < 4) are exempt from the contagion rule and fall back to their individual monitors.
inputs: daily return series for every live idea
rolling 60-day Sharpe and its 750-day percentiles per idea
ideas.why: This is the statistical-power argument, and it is the single biggest practical weakness of every per-strategy monitor above. Detecting a halving of a Sharpe of 0.5 on one strategy at conventional significance needs years of daily data - by which time the money is gone. But if twelve ideas in the corpus are all variants of the same mean-reversion trade, their decay is one event with twelve noisy measurements of it, and pooling gives roughly twelve times the observations. That is the difference between detecting death in two months and detecting it in two years. It is also the right economic model: McLean and Pontiff's and Chordia, Subrahmanyam and Tong's results are about whole categories of anomaly attenuating together as arbitrage capital and liquidity rise, not about individual rules failing independently. Killing a healthy-looking member of a dying cohort is the intended behaviour, not a bug - its apparent health is most likely noise.
ideas.source: Synthesis. The power-pooling rationale is mine; the cohort-level decay premise follows McLean, R.D. & Pontiff, J. (2016), 'Does Academic Research Destroy Stock Return Predictability?', Journal of Finance 71(1):5-32, and Chordia, T., Subrahmanyam, A. & Tong, Q. (2014), 'Have Capital Market Anomalies Attenuated in the Recent Era of High Liquidity and Trading Activity?', Journal of Accounting and Economics 58(1):41-58, both of which document category-wide rather than idiosyncratic attenuation. The magnitude of the effect being pooled (post-publication returns roughly 50% below in-sample, non-statistical deterioration 34% of in-sample return) is from Chen & Zimmermann, FEDS 2018-033.
